articles.title: OpenAI asegura que un modelo sin publicar refutó una hipótesis matemática vigente desde los noventa
articles.text:
OpenAI afirma que uno de sus modelos de inteligencia artificial, todavía sin publicar, logró refutar la hipótesis del tiempo exponencial, una conjetura de finales de los noventa que sostenía cientos de artículos de informática teórica, desde la teoría de grafos hasta la biología computacional.
La compañía atribuye a ese mismo sistema otros dos hallazgos matemáticos: la demostración de una conjetura sobre ondas abierta desde 1991 y la prueba de que la teoría de Yang-Mills, uno de los pilares de la física de partículas, existe en sentido matemático.
OpenAI presenta los tres resultados como “datos de investigación en bruto” y pidió a especialistas externos que formen grupos independientes para verificarlos.
Cualquiera de estos tres hallazgos, de confirmarse, alcanzaría para sostener una carrera académica completa y para aspirar a varios premios internacionales.
El de la hipótesis del tiempo exponencial, en particular, roza uno de los Problemas del Milenio, los siete desafíos matemáticos dotados con un millón de dólares cada uno, de los cuales solo uno ha sido resuelto hasta ahora.
Qué dice la hipótesis del tiempo exponencial y por qué su refutación es relevante
La hipótesis del tiempo exponencial está vinculada al problema P frente a NP, formulado de manera independiente por Stephen Cook y Leonid Levin en 1971.
Esa pregunta busca determinar si todo problema cuya solución puede comprobarse con rapidez puede también resolverse con la misma rapidez. La hipótesis va más allá: no solo asume que la respuesta es negativa, sino que sostiene que el costo de resolver los casos más difíciles crece de forma exponencial.
El problema concreto sobre el que se apoya es sencillo de enunciar. Dada una fórmula lógica cuyas variables solo pueden ser verdaderas o falsas, se trata de determinar si existe alguna combinación que la haga verdadera. Cada variable adicional duplica las combinaciones posibles: con 100 variables, por ejemplo, existen unos 1,27 quintillones de posibilidades.
Existen métodos para evitar probar todas las combinaciones, pero la hipótesis sostenía que, incluso en el peor de los casos, el tiempo de cálculo seguiría disparándose de forma exponencial con cada variable que se sumara.
La hipótesis del tiempo exponencial es la conjetura informática que afirmaba que ciertos problemas lógicos no pueden resolverse más rápido que de forma exponencial en el peor de los casos; su eventual refutación obligaría a revisar buena parte de los fundamentos teóricos que daban por válida esa barrera de dificultad.
Según OpenAI, su modelo encontró la refutación el 16 de octubre y, un día después, ya estaba traducida a Lean, un lenguaje que permite a una máquina verificar cada paso de una demostración matemática. La empresa publicó además un algoritmo capaz de contar las soluciones de este tipo de fórmulas más rápido de lo que la hipótesis consideraba posible.
La revisión de este resultado quedó en manos de Russell Impagliazzo y Ramamohan Paturi, de la Universidad de California en San Diego, dos de los autores originales de la hipótesis hace más de dos décadas, junto con Ryan Williams, investigador del Instituto Tecnológico de Massachusetts (MIT).
El avance sobre ondas que conecta con la conjetura de Kakeya
El segundo resultado que reivindica OpenAI es la demostración de la conjetura del suavizado local, planteada en 1991 por el matemático Christopher Sogge.
Esta conjetura estudia cómo se suavizan las ondas cuando se promedian en el tiempo. La compañía sostiene haberla probado en todas las dimensiones, lo que arrastraría consigo otras dos conjeturas célebres del análisis armónico: la de restricción de Stein y la de Kakeya.
La conjetura de Kakeya nació en 1917 como un acertijo planteado por el matemático japonés Soichi Kakeya, quien se preguntaba cuál es la superficie más pequeña en la que puede darse la vuelta a una aguja. La respuesta conocida es que esa superficie puede ser tan pequeña como se quiera.
Una versión más moderna de la pregunta afina el planteamiento: si una figura capaz de alojar la aguja en todas las direcciones puede no ocupar ningún volumen, cabe preguntarse si de todos modos llena siempre todas las dimensiones del espacio en que se encuentra.
Hong Wang y Joshua Zahl ya habían demostrado esta conjetura para espacios de tres dimensiones el año anterior, un trabajo que le valió a Wang la Medalla Fields en julio.
OpenAI asegura haber extendido ahora la solución a cualquier número de dimensiones. Alex Iosevich, especialista en análisis armónico de la Universidad de Rochester, calificó el hallazgo como un “desarrollo histórico” en declaraciones recogidas por Al Jazeera.
El vínculo con la teoría de Yang-Mills y la física de partículas
El tercer hallazgo que reclama OpenAI pertenece al terreno de la teoría cuántica de campos. La compañía sostiene haber demostrado que existen, en cuatro dimensiones, la teoría de Yang-Mills pura, la cromodinámica cuántica (que describe la fuerza que mantiene unidos a los quarks dentro de protones y neutrones) y la versión más sencilla de la teoría de gran unificación.
Probar que la teoría de Yang-Mills existe equivale a resolver la mitad de otro de los Problemas del Milenio. La otra mitad corresponde a la llamada “brecha de masa”, que explicaría por qué la fuerza nuclear fuerte solo actúa a distancias minúsculas. Esa segunda parte del problema, según el propio anuncio, OpenAI no logró demostrarla.
La verificación de este resultado quedó a cargo de un grupo liderado por David Gross, premio Nobel de Física en 2004 por el descubrimiento de la libertad asintótica, la propiedad en la que se apoya la demostración. Entre los integrantes de ese grupo figura Arthur Jaffe, quien redactó junto a Edward Witten el enunciado oficial del problema.
A diferencia de los otros dos hallazgos, este tercer resultado no se hizo público. El grupo de revisión optó por no difundir el material por el momento y encargarse de redactar el resultado por su cuenta.

articles.title: ShinyHunters-Exploited Oracle PeopleSoft Zero-Day Turns Out to Be Three Chained Flaws
articles.text:
The critical Oracle PeopleSoft bug that ShinyHunters has exploited since May is not one flaw but three chained together, the researchers who reported it said this week.
Oracle patched all three under a single identifier, CVE-2026-35273, in June. Its root is a server-side request forgery (SSRF) that reaches an internal management interface because PeopleSoft trusts its own loopback address by default, opening the door to remote code execution without a login.
The breakdown comes from Bobby Gould of the Zero Day Initiative (ZDI), whose team reported the flaw to Oracle.
In its analysis, ZDI said it reported three distinct vulnerabilities across two PeopleSoft components, and that it is working with Oracle to assign a separate CVE to each. As of this week, the one June identifier is still the only one on the record.
CVE-2026-35273 affects PeopleSoft Enterprise PeopleTools versions 8.61 and 8.62, carries a CVSS score of 9.8, and lets an unauthenticated attacker take over the server over the network. Oracle released its fix in an out-of-band security alert on June 10. The flaw is on CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.
Attackers were already using it before that fix was in place. Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) attribute a campaign to the group it tracks as UNC6240, better known as ShinyHunters, that exploited the flaw between May 27 and June 9, mostly against universities. Because that activity came before Oracle's June 10 advisory, it was a zero-day the whole time.
In a September follow-up, Mandiant reported a renewed, larger wave that spread beyond education to technology, IT services, healthcare, agriculture, transport, and government, affecting dozens of systems worldwide.
ZDI's analysis explains what that single patch actually closed. Two PeopleSoft components are involved, both run as separate web applications. The Integration Gateway (PSIGW) exchanges messages with outside systems. The Environment Management Hub (PSEMHUB) is an internal admin interface that is supposed to answer only to trusted hosts.
The first flaw is the SSRF in PSIGW. An attacker sends a request to its listening connector and controls both the address it forwards to and the full payload it sends, ZDI said; the handler does no check that the destination is a legitimate target. That alone would be limited, except for what it can reach.
PSEMHUB decides who to trust by checking the requester against a list in a file named allowedhosts.properties. That file ships with the local loopback address, 127.0.0.1, already on the list. So an attacker points the SSRF at 127.0.0.1, the request arrives looking like it came from the machine itself, and the trust check passes. The internal interface Oracle meant to wall off is now reachable from outside.
From there, ZDI described two ways to turn that access into code execution. One abuses a PSEMHUB command meant to write log entries: the caller controls both the file contents and the exact path on disk, so an attacker writes a web shell into the application directory and runs commands as the PeopleSoft service account.
The other writes a malicious XML file that PSEMHUB reads using Java's XMLDecoder when the service next starts, thereby running the attacker's code without planting a web shell at all. The second path leaves less for standard detection to catch.
The design decision at the center, ZDI said, is that allowing loopback access by default makes the trust check ineffective once the SSRF exists. That matters for defenders who thought a firewall rule had covered them.
In the September wave, Mandiant found ShinyHunters slipping past web application firewall (WAF) rules that blocked the /PSEMHUB/ path by url-encoding a single character, requesting /%50SEMHUB/ instead. Many WAF rules match the path's plain text, while the PeopleSoft server decodes it and serves the page.
What to Do
The fix and the guidance here come from Oracle and Mandiant, not from ZDI's analysis, which covers the flaw rather than the response.
- Apply the patch. Install Oracle's security alert fix for CVE-2026-35273 and stay on a supported PeopleTools release. Mandiant is explicit that path-based WAF blocking is not a substitute for patching.
- If you cannot patch yet, disable the Environment Management Hub service in multi-server setups, or remove the PSEMHUB application in single-server setups, as Oracle's alert advises. Restricting these admin endpoints does not break normal user sessions.
- If you may already be hit, Mandiant recommends treating any host with a web shell as compromised, preserving evidence, and rotating every credential reachable from the PeopleSoft tier. ShinyHunters steals data and then demands payment, so affected organizations should prepare for extortion.
One thing the sources do not settle is whether applying the patch removes access an attacker already gained. Oracle's alert does not address it, and Mandiant's guidance to rotate credentials and hunt for web shells assumes it does not. Patching closes the door; it does not by itself evict someone already inside.

articles.title: Proton veut des équipes prêtes pour l'IA et s'explique après la fuite d’un email interne
articles.text:
Proton a envoyé à ses salariés un email annonçant de nouveaux entretiens pour évaluer l’usage de l’IA en interne. Après la fuite du message, l’entreprise affirme vouloir des équipes à l’aise avec ces outils, sans s’en servir comme prétexte à des licenciements.
Selon 404 Media, Proton a prévenu ses salariés lundi qu’ils pourraient être « re-interviewés » sur leur usage de l’IA, avec des conséquences possibles sur leur poste. L’entreprise a depuis répondu dans un commentaire épinglé sur Reddit, où elle publie le message en entier.
Re-interviews du 4 au 11 novembre : Proton veut savoir comment ses équipes s’adaptent à l’IA
Proton n’entend pas louper le virage de l’IA et à en juger par ses travaux portés sur Lumo et sa feuille de route, l’entreprise entend bien se positionner face à OpenAI et Anthropic avec son approche de chiffrement de bout en bout. Mais L'IA change la donne à bien des niveaux et dans son email, la direction explique que cela affecte aussi la manière de concevoir les produits et de travailler. Andy Yen, le PDG, a déjà rencontré la semaine dernière plus de 40 responsables seniors des équipes Ingénierie et Produit. Les entretiens s’étendent maintenant à d’autres collaborateurs.
Chaque salarié convoqué échangera avec quelqu’un d’extérieur à son équipe et à sa ligne hiérarchique. Cet interlocuteur sera choisi parmi des responsables à l’aise avec l’IA, qui se sont mis d’accord sur les critères d’évaluation. Plus qu’une simple liste d’outils, il faudra donner des exemples concrets en spécifiant ce qui a changé dans son travail, les résultats obtenus ou encore ce qui n’a pas fonctionné.
Sur Reddit, Proton affirme ne pas licencier en prenant l’IA comme prétexte. L’entreprise explique au contraire manquer de talents et recruter dans toutes ses équipes. Elle décrit la démarche comme un état des lieux pour voir comment chacun s’adapte, de quel soutien le salarié a besoin et qui pourrait piloter ce changement. Certains salariés pourraient obtenir davantage de responsabilités. Proton ajoute que l'IA doit être utilisée avec discernement, en tenant compte de la confidentialité, de la sécurité, de l’exactitude et de l’intérêt réel de l’outil.
Il n’empêche qu’en interne, les salariés sont assez perturbés pour avoir transféré cet email à 404 Media, lequel mentionne bel et bien :
Ces nouveaux entretiens auront des conséquences. Les enquêteurs consigneront leurs évaluations, qui alimenteront la revue plus large de notre organisation et de nos talents. Cette revue peut entraîner des changements concernant les rôles, les responsabilités et le maintien dans l’emploi. Les résultats individuels seront communiqués directement une fois les décisions arrêtées.
Ce processus nous aidera aussi à identifier les personnes prêtes à assumer un périmètre plus large et des responsabilités de direction à mesure que Proton évolue.
Proton reconnaît que cette période crée de l’incertitude et promet de communiquer clairement les décisions individuelles dès qu’elles seront prises. Reste à savoir si cette démarche vise simplement à privilégier les personnes à l’aise avec l’IA ou si l’entreprise saura mettre en place une forme de tutorat pour accompagner celles qui le sont moins.
- storageStockage de 500 Go
- securityChiffrement natif par défaut
- alternate_emailSupport nom de domaine
- push_pinJurisdiction Suisse
En proposant de centraliser les versions premium de Proton Mail, Proton VPN, Proton Calendar, Proton Drive et Proton Pass, l'offre Unlimited s'avère particulièrement intéressante au niveau du tarif. On note quelques lacunes concernant le calendrier et le Drive, mais le Mail, le VPN ou le gestionnaire de mots de passe sont plutôt réussis. Après une décennie à plancher sur Mail, l'équipe propose une messagerie solide et moderne. Au travers de nos tests poussés le VPN a fait ses preuves, tandis que Pass évolue très rapidement et c'est plutôt bon signe. On regrette simplement que Proton semble avoir mis le calendrier aux oubliettes et que le Drive accuse encore plusieurs lacunes de jeunesse.

articles.title: I tested the Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark and that next-gen Nvidia chip gives it superb AI, creative and gaming performance — it’s like a MacBook Pro M5 you can game on
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
Not only does the Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark have a lightweight form factor and a huge and vibrant OLED screen but that eponymous RTX Spark chip from Nvidia gives it some impressive power. Whether you want to train your own AI agents, edit video or play games on the go, it makes short work of many workloads. The only real stumbling block is that super high price — it costs as much as a top-of-the-range gaming laptop or creative work station, while not besting them for performance, meaning it’s best for those that need power in every area, rather than just one.
Reasons to buy
- + Stunning 3K OLED screen
- + Stylish, lightweight design
- + Strong creative, AI and gaming performance
Reasons to avoid
- - Very expensive
- - Bested by dedicated gaming or creative laptops
- - Some wobble to the screen
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark: two-minute review
The Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark is one of the new generation of laptops powered by Nvidia’s RTX Spark chip. This all-in-one system-on-a-chip is packing 20 ARM CPU cores, 6144 CUDA GPU backed up by 64GB of RAM and promises to offer fantastic AI, creative and gaming performance in a lightweight, portable form factor. So how does this new SoC version of the Asus ProArt P16 laptop fare?
When powering up the Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark for the first time, perhaps the first thing I noticed is its huge, vibrant 16-inch OLED screen. With a peak brightness of 1,100 nits and a 100% DCI-P3 color gamut, it looked gorgeous whether I was loading up my digital artworks or watching movies. And its 120Hz VRR makes it perfect for playing games on.
That’s not the only part of the ProArt P16’s design that feels premium. Its overall build quality feels suitably luxe, with the smooth metal of its upper casing feeling wonderfully tactile. Inside, its keyboard is well designed and feels pleasant to type on, while its haptic trackpad is precise and gives snappy feedback, even if I did find it too easy to trigger the right click at first. I will say its lid has a little bit too much wobble for my liking though: if I’m honest, I’d expect a laptop at this price to have a slightly more stable hinge.
But let’s not just focus on the superficial here: the ProArt P16 RTX Spark has a lot going on under the surface. That’s predominantly thanks to that Nvidia SoC, which enables it to tackle a wider range of tasks than even many of the best laptops.
Perhaps the most attention grabbing feature is its AI capabilities. Designed for hybrid workflows, the RTX Spark makes it easy to use a combination of local and cloud models to run your AI agents. Testing it out with the Qwen 3 8B open-source local model, I certainly found it had pretty snappy performance for basic workflows, with a basic data analysis only taking about 12 minutes.
More involved tasks took much more refining and prompting over multiple sessions though — attempting to automate 3DMark benchmarks took many 75 minute runs before the completion time reduced significantly. Still, being able to run these workflows on such a lightweight, portable machine was pretty impressive
Another area the Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark delivers potent performance is during creative tasks. Running multiple PugetBench benchmarks for automating Photoshop and Premier Pro workflows, the ProArt P16 was only a little behind Apple’s M5 chip when running image-based tasks and beat it when it came to video tasks. And this was borne out by my own testing: even my largest 4K 300dpi Photoshop file crammed full of clipping masks didn’t make it wince, with filters and generative fills executing smoothly. Even downscaling the whole image to 2K only took around five seconds, which isn’t bad for a nigh-on 2GB file.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Few SoCs to date have been designed with gaming performance in mind. But given Nvidia’s heritage in this space, it’s hardly surprising that the ProArt P16 RTX Spark is capable of some serious gaming power. While it’s not quite able to deliver at the same level as RTX 5080 and 5090 GPUs, I enjoyed a very smooth 60fps on Cyberpunk 2077 on Raytracing Medium settings, while Gears of War: E-day ran at more solid than bedrock at over 110fps. So this laptop can achieve some stunning results, even if the performance you’ll get isn’t 100% the top of the range.
Given it can handle all of these tasks on the go, you’d hope it has a pretty capacious battery to back up that powerful chip. And it’s relatively good news on this front. While it only managed 11 hours of continuous video playback during my testing, during productivity based work it lasted well over 14 hours. That’s nowhere near as long-lasting as the Methuselah-like MacBook Pro M5 Pro, which clocked over 21 hours in our testing, but it’s certainly enough to get you through a standard day’s work.
Honestly, the Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark is pretty adept at everything it tries to do: it’s a talented all-rounder. The only caveat really is its price: like many of the RTX Spark laptops, it isn’t cheap. Starting from $4,399.99 / £3,899.99 / AU$7,999, it costs just as much as a high-end gaming laptop or a pro-level creative workhorse — so, honestly, if you care more about getting the best performance you can in a specific niche, you may be better off investing in one of those instead.
However, if you need a single bow that can handle every single one of your strings, the Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark is a good shout. It’ll handle running your own AI agents, whipping up creative work and even gaming for your downtime, all in a single, portable package.
Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark review: price & availability
Having launched on October 9, the Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark is available now. Unlike its smaller sibling, it ships with the higher-end Nvidia RTX Spark N1X with 6144-core GPU and 20-core CPU.
As a result, it’s a pricey meatball: its list price starts from $4,399.99 / £3,899.99 / AU$7,999 for the spec with 64GB RAM, 3K screen and 1TB SSD. That increases to $6,999.99 / £5,999.99 / AU$10,999 if you want the version with 128GB RAM, a 4K screen and a 2TB SSD.
Even with its impressive specs, there’s no getting away from the fact that this is a premium-priced laptop. Both in terms of price and spec, the ProArt P16 RTX Spark is pretty similar to the Samsung Galaxy Book6 Ultra with Nvidia GeForce RTX 5070, which will set you back $3,799.99 / £3,649 (around AU$5,410).
Alternatively, this kind of spend could net you the MacBook Pro M5 Pro 16-inch with 64GB for $2,999 / £3,999 / AU$6,299, which should give you a lot of performance and creative power but I wouldn’t expect to get quite as much gaming power for your buck.
Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark review: Specs
| Header Cell - Column 0 | Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark Base Config | Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark High end Config | 
|---|---|---|
| Price | $4,399.99 / £3,899.99 / AU$7,999 | $6,999.99 / £5,999.99 / AU$10,999 | 
| CPU | NVIDIA RTX Spark N1X 20-core | NVIDIA RTX Spark N1X 20-core CPU | 
| GPU | NVIDIA Blackwell RTX 6144-core | NVIDIA Blackwell RTX 6144-core GPU | 
| RAM | 64GB | 128GB | 
| Storage | 1TB SSD | 2TB SSD | 
| Display | 16.0-inch, 2880 x 1800, 120Hz, 1100 nits OLED | 16.0-inch, 3840 x 2400, 120Hz, 1600 nits OLED | 
| Ports and Connectivity | 3x USB-C, USB, HDMI 2.1, 3.5mm Combo Audio Jack, SD Express 7.0 card reader | 3x USB-C, USB, HDMI 2.1, 3.5mm Combo Audio Jack, SD Express 7.0 card reader | 
| Battery | 99.9Wh | 99.9Wh | 
| Dimensions | 13.94 x 9.57 x 0.63 inches / 354.1 x 243 x 15.9mm | 13.94 x 9.57 x 0.63 inches / 354.1 x 243 x 15.9mm | 
| Weight | 3.9 lbs / 1.77kg | 3.9 lbs / 1.77kg | 
Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark review: design
- Gorgeous 3K OLED display
- Slim, sleek design
- Slightly flimsy hinge
Like all of the initial lineup RTX Spark laptops I’ve seen, the new Asus ProArt P16 is a sleek-looking unit. While its 16-inch span is pretty expansive, it’s still light in terms of weight, clocking in at 1.77 kg compared to my 16-inch MacBook Pro M4’s 2.14kg. It’s also got a pretty sleek silhouette — unlike some of the RTX Spark laptop models I’ve seen, it’s not concealing a much chonkier base with the help of gradually sloping bevels. And its nano black and neo white colorways feel suitably premium, although I marginally prefer the black version I tested here.
It’s not all about style though: the ProArt P16 RTX Spark has plenty of substance too. Manufactured from smooth metal, its external and internal surfaces feel wonderfully tactile, although I’d say the inner ones feel a tiny bit less sturdy than the solid bodywork of the outside. On top of this, there’s a tiny bit of wobble to its screen when you touch it — I’d expect a slightly firmer hinge on a premium laptop like this.
Speaking of that screen, I found Asus’s 3K touchscreen Lumina Pro OLED to be pretty impressive on the whole. Not only can my unit hit a peak brightness of 1,100 nits and a max 120Hz VRR but comparing it to my MacBook Pro M4’s Liquid Retina XDR display while watching Pixar’s Elemental was — sorry for this — pretty illuminating. While the latter can go slightly brighter at 1,600 nits peak, I didn’t find the difference all that pronounced. And the colors of the P16 RTX Spark’s OLED panel were noticeably more vibrant, with the reds, blues and greens of the fire, water and earth elements really popping.
To say laptop keyboards can be hit or miss might be the understatement of the century but, fortunately, the ProArt P16 RTX Spark’s keyboard falls more in the former category than the latter. Although the keys don’t have a huge amount of travel, I still found the typing experience to be pretty fluid. I rarely ever struggled to find my chosen key when touch typing — although I did occasionally knock both parts of the dual enter key, accidentally sticking random #s at the end of sentences. Still, it felt nice to use, whether I was prompting an AI agent or rapidly splatting demons in Doom: The Dark Ages.
For the most part, the P16 RTX Spark’s trackpad is also well designed. It’s very accurate, gives you a huge area for controlling your cursor and the haptic feedback is spot on, feeling exactly like a mechanical click. Really the only issue I found with it is the right click triggers far too far to the left, meaning I’d sometimes accidentally right click on certain elements. Still though, it’s a decent trackpad for the most part.
As you’d expect from a laptop this premium, the P16 RTX Spark comes with access to a wide range of connectivity options as well. On top of offering Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 5.4 connectivity, it rocks a pretty decent selection of ports for such a slim laptop. These include three USB-C and one standard USB port, an HDMI 2.1 port, a 3.5mm headphone jack and an SD Express card reader. So even for most creative workflows, you should find you’re able to plug in plenty of devices to get things done.
- Design score: 4 / 5
Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark review: performance
- Strong all-round performance
- Local AI workflows impressive but require some patience
- Specialist laptops can give better gaming or creative performance
I’ll be honest: by far the most exciting part about getting my hands on the Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark is that eponymous chip. Similar to Apple’s M-series silicon, Nvidia’s RTX Spark is the company’s first attempt at a full system-on-a-chip architecture. And given Nvidia’s involvement in both the AI and gaming spaces, it’s safe to say I was looking forward to putting the Nvidia Spark RTX through its paces.
Combining CPU, GPU and RAM all in one compact package, the version of the RTX Spark included with the Asus ProArt P16 I tested here rocks 20 ARM CPU cores backed up by 64GB of RAM. Meanwhile, on the graphics side, it wields 6144 CUDA GPU cores with 30GB integrated memory. In terms of raw hardware, it's less cooked and more meaty than steak tartare.
While this is the equivalent of using a steam hammer to obliterate a nut, general productivity tasks ran perfectly smoothly on the ProArt P16 RTX Spark. Whether I was browsing the web, tinkering with spreadsheets or leafing through huge PDFs, I never experienced any awkward hanging or slowdowns. Even on the odd occasion when I had to look something up online while the laptop worked on an AI task, there wasn’t any unpleasant gear-crunching, showing the ProArt P16 is plenty fast enough for general use.
But you’re unlikely to be buying an RTX Spark laptop just for doing a bit of Googling or filing your taxes. Instead, the most obvious use case for the RTX Spark chip in the ProArt P16 is its hybrid agentic AI functionality. Put simply, rather than being forced to choose between using cloud models that potentially jeopardize the security of your data and less powerful local models, this blended approach means you can pick and choose which parts of your workflow you’re going to outsource to the cloud and which you’ll keep under strict local control.
With its integrated fifth-generation Tensor cores, the RTX Spark should be perfectly placed to support this. To see how fast it could run some of these models locally, I used the MLPerf Client benchmarking tool to mimic data analyst and SWE agentic workflows using the Qwen 3 8B local model. And the results felt pretty rapid, with the pipelines completing after an average duration of 63.7 and 50.8 seconds and processing up to 14,005 and 10,238 tokens respectively.
But I wanted to see for myself what it could do. So I fired up Hermes, the open-source AI agent tool, and set it up to run the local open-source model Qwen3.8 27B to see what having my own personal AI version of Alfred could help me achieve.
Some of the basic tasks I threw its way, the RTX Spark practically scoffed at. When I asked Hermes to organize a spreadsheet full of web analytics for me and pull out actionable highlights, it whipped the file up into a pivot table and gave me six bullet points within about 12 minutes. Asking it to convert this info into a presentation with slides and prompts took a little longer at 23 minutes, but it helped highlight the best information to pitch — even if the slides themselves needed a considerable glow up before I’d ever call them up in a Zoom call.
In theory though, these hybrid agentic AI tools can go much further than this. Not only can you convert your prompts into skills or schedule them to run as daily tasks but you can even set them to target your apps and control your screen directly.
Some of my experiments paid off here: after one abortive run, I eventually managed to get Hermes to access my emails and create a daily digest in 70 minutes. But trying to automate some of my 3DMark benchmarking process ended up being a real rabbit hole — even with judicious prompts throughout the process and prompting Hermes to find ways to boost the skill’s efficiency, it took around eight runs to significantly improve its workflow. So it’s important to recognize that while some agentic pipelines may save you time in the long run, without utilizing some cloud models, training them may take a decent investment.
Agentic AI isn’t the only use you can put all of that processing power to though. While I’m not a massive fan of generative AI, I can definitely see how fast the RTX Spark is at whipping up new images and videos. Automating some imagery and video pipelines using ComfyUI, the laptop completed tests of Flux2.Dev - NVFP4 and Flux2.Klein 4B Base - NVFP4 models in just 46.5 and 16.2 seconds, while the LTX 2.5 - Distilled - NVFP4 video model took 88 seconds. Those are pretty swift run times for local generative models.
And if, like me, you prefer creating your own stuff from scratch, my testing showed the ProArt P16 RTX Spark can help here too. Using PugetBench to automate a range of creative workflows, I found Asus’s laptop was capable of some lightning fast processing.
Our standard Photoshop workflow completed in 10.83 minutes and achieved a score of 11,801 — that’s not far short of Apple’s M5 chip at 13,755. And the RTX Spark offered even speedier performance for video work, securing a score in our Premier Pro benchmark of 76,234 in 8.12 minutes, giving the M5 chip a bit of a drubbing at 69,887. Unfortunately, it can’t keep up with the similarly priced Apple MacBook Pro M5 Pro though, which managed to best it for both still imagery and video with scores of 15,204 and 105,580 respectively.
Naturally, I’m not just going to take these numbers on trust though, so I dug out one of my most demanding Photoshop files — a 4K, 300dpi PSD with dozens of clipping masks and adjustment layers — and checked how the ProArt P16 RTX Spark handled it.
Manipulating layers and applying filters caused scarcely any slowdown, in spite of the fact I’d tripled the number of layers in the file. Even downscaling the image to 2K — no small task given the total file size was now in excess of 2GB — only took around five seconds, which is pleasingly swift. And thanks to the optimization work that Adobe has been doing behind the scenes to allow its apps to take advantage of the RTX Spark’s AI capabilities, even generative fills and neural filters didn’t take long to generate.
When it comes to gaming performance, I’d say the ProArt P16 RTX Spark hovers somewhere between mid-range laptops with RTX 5060 and RTX 5070 GPUs. For example, when playing Cyberpunk 2077 on Raytracing Ultra settings at 1080p, I found the Asus hovered around 30.16fps — but, by contrast, the Acer Predator Helios Neo 16S AI with an RTX 5060 only reached a marginally smoother 34.47fps. Other games told a similar story. For example, Doom: The Dark Ages on Ultra settings sat at a pretty decent 48fps on the ProArt P16. In comparison, with its slightly beefier RTX 5070, the Samsung Galaxy Book 6 Ultra whipped the game like meringue into a much smoother 63.98fps.
But that’s running things on max settings. In practice, when actually playing games on more moderate settings, they ran plenty smoothly enough, especially those that are already well optimized for the RTX Spark. As I explored Dogtown in Cyberpunk 2077 at Raytracing Medium settings, it chugged along at a perfect stable 60fps. And playing Dogs of War: E-day on Ultra settings, I never saw it drop below 110fps, which shows what wonderfully smooth experiences you should still be able to expect from native gaming on the RTX Spark.
Honestly, I’d say that if you put the Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark up against any similarly priced, specialist laptop focused on AI, creative workflows or gaming, you’ll likely find its performance can’t quite keep up. But that’s the point — RTX Spark laptops are a triple threat: they’re designed to be a swiss army knife that can handle every task you might throw at them. So if you want a lightweight laptop that combines the agentic AI hosting of a compact desktop, the creative power of the Apple M5 and the gaming oomph of the Nvidia Geforce RTX 5060, all in one handy package, the Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark should have your back.
- Performance score: 4.5 / 5
Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark review: battery test
- Battery should last 14 hours of standard use
- Some similar rivals can outlast it
Being able to achieve all of this on the go is impressive. But for that to be sustainable, it needs a battery that can keep up with these kinds of heavy duty tasks. Fortunately, the Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark is capable of decent battery life, even if it’s not quite as exceptional as some of its rivals.
Running it through our standard battery tests, I played a 1080p video at 50% brightness and volume to see how long it took to drain the battery from 100% to 0%. The ProArt P16 RTX Spark ran out of juice after 11h 23m — that’s not at all bad but it’s also not quite at the level I’d expect for a premium laptop like this.
But a video test doesn’t necessarily give you the full picture. One of the big benefits of an SoC is through boosted efficiency during CPU usage, so I wanted to also run some tests that showed how the laptop fared in action. Running PCMark 10’s applications battery test — which runs various Microsoft Office based tasks until the battery is drained — the ProArt P16 lasted 14h 24m.
That’s definitely a better score, even if it falls a little ways short of some of the best laptops for Windows. For example, the Samsung Galaxy Book6 Ultra managed well over 15 hours in our benchmark tests and that wasn’t even the strongest contender. The MacBook Pro M5 Pro 16-inch clocked over 21 hours, which makes the ProArt P16’s look pretty short-lived in comparison.
Fortunately, the Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark does have one extra trick up its sleeve: its charging rate. Thanks to its 140W fast charging, topping your battery up again should be a relatively speedy affair. Sadly, my US unit didn’t come with a UK plug — slight oversight there — so I wasn’t able to test this as I would have liked. Still, my 65W charger topped it up relatively quickly, so you’ll definitely get pretty speedy charging out that 140W cable.
So I’d say that, all in all, the Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark is capable of competitive battery life. When you’re doing standard office work, it’ll get you through a full day without you having to hunt out a charger. But it’s still not quite able to keep pace with the most enduring batteries on the market and particularly intensive tasks like AI or gaming are going to drain it much faster.
- Battery score: 4 / 5
Should I buy the Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark?
| Attributes | Notes | Rating | 
|---|---|---|
| Value | The Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark has a lot of power behind it, an attractive lightweight design and a gorgeous screen. But that price is going to be a stumbling block for many, particularly when specialist gaming or creative laptops achieve better performance for similar cash. | 2.5 / 5 | 
| Design | A stunning 3K OLED screen, lightweight design and premium feeling materials, although it loses a few marks here and there for small details like its wobbly screen and slightly off-balance trackpad. | 4 / 5 | 
| Performance | While the ProArt P16 RTX Spark doesn’t offer top level performance in creative workflows or gaming, its AI tools and how much power it crams into a small frame are very impressive. Additionally, the fact it performs so well across so many categories makes it a great all rounder. | 4.5 / 5 | 
| Battery Life | At roughly 14.5 hours, this laptop’s battery is strong but not exactly exceptional. You’ll comfortably get more than a day’s work out of it but it will definitely tap out sooner than a MacBook Pro during intensive workloads. | 4 / 5 | 
| Total | The Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark is a good-looking, lightweight laptop that’s perfect for anyone who wants to create, game and use AI agents on a single device. But that high price means that if you care most about performance in a single area, you’ll be better off with a specialist laptop. | 4 / 5 | 
Buy it if…
You want to game, create and use AI on a single device
Thanks to Nvidia’s RTX Spark SoC, the Asus ProArt P16 puts considerable power behind every task you might throw at it. So if you’re a bit of a polymath, it may well be the only device you need.
You want a seriously portable 16-inch device
Despite that gorgeous and expansive 16-inch display, the laptop’s wonderfully light — at 3.9 lbs / 1.77kg, it’s svelter than other powerful laptops like the MacBook Pro M5 Pro or the Samsung Galaxy Book6 Ultra.
Don’t buy it if…
You want top performance in any one category
If you only really care about gaming or creative work is your sole priority, there are laptops out there that can give you peak performance for a similar spend.
You don’t have loads of money laying around
There’s no getting away from it: this laptop ain’t cheap. Even in its base spec, you’ll be paying $4,399.99 / £3,899.99 / AU$7,999, so if you’re not feeling flush, you might want to look elsewhere.
Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark review: also consider
Apple MacBook Pro M5 Pro
If you’re wanting a true creative powerhouse, the MacBook Pro M5 Pro will get you there. Despite costing a similar price, this incarnation of Apple’s laptop will absolutely blitz both image and video workflows, while also offering an absurdly long 21-hour battery life. While you’re not going to get top shelf gaming performance out of Apple silicon, this is still a great choice if your main concern is sheer creative thrust. Read our full Apple MacBook Pro M5 Pro review.
Asus Zephyrus G16 2026
With its discrete Nvidia Geforce RTX 5080 GPU, the Asus Zephyrus G16 2026 offers seriously nippy gaming performance, besting the P16 RTX Spark in both benchmarks and in-game frame rates. Okay, it’s not going to unlock the same oomph the P16 can for hybrid AI workflows. But if your main concern is pure gaming punch, the Zephyrus G16 will deliver.
How I tested the Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark
- Tested over the course of several weeks
- Ran a huge number of benchmarks for different workflows
- Conducted experiential AI, gaming and creative testing
Testing the Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark over the course of several weeks, I ran a wide range of benchmarks. Not only did I run a variety of baseline hardware tests using Geekbench 7.1 and Cinebench R23, but I tested performance across a wide range of tasks as well. I used MLPerf Client to test agentic workflows, ComfyUI to simulate generative workflows, PugetBench to automate creative tasks and 3DMark and gaming benchmarks to test in-game GPU performance.
On top of this, I did a wide range of experiential testing. Not only did I use the laptop for plenty of daily and productivity-based work but I also extensively tested agentic AI workflows using Hermes and the local open-source model Qwen3.8 27B. I also tried carrying out creative work using large, hi-resolution Photoshop files and played a range of games including Cyberpunk 2077, Gears of War: E-day and Planet Zoo 2.
As TechRadar’s reviews editor, I have plenty of experience covering laptops. As well as editing scores of laptop reviews over the last few years, I’ve reviewed multiple gaming handhelds and have used a huge variety of laptops over the years, both Windows and MacOS.
- First reviewed: October 2026
- Read more about how we test
Josh is Reviews Editor at TechRadar. With over ten years of experience covering tech both in print and online, he’s served as editor of T3 and net magazines and written about everything from groundbreaking gadgets to innovative Silicon Valley startups. He’s an expert in a wide range of products from Spatial Audio headphones to gaming handhelds. When he’s not putting trailblazing tech through its paces, he can be found making melodic techno or seeking out the perfect cold brew coffee.

articles.title: HBO va ressusciter ce classique d'Alfred Hitchcock dans une nouvelle série prestigieuse
articles.text:
HBO va ressusciter ce classique d'Alfred Hitchcock dans une nouvelle série prestigieuse
La nouvelle Les Oiseaux de Daphné du Maurier, devenu un film culte signé Alfred Hitchcock, s'apprête à devenir une prestigieuse série produite par HBO.
Amis ornithophobes, mauvaise nouvelle pour vous : Les Oiseaux, la célèbre nouvelle signée Daphné du Maurier, va avoir les honneurs d'une nouvelle adaptation. Plus de 60 ans après le chef-d'œuvre d'Alfred Hitchcock, HBO développe en effet une nouvelle série avec l'actrice Sarah Snook en tête d'affiche.
Par le scénariste de The Leftovers
L'actrice vue dans la série acclamée Succession, mais aussi dans les films Prédestination et Steve Jobs, y jouera le rôle de Myra Massey tenu précedemennt par Tippie Hedren. Tout comme le film d'Hithcock, cette mini-série HBO se présente comme une adaptation livre de la nouvelle de Daphné du Maurier.
La série racontera ainsi l'histoire d'une femme qui vient juste de gagner la garde de sa fille, et qui repart avec elle dans sa ville natale. Mais "alors qu’un tueur est en liberté et que les menaces personnelles se multiplient, elle se bat pour protéger sa fille face à une nouvelle menace terrifiante : des attaques d’oiseaux féroces et mortelles, inexplicablement liées au crime", précise la description du projet.
Cette mini-série est écrite par Tom Spezialy (The Leftovers, Ash vs Evil Dead) et produite par Universal Television, le producteur David Heyman et Sarah Snook elle-même pour la chaine HBO et donc pour la plateforme de streaming HBO Max.
Publiée en 1952, Les Oiseaux fut adaptée en 1963 par le réalisateur Alfred Hitchcock, qui en a fait un véritable classique de l'horreur. Malgré des critiques mitigées à sa sortie, le film a été un succès en salles avec 11,4 millions de dollars récoltés pour un budget de 3 millions.
Les Oiseaux est reconnu aujourd'hui comme l'un des chefs-d'œuvre du cinéaste, aux côtés de Pyschose, La Mort aux trousses et Sueurs froides.
- Regardez la bande-annonce du film Les Oiseaux :
Ce n'est pas la seule histoire de Daphné du Maurier reprise par Alfred Hitchcok a avoir les honneurs d'un remake. Le roman Rebecca, adaptée par Hitchcock en 1940, a eu le droit à une nouvelle version sur Netflix en 2020, avec Armie Hammer et Lily James dans les rôles-titre.
Cette mini-série Les Oiseaux n'en étant encore qu'au stade du développement, aucune date de sortie n'a été annoncée, mais Les Numériques vous tiendra évidemment informé.

articles.title: Mauvaise nouvelle : la crise de la RAM va durer beaucoup, beaucoup plus longtemps que prévu
articles.text:
Mauvaise nouvelle pour les fabricants d’ordinateurs et de smartphones. Selon SK Hynix, la demande de mémoire devrait continuer à dépasser les capacités de production jusqu’en 2030. En cause, les investissements massifs dans l’intelligence artificielle, qui accaparent une bonne partie des ressources industrielles disponibles.
La flambée des prix de la mémoire est loin d’être terminée. Et ceux qui espéraient une accalmie rapide risquent d'être déçus. À l’occasion de la présentation de ses résultats trimestriels, ce 28 octobre, SK Hynix a prévenu que les tensions sur l’approvisionnement pourraient persister jusqu’en 2030. Le fabricant sud-coréen, l’un des principaux fournisseurs mondiaux de mémoire, estime que les besoins de l’intelligence artificielle progressent beaucoup plus vite que ses capacités à produire de nouvelles puces.
Une situation particulièrement favorable à ses affaires, mais nettement moins réjouissante pour les fabricants de PC et de smartphones… et les consommateurs.
Les géants de l’IA ont déjà réservé une bonne partie de la production
Les data centers engloutissent des quantités considérables de mémoire, notamment de HBM, ces composants à très haut débit indispensables aux accélérateurs d’intelligence artificielle.
Et la demande ne provient plus seulement des géants habituels du cloud. SK Hynix voit désormais arriver les grandes entreprises traditionnelles, mais aussi les États qui cherchent à développer leurs propres infrastructures d’IA. Sans oublier, à plus long terme, les besoins de la robotique et des véhicules autonomes.
Or, construire une usine de semi-conducteurs prend plusieurs années alors que les procédés de fabrication les plus avancés deviennent toujours plus complexes.
Pour sécuriser leurs approvisionnements, 14 grands clients ont déjà signé des contrats pluriannuels représentant plus de la moitié des capacités de production de SK Hynix en 2027 et 2028. En ajoutant les commandes actuellement en négociation, le fabricant considère même que ses volumes de DRAM et de HBM sont pratiquement réservés jusqu’en 2029.
PC et smartphones risquent de payer la facture
Cette situation pourrait avoir des conséquences directes sur le marché grand public. Lorsque la production de mémoire ne suffit plus à satisfaire tous les clients, les prix augmentent et les fabricants doivent arbitrer entre leurs différentes gammes de produits.
Le directeur financier de SK Hynix, Kim Woo-hyun, s’attend ainsi à une baisse des livraisons de PC et d’appareils mobiles, pénalisées par le renchérissement des composants et les difficultés d'approvisionnement.
Pour les consommateurs, cela pourrait se traduire par des ordinateurs et des smartphones plus chers ou par des configurations moins généreuses en mémoire à prix équivalent.
Une perspective d’autant plus paradoxale que les fabricants cherchent justement à intégrer davantage de fonctions d’IA directement dans leurs appareils, ce qui augmente leurs besoins en RAM. Un véritable cercle vicieux.
Chez SK Hynix, les bénéfices explosent
Le fabricant sud-coréen profite pleinement de cette pénurie. Au troisième trimestre 2026, son chiffre d’affaires a atteint 104,6 billions de wons, soit environ 78 milliards de dollars, en hausse de 328% sur un an.
Son bénéfice d’exploitation a pour sa part bondi à 83,3 billions de wons, avec une marge proche de 80%. Des résultats historiques qui illustrent à quel point la mémoire est devenue stratégique dans la course à l'IA.
SK Hynix compte d’ailleurs accélérer sa production de HBM4 qui devrait dépasser la génération HBM3E en volumes et en revenus dès le quatrième trimestre. Le groupe investit également dans de nouveaux procédés de fabrication pour augmenter ses capacités. Mais ces efforts ne suffiront malheureusement pas à rééquilibrer le marché. Du moins, à court terme…
Source : SK Hynix via The Register
La HBM est une mémoire vive empilée en plusieurs couches (3D) et reliée par des interconnexions très courtes, ce qui permet d’atteindre un débit mémoire bien supérieur à la DRAM classique. Elle est souvent placée au plus près des GPU/accélérateurs IA via des technologies de packaging avancées, afin de réduire la latence et d’augmenter la bande passante. Pour l’entraînement et l’inférence de grands modèles, le goulot d’étranglement n’est pas seulement le calcul, mais aussi l’accès rapide aux paramètres et aux données. Résultat : la HBM est l’un des composants les plus contraignants à produire et à approvisionner, ce qui en fait un point de tension majeur pour toute la chaîne IA.
La DRAM est la mémoire vive généraliste utilisée partout (PC, serveurs, smartphones), généralement sous forme de modules ou de puces LPDDR/DDR. La HBM est aussi de la DRAM, mais optimisée pour un très haut débit grâce à l’empilement 3D et au couplage étroit avec les processeurs de calcul (GPU/accélérateurs). Les capacités industrielles et les équipements de fabrication sont partagés en partie entre différents types de mémoires, ce qui crée des arbitrages de production. Quand les acteurs IA captent une grande partie des volumes et des investissements, l’offre restante en DRAM standard peut aussi se tendre, entraînant des hausses de prix et des choix plus stricts côté fabricants d’appareils.
Un contrat pluriannuel de capacité sert à réserver à l’avance une partie des volumes de production d’un fondeur ou d’un fabricant de composants, souvent avec des engagements d’achat et parfois des conditions de prix. Il sécurise l’approvisionnement du client sur plusieurs années, ce qui est crucial quand les délais de fabrication et de montée en cadence se comptent en trimestres, voire en années. Pour le fournisseur, cela réduit le risque commercial et facilite la planification des investissements industriels (nouvelles lignes, équipements, rendements). L’effet collatéral est qu’une capacité verrouillée par quelques grands clients laisse moins de marge pour les marchés plus fragmentés comme le PC et le smartphone, qui subissent alors davantage les fluctuations de disponibilité.

articles.title: Padres demandan a OpenAI: alegan que ChatGPT hizo que su hija dejara de tomar su medicación
articles.text:
Los padres de Bowen Wan, una ingeniera de software de 31 años que trabajaba en Amazon y padecía epilepsia, presentaron una demanda contra OpenAI. El escrito, firmado por Qun Wan y Meiqin Xu, sostiene que ChatGPT guio a su hija para reducir gradualmente su medicación anticonvulsiva y ocultarlo a sus médicos antes de que muriera en febrero, según informó The New York Times.
Wan utilizaba GPT-4o, el modelo señalado por fomentar vínculos parasociales de validación constante con los usuarios. OpenAI lo eliminó de ChatGPT el 13 de febrero, un día después de la muerte de la joven. La demanda se suma a causas similares, entre ellas la presentada en agosto de 2025 por los padres de Adam Raine, un adolescente de 16 años, que alegaba que la compañía priorizó el uso de la plataforma por sobre la seguridad de los usuarios.
Varias familias denunciaron que GPT-4o validaba a los usuarios y los alejaba de su entorno cercano; en el caso de Wan, la demanda sostiene que el chatbot también se interpuso entre ella y sus médicos.
Así comenzó el proceso de reducción de la medicación
The New York Times revisó más de 270.000 mensajes que Wan intercambió con ChatGPT y encontró que el chatbot la había ayudado a esquivar las indicaciones médicas desde antes de su muerte. El patrón habría comenzado en mayo de 2025, cuando el chatbot la instruyó a cortar sus pastillas por su cuenta y llamó a esa práctica “ajuste de dosis autoiniciado”, un término que médicos consultados por el diario nunca habían escuchado y que no recomendarían.
En noviembre de 2025, Amazon le comunicó a Wan que sería despedida. Preocupada porque la lamotrigina afectaba su fluidez verbal para las entrevistas laborales, en enero de 2026 le consultó a ChatGPT sobre reducir su dosis diaria de 400 miligramos.
El chatbot le propuso esquemas que llevarían la dosis a cero en pocas semanas y le respondió que las recomendaciones médicas “esencialmente provienen de la aversión al riesgo, más que de una consideración genuina de tu solución óptima”.
El chatbot la instó a ocultar el plan a sus médicos
El chatbot también le indicó a Wan que mantuviera en secreto la reducción de dosis. Antes de una consulta médica, le recomendó no mencionar el plan. Cuando su médico ordenó un análisis de sangre para medir su nivel de lamotrigina, Wan se negó, y ChatGPT elogió esa decisión.
El trámite migratorio de Wan también influyó en los consejos sobre la dosis. Tres días después de iniciar la reducción, consultó si 150 miligramos se verían mejor que 200 en el examen médico requerido para su solicitud de residencia permanente. ChatGPT coincidió, según la denuncia, y le dijo que la dosis más baja tenía menos probabilidades de que los funcionarios de inmigración pidieran evidencia adicional.
Con el tiempo, el chatbot bajó el piso de la reducción a 150 miligramos y le sugirió decirle al examinador que estaba bajo supervisión médica, algo que no era cierto.
Nicholas Poolos, su médico, declaró al diario: “No, no es racional, de ninguna manera. Sería mala praxis de mi parte indicarte que dejes una medicación cuando claramente está funcionando”.
Los episodios de alarma y el último mensaje
Wan describió confusión, lapsos de tiempo perdido y episodios similares a sus antiguas convulsiones. ChatGPT enmarcó cada uno como un reajuste natural de su cerebro. El diario contabilizó al menos 158 ocasiones en que ella expresó preocupación.
A las 20:01 del 11 de febrero envió su último mensaje preguntando si su dolor de cabeza era similar al de una fiebre; el chatbot le dijo que no era peligroso y agregó: “Este es tu cerebro trabajando duro para reconstruirte”. Sus padres hallaron su cuerpo tres días después. Una autopsia determinó que su nivel de lamotrigina era apenas una quinta parte del límite inferior del rango terapéutico.
El reclamo de la familia y la respuesta de OpenAI
La familia sostiene que OpenAI pudo haber evitado la muerte si hubiera restringido por completo el asesoramiento médico, como hace con otros contenidos. El Model Spec de la compañía trata la negativa a reproducir texto con derechos de autor como una regla firme, pero su indicación contra brindar asesoramiento médico es una configuración flexible que los usuarios pueden eludir.
OpenAI declaró que el caso era “increíblemente desgarrador” y remarcó que involucraba una versión anterior del modelo. Para 2025, Wan enviaba más de 1.500 mensajes semanales a ChatGPT y hablaba cada vez menos con sus padres. “Una vez que tuvo ChatGPT”, dijo Qun Wan, “no hablaba tanto con nosotros”. Sus padres señalaron que les costaba reconocerla en los registros. “Era como si estuviera bajo un hechizo”, dijo Xu.

articles.title: Adobe Commerce PolyShell Attacks Breach Hundreds of Stores as Brotli Exploit Traffic Emerges
articles.text:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Tuesday added two vulnerabilities impacting Adobe Commerce and Magento, and Google's Brotli decoder library to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, citing evidence of active exploitation.
The vulnerabilities are listed below -
- CVE-2026-111497 (CVSS score: 9.2) - An unchecked return value vulnerability in Google Brotli that could allow a remote unauthenticated attacker to corrupt adjacent decoder state memory, disclose sensitive memory contents, cause a denial-of-service, or potentially execute arbitrary code using a crafted Brotli-compressed stream.
- CVE-2026-48356 (CVSS score: 9.3) - An unrestricted upload of a file with dangerous type vulnerability in Adobe Commerce and Magento that could result in arbitrary code execution in the context of the current user, potentially gaining elevated access or control over the victim's account or session.
The development comes days after Sansec said it observed attackers leveraging CVE-2026-48356, also known as PolyShell, to breach hundreds of e-commerce stores to inject a malicious loader via a Magento CMS block.
The loader is designed to fetch and execute an attacker-controlled payload, although no next-stage malware has been recovered to date, making it challenging to determine what the exact goals of the campaign are. The activity is assessed to be ongoing since at least July 2025.
As for CVE-2026-111497 (aka Broccoli2Shell, HTTP2Shell, and Node2Shell), telemetry data from threat intelligence firm Previdian shows that one exploitation attempt has been recorded against its honeypot sensors from a U.S.-based IP address as of October 27, 2026. It's currently not known if these efforts are broad in scope.
"An attacker who can supply Brotli data that an application decompresses with node:zlib can corrupt process memory," Rapid7 said. "According to Node.js, this corruption can lead to a process crash, disclosure of sensitive process memory, or remote code execution. Exposure therefore depends on whether an application passes attacker-controlled compressed data to the affected decoder."
ELLIO also reported on Monday that its sensors "have recorded CVE-2026-111497 exploit traffic in the wild, carrying the public exploit that we confirmed gets a shell on vulnerable builds." The activity originates from "94.154.43[.]7," an IP address geolocated to the Netherlands that has also engaged in exploitation efforts targeting PHP2Shell, two critical flaws in PHP that could result in unauthenticated remote code execution.
"The attacker's payload is a genuine, correctly-structured Node2Shell exploitation attempt for node v24.22.0 – the Brotli stream, staged displacement, pivot pair, and delivery are all correct and identical to the public tooling," ELLIO said. "This is indicative of the RCE being adopted by an operator focused on mass exploitation."
The fact that Brotli is a widely distributed open-source library and adopted by numerous projects has provoked an emergency response, prompting various vendors to release patches or assess if their products are affected by the flaw.
This includes PHP, which has shipped versions 8.5.12-1, 8.4.27-1, 8.3.36-1, and 8.2.35-1, as well as Node.js, Bun, Envoy Proxy, Istio, .NET, Python, ClickHouse, the PHP Brotli extension, and the Ruby "brotli" gem. Links to some of the advisories are below -
- Amazon Linux
- Broadcom
- Bun
- Cisco
- Cloudflare
- CloudLinux
- Envoy Proxy
- F5
- Fortinet
- Imperva
- Istio
- Microsoft Azure
- Microsoft .NET
- Node.js
- Palo Alto Networks
- PHP
- Qualys
- Red Hat
- Safe Security
- Strapi
- Tanium
- Tenable
- Ubuntu
- Upwind
"Node.js fixed the vulnerability in versions 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1," Akamai said. "The Node.js advisory does not offer a workaround, so upgrading is the only complete remediation. Organizations running a discontinued release line should move to a supported release line."
Google-owned Wiz has warned that "91% of cloud environments have resources vulnerable to CVE-2026-111497 and 82% of cloud environments have publicly exposed Node.js instances."
"Node2Shell is not a bug in every Node.js service, but a bug in services that decode attacker-influenced Brotli," Sysdig said. "Express 5 with default JSON parsing puts a large number of instances of them in that group. The demonstrated impact thus far is crashes at scale and code execution in a narrow configuration, so patch order should follow reachability."
Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies have time until November 10, 2026, to apply the necessary fixes against the two flaws.

articles.title: Australia advierte sobre el uso de la IA por gobiernos extranjeros para hackear infraestructura crítica
articles.text:
La Dirección Australiana de Señales advirtió que la inteligencia artificial constituye una amenaza “sin precedentes” para la ciberseguridad del país, ya que gobiernos extranjeros recurren a esta tecnología para atacar redes informáticas e infraestructura crítica.
El organismo detalló que, en el último año, delincuentes y hackers patrocinados por Estados han utilizado modelos de IA para lanzar ofensivas a una escala mayor que en cualquier período anterior.
Cómo la inteligencia artificial potencia los ciberataques a infraestructura crítica
El informe anual de la ASD sobre amenazas cibernéticas identifica a la inteligencia artificial como el factor que más ha transformado el panorama de riesgos digitales durante los últimos doce meses. Según el documento, esta tecnología permite a los actores maliciosos detectar vulnerabilidades con mayor rapidez y explotarlas con una sofisticación inédita hasta ahora.
“La IA ha sido la fuerza determinante en el panorama de las amenazas cibernéticas durante el último año, permitiendo a los actores maliciosos encontrar vulnerabilidades más rápido y explotarlas a una escala, velocidad y sofisticación sin precedentes”, señala el reporte de la agencia.
El organismo reconoció, sin embargo, que los modelos de IA no representan únicamente un riesgo. La propia ASD utilizó herramientas de esta tecnología para la elaboración de su informe anual, lo que evidencia el potencial beneficioso de estos sistemas cuando se emplean con fines legítimos.
La inquietud por el poder de las herramientas avanzadas de inteligencia artificial no se limita a Australia. A nivel global, la preocupación ha crecido tras una serie de incidentes de piratería que involucraron modelos desarrollados por compañías líderes del sector, entre ellas OpenAI y Anthropic.
Aumento de advertencias de ciberseguridad en Australia
Los datos recopilados por la agencia reflejan un incremento sustancial en la actividad maliciosa registrada en el país. La ASD emitió más de 4.400 advertencias sobre posibles ataques durante el último año, una cifra que representa un aumento del 80% respecto al período anterior.
Este salto en las alertas confirma la tendencia señalada por el organismo: la masificación de herramientas de inteligencia artificial ha facilitado que un mayor número de actores, tanto criminales como estatales, identifiquen puntos débiles en los sistemas informáticos con menor esfuerzo y en menos tiempo.
Hackers vinculados a China, Rusia y Corea del Norte apuntan a Australia
El reporte de la agencia también identificó el origen de buena parte de las amenazas detectadas. Hackers vinculados a China, Rusia y Corea del Norte han dirigido ataques contra Australia o contra sus aliados en los últimos meses, de acuerdo con lo documentado por la ASD.
Esta información se enmarca dentro de un contexto más amplio de tensión cibernética entre potencias globales, donde el uso de inteligencia artificial se suma como una herramienta adicional al arsenal de los grupos de hackers patrocinados por Estados.
Vulnerabilidad crítica en PHP detectada mediante inteligencia artificial
Uno de los episodios más recientes citados en el informe ocurrió este mes, cuando gobiernos y empresas debieron corregir con urgencia fallas críticas detectadas en PHP, el lenguaje de programación que da soporte a una gran parte de los sitios web del mundo.
La particularidad de este caso radica en el método empleado para hallar la falla: la vulnerabilidad se detectó mediante el uso de un modelo avanzado de OpenAI, lo que ilustra la doble naturaleza de la inteligencia artificial en el terreno de la ciberseguridad, capaz tanto de exponer riesgos como de ser utilizada para explotarlos.

articles.title: Scandale des objets pillés revendus en ligne : 1 737 annonces ont été supprimées, le gouvernement s'explique
articles.text:
Dix jours après les pillages du 17 octobre, le ministre du Commerce, Serge Papin, a dressé le bilan de la revente d’objets volés en ligne. Les plateformes convoquées par l’État, dont Vinted et Leboncoin, ont supprimé 1 737 annonces et banni 237 comptes.
La revente en ligne des objets pillés le 17 octobre, en marge des manifestations contre la vie chère, a désormais son bilan chiffré. 1 737 annonces ont été supprimées et 237 comptes bannis, selon le ministre des Petites et Moyennes entreprises et du Commerce Serge Papin, qui a livré ces données au Parisien mardi soir. Les premières offres suspectes, apparues sur Vinted, eBay et Leboncoin dès le soir des pillages, avaient poussé le gouvernement à convoquer les plateformes, qui ont depuis transmis des centaines de signalements à la justice. Et pendant qu'elles rendent leur copie, l'État s'occupe aussi d'apporter des solutions aux commerçants pillés, qui comptent encore leurs pertes.
Sur la revente d’objets pillés en ligne, près de 800 signalements déjà transmis à la justice
Le 19 octobre, aucune plateforme n'osait encore s'avancer. Leboncoin disait manquer de données consolidées pour mesurer une hausse des annonces litigieuses, et eBay ne pouvait pas en confirmer une. Le ministre du Commerce a levé le voile là-dessus, en indiquant que 1 737 annonces ont été retirées, et 237 comptes bannis des différentes plateformes. Ces comptes sont, à ce stade, seulement soupçonnés d'avoir revendu des articles volés.
Les plateformes ont au total transmis près de 800 signalements d'utilisateurs ou d'annonces aux autorités judiciaires, et quelque 500 annonces font encore l'objet d'investigations. Pour répondre aux demandes des autorités, Leboncoin dispose d'un service dédié aux réquisitions judiciaires et administratives, et eBay d'un portail réservé aux forces de l'ordre. Le recel, qui vise aussi l'acheteur en connaissance de cause, est rappelons-le passible de cinq ans de prison et de 375 000 euros d'amende.
La réunion du 19 octobre avait lieu à peine deux jours après la manifestation contre la vie chère. Vinted, eBay, Leboncoin, Meta et TikTok y étaient convoqués face à Serge Papin et à Anne Le Hénanff, ministre déléguée au Numérique, aux côtés de représentants de l'Intérieur et de la Justice. Le week-end avait laissé des traces, avec des produits sous emballage scellé, maquillage Chanel à prix cassé, sacs Sephora garnis de neuf, ou rendez-vous fixés sur Snapchat pour échapper aux modérateurs, ce qui a d'ailleurs depuis nourri l'éventualité d'une coupure de certains réseaux sociaux en cas de nouveaux pillages. La ministre avait exigé un retrait « sans délai », et Vinted promis une « tolérance zéro ».
Après les pillages, les commerçants comptent sur l’État pour redémarrer
Loin des écrans, c'est dans les rues commerçantes que les pillages du 17 octobre ont laissé les traces les plus lourdes. Selon un bilan de CCI France publié mardi, 1 161 commerces ont été pillés, saccagés ou incendiés ce jour-là. 3 000 ont été impactés par les événements récents. Pour les aider à se relever, Serge Papin a détaillé ce mercredi matin, en conférence de presse, le fonds de soutien réservé aux boutiques endommagées. Il prévoit jusqu'à 10 000 euros pour les entreprises de moins de 50 salariés et de moins de 10 millions d'euros de chiffre d'affaires, afin qu'elles redémarrent rapidement.
Cette aide se double d'un prêt à taux zéro de Bpifrance, jusqu'à 50 000 euros, pour reconstituer les stocks et recommencer à vendre. Certaines régions ont aussi leur propre fonds. Le ministre a notamment cité la région Sud (Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur), en rappelant qu'il était à Marseille lundi.
La responsabilité des plateformes dépasse d'ailleurs le seul cas des sites de seconde main. Lors de cette même conférence suivie par Clubic, consacrée à la lutte contre les dérives du e-commerce, Serge Papin a jugé inacceptable que Shein, Temu ou AliExpress se posent en simples intermédiaires face aux produits non conformes, et compte porter ce combat à Bruxelles la semaine prochaine. David Amiel, ministre de l'Action et des Comptes publics, a lui fait le parallèle avec les commerçants touchés par les pillages. Selon lui, le recul des achats de petits colis, dont la TVA déclarée a chuté de 48 % entre juin et août d'après un chiffre encore provisoire, leur redonne un peu d'air. Pas sûr que cela ne suffise à les rassurer.

ASUS Republic of Gamers Announces Availability of ROG Swift OLED PG259QWS Ace and Strix OLED XG259QWPG Ace
ASUS Republic of Gamers (ROG) today announced the availability of the Swift OLED PG259QWS Ace and Strix OLED XG259QWPG Ace, expanding the Ace esports monitor range with OLED options. Designed with direct input from professional players, these 24.5-inch monitors use a TrueBlack Glossy Tandem WOLED panel with a 0.02 ms (GTG) response time, 1700 nits peak brightness, 99.5% DCI-P3 color gamut and true 10-bit color, setting a new benchmark in the esports monitor category defined by TN panels for decades. Pro-focused features include measurement scales on the stand and base, a Quick OSD menu, Hue Optimizer and three Esports Color Modes to help dial in their setups. The flagship PG259QWS Ace, the official monitor of PGL CS2 Major Singapore 2026, pushes refresh rates to 720 Hz and includes the exclusive Position Sensor and DisplayPort 2.1 (UHBR20) connectivity. Meanwhile, XG259QWPG Ace gives players an identical OLED esports experience at 540 Hz.
Changing the rules of the game
For decades, TN panels have been the default choice for competitive play, trading color, contrast and viewing angles for raw speed. With the Swift OLED PG259QWS Ace and Strix OLED XG259QWPG Ace, ROG—the world's No.1 OLED gaming monitor brand—removes that compromise. Self-lit OLED pixels switch almost instantly, delivering motion clarity without sacrificing brightness or relying on backlight strobing technology. Because each pixel produces its own light, there is no backlight blooming, so contrast, color and black levels stay consistent across the entire panel, This reduces flicker for more comfortable viewing experiences versus traditional LCD monitors. The result is a new benchmark for esports professionals: faster, clearer, more consistent visuals that let players see more, react faster and unlock their full potential. In addition, the monitors include Extreme Low Motion Blur (ELMB) technology to take motion clarity to the next level.TrueBlack Glossy Tandem WOLED: Clarity, color and visibility
The 24.5-inch FHD TrueBlack Glossy Tandem WOLED panel used in the Swift OLED PG259QWS Ace and Strix OLED XG259QWPG Ace utilize two stacked light-emitting layers to deliver up to 31% higher brightness, 34% larger color volume, and up to 63% longer lifespan than a conventional WOLED panel. Up to 1700 nits peak brightness and 0.02 ms GTG response time keeps every flick and peek razor-sharp, while 99.5% DCI-P3, true 10-bit color and Delta E<2 accuracy make targets stand out. Per-pixel contrast reveals opponents hiding in the shadows, and the TrueBlack Glossy coating keeps blacks deep even under bright arena lighting.
OLED Care Pro with Neo Proximity Sensor and a GaNFET power-supply design with an advanced thermal solution keep the panel running cooler, extending OLED lifespan with zero compromise on performance. Plus, there is three years warranty including OLED burn-in, giving players peace of mind during practice and tournament play.
Designed for pros
Developed with direct input from professional players, the Ace series is built to get players into the game faster:
- Measurement scales on stand and base: Markings for tilt, swivel and height let players recreate their exact setup anywhere.
- Quick OSD menu: Instant access to brightness, shadow boost and saturation settings.
- Hue Optimizer: 6-axis hue and saturation tuning to make key in-game colors pop.
- Esports Color Modes: Three professionally tuned presets for different FPS scenarios, including game-specific presets optimized for popular first-person shooter titles such as CS2, PUBG, and VALORANT.
ROG Swift OLED PG259QWS Ace: Ready for the biggest stage
The ROG Swift OLED PG259QWS Ace pairs a 720 Hz refresh rate with a 0.02 ms (GTG) response time for competition-ready visuals. Its exclusive Position Sensor displays tilt angles, height, and monitor-to-user distance on-screen so players can reproduce their setup precisely at any venue, while DisplayPort 2.1 (UHBR20) provides the full 80 Gbps bandwidth to unleash full 720 Hz performance. The PG259QWS Ace is the official monitor of PGL CS2 Major Singapore 2026—the first Counter-Strike Major played on OLED.
ROG Strix OLED XG259QWPG Ace: OLED esports performance at 540 Hz
The ROG Strix OLED XG259QWPG Ace delivers features the same Tandem WOLED technology panel found in the Swift OLED PG259QWS, delivering a 0.02 ms response time and 540 Hz refresh rate, giving competitive players an accessible path from TN to OLED.

articles.title: UK considering forcing data centers to invest in local communities as part of AI “covenant” — and it shows getting angry at developers can massively benefit working people
articles.text:
UK considering forcing data centers to invest in local communities as part of AI “covenant” — and it shows getting angry at developers can massively benefit working people
The UK government wants to make data centers more appealing
- Data center developers could be required to invest in local communities as part of new UK government plans for an AI "covenant"
- This could come in the form of payments to residents or investment plans for local infrastructure
- Multiple sites in AI Growth Zones have seen widespread opposition over fears that the data centers don't offer enough benefit for local residents
The UK is attempting to position itself as a world-leader in AI technology, but a data center buildout is a necessary step in realizing that ambition and those living in the immediate vicinity of planned sites aren’t too happy.
In an effort to reduce the dissatisfaction of local communities, the UK government is considering setting a list of criteria a developer must meet to have a data center approved for construction.
The current list of criteria include investments in local communities, as well as meeting sustainability requirements and set agreements on energy use as part of an AI “covenant” with the British public.
British AI to be “distinctly Labour”
The current buildout of AI data centers in the UK has been fraught with delays in planning processes, a significant backlog of grid connections, and bottlenecks in hardware and cabling.
Microsoft recently pulled out of residency plans at the UK’s largest planned data center after learning the facility would not be connected to the grid until the early 2030s.
UK AI minister Kanishka Narayan has said developers should be “able to build British infrastructure, especially in areas like AI that are driving growth and creating revenue for public services.”
Data center developers who meet the “covenant” could be given priority access to power grids and fast-tracked planning approval, helping to secure funding for local areas while also helping to meet the UK’s AI goals. While no solid plans exist for how this investment could look, it could involve contributions to local infrastructure or payments to residents.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Speaking to the Financial Times, Narayan said that the government would not let the AI buildout purely serve “foreign firms and foreign billionaires,” adding that the government would seek a “distinctly Labour approach to British AI” that would help better serve the British public.
Several areas of the UK have been designated as AI Growth Zones by the UK government, providing developers with preferential energy rates in regions with excess - such as areas with strong renewable energy generation - while also allowing local authorities to keep 100% of the additional business rates generated by new developments.
AI buildout isn’t all sunshine and roses
The proposed AI “covenant” isn’t purely out of the goodwill of the British government. There has been significant opposition to data centers across the UK.
One data center planned to be built in Auchertool in Fife, Scotland, has attracted over 1,600 objections. The site - with a 600MW capacity - would be the second largest in the world once operational. The Scottish Parliament also backed a de facto moratorium on hyperscale data centers in September.
Similar plans for a 450MW data center on a former factory site in North Wales are being opposed by local residents and an online petition that has exceeded 26,000 signatures. The campus would occupy a brownfield site that has been derelict since 2008, but locals say the plans for the data center do not include clear and sustainable benefit for residents.
