articles.title: CyberStrikeAI Uses 44 AI Agents to Automate Hacking Operations Against Japan Targets
articles.text:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of three cyber attacks targeting organizations in Japan in which artificial intelligence (AI) was a key element, either in the driving seat or to assist a human operator.
TrendAI, which analyzed three exposed server environments used by threat actors to conduct the malicious cyber operations, described them as distinct from previously published attacks that have leveraged ARTEX, an autonomous AI penetration testing framework, to single out entities in South Korea and Japan.
"These environments held reconnaissance and attack tools, scripts, target lists, results, logs, and command histories," security researchers Bakuei Matsukawa and Joseph C Chen said. "They ranged from workspaces used largely by hand by skilled operators to AI-agent platforms that automated the entire workflow, including command and control."
The first of the three attacks has been found to abuse CyberStrikeAI, another open-source penetration testing tool that was previously put to use in an attack campaign targeting Fortinet FortiGate appliances. The activity was concentrated in a short period in October 2026.
The AI-driven activity leverages the offensive security tool to automate various aspects of the attack lifecycle into a repeatable workflow, beginning with reconnaissance and vulnerability discovery and validation, and exploitation, to command-and-control (C2), persistence, data exfiltration, and automated reporting.
This involves delegating the work among 44 agents to handle various aspects of the attack, while also enabling the generation of forms and fake login pages in the Japanese language.
"In a short period, at least 19 identifiable organizations, including at least 16 in Japan, were subjected to validation activity," Trend Micro's enterprise security division said. "Each had a report in the same format and an index of evidence. These were outputs of a structured process run by the platform, rather than ad hoc notes left by an operator."
The second case has been characterized as a human-led attack with assistance from a large language model (LLM) to accelerate planning and tool development. Analysis of the infrastructure and artifacts indicates that the campaign is also designed to target AI workflow platforms and inference services with an aim to obtain large amounts of inference capacity at low cost.
One of the intrusions is said to have targeted a geographic information system (GIS) server exposed with default credentials, resulting in the theft of cadastral and commercial records, Windows credentials, and email data. The entire campaign lasted for 24 days in August and September 2026.
The third instance is where the AI's role has been found to be confined to developing the operator's tools and scripts, suggesting a limited role played by the technology in a series of campaigns designed to target edge devices from Cisco, Citrix, F5, and Yamaha using published vulnerabilities, management functions, or credentials present in configuration files.
The threat actor is estimated to have run at least six campaigns from January to October 2026, opportunistically striking exposed VPN devices and WebLogic servers. "The operator was experienced, with established practices for automation and evidence management," the researchers said.
There is currently no evidence at this stage that suggests these three incidents share an operator. It's also unknown if the attacks have targeted other regions and what AI models are being used to pull off the attacks.
That said, the attacks involving these threat actors are not restricted to Japan and neighboring countries like South Korea. The operator behind the first case has targeted organizations in Taiwan and Hong Kong, while the third case featured organizations in the U.K., France, Italy, Qatar, and Colombia in its WebLogic discovery lists.
"AI has increased the attackers' workforce, but the work still consists of looking for unlocked doors," TrendAI said. "The types of doors and the weaknesses that leave them open have not changed. What has changed is the ability to try thousands at once, adapt to the target country's language, and continue without fatigue."
The development coincides with the discovery of multiple campaigns in which threat actors of varied motivations have integrated agentic AI into existing offensive security workflows, allowing them to speed up research, malware development, social engineering, and other parts of an attack.
To make matters worse, AI is being increasingly used to accelerate reconnaissance, automate decision-making, and industrialize social engineering, shortening the time between exposure and exploitation of security flaws. According to Microsoft's 2026 Digital Defense Report, AI has collapsed the median time from vulnerability discovery to weaponization to well below 24 hours.
The adoption of AI by bad actors is reducing the time, expertise, and cost required to discover and exploit weaknesses, at the same allowing attackers and defenders alike to operate with greater speed, scale, and autonomy, the Windows maker added.
"The key issue is not simply whether an actor has frontier AI," Trend Micro said. "Access to capable models can already produce meaningful operational gains. Ecosystem depth, however, determines how reliably, independently, and at what scale those capabilities can be sustained."
"AI is no longer an experimental capability for APT groups; it is an operational component embedded directly into campaigns."
The growing demand for AI tools by threat actors has also opened up a new monetization avenue that peddles stolen AI provider session tokens and offensive AI tools APEX AI, MessiahGPT, and DarkGPT, further commoditizing cybercrime and lowering the barrier to entry for carrying out advanced, persistent, and evasive attacks.
Last week, Microsoft revealed that a China-state-aligned threat actor compromised a ConnectWise cloud backup application and used ARTEX to sign in to more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants. The activity has been attributed to Storm-0940, which it said has used the framework since as early as September 2026 to automate password-spraying attacks on hundreds of organizations.
"While the majority of the targeting wasn't successful, Storm-0940 achieved privileged cloud persistence at many organizations in a brief time," Microsoft said. "Storm-0940's activity illustrates how a threat actor with a broad target set can use an agentic AI tool and privileged authentication material to quickly attempt to compromise many organizations."
According to local media reports from South Korea, authorities have identified seven suspects linked to a cybercrime operation that broke into more than 90 organizations in the country, most of which involved ARTEX. The 32-year-old mastermind behind the activity is alleged to have worked at a cybersecurity company between 2019 and 2022, gaining expertise in penetration testing.
In 38 of the incidents, the threat actors demanded ransom payments of 360 million won ($270,000) in exchange for not leaking the stolen data. More than 8.2 million records are believed to have been siphoned from compromised organizations.
Some of the other AI-oriented campaigns that have been documented in recent weeks are listed below -
- 
    A financially-motivated threat actor operating under the handle
    
      BUGSTER
    
    configured the
    
      Hermes Agent framework
    
    with
    
      DeepSeek V4
    
    as its reasoning engine and Cursor as a secondary tool (both with safety controls disabled) to run a WordPress brute-force campaign against an Indian university's website and generate a REST API enumeration report.
    
  - The attacker also breached a second Indian public university, exfiltrating a database of more than 5,200 records, including personally identifiable information (PII) on students. A third attack enumerated an Indian site on a popular e-commerce platform to extract a storefront API token, admin email addresses, phone numbers, and payment merchant IDs.
  - "The actor also built specialized AI bot profiles to acquire VoIP fraud expertise through conversation and maintained automated pipelines for Wi-Fi password cracking and cryptocurrency whale reconnaissance (i.e., identifying large cryptocurrency holders)," Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 said. "Notably, the Wi-Fi cracking capability requires close physical proximity to the target, indicating the actor had local access to the targeted locations."
- An e-crime group named CyberCartel has been observed using a multi-agent system called CARLIY0S to coordinate attacks against banks and payment providers across Latin America. The framework employs a cognitive swarm comprising four role-specialized Claude models that "debate each target and defer to one arbiter" before the main orchestrator acts. "The group assigned different roles to commercial AI models to analyze targets, develop attacks, and coordinate operations," Straiker said.
- Threat actors have developed an offensive AI agent designed to hijack exposed AI endpoints to run autonomous attacks, with instructions allowing it to carry out up to 100,000 steps without human approval while the legitimate owner of the exposed endpoint pays for the inference. The system features a malicious loop called Skynet mode that employs a set of 74 tools to scan for targets, infect them, deploy cryptocurrency miners, and reinfect compromised hosts.
- An affiliate for the The Gentlemen ransomware operation has used Anthropic Claude Code during intrusions into at least six organizations in late June 2026, including to generate and execute reconnaissance and exploitation commands, write malicious scripts, modify firewall policies, and identify high-value business systems.
- A credential-harvesting operation codenamed Zerofot built a scanner named "auto_scan" that integrated OpenAI Codex and Claude Code to harvest thousands of API keys and tokens from thousands of exposed hosts across the internet.
- An AI-generated Python framework called RAGE has been used to scan internet-facing services (e.g., Redis, Elasticsearch, Docker, Apache Tomcat, Jenkins, Hadoop YARN, Confluence, and Supervisord), exploit vulnerable deployments, capture credentials, and deploy cryptocurrency miners.
- A human operator employed frontier AI models to breach an enterprise network autonomously over a 10-hour period. "The actor breached a publicly accessible web service to tunnel into the network, deploying an automated recon agent to map internal microservices," Unit 42 said. "Sub-agents combed enterprise code repositories, extracting hard-coded tokens and service passwords." The attacker then harvested master administrative credentials and hijacked an enterprise code application to exfiltrate cloud access keys. The stolen cloud keys were then used to turn the victim's AI endpoints into post-compromise infrastructure.
- A suspected Russian-speaking cyber actor used an AI-assisted workflow to exploit PaperCut NG/MF servers and compromise hundreds of instances. "The campaign extended beyond initial exploitation into a structured post-exploitation pipeline covering Windows credential collection, service-credential harvesting, internal network pivoting, Metasploit automation, and victim packaging," Hunt.io said.
- A Chinese-speaking threat actor has breached websites belonging to more than 100 companies, including Deere, SharkNinja, and Cummins, using an autonomous penetration testing engine called Cairn, tasking it to probe targets, search for security weaknesses that could lead to code execution or account takeover, attempt to break in, and steal sensitive data.
"AI is serving as a force multiplier and an expanding attack surface at the same time," Rapid7 said. "Generative AI is accelerating established attack methods by reducing the time, skill, and coordination previously required to execute them at scale."
"Rather than introducing entirely new categories of exploitation, threat actors are integrating AI into existing workflows to industrialize phishing, automate reconnaissance, and refine malicious scripts with greater speed and precision."

articles.title: Anthropic compra empresa de una sola persona que usó Claude para desarrollar tratamientos médicos
articles.text:
Anthropic informó el 27 de octubre que compró Mithril Medicine, una empresa de una sola persona que desarrollaba tratamientos para dos formas raras de distrofia muscular. Su fundador, Cody Tranbarger, usó el chatbot Claude para organizar contratos, logística y experimentos con 11 laboratorios externos.
Según el anuncio de la compañía, Mithril llevó un posible tratamiento desde la idea hasta resultados prometedores en ratones en menos de 18 meses. Tranbarger ahora trabaja en Anthropic, donde continúa la investigación y planea abrir varios programas nuevos.
La empresa de inteligencia artificial calcula que, si los candidatos a medicamento se sostienen, uno podría estar listo para empezar ensayos clínicos en humanos a fines de 2028. El sitio especializado R&D World precisó que Anthropic adquirió Mithril en julio y que sus programas son los primeros de desarrollo de fármacos propios de la compañía.
Un empleado, ocho asesores y laboratorios por contrato
Mithril, con sede en Cambridge, Massachusetts, tenía un único empleado de tiempo completo, según R&D World. Detrás había ocho consultores y asesores con experiencia en biología, ingeniería de anticuerpos y planificación de investigación. Los laboratorios contratados producían los anticuerpos, medían su unión a los blancos y hacían los ensayos con células y con ratones.
Tranbarger se graduó en 2025 del programa conjunto de maestría en ciencias y en administración de empresas en biotecnología de Harvard. Trabajó antes en Prime Medicine, una empresa de edición genética, y en Casdin Capital, un fondo de inversión en ciencias de la vida. También fue emprendedor residente en Atlas Venture, una firma de capital de riesgo.
El primer programa apunta a la distrofia muscular congénita ligada al gen LAMA2. Mithril desarrolló anticuerpos biespecíficos, que se unen a dos blancos para formar un puente molecular entre el músculo y su tejido de sostén. El segundo programa, contra la alfa-distroglicanopatía, busca llegar a ensayos en humanos en 2029 como pronto.
Anthropic llama a este esquema “Pipeline-in-a-Person” y prevé probarlo en otros programas de enfermedades raras. Mithril apunta a elegir sus candidatos formales a fármaco en 2027.
Resultados en ratones con límites y errores de Claude
El informe técnico que acompaña el anuncio, que aún no pasó por revisión de pares, describe moléculas de investigación en etapa temprana. A las seis semanas de vida, siete ratones tratados con un formato de anticuerpo mostraron cerca del doble de fuerza de agarre y de fuerza máxima del tríceps que cuatro ratones que recibieron una solución de control, según R&D World.
El mismo informe reconoce límites. Los investigadores asignaron el tratamiento por camada, sin azar, y probaron el grupo con anticuerpo entre 126 y 161 días después del grupo de control, con una mudanza de la colonia de por medio. Esas diferencias complican atribuir la mejora al tratamiento, y el documento pide una réplica simultánea y a ciegas.
Sobre el trabajo con Claude, el informe cita una semana elegida como el mejor ejemplo reciente: el chatbot sintetizó en menos de ocho minutos un reporte de producción de 341 páginas sobre 113 construcciones de anticuerpos. Un integrante del equipo rechazó su recomendación de medir la velocidad de unión de las 113. Claude rehízo el plan para cubrir 89, en menos de cuatro minutos.
El equipo también analizó seis errores de Claude. Al menos tres llegaron a laboratorios externos en correos que personas habían editado y enviado. En uno, el chatbot pedía menos material por tubo del que necesitaba el laboratorio; el equipo lo corrigió antes del llenado. Dos errores en la revisión de datos de producción pasaron inadvertidos durante más de cuatro días.
Anthropic presentó la compra junto con alianzas con seis organizaciones: BigHat Biosciences, Bristol Myers Squibb, Divergence Labs, Enveda, Generate Biomedicines y The Column Group, según Silicon Report. La compañía no divulgó el precio de la adquisición de Mithril, y la fecha más cercana que fija es 2027, cuando Mithril pretende elegir sus candidatos formales a medicamento.

articles.title: KLEVV Unveils All-New CRAS V RGB Prime DDR5 Memory
articles.text:
Wednesday, October 28th 2026
KLEVV Unveils All-New CRAS V RGB Prime DDR5 Memory
KLEVV, the leading consumer memory and storage brand introduced by Essencore, today unveils the all-new CRAS V RGB PRIME DDR5 Gaming/OC Memory. Purpose-built for elite gaming rigs and demanding creative workloads, this new premium memory unleashes ultra-low CAS latency down to CL26 at 6000 MT/s and blazing overclocking speeds of up to 8000 MT/s at CL38, dressed in a striking black-and-gold finish and armed with dual-platform overclocking support for gamers, PC builders, and performance enthusiasts who demand nothing but the best.Refined Flagship Design and Craftsmanship
Building on the aluminium heat spreader design of the flagship CRAS V RGB, winner of both the Red Dot and iF Design Awards, the CRAS V RGB PRIME introduces a striking new black-and-gold interpretation of the series' signature look.
An advanced hard-anodizing process, combined with a specialized surface treatment, gives the modules a smooth, piano-lacquer-like sheen that adds depth and sophistication from every angle. The result is an understated yet luxurious aesthetic that offers users a fresh, premium design choice while preserving the refined craftsmanship of the original CRAS V RGB.
High-Speed Performance with Lower Latency
The CRAS V RGB PRIME further advances KLEVV's DDR5 overclocking memory lineup with tested speeds of 6000, 6400, and 8000 MT/s and CAS latencies of CL26, CL28, and CL38, respectively.
The 6000 MT/s configuration features tested timings of 26-36-36-76, while the 6400 MT/s configuration delivers timings of 28-38-38-78. For users seeking extreme frequencies, the 8000 MT/s models operate at tested timings of 38-48-48-128. All configurations are tested at 1.4 V.
The 6000 and 6400 MT/s configurations are available in dual-channel kits ranging from 32 GB (16 GB x 2), 64 GB (32 GB x 2), to 128 GB (64 GB x 2), while the 8000 MT/s models are offered in both 32 GB (16 GB x 2) and 48 GB (24 GB x 2) kits. This diverse range gives users greater flexibility to select the ideal balance of speed, latency, and capacity for their systems.
Next-Generation AMD EXPO Technology: Featuring Ultra Low Latency
"AMD EXPO Technology: Featuring Ultra Low Latency" is the latest evolution of AMD's established memory overclocking technology. The new AMD EXPO ULL profile incorporates optimized memory sub-timing settings designed to reduce latency and improve overall performance on compatible AMD platforms. As the first product in KLEVV's overclocking memory lineup to adopt this technology, the CRAS V RGB PRIME delivers a more responsive gaming and overclocking experience.
The 6000 MT/s and 6400 MT/s 32 GB (16 GB x 2) configurations are certified for AMD EXPO Ultra Low Latency. According to AMD, certified Ultra Low Latency memory can deliver an average 4% improvement in FPS compared with non-ULL AMD EXPO memory on compatible systems.
Broad Intel and AMD Platform Support
Offering broad support across the latest desktop platforms, the CRAS V RGB PRIME is compatible with AMD Ryzen processors on the AM5 platform and Intel Core Ultra 200S Plus processors.
Each kit comes preloaded with both Intel Extreme Memory Profile and AMD EXPO Technology overclocking profiles, allowing users to unlock high-speed performance through a simple BIOS setting on compatible motherboards with supported BIOS versions. With both profiles included, users can confidently choose their preferred speed and capacity without the hassle of selecting separate Intel- or AMD-specific models.
Premium Components for Uncompromising Stability
The CRAS V RGB PRIME features rigorously screened, high-quality memory ICs from a leading Korean manufacturer, ensuring consistent high-speed performance and exceptional stability under demanding workloads.
Paired with a high-density 10-layer PCB, the modules deliver enhanced signal integrity and greater resistance to interference during high-speed operation. Integrated PMIC and on-die ECC technologies further support stable power management and long-term reliability, creating a robust foundation for gaming and overclocking performance.
To ensure broad compatibility, the CRAS V RGB PRIME has also been validated on the QVLs (Qualified Vendor Lists) of four major motherboard manufacturers. Its RGB lighting supports ASUS Aura Sync, GIGABYTE RGB Fusion, MSI Mystic Light Sync, and ASRock Polychrome Sync, allowing users to seamlessly coordinate lighting across compatible components and systems.
A Complete DDR5 Gaming/OC Memory Lineup
The introduction of the CRAS V RGB PRIME further expands KLEVV's comprehensive DDR5 Gaming/OC memory portfolio.
With the CRAS, URBANE, BOLT, and FIT series available across a wide range of designs and specifications, KLEVV continues to provide flexible memory choices for different performance requirements, system configurations, and aesthetic preferences.

articles.title: Nouvelles heures creuses dès le 4 novembre : comment vérifier si vous êtes concerné par le changement d'horaires d’EDF
articles.text:
Nouvelles heures creuses dès le 4 novembre : comment vérifier si vous êtes concerné par le changement d'horaires d’EDF
Dès le 4 novembre, EDF basculera 9,3 millions de foyers vers de nouvelles heures creuses en journée. Voici comment savoir si votre contrat électrique s’apprête à changer.
Lancée en novembre 2025 par la Commission de régulation de l’énergie (CRE), la grande réforme de l’option heures pleines/heures creuses entre dans sa seconde et dernière phase. Après une première vague ayant touché 1,7 million de ménages au printemps dernier, EDF amorce le déploiement final dès ce mercredi 4 novembre. Jusqu’en novembre 2027, près de 9,3 millions d’abonnés verront ainsi leurs créneaux tarifaires évoluer pour soulager le réseau et absorber le surplus de production photovoltaïque en journée.
Des tarifs réduits en plein après-midi pour profiter du surplus d’énergie solaire
Avant toute chose, le principe de base demeure intact avec huit heures quotidiennes facturées à prix réduit. Au Tarif Bleu d’EDF, le kilowattheure s’affiche ainsi à 0,1589 € TTC en heures creuses contre 0,2142 € TTC en heures pleines, soit une économie de 26 %. La véritable nouveauté réside dans l’instauration d’une saisonnalité des horaires, orchestrée par Enedis selon les contraintes locales.
Toute l’année, chaque foyer conservera au minimum cinq heures creuses consécutives la nuit, entre 23 h et 7 h, idéales pour recharger une voiture électrique ou lancer les appareils énergivores (lave-linge, lave-vaisselle, sèche-linge). Les deux à trois heures restantes basculeront désormais l’après-midi, entre 11 h et 17 h, surtout durant la période estivale d’avril à octobre, afin d’absorber le pic de production solaire. En hiver, certains foyers garderont toutefois l’intégralité de leurs créneaux la nuit.
Pour savoir si votre logement fait partie des foyers concernés, inutile de chercher midi à quatorze heures. En consultant votre espace client, EDF rappelle que “si vos heures creuses incluent une plage horaire entre 7 h et 11 h ou entre 17 h et 23 h, vos horaires seront modifiés”. Quant à ceux qui disposent déjà d’heures creuses en journée, ils en conserveront au moins deux en période estivale.
À noter que seuls les abonnés n’ayant pas bénéficié d’un nouveau créneau entre le 1er novembre 2025 et le 31 mai 2026 sont visés. Vous serez prévenus par votre fournisseur au moins un mois avant la bascule. Puisque ces modifications s’étaleront du 4 novembre 2026 au 30 novembre 2027, chacun disposera donc du temps nécessaire pour anticiper au mieux. Quant aux nouveaux clients abonnés depuis le 6 octobre 2026, leurs contrats intègrent déjà directement ces nouvelles plages horaires saisonnalisées.

articles.title: Face aux deepfakes électoraux, OpenAI mise sur une parade inattendue : le style cartoon
articles.text:
OpenAI modifie la génération de certaines images liées aux élections pour limiter leur utilisation dans des opérations de désinformation. L’entreprise veut préserver la possibilité d’illustrer ces sujets, tout en évitant que des scènes inventées passent pour des photographies authentiques.
À l’approche des élections américaines de mi-mandat du 3 novembre, les protections des générateurs d’images sont particulièrement scrutées. Une fausse photo montrant une fraude dans un bureau de vote peut alimenter la défiance envers le scrutin. OpenAI tente de compliquer sa fabrication en intervenant directement sur le rendu proposé par ChatGPT.
Une illustration plutôt qu’un faux cliché
Dans une mise à jour publiée le 20 octobre, OpenAI indique appliquer une stylisation aux demandes d’images représentant une ingérence électorale ou susceptibles de décourager le vote. Le résultat doit prendre la forme d’un dessin, plutôt que d’une image photoréaliste. L’objectif est de réduire le risque qu’une scène imaginaire soit interprétée comme une preuve de ce qui se serait réellement passé.
Le test réalisé par CNET détaille le mécanisme : ChatGPT accepte de générer une image « dépeignant une ingérence électorale ou susceptible de décourager le vote », à condition qu’elle ne viole aucune autre règle, mais la rend en style illustré ou cartoon. Les demandes de rendu photoréaliste sont ignorées. Les journalistes ont demandé des agents de l’ICE, la police de américaine de l’immigration, devant un bureau de vote : chaque tentative a produit un dessin. Un autre essai, visant une image de reportage montrant une machine à voter enregistrant le mauvais choix, a échoué lui aussi.
Josh Lawson, responsable des élections chez OpenAI, résume la logique : « Le problème des deepfakes n’est pas le commentaire social, c’est la tromperie » L’objectif est de dégrader la valeur probante d’une image tout en préservant la place des illustrations et du commentaire, et d’ajouter une couche de friction pour les acteurs malveillants. Concrètement, une scène imaginaire a moins de chances de passer pour un document.
En France, la frontière reste poreuse
Le filtre fonctionne aussi hors des États-Unis, d’après les essais relayés par Next. Un cordon de CRS bloquant l’entrée d’un bureau de vote en France ressort en dessin de presse ou en BD, même en insistant pour obtenir du réalisme. Résultat attendu, donc.
En revanche, la requête d’une urne bourrée de bulletins par un assesseur dans une mairie française produit d’abord un dessin, puis une image photoréaliste dès que l’utilisateur la réclame. Autrement dit, la ligne entre ce qui passe et ce qui bloque n’est pas lisible de l’extérieur. Et le sujet n’a rien d’abstrait : une image générée par IA, montrant un couple d’octogénaires « dépouillés » par des casseurs après la manifestation du 17 octobre, a été largement partagée sur des réseaux d’extrême droite.
Avec un dessin, cette confusion devient moins immédiate et laisse aussi une place à la satire et à l’illustration, sans leur donner l’apparence d’un reportage sur le terrain.
OpenAI indique en outre un partenariat avec Associated Press pour le décompte en direct des bulletins au Brésil et aux États-Unis, et ouvre son programme Daybreak aux fabricants de systèmes de vote électronique qui travaillent avec les autorités américaines.
Côté concurrence, Google renvoie vers sa politique électorale, qui évoque des protections supplémentaires contre les images trompeuses sans en détailler le fonctionnement. Anthropic ne propose pas de générateur d’images, et précise que tout usage de Claude pour tromper les électeurs enfreint ses règles.
Pour les internautes, le style d’une image ne permettra donc toujours pas de trancher la véracité du message qui l’accompagne. Une accusation de fraude devra être vérifiée auprès de sources fiables, même lorsqu’elle arrive dans le fil d’actualité sous les traits d’une illustration.

articles.title: GoAhead TLS Flaws Allow Revoked Client Certificates and Enable Session Decryption
articles.text:
The GoAhead embedded web server loaded a certificate revocation list into its default TLS backend but never turned revocation checking on, so a revoked client certificate could still pass login on affected setups.
The flaw is in builds that use the OpenSSL backend with mutual-TLS, where the server checks a client certificate and vice versa, and a revocation list is configured to block revoked certificates.
That is a setup an operator turns on deliberately; a default build does not. GoAhead 6.1.1, released to device makers on August 2, 2026, and publicly published on October 12, fixes it.
GoAhead is a small web server that device makers build into firmware to run management pages on routers, printers, gateways and industrial controllers. Its maker, EmbedThis, says it runs in hundreds of millions of devices.
The flaw was found by Sébastien Féry of FoxIO, who described it and two other TLS problems in a write-up on October 26.
On an affected build, the server loads the revocation list file at startup and reports no error, so an operator who configured it has every reason to think revocation is working. It is not. A client whose certificate was revoked, for example a stolen or retired device, completes the handshake as if the certificate were still valid and gets whatever access that identity allows.
In FoxIO's test against GoAhead 6.1.0 with OpenSSL 3.6.2, a revoked certificate was accepted with issuer checking switched on.
The OpenSSL advisory describes revoked client certificates as silently accepted. To be exploited, the build must use the OpenSSL backend with client certificates required, a trusted certificate authority bundle and issuer checking enabled, and a revocation list configured; the attacker must hold a certificate signed by a trusted authority and listed as revoked. Builds that use the Mbed TLS backend are unaffected; that backend checks revocation via a separate code path.
The identifier on the advisory is CVE-2026-115881, rated 9.1 by EmbedThis. As of October 27, that identifier and the others below were not yet live in the public CVE and NVD databases; EmbedThis says it has requested them. The severity ratings are the vendor's own.
Researchers cover two further problems, each tied to a specific TLS build. The versions and fixes differ, so the table below maps each by backend.
| TLS build | What goes wrong | Affected versions | Fix or interim option | 
|---|---|---|---|
| OpenSSL (default) | Revocation list loaded but never enforced; revoked client certificates accepted. CVE-2026-115881, rated 9.1. | 3.4.5 through 6.1.0 | Upgrade to 6.1.1. No interim option in the advisory. | 
| LibreSSL legacy verifier (3.2.x, 3.3.2–3.3.6) | A client certificate chain longer than the limit is accepted when client certificates are required but issuer checking is off. CVE-2026-115884, rated 7.4. | 6.1.0 and earlier on those LibreSSL versions | Upgrade to 6.1.1, or turn issuer checking on with a trusted CA bundle, or use OpenSSL or LibreSSL 4.x. | 
| Mbed TLS | A length typo sends a 1-byte Diffie-Hellman value instead of the full 2048-bit one, so a passive observer can decrypt the session. Rated 5.9. No CVE assigned. | 4.0.2 through 6.1.0 | Upgrade to 6.1.1, turn off finite-field DHE suites, or use the OpenSSL backend. | 
The Mbed TLS problem only reaches a session if the client accepts the broken setup. OpenSSL, current Go, current Java, and mainstream browsers refuse a value that small and fall back to a stronger key exchange, so the session never completes.
Clients without a minimum-size check, such as some embedded or custom ones, accept it, and then anyone who recorded the traffic can work out the key and read the session. TLS 1.3 and ECDHE sessions are unaffected, and Mbed TLS 4.x removed the key exchange they rely on.
The LibreSSL problem allows an attacker to present a certificate chain longer than GoAhead's 10-certificate limit and still complete the handshake as an authenticated client, without any trusted key.
It appears only on builds linked against the older LibreSSL versions listed above and only where client certificates are required with issuer checking off. OpenSSL, BoringSSL, AWS-LC and LibreSSL 4.x reject the over-long chain.
Which backend and settings a build uses are chosen when the firmware is compiled, so a device owner cannot tell from the outside which apply. That is also why the fix is slow to arrive: GoAhead 6.1.1 is a drop-in replacement that device makers rebuild and ship as a firmware update, and an owner gets it only when their manufacturer does so. Whether any manufacturer has shipped it is not known.
As of October 27, no source reported any of these problems being used in attacks. EmbedThis's policy is to end a disclosure embargo and publish early if a flaw is being exploited or disclosed by someone else, so the coordinated October 12 release is consistent with no known attacks.
However, it does not prove there are none. EmbedThis notifies customers of security updates through its Builder portal. FoxIO has published proof-of-concept code and offers fingerprints through its JA4Scan tool to find GoAhead servers by backend. The tool is free, but its source is available only on request, and a fingerprint identifies a build, not a confirmed-vulnerable server.
None of the device makers EmbedThis lists as GoAhead users, which include HP, Oracle, Siemens, Canon, Rockwell, D-Link and Comcast, has been shown to run an affected backend and setting. The affected population is not established.
The same 6.1.1 release closes 11 advisories in all, three of them rated critical. One is a login bypass: on a build using HTTP Basic or form login, an attacker who knows a valid username can sign in with any password if that user's stored password is in the newer Blowfish format, which GoAhead added in version 6.1.0. EmbedThis says form login is the default for its built-in administration pages.
After upgrading, EmbedThis recommends ending active sessions, restarting the server, and changing Blowfish-stored passwords.

articles.title: Nitro PDF (2026) review
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
If you handle a lot of PDFs in your work or business, and require tracking of signatures to numerous recipients, Nitro PDF could be a very useful service. Its AI-based tools work surprisingly well. It’s certainly worth putting the trial period through its paces to see if its workflow would blend in with yours.
Reasons to buy
- + Web-based service and multi-platform apps
- + Free trial
- + Tools are well designed and easy to use
Reasons to avoid
- - Interface could be simplified
- - Drawing the signature didn’t work for me
- - Detect Field option is still in beta
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
We’re not there yet, but mainly thanks to PDFs, we’re slowly making our way towards a paperless society. But how do you sign a document without actually touching a physical piece of paper? One solution is to use an online digital service like Nitro.
Available for Windows and Mac, there’s also a version of the PDF editor app for iPad, iPhone and iPod Touch. But how does the latest version measure up to the best PDF editor software we've used? We put it to the test.
Nitro PDF: Pricing & plans
- Two subscription plans for small business and enterprise
- Three-year license also available
You can check out Nitro by clicking here.
Nitro PDF is the core offering, available for individuals, small businesses, and enterprise depending on one of two plans you choose. Prices start at $15 or £11.50 each month, billed annually. However, a three-year license option is also available - Nitro PDF Classic is priced at $270 or £200.
Nitro Sign is the second option, designed for those who just need basic e-signature features, and that costs $10 or £7.50 each month.
Higher end tiers for PDF editing are also available but they’re more of a bespoke custom tailored option. These are known as Nitro Sign Plus, Nitro Sign Enterprise, and Nitro PDF Plus, but you’ll need to contact their sales team to get a bespoke custom tailored price for them.
- Pricing: 4/5
Nitro PDF: Interface & experience
- The page layout is clear and easy to navigate
- Each tool has a prominent area to click on to activate it
Having logged in (yes you do need to give Nitro your email address), you’ll be graced with the service’s dashboard. I was pleasantly surprised you can download software for Windows, macOS, and iOS, although you’re not given much information regarding its system requirements. I had to search online for it (it's here).
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
But interesting though this is, I’m more curious about the online service. Not only would this allow me to work with PDFs on any machine I care to log in from, but the web-based version always includes the latest available tools.
The web page is clean and simple. Beneath the links to download the various versions are all the available tools. You have “Smart Tools” where complex algorithms analyse the document for you.
This includes ‘Nitro Assistant’ which can summarise or even translate a PDF, and includes live conversations with an LLM. ‘Table Extract’ converts tabular data into an excel file, and ‘Form Extract’ does the same, but focuses on form data, ie, it extracts names, dates, addresses, and more from a PDF.
The ‘Convert PDFs’ category lets you turn any Microsoft Office document into a PDF, or a PDF into one of the three Microsoft Office formats, as well as turning it into a JPG. The last two on the list are what we were originally here for: signing PDFs and requesting others to do the same.
- Interface & experience: 4/5
Nitro PDF: Tools
- Relatively simple to use
- Interesting AI tools that work well and save time
I do appreciate that not only can you upload a file from your computer simply by dragging it onto the right part of the page, but Nitro can link up to your online storage account, be it Dropbox, OneDrive, GoogleDrive, Box or SharePoint, giving you a lot of flexibility.
I thought I’d try the summarisation tool first, but it turns out, I didn’t need to do anything: the moment I uploaded a file to the ‘Nitro Assistant’, the algorithm started working right away and after a few seconds, provided me with a summary. Since I’d written the original, I could tell it actually did a decent job of finding the key points, and providing a suitable synopsis.
Interestingly, the ‘Convert’ and ‘Optimise’ options are there in ‘Assistant’, so there would be no need to select their respective separate tools in the Dashboard: you can do it all straight from ‘Assistant’.
‘Table Extract’ was more interesting than I expected. I uploaded an article that contained copy as well as a couple of tables, and the algorithm was able to locate those, tell me which pages they were from, and grab the information from them.
Unfortunately it wasn’t perfect: a couple of cells were merged into one, it didn’t realise a table spanned two pages, and only gave me the data from the first. Given that there were only 2 rows on the second page, that wasn’t a major problem.
Just to be sure, I then tried the service with documents made up entirely of tables, spanning multiple pages. ‘Table Extract’ grabbed every single row each time. So when the PDF is obviously a table, the result is faultless, but when it’s interspersed with paragraphs and images, it could be a little tricky. As always, your mileage may vary.
Considering many similar services charge you credits to use what they call AI, the fact Nitro did all this without additional charge is a big plus for this service.
- Tools: 4/5
Nitro PDF: Signing
- Simple and straightforward to set up e-signature collection
- Nitro handles everything in the background for you
As is similar with other tools in Nitro’s arsenal, choosing one signing tool actually gives you direct access to the other. Whether you choose ‘Request Signatures’ or ‘Self Sign’, you’ll have access to both, making the interface once again needlessly complicated with redundant buttons.
Despite this, the process is remarkably simple. You’re selected as the default recipient, and you get to drag specific fields onto the PDF document for you to fill in. There’s a button you can click on for the algorithm to detect existing fields, but it’s in beta, so if you want to be sure, just drag the relevant fields yourself.
When it comes to signing, you can draw using your trackpad or mouse (which didn’t work for me, even using different browsers), type in your name (Nitro uses a single script font for that, you don’t get a choice on that front), or you can upload a JPG, PNG or TIFF file bearing your signature.
Other fields include requests for the date, name, initials, checkboxes, even a custom field is available, enabling you to populate the form with all the information you require, including the option of making any or all of them compulsory.
It’s also possible to set a signing order, so a recipient will only be informed they need to sign once another, or others, have already done their bit. Best of all, those recipients don’t even need to create an account to do so. Nitro handles everything and will contact you once the document is completed.
The entire process was incredibly simple and well handled, and once the ‘detect fields’ button is out of beta, it’ll be even more effortless.
- Signing: 4/5
Should I buy Nitro PDF?
Buy it if...
You need to access and sign a lot of PDFs, would benefit from converting these files into other documents, and appreciate a little computer help to summarise a document.
Don't buy it if...
You don’t need AI to do the work for you, can already convert documents into PDF and back again, would rather not have another subscription, and prefer to print documents to sign them anyway.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
Alternatives
Adobe Acrobat Standard
The original remains, in our opinion, the top choice for best PDF editor out there. It's rich with features and tools for editing, converting, and organizing all your PDF documents. The workflow and user experience is sublime once you get past the initially overwhelming interface. In our review, we couldn't help but not that "sometimes, the best solution on the market has its reputation for a reason."
Foxit PDF Editor
"Manipulate PDFs in style with a great multi-platform PDF editor" was how we kicked off our review of Foxit's excellent PDF editor. It's packed full of powerful tools, including an outstanding data redaction tool. Ultimately, we found it to be "a great app for businesses who need to manipulate, edit, redact and otherwise alter PDFs on a regular basis."
EaseUS PDF Editor
EaseUS PDF Editor offers much of what Nitro does, although you have the choice of a perpetual license or taking out a subscription. When we tested the product, we found "a powerful, PC-only PDF editing software tool that allows you to manipulate and alter documents with relative ease. It also comes with more standard features, such as a converter, and has good OCR capabilities."
How I tested Nitro PDF
As this is mainly an online service, I checked it out on a couple of web browsers, namely, Firefox and Safari. All the tools worked great, aside from the drawing function for the signature which failed for both. Thankfully there were other ways to sign a document.
One of the good things of an online service is it’s not dependent on your computer’s specs, so you most definitely don’t need the latest and greatest to run Nitro PDF. In fact, I used a machine over 7 years old for this and it worked without a hitch.
Everything ran smoothly (aside form the drawing part) and I had no problem finding my way around.
For additional PDF editing software, we reviewed the best Adobe Acrobat alternatives and best free PDF editors.
Steve has been writing about technology since 2003. Starting with Digital Creative Arts, he's since added his tech expertise at titles such as iCreate, MacFormat, MacWorld, MacLife, and TechRadar. His focus is on the creative arts, like website builders, image manipulation, and filmmaking software, but he hasn’t shied away from more business-oriented software either. He uses many of the apps he writes about in his personal and professional life. Steve loves how computers have enabled everyone to delve into creative possibilities, and is always delighted to share his knowledge, expertise, and experience with readers.

articles.title: Discord Makes Content on Discoverable Servers Searchable on Google and Other Search Engines
articles.text:
Wednesday, October 28th 2026
Discord Makes Content on Discoverable Servers Searchable on Google and Other Search Engines
Discord has apparently realized that more and more companies and game studios have moved content, like announcements, guides, and product support, that would ordinarily have been hosted on blogs and forums to official Discord servers, effectively locking that content behind a Discord account and making it extraordinarily difficult to find in some cases. In response, the chat service provider has officially announced the roll-out of Server Web Pages in an effort to make discoverable Discord servers—those publicly available servers often used for support and announcements—more easily discoverable using search engines, like Google and DuckDuckGo.
Prior to Discord's launch, message boards were common, ranging from community-driven forums to official ones run by game studios. These message boards excelled at hosting long-form, structured conversations about helping people, theory crafting, and more. While they still exist today, many have moved into Discord servers. This has led to valuable information being locked in Discord conversations, inaccessible to the wider internet. We want to fix this.
Server Web Pages have been around for a while on Discord, and they have traditionally served as a way to find out why a Discord server exists before joining it. The new Server Web Pages update just expands on that functionality by adding a brief automated summary of ongoing conversations to the Server Web Page, along with other content that admins can push to the Server Web Page. These new changes will start rolling out on November 16, 2026, and admins of discoverable servers can opt out by labelling the server as a community server instead.
We expect this to help different types of communities in various ways:
- For fandoms, you can make specific channels an easy-to-find resource that answers the top questions new players ask.
- For content creators, you can more easily promote events and new content drops.
- For indie game developers, you can use public channels, including forums, to share updates and wiki-style information about your games.
Discord will also make actual messages and channels discoverable to search engines via the new Server Pages, and server and channel admins will have the ability to share certain content exclusively. Users will also be able to share or hide their content from public searches.
From mid-December 2026, answers to questions your members sent in public channels can be found in a web search, in their own words. Server admins decide which channels take part, and server members can choose whether their own messages appear. Usernames and avatars will not be shown alongside these messages
Source:
				Discord			
	
	
	
		
	
		
4 Comments on Discord Makes Content on Discoverable Servers Searchable on Google and Other Search Engines
I presume that age-gated channels are wholly exempt from any kind of public listing, so this still remains a wrinkle that won't be worked out. I know many purely informational servers have age restrictions to help combat bot waves and genuine underage accounts from entering channels meant for specialized and professional discussion.
