articles.title: Congress is questioning Delaware's plan to let AI agents run companies
articles.text:
WTF?! The idea of an entire business being run by an AI agent sounds like a nightmare, but it's a scenario that Delaware is pushing for. Now, the state's plan is facing pushback from a senior lawmaker who says having an AI in charge could protect owners and investors from liability for harmful actions.
House Oversight Committee chairman James Comer wrote to Governor Matt Meyer on October 26, requesting documents about the proposed Artificial Intelligence Company, or AIC.
The Kentucky Republican wants details of safety assessments and industry involvement, warning that the investigation could lead to federal legislation restricting state AI initiatives.
Under the draft bill, Delaware would establish a 30-month regulatory sandbox to test the concept. An AIC could pursue any lawful purpose except banking, with an AI agent handling business decisions without routine human supervision. The company itself could sue and be sued.
Each AIC would have one member, either a person or an entity, responsible for keeping it adequately funded. That member would generally be protected from the company's liabilities. However, the draft includes exceptions for fraud, willful lawbreaking, and allowing activities the member knew, or should have known, fell outside the company's stated purpose.
The proposal would not make every AI-related disaster somebody else's problem. But critics question whether those exceptions offer enough protection when software makes the decisions and humans collect the profits.
UC Berkeley law professor Andrew Baker told the Financial Times that the proposed liability shield appeared excessively generous and lacked a sufficiently developed justification.
Supporters argue that giving autonomous systems a legal identity would make their actions traceable and provide a target for liability. Delaware Secretary of State Charuni Patibanda-Sanchez outlined the proposal with Norm Ai CEO John Nay in Fortune.
There's also a financial incentive, naturally. Spotlight Delaware reports that Patibanda-Sanchez highlighted the formation fees these companies could generate. Corporate taxes and fees already contribute more than $2 billion annually to Delaware's budget, roughly a third of its revenue.
The idea of putting AI in charge of a company isn't new. In October 2025, Logitech CEO Hanneke Faber called for AI agents in every board meeting. A month later, OpenAI boss Sam Altman said he wants his company to become the first big firm run by an AI.
For now, this remains a proposal. Spotlight Delaware reported that the bill was likely to be introduced next year, while Meyer's office told Ars it was reviewing Comer's letter.
Given the many recent incidents in which AI agents have gone rogue and hacked other companies, putting the technology in charge of a company seems like a rash move. That's without mentioning the repeated warnings from experts about an AI apocalypse. Or maybe it's exactly what the sneaky AI wants?

articles.title: Mini cerebros cultivados en laboratorio logran identificar letras braille en un experimento revelador
articles.text:
Un equipo de la Universidad de Bristol logró que tres organoides cerebrales —mini tejidos cerebrales cultivados en laboratorio— produjeran señales asociadas con letras braille con un 83% de precisión, un resultado que explora la conexión entre sensores artificiales y redes neuronales vivas para desarrollar sistemas de computación biohíbrida de menor consumo energético, informó TechXplore, portal especializado en ciencia y tecnología.
La conexión entre sensores artificiales y sistemas neuronales biológicos ofrece una posible vía hacia dispositivos informáticos más eficientes en el uso de energía. El cerebro humano procesa información con un consumo energético reducido, mientras que los procesadores de silicio que intentan imitar su funcionamiento también pueden ahorrar energía frente a sistemas convencionales.
Los organoides, modelados a partir del prosencéfalo humano, miden menos de un milímetro y contienen alrededor de 10.000 neuronas, además de células de soporte. Carecen de varias estructuras presentes en un cerebro humano, pero pueden recibir estímulos eléctricos a través de matrices de múltiples electrodos, dispositivos que envían y registran impulsos eléctricos en el tejido.
El experimento, publicado en la revista Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence, buscó determinar si estas redes neuronales podían recibir información táctil y retransmitirla de forma reconocible.
Del braille a las neuronas: metodología y resultados
Los investigadores aplicaron un sensor que registra datos táctiles a las 26 letras del alfabeto braille. Luego transformaron esos registros en patrones de estimulación eléctrica y los enviaron a los organoides para observar si su actividad neural permitía identificar el estímulo recibido.
“Podemos tomar información de un sensor táctil real, convertirla en una forma que una red neuronal viva pueda recibir y luego recuperar información significativa de la respuesta del organoide”, explicó Tianyi Liu, estudiante de doctorado de la universidad y autora principal de la investigación.
La actividad neural de los organoides fue analizada con un algoritmo de aprendizaje automático —conocido técnicamente como máquina de vectores de soporte— capaz de clasificar patrones y determinar si una señal correspondía a una letra específica. Un solo organoide generó respuestas que podían decodificarse correctamente como una letra en torno al 61% de los casos.
La combinación de tres organoides elevó la capacidad de reconocimiento al 83%. “Después del procesamiento por los organoides, los datos táctiles todavía contienen suficiente información para clasificar letras braille con buena precisión”, afirmó Benjamin Ward-Cherrier, también investigador de la universidad y autor sénior del trabajo.
Los científicos todavía no determinaron por qué la combinación de tres organoides superó el desempeño de uno solo. Una posible explicación es que las variaciones individuales entre ellos aporten matices distintos al procesamiento: “Distintos organoides pueden tener conexiones de red, estados de desarrollo y actividad continua ligeramente diferentes, de modo que la misma entrada puede producir respuestas similares, pero no idénticas. Combinar esas respuestas puede proporcionarnos información complementaria que no obtendríamos de un único organoide”, señaló Liu.
Esa diversidad también plantea un obstáculo para diseñar un sistema previsible y estandarizado. Si cada organoide responde de forma demasiado distinta, resulta más difícil anticipar el comportamiento del conjunto ante un mismo estímulo.
Ruido, aprendizaje y comprobación
Para aumentar la dificultad de la prueba, el equipo aplicó distintos filtros de ruido a las señales correspondientes a las letras braille. Después comparó la decodificación de las respuestas de los organoides con la identificación directa de las señales deliberadamente alteradas.
El algoritmo que analizó las señales sin intervención de los organoides resultó más vulnerable al ruido artificial. En cambio, las respuestas neuronales conservaron una mayor capacidad para distinguir qué letra había sido codificada.
El ensayo no demostró que los organoides puedan aprender con el tiempo ni que experimenten cambios duraderos tras recibir estímulos. Solo confirmó que la información táctil podía codificarse, procesarse en los organoides y decodificarse posteriormente.
Liu precisó que se utilizó una única tarea táctil, un esquema de codificación fijo y una medida relativamente simple de actividad neural. Los próximos experimentos buscarán incorporar texturas, bordes y otras formas de contacto.
La meta final es evaluar tareas de circuito cerrado, en las que el organoide reciba retroalimentación sobre sus propias respuestas y pueda ajustar su comportamiento en función de los resultados. Ese tipo de prueba permitiría analizar si puede adaptarse a partir de la experiencia.

articles.title: PowerToys 0.102: "canivete suíço" do Windows agora facilita uso do mouse • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
PowerToys 0.102: “canivete suíço” do Windows agora facilita uso do mouse
Novo PowerToys para Windows permite manter um botão do mouse pressionado virtualmente e pode ocultar o cursor em certos momentos.
A Microsoft continua atualizando o seu “canivete suíço” para Windows. O PowerToys 0.102, a versão mais recente, traz dois utilitários novos e interessantes relacionados ao mouse: um permite arrastar algo sem manter o botão do mouse pressionado; outro oculta o cursor do mouse sob determinadas circunstâncias.
O primeiro recurso foi batizado como Bloqueio do Botão do Mouse (Mouse Button Lock). Quando ativado, ele permite que você pressione um dos botões do mouse por apenas um curto momento, mas faz o Windows entender que esse botão continua sendo pressionado.
Com isso, você pode selecionar textos, arrastar arquivos, dimensionar elementos, entre outras ações que exigem que um dos botões do mouse fique bastante tempo pressionado, mas sem se cansar. Presumivelmente, a novidade também pode ser útil para usuários com dificuldades motoras.
É possível aplicar o recurso a qualquer botão do mouse (esquerdo, central e direito). Você também pode definir quanto tempo o botão deve ficar pressionado para que o bloqueio automático seja ativado. Um novo toque cancela imediatamente o bloqueio.
A outra novidade relacionada ao mouse é o recurso CursorHide. Com ele, você pode ocultar automaticamente o cursor (seta) do mouse enquanto digita, em momentos de inatividade ou em ambas as circunstâncias. A simples movimentação do mouse faz o cursor surgir na tela novamente.
O CursorHide pode ser útil para evitar que o cursor fique por cima de alguma informação importante na tela ou, de alguma forma, atrapalhe o seu foco.
Entre as demais novidades do PowerToys 0.102 (são várias) estão:
O PowerToys 0.102 está disponível no GitHub. Na página, escolha a versão x64 para computadores com chip Intel ou AMD, e ARM64 para chips Arm.
Para quem usa versão anterior do PowerToys, basta abrir o aplicativo. Um aviso de atualização para a nova versão será exibido na tela de início.
Apesar de ser focado no Windows 11, o PowerToys 0.102 também funciona no Windows 10, vale enfatizar.
Uma última dica: em maio, revelei quais utilitários do PowerToys uso no meu dia a dia. Talvez alguma das dicas mostradas ali possa ser útil a você.

articles.title: Russian gasoline-powered drone spotted on the front lines
articles.text:
Ukraine spots Russia deploying a mystery new petrol-powered drone that could fly further than ever before
Russian loitering drone swaps electric motor for a gasoline engine
- Ukraine identifies a mysterious Russian drone powered by gasoline
- Red-starred wings distinguish the unfamiliar aircraft in photographs
- Russia's new drone resembles the Lancet with different propulsion
Ukrainian defense specialists have identified a previously unknown Russian aircraft powered by gasoline, which adds to Moscow's growing range of unmanned weapons.
The drone reportedly resembles Russia's Lancet loitering munition, although its combustion engine sets it apart from the electrically powered weapon.
“A new enemy drone has been spotted on the front. It resembles the Lancet in shape but has a gasoline engine. We are waiting for captured examples to study. Get in touch,” said Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on defense technologies.
Gasoline engine distinguishes the aircraft from Lancet
Images show red stars painted on the wings, but nothing visible in the photographs identifies the aircraft or what it is designed to do.
According to Beskrestnov, the name, manufacturer, and specifications have emerged, yet he has declined to release them until they are confirmed.
The propulsion system is the clearest reported difference from the Lancet, a Russian loitering munition developed by ZALA Aero Group that uses an electric motor.
Burning gasoline could allow longer missions without reliance on battery capacity, since combustion engines can offer greater endurance depending on fuel use and design.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
However, the drone's flight duration, operational range and payload capacity have not been disclosed, which prevents any comparison with existing Russian unmanned aircraft.
Russia continues developing battlefield drone capabilities
The Lancet is designed to strike artillery systems, armored vehicles, and radar installations, launches from a catapult, and comes in versions with varying warheads.
Russia has modified the Lancet family before, and the Ukrainian defense has identified an updated version with a redesigned antenna system.
That change potentially affected the drone’s communications, though Ukrainian defense reporting says its forces kept intercepting the upgraded systems, a claim that has not been independently confirmed.
The new drone could give Russian forces another propulsion option for missions where extended endurance is an advantage, though its deployment extent is unknown.
At a defense forum in Kyiv last month, Ukrainian military officials and industry representatives warned that battlefield technologies were evolving rapidly.
Participants urged faster innovation and wider use of AI tools, along with autonomous systems, and asked engineers to forecast Russian developments six months to one year ahead.
Ukraine has also expanded its domestic drone manufacturing, with locally produced systems accounting for 95% of unmanned aerial vehicles procured for its armed forces.
Similarly, Russia has expanded its drone manufacturing, with satellite imagery showing that the Alabuga zone in Tatarstan grew by 340 hectares in a year.
Ukraine’s military intelligence said Russia produces about 3,000 Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones per month and that Moscow seeks more capacity at Alabuga.
Bloomberg reported plans for more than 7 million FPV drones, while Beskrestnov estimates Russia’s yearly strike drone capacity at 36,000 to 40,000 units.
With both sides expanding their drone factories, the gasoline-powered aircraft is an indication of what may follow as manufacturers keep testing new engines and designs.

articles.title: Military drone outfit Anduril partners with Qualcomm to build laptops on US soil with new BlueChip venture — defense contractor targets a 100% domestic supply chain in the future
articles.text:
Military drone outfit Anduril partners with Qualcomm to build laptops on US soil with new BlueChip venture — defense contractor targets a 100% domestic supply chain in the future
“It’s time to bring silicon back to the valley.”
Defense contractor Anduril, which is known for its military drones, just announced that it’s building laptops in the U.S., with the company saying that it will begin taking orders in 2027. According to its press release, it will call its laptop product line BlueChip and will use a Snapdragon X Series SoC for its core computing capabilities. It also said that it already has functional prototypes, with 90% of the procurement cost of the components used to build it coming from suppliers in the U.S. and other allied countries. However, it’s also aiming for a fully domestic supply chain in the long term.
This means that Anduril is not only sourcing domestically produced semiconductors but also uses other made-in-the-U.S. parts, like batteries, the external casing, and even the glass for its screen. “Other companies might design their computers in the U.S., Anduril makes them here,” the Anduril founder Palmer Luckey said in the Anduril YouTube video. “We’re making parts out of metals that the U.S. knows how to extract, knows how to refine, knows how to process, and knows how to mill at scale at a reasonable price; and that goes for the entire laptop. The same thing goes for the battery technology.”
Luckey has been planning to launch a fully U.S.-made laptop since last year but said that it’s going to cost 20% more than a comparable device. Still, it seems that the company is targeting critical industries — government, defense, first responders, and public safety — which might be willing to spend more to ensure the security of their computer systems. Anduril is also better placed to start building a domestically designed, built, and sourced laptop today as the White House’s efforts to bring back semiconductor manufacturing have resulted in massive fabs like TSMC Arizona and Samsung’s Taylor, Texas site. Taiwan’s plan to support smaller companies key to TSMC’s supply chain by funding industrial parks in the U.S. will also likely benefit BlueChip, as it would make it easier for the company to source needed parts it would otherwise have to order from abroad.
Anduril has acknowledged the progress in the U.S.’s efforts to bring back computer manufacturing to its shores but also acknowledged the challenges that it faces when it comes to building a 100% domestic supply chain. “…manufacturing complete computers also requires circuit boards, displays, batteries, and other components still largely produced overseas. Restoring domestic computer manufacturing requires rebuilding that broader industrial base,” it said in its press release. “BlueChip will take a phased approach, beginning with expanding domestic sourcing and manufacturing, progressing toward eliminating reliance on foreign suppliers, and ultimately establishing an end-to-end American supply chain.”

articles.title: Kingdom Come Developer Warhorse Studios Confirms Cyberattack, Company Data Accessed
articles.text:
Tuesday, October 27th 2026
Kingdom Come Developer Warhorse Studios Confirms Cyberattack, Company Data Accessed
Warhorse Studios, the Czech developer behind Kingdom Come: Deliverance II, has confirmed that it was hit by a cyberattack. In an official statement on its website, the studio says the attack involved unauthorized access to company systems and company data. Warhorse is working with cybersecurity experts to secure its systems and assess the full impact, and says it is coordinating with the relevant authorities, though it didn't name them. A much shorter message also went up on the studio's X account on October 27, telling players it was sorry to share the news and thanking them for standing with the studio.
CEO Martin Frývaldský called it "a serious incident for Warhorse Studios and everyone affected," adding that the priority is to secure systems, establish the full extent of the breach, and protect employees, partners, and the community. Other details are thin, however. Warhorse hasn't said when the attack happened, who is behind it, what kind of data was accessed, or whether anything was actually taken, and it isn't giving interviews or further comments while the investigation is ongoing.The timing is unfortunate, as the Embracer-owned studio is busy with a new Kingdom Come game and an open-world Middle-earth RPG, with the former penciled in for April 2027 to March 2028 if everything goes right. So far, it doesn't look like anything about either project has leaked. The attack also comes just days after Capcom confirmed a breach affecting 11.7 million CAPCOM ID records, though there's nothing to suggest the two incidents are connected.

articles.title: Israeli ad tech firm tied to suspected Starlink tracking effort, report claims — researchers say it outbid everyone for Starlink-linked ads in 100+ countries, including where the service is banned
articles.text:
Israeli ad tech firm tied to suspected Starlink tracking effort, report claims — researchers say it outbid everyone for Starlink-linked ads in 100+ countries, including where the service is banned
Israeli ad-tech firm linked to suspected surveillance campaign exploiting online advertising auctions across sensitive networks.
Discover-Tech, an Israeli advertising technology company, has reportedly been linked to a suspected surveillance effort aimed at Starlink users, according to Reuters. The report, which cites six people familiar with the matter, claims the firm was the top bidder for ad space tied to Starlink traffic in more than 100 countries. Researchers suspect the aggressive bidding was meant to reveal where users are located or to enable further monitoring — though the findings do not show that anyone was actually tracked.
The data comes from TrendAI, the research arm of Trend Micro. Its October 15 report referred to the activity as ‘Shadow-Earth-79’ without naming a company, but the report claims the codename belongs to Discover-Tech. TrendAI says its attribution process is designed to avoid ‘hype-driven labels’ that could mislead security teams. “Our approach reduces the risk of misattribution, hype-driven labels, and unstable actor names that can mislead defenders, distort risk prioritization, and trigger inappropriate response actions.” The report says.
The method exploits how online ads are sold with advertisers bidding in real-time auctions for space on websites and in apps, and each bid request can carry details about the person on the other end. Collected over time and combined with other data, that information could be used to identify people, follow their activity across the web, or select targets for spyware.
The geography is what raised eyebrows. Shadow-Earth-79 was reportedly the largest ad buyer in Syria, Libya, Yemen, and South Sudan, and the second largest in Afghanistan, while also claiming unusually large shares of bids in Hungary, Israel, Egypt, Azerbaijan, and Venezuela. TrendAI says the pattern points to ‘targeting and tracking infrastructure rather than a commercial advertising operation.’ That is plausible, given how little legitimate Western advertising demand exists in sanctioned or war-torn markets.
Notably, Discover-Tech was already under scrutiny. On the same day as TrendAI’s report, Citizen Lab and ad security firm Confiant separately named the company, alleging that it used ad auctions to collect data on users across sensitive networks, including those tied to media organizations, governments, and tech firms. “The malicious advertisements were purchased by Discover-Tech, an Israeli company that presents itself as a legitimate advertising company, but which we found operates as a facilitator for multiple mercenary spyware partners.” Citizen Lab wrote.
Google and Comcast have since said they removed Discover-Tech from their advertising platforms, while the report says that a major U.S. technology company and an international organization have opened internal inquiries into whether the firm’s ads targeted their employees.
For Starlink, the stakes are obvious — the service works outside conventional telecom networks, which makes it a lifeline where governments restrict internet access, and makes its users an attractive target for those same governments. In April, Iran’s nationwide internet blackout passed 1,000 hours, with authorities reportedly going after Starlink terminals and imposing severe penalties for possessing one. Earlier this month, SpaceX also limited Starlink service for Ukraine’s high-speed military drones, which Ukrainian officials say complicates logistics and operations.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Advertising and consumer tech have been abused for tracking before. A backdoor was previously found in a popular iOS ad library that could collect device-location data and capture screenshots, while Chrysaor, Android spyware linked to the Pegasus family, was discovered by Lookout and Citizen Lab on a small number of devices. More recently, a researcher claimed to have found extensive data collection, including ad-related telemetry, inside a Samsung smart TV’s Tizen operating system, though those findings are still being investigated.
That said, it is still unclear if Discover-Tech actually used Starlink-related data to single out specific subscribers remains unverified, and neither the company nor SpaceX has commented.

articles.title: Le MacBook Pro M6 est lancé, mais le 16" M5 Max est bradé à -22% chez Amazon 🔥
articles.text:
Apple a présenté le 27 octobre ses MacBook Pro à puce M6, de quoi relancer la question pour qui hésitait sur la génération M5 et sa puce Max, taillée pour la vidéo, la 3D et l’IA en local. Amazon affiche le MacBook Pro 16 pouces M5 Max (36 Go, 2 To) à 3 999 €, 1 100 € sous le prix de Darty : une machine de création qui reste chère, et livrée sans chargeur.
Lancé au printemps 2026, le MacBook Pro 16 pouces M5 Max associe ici une puce à processeur 18 cœurs et GPU 32 cœurs à 36 Go de mémoire unifiée et 2 To de SSD, en coloris Noir sidéral. Amazon le vend à 3 999 €, alors que Darty l’affichait encore à 5 099 € le 27 octobre.
L’offre s’adresse aux monteurs vidéo, aux graphistes 3D et aux développeurs qui font tourner des modèles d’IA en local, pour qui la puissance graphique compte davantage que le prix. Pour la bureautique, cette configuration reste nettement surdimensionnée.
Le MacBook Pro 16 pouces M5 Max 36 Go et 2 To est à 3 999 € chez Amazon, contre 5 099 € chez Darty lors de notre dernier relevé.
Pourquoi choisir le MacBook Pro 16 pouces M5 Max ?
- Un GPU de 32 cœurs : Chaque cœur graphique intègre un accélérateur neuronal, et la mémoire atteint 460 Go/s de bande passante. Les exports vidéo, le rendu 3D et l’inférence de modèles d’IA en profitent directement.
- Un écran taillé pour l’image : La dalle Mini-LED de 16,2 pouces monte à 1 600 nits en HDR, à 120 Hz. Notre test de la version M5 Pro, qui partage cet écran, y a mesuré des couleurs très fidèles.
- Jusqu’à quatre écrans externes : Trois ports Thunderbolt 5, un HDMI et un lecteur SDXC accompagnent une puce M5 Max qui pilote quatre moniteurs, un de plus que la M5 Pro. Les cartes SD de vos caméras se lisent sans adaptateur.
Montage, 3D, IA locale : là où la puce Max fait la différence
Les 36 Go de mémoire unifiée sont partagés entre le processeur et le GPU, ce qui laisse de la marge aux timelines 4K chargées et aux scènes 3D lourdes. Le SSD de 2 To accueille plusieurs projets vidéo sans disque externe. Apple la présente aussi comme capable de faire tourner et d’entraîner des modèles de langage en local, un argument concret pour les développeurs.
Ce modèle vise d’abord les monteurs, les motion designers et les studios qui facturent leur temps de rendu. Il pèse en revanche plus de 2 kg et ne se recharge qu’avec un adaptateur d’au moins 94 W, absent de la boîte : un nomade s’en lassera vite. Le jeu n’est pas non plus sa vocation, puisque notre test de la version M5 Pro situait ses performances au niveau d’une RTX 4060.
M5 Pro, M5 Max ou M6 : ce que vous payez vraiment
Face au MacBook Pro 16 pouces M5 Pro, proposé à partir de 2 999 € à sa sortie, la version M5 Max apporte surtout un GPU de 32 cœurs, contre 20 sur le modèle que nous avons testé, et la prise en charge d’un quatrième écran. Le processeur de la M5 Pro testée comptait déjà 18 cœurs, si bien que le gain se concentre sur le rendu graphique et l’IA. Les MacBook Pro M6 présentés le 27 octobre restent à confronter à cette offre, faute de test à ce jour. Face aux alternatives sous Windows, notre comparatif des meilleurs PC portables fait le point.
✅ Les points forts
- GPU de 32 cœurs avec un accélérateur neuronal dans chaque cœur
- 36 Go de mémoire unifiée à 460 Go/s
- Écran Mini-LED de 16,2 pouces à 120 Hz, 1 600 nits en HDR
- Thunderbolt 5, HDMI, lecteur SDXC et jusqu’à quatre écrans externes
- 1 100 € sous le prix affiché par Darty
❌ Les limites
- Adaptateur secteur non fourni, 94 W minimum requis
- Mémoire et stockage impossibles à faire évoluer après l’achat
- Plus de 2 kg, peu adapté aux déplacements quotidiens
- Wi-Fi 7 limité aux canaux de 160 MHz, selon notre test de la version M5 Pro
Amazon n’indiquait plus que deux exemplaires en stock lors de notre relevé de 6 h : vérifiez la disponibilité de cette configuration avant de commander.
À 3 999 €, le MacBook Pro 16 pouces M5 Max reste un investissement lourd, mais il coûte 1 100 € de moins que chez Darty pour une configuration de création complète. Son GPU, son écran et sa connectique justifient l’écart avec la version M5 Pro pour qui exporte, rend ou entraîne des modèles au quotidien. Ajoutez au budget un adaptateur d’au moins 94 W.
Si votre activité se mesure en heures de rendu, l’offre mérite un examen sérieux, d’autant que la mémoire et le stockage ne se changent pas après l’achat : 36 Go et 2 To doivent tenir plusieurs années. Pour de la retouche photo ou du montage occasionnel, en revanche, une version M5 Pro ou un MacBook Air répondront au besoin pour bien moins cher. Les premiers tests des MacBook Pro M6 diront ce que la nouvelle génération change.

articles.title: I wish the iPhone Duo haters would stop telling me to buy an iPhone 18 Pro and OLED iPad mini instead — they are not like-for-like experiences
articles.text:
It’s been an exceptionally busy few months for Apple. In just seven weeks, the Cupertino giant has refreshed its store shelves with the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, iPhone Duo, HomePod mini 2, HomeView, OLED iPad mini, iMac M6, and MacBook Pro M6.
That’s eight new products for your perusal, but by offering more choice than ever, Apple has also thrown up some unique new buying conundrums.
For instance, if it’s cheaper to buy an iPhone 18 Pro and Apple’s new iPad mini than it is to buy the iPhone Duo (spoiler: it is), should you? That’s the argument currently doing the rounds on Reddit and TechRadar sister site Tom’s Guide, where my colleague says the iPhone 18 Pro/iPad mini combo is “cheaper and better” than Apple’s first foldable.
I can absolutely see the logic in this position. The iPhone 18 Pro costs $1,199 / £1,199 / AU$2,099. The new OLED iPad mini costs $699 / £699 / AU$1,099. Together, they cost $1,898 / £1,898 / AU$3,198, while a single iPhone Duo costs $1,999 / £1,999 / AU$3,499. You’d be getting two great products instead of one, and saving $101 / £101 / AU$301 in the process.
The iPhone 18 Pro is also a better phone in many ways than the iPhone Duo. It’s thinner, lighter, has better cameras, and doesn’t rely on Touch ID. The OLED iPad mini, meanwhile, offers a Duo-comparable entertainment experience, and can even be equipped with the same Nano-Texture display technology as Apple’s first foldable. So buying the Pro and mini over the Duo is a no-brainer, right?
Well, I'm not so sure. The fundamental difference between these two purchase decisions is that one involves two devices, and the other only one. These are not like-for-like experiences. Owning and using an iPhone 18 Pro alongside an iPad mini is not comparable to the experience of owning and using a single iPhone Duo. But, crucially, the reverse is true.
The Duo is a compromise, yes, but it still offers an undeniably iPad-like experience in pocketable form. You’re paying a premium for its versatility and portability. The whole point of the Duo (and foldables generally) is that it lets you experience a tablet whenever and wherever you are. It’s like using a spork while camping to save you packing a spoon and a fork. Or buying a Range Rover Sport instead of a Ferrari and a family-sized minivan.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
The new iPad mini is small, sure — but are you really going to walk around with an 8.5-inch tablet in your pocket? Tom’s Guide’s assertion that “Apple has inadvertently priced its own foldable out of the market for anyone willing to carry a small bag” makes a rather big assumption about the number of people willing to carry a small bag on their person at all times. I am not one of those people, and I don’t know many of them.
All this being said, I am no great iPhone Duo defender. For me, the compromises of getting an iPad-like experience in an iPhone-sized device are, at the time of writing, too great, and I would personally rather stick with my iPhone 18 Pro (and, yes, maybe even buy an iPad mini for watching movies in bed or on the plane).
But that does not mean I think I'd be recreating the experience of owning the iPhone Duo by buying two separate Apple products — watching movies in bed or on the plane is not the same as watching movies wherever I please.
So, yes: buying the iPhone 18 Pro and the new iPad mini might be better value for money than buying a single iPhone Duo, but value and compatibility are two different things. There’s definitely something to be said for owning one device that offers the best of both worlds, and anyone considering the iPhone Duo should remember that before being swayed one way or the other.

articles.title: Ce SUV électrique chinois devient éligible au bonus écologique en France grâce à Stellantis
articles.text:
Le constructeur chinois est bien aidé dans son implantation en Europe par Stellantis. En effet, la marque chinoise est gérée en Europe par Stellantis sous une société appelée Leapmotor International, dont Stellantis est actionnaire majoritaire. Le groupe franco-italien ne compte pas qu’importer les Leapmotor en Europe : les produire dans ses usines est aussi un projet important pour la réussite de la marque, et un modèle vient justement de profiter de cette stratégie pour devenir beaucoup plus intéressant en France et en Europe.
De nouveaux modèles produits en Espagne
Stellantis a trouvé de la place dans ses usines pour les modèles Leapmotor. L’usine espagnole de Saragosse, produisant actuellement pour le groupe la Peugeot 208, l’Opel Corsa ou encore la Lancia Ypsilon, vient de voir arriver le Leapmotor B10. Il s’agit d’un SUV compact d’origine chinoise désormais assemblé par Stellantis en Espagne pour le marché européen.
Mais ce n’est pas tout, Stellantis prévoit d’ajouter à l’usine de Saragosse dans les prochaines semaines la Leapmotor B05, une berline compacte électrique dont le prix pourrait défier toute concurrence. Pour Stellantis, cela assure l’occupation de son appareil industriel, que ce soit ses chaînes de production, mais aussi ses collaborateurs. Tandis que pour Leapmotor, cela permet d’avoir des produits plus concurrentiels en Europe, évitant les barrières à l’entrée que l’Union européenne a mises en place pour les constructeurs chinois.
Un nouveau SUV électrique chinois éligible au bonus écologique
En profitant de sa production en Espagne, le Leapmotor B10 peut prétendre désormais au bonus écologique en France, ce qui peut créer de l’inquiétude du côté des constructeurs européens qui luttent contre les nouvelles marques chinoises.
Et cela n’a pas traîné puisque le Leapmotor B10 valide déjà l’éco-score, précieux sésame pour profiter du coup de pouce CEE en France. Pourtant, cet éco-score a été pensé justement pour éviter de financer des véhicules électriques chinois, enfin davantage des véhicules électriques produits en dehors de l’Europe, visant intrinsèquement les constructeurs chinois très agressifs face aux constructeurs européens. Il y avait une volonté de la France de favoriser les constructeurs français et européens avec cet éco-score que vient de déjouer Stellantis, constructeur ayant pourtant intérêt à ne pas voir la concurrence chinoise s’installer.
En aidant à l’obtention de l’éco-score de 3 650 à 7 000 € pour le Leapmotor B10, on peut dire que Stellantis a fait entrer le loup dans la bergerie. D’autant que ce lieu de production en Espagne évite également la taxe d’importation en Europe majorée pour les voitures électriques produites en Chine. Le Leapmotor B10 passe désormais à 25 750 euros pour tous, en déduisant le bonus de 3 650 euros, ou 22 400 euros avec le bonus pour les foyers modestes.
À ce prix, le Leapmotor B10 Life Pro embarque une batterie de 60,8 kWh pour une autonomie de 400 km WLTP. Leapmotor vient récemment d’améliorer la capacité de la batterie. En haut de gamme, il y a la version Pro Max, qui utilise une batterie de 68,7 kWh pour 450 km d’autonomie WLTP. Les autonomies ne sont pas impressionnantes, mais elles sont plus que raisonnables pour les prix auxquels sont proposées les variantes du Leapmotor B10. Et pire encore pour la concurrence européenne, la Leapmotor B05 devrait également avoir droit prochainement au bonus écologique, réduisant encore son prix déjà très agressif.

articles.title: Smart TVs spy on you, even when you opt out: study
articles.text:
A new study has shown that your smart TV might be tracking you and what you watch, even when you opt out of tracking.
The study, named Watching the Watchers, was conducted by researchers affiliated with Northeastern University in Boston, Massachusetts.
- Essentially, it examines automatic content recognition (ACR) features, which the study noted are built into most available smart TVs—and whether turning ACR off actually stops TVs from sending whatever is on your screen to providers.
The researchers tested TVs running Tizen OS (Samsung), Roku OS (Roku, TCL), webOS (LG), SmartCast OS (Vizio), Google TV OS (Sony, Hisense, TCL), Fire TV OS, and others like VIDAA and Xumo.
To add some context, here is how ACR works: essentially, the TV takes short audio or video snapshots of what is on screen, and those snapshots (or the digital fingerprints made from them) are then sent to the internet or ACR provider. From there, the provider compares what was sent to a library of known content to determine exactly what you are watching. The data can reveal your viewing habits and can be used for targeted ads or sold to other companies.
Interestingly, the researchers found out that antenna broadcasts were almost always tracked on every analyzed system. On the streaming side, no TV tracked YouTube or Netflix, but free ad-supported streaming platform Tubi was tracked on Tizen OS, Google TV on Sony, and VIDAA OS.
The researchers also noted that most operating systems tracked their own streaming services, except Fire TV OS and Google TV on Sony.
Outside of antenna and streaming services, the researchers said that devices on HDMI ports were tracked on five screen systems, but not on Roku OS or SmartCast OS. Interestingly, screen mirroring was only tracked on one of the tested brands: VIDAA OS. Even more concerning, Vizio’s SmartCast OS sent ACR-pattern traffic back to its provider, even when the TV sat idle.
The researchers also said turning these features off didn’t always work. After running each scenario more than 30 times across each operating system, only four (webOS, Google TV on Sony, VIDAA OS, and Fire TV OS) were found to actually shut off the feature if the user opted out of ACR. Interestingly, another recent report that dove into LG’s smart TVs found other concerning practices, like capturing data when offline or in standby mode, recording people, scanning Wi-Fi networks, and more.
Samsung’s built-in streaming service still showed ACR-consistent traffic, and the same thing happened with Vizio, where traffic was sent to its Amazon Kinesis ACR endpoint.
If you own a smart TV, Watching the Watchers also shared some tips for what to do if you don’t like being spied on. Turning ACR off is the first step, especially if you have a TV that actually lets you turn it off. Further, you can disconnect the TV from the internet and use an external streaming device that doesn’t use ACR. Finally, for those using TVs that don’t respect the ACR toggle, the researchers also shared a blocklist that you can use to prevent the TV from communicating with the ACR endpoints.
Source: Watching the Watchers

articles.title: TSMC reportedly weighs 20% CoWoS price increase as Nvidia Blackwell and Rubin chips put pressure on packaging capacity — equipment lead times stretch to eight months
articles.text:
TSMC reportedly weighs 20% CoWoS price increase as Nvidia Blackwell and Rubin chips put pressure on packaging capacity — equipment lead times stretch to eight months
TSMC’s reported 20% CoWoS price hike comes as AI demand strains packaging capacity
TSMC is weighing raising prices for its Chip on Wafer on Substrate (CoWoS) advanced packaging technology by as much as 20%, reports Trendforce, citing supply chain sources and local media. The increase reflects strained capacity amid AI demand and longer delivery times for chipmaking tools. Such a hike would be significant, as CoWoS is already one of the tightest links in the AI supply chain. TSMC has yet to confirm the report.
CoWoS combines logic dies and high-bandwidth memory (HBM) stacks within a single package, which is how AI accelerators get the data bandwidth that demanding workloads require. Building these packages is only getting harder as chip designers cram in more compute and memory. Nvidia’s Blackwell already pairs two large GPU dies with eight HBM3E stacks, whereas the upcoming Rubin and Rubin Ultra are expected to push integration further, which will increase pressure on packaging and the supply chain that supports it.
Testing is turning into another bottleneck. Blackwell reportedly takes three to four times longer to test than Nvidia’s previous-generation Hopper, and Rubin could need as much as seven times longer. Extended test cycles keep equipment occupied for longer, which makes it harder to increase output as demand grows. GPUs are not the only products competing for capacity either, as server CPUs and custom ASICs also need advanced packaging, adding more strain to an already crowded supply chain.
Tools are also taking longer to arrive, as equipment lead times have reportedly stretched from three to six months to as long as eight months, making timely access to fab equipment increasingly important. As a result, TSMC has reportedly placed this year’s equipment orders at existing prices instead of negotiating discounts or extra features — a departure from its customary approach of using its purchasing power to secure better terms. Essentially, getting the tools on time now appears to matter more to the company than getting them cheaply.
The squeeze echoes a report from September, which said that TSMC’s projected semiconductor equipment requirements had almost doubled in six months as the company expanded production to meet AI demand. Cliff Hou, deputy co-COO at TSMC, said that by July the company’s expected equipment needs had reached 1.9 times its original estimate as AI demand accelerated. “Compared with the pattern 30 years ago, we have never seen the demand increase that much, that frequency of changes,” Hou said at the time.
TSMC is also trying to broaden its packaging supply chain. Earlier this month, GlobalFoundries agreed to produce silicon interposers for TSMC’s CoWoS in the U.S. under a five-year contract worth $2 billion, with production expected to ramp up in the first half of 2028. However, interposers are only one part of the packaging flow, so the agreement alone will not eliminate shortages.
Higher costs are not limited to packaging. TSMC is reportedly considering broader price increases for 2027, with wafer prices on advanced process technologies expected to rise by 5% to 10%. Customers using 2nm and 3nm-class nodes could face the steepest hikes, whereas those seeking capacity beyond their original allocations may have to pay additional premiums, which could push some costs up by as much as 25%.

Industry estimates cited by Trendforce put TSMC’s monthly capacity at over 106,000 wafers in 2026, with a target of 227,000 wafers in 2027 as the company works to keep pace with demand for increasingly complex AI processors. If both the packaging and wafer price increases materialize, the cost of AI hardware will likely climb further, and some of that will inevitably be passed down the chain.

articles.title: Unos científicos desarrollan un dispositivo capaz de unir la luz de varios telescopios y lo probarán en Calar Alto, Almería
articles.text:
La astronomía ha evolucionado muchísimo en los últimos años. Cada vez se pueden captar objetos más difusos y lejanos, pero todo tiene un límite. Para llegar más lejos, es necesario que los telescopios puedan captar más luz. Eso se consigue con telescopios más grandes, pero, técnicamente hablando, es algo que tiene un límite. Por eso, la ciencia se centra también en la búsqueda de formas de combinar la luz de muchos telescopios pequeños en una sola señal que los instrumentos puedan manipular. Justamente eso es lo que pretende hacer un equipo internacional de científicos, dirigido por el Instituto de Astrofísica de Andalucía (IAA), con su linterna fotónica.
Siete telescopios como si fuesen uno. Las linternas fotónicas son componentes de fibra óptica que sirven para adaptar dos tipos de fibra. Generalmente, se usan para dividir la luz de una sola fibra óptica en varias señales independientes. Sin embargo, estos científicos han logrado hacer justo lo contrario: unir las señales de siete fibras ópticas en una sola. El resultado se puede usar para alimentar cualquier instrumento de los que normalmente emplean la luz captada por los telescopios para obtener información.
En pruebas de laboratorio, se ha logrado conservar más del 90% de la luz original, por lo que sería una herramienta muy útil para observar objetos débiles.
De multimodo a multimodo. Esta es la primera demostración de una linterna fotónica capaz de unir siete señales ópticas multimodo en una sola señal, también multimodo. Que sea multimodo significa que puede admitir muchos patrones de luz a la vez, por lo que es muy adecuado para procesar luz distorsionada por la interacción con una atmósfera turbulenta.
Photonic E-MARCOT. Así se llama el proyecto internacional en cuyo marco se ha llevado a cabo esta investigación. Su objetivo es desarrollar un telescopio de gran apertura, dotado de varias unidades telescópicas, cuya luz se fusione en una sola. De momento, su demostrador, llamado MARCOT Pathfinder, se encuentra en el Observatorio de Calar Alto, en Almería, por lo que ha sido ahí donde se ha recogido la luz para los experimentos.
Un equipo internacional. Si bien la investigación ha sido dirigida por el Instituto de Astrofísica de Andalucía, con un demostrador ubicado en Almería, este trabajo ha sido realizado también por científicos de otros dos centros extranjeros: la Universidad de Sydney y el Leibniz Institute for Astrophysics Potsdam.
Más aplicaciones. Todo esto puede tener muchas aplicaciones en astronomía, pero también puede ser útil sin salir de la Tierra. Por ejemplo, en una nota de prensa del IAA, los investigadores señalan que podría ser útil en otros ámbitos de la fotónica, como las comunicaciones ópticas, la teledetección o los sensores ópticos.
En realidad, esto es algo muy común en el campo de la tecnología espacial. Muchos inventos de nuestro día a día, desde la cámara del teléfono móvil hasta el termómetro de infrarrojos que usamos cuando estamos enfermos, se desarrollaron o inspiraron en el ámbito espacial. Es cierto que se invierte mucho dinero en el espacio, pero parte de esa inversión vuelve a nuestra vida cotidiana. Los telescopios basados en linternas fotónicas podrían llevarnos a lugares del Universo que no conocemos, pero también tendrían aplicaciones sin salir del salón de nuestra casa.

articles.title: Exclusive: Prophecy launches DataGPT to run data workflows inside ChatGPT, Claude and Copilot - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Exclusive: Prophecy launches DataGPT to run data workflows inside ChatGPT, Claude and Copilot
Data preparation startup Prophecy Inc. today launched DataGPT, a new service that allows business analysts to run complete data workflows from inside OpenAI Group PBC’s ChatGPT, Anthropic PBC’s Claude and Microsoft Corp.’s Copilot.
Each answer arrives with a visual map of the steps that produced it. The service goes after a workaround that has become common in finance and operations teams: An analyst uploads a spreadsheet to a chatbot, often without sign-off from the information technology department, and asks it to reconcile a quarter of transactions. The chatbot answers by writing a script of its own.
Most people in those jobs cannot read code, according to Prophecy, so they end up taking the numbers on trust. Closing the chat wipes the logic, along with whatever revenue definitions or approved exceptions the user explained during the session. Prophecy cites a January forecast from Gartner Inc. that half of all organizations will adopt a zero-trust posture for data governance by 2028 as unverified data generated by artificial intelligence spreads.
Raj Bains, Prophecy’s founder and chief executive, said software developers already have AI that helps them write code and take it all the way to production. “Business data users got question answering, and nothing changed,” he said. DataGPT is meant to put those users on the same footing, with the workflow behind every result in a form they can verify and change.
In a single DataGPT conversation, an analyst can load a messy Excel file and cross-check it with an audit list and records held in SharePoint or Snowflake Inc.’s data cloud. A pricing rule for discounted product bundles might come next. Prophecy’s own walkthrough ends with that workflow set to run again every month without anyone rebuilding it.
No workflow goes on a schedule until a person has looked it over. DataGPT lays out each stage on screen beside its results, and an analyst who spots a problem can fix that stage before approving the whole thing.
Every workflow is backed by open code in Git. Because reruns follow that code exactly and never go back to the AI model, they carry no added AI cost. Signed-off workflows also feed a knowledge graph Prophecy builds for each customer from its own business rules and data catalogs.
Prophecy is also pitching DataGPT as a way to bring shadow AI under IT’s control. Uploaded files never sit inside the chat. They go through Prophecy to the organization’s own data platform, where IT staff and the people who run that platform can see every workflow and govern it like anything else they manage. Scheduled runs happen on Snowflake, Databricks Inc.’s data platform or Google LLC’s BigQuery, whichever the customer already owns.
DataGPT is available today through the connector marketplaces in ChatGPT, Claude and Copilot. Companies that have not yet approved those AI tools can run it in Prophecy’s own app. Individuals can start with a free account, and the product can also be rolled out centrally by an administrator.
Prophecy has raised more than $100 million since its founding in 2017, most recently a $47 million Series B extension led by Smith Point Capital in January 2025. SAP SE, HSBC Holdings plc and Pfizer Inc. are among the customers it names.

articles.title: PrivacyHawk data removal service review
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
PrivacyHawk is a decent data removal service, but more could be improved, like its customer support channels and data broker coverage. However, it provides a broad feature set outside data removal, like dark web monitoring, spam call blocking, and more.
Reasons to buy
- + User-friendly interface
- + Deep scanning
- + iOS & Android mobile apps
Reasons to avoid
- - No live chat support
- - U.S.-centric data broker coverage
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Any personal information posted online could be harvested by data broker sites and remain in their databases for a long time. These sites pose privacy risks that need to be mitigated. A data removal service like PrivacyHawk is an effective mitigation strategy: it scans data broker sites for your data and sends deletion requests where it’s discovered.
PrivacyHawk is one of many data removal services and identity theft protection tools out there. And you’re probably wondering, “Why should I choose it over other options?” I reviewed the platform to answer this question. Read on to learn about its features, pros, cons, and other factors to help decide whether it’s your ideal choice.
PrivacyHawk: Plans and pricing
You can check out the PrivacyHawk platform by clicking here.
It has a simple pricing system. Individuals can choose either the Premium or higher-priced Platinum plan. The former offers mostly data removal, while the latter offers extra features like dark web monitoring, identity theft protection, and priority support.
The Premium plan costs $20 per month, and the Platinum plan goes for $30 per month. However, PrivacyHawk offers steep discounts for users who choose to pay annually. An annual Premium subscription goes for $74, compared to $240 if paid month-to-month, and an annual Platinum subscription costs $125, compared with $360 if paid month-to-month. These steep discounts make an annual payment the best option.
PrivacyHawk also offers family discounts for both the Premium and Platinum plans. For Premium, a Family package (covering 4 people) goes for $200 annually, and the Platinum Family package costs $300 annually.
If paid month-to-month, the Premium Family plan costs $40, while the Platinum Family plan costs $50. This sums up to $480 over 12 months for the Premium plan, and $600 for the Platinum plan, which are overly high prices. I wouldn't advise paying month-to-month for the Family package—choose it only if you can afford the annual payment.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
PrivacyHawk doesn’t offer a standard free trial, which is a drawback, but there’s a 30-day window to request a refund if you're unsatisfied with what you get. After downloading PrivacyHawk, I discovered that I could run some free scans (as part of a so-so, unofficial free tier package), but this isn’t a substitute for a standard free trial.
PrivacyHawk: Setup
Setting up PrivacyHawk doesn’t take much effort. It has designated iOS and Android apps, a feature that sets it apart from most data removal platforms I’ve tested. Setting up PrivacyHawk starts with downloading the app from the Play Store (Android) or App Store (iOS).
After downloading the app, you can sign in with an existing Google or Apple account. Provide the necessary sign-in permissions, and you’ll enter your PrivacyHawk dashboard.
PrivacyHawk welcomes new users with a free scan, as I noted when discussing the lack of a standard free trial. To begin the scan, you’re prompted to enter your name, last name, and age. PrivacyHawk then runs this data against a network of 100+ people-finder sites to discover where your personal data may be present.
Notably, this scanning is geared towards U.S.-centric data broker sites. Non-U.S. residents can run a digital footprint scan, but can’t scan or send deletion requests to data broker sites.
I wasn’t comfortable with the fact that I needed to sign into my email again to run a digital footprint scan (although I did eventually). For most platforms I’ve reviewed, typing the email address is what’s needed to run the scan.
However, PrivacyHawk claims it works by analyzing email inboxes to see which companies could expose personal data. It also compiles a list of junk email senders that you can quickly unsubscribe from. If you’re comfortable with signing into your email address for a deep digital footprint scan, you can do it.
PrivacyHawk covers a network of 100+ data broker sites. This figure isn’t large compared to several competitors, but PrivacyHawk only focuses on U.S.-centric data broker sites, rather than providing global coverage. A scan can take anywhere from a few minutes to a few hours, after which you’ll see a list of the data broker sites hosting your data. You can quickly initiate deletion requests, and this is where the real work begins.
PrivacyHawk sends automated deletion requests to data broker sites, asking them to remove your personal information from their database. If an automated request isn’t sufficient, PrivacyHawk’s team can send a manually drafted legal request to the data broker sites. Processing removal requests can take a long time, maybe 30 to 90 days, depending on the data broker site. Fortunately, I could monitor the progress of each request from the smartphone app.
You may have discovered your data present on a data broker site that isn’t covered by PrivacyHawk. In that case, you can initiate a manual removal request for that site from your dashboard. PrivacyHawk’s team will send a deletion request on your behalf and follow up on it.
After the initial scan and deletion requests, PrivacyHawk runs monthly rescans of your personal data and sends email alerts if your data is found on any site. You can then initiate new deletion requests. Overall, I found PrivacyHawk to be a reliable data removal platform, although with limited U.S.-centric coverage.
PrivacyHawk: Ease of use
PrivacyHawk scores high when it comes to user-friendliness. The mobile app felt very smooth to navigate, with features neatly arranged and an uncluttered dashboard for scanning, initiating, and monitoring deletion requests.
The interface features a white background with brightly-red-colored icons & buttons that are easy to find. From signing up to scanning and managing deletion requests, I have no complaints about PrivacyHawk’s ease of use.
PrivacyHawk: Security and privacy
PrivacyHawk may not be the best data removal platform, but its complementary features make it practically a full-fledged security suite. With a single app, you can check if your data was discovered in data breaches, identify and block robocall numbers, and counter spam emails. A PrivacyHawk subscription significantly boosts your online privacy and security.
PrivacyHawk: Support
PrivacyHawk users have access to a detailed Help Center with user guides and manuals related to all its features. This Help Center proved very valuable as a new user navigating through data broker and digital footprint scans.
When I needed direct help, I contacted PrivacyHawk’s team via email. I saw what looked like live chat support, only to discover it was an AI chatbot, and I couldn’t chat with human support staff. Given the price of a PrivacyHawk subscription, I think live chat or telephone support should be provided, but they aren’t available.
PrivacyHawk: Competition
I’ll highlight OneRep as the main competitor to PrivacyHawk. It offers broader coverage, with a network of 300+ public data broker sites and 500+ non-public ones, compared to PrivacyHawk’s 100+ coverage. Its plans are more affordable than PrivacyHawk’s.
However, PrivacyHawk offers complementary features like dark web monitoring, identity theft protection, and robocall blocking, while OneRep offers email breach monitoring and little else. I think PrivacyHawk is a more complete security suite, but OneRep is a better option for data removal.
PrivacyHawk: Final verdict
PrivacyHawk has its pros and cons. Its data broker coverage is limited, but for the covered sites, it offers deep scans and effective deletion requests.
For sites not covered, you can still initiate manual deletion requests, although success rates may be lower. PrivacyHawk offers advanced complementary features that make it feel like an enterprise security suite.
The most notable drawbacks are the limited customer support, the lack of a standard free trial, and the limited broker coverage. However, PrivacyHawk remains a decent data removal platform.
