articles.title: Apple refreshes 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 chip and faster wireless
articles.text:
In brief: Apple's slow drip of new product releases continues on Tuesday with the introduction of a refreshed MacBook Pro featuring the company's new M6 processor. The chip is comprised of a 12-core CPU, a 12-core GPU with neural accelerators in each core, a dual 16-core Neural Engine for AI workloads, and unified memory for faster overall performance.
The M6 features two additional CPU and GPU cores compared to the previous M5. According to Apple, the GPU delivers up to 30% faster graphics performance and 25% faster on-device AI performance.
The dual 16-core Neural Engine, meanwhile, is said to be 1.9x faster than the M5. Memory bandwidth tops out at 170GB/s, up from 153GB/s, but you'll need a model with 24GB or 32GB of RAM to realize the additional bandwidth (the base model includes just 16GB of memory).
Battery life is rated at up to 24 hours overall, which Apple claims is about four hours more for those coming from an M1 chip and a whopping 14 hours more for "Intel-based upgraders." Wireless connectivity has been upgraded to Wi-Fi 7 (802.11be) and Bluetooth 6, from Wi-Fi 6E and Bluetooth 5.3.
Much of the rest of the laptop remains unchanged from the base M5 model, including the 14.2-inch Liquid Retina XDR display with 120Hz ProMotion refresh rate, 1TB of base local storage, a six-speaker sound system with support for Spatial Audio, and a 12MP Center Stage front-facing camera. Port selection is the same as well, with three Thunderbolt 4 (USB-C) ports, an HDMI port, and an SDXC cart slot.
Even the dimensions and weight are identical to the previous model, measuring 0.61 inches (H), 12.31 inches (W), and 8.71 inches (D), and tipping the scales at 3.4 pounds.
The new 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 will be available to pre-order starting tomorrow (October 28) from $1,999 in your choice of black or silver. Like other recent Apple devices, there is an option to upgrade to a nano-texture display that reduces glare for an additional fee. Look for it to ship on November 6.

articles.title: Cuánto espacio ocupará GTA 6 en PS5: revelan que será casi lo mismo de tres juegos
articles.text:
El dato llega apenas unas semanas antes de la fecha de estreno, fijada para el 19 de noviembre, y obliga a los jugadores a revisar cuánto espacio libre tienen disponible en sus consolas antes de que el título llegue a las tiendas digitales.
Qué se sabe del espacio que ocupará GTA 6 en PS5
La cifra proviene de PlayStation Game Size, una cuenta de X dedicada a compartir información basada en los registros disponibles en la base de datos de PSN, la red de PlayStation.
Según esta fuente, el recorrido por Leónida y Vice City demandará 210 GB en PS5. Se trata de un número que todavía no cuenta con confirmación oficial por parte de Rockstar Games, aunque se espera que sea idéntico en Xbox Series X|S, ya que por ahora no existe una cifra específica para la consola de Microsoft.
Al tratarse de un título exclusivamente digital, todos los usuarios que quieran jugar desde el primer día tendrán que hacer espacio en sus sistemas para albergar la descarga completa, sin posibilidad de recurrir a una versión física que reduzca ese peso inicial.
La misma cuenta informó, además, que el lanzamiento del juego está previsto para la medianoche, de acuerdo con los datos disponibles en PSN. Ese detalle podría significar que los jugadores más impacientes recurran al truco de cambiar la región de su consola a Nueva Zelanda para acceder a Leónida y Vice City horas antes de que la medianoche llegue a su propio país, aunque todavía queda por verse si Rockstar opta por un lanzamiento simultáneo en todo el mundo.
Además, las personas que hayan hecho la reserva del título podrán realizar la descarga desde el 12 de noviembre, lo que les daría el tiempo adecuado para disfrutarlo desde el primer día sin esperas.
Cómo se compara con Red Dead Redemption 2 y otros títulos recientes
El tamaño de GTA VI duplica al de Red Dead Redemption 2, el anterior gran lanzamiento de Rockstar Games, que requirió unos 105 GB en PS4 Pro, aunque el espacio recomendado para su instalación completa ascendía a 150 GB.
La comparación también deja mal parado a otro estreno de este mismo año: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 se puede descargar con unos 120 GB de almacenamiento disponible, contando campaña y modo multijugador, bastante por debajo de lo que exigirá el nuevo trabajo de Rockstar.
El contraste resulta llamativo si se tiene en cuenta que GTA VI promete el mapa más grande jamás construido por el estudio, acompañado de un nivel de detalle gráfico y sistemas de realismo que, según se ha explicado en distintas ocasiones, justificarían ese peso superior al de sus predecesores directos.
Cuáles son los videojuegos más grandes de la historia reciente
Pese a la magnitud de la cifra, GTA VI no alcanzaría el podio de los juegos más pesados jamás lanzados. ARK: Survival Evolved supera los 400 GB una vez instalados todos sus contenidos descargables y expansiones, mientras que Microsoft Flight Simulator puede dispararse por encima de esa misma marca al sumar paquetes de texturas fotogramétricas y ciudades completas en local.
En la categoría de experiencias para un solo jugador, Final Fantasy VII Rebirth ronda los 155 GB y Final Fantasy XVI, en su versión para PC, se aproxima a los 170 GB. Ambos quedan por debajo de los 210 GB que demandaría GTA VI, lo que refuerza la idea de que el nuevo título de Rockstar se ubicará entre las instalaciones más voluminosas del catálogo actual para un solo juego de mundo abierto.

articles.title: Wrangling Telemetry at Scale: A Guide to Self-Hosted Observability
articles.text:
Transcript
Colin Douch: Do you ever feel a looming threat of complexity? I feel as I've developed in my infrastructure life, I've developed the ability to almost smell it. It feels like even in simple systems, we're always fighting this uphill battle against this ever-encroaching demon. It's so easy to make something complex, and sometimes that complexity is out of necessity. Our world is complex, so our systems must sometimes also be complex. Sometimes it's out of false necessity. I thought it needed to be complex, or perhaps these days my AI thought it needed to be complex. Sometimes it's out of organic growth. Something started simple and became more complex over time. Sometimes it's just out of a lack of care. No matter what, we live in a world of complexity. For those of us who have to build, run, and operate these complex systems, tough luck, like that's our collective punishment for sins in a previous life.
There's a few escape hatches that sneaky folks like us like to run to when we try and escape that complexity beast. We can scoff and decide to rewrite it. Surely if we rewrite it, then all of the complexity will fall away and reveal the soft underbelly of a simple system that does all the things the complex one did with none of the complexity. Or we might try to ignore it, put it in a box, shield it from solar rays and funny looks, and try not to think about it. Or if we have to touch it, we might fob it off onto whoever is unlucky enough to be our next hire. Increasingly with distributed systems, our old methods don't work. These things become too large to rewrite, too complex to throw in a corner, and so scary that if you gave them to a new hire, they might just run away.
In those scenarios, when we have to stop running and actually have to start to tame the complexity that has been wrought upon us, we have to turn to observability. I often get asked by engineers, because I do have some experience in this field, should I run my own observability stack? My answer is, no. You don't need that hassle. In fact, I think you should put as much effort as you can possibly muster into fighting the urge to do so. You see, it's that complexity demon again. He's invading your mind. As soon as I say that, I often get a Datadog bill or a Splunk bill thrown in my face. Can people stop doing that? I have so many paper cuts on my face. How many folks out there spend at least part of your day trying to tame a Datadog or a Splunk bill? That's crazy that that's something that people have to do.
Doesn't the thought of just chucking Prometheus and Grafana on a $10 a month VPS sound so alluring? No. Back, complexity demon. There is a reason that even in the face of those monumental bills, I will say, do not run your own thing. I will recommend that you stick with a provider. That doesn't mean not changing a provider. You can certainly do better than Datadog and Splunk these days. Please, unless you need to, buy your way out of this problem, you'll save yourself so many gray hairs and so much alcoholism.
There will come a time when your life starts to go downhill where you do need to start doing things for yourself. That billing thing is a real problem. It does get exponentially worse as your telemetry volumes get bigger and you outgrow your providers, or perhaps auditors are coming around asking tricky questions like, why do we shovel so much data to this random third party? Or maybe you've decided your BI folks need a feature that you don't have the clout with your SaaS provider to build for you. Or maybe that complexity demon has finally just sapped your will to live. As complexity starts to consume the systems we run, so too does it consume our observability itself. That's what I want to talk about today. How can we run our own observability stack? What does that look like? What are the tradeoffs? How can we weave a bunch of disparate tooling together into one debugging canvas?
Background
I'm Colin Douch. I, at the moment, am a site reliability engineer at DuckDuckGo. Before that, I created and then co-led the observability team at Cloudflare. Before that, I was a founding member of the SRE team at Xero doing cloud accounting stuff, doing basically the same observability work. Before that, I was doing observability work in the real-world mining sector. DuckDuckGo in particular has been a real trip, because DuckDuckGo still uses Carbon, and Graphite, and Icinga 1, not Icinga 2. Using that to provide observability into a massive Perl monolith has been a challenge, to say the least. All that being said, I have quite a bit of experience building self-hosted observability systems. Today, I want to share that, what I've learned and how people can better build, maintain, and monitor the complexity that seems to have become inevitable these days. Whatever the reason, and there are a myriad, you need to be prepared for the baggage that building your own observability system comes with.
Be prepared to dedicate at least two to three engineers, that's at least to run it. Spend more time and money than you ever thought you would need to. Spend more time in GitHub Issue pages than you ever have in your entire life. Put in an amount of effort that would make you wistfully look at your Datadog bill like you're hoping your ex will take you back.
What Does a Self-Hosted Observability Stack Look Like?
What does a self-hosted observability stack even look like? For most people who haven't been indoctrinated into the all you need is tracing crowd, it's going to look like the three pillars. We're talking systems for metrics, logs, traces, but crucially, ways to tie them together. Observability is not about the data you're storing. It's about how you can move between that data to find what you want. That's the hardest part of building it yourself because there aren't any great open-source tools that allow you to do that, at least by default. No matter what, we're going to need telemetry storage. Let's talk about that. We can start with metrics.
Metrics
If I asked you, what should I use to store my metrics, what answers would I get? I imagine some of you are rolling your eyes and saying, Prometheus, obviously. The more well-researched or newer to the game might say, VictoriaMetrics smugly, and then put on a top hat and a monocle, and show how efficient it is, before laughing and cackling at the Prometheus people. The older folks might suddenly grow another wrinkle and say, Graphite, or RRD, or Carbon. In this instance, I think the Prometheus folks are right, but not for the reason you think. Don't get me wrong. As a time series database, VictoriaMetrics is just better. It just is. If you need a strict what you put in is what you get out type of database, VictoriaMetrics is lossy in that way, so maybe not. In terms of efficiency, in terms of scalability, in terms of ease of running, VictoriaMetrics is what we want.
That's just if you want metrics. We want observability. Prometheus has one feature that VictoriaMetrics refused to implement, exemplars. Exemplars are what allow us to start stitching together metrics into our other types of telemetry. You have to enable them in Prometheus with a feature flag at the moment. They are included in the OpenMetrics spec, the attempt to formalize the Prometheus text exposition. Hopefully that will change soon and everyone will be able to enjoy them. What exemplars allow you to do is attach a second labelset to your metric. The special thing is that that labelset can change but still be attached to that same metric, which allows you to provide an exemplar. For example, let's say we have this nice little error metric. He's running along, all good, no errors. Then suddenly, no, he's fallen over. No, we've got an error. This is standard monitoring. We know this.
Something went wrong, but we don't know what. We just got an error. If we're exporting traces or logs with a correlation ID, we can add that to the error metric as an exemplar. This trace ID is an example of a request that triggered this increase in the error metric. Now we have something to go on. We can start to move between systems. Grafana even has the ability to show these in graphs alongside the metrics themselves, which allows you to one-click jump from your graph that went wrong to traces that tell you why. If you go with Prometheus, eventually you're going to start hitting scaling issues. This is where the VictoriaMetrics folks like to jump back at me and get all smug and point out that VictoriaMetrics has a clustering which allows it to horizontally scale. Prometheus just doesn't. It doesn't horizontally scale at all, really.
It was built with this natural tree structure in mind, like one Prometheus server or a pair of them for redundancy for a set of servers. If you run out of space, you vertically scale or you shard it and split your metrics across different servers. Neither of which are particularly good solutions. Scaling up, you start to hit scaling issues, especially if you're on a cloud provider, pretty quickly. Sharding requires a huge amount of manual effort, especially when there's no natural boundary to shard on, because you then have to create another federated instance to share metrics. It becomes a huge mess.
It begs the question, how do you scale this thing? There are a few dimensions to consider. The number of active time series, which is the number of time series that have had a sample in the last two hours, and your retention, which starts to bound your CPU for queries and things like that. For your active time series, Prometheus buffers the last two hours' worth of metrics in memory, which is known as the head chunk before it's finalized to disk. Unfortunately, that's just Prometheus's design. There's not much you can do about it. At Cloudflare, we found that for each time series in that head chunk, it takes about 4 kilobytes, so use that for your capacity planning. What makes this a little bit easier and solves the retention issue as well is long-term storage systems. You can probably name a few: Thanos, Mimir, Cortex. They all serve to solve the retention problem in different ways.
Mimir and Cortex, through Prometheus's remote write system, directly writing metrics to a receiver service, which removes the need for that head chunk, and then writes them to blob storage. If you are running into head chunk issues, go there. Thanos, on the other hand, because it can only upload completed blocks, which are finalized every two hours, it relies on having to pull directly from the sidecars that run next to each Prometheus instance before it can run a computation, which tends to make highly distributed environments quite difficult with Thanos. There are a couple of tips here that I think, in the general case, make Thanos shine over Mimir and Cortex. The first is the distributed query engine. Usually, when Thanos does a query, it fetches data from all the sidecars and centralizes it and then runs the query over that data, which, if you're querying over a large number of data centers, is disastrous.
It's way too much data. If you use the distributed query engine with that flag there, it pushes that computation down into the sidecars, which then send partial results back and those get combined centrally, which, if you have the architecture to require it, a more distributed system rather than one or two data centers, this unlocks the ability to horizontally scale your Prometheus query layer, which is pretty great when it's for free. The other is the Parquet storage engine. One thing that's really frustrating about the Prometheus world is that Prometheus people tend to be very protective of Prometheus. I remember at PromCon, I think in 2017, 2018, when Alexander first announced VictoriaMetrics, and Brian Brazil and a couple of other maintainers threw together a very quick lightning talk that basically amounted to, no. So too today, because Thanos has a new neat little experiment they're running, rewriting Prometheus blocks into Parquet.
If you use it, the benchmarks are incredibly impressive. They take you to basically the performance of VictoriaMetrics, but without any of the micro-optimizations that VictoriaMetrics does, which is quite exciting. You can have a look at it there. It's just an experiment at the moment, but I'm hoping that maybe that will start to get pulled into Prometheus itself, maybe in Prometheus 3.
Logs
Enough about metrics. They're boring. They're so retro. What we want is logs. We want observability, these things. To me, logs are the most fun part of an observability stack. They're ubiquitous, and they're simple. Just about everyone has done a hello world, which is a log, albeit a terrible one. At the same time, a lot of people get logging wrong. Lots of companies will try and tell you, logs are bad, you should do tracing. There is some merit to that. There's that complexity demon raising his head again, because I can call println, or I can import 10 megs of OTel libs and use their convoluted APIs. I would argue that in most cases, if you can get away with logs, do logs. Here's how you do them right. For starters, as you get more and more loglines, finding things becomes harder and harder. Things like Elasticsearch excel at full text search, which makes this work.
Elasticsearch is commonly used for this sort of thing. Full text search is slow, and even with the indexing that Elasticsearch does, especially if you want to start introducing regexes and wildcards, it starts to fall down. The simplest example I can give is searching for user records. Let's say we're logging a user ID, and we want to search for user 20. This pattern is very common in nginx logs, for example, older things that don't structure logs. Let's search for it. Because we're doing full text search, we also get user 202 and 2070. We can chuck in some anchors and search for breaks between words, but then we start to hit other issues. What if other call sites structure the data differently and it starts to get messy? No, plain-text logs, they suck. What you want is structured logging. People equate structured logging with JSON, and that's what it boils down to these days.
Really, the difference is in the storage engine, rather than how that structure is ultimately produced. You need a storage that allows storing and indexing on those structured fields, ideally with support for dynamic schemas, so you don't have to define up front what your data looks like. Elasticsearch, again, was the go-to for this for a long time. Dynamic field support in Elasticsearch just sucks. You can only have a certain number of dynamic fields in your index before ingestion just stops, and you have to bump the limit in your YAML file. If you bump the limit too high, the performance of your Elasticsearch server just tanks.
I haven't used it, but from what I've heard, OpenSearch, Amazon's fork of Elasticsearch from when things started to go weird with their licensing, does this a bit better. There are more specialized log storage things that seem to fit the bill. The first real competitor to come out was Loki from Grafana, which flips the storage model on its head. Instead of storing one big indexed stream, like a standard database, Loki stores logs in individual streams with stream labels. If you're not a big fan of the whole cattle not pets thing, you could have a stream for Node, or Node and services, like a couple. Crucially, that's all the indexing you get with Loki. If you want a field to be indexed, you have to say that at ingest time, which basically brings us back to that full text search problem. Anything you didn't say you wanted to be indexed goes back into that full text search, which means that you either have to know what you want to search for ahead of time or suffer the penalty of full text search.
That's not very observability of you, Grafana. VictoriaLogs, on the other hand, does not have that limitation. It's a full columnar database like its metrics counterpart. If you're starting from scratch or looking to move, VictoriaMetrics would be my recommendation. Of course, you could just go with a dedicated columnar database, like inserting logs directly into ClickHouse and using SQL to query them, or a gateway like Quesma. Those tend to be a lot higher maintenance in my experience. If you're not already running one, it's not worth starting just to run your logging system. Cloudflare got away with this by having a whole dedicated ClickHouse team to run the stack for us. Not everyone has that luxury or the ability to poach half of ClickHouse Inc. Remember the complexity demon? You really do need a columnar database with support for dynamic indexing. The reason for that is inherent in observability itself. We don't know what we don't know. Having to decide ahead of time what fields to index just doesn't work when we start to look at those unknown problems.
Speaking of observability, how can we actually start using logs to answer those questions? We have to think about the usability of our data. A lot of time, logs are sprinkled around. We're like a chef, just sprinkling them in wherever you need one. That leads to this annoying situation where for a single error, you have a bunch of disparate logs that are all unordered and all just strewn about, like old clothes you can't be bothered to put away. What we really need is a way to tie all of those logs together into one event, which is where canonical logging comes in. I think Stripe came up with this idea originally. It's a really simple idea that bridges the way between logging and tracing. Instead of doing this, where we have a bunch of individual log calls, we instead collect all our fields into a context block as we go through a function.
Then at the end, or in Go's case in a defer func, we emit it as one thing. Instead of having a bunch of disparate logs, we have one log per block of work. With one logline, there's no chasing through different streams to try and find what you need. It's all just there in one event. Generally, we do this at the handle level. If your service is an HTTP microservice, or in some sort of logic or top-level function, like a processing function, if not. You can even be super fancy and generate a UUID and add it in. Look, we've got a correlation ID that we can add to our exemplars. Between structured logging into a proper columnar database and canonical logging, we have a pretty good way to debug individual services, which might be enough if that's your architecture. Remember that complexity demon? Fight it off as much as you can.
Tracing
If you must, and we're here to talk about distributed systems after all, we need to talk about how we can debug across multiple systems that all talk to each other. We need to talk about tracing, which is what we're all here for. This is the debugging distributed systems track after all. I hope I've made a case that you can actually get pretty far with metrics, with exemplars, and canonical logs. As with so much here, keep fighting that complexity demon. Tracing explodes your complexity. Suddenly, you have to decide what tracing libraries to use. You have to worry about how you're going to export your data and in what format and what context format you're going to use, and how that gets serialized and deserialized between your systems and your RPC. There's a little secret here, one that tracing advocates don't want to tell you. Tracing is only tracing if it comes from the distributed tracing region of San Francisco.
Anything else is just sparkling logs, because that's really what they are, just logs with a little bit of structure dictated on top of them, rather than being arbitrarily freeform. Take a structured log, add a random ID, we'll call it a span ID, shall we say. Add a couple of passed in IDs, one that represents the request, we'll call that maybe a trace ID. We'll generate another one that we take in, and we'll call that the parent span ID. We've got a span. We collect a bunch of those spans together based on that top-level request ID, and we've got a trace. Why is tracing important? It's because of those parent-child relationships. It's a simple idea, but a pretty crucial one. Logs come in and get ordered by time, but on computers, time is weird and flexible and sometimes goes backwards, which is a crazy thing that time can do.
There's no real guarantee that a log coming in was actually produced before another log that came in later. The idea of a parent span ID strips that causal relationship there and models what we actually want. This function called this other function, rather than having to infer that based on temporal information. Having that alongside the wide context is tremendously useful in debugging, especially when you can communicate those IDs over a network between services, and stitch together spans from all over the place where those time issues become infinitely worse.
Because tracing has become this hot buzzword, there are so many tools that have popped up to try and be the one to take, process, and store your traces, which brings me to OpenTelemetry, or OTel. OTel, the spec, and the associated libraries attempt to try and mask over that complexity demon that is inherent in tracing. The OTel libraries make sane default choices for you so that if your entire stack is using them, they just work masking over a lot of those choices. Useful if you're just getting into tracing and you don't really care, or if you're instrumenting multiple different services in multiple languages and want to make sure that you've made the same decisions in each one. It's worth mentioning as an aside, OTel also has a spec for metrics and logs, but there's a reason I haven't mentioned them until now. I would recommend you don't use them.
Remember that complexity demon? Don't make things any more complicated than they need to be. The OTel project attempting to ingratiate themselves into existing open-source communities like Prometheus has caused quite a stir because they're completely ignoring what exists and just trying to dictate a spec. I highly recommend looking at the Prometheus mailing list for all the OTel discussions, if you need a dose of cortisol in your system, because it's quite a read. I would recommend the OTel libs for tracing. They're the most stable of the telemetry types, and the complexity they introduce becomes worth it because tracing is so useful. There are older alternatives out there. You can instrument with Jaeger or Zipkin, but both of which are older and being deprecated or are deprecated in favor of the OTel format. OTel is really your only choice here.
It's all well and good exporting a bunch of data. A lot of people just import OpenTelemetry, chuck in a bunch of auto-instrumentations and call it a day, but we're doing observability and observability isn't about collecting a bunch of data. We actually care about being able to use that data to solve problems. We want to store it and we want to care about what that storage can provide us in terms of useful queries and links to other systems. Yet again, we have a few options here, mostly Jaeger or Tempo. In the past, I would have recommended Jaeger as the original, but I think Tempo starts to tip it over because it starts to provide those observability features. Jaeger has made some impressive strides here. The new monitoring page in Jaeger, which I'd recommend you upgrade to, provides RED metrics for free from your tracing data. When it actually comes down to getting actionable insights out of your data, Tempo wins every day.
It actually has a bunch of features that make it quite useful. Things like TraceQL is tremendously powerful for searching through your spans. The ability to generate metrics from your traces is fantastic to enable those cross-telemetry bridges. The main problem I have with it is that it uses its own storage engine. From what I've seen, that doesn't scale well beyond a few tens of thousands of traces per second. Maybe that's just a me problem. Jaeger on the other hand, can scale as you go, which is why we went for it at Cloudflare. It's storage system agnostic, so you can start with Elasticsearch and then graduate to ClickHouse if necessary. Which provides a much nicer scaling path, but at the cost of losing out on a bunch of features, a lot of which we ended up implementing in our own private fork as much as I wanted to open source them.
Which is really frustrating because that's the point of tracing, collecting large amounts of data and then being able to sift through it. I really think there's an opportunity here for Jaeger to improve or a new system to blossom, because the lack of a fully featured scalable tracing system is probably one of the biggest downsides of the open-source observability world. The VictoriaMetrics folks are cooking up VictoriaTraces, which might be a solution here. It uses the same columnar DB as their logs offering, so provides that necessary wide event storage, but it's a little too new and untested for me to consider at the moment. Even though the point is to collect large numbers of wide events, you can't collect everything, at least not without bankrupting yourself.
We should probably talk about sampling. There are two types of sampling we can consider here. One easy, one more complex, head sampling and tail sampling respectively. Head sampling is a no-brainer. Probabilistically determine whether or not we should keep a span or a trace. Where this gets messy is when we then try and reason about our traces afterwards. For example, if we're only keeping 10% of our spans, we have to remember to multiply every stat we generate from those by 10. If we then change that ratio, we have to remember when we changed that ratio and apply different multipliers at different times. The hack here, if you're doing head sampling is to embed the sampling rate into your spans itself, so your query engine at query time can do that multiplication in line, which is quite useful. In a proper columnar database, because those numbers don't change very often, they compress to basically nothing.
Tail sampling is where things get interesting and messy, to the point that I would actually recommend against tail sampling, unless you are starting to get into the types of issues that head sampling causes. Tail sampling adds a little bit more logic to the flipper coin and choose whether you accept a span or not. Instead, we put an if statement in the mix. If it's an error, sample it at this rate. If it's not an error, sample it at a different rate. Useful if your errors are being drowned out by the noise of all your successes, which is a nice problem. There's that complexity demon again. Tail sampling requires you to have somewhere to buffer a trace because you don't know until all the spans come in whether or not something is an error. It requires you to have that resource usage that comes with buffering things and complexity and hard decisions, like how long to buffer for, which there is no real answer to because it entirely depends on where all your spans are coming from, and how to shard your traces so that all the spans from one trace end up on the right nodes so you can make the decision with all the data is a giant mess. Generally, if you are trying to host your own tracing system, I would recommend against it unless you are hitting tens of thousands of spans per second level. If you are considering it though, all of those sampling decisions we just talked about have to happen somewhere and that somewhere is a telemetry pipeline.
One of the most annoying things about modern observability in general is that because it pushes you to higher cardinalities and higher rates of data, that implies higher processing, and that processing has to happen somewhere. Generally, it means you're running a collector of some kind that takes your telemetry, runs logic over it, transforms them, drops them, that sort of thing. In the old world of logs and metrics, we can get away with just shipping things to the backend. Not so much these days unless you want your budgets to run away from you. You need some sort of processor. Again, a few options here. OTel itself provides one, the OTel Collector written in Go. Grafana Alloy is similarly based off of the OTel Collector. Vector recently acquired by Datadog, so take what you will from that, but written in Rust. Again, it starts to get messy. I love the OTel project.
It's a great effort. The idea of standardizing all of your telemetry formats so you can move between providers is a noble one even if it doesn't work in practice. The OTel Collector is a bit of a mess. That's speaking as a contributor to it. Because it's run by the CNCF, there's a certain amount of bureaucracy involved. Because it's run by unpaid volunteers, even minor changes can take weeks. If you want timely changes, that requires you to fork internally and run your own builds of a collector. It's a real pain point if you actually want to manage one. I'm not sure, at least until the components start to get a bit more stabilized that I can recommend running it. You've got a lot of data, lots of it. Data isn't observability, like a warehouse full of unlabeled boxes isn't a library. A Grafana instance full of graphs that no one understands isn't a debugging tool.
UI - Tying It All Together
The last thing we need is something to tie it all together. Something that we can actually use to solve problems. Generally, that comes in the form of a UI, because fortunately AIs and APIs haven't taken over the world quite yet. Again, Grafana may seem like the optimal choice here, or perhaps the only choice, save for those individual UIs out there. I would present you with another, Perses. It's a CNCF project that is designed to try and be a bit more of a user friendly and open-source friendly version of Grafana. Grafana in particular has the annoying problem of being owned by a company, which unfortunately in our capitalist society means they have to make money, which I mean, fair dues, no problem with that. I acknowledge the realities of our society. In pursuit of less, they end up locking a bunch of features behind paying them money.
Features that are really useful for making a better observability system, like usage tracking on certain dashboards or proper data source permissions. Even when folks try and contribute those features open source upstream, they get shut down. It's a bit disappointing. On the other hand, Perses provides all those features along with a few others, like better support for automated dashboards and things like ephemeral dashboards, dashboards that disappear after a certain amount of time. Because I think that's actually something a lot of people get wrong with dashboarding in particular. I've seen Grafana instances with thousands of built-up dashboards, copies of copies of copies of minor things changed. Because Grafana locks down those features behind its paywall, then most self-hosting people are not going to pay. You can never be quite sure whether a dashboard is safe to delete. I think there's an interesting distinction to be made in your dashboarding about two different use cases.
You have your BI dashboards. The ones that tell product folks things that keep the business going. How many users are there? Your click-through rate for things. Even your SLOs are a BI dashboard to some extent. These tend to be much longer lasting because business metrics don't really change that much. Then you have debugging dashboards. These display things like service metrics, specific drill-downs on known failure modes, things like that. I hate these because they tend to just stick around despite the fact that when you're debugging a problem, it tends to be different each time. If they're not, that's another question to ask yourself. Why are you getting the same problem over and over again? I would encourage you if you're running a dashboarding solution to go and tag each of your dashboards with one of these two labels and then audit your debugging dashboards for deletion.
It'll make it so much easier to use, which brings me back to Perses. Ephemeral dashboards automate that whole process for you. No manual cleanup required. They can get automatically deleted after a certain amount of time. They can even be automatically created by your alerting tool via webhooks specifically for any firing alert. Once you've got everything flowing together, we have to have to start thinking about how all this data weaves together into a cohesive structure. That all stems from our correlation IDs or trace IDs, if you're doing tracing. You see, by embedding those into our metrics with exemplars into our canonical logs as a context field and into our traces, we start to get this neat flow where our telemetry data merges together. This becomes a typical flow. Your alert fires, you have a metric spike. You picked Prometheus, so you have an exemplar on that metric, a trace ID attached to an example request that triggered it.
You click through to Tempo or Jaeger, you're now in a trace. You can see exactly what service in your distributed system starts behaving. You can see what downstream calls it caused. Because you've instrumented canonical logs, each span has a corresponding single logline. If you put enough context into them, because we all love high context as we should, you can see exactly what failed where.
What About the Future?
What about the future? Because observability stacks do have one thing, multiple separate tools do kind of suck even though you can make them better by weaving them together. There's a lot of duplication when you have multiple different systems, because what you really have is metrics, logs, and traces. It's the same data with different granularities. Your logs are basically subsets of your traces, and your metrics are just counts and aggregations over them as well. Effectively, if your traces are good enough for the wide enough context, you don't actually need to generate the others in your application because you can synthesize them in your observability tool. It means that one instrumentation of your wide events just gives you the rest of the telemetry. There are starting to be tools that do this well. SigNoz for one does an ok job at being an all-in-one solution, although it suffers from the problem of doing everything fine and nothing great.
Your pipelining tools are starting to develop these features as well with OTel Collectors connector format, and vectors log to metric function to do similar. I think the key thing here is that logs and metrics aren't going away. They're just changing. I do see a future where in the open-source world, not just the SaaS world, you only have to instrument your applications once with these wide high-context events. From those, all your other types of telemetry are derived. Metrics for graphing and alerting, logging for debugging and tracing for locating problems, all just the one original source of data where the three pillars aren't gone, but they're instead pushed up the stack. In doing so all work in harmony on one grand observability canvas.
Questions and Answers
Liz Fong-Jones: You said that the state of open-source tracing tools is less mature than the other signals. Why do you think that is? What can people do to solve that problem?
Colin Douch: There's a lot of aspects to a good tracing tool and a lot of open-source projects do some of the things required. Open-source contributions are always welcome. The CNCF Jaeger project is tremendous. Please go contribute, if you're welcome to it. The other upcoming things like HyperDX from ClickHouse and things like that are also worth keeping an eye on because they are up and coming.
Liz Fong-Jones: I noticed you didn't mention the word AI anywhere in this talk. What thoughts might you have about how can AI help us build or run these telemetry systems?
Colin Douch: I have a lot of thoughts around, especially like SRE workloads and AI because what it amounts to for AI observability at the moment is chucking a bunch of traces into a context window and hoping that something gets spat out the other end. There's work to do in distilling information before it hits an AI agent. AI agents are very useful at summarizing information, but especially with wide high context events, that context window gets burned very quickly. There needs to be some intermediate layer that helps in the meantime.
Liz Fong-Jones: You're saying that I shouldn't just shove an MCP server directly on top of the logging API and have it spit out 500 kilobytes of logs?
Colin Douch: You're welcome to try, but I'd love to know how much hallucination is there.

articles.title: Cet airfryer cuit aussi à la vapeur, ça donne quoi ?
articles.text:
| Commodité d'emploi |  | 
| Dimensions (L x H x P) | 303 x 366 x 404 | 
| Capacité | 7 L | 
| Programmes de cuisson | Oui | 
| Cuisson |  | 
| Puissance | 1850 W | 
| Température min | 30 °C | 
| Température max | 230 °C | 
Avec un panier de 7 l et son réservoir d'eau, le Xiaomi Mijia Smart Steam Air Fryer associe air chaud et vapeur. De quoi varier les préparations dans une seule et même cuve. Nous avons confronté les modes proposés à nos sondes et quelques plats.
Xiaomi ajoute de l'eau à son airfryer. Le Mijia Smart Steam Air Fryer 7L conserve le panier à tiroir et le fonctionnement classique d'une friteuse sans huile, mais y associe un réservoir de 1,5 l dédié à la cuisson à la vapeur. Les deux méthodes peuvent être utilisées séparément ou combinées au sein d'un même programme, selon le résultat recherché et les préférences de cuisson.
L'appareil déploie une puissance de 1850 W pour la production de vapeur. 10 fonctions sont proposées, parmi lesquelles la friture à l'air, la cuisson vapeur, le mode combiné, la déshydratation, la fermentation ou encore le réchauffage. La température peut grimper jusqu'à 230 °C selon le programme sélectionné. Enfin, une connexion à l'app Xiaomi Home complète les commandes physiques, offrant l'accès à un catalogue de recettes et quelques réglages supplémentaires.
Le Mijia Smart Steam Air possède des dimensions de 30,3 cm de largeur, 40,4 cm de profondeur, 36,7 cm de hauteur et pèse 7,8 kg. Sa façade sombre accueille un bouton rotatif avec écran intégré et deux touches alimentation et retour.
Le tiroir offre une surface de cuisson de 400 cm² et une hauteur intérieure de 11,5 cm. Une plaque amovible prend place au fond et Xiaomi fournit une grille pour disposer les aliments sur deux niveaux. Toutefois, les deux étages restent soumis au même programme et, en l'absence de pieds sur la grille, l'espace inférieur est plutôt restreint.
Au-dessus de la cuve, nous retrouvons une résistance en spirale associée à la ventilation.
Le réservoir d'eau s'installe pour sa part sur le dessus de l'appareil. Son remplissage se fait par une petite trappe et sa position impose de garder un accès libre en hauteur.
La fenêtre permet de surveiller la coloration des aliments sans retirer le panier. L'éclairage intérieur facilite ce contrôle et s'active pendant une minute lorsqu'on manipule la molette ou une touche durant la cuisson. On peut ainsi vérifier l'avancée du repas sans laisser s'échapper la chaleur à chaque coup d'œil.
La molette est plutôt agréable à utiliser. On la tourne pour parcourir les fonctions ou modifier les réglages, puis on appuie pour valider. Il est possible d'ajuster les paramètres pendant la cuisson. La prise en main est très simple, mais le petit écran oblige à laisser certains intitulés défiler. Quelques centimètres supplémentaires auraient évité d'attendre la fin de la phrase pour savoir ce que l'appareil a à nous raconter.
Avant le premier repas, un passage par le nettoyage et la désodorisation est conseillé dans le mode d'emploi. Nous avons donc lavé le panier, puis lancé le programme prévu avec une tranche de citron. Une forte odeur de plastique s'est en effet dégagée pendant cette opération, mais elle a disparu lors de la cuisson suivante.
Le maintien au chaud automatique est appréciable lorsqu'on ne passe pas immédiatement à table. En revanche, aucun rappel de mélange n'est proposé. Cela semble volontaire de la part du fabricant qui évoque une “circulation d'air cyclonique à 360°”. Les écarts de température constatés plus loin ne semblent toutefois pas nous dispenser de cette tâche.
L'ajout dans Xiaomi Home passe par la détection de l'appareil, la sélection du réseau wifi et l'attribution d'une pièce. Le Mijia rejoint ainsi les autres équipements de la marque déjà présents dans l'application, sans nécessiter une app supplémentaire.
On y retrouve les différents modes avec des intitulés plus faciles à consulter que sur le petit écran de la façade. Les possibilités de commande restent toutefois limitées. Nous avons notamment pu sortir l'appareil de veille, mais le lancement de la cuisson doit être confirmé sur la machine pour des raisons de sécurité.
L'intérêt principal réside finalement dans les nombreuses idées de recettes, réparties par catégories et pouvant être placées en favoris. Xiaomi en annonce plus d'une centaine en ligne, de quoi trouver quelques pistes pour utiliser les fonctions autres que la friture à l'air. Les paramètres permettent aussi de choisir les notifications de fin de cuisson et de maintien au chaud.
Le panier et ses éléments amovibles se nettoient facilement à la main avec une éponge douce et du liquide vaisselle. Il faut en revanche renoncer au lave-vaisselle pour la cuve.
La fonction vapeur ajoute l'entretien du circuit d'eau. Xiaomi recommande une eau purifiée pour limiter les dépôts de calcaire et prévoit une fonction de nettoyage des tuyaux avec de l'acide citrique ou du vinaigre blanc, puis un rinçage à l'eau claire. Une fonction de séchage est également proposée pour limiter l'humidité résiduelle.
Comme d'habitude, nous avons installé trois sondes dans le panier, au centre et dans deux coins opposés, avant de lancer des cuissons à 160 et 200 °C. La montée en température est rapide puisque la première sonde atteint 160 °C en environ 1 min 30 s et 200 °C en quelque 2 min 35 s. La chauffe manque toutefois de régularité et d'homogénéité.
À 160 °C, la température moyenne au centre est respectée, contre 173,6 et 176,1 °C dans les coins. La courbe centrale est la plus régulière, tandis que les deux autres dessinent des cycles nettement plus marqués au gré des relances de la résistance. Les bords ont donc tendance à chauffer davantage que demandé.
À 200 °C, nous retrouvons le même comportement. Le centre reste assez proche de la cible, mais les deux coins atteignent respectivement 213,3 et 216,1 °C. Ces relevés nous invitent donc à mélanger ou déplacer les aliments pour limiter les différences de cuisson.
Nous avons essayé la cuisson vapeur seule avec des carottes, qui s'est montrée efficace, puis le programme combinant vapeur et air chaud. Pour ce second essai, nous avons placé du poulet et des carottes dans le même panier. Au final, les légumes étaient parfaitement cuits, mais le poulet manquait de croustillant.
Quelques minutes supplémentaires en mode Airfryer ont donc été nécessaires pour obtenir la finition souhaitée.
Nous avons ensuite utilisé le mode combiné avec des pommes de terre coupées façon potatoes. L'appareil semble réserver la phase à l'air chaud pour la fin du programme. Le résultat s'est révélé plutôt satisfaisant. Ceux qui préfèrent une croûte plus marquée pourront prolonger la cuisson à l'air chaud ou privilégier ce mode dès le départ.
L'ajout de la vapeur apporte donc une possibilité intéressante pour varier les préparations et adapter leur texture.
À 200 °C, nous avons mesuré 48 dB à 1 m de l'appareil. La ventilation reste audible, mais le niveau sonore est plutôt raisonnable pour un airfryer. En mode vapeur ou combiné, la pompe à eau fonctionne par intermittence et se fait aussi entendre.
Le Xiaomi Mijia Smart Steam Air Fryer 7L apporte une véritable polyvalence grâce à sa cuisson vapeur, utilisable seule ou associée à l'air chaud. La maîtrise des températures s'avère toutefois perfectible avec des bords de cuve plus chauds, qui imposent de mélanger malgré l'absence d'alarme de rappel. Nos préparations ont néanmoins donné des résultats très satisfaisants, quitte à ajuster le tir en changeant de mode en fin de cycle pour obtenir davantage de croustillant. Au final, cette machine peut mettre tout le monde d'accord en cuisine, qu'il s'agisse des inconditionnels de l'airfryer ou des amateurs de plats vapeur.
Le Nutribullet Crisplite Vision offre un panier plus généreux de 8 l, une large fenêtre éclairée et des commandes tactiles plus lisibles, avec une cuve compatible lave-vaisselle. De son côté, le Moulinex Easy Fry Infrared 7L se distingue par une meilleure homogénéité et une plus grande stabilité des températures, ainsi que par sa fonction Crispy pour accentuer la coloration des aliments en fin de cuisson.

articles.title: Motorola Razr 70 atinge 2º menor preço desde lançamento • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Motorola Razr 70 atinge 2º menor preço desde lançamento
Motorola Razr 70 (256 GB) com tela AMOLED flexível de 120 Hz e câmeras de 50 MP recebe desconto de 28% sobre o preço original, em oferta no Pix com cupom no Mercado Livre
O Razr 70 de 256 GB está saindo por R$ 4.299 no Pix com cupom HOJETECH no Mercado Livre. O novo dobrável da Motorola, com tela AMOLED flexível de 120 Hz e câmeras de 50 MP, atinge o 2º menor preço desde o lançamento com desconto de 28% sobre o original de R$ 5.999.
O Razr 70 é um dos melhores dobráveis do mercado, possuindo tela AMOLED interna flexível de 6,9″ com taxa de 120 Hz, brilho de até 3.000 nits e certificação Pantone com 100% do DCI-P3. Tal combinação entrega cores vibrantes, alta fluidez e visibilidade garantida. E seu formato compacto quando dobrado contribui para a portabilidade.
O kit principal de câmeras é formado por uma wide com OIS e uma ultrawide com ângulo de 122º, que captam belas imagens ao ar livre, ambas de 50 MP, enquanto a frontal de 32 MP tira ótimas selfies. Todas filmam em 4K.
O chip MediaTek Dimensity 7450X e os 8 GB de RAM física suportam a execução de apps pesados em multitarefa e funções da suíte Moto AI. Os 256 GB de armazenamento disponibilizam espaço interno adequado para guardar fotos e vídeos.
O corpo de alumínio com dobradiças de titânio do Razr 70 resiste a centenas de movimentos de abre-e-fecha, e é reforçado pela certificação IP48, que confere proteção em cenários como poeira moderada e mergulhos acidentais. O vidro Gorilla Glass Victus protege a tela externa contra pancadas e arranhões.
Sua bateria de 4.800 mAh resiste a até 36 horas de uso, segundo a fabricante. O suporte ao carregamento rápido de 30 W permite receber uma carga para um dia inteiro em 15 minutos, recurso ideal para quem não quer perder tempo com tomadas.
O Motorola Razr 70 de 256 GB (R$ 4.299 no Pix com cupom HOJETECH) será atualizado até o Android 19 e possui conectividade 5G, Wi-Fi 6E, Bluetooth 5.4 e NFC.
Aviso de ética: ao clicar em um link de afiliado, o preço não muda para você e recebemos uma comissão.

articles.title: Post-quantum cryptography: Dell secures the root of trust - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Dell brings post-quantum cryptography to the root of trust
Post-quantum cryptography is gaining urgency as attackers collect encrypted data they hope to decrypt later with quantum computers.
Stolen data is only part of the problem. A future quantum computer could also forge the signatures that tell a laptop or server its firmware is genuine, according to Rick Martinez (pictured, right), fellow and vice president of client solutions at Dell Technologies Inc. Code written by an attacker would then pass the same checks as code from the manufacturer.
“We think of this in terms of trust now, forge later,” Martinez said. “Instead of kind of attacking that confidentiality of encryption of data, these quantum computers will actually be able to attack the integrity of the actual system that runs everything from the bottom up.”
Martinez and Judy Furlong (center), senior distinguished engineer at Dell, spoke with theCUBE’s Krista Case (left) at the AI Cybersecurity and Resilience Summit, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how enterprises can protect firmware and storage as they transition to post-quantum cryptography. (* Disclosure below.)
Post-quantum cryptography starts at the first line of code
Dell has already made changes on the PC side. Dell Pro systems now use a post-quantum algorithm in the embedded controller, which is the first part of the system to fetch code at startup. The company has also moved to quantum-resistant hashing for its off-host BIOS checks, Martinez explained.
“We want to make sure that that verification algorithm that is baked into the system when you buy it already understands PQC — already uses the stronger resilient algorithms so that we can avoid that tamper opportunity for those future adversaries that may have quantum computers,” he said.
Storage is harder to secure because cryptography shows up at every layer. It runs through hardware and software and into the identity and intrusion-detection tools each array connects to, according to Furlong.
“We can’t say we’re done until every piece of the quantum vulnerable cryptography has actually been migrated to something that’s quantum resistant,” she said. “It’s going to occur over multiple releases and actually is heavily involved with our supply chain and the vendors, because we obviously have dependencies on when they’re going to have their particular components available and migrated to the post-quantum algorithms.”
Here’s the complete video interview, part of SiliconANGLE’s and theCUBE’s coverage of the AI Cybersecurity and Resilience Summit:

articles.title: Kodiak lands first commercial deal to supply driverless trucks for public highways | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Kodiak AI will deliver 75 self-driving trucks to freight company DTL Transport starting in 2028. It’s the company’s first binding commercial deal for driverless big rigs that will run on public highways.
The contract, announced Wednesday, comes just ahead of Kodiak’s next big milestone: pulling human safety operators out of the cab to begin operating a driverless highway service in December. The company, which went public in September 2025, plans to launch that service by carrying goods for Ikea on Interstate 45 between Dallas and Houston.
DTL Transport, a California mid-market trucking company that hauls fresh produce and goods to grocery chains, plans to use the self-driving trucks on multiple interstate highway routes, starting with Dallas to El Paso, Texas, and Interstate 20 between Dallas and Atlanta. Kodiak has already conducted testing and operations on those two routes.
“One of the things that we love about mid-market carriers (like DTL) is that they are able to move with fast execution speed, much more at the speed of a startup or a small company or a tech company like Kodiak, and that they just want to get stuff done,” Kodiak founder and CEO Don Burnette told TechCrunch in an exclusive interview. “It’s easier for them to integrate into their fleet because they’re not as large, and we think that this is a real turning point for the self-driving industry in general.”
The contract should give Kodiak a revenue boost and a positive benchmark. Its shares have fallen 87% from their opening-day price. It also puts Kodiak on a path to become an “asset-light” technology supplier, meaning it would sell its technology rather than own and run trucks itself — a goal it shares with competitor Aurora Innovation.
Today, Kodiak has a number of customers under a Trucking-as-a-Service (TaaS) model, including Charger USA, Roehl Transport, and Werner Enterprises. Under this business model, Kodiak owns and operates the self-driving trucks as a third-party carrier on behalf of other companies. It currently carries freight for these companies on a few routes in Texas. Kodiak generates revenue carrying freight daily for these companies on three active routes, but Burnette described these operations as still being in pilot stage.
Ultimately, Kodiak wants to move to a Driver-as-a-Service (DaaS) model, in which customers own and operate the trucks. Kodiak licenses its technology, charging customers by the mile for the duration of the contract. DTL is Kodiak’s first on-highway DaaS customer, a relationship that was forged during a pilot program last month in California. In that pilot, Kodiak autonomously hauled perishable goods for DTL about 225 miles along Interstate 5 and California State Route 99 between Fresno, California, and Los Angeles, with a human safety operator behind the wheel.
“You have to prove out the technology first using your own truck, show them that it works, show them that it’s safe, show them that it integrates,” Burnette said, describing the Trucking-as-a-Service model. “And then we want to be asset light. We don’t want to be in the business of running a trucking company.”
Atlas Energy Solutions has been a Driver-as-a-Service customer since 2024. Technically, Atlas was Kodiak’s first customer under a binding commercial contract, but its driverless trucks operate in off-road settings in West Texas’ remote Permian Basin. Atlas currently owns and operates 35 driverless trucks equipped with Kodiak’s self-driving system. Burnette said Kodiak is on track to have as many as 100 in service there by mid-2027.
Kodiak didn’t reveal the value of the deal with DTL Transport. However, its public 2025 investor presentation offers some clues about the contract’s potential value.
In that document, Kodiak forecast annual recurring revenue of $150,000 to $190,000 per truck. That forecast rests on several assumptions, including a per-mile licensing fee of about $0.97 (in line with current human driver costs per mile), annual mileage of about 225,000 miles a year per truck, and other factors.
Assuming those projections bear out, the deal with DTL Transport could generate at least about $11.2 million in annual recurring revenue once all 75 trucks are delivered.

articles.title: ‘The open-ear market has a strong new contender’: Sennheiser’s first clip-style open earbuds are a surprisingly solid first attempt, but they're not perfect
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
Sennheiser’s Accentum Clip have their quirks — some connectivity issues I hadn’t expected, oddly-placed touch controls, and a slightly more noticeable fit than some other cuff-style buds — but they’re a great clip-on debut from the brand and one I’d recommend for a few key reasons. Firstly, they deliver when it comes to Sennheiser’s natural sound profile, especially at moderate volume, where there’s a good amount of bass and clarity. They’ve also got a neat battery protection feature, LDAC support, and a great value price. There’s so much competition in this area that there are still cheaper options I’d suggest over them, but they’re a highly impressive entrant into the open-ear category for Sennheiser.
Reasons to buy
- + Excellent natural sound signature
- + Useful battery protection feature
- + Great for situational awareness
Reasons to avoid
- - A couple of wireless connectivity and multipoint issues
- - Touch controls are easy to accidentally activate
- - Cheaper alternatives available in a crowded market
Why you can trust TechRadar
We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test.
Sennhesier Accentum Clip: two-minute review
Clip-on (or cuff-style) examples in our best open earbuds guide once felt like a niche trend alongside the more sensible shape — the one that arcs behind your ear. But these ear cuff-esque offerings may now be the next major personal audio craze.
The first ones to hit were Huawei’s FreeClip, and they were followed soon after by the premium Bose Ultra Open Earbuds. That was in early 2024, and they’re still among the best options you can buy today.
These days, everyone from Soundcore and Shokz to Earfun and Sony offers a clip-on set of buds, made to attach to the back of your ears and direct audio with tiny speakers pointing to your ear canals. They’re good for hearing everything around you at the same time as your music, and Sennheiser has just got in on the action with its Accentum Clip, available in Black and Cream colors.
The naming of Accentum (as opposed to Momentum) means they’re part of Sennheiser’s more affordable range, but they still promise the brand’s well-known rich and natural sound. The press release for the new buds says that “the growing demand for truly open earbuds has come with sonic compromises” and that these buck that trend by offering “brilliant Sennheiser sound in every situation”.
But we’ve also been here before with the cheap and slightly disappointing Sennheiser Accentum Open. I was keen to try the Accentum Clip and hoped they improved upon the previous attempt.
The good news is that these offer great performance in most of the areas that matter. Once you get a comfortable fit (which I found a tiny bit more challenging than usual), they deliver a clean and accurate sound. You have to be careful with volume levels, as too much volume introduces distortion, but they’re overall pretty delightful-sounding for this category.
And they’ve got excellent battery life, although I did encounter a couple of connection and multipoint quirks. Rivals from Shokz beat these on comfort and weight, while Soundcore undercuts them in the price department. That said, I still reckon they’re some of the best-sounding clip-ons I’ve heard, and that is important in a congested market.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
The bad news? If you’re in the US, you seemingly can’t buy these at launch. They could be coming at a later date, but for now, US buyers will have to look at other clip-on contenders. As to why, Sennheiser told prospective buyers that it’s a "strategic decision based on the legal environment”, in a comment on Reddit. But decisions can be rethought, can't they…
Sennheiser Accentum Clip review: Specifications
| Component | Value | 
| Water resistance | IP54 | 
| Battery life | 9 hours; 36 hours with case | 
| Bluetooth type | Bluetooth 6.0 | 
| Weight | 6.8g per earbud | 
| Driver | 12mm dynamic | 
Sennheiser Accentum Clip: Price and release date
- Launched on July 23, 2026
- Sells for £149 / AU$289 (around $180, although not officially available yet)
- Sennheiser’s first-ever clip-on buds
The Sennheiser Accentum Clip went on sale on July 23, 2026, after being announced almost a month earlier, on June 18. While they’re Sennheiser's first-ever challenger in the clip format, the brand previously tried its hand at a “semi-open” AirPods-style with the Accentum Open, which lacked app support and had flimsy build quality.
You can buy the Accentum Clip for £149 / AU$289. That puts them firmly in the middle of the pack for this style of earbuds. You can get the Soundcore AeroClip or new Shokz OpenDots Air for a competitive $129 / £129.99 / AU$219, or increase your budget to get the Bose Ultra Open Earbuds for $299 / £299 / AU$449.95.
Another top pick, the Shokz OpenDots 2, costs $199.95 / £179.99 / AU$339, while budget contenders like the EarFun Clip 2 set you back as little as $79.99 / £69.99 (about AU$120).
So, stiff competition — and Sennheiser's come in at a busy time.
Sennheiser Accentum Clip review: Features
- 9 hours of playback on a charge; 36 hours with the charging case
- 5-band graphic equaliser in the Sennheiser Smart Control Plus app
- LDAC support and a battery protection mode to enhance longevity
The Sennheiser Accentum Clip are easy to set up and customise, and they support the Sennheiser Smart Control Plus app, which is one of the best companion apps in the business.
Right after adding them to the app, I was able to do a firmware update, turn on battery protection (more on that in a moment), Bluetooth multipoint, and customise the default touch controls. Here, you can also enable “advanced sound quality”, which turns on the buds’ LDAC capabilities.
As they’re open earbuds, you’re not getting any noise-cancellation (very few buds like this offer it, although the Shokz Openfit Pro and Honor Earbuds Open are two that do), which would draw more battery, so the promised battery life is 9 hours of listening, which extends to up to 36 hours when you factor in recharging via the case.
I checked battery life after three hours of continuous playback and they'd dropped by 40%, indicating a respectable 7.5 to 8 hours of total playtime at 50% volume. That's not quite Sennheiser's official figure, but still a solid real-world showing for open-ear buds — matching rivals like the Bose Ultra Open and Huawei FreeClip.
There’s not a long list of features here, although I do think they nail the basics. The battery protection mode, which makes them charge more slowly and prevents them from charging to 100%, is a fantastic feature to increase the longevity of your earphones. It reduces stress on battery cells and means you could vastly improve their lifespan.
There’s a 5-band EQ for tinkering with the sound, the ability to turn on the high-res LDAC codec and connection management. I’ll talk more about sound in a separate section, but it’s worth saying that one of my few disappointments here was with connectivity. Multipoint just didn’t really work effectively.
It connected to two devices, but audio would restart on the wrong device when pausing and playing again, or sound wouldn’t come out when watching some Instagram Reels. With multipoint off, you also can’t “pull” the connection from one device to another like you can on others. You have to manually disconnect and reconnect. These were all unexpected flaws for buds running Bluetooth 6.0, and hopefully will be fixed via firmware.
- Features score: 4 / 5
Sennheiser Accentum Clip review: design
- Comfort takes a little getting used to
- As do the touch controls…
- IP54 dust- and splash-resistant
Most cuff-style buds look pretty similar, but there are some notable deviations from the formula in Sennheiser’s design. They’re a little heavier than some rivals, at 6.8g per bud, and a little more of that mass is at the back, where the battery is held in the part that clips behind your ear.
In use, this makes them “pinch” ever so slightly more than some comparable rivals, and it’s essential to find the right position to angle the driver to fire audio into your ears. Get it slightly wrong, and you’ll have a less-engaging sound.
The stretchy part is a little chunkier than on some rivals, too, which may also affect how they feel to wear. I was able to get them sitting comfortably, but it takes a little trial-and-error.
Once they were on, the other big difference I noticed is that they use touch controls at the front of the buds (on the speaker part) rather than at the back on the battery container. This, unfortunately, does mean several more accidental taps. But, luckily, you can tweak and turn off capacitive control in the app.
They’re IP54-rated, so they can survive dust and light splashes, and they go in a fairly compact and discreet charging case with the Sennheiser logo on the top. I like that the case stands upright on a tabletop, and it’s small enough to be pocketable.
They’re just in white or black shades, and the plastic of the buds and case doesn’t feel quite as premium as Sennheiser’s flagship true wireless pair; but this is the Accentum line, so that isn’t a huge shock.
- Design score: 3.5 / 5
Sennheiser Accentum Clip review: Sound quality
- Natural, warm Sennheiser sound
- Best suited for indoor listening
- They have LDAC support, but it doesn’t make a difference
Open earbuds always have to make a couple of compromises to bring you audio while maintaining your awareness of the outside world. Keeping your ear canals unplugged means you don’t have the acoustic seal required for deep low frequencies, for example.
That said, Sennheiser has managed to bring much of its natural and balanced sound signature across to the Accentum Clip, and these offer a pleasant, warm listen. Vocals and instrumentation sound as I expected, and there’s none of the harshness or hollowness I’ve heard on some cheaper clip-ons.
Across a wide range of listening (including ambient focus playlists, the new Myles Smith album, summer pop playlists, and Michael Giacchino’s Spider-Man: Brand New Day soundtrack), I found the 12mm drivers deliver impressive clarity and refinement. At moderate listening levels (up to about 70%) I felt they had a good bass presence with a bit of weight to kick drums.
But, crank the volume up and it does change things a bit. I’d definitely prefer to use these in quieter indoor environments over the busy outdoors, because increasing the volume introduces distortion, takes some of the texture out of the bass, while fine details end up getting a bit lost.
Audiophiles will be happy to see that the Accentum Clip support the high-res LDAC codec, alongside standard AAC and SBC. In use, though, I couldn't detect any meaningful audible difference when switching between streaming via LDAC on a Google Pixel 10 Pro and AAC on an iPhone 17 Pro. High-res support is great, but it doesn’t make an obvious difference in this product and using LDAC will probably just burn through your battery life a little quicker.
- Sound score: 4 / 5
Sennheiser Accentum Clip review: Value
- Great value compared to Sennheiser’s last 'open' pair
- But they’re undercut by quite a few other cuff buds
While the Sennheiser Accentum Clip are a good pair of clip-on buds, you’re paying mid-range money for a pair that feels ever so slightly below-mid-range, given how many elements are evidently a “first try” at this form factor.
I like them for sound quality, but because I found comfort, control and connectivity a little less convincing, I think there are cheaper rivals with better features.
When compared to Sennheiser’s last open earbuds attempt, the Accentum Open, these are a far better value proposition because they include app support and features like battery protection, control customisation, and LDAC.
But if compared to the rest of the open bud market, there are serious challengers available at lower prices from the likes of Shokz, Earfun, Soundcore, CMF by Nothing and Soundpeats.
- Value score: 4 / 5
Should I buy the Sennheiser Accentum Clip?
Score card
| Features | Solid battery performance, useful battery protection, and extensive app controls (including EQ and customizable touch gestures) make for a strong feature set. | 4 | 
| Design | Cuff-style clip with an IP54 build, though the touch controls are prone to accidental taps. The fit does also feel slightly heavier than some rivals. | 3.5 | 
| Sound quality | Impressively warm and natural at moderate volumes, though bass and detail fall off when pushed louder. | 4 | 
| Value | More affordable than flagships like the Bose Ultra Open, offering great audio and features for the price despite having several cheaper rivals. | 4 | 
Buy them if…
You need Sennheiser sound in the clip-style
At moderate volume, I loved the sound on offer from the Sennheiser Accentum Clip — they’re detailed, warm, and engaging.
You need LDAC support
LDAC is extremely rare for the open clip-on category; even the major players stick to the basic codecs, and while I can’t say it made the biggest difference in sound, some high-res purists will appreciate its presence.
You want to hold onto them for a very long time
That battery preservation feature is a big deal — controlling how fast they charge and setting a charge limit could double or triple how long they last compared to others.
Don’t buy them if…
You need a fuss-free fit
An ever-so-slightly chunkier build (for this category) meant I needed a few attempts to get the right fit, and that can be frustrating with the oddly-placed touch control panel.
You’re on a tight budget
This may be a lower price for Sennheiser, but there’s healthy competition among open buds, and these aren’t quite among the best budget options.
You’d like to use multipoint
While it may be fixed in a firmware update, I can’t pretend the multipoint issues aren’t a strange issue and one I wouldn’t have expected in 2026 from buds at this price — especially a pair with Bluetooth 6.0.
Sennheiser Accentum Clip review: Also consider
EarFun Clip 2
These prove you don’t need to spend loads of money to get comfortable, secure clip-on open earbuds that actually sound good. While the cheap build reflects the budget price tag, the inclusion of LDAC, an impressive 11-hour battery life, and IP55 water resistance make them a great entry point for those new to open earbuds.
Read our full EarFun Clip 2 review
Bose Ultra Open Earbuds
It's been two years since they launched, and the Bose Ultra Open Earbuds are still a benchmark for open-ears, delivering rich sound and Bose’s immersive audio while keeping your spatial awareness intact. They're undeniably expensive, but the featherlight cuff design is so comfortable and surprisingly secure that I often forget I'm wearing them.
Read our full Bose Ultra Open Earbuds review 
How I tested the Sennheiser Accentum Clip
- Tested for two weeks
- Paired with Android, iOS and macOS devices
- Used during multiple activities
I tested the Sennheiser Accentum Clip over two weeks, pairing them with my iPhone 17 Pro, MacBook Air, and Google Pixel 10 Pro, which allowed me to thoroughly test multipoint connectivity and LDAC support.
I wore them mostly at home while working, cooking, and during full-day listening sessions, as well as outside on walks in the park. I used them to play a wide variety of media, including music of several genres, podcasts, and YouTube videos.
I also ran a battery test on these to see if the real-world performance lived up to the claims.
I've been testing gadgets since 2020, and I've reviewed countless headphones and earbuds, including dozens of open-style models from brands like Shokz, Nothing, Soundcore, Bose and Huawei.
Read more about how we test at TechRadar
- First reviewed: October 2026

With over a decade of experience, Simon has written for several major titles, including Esquire, Digital Spy, Shortlist, and Men’s Health. He specializes in testing out the latest gadgets, and has reviewed smartphones, headphones, speakers, e-readers, and much more.
