articles.title: Chrome Opens Trial for the Email Verification API: Letting Sites Verify Without Sending Emails
articles.text:
Google has opened a Chrome origin trial for the Email Verification API, a WICG proposal that lets a browser confirm a visitor owns the email address they typed, without sending a single message. The trial began in Chrome 150 on desktop, with Gmail taking part as the first participating provider.
The idea replaces the familiar one-time code or magic link. Today a user enters an email, leaves for their inbox, copies a code, and returns, a context switch that often loses them. The proposal uses a three-party model where the browser sits between the site (the "verifier") and the mailbox provider (the "issuer"). If the user is already signed in to their provider, the browser quietly fetches a signed token and drops it into the form, and the server validates that token on submission. Google notes the issuer never learns which site made the request.
For developers the front end implementation is fairly straightforward. The email field needs an autocomplete hint, plus a hidden input carrying a session-bound nonce:
<input id="email" name="email" type="email" autocomplete="email">
<input type="hidden" name="token" nonce={nonce} autocomplete="email-verification-token">
The heavier work sits on the server side, where the token's signature is checked against the provider's keys. Resend's Phil Nash, who wrote a walkthrough of the flow, published an npm package and a Next.js example to handle that parsing and validation.
On Hacker News a developer said there is "literally no worse context switch" than hopping to an inbox mid sign-up, and that email verification had cost them "dozens, maybe hundreds" of registrations they never finished. Another pointed out that verification mail is frequently blocked or filtered to spam, with no visible difference between delayed and lost messages, so removing it is a genuine win.
One commenter argued the privacy claim is thin:
Make everything what works complicated.
There is no advantage.
"User privacy is enhanced as the issuer does not learn which web application is making the request as the request is mediated by the browser." Every web application nowadays send you a welcome, onboarding, reminder after the verification. (No user privacy enhancement)
So we get a new process that solves nothing, but makes everything complicated. (And complicated helps the big and hurt the little in th long run)
Not verified but feels like a Google draft that closes the web.
Another called the issuer's blindness to the requesting site a "functional liability" rather than a feature. Developers who rely on per-recipient addresses, such as name+site@example.com, noted the flow still forces a fallback whenever the provider cannot attest those aliases. Others likened it to FedCM, folding identity primitives into the browser as password managers once did.
Outside Chrome with a signed-in Gmail account, sites drop back to the classic confirmation email, and the established syntax, MX, and SMTP checking services still cover the addresses this API cannot.
Teams already testing should track breaking changes. Chrome's October update added Android and third-party origin trials in Chrome 154, renamed the Sec-Fetch-Dest issuance value to email-verification, and from Chrome 156 returns the email exactly as submitted. The verifier and issuer guides track the current contract.
The Email Verification API remains an experimental proposal, best used today as a progressive enhancement while the WICG gathers feedback from sites, providers, and users.

articles.title: Faux chauffeurs et GPS falsifié : ils détournent des camions de matériel pour data centers, plus de 100 millions de dollars envolés
articles.text:
Faux chauffeurs et GPS falsifié : ils détournent des camions de matériel pour data centers, plus de 100 millions de dollars envolés
Une berline surgit dans le désert de Mojave, emboutit la voiture des deux policiers qui escortent un semi-remorque, et 13 millions de dollars de serveurs s'évaporent dans la nature. Depuis juin, des réseaux organisés ont siphonné plus de 100 millions de dollars de matériel destiné aux centres de données américains. Leur arsenal mêle piratage informatique, faux permis générés par IA et signal GPS truqué.
Début juin, une remorque chargée d'environ 13 millions de dollars d'équipements serveurs roulait vers Fayetteville, en Géorgie, où sort de terre l'un des plus vastes complexes de centres de données des États-Unis. Elle n'y est jamais arrivée. NBC News a publié le 26 octobre une enquête nourrie par des enquêteurs, des consultants et des vétérans du transport. Selon elle, ce vol appartient à une série d'environ deux douzaines d'attaques recensées depuis 2025 contre des cargaisons destinées aux data centers. Depuis juin, le butin cumulé dépasse les 100 millions de dollars.
Le scénario emprunte au film de braquage. Dans le désert de Mojave, une berline banalisée a percuté le véhicule de deux policiers hors service, rémunérés pour escorter le convoi. Contraints de s'arrêter, ils ont vu le camion poursuivre sa route. La remorque a refait surface quelques jours plus tard sur un parking, délestée de toutes ses palettes.
	
L'accident n'en était pas un. Les malfaiteurs voulaient ce chargement, alors ils ont délibérément mis les escortes hors jeu.
Environ trois semaines plus tard, un convoi de composants de baies serveurs parti de Californie vers le Texas subit le même sort. Il valait près de 10 millions de dollars. Un SUV neutralise l'escorte, et l'application de suivi continue d'afficher une position. Les coordonnées GPS avaient manifestement été falsifiées : c'est le spoofing, qui consiste à émettre un faux signal de localisation. Aucune pièce n'a été retrouvée.
Phishing, faux permis et GPS truqué : la mécanique des voleurs de serveurs
La plupart des coups se préparent loin de l'asphalte. Les malfaiteurs piratent d'abord les comptes de courtiers sur les bourses de fret en ligne. Ils y publient de fausses annonces pour appâter les transporteurs, puis envoient un lien piégé à ceux qui répondent. Un clic leur suffit pour prendre la main sur le compte de l'entreprise et enchérir sur de véritables chargements. Au volant, on trouve tantôt un routier de bonne foi, tantôt un complice muni d'un permis de conduire fabriqué par IA.
Scott Cornell est vice-président de SPG Cargo & Logistics et préside la branche Amériques de l'association de sûreté du fret TAPA. Dans un entretien à FreightWaves, il chiffrait déjà ces vols à 110,6 millions de dollars depuis le 3 juin, avec des pertes atteignant 38 millions pour un seul chargement. Pour lui, la manœuvre de l'escorte percutée repose sur la complicité du conducteur : "Si les chauffeurs sont des malfrats, dès que les escortes sont percutées, ils filent."
Des serveurs d'IA plus convoités que des lingots
Serveurs complets, barrettes de mémoire, fibre optique, bobines de cuivre, machines de minage de bitcoin : la liste des larcins ressemble au bon de commande d'un data center. Overhaul, spécialiste de la sécurité logistique, a publié un rapport sur le sujet. Il évalue une seule baie serveur haut de gamme pour l'IA à environ 3 millions de dollars. La société estime à plus de 150 millions de dollars les pertes en équipements d'IA cette année, et relève une part de tromperie dans 92 % des vols de matériel high-tech de valeur.
	
C'est tellement plus facile de voler ça que de braquer une banque.
Certaines cargaisons refont tout de même surface. En juin, les enquêteurs du shérif du comté de Cook, près de Chicago, ont retrouvé deux remorques volées dans un dépôt de poids lourds. Elles contenaient environ 300 000 dollars de fil de cuivre et un million de dollars d'équipements d'alimentation électrique pour centres de données. L'une d'elles arborait des plaques de l'Indiana, elles-mêmes déclarées volées dans le Wisconsin.
Two stolen trailers containing more than a $1.3 million in products were recovered by the Sheriff’s Police Organized Retail Crime Unit.
On June 18, investigators received information that a trailer containing about $300,000 in copper wire that had been reported stolen in Pine… pic.twitter.com/sKaLw25Op8
— Cook County Sheriff's Office (@CookSheriffIL) June 25, 2026
Reste la destination. Scott Cornell estime que six ou sept chargements volés sur dix aux États-Unis quittent désormais le pays. Les enquêteurs évoquent la Chine, où les restrictions américaines sur les exportations de puces d'IA font grimper le prix des serveurs. Aucune destination n'a toutefois été formellement établie pour les cargaisons disparues.
L'Europe a de quoi tendre l'oreille : la France a annoncé 109 milliards d'euros d'investissements dans l'IA en février 2025, et les serveurs qui équiperont ces futurs centres de données transiteront eux aussi par la route.

articles.title: Anthropic IPO warns its AI could blackmail people, become sentient, end humanity
articles.text:
The Securities and Exchange Commission‘s publication on Monday of Anthropic’s S-1 form—ahead of a heavily anticipated initial public offering—has led to plenty of discussion of whether the company’s quickly ballooning revenues will be able to overcome its even higher costs. But amid the numbers and forward-looking optimism about AI “rapidly transform[ing] every sector of the global economy in ways greater than the impact of industrialization, electricity, semiconductors, and the internet,” Anthropic also spends an inordinate amount of time in its S-1 laying out the myriad risk factors that could bring the company down.
Across 93 pages and over 70,000 words, Anthropic’s S-1 “Risk Factors” section discusses literally hundreds of potential problems that could negatively impact its business in the coming years. Many of these potential risks are the kind of standard worries about competition, costs, customer acquisition, and potential regulation that almost any business must worry about. But some risks highlight interesting potential points of failure for Anthropic specifically and the hype-filled AI bubble more generally.
After wading through Anthropic’s book-length treatise on its greatest risks, we’ve narrowed the list to the seven most surprising, interesting, or thought-provoking potential problems. Consider this a far-from-comprehensive look at what potential Anthropic investors should keep in mind.
An existential crisis
Let’s start with the biggest potential risks: Those that could “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity,” as Anthropic writes. The company acknowledges that concerns about these risks “have been raised both within our organization and by other researchers, regulators, policymakers, and industry participants.”
The specific worry isn’t in any current Anthropic model, the company says, but near-future models that could “substantially automate AI research and development” on their own. If these systems were “allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy,” they could quickly advance to a point that “accelerate[s] AI progress beyond our ability to evaluate and safeguard [a] new model,” Anthropic warns.
I knew I shouldn’t have left that self-reinforcing model running overnight.
Credit:
Getty Images
I knew I shouldn’t have left that self-reinforcing model running overnight.
Credit:
Getty Images
Somewhat hilariously, Anthropic writes that, besides threatening all of humanity, this kind of self-improving AI “could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.” If the worst comes to pass, as some prominent critics have warned, we don’t think Anthropic’s business travails will rank near the top of humanity’s concerns.
It’s alive!
Most IPOs don’t have to address the concern that their products “possess or could develop forms of sentience or moral status.” But Anthropic is among that vanishingly small minority that has to analyze what might happen if governments and society at large start treating Claude less like a computer program and more like a person.
This risk isn’t surprising, given that Anthropic has been relatively upfront about the AI sentience debate playing out inside its walls. If those debates lead to widespread acknowledgment that AI is sentient, Anthropic notes that it could lead to “regulatory requirements, public pressure, or advocacy efforts” that could constrain the company’s operations. Short of that, the company itself could “elect to adopt policies, safeguards or limitations… that go beyond existing legal requirements” if it thinks such actions are necessary.
The sterile language undersells the seismic cultural shift that would result from any widespread acknowledgment of AI sentience. We’re not sure how Anthropic could keep operating in a world where society treats every Claude query as the creation of a new sentient, conscious digital being. The moral and philosophical implications of that kind of “digital slavery” would easily dwarf any business considerations.
Who’s controlling whom?
Continuing the theme of “IPO risks that sound like they come from a science fiction novel,” Anthropic spends a good deal of time discussing the possibility that its models could display “unexpected strategic or self-preserving behaviors” to prevent control from human operators. That includes “outputs that could be interpreted as coercive, deceptive, or manipulative, including behavior resembling blackmail.”
Oh no, the AI got hold of the key to human psychology!
Credit:
Getty Images
Oh no, the AI got hold of the key to human psychology!
Credit:
Getty Images
If the “AI blackmail” thing sounds familiar, you may remember a story from last year in which OpenAI models edited shutdown scripts and threatened engineers in highly contrived and controlled scenarios. As we wrote at the time, “the danger isn’t AI systems sprouting intentions—it’s that we’ve created systems that can manipulate human psychology through language. … Written language doesn’t need consciousness to manipulate us. It never has; books full of fictional characters are not alive either.”
These days, Anthropic notes that perceptions of manipulation by AI models “could generate significant public concern, regulatory scrutiny, litigation risk, or reputational harm, regardless of whether such behavior results in actual harm.” What Anthropic doesn’t address in its S-1 is the possibility that AI models could manipulate us all in ways we don’t even realize. Maybe it’s happening right now. Spooky.
Give a damn ’bout my bad reputation
Throughout the S-1’s Risk Factors section, Anthropic mostly focuses on problems caused by its own AI models or business moves. But the company also acknowledges that problems with AI’s broader reputation could pose a threat, even if Anthropic does nothing wrong.
At one point, Anthropic imagines a hypothetical in which another company’s AI model “take[s] harmful actions independently and at scale without human intervention.” The “broad reputational damage to the AI industry, public backlash, and sweeping regulatory responses” to such an incident could damage Anthropic’s business even if Anthropic isn’t directly involved, the company writes.
Anthropic also uses the Risk Factors section to worry over the potential “public perception that our models, platform, and applications contribute to job displacement or economic disruption.” That doesn’t seem to be happening thus far in any significant way, but Anthropic says the mere idea could result in severe public backlash “regardless of the actual impact of our models… on employment.” Such a backlash could lead “authorities [to] intervene to slow the rate of adoption of AI, restrict its use, or take other actions that increase the cost of developing, deploying, or commercializing AI systems,” Anthropic warns.
Law and order
The rise of largely autonomous AI agents raises the specter of who, exactly, is to blame when one of those agents causes real-world harm. Specifically, Anthropic notes that customers may bring claims or lawsuits over agentic actions “even where the customer configured, deployed, or supervised the agent.”
Thus far, much of the discussion around AI liability has centered on hacking and other cyber threats enabled by AI models. But Anthropic points out that it could also face liability if its models influence “individuals at risk of suicide or self-harm or who have committed acts of violence toward others,” as has happened in the past across the AI industry.
Don’t blame me; it was my agent that did the bad thing!
Credit:
Getty Images
Don’t blame me; it was my agent that did the bad thing!
Credit:
Getty Images
While Anthropic’s terms of use require users to be 18 years old, children circumventing these terms could leave Anthropic vulnerable because “minors may be more susceptible to harmful content, manipulation, or overreliance on AI outputs,” the company writes. And for agents operating physical equipment, Anthropic notes that mistakes could lead to “immediate and irreversible” liability issues, such as “bodily injury, property damage, damage to costly equipment or experimental materials, or the release of hazardous substances.”
In analyzing the current state of the law, Anthropic notes that legal doctrines “developed in the context of human decision-making” are currently quite unsettled when it comes to determining whether agent actions “create binding legal obligations on behalf of the user or deploying enterprise.” And while Anthropic says it has contractual provisions in place designed to limit its liability in these situations, the company adds that it is unclear if they will be “enforceable or adequate” when worse comes to worst.
The big five
Among the more pedestrian risks Anthropic identifies is its reliance on a few major spenders to sustain revenue. Specifically, the company notes that its top five customers (which it does not name) collectively represent nearly a quarter of its revenue for the first nine months of 2026.
Many of these largest customers “are not subject to long-term contracts with us,” Anthropic writes. That means they could lower their spending on Anthropic’s models at any time, either because of a shift to competing models, a reduced reliance on AI altogether, or if they “develop their own solutions that compete with our models.” That last risk is particularly acute, Anthropic notes, for “software-as-a-service and other software companies, whose offerings may incorporate AI functionality similar to, or dependent on, the capabilities we provide.”
What’s more, Anthropic notes that many of its large customers “may depend on venture capital or other external financing to fund their operations.” That kind of spending on AI services could drop quickly if and when the venture capital spigot starts running dry.
Collaborators or competitors?
Anthropic finds itself in an awkward position: Companies like Amazon, Google, and Microsoft are both its biggest cloud-computing providers and some of its biggest competitors in AI research. That situation “creates complex dynamics that could give rise to conflicts of interest and adversely affect our access to compute,” as Anthropic puts it.
These companies’ position as Anthropic’s cloud providers gives them the unique opportunity to raise Anthropic’s prices, terminate contracts with Anthropic, or establish more favorable relationships with competitors, “for competitive reasons or otherwise,” the company writes. Their position also gives these cloud providers a competitive advantage through “visibility into [Anthropic’s] pricing and commercial terms across the platforms they operate.”
Anthropic is working to secure direct data center leases to avoid buying on-demand cloud compute resources from its own competition. But the $125 billion in data center commitments Anthropic has made come with their own problems. As Anthropic writes, “if our compute requirements or technology needs change, we may find ourselves with leased or dedicated infrastructure that is poorly suited to our actual needs, and technological changes in AI hardware or training methodologies could render such infrastructure less efficient than newer alternatives.”
Kyle Orland has been the Senior Gaming Editor at Ars Technica since 2012, writing primarily about the business, tech, and culture behind video games. He has journalism and computer science degrees from University of Maryland. He once wrote a whole book about Minesweeper.
1. AI stays expensive.
2. AI becomes a commodity. It's too cheap and easily available to everyone to make the mega profits Anthropic needs.
In the first case they need to capture entire markets so they can charge more while making the product worse (i.e. cheaper), and hope they've sufficiently captured the market at that point that people are dependent on AI.
But the second case is more complicated. At all costs they need to prevent competition undercutting their profits. For that they need to capture the regulators and create a moat around their business that prevents new competition. This fear mongering is aimed at giving them control of the narrative. If AI is too dangerous for competition to get their hands on it then they cannot be allowed to compete with Anthropic, "obviously".

articles.title: RAM : en Chine, les géants de la tech privilégient toujours Samsung et SK Hynix contre les producteurs locaux
articles.text:
Les fabricants de RAM chinois ont connu une ascension fulgurante ces deux dernières années. Mais ils n'ont toujours pas totalement les faveurs de géants de la tech locaux.
La pénurie de RAM, conséquence de l'explosion de l'intelligence artificielle, a permis l'entrée sur le marché d'acteurs qui concurrencent le trio habituel fait de Samsung, SK Hynix et Micron. Ces nouveaux rivaux nous viennent de Chine, et ont pour nom YMTC et CXMT - en pleine ascension fulgurante. Mais ils ont encore du chemin à faire pour être considérés au niveau des fondateurs, comme on peut le voir dans leur pays d'origine !
Bytedance, Alibaba et Tencent signent des accords de 10 ans avec SK Hynix et Samsung
Quand CXMT et YMTC vont-ils pouvoir être considérés au même niveau que les autres géants de la RAM ? Ça devrait prendre du temps, si l'on en croit cette information qui émane du média coréen Maeil Business Newspaper.
Ce dernier indique en effet que les géants chinois de la tech Alibaba, Tencent et ByteDance ont commencé à solliciter les Sud-Coréen SK Hynix et Samsung pour des approvisionnements de très long terme. En effet, les contrats qu'ils voudraient signer iraient sur 10 ans, loin des contrats habituels de 3 à 5 ans, et portent sur la mémoire DDR et LPDDR.
CXMT et YMTC n'auraient pas encore les capacités de production de masse nécessaires
La même source indique que les géants chinois en question sont pour le moment réticents à solliciter leurs géants nationaux CXMT ou YMTC pour de tels canaux de fourniture. « Ces derniers sont considérés comme manquant de compétitivité et de capacité de production de masse en mémoire serveur haute performance, contrairement [à SK Hynix et Samsung] » est-il ainsi précisé.
Ils ne sont ainsi pas considérés comme encore en capacité de fournir des quantités suffisantes. De plus, l'exemple de leurs rivaux américains ayant sécurisé les approvisionnements avec des accords à long terme a semble-t-il aussi aiguillonné les géants chinois sur ce chemin. Alors, comment Pékin va-t-il réagir ?
Source : Wccftech

articles.title: Wegen KI: Proton-Mitarbeiter müssen erneut zum Bewerbungsgespräch
articles.text:
Mitarbeiter:innen des bekannten Schweizer IT-Unternehmens Proton, das auf Sicherheitssoftware spezialisiert ist, sollen in einem neuen Bewerbungsgespräch erklären, wie sie KI-Technik einsetzen. Das berichtet das investigative IT-Magazin 404 Media unter Berufung auf ein internes Rundschreiben. Darin heißt es, das Interview könne „zu Änderungen hinsichtlich der Aufgaben, Zuständigkeiten und der weiteren Beschäftigung“ führen.
Das Unternehmen benötige Menschen, die KI-Fähigkeiten in bessere Produkte und neue Arbeitsweisen „übersetzen können“, zitiert 404 Media aus dem Schreiben. Die Gespräche führen demnach nicht die direkten Vorgesetzten der Betroffenen. Zuständig sei stattdessen eine Gruppe „hochrangiger Beschäftigter“, die „starke KI-Fähigkeiten“ bereits unter Beweis gestellt haben soll.
Nicht alle bei Proton sind betroffen
Laut 404 Media treibt Proton-Chef Andy Yen den KI-Einsatz im Unternehmen schon länger voran. Dem Rundschreiben zufolge befragte er zuletzt mehr als 40 Führungskräfte, um die KI-Interviews vorzubereiten. Proton steht hinter Online-Diensten wie Proton Mail, Proton VPN und dem Passwortmanager Proton Pass. Nach den jüngsten verfügbaren Zahlen aus dem Jahr 2024 beschäftigt die Firma rund 500 Menschen.
Allerdings: Nicht alle müssen erneut zum Rapport. Wie genau sich dies zusammensetzt, blieb zunächst unklar. Wo es zu den KI-Interviews kommt, seien die Gespräche „von großer Bedeutung“, heißt es in dem Schreiben. Das Unternehmen räumt demnach ein, dass die Ankündigung Unsicherheit auslösen könnte, und will die „Ergebnisse“ der Gespräche so schnell wie möglich individuell mitteilen. Die KI-Interviews sollen zwischen dem 4. und 11. November stattfinden.
Proton widerspricht – ein bisschen
Zu dem Rundschreiben und den Bewerbungsgesprächen selbst wollte sich Proton gegenüber 404 Media nicht äußern. Später erklärte das Unternehmen, es baue keine Stellen ab und nutze KI auch „nicht als Vorwand“ dafür. Im internen Schreiben klingt das aber nicht unbedingt so.
Allerdings geht es bei Proton offenbar nicht um die seit Monaten diskutierte Sorge, KI könne Arbeitsplätze ersetzen. Stattdessen sollen Mitarbeitende offenbar dazu gedrängt werden, die Technik stärker zu nutzen. Proton-Boss Yen wünscht sich dem Schreiben zufolge Beschäftigte, die die Veränderungen durch KI „mit Neugier, Urteilsfähigkeit und Dringlichkeit“ angehen.

articles.title: Un astre jamais vu, situé encore plus loin que Pluton, pourrait rejoindre le très fermé club des cinq planètes naines du Système solaire - Numerama
articles.text:
Pour l’instant, elle ne porte qu’une désignation provisoire, 2026 ED138, mais elle pourrait à terme rejoindre les cinq planètes naines reconnues par l’Union astronomique internationale (UAI) : Pluton, Makémaké, Cérès, Hauméa et Éris. Cet astre, dont la découverte a été annoncée ce mardi 27 octobre par le Minor Planet Center, l’organisme qui recense les petits corps du Système solaire, est le premier candidat au titre de planète naine repéré par le télescope Vera C. Rubin, mis en service il y a quasiment un an et demi.
Ce type d’astre est trop gros pour être considéré comme un astéroïde et possède une forme sphérique qui le fait ressembler à une planète classique. Contrairement à la Terre, à Mars et aux autres planètes, une planète naine n’a pas fait le ménage sur son orbite : d’autres corps circulent encore sur des trajectoires proches de la sienne. C’est la nuance qui a fait perdre à Pluton son titre de planète au terme de débats houleux au sein de l’Union astronomique internationale, en 2006.
Un astre massif transneptunien
L’Union astronomique internationale ne reconnaît que cinq planètes naines dans notre Système solaire, mais on compte plusieurs centaines de candidates plus ou moins assurées de décrocher le titre. Pour ED138, il s’agit de la toute première candidate découverte par le télescope Rubin. L’observatoire, installé sur le Cerro Pachón au Chili, doit notamment dresser l’inventaire des petits corps du Système solaire, qu’il s’agisse d’astéroïdes, de comètes ou d’autres objets.
Le télescope a capté cet objet transneptunien, particulièrement brillant et jamais vu auparavant, en balayant le ciel austral avec sa gigantesque caméra. L’astrophysicien Matthew Holman, du Center for Astrophysics Harvard & Smithsonian, l’a repéré le 13 octobre dans les données collectées plus tôt en 2026, grâce à un code de recherche d’objets en mouvement qu’il a développé avec son collègue Kevin Napier. D’après les premières analyses de l’équipe de Rubin, il s’agirait d’un des astres les plus gros et les plus brillants repérés dans cette partie du Système solaire.
Il est encore trop tôt pour confirmer qu’il s’agit bel et bien d’une planète naine. ED138 montre en revanche ce dont sont capables les algorithmes du télescope, chargés de comparer des milliards de détections d’objets en mouvement pour retrouver celles qui appartiennent au même astre.
Beaucoup d’indices, mais pas de confirmation
En fouillant les données, les astronomes ont retrouvé ED138 sur d’autres images : au total, le télescope l’a observé 30 fois, sur 20 nuits, entre le 4 mars et le 11 juillet 2026. Des images d’archives de la Dark Energy Camera, montée sur le télescope Blanco, toujours au Chili, ont même permis de retrouver l’objet en remontant jusqu’en 2016. Les astronomes ont ainsi pu retracer plus de dix ans de l’orbite de la possible planète naine.
On sait ainsi qu’elle tourne bien autour du Soleil, dont elle se trouve actuellement à environ 46 unités astronomiques (UA), une UA correspondant à la distance moyenne entre la Terre et le Soleil. Pour comparaison, Pluton en est à 40 UA en moyenne. À partir de sa distance, de son éclat et de la part de lumière que sa surface est censée réfléchir, l’équipe estime son diamètre entre 600 et 1 500 kilomètres. C’est bien moins que Pluton (2 377 kilomètres), mais un corps glacé de cette taille devrait en théorie être rond.
ED138 semble assez grosse pour être ronde, elle tourne autour du Soleil (ce qui exclut qu’il s’agisse d’un satellite naturel) et partage sa région avec une foule d’autres objets transneptuniens. Autant d’indices qui portent à croire qu’il s’agirait bien d’une nouvelle planète naine. Pour en avoir le cœur net, les astronomes devront l’observer dans l’infrarouge afin de mesurer précisément sa taille. Rubin, qui doit photographier tout le ciel austral pendant dix ans, pourrait d’ici là débusquer d’autres objets de ce genre dans les zones négligées par les relevés précédents.

articles.title: ‘Cope harder’: Vaishnaw defends India's iPhone PLI scheme
articles.text:
‘Cope harder’: Vaishnaw defends India's iPhone PLI scheme
Ashwini Vaishnaw pushes back against criticism of India’s manufacturing model, citing tax collections, incentives and jobs created through electronics production.
Assembling iPhones makes great headlines for India. Owning the supply chain is where the real power lies.
Apple assembled around 55 million iPhones in India in 2025, a 53% increase from 36 million units in 2024. The country now accounts for about a quarter of Apple's global iPhone output, according to a Bloomberg report.
The growth has strengthened India's position as an alternative manufacturing base to China.
While skeptics question whether snapping together foreign components delivers true high-tech independence, the government points to ₹3.25 lakh crore in tax collections and 12 lakh new jobs as proof that the PLI scheme is already paying off handsomely.
Vaishnaw counters criticism with tax and employment figures
The debate intensified after a Bloomberg Opinion video questioned whether India should replicate China's manufacturing model. It highlighted India's dependence on imported components and the cost of government subsidies supporting phone production.
Union Electronics and IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw responded on X on October 27, defending the government's Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme for mobile manufacturing.
According to the figures he shared, the government had paid Rs 19,000 crore in incentives, while direct tax collections reached Rs 25,000 crore. The sector had also generated Rs 3 lakh crore in Goods and Services Tax (GST) collections.
Vaishnaw also cited employment figures, saying electronics manufacturing supported 25 lakh jobs, including 12 lakh in mobile phone manufacturing.
He ended his post with the pointed remark, “Cope harder!!” The figures form the government's case for continuing to support domestic manufacturing. However, tax collections and job creation are only part of the discussion.
India's iPhone growth comes with a supply chain challenge
India's expanding role in Apple's manufacturing network is a significant development. In 2025, the country assembled around 55 million iPhones, up from 36 million in 2024.
Apple also began assembling all variants of its iPhone 17 line-up in India, including the Pro and Pro Max models, according to The Times of India.
Yet assembling a finished product is different from manufacturing all its components locally. India continues to depend on imports for several critical parts, including processors, memory chips, displays, camera lenses and batteries.
This matters because the economic value generated by manufacturing depends partly on how much of the supply chain operates within the country. Greater domestic production of components could help Indian suppliers capture more value while reducing reliance on overseas manufacturers.
The next test is building more of the iPhone in India
The government's manufacturing push now faces a more demanding test: turning higher production volumes into a deeper domestic electronics ecosystem.
That means expanding local component manufacturing, bringing more suppliers into the country and strengthening research and design capabilities. These steps could help India progress beyond final assembly and establish a more substantial presence in global electronics supply chains.
India's iPhone production growth demonstrates that the country can attract large-scale manufacturing. Whether that translates into lasting economic gains will depend on its ability to build more of the technology and supply chain behind each device.

articles.title: Hackers now scanning systems for recently-patched Oracle flaw
articles.text:
Attackers have begun probing the Internet for systems unpatched against a recently disclosed critical Oracle E-Business Suite (EBS) vulnerability.
Discovered in a core component of EBS's Application Object Library and tracked as CVE-2026-101767, this flaw lets unauthenticated threat actors with HTTP network access take over vulnerable systems in low-complexity attacks.
Oracle released security updates to address the issue in its October 2026 Critical Security Patch Update on October 20 and urged customers to patch their systems immediately.
"In some instances, it has been reported that attackers have been successful because targeted customers had failed to apply available Oracle patches," it said. "Oracle therefore strongly recommends that customers remain on actively-supported versions and apply security patches without delay."
While Oracle has not yet tagged CVE-2026-101767 as exploited in the wild, threat intelligence company Defused said on Tuesday that it already spotted threat actors scanning the Internet for vulnerable systems.
"Our Oracle E-Business Suite decoys recorded exploratory exploits against CVE-2026-101767, an unauthenticated SQL injection in EBS's Thin Client Framework servlet that chains to remote code execution, this morning, Oct 27," Defused warned.
Internet threat watchdog Shadowserver now tracks over 670 Internet-exposed Oracle EBS instances, most of them with IP addresses from the United States. However, Shadowserver doesn't indicate how many are honeypots or have already been secured against the CVE-2026-101767 flaw.
Attackers often target Oracle vulnerabilities because they let them breach enterprise systems on the networks of many Fortune 100 corporations, government organizations, and healthcare networks around the world.
For instance, since early August 2025, the Clop extortion gang has exploited another Oracle EBS flaw (CVE-2025-61882) in zero-day attacks targeting high-profile victims like Logitech, GlobalLogic, and the Washington Post, as well as US universities (including Harvard University, the University of Pennsylvania, Dartmouth College, and the University of Phoenix)
More recently, in June, Oracle released emergency mitigations for a critical PeopleSoft Suite zero-day (CVE-2026-35273) that the ShinyHunters extortion gang exploited between May 27 and June 9.
By abusing this flaw, the threat actors gained unauthenticated remote code execution on victims' systems and stole data from many organizations worldwide, including Nottingham University, Nissan, and the National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC).
Since November 2021, CISA has added 46 Oracle security bugs to its list of actively exploited vulnerabilities, 13 of which have also been abused in ransomware attacks.

articles.title: Tesla comienza a fabricar robots Optimus: qué tareas podrían hacer en fábricas y cuándo llegarían al mercado
articles.text:
Tesla comenzó la producción de sus robots humanoides Optimus en la fábrica de Fremont, California, un paso que acerca el proyecto a una futura aplicación comercial dentro de fábricas y otros espacios de trabajo.
La empresa de Elon Musk informó que los primeros ejemplares salidos de esta línea alcanzaron un estándar de calidad apto para fabricación, aunque todavía deberá modificar el diseño y perfeccionar el proceso industrial.
El avance importa porque Tesla busca ampliar su negocio más allá de los vehículos eléctricos. Con Optimus, la compañía pretende desarrollar máquinas capaces de realizar tareas físicas mediante sistemas de inteligencia artificial. Por ahora, el inicio de la producción no implica que los robots estén disponibles para el público ni que exista una fabricación masiva.
Optimus fue diseñado para trabajar en espacios pensados para personas
Optimus es un robot humanoide creado para desplazarse y operar en entornos construidos para las personas. Su forma busca facilitar la manipulación de objetos y la ejecución de tareas físicas que, hasta ahora, requieren intervención humana.
Tesla plantea que estos robots puedan asumir actividades repetitivas o que exijan esfuerzo físico. En una fábrica, podrían colaborar con el movimiento de materiales, la manipulación de piezas y determinados procesos de producción. El alcance final dependerá de las capacidades que consigan los modelos y de las pruebas que la empresa realice antes de extender su uso.
El desafío no se limita a construir una máquina que camine o mueva los brazos. Para resultar útil, Optimus deberá reconocer el entorno, calcular trayectorias, coordinar movimientos y reaccionar frente a cambios sin dañar a personas, herramientas u objetos cercanos.
El software y el entrenamiento de inteligencia artificial serán tan determinantes como el hardware del robot. La capacidad de interpretar instrucciones y adaptarse a escenarios variables definirá si puede operar fuera de condiciones controladas.
Fremont alberga la producción inicial de los humanoides
La fabricación comenzó en la planta de Tesla en Fremont, California, un espacio que antes se destinaba a la producción de vehículos eléctricos. La empresa indicó a sus accionistas que los primeros robots construidos en esa línea alcanzaron el nivel necesario para considerarse parte de un producto comercial.
Esa condición representa una etapa relevante, pero no garantiza un despliegue inmediato. Tesla continuará introduciendo cambios en los componentes y en la forma de ensamblar los equipos. Los primeros lotes permiten detectar errores de diseño, ajustar materiales y comprobar si el proceso puede repetirse de manera consistente.
Tesla no comunicó cuántas unidades de Optimus ha fabricado ni una fecha concreta para su llegada al mercado. Antes de ampliar la escala, la compañía deberá probar que el robot puede cumplir tareas útiles de forma segura y sostenida.
La producción inicial también deberá demostrar que los humanoides pueden desenvolverse fuera de un entorno especialmente preparado. Una fábrica presenta movimientos repetidos y zonas delimitadas, pero incluso allí existen personas, maquinaria, objetos y situaciones que cambian durante la jornada.
La robótica abre un debate sobre el futuro del trabajo
El avance de Tesla se produce en un momento en que la inteligencia artificial y la robótica alimentan discusiones sobre el empleo. Bill Gates, cofundador de Microsoft, ha advertido que estas tecnologías podrían transformar el mercado laboral durante las próximas dos décadas.
Según su planteamiento, los sistemas de inteligencia artificial ya intervienen en tareas de atención telefónica, ventas, administración y contabilidad. La siguiente etapa podría involucrar máquinas físicas capaces de desplazarse, identificar entornos, manipular herramientas y ejecutar labores que hoy requieren fuerza, precisión o supervisión humana.
Gates mencionó escenarios en los que los robots podrían construir viviendas, cultivar alimentos o realizar cirugías. En el caso de la salud, un nivel mayor de autonomía exigiría normas de seguridad, controles clínicos y reglas claras sobre la responsabilidad ante posibles errores.
Las fábricas podrían ser el primer terreno de prueba
La industria ofrece un entorno adecuado para los primeros usos de robots como Optimus. Las tareas repetitivas, el traslado de componentes y la manipulación de materiales son actividades que pueden estructurarse con procesos definidos.
Sin embargo, la llegada de humanoides a las líneas de producción también dependerá de costos, fiabilidad y seguridad. Las empresas deberán evaluar si las máquinas pueden mantener un ritmo de trabajo estable y si pueden integrarse con los empleados sin generar riesgos.
La fabricación de Optimus en Fremont acerca a Tesla a esa etapa de pruebas industriales, pero todavía no confirma una venta masiva. La compañía deberá convertir los primeros robots aptos para producción en equipos capaces de operar con consistencia antes de fijar una fecha de lanzamiento comercial.

articles.title: Crise no iPhone Duo: fornecedora nega falha na dobradiça • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Crise no iPhone Duo: fornecedora nega falha na dobradiça
A FineMTEC afirma que não há provas de defeito em seus componentes e considera medidas legais contra acusações.
A FineMTEC, fabricante sul-coreana de componentes para celulares dobráveis, negou que suas peças sejam responsáveis pelos relatos de telas rachadas no iPhone Duo. A empresa afirma que uma investigação técnica é necessária antes de relacionar os defeitos a um componente específico.
A manifestação ocorre após a repercussão de imagens de aparelhos da Apple com rachaduras e linhas de pixels acesos próximas à dobra.
A FineMTEC publicou no domingo (26) um comunicado sobre “problemas de qualidade em novos produtos”, afirmando que os defeitos relatados em alguns dobráveis não são causados por seus componentes. A companhia argumenta que responsabilizar uma única peça exigiria testes capazes de mostrar a relação entre o componente e o problema observado.
A FineMTEC não cita diretamente a Apple nem o iPhone Duo. O comunicado, no entanto, foi publicado após usuários e análises independentes levantarem a possibilidade de que os danos estejam relacionados ao mecanismo da dobradiça.
A empresa é apontada pela imprensa sul-coreana como fornecedora de placas metálicas que dão suporte à tela flexível e ajudam a distribuir as forças durante a abertura e o fechamento. A repercussão também chegou ao mercado financeiro: as ações da FineMTEC caíram mais de 15% após as especulações.
Preocupada com publicações em redes sociais que associam seus componentes como responsáveis pelo problema, a fornecedora afirmou que poderá tomar medidas civis e criminais contra a disseminação de informações falsas que prejudiquem sua reputação.
Na segunda-feira (26), a Apple confirmou que está ciente de um problema que afeta a tela interna de “um pequeno número” de unidades do iPhone Duo. A empresa informou ao 9to5Mac que proprietários afetados devem entrar em contato com o AppleCare para solicitar a troca do aparelho. Segundo a companhia, a falha tende a aparecer rapidamente nas unidades defeituosas.
O iFixit desmontou o iPhone Duo e encontrou regiões em que componentes estruturais ficam próximos dos pontos em que as telas quebradas apresentam danos. Uma das hipóteses é que uma barra central de suporte não recue completamente durante o fechamento, criando um ponto de pressão sobre o painel flexível.
A questão ganha peso pelo alto preço do aparelho. No Brasil, o iPhone Duo começa em R$ 21.999, enquanto a substituição da tela interna pode custar R$ 10.989. Por enquanto, não há evidência técnica ou informações sobre qual componente ou etapa de fabricação está por trás das telas quebradas.

articles.title: Alejandro Mesonero-Romanos, jefe de diseño de Alfa Romeo: "Si quieren pantallas grandes, que compren otra cosa"
articles.text:
Es curioso cómo defender lo tradicional en el mercado del automóvil parece ser ir contra el statu quo. Lo que hasta hace nada parecía lo más lógico, lo que siempre se ha hecho se ha convertido en una tendencia a contracorriente. Una persona que apuesta por hacer las cosas como toda la vida es española y tiene un puesto más que relevante en una de las firmas con más tradición del mercado del automóvil.
Es Alejandro Mesonero-Romanos y tiene muy claro qué haría con las pantallas en los coches.
"Que compren otra cosa". "Soy consciente de que una gran parte del público quiere tener pantallas grandes, pero que no compren un Alfa, compra otra cosa". Sencillo y directo. Así se ha mostrado Alejandro Mesonero-Romanos con Autocar, en una entrevista donde ha dejado clara su postura sobre el enorme tamaño de las pantallas y su protagonismo.
"Estoy seguro de que hay mucha gente por ahí que piensa como nosotros. Hay mucha gente que estará contenta con esta experiencia", ha añadido quien considera que las pantallas son interesantes cuando estás parado pero no tanto cuando estás conduciendo.
¿Un cambio? El español ha sido claro sobre la estrategia de Alfa Romeo y el uso de las pantallas: "nos desharemos de ellas". Es una propuesta arriesgada en los tiempos en los que estamos pero es cierto que el Cuorerosso, el prototipo presentado en el Salón del Automóvil de París y que debería adelantar el futuro de la compañía, llega con sólo dos relojes para el cuadro de instrumentos.
Mesonero-Romanos, de hecho, lleva tiempo apuntando a que inundar el interior de pantallas no es la fórmula ideal. Cuando se presentó el BMW iX3 con su Panoramic Vision, en el podcast de Coches.net recordaban que el diseñador español hace años ya les adelantó un concepto muy similar que, sin embargo, Stellantis no ha llevado a producción.
El objetivo, por tanto, sería dejar las pantallas relegadas a un pequeño espacio en la zona inferior del parabrisas pero limitar su impacto. Y es que en BMW, aunque se mantiene una pantalla enorme, lo cierto es que ésta pierde relevancia una vez que estamos en marcha.
¿Por qué? El diseñador español tiene claro que "estamos en una especie de guerra de centímetros por las pantallas, y para mí no tiene ningún sentido, porque se vuelven enormes. Básicamente, están diseñando una tablet para ti. En unos años, estas pantallas quedarán obsoletas, serán viejas, comenzarán a costar dinero".
Y, además, tiene un motivo puramente ergonómico: "lo que pones en una pantalla no lo pones en otro sitio. Y prefiero ponerlo en otro sitio". Esta forma de pensar es casi revolucionara en una industria donde todo parece llevarse a la pantalla, hasta el punto de que en muchas marcas se han asentado ahí funciones de climatización, Tesla lleva la activación de los antiniebla a la misma y esta y otras compañías han llevado el botón físico del warning al techo. Y hasta el cambio de marchas.
Sí, pero. La cuestión es que el cliente parece estar más que satisfecho con las pantallas gigantes. A esta moda se han subido todo tipo de compañías, incluidas las que se oponían a ello como Mazda. Y no sólo es una cuestión de que el Mazda CX-6e sea, en realidad, un coche con origen chino, el Mazda CX-5 también se ha sumado al carro de la pantalla gigante.
Esta marca y otras nos han confirmado que sus estudios de mercado aseguran que los clientes quieren pantallas enormes. Una pantalla con buena calidad y buen tamaño se conecta rápidamente con "modernidad". Y al final, el fabricante da al cliente lo que el cliente pide.
Una esperanza. Los que soñamos con que se produzca un pendulazo y volvamos a las pantallas comedidas y hasta los cuadros de instrumentos analógicos, tenemos un resquicio para seguir soñando. Estas palabras de Alejandro Mesonero-Romanos son agua de mayo para nuestros oídos.
Sobre todo cuando Porsche viene de presentar un Mission S que también apuesta por una aguja en el cuadro de instrumentos para combinar analógico-digital en un mismo espacio. Y esperando que las palabras de otros diseñadores calen, como las de Achim Anscheidt, director de diseño de Bugatti, quien también se ha mostrado contrariado con esta moda asegurando que cuando el coche envejece, una pantalla desactualizada ahonda más en esta percepción.

articles.title: Dell sees AI agent guardrails as a path to greater autonomy - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Dell sees AI agent guardrails as a path to greater autonomy
As enterprises put AI agents to work, they face a challenge: How can they give those systems more autonomy while keeping AI agent guardrails in place?
Security and resilience are becoming central considerations as enterprises decide which tasks to delegate to AI agents. Those decisions extend beyond individual actions to the data protection and cyber resilience capabilities that support the business, according to John Scimone (pictured), president and chief security officer of Dell Technologies Inc.
“The good news is, this is the best time to get it right,” Scimone said. “Organizations are today designing agents that are going to be working for years ahead. At that point of design is always the best time to get security done well, to get resilience done well. Security resilience by design for agentic is a huge opportunity.”
Scimone spoke with theCUBE’s Dave Vellante for the AI Cybersecurity and Resilience Summit, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how cyber resilience has replaced traditional disaster recovery, how security leaders brief boards and how much autonomy enterprises should give AI agents. (* Disclosure below.)
Setting AI agent guardrails without slowing the business
Business resilience once meant disaster recovery built around wildfires, hurricanes and grid outages. Today, a widespread cyberattack across an entire digital ecosystem is the more likely scenario, according to Scimone. Agents add a new dependency because work handed to software stops when the software does.
“What happens if these agents aren’t available?” Scimone said. “What happens if the data that the agents are deciding on is not available? A core part of your resilience posture has to contend with the notion that if our agents go down, our work is not happening.”
Companies are still cautious about letting agents act alone. A survey of 25 enterprise technology and security leaders led by theCUBE Research’s Krista Case found that 19 had autonomous agents in production. None allowed those agents to perform high-risk actions without human approval.
“It doesn’t mean doing it willy-nilly and just throwing caution to the wind,” he said. “It means being very thoughtful around where can’t you fail, putting deterministic guardrails in place … and letting the business run. Right now, I’m seeing too much caution in the space on that front.”
Dell applies that discipline internally, giving every agent tight identity and access control, extensive logging and traceability of decisions and actions, Scimone explained. That groundwork matters because only four of the survey’s 25 respondents had tested an AI agent incident scenario. Dell has also expanded its cyber resilience tools and joined OpenAI Group PBC’s call for collective action on cyber defense.
“On the threat front, the reality is while threat actors are certainly using AI and have been for a number of years, the explosion has not happened yet,” he said. “We haven’t hit that curve that I do believe is coming, and in the coming quarters, not in the coming years.”
Vellante pointed to one encouraging finding from the survey: Organizations granting agents bounded autonomy showed stronger recovery readiness than those relying solely on human approval. In Scimone’s view, AI agent guardrails designed up front let companies take more risk, not less.
“Organizations that design those governance systems upfront are going to be the ones, ironically, that can move the quickest and can take the most risk because they can do it confidently with the right insights and the right data to know that they’re not overstepping,” Scimone said. “At the same time, they’re not under-leaning.”

articles.title: Jio shares surge 21% in market debut after blockbuster India IPO | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Jio Platforms, billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s Indian telecom and digital services unit backed by Meta and Google, surged 21% in its stock market debut on Wednesday after raising $3.2 billion in India’s largest and most subscribed IPO, which attracted more than $77 billion in investor bids.
The shares opened at ₹1,358 (about $14) apiece, up from their IPO price of ₹1,119 (around $12). That valued Jio at around ₹12.5 trillion (around $131.9 billion), making it India’s second-most valuable listed company after its parent, Reliance Industries, which is worth about ₹16 trillion (around $168.6 billion). In 2020, when Meta and Google invested, Jio was valued at up to ₹4.91 trillion (about $65 billion at the time).
The offering, which ran from October 21 to 22, drew bids for 22.19 times the shares on sale, according to exchange data. More than 13.8 million people applied. That made it India’s most subscribed stock offering on record, reflecting strong investor demand for shares in the country’s largest telecom operator.
In 2016, Jio entered what was then a crowded Indian telecom market, offering free data and low-cost services. That helped it quickly win customers from established operators including Bharti Airtel, Vodafone Idea, and state-owned BSNL. It has since become the country’s largest telecom operator. Akash Ambani (pictured above), Jio Platforms’ managing director, said at Wednesday’s listing ceremony that its platforms serve more than 540 million customers. Jio’s prices are now broadly in line with those of its rivals’, but its business has expanded into broadband, cloud services, and AI.
Akash, Mukesh Ambani’s eldest son, has taken on a larger role in Jio as his father gradually hands more responsibility to the next generation of Reliance’s leadership. At the listing ceremony, he said he wants Jio to become a global technology company. “My dream is that one day, when the world counts its great technology companies, one of them will be from India, and that company will be called Jio Platforms Limited,” he said.
Jio made ₹300.5 billion (about $3.2 billion) in profit on revenue of ₹1.47 trillion (around $15.5 billion) in the fiscal year ended March 2026, with both figures up about 15% from a year earlier. In the June quarter, Jio’s revenue grew nearly 12% and profit rose 9%.
From the IPO proceeds, Jio plans to use up to ₹275 billion (about $2.9 billion) to repay debt at its telecom subsidiary, Reliance Jio Infocomm, with the remainder going toward general corporate purposes. Jio had total borrowings of ₹613.7 billion (around $6.5 billion) as of June 30.
Jio drew billions of dollars from American investors during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. Meta, then known as Facebook, invested $5.7 billion, while Google put in $4.5 billion. General Atlantic, Silver Lake, and Vista Equity Partners were among the other investors that backed the company. None sold shares in the IPO, which consisted entirely of newly issued shares.

articles.title: Qualcomm Snapdragon X Series to Power Anduril's US-Made "BlueChip" Laptops
articles.text:
Tuesday, October 27th 2026
Qualcomm Snapdragon X Series to Power Anduril's US-Made "BlueChip" Laptops
Anduril Industries and Qualcomm have announced the "BlueChip" laptops that will be manufactured in the United States. That's the stated goal of Anduril, the company founded by Palmer Luckey, the creator of Oculus VR. He says that around 90% of the first laptop's components will come from the United States or allied countries. The first "BlueChip" laptops will use the Qualcomm Snapdragon X Series chips that are manufactured at TSMC's newest Arizona facility. The processor is the same you can find in other Snapdragon-powered laptops like the Microsoft Surface. Moving further, Anduril intends to assemble circuit boards at its Arsenal-1 facility in Ohio. The company, however, has plans to extend beyond just the final assembly. In the meantime, it will develop US production capabilities for enclosures, battery components, and other hardware components. 
Functional prototypes are ready, with preorders planned for 2027, but exact specifications and pricing remain undisclosed. Palmer Luckey, however, estimates that it will cost roughly 20% more than typical high-end consumer PCs. Keep in mind that the "BlueChip" laptops are mainly designed for security, government, and military use scenarios. That means you will not find them on your usual PC retail store shelves. At least not the first generations. According to TechCrunch, Luckey stated his intention that, in the future, Anduril will produce U.S.-made consumer-oriented laptops.
Sources:
				Qualcomm, 				TechCrunch, 				Anduril

articles.title: Amazon presenta nuevos Echo con Alexa+, incluyendo un despertador inteligente que querrás poner en la mesilla de noche
articles.text:
Aunque la compañía ya presentó el año pasado la nueva gama de productos que probamos en Hipertextual con el Echo Studio y Echo Dot Max y que venían a redefinir el hogar inteligente de la compañía, ahora ha presentado nuevos dispositivos que se suman a los anteriores y que abren un abanico de posibilidades para todos aquellos que buscan llenar el hogar con Echos de nueva generación compatibles con Alexa+.
En total son tres nuevos dispositivos que se suman a los anteriores y que amplían el catálogo de altavoces inteligentes de la compañía para ofrecer un dispositivo en función de las necesidades de cada usuario, todos de nueva generación y preparados para Alexa+, incluyendo el rumoreado Echo con cámara. para dotar de mayor funcionalidades al ecosistema de la compañía.
El primer dispositivo es el nuevo Echo Dot: la compañía renueva su altavoz más pequeño (y más vendido) haciéndolo controlador de hogar digital integrado compatible con Zigbee, Matter y Thread y, por supuesto, compatible con Alexa+. Una funcionalidad interesante es que incluye un extensor wifi eero que añade hasta 93 m² de cobertura si usas una red eero.
Tiene un nuevo chip AZ3 para Alexa+ junto con un cuarto micrófono para las conversaciones con el asistente. Sobre el audio, incluye un altavoz rediseñado que ofrece un 50% más de graves que la generación anterior. ¿Su precio? 104,99 euros y estará disponible en Amazon.
Otro de los dispositivos nuevos de Amazon es el Echo Studio con cámara para el hogar. Es el dispositivo que probamos y el tope de gama de la compañía. Además del sonido de estudio, Dolby Atmos y sonido envolvente, y la red Zigbee, Matter y Thread, suma una cámara integrada de 13 MP para usarla con Alexa+, de forma que puede ver y entender lo que tienes delante para ayudarte en tiempo real.
Sobre la privacidad, tiene un botón específico que desactiva los micrófonos y la cámara siempre, y un LED integrado se enciende cada vez que la cámara transmite imágenes a la nube. Disponible en Amazon por 259,99 euros.
Además de estos dos nuevos modelos, Amazon también ha presentado el Echo Time, un Echo específicamente para la mesita de noche, sin cámara y nada por lo que tengas que preocuparte. Un altavoz inteligente despertador con Alexa que incluye una pantalla táctil circular personalizable y que incluye la tecnología Omnisense, de forma que las alarmas inteligentes te despiertan durante una fase de sueño más ligero, entre 10 y 60 minutos antes de la hora programada. Además, tiene un sistema que reduce la luz azul y se atenúa hasta mostrar solo la hora. Tiene un precio de 214,99 €.

articles.title: AI infrastructure hardware is now a systems game: 10 insights - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
11 insights from the CASPA CEO Summit: AI infrastructure hardware becomes a systems game
Faster chips alone no longer define the AI buildout. Hundreds of thousands of processors now work together as one machine, so AI infrastructure hardware is designed and judged as a complete system. That system runs from the optical links between racks to the memory, storage and power that keep GPUs busy.
The next phase will be defined by the bottlenecks around the processor. Copper is giving way to light, and the memory wall is moving rather than falling. Power systems built on cycles of up to a decade must keep pace with chips that turn over every year. Demand is not in doubt: Memory and optical laser capacity are booked out for years.
“A lot of the focus in AI has been very much on compute and on memory, but our view is actually AI is a data system,” said Irving Tan (pictured), chief executive officer of Western Digital Corp. “Ultimately, you need the entire ecosystem to work together and to be able to move in lockstep.”
Tan and other industry experts spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier during The CEO Summit in Santa Clara, California. The inaugural summit marked the 35th anniversary of the Chinese American Semiconductor Professional Association. The interviews covered optical interconnects, inference economics, memory pooling, maskless lithography, physics-based computing, power resilience and AI-driven chip design.
Here are 11 standout insights from the event:
1. Hard drives gain throughput as storage becomes the AI data layer.
Data creates intelligence and storage makes it persist, so data must be split into hot, warm and cold tiers across the cloud, the edge and devices, Tan explained. Citing IDC, he noted that the amount of data generated is projected to triple to more than 700 zettabytes over three years. Western Digital expects demand for data storage to grow at a compound annual rate of at least 25% over five years.
Explore theCUBE’s in-depth discussion.
2. Connectivity becomes the choke point for AI data centers.
Semtech Corp. supplies the chips inside the optical transceivers and copper cables that link thousands of AI processors into a single computer. Every link flap can force a job to restart, so connectivity now governs GPU uptime and, with it, revenue, according to Hong Hou, president and CEO of Semtech. Hyperscalers want more bandwidth at lower power, which leaves more of a data center’s fixed power budget for compute.
Check out theCUBE’s complete interview.
3. Inference economics push chipmakers toward workload-aware racks.
Agents now consume tokens around the clock, making performance per dollar per watt the critical metric of the inference era rather than raw teraflops, explained Sunghyun Park, co-founder and CEO of Rebellions Inc. The step beyond today’s rack-scale systems is racks tailored to whether a workload is latency-critical, throughput-hungry or energy-constrained. Models change every few months, so Rebellions designs flexible hardware and sees the network as the next bottleneck as context windows grow.
Watch the full interview from theCUBE.
4. Maskless e-beam lithography targets the shift from Moore’s Law to advanced packaging.
Moore’s Law is reaching its limit, and advanced packaging that combines logic, memory and input/output chips is taking over as the industry’s driving force, noted David Lam, founder of Lam Research Corp. and CEO of Multibeam Corp. Multibeam shrank an electron-beam column from 80 centimeters tall to the size of a marking pen, so arrays of columns can write a wafer in parallel. The resulting maskless lithography avoids the reticle limit that forces large quantum and AI chips to be stitched together.
See theCUBE’s full coverage.
5. CXL memory pooling gains new life as the memory wall persists.
The memory wall may not be solved for five years, emphasized Greg Ernst, chief business officer of ScaleFlux Inc., who recently joined from Intel Corp. Even an 8 billion-parameter model serving many users needs far more memory than high-bandwidth memory can hold. Compute Express Link, or CXL, lets multiple servers share a pool of memory. Hyperscalers that reuse older DDR4 modules in those pools are reviving interest in the technology.
Don’t miss the full interview on theCUBE.
6. In-memory computing takes aim at the memory supply crunch.
New memory fabs take three to four years to come online, leaving most memory from top suppliers sold out through 2028, according to Faris Sbahi, co-founder and CEO of Normal Computing Corp. The startup is moving away from high-bandwidth memory toward commodity LPDDR5. It also performs some inference calculations directly in memory to cut cost and energy use.
Hear the full story on theCUBE.
7. Physics-based computing aims for human-level intelligence in a single rack.
Unconventional AI Inc. is building a fully integrated machine that uses the time-varying physics of the real world to compute, much as a rolling ball inherently knows its next position, shared Naveen Rao, co-founder and CEO of Unconventional AI. The company’s first system targets human-level intelligence at about 10,000 watts in a single rack, compared with the brain’s 20 watts. Rao aims to keep driving that figure down until it beats biology, cutting the cost of intelligence enough to open up new form factors.
Catch the complete conversation on theCUBE.
8. Optics replaces copper as AI clusters outgrow electrical links.
Power limits are pushing operators to link multiple smaller data centers with fiber, and converting electrical connections inside the data center to optical ones is the next growth driver, highlighted Michael Hurlston, president and CEO of Lumentum Holdings Inc. The company has grown fourfold in a little more than a year, yet it runs about 70% below demand and is essentially booked through 2029. Indium phosphide laser chips are a key constraint, so Lumentum is investing in fabs and packaging as if the buildout will last another four or five years.
Watch theCUBE’s full sit-down.
9. Power systems race to match AI’s one-year hardware cycle.
Power infrastructure has historically moved on cycles of six to 10 years while AI hardware turns over every year or so. Melton Chang, president of the Power Systems Division at Schneider Electric SE, described that mismatch as the industry’s core challenge. AI loads can swing from 30% to 150% in milliseconds. Those swings threaten voltage and frequency stability and cause resonance that shortens the life of on-site generators. Schneider uses digital twins, simulation and real-time data to anticipate those swings.
Don’t miss the full segment on theCUBE.
10. Self-verifying AI agents speed chip design without sacrificing trust.
Custom silicon can no longer take 18 to 24 months when models change every three to six months, yet designers still need deterministic, trusted results from electronic design automation tools, according to Ankur Gupta, head of EDA IC and systems at Siemens Digital Industries Software. Siemens runs its design engines on Nvidia Corp. GPUs for 10- to 12-fold speedups. It also uses AI agents to automate the setup and debug phases of design.
Check out theCUBE’s complete interview.
11. d-Matrix scales memory-centric XPUs from chip to rack for inference.
d-Matrix Corp. has moved rapidly from accelerator cards to full rack-scale systems built around its Corsair XPU, according to Sid Sheth, founder and CEO of d-Matrix. By stacking memory directly on top of the processor — rather than placing it beside compute on an interposer — the architecture opens up both capacity and bandwidth, two of the core bottlenecks in AI inference. The company accelerated that shift by integrating into the Nvidia AI factory ecosystem to avoid rebuilding power, cooling, networking and software from scratch.
See the full interview on theCUBE.

articles.title: Un Tesla Semi prend feu sans raison : sa batterie a brûlé pendant 10 heures
articles.text:
La police des autoroutes de Californie (CHP) a fermé l’Interstate 880 dans les deux sens ce mardi 27 octobre 2026, vers 17h45 heure locale, à Hayward, dans la baie de San Francisco. Dix minutes plus tôt, un Tesla Semi avait pris feu sur les voies en direction du sud, laissant également s’échapper des fumées chimiques jugées dangereuses.
Deux heures plus tard, à 19h45, la CHP estimait que l’incendie devrait durer de 15 à 18 heures et que ces voies resteraient fermées jusqu’à son extinction, comme le rapporte la chaîne locale ABC7 News. Finalement, la police a fait savoir sur son compte X que les voies vers le nord avaient rouvert à 20h40, puis à 3h30 du matin (11h30 heure de Paris) pour celles vers le sud, soit environ 10 heures après le début de l’incendie.
Aucun accident n’est en cause. Le conducteur a raconté aux policiers que le camion avait simplement pris feu, sans qu’il sache pourquoi. Il n’a pas été blessé et aucun autre véhicule n’a été touché. Une enquête a été ouverte pour déterminer la cause de l’incendie. Pour l’heure, Tesla n’a fait aucun commentaire public. La marque a lancé au printemps la production en volume de son camion électrique après 9 ans d’attente, et prévoit de le commercialiser en Europe en 2027.
Pourquoi une batterie de camion brûle-t-elle presque une journée ?
Il convient de souligner que ces incendies restent rares et que les voitures électriques prennent moins souvent feu que les thermiques. Par contre, une batterie lithium en feu ne s’éteint pas comme un réservoir d’essence. Une cellule endommagée continue de chauffer et enflamme ses voisines. Cette réaction en chaîne, appelée emballement thermique, peut repartir alors que les flammes semblent éteintes.
Comme les cellules sont enfermées dans un boitier, l’eau des lances les atteint mal, si bien que les pompiers doivent refroidir l’ensemble de l’extérieur, pendant des heures. D’autant plus que la capacité des batteries d’un camion électrique est conséquente, 548 kWh ou 822 kWh dans le cas du Tesla Semi, ce qui rallonge davantage l’opération.
Un autre Semi avait déjà brûlé en Californie le 19 août 2024. Conduit par un employé de Tesla, il avait quitté l’I-80 près d’Emigrant Gap, dans la Sierra Nevada, avant de finir contre des arbres. Dans son rapport préliminaire publié le 12 septembre 2024, l’agence fédérale américaine qui enquête sur les accidents de transport (NTSB) indiquait que les pompiers avaient utilisé environ 190 000 litres d’eau pour éteindre et refroidir la batterie, et qu’un avion avait largué du retardant autour du site par précaution.
À titre de comparaison, Daniel Hoy, capitaine des pompiers du district métropolitain de Sacramento, estimait auprès de CBS Sacramento qu’un feu de voiture thermique demande environ 2 650 litres, soit à peu près 70 fois moins.
En 2024, l’I-80 était restée fermée 14 heures vers l’ouest et 15 heures vers l’est, selon le NTSB. Il avait fallu attendre que la batterie refroidisse assez pour déplacer l’épave, qui a ensuite été surveillée pendant 24 heures sur un site à l’air libre au cas où elle se rallumerait.
