articles.title: Rachat de SFR : Orange garde le cap et fait une promesse aux salariés
articles.text:
Orange vient de publier ses résultats trimestriels. L’opérateur y présente bien entendu ses résultats financiers, mais revient aussi brièvement sur le rachat de SFR. Pour rappel, le consortium réunissant Orange, Bouygues Telecom et Free a signé un accord le 6 juin dernier avec Altice France en vue du rachat de SFR, pour un montant de 20,35 milliards d’euros. Cependant, l’opération n’est pas encore définitivement actée : elle doit encore obtenir le feu vert des autorités compétentes, et sa finalisation pourrait intervenir au second semestre 2027. En attendant, Orange confirme une nouvelle fois ce calendrier, tout en affirmant être attaché à la qualité du dialogue social.
Orange confirme le calendrier prévu
Dans ses résultats trimestriels, Orange annonce que le calendrier du rachat de SFR « reste inchangé ». La finalisation du rachat devrait donc s’effectuer au second semestre 2027, si les régulateurs l’approuvent. Mais l’opérateur ajoute également une ligne : « Alors que des décisions sont attendues dans le cadre des procédures engagées par des comités sociaux et économiques au sein du groupe Altice France, Orange reste attaché à la qualité du dialogue social qui se poursuit ».
Orange mentionne donc ici le Comité social et économique (CSE) de SFR, soit les représentants du personnel de l’opérateur au carré rouge, qui a attaqué en justice Bouygues, Orange et le groupe Iliad. Le CSE a notamment pointé du doigt un manque de transparence sur le découpage de SFR, laissant ainsi plus de 5 000 employés dans l’incertitude. À noter que l’issue du référé du 26 octobre dernier n’a pas été dévoilée, tandis qu’une audience au fond est prévue début décembre. Au passage, rappelons qu’environ un tiers des 8 000 salariés de SFR (selon les syndicats) s’est mis en grève le 24 septembre dernier, dénonçant un manque de transparence concernant leur sort.
Le consortium promet une solution pour chacun des 8 000 salariés de SFR
À la suite de l’un de nos articles concernant le sort incertain de 5 000 salariés de SFR, le consortium nous avait transmis un communiqué promettant « une solution d’emploi à chacun des 8 000 salariés du périmètre repris », tout en assurant que : « sur la base de notre proposition, environ 5 000 pourront rejoindre les trois opérateurs au lendemain de l’opération et 3 000 poursuivront leur activité chez SFR pour conduire la migration sur plusieurs années ». Cette annonce ne semble pas avoir rassuré l’intersyndicale, qui réclame trois offres de reclassement par personne et des indemnités de départ plus généreuses. Il reste maintenant à voir dans quelle mesure Orange sera « attaché à la qualité du dialogue social ».

articles.title: UEFI-Lücke: Kritischer Bug versteckt sich seit 16 Jahren in vielen Servern
articles.text:
UEFI-Lücke: Kritischer Bug versteckt sich seit 16 Jahren in vielen Servern
Erst Mitte Oktober 2026 sorgte die Entdeckung schwerwiegender Sicherheitslücken in der weit verbreiteten Programmiersprache PHP für Aufregung. Angreifer:innen sollen die php2shell genannten Schwachstellen schon aktiv ausnutzen und versuchen, ganze Server zu kapern. Allein in Deutschland sollen vier Millionen Dienste betroffen sein.
Schwachstelle in Baustein für UEFI-Firmware
Jetzt ist eine weitere kritische Sicherheitslücke bekannt geworden, von der ein großer Teil der Server weltweit betroffen sein soll. Dabei handelt es sich um eine Schwachstelle in EDK II, dem Open-Source-Code, der vielen UEFI-Firmwares als Basis dient. Diese Firmware ist der moderne Nachfolger von BIOS und startet beim Einschalten eines Computers als erstes, noch vor dem Betriebssystem. Laut Ars Technica setzen die meisten UEFI-Anbieter wie AMI, Insyde und Phoenix auf den Code.
Die Sicherheitslücke in EDK II (CVE-2026-97631), die auf der Schweregradskala CVSS 4.0 9,5 von 10 Punkten erreicht, befindet sich konkret im ICMP-Code des PXE-Netzwerkstarts. PXE sorgt dafür, dass Computer über ein Netzwerk statt von einer eingebauten Festplatte oder SSD starten. In Unternehmen dient diese Funktion dazu, viele Rechner zentral einzurichten oder zu warten.
Nur Geräte mit PXE-Start betroffen
Eine fehlerhafte Speicherbegrenzung bei dieser Art von Start per PXE kann es Angreifer:innen ermöglichen, eigenen Code auszuführen, bevor das Betriebssystem und Schutzmechanismen wie Secure-Boot starten. Dazu benötigen Angreifer:innen Zugang zu dem entsprechenden Netzwerk. Und: Computer, die von Festplatte oder SSD aus starten, sind nicht betroffen.
Bis ein Firmware-Update die Geräte erreicht, sollten Admins prüfen, ob Server und Netzwerkgeräte per PXE starten und ob die Firmware auf EDK II beruht, wie Dr. Web empfiehlt. Sollte PXE nicht benötigt werden, sollte die Funktion bis zu einem Update deaktiviert werden. Andernfalls sollten Admins das Bootnetz abschotten, so dass Arbeitsplatzrechner und Geräte im Gästenetz keine Pakete schicken können.
Verfrühte Korrektur erleichtert Angriffe
Erschwerend für die Bereinigung der schon seit 16 Jahren bestehenden Sicherheitslücke sind die offenbar unzureichend koordinierten Korrekturschritte. So wollten die Entdecker der Lücke, Alex Matrosov von Anthropic und Dan Holmes-Mitra von Google, den Fund eigentlich bis Januar 2027 geheimhalten. Allerdings ist schon Mitte Oktober 2026 eine Korrektur öffentlich einsehbar veröffentlicht worden. Diese zeigt potenziellen Angreifer:innen, wo der Fehler lag.

articles.title: Roblox accused of downloading 145GB of 3D assets, including adult content, for AI training purposes during scraping spree — 1,000 files scraped by automated crawler that ignored Open3DLab's site rules
articles.text:
Roblox accused of downloading 145GB of 3D assets, including adult content, for AI training purposes during scraping spree — 1,000 files scraped by automated crawler that ignored Open3DLab's site rules
Another crawler vacuuming up the internet for undisclosed reasons
Independent 3D modeling community Open3DLab has publicly warned that a web crawler, linked to the gaming platform Roblox, mapped "almost every project" on its website, along with sister sites SFMLab and SmutBase, downloading 145.5GB of data in the process. In a blog post, Open3DLab reports that "complete copies" of 1,027 files from 712 projects were sourced in the process, which it believes were taken for "AI training purposes."
The blog post goes into the specifics of the incident, along with some changes that Open3DLab has made since to try and avoid a repeat. According to the post, Open3DLab's staff noticed a crawler "making a large number of requests to our sites and download infrastructure" on October 18. The crawler used trellis2-data-sourcing/1.0 (3D foundation model research; [redacted]@roblox.com) as its user agent, with the data coming from a single Amazon AWS address. The crawler didn't respect the site's robots.txt file or Terms of Service, which explicitly forbid scraping. It also, according to the report, ignored creator licenses for the projects, which prohibit non-commercial use.
The crawler read "practically [its] entire catalogue" of 18,926 projects in a span of 34 hours over a total of 26,429 requests. Once it was done, the crawler downloaded 1,027 files from 712 projects before it "suspended operations." Files downloaded include 364 files, or 54.8GB worth, from 224 projects hosted on SmutBase, OpenLab's sister site focused on adult content. A further 345 projects of adult-marked SFMLab projects, or 62.6GB worth, were also taken.
According to Open3DLab, the crawler's "main limiting factor" was its use of free download servers that capped speed and concurrent downloads. The scraping was detected on the same day, and blocked by the following morning. Further download attempts were detected on October 19, "neatly within office hours, only briefly pausing for an hour around lunchtime," and despite being blocked, "did not reduce its download attempts."
A final attempt on October 20, with requests tapering, "likely in an effort to test... rate limiting," was made, with requests stopping completely later that day. Open3DLab made another request at this point for comment, although without reply.
The Roblox user agent mentions "3D foundation model research." As Open3DLab's blog post notes, Roblox has been building such a model since March 2025, when it introduced Roblox Cube, its "core generative AI system" for 3D modeling for character rigging, with characters and avatars listed as future goals. Further AI tech that could build in-game models using natural language prompts, called "4D generation," was beta launched in February 2026. The email address listed in the user agent matches one of the researchers listed on the Roblox Cube research paper, according to Open3DLab, although it redacted the name here.
Noting Roblox's "track record," Open3DLab's "most likely explanation" is that the crawler was collecting "training or evaluation data" for its 3D foundation model, although it notes that it can't prove it.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Roblox is a gaming platform and game creation system with over 33 million users and billions of "game experiences" for its player base, 40% of whom are reportedly aged under 12 years old. Open3DLab is clear to state that it "doesn't think Roblox set out to collect adult content" but that "as far as [its] logs show, nobody checked," which, it believes, is "not a good position" for Roblox to be in.

articles.title: La série Harry Potter agrandit encore un peu plus son casting et donne un gros indice
articles.text:
Alors que la première saison de la série Harry Potter, adaptée du premier tome Harry Potter à l’école des sorciers, arrive le 25 décembre 2026 sur HBO Max, HBO continue d’étoffer la distribution de sa superproduction.
HBO a annoncé ce mardi 27 octobre l’arrivée de trois nouveaux acteurs : Jasper Talbot, Hannah Chinn et Harry Gilby. La chaîne promet une adaptation « fidèle » des romans, et ce casting montre que la showrunner Francesca Gardiner (Succession) veut faire exister des personnages que les films avaient laissés de côté.
Les parents de Harry et Charlie Weasley prennent enfin de la place
En étalant l’adaptation sur une décennie, à raison d’une saison par roman, HBO promet de combler les manques des films. Le choix de Harry Gilby (The Last Kingdom) pour jouer Charlie Weasley va dans ce sens. C’est un gros indice pour la série.
Le deuxième fils Weasley, qui travaille avec les dragons en Roumanie, n’apparaissait au cinéma que sur une photo de famille dans Harry Potter et le Prisonnier d’Azkaban. Il aura un vrai rôle dès la première saison.
Côté souvenirs et fantômes du passé, la production a validé Jasper Talbot et Hannah Chinn pour camper respectivement James et Lily Potter. Jasper Talbot est passé par Broadchurch, Hannah Chinn par Conjuring : L’heure du jugement. Dans les films, les deux rôles revenaient à Adrian Rawlins et Geraldine Somerville, le temps de quelques brèves apparitions.
Une série prévue pour durer dix ans
Ces annonces tombent alors que la saison 2, adaptée de Harry Potter et la Chambre des secrets, est déjà en tournage, avant même la diffusion de la première. HBO enchaîne les saisons pour que ses jeunes acteurs ne grandissent pas plus vite que leurs personnages. La chaîne a aussi changé de propriétaire : depuis le 6 octobre, elle appartient à Skydance, le groupe né du rachat de Warner Bros. Discovery par Paramount, et David Zaslav a quitté la direction.
Avec une saison par roman, la série Harry Potter se donne le temps de développer des personnages que les films expédiaient en quelques plans. Le public découvrira les trois nouveaux venus à partir du 25 décembre sur HBO Max, au rythme d’un épisode par semaine jusqu’au 14 février 2027. HBO n’a pas précisé quelle place ils occuperont dans les huit épisodes.

articles.title: Plus d'un an après sa sortie, la Galaxy Watch 8 passe à 200,59€
articles.text:
Plus d’un an après son lancement, la montre que nous avions désignée meilleure montre connectée de 2025 voit son prix baisser nettement. AliExpress affiche la Samsung Galaxy Watch 8 à 200,59 € au lieu de 259,16 €, son prix le plus bas des 30 derniers jours, une offre réservée aux smartphones Android et à ceux qui acceptent une recharge presque quotidienne.
Sortie à l’été 2025, la Galaxy Watch 8 est le modèle de base de la gamme Samsung, sous Wear OS 6 et One UI 8 Watch, avec Gemini intégré. Son boîtier en aluminium ne pèse que 30 g en 40 mm et 34 g en 44 mm, et son écran AMOLED monte à 3 000 nits.
AliExpress la propose à 200,59 € en coloris graphite et en version Bluetooth, contre 259,16 € pour son prix le plus bas des 30 derniers jours, soit 22 % de remise. Elle s’adresse aux utilisateurs Android qui veulent un suivi santé et sport complet dans une montre légère.
La Samsung Galaxy Watch 8 Bluetooth est affichée à 200,59 € sur AliExpress, au lieu de 259,16 €, son prix le plus bas des 30 derniers jours.
Pourquoi choisir la Samsung Galaxy Watch 8 ?
- Un écran lisible en plein soleil : Sa luminosité maximale passe à 3 000 nits, contre 2 000 sur la Galaxy Watch 7. Lire son temps de parcours ou l’heure en extérieur ne demande plus de chercher l’ombre.
- Des coachs pour la course et le sommeil : Le Coach Running calcule votre VMA lors d’une première course de 12 minutes, puis propose des séances adaptées à votre niveau. Le coach Sommeil suggère vos heures de coucher et de lever après une semaine de mesures.
- Gemini au poignet : L’assistant de Google remplace Google Assistant et sait aussi répondre à des questions complexes. Sur cette version Bluetooth, il a besoin du smartphone à proximité pour fonctionner.
Du footing aux nuits de sommeil, ce qu’elle suit vraiment
Côté sport, la montre garde le GPS double fréquence L1+L5, avec un traitement logiciel revu après les critiques sur la fiabilité du tracé. Dans notre test de la Galaxy Watch 8, le tracé d’une marche signalait jusqu’au changement de trottoir, et le Coach Running nous a paru assez bien intégré pour motiver à sortir de son parcours habituel, sans remplacer un vrai entraîneur. Côté santé, les capteurs BioActive suivent notamment fréquence cardiaque, VO2max, ECG, tension artérielle et SpO2, plus un score d’énergie. Le nouvel indice antioxydant, lui, oblige à retirer la montre pour poser le pouce sur le capteur.
Elle convient à un utilisateur Android qui veut une montre légère à porter jour et nuit, pour le sport, les notifications et le paiement mobile. Elle est en revanche incompatible avec l’iPhone et demande Android 12 ou plus récent. L’autonomie limite son intérêt pour les profils très actifs : avec appels, messages et une heure de sport par jour, nous n’avons jamais dépassé 40 heures. Enfin, la nouvelle attache rend vos anciens bracelets Galaxy Watch inutilisables.
Face à la Watch 8 Classic et aux montres plus endurantes
Dans la gamme, la Galaxy Watch 8 Classic ajoute un boîtier en acier, une couronne rotative autour de l’écran et une touche Action, mais elle pèse 63,5 g et n’existe qu’en 46 mm. La Watch 8 standard garde l’essentiel du suivi santé et Gemini dans un format bien plus léger. Face aux montres spécialisées dans le sport, elle reste en retrait sur l’autonomie, contrepartie de sa polyvalence. Pour la situer parmi les modèles que nous avons testés, notre comparatif des meilleures montres connectées les départage sur l’autonomie, la précision des capteurs et la compatibilité.
✅ Les points forts
- Écran AMOLED de 3 000 nits protégé par un verre saphir
- Boîtier en aluminium de 30 à 34 g, discret au poignet
- Coach Running et coach Sommeil intégrés
- Gemini et une interface One UI 8 Watch plus ergonomique
- Suivi santé complet, ECG et tension artérielle compris
❌ Les limites
- Moins de deux jours d’autonomie, recharge quasi quotidienne
- Incompatible avec l’iPhone
- Trop d’applications Samsung à installer sur le smartphone
- Nouvelle attache : anciens bracelets incompatibles
La fiche AliExpress propose la Galaxy Watch 8 graphite en 40 et en 44 mm : vérifiez la taille sélectionnée avant de valider la commande à 200,59 €.
À 200,59 €, la Galaxy Watch 8 coûte 58,57 € de moins que son prix le plus bas des 30 derniers jours, une référence réelle et non un prix conseillé. Nous lui avions attribué 9/10 et le titre de meilleure montre connectée 2025, pour son design allégé, son écran très lumineux et l’arrivée de Gemini. À ce tarif, elle devient une porte d’entrée solide pour suivre sport, sommeil et santé sur un smartphone Android.
Si vous utilisez un iPhone, passez votre chemin : la montre ne fonctionnera pas avec. Si l’autonomie prime sur tout le reste, une montre de sport plus spécialisée vous conviendra mieux. Reste à choisir la taille : le 40 mm et sa batterie de 325 mAh pour la légèreté, ou le 44 mm, avec son écran de 1,47 pouce et sa batterie de 435 mAh.

articles.title: Le rapport performances/prix du Mac Mini M6 d'Apple devient imbattable avec cette offre — Frandroid
articles.text:
Avec son format minuscule et ses performances solides, le Mac mini M4 avait été l’un des ordinateurs les plus intéressants de ces deux dernières années. Le modèle 2026 reprend exactement le même boîtier et passe à la puce M6. Apple propose aussi une déclinaison M5 Pro pour les profils les plus exigeants, mais c’est bien le modèle d’entrée de gamme qui plaira au plus grand nombre. En pleine crise des composants, qui tire les prix de nombreux ordinateurs vers le haut, le voir passer sous les 1 000 euros change un peu la donne.
Ce qu’on apprécie du Mac mini M6 (2026)
- La taille ultra-compacte
- Les performances de très haut niveau
- Un fonctionnement silencieux et les capacités IA
L’Apple Mac mini M6 (2026) avec 16 Go de mémoire unifiée et 256 Go de SSD a un prix de référence de 1 049 euros. Chez PC Componentes, le mini PC est affiché à 969,68 euros. Sur Amazon, on le retrouve aussi en promotion à 1 019 euros.
Si, par la suite, l’offre mentionnée dans cet article n’est plus disponible, merci de jeter un coup d’œil ci-dessous afin de dénicher d’autres offres concernant l’Apple Mac mini M6 (2026). Le tableau s’actualise automatiquement.
Protégez votre vie numérique avec Bitdefender, la protection européenne de confiance. Bitdefender vous protège contre les arnaques et les fraudes du web. Profitez de vos activités en ligne en toute tranquillité.
Un boîtier toujours aussi minuscule, avec quelques compromis
Le design n’a pas changé depuis le Mac mini M4. Le châssis monobloc en aluminium recyclé mesure 12,7 cm de côté pour 5 cm de hauteur. Il se glisse sans difficulté sous un écran, voire derrière. La connectique reste complète pour un si petit format, avec trois ports Thunderbolt 4, deux USB-C et une prise casque en façade et un port HDMI plein format. Nouveauté de cette génération, l’Ethernet passe à 2,5 Gb/s et le Wi-Fi 7 fait son apparition. Jusqu’à trois écrans externes peuvent être branchés.
Tout n’est pas parfait pour autant, et cette génération impose son lot de petites concessions. Le bouton d’alimentation reste placé sous le châssis, à l’arrière, un choix que nous trouvons toujours peu pratique. Autre regret : là où l’ancien modèle laissait la possibilité de remplacer le SSD — au prix d’un démontage acrobatique —, ce n’est plus du tout le cas ici. Les 256 Go de stockage de cette version de base risquent donc de se remplir très vite et les options de stockage chez Apple coûtent cher. Mieux vaut donc bien estimer vos besoins avant l’achat.
Une puce M6 qui travaille en silence
Le modèle M6 inaugure la première puce Apple gravée en 2 nm et ça se sent : les performances sont en très nette hausse sur la partie processeur mais aussi graphique. La machine est à l’aise que ce soit pour la bureautique, le montage ou les tâches créatives plus lourdes. Elle reste silencieuse même en pleine charge, un vrai confort sur un bureau.
Les capacités IA font aussi partie des points forts relevés dans notre test. En revanche, si vous pensez faire tourner de gros modèles de langage en local, la question est plus nuancée : nous expliquons dans un article dédié pourquoi le Mac mini M6 est souvent un mauvais choix pour l’IA locale.

articles.title: Nefilim and Hive ransomware affiliate gets 70 months in prison
articles.text:
A Ukrainian national was sentenced to 70 months in prison for his role in Nefilim and Hive ransomware attacks targeting hospitals, government entities, and high-revenue businesses worldwide between 2018 and 2021.
The sentence follows the extradition of 35-year-old Artem Aleksandrovych Stryzhak to the United States on April 30, 2025, after authorities arrested him in Spain in June 2024.
"Artem Stryzhak is a prolific cybercriminal who worked with multiple ransomware groups to target U.S. businesses and hospitals," said Brett Leatherman, the FBI's Cyber Branch Operations Director. "These groups disrupted patient care and caused more than $100 million in losses. Today's sentence reflects the seriousness of Stryzhak's crimes and demonstrates the FBI's global reach and extensive network of international partners."
According to court documents, he paid for 20% of all ransom payments collected for access to custom Nefilim ransomware and decryption keys starting in June 2021.
While active as a Nefilim affiliate until October 2021, Stryzhak used the custom-tailored malware to target large corporations in the United States, Canada, and Australia with revenues exceeding $100 million each year. However, one of the Nefilim administrators later encouraged him to focus on large companies that were generating more than $200 million annually.
To pressure victims into paying, the ransomware operation also threatened to leak data stolen during attacks on dark web "Corporate Leaks" websites managed by the Nefilim admins unless victims met the ransom demands.
Stryzhak also joined Hive ransomware as an early affiliate, breaching and encrypting the systems of seven victims, including a dentist's office, multiple law firms, and a healthcare provider during the COVID-19 pandemic.
In December 2025, Stryzhak pleaded guilty and admitted to computer fraud conspiracy charges brought by US prosecutors in connection with ransomware attacks targeting businesses in the United States, Norway, France, Switzerland, Germany, and the Netherlands.
"Disrupting a ransomware group that attacked approximately 1,500 victims worldwide and sentencing a defendant who had targeted healthcare during the COVID-19 pandemic is of significant importance to this office," added US Attorney Gregory W. Kehoe.
"Ransomware attacks like those committed by the defendant wreak enormous havoc — harming victim companies that pay millions in remediation and ransoms, preventing hospitals and other critical facilities from accessing data, and putting sensitive information in the hands of bad actors," US Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. noted.
The US State Department also offers up to $11 million for any details that could lead to the arrest of Ukrainian national Volodymyr Tymoshchuk, one of Stryzhak's alleged accomplices, who is still at large.
Tymoshchuk is on the most-wanted lists of the European Union and the FBI, and the US Justice Department charged him in September for his roles as an administrator for the LockerGoga, MegaCortex, and Nefilim ransomware gangs. He was also allegedly involved in ransomware attacks that caused millions of dollars in damages to hundreds of companies around the world between July 2020 and October 2021.

articles.title: Modders unlock hidden AI power on Nvidia RTX 20, 30, and 40 series GPUs, nearly doubling some benchmarks
articles.text:
Sounding off: A used RTX 3090 has become the go-to card for running AI models at home, mostly because 24GB of memory costs far less on a gaming card than on a workstation one. That bargain comes with a catch Nvidia prints in its own spec sheets, though. On GeForce cards, one of the most common kinds of AI math runs at exactly half speed. A few open-source projects now claim to remove that limitation on RTX 20-, 30-, and 40-series cards.
The limit lives in the tensor cores. When they multiply FP16 or BF16 numbers and add up the results in higher-precision FP32, GeForce cards issue those instructions at half the rate of the FP16-accumulate mode. That FP32 mode is the one most training and plenty of inference actually rely on. The workstation cards Nvidia builds on the same chips – the RTX A6000, for example – run it at full speed.
The first fix came from GitHub user Zagitta, who published "gpu-unlock" for RTX 30-series cards. It's a Linux kernel module that kicks in before Nvidia's driver loads. That's when it rewrites two speed-select registers on the GPU and resets the card. Nvidia's regular driver then takes over as usual, so nobody has to flash a VBIOS or patch a driver.
On an RTX 3090 Ti capped at 450W, the developer's matrix-multiply tests show BF16 throughput climbing from 87.5 to 157.4 TFLOPS. TF32 nearly doubled, too. FP16 saw a smaller gain of 35%.
Other developers have since adapted the module for the remaining two generations. A version called gpu-unlock-ada doubled an RTX 4090's FP16 instruction rate from 165.6 to 331.6 TFLOPS. That's a raw issue rate, though – the README is upfront about it – so real matrix workloads on a card tested by an independent owner saw smaller gains of 12% to 34%.
On the older side, turing-unlock targets the RTX 2080 Ti and was tested on one of the 22GB memory-modded cards popular with budget AI builders. Its developer measured 36% to 64% faster FP16 matrix math, depending on matrix size. BF16 doesn't apply here, since Turing never had hardware for it.
Unfortunately, gamers won't really notice any difference, since games barely touch this kind of math. Chatbot token speeds hardly move either, mostly because generating text is limited by memory bandwidth rather than raw compute. Prompt processing reportedly runs 14% to 36% faster, though. Image generation and fine-tuning should benefit the most, since both lean heavily on FP32-accumulate tensor math.
For now, support is largely limited to Linux, apart from a couple of experimental Windows ports validated on specific hardware.
Zagitta considers hardware damage very unlikely, pointing out that the card's usual throttling and power management stay in place. The turing-unlock README is more cautious, warning that tensor cores draw a lot of power and that running them flat out may damage hardware.

articles.title: From human clicks to agentic velocity: What OpenAI’s 1.2 billion scale means for your auth
articles.text:
From human clicks to agentic velocity: What OpenAI’s 1.2 billion scale means for your auth
When OpenAI announced at DevDay that ChatGPT had crossed 1.2 billion weekly active users (WAUs), roughly 15% of the human population, most engineering discussions naturally centered on model context windows, compute clusters, and distributed GPU inference.
However, behind every chat session, API call, and model invocation sits an equally monumental infrastructure challenge: Identity and Access Management (IAM) at extreme web scale.
“Behind every chat session, API call, and model invocation sits an equally monumental infrastructure challenge: Identity and Access Management (IAM) at extreme web scale.”
Before OpenAI can serve a token from an LLM, its backend systems must authenticate the request, validate OAuth2 access tokens, inspect fine-grained permissions, and maintain secure session contexts globally. To manage this massive transaction volume without introducing latency bottlenecks, OpenAI turned to Ory, utilizing its lightweight, decoupled authentication engine and OAuth2/OIDC infrastructure.
Here is an architectural breakdown of how identity scale shifts when moving from human traffic to agent workloads, why legacy IAM platforms break at this volume, and how decoupled, edge-ready authorization handles extreme throughput.
The scale problem: human traffic vs. agentic workloads
To understand why traditional IAM platforms fail at extreme scale, consider how user authentication patterns change as architectures evolve from standard web applications to agentic AI platforms.
“When an enterprise moves from human-initiated UI clicks to autonomous AI agents… the ratio of token validations to human interactions scales non-linearly.”
When an enterprise moves from human-initiated UI clicks to autonomous AI agents (e.g., OpenAI’s Work and Codex suites), the ratio of token validations to human interactions scales non-linearly:
- Transaction velocity: A single user request to an AI agent can trigger dozens of downstream sub-tasks, database queries, and third-party API tool calls. Each step requires session verification and token introspection.
- Token introspection overhead: Legacy central identity providers (IdPs) typically validate access tokens via centralized RPCs or database lookups. At billions of requests per minute, centralized introspection introduces severe network hops and database lock contention.
- Stateless edge verification: To prevent authorization from becoming the primary bottleneck in the request path, session validation must happen synchronously at the edge using lightweight cryptographic verification (such as JSON Web Key Sets / JWKS caching) rather than stateful network calls.
Architectural comparison: modern composable IAM vs. legacy monolithic SaaS
When evaluating identity platforms for ultra-high throughput, engineering teams frequently hit performance and cost walls with traditional multi-tenant identity SaaS products (e.g., Auth0, Okta, Ping Identity).
| Architectural dimension | Legacy monolithic identity SaaS | Self-hosted composable IAM (e.g., Ory) | 
| Token validation mechanism | Centralized IdP round-trips or heavy server-side SDKs | Edge-native stateless JWT validation & local session caching | 
| Data residency & ownership | User store hosted in vendor-managed SaaS clouds | Complete data sovereignty (runs directly in your VPC / multi-cloud k8s) | 
| Database persistence strategy | Proprietary SaaS database clusters subject to vendor rate limits | Highly available distributed SQL layers (e.g., CockroachDB, Spanner, Postgres) | 
| Cost scaling model | Per Monthly Active User (MAU) or per-API request execution fees | Infrastructure-based scaling; cost correlates with compute/memory footprint | 
| Customizability & velocity | Restricted to vendor webhooks, rules, or custom code sandboxes | Go-native microservices with clean API boundaries and headless UI integration | 
“OpenAI wanted a partner that could help enable our vision for owning our identity processes, data, and success. We have a lot of partners, and Ory is one of our best.”
- Benjamin Billings, Engineering Manager, OpenAI (Case study)
Key infrastructure requirements for billion-user identity systems
Securing identity at scale requires a clear separation of concerns across the auth stack. Based on high-throughput deployments like OpenAI’s, modern identity architectures depend on four core principles:
1. Separation of identity state from business logic
Monolithic frameworks often bind user profiles, authentication state, and business roles together in single relational databases. High-throughput architectures decouple these responsibilities into distinct microservices:
- Identity storage & auth engines: Dedicated microservices handling identity lifecycle, credential hashing, and session management (e.g., Ory Kratos).
- OAuth2 / OIDC token issuance: High-performance OAuth2 server implementations capable of issuing signed access tokens and managing grant flows with minimal latency (e.g., Ory Hydra).
- Fine-grained access control (FGAC): Relationship-based access control engines based on Google’s Zanzibar model (e.g., Ory Keto) to evaluate tuple relationships (ObjectRelationSubject) in sub-millisecond execution times.
2. Distributed persistence across cloud regions
To support global edge routing, the underlying storage layer must support geo-distributed writes and low-latency local reads. Combining a self-hosted identity engine with distributed SQL engines (such as CockroachDB or cloud-native multi-region databases) ensures token-verification state can be replicated globally without split-brain risks or cross-continental network latency.
3. Agent security: transitioning from “enforce first” to “observe mode”
As enterprises deploy autonomous agents that execute commands on users’ behalf, writing restrictive IAM policies immediately can break workflows or cause silent failures. Modern security practices emphasize runtime observability before strict policy enforcement:
- Step 1: agent fingerprinting: Map every machine-to-machine (M2M) credential and agent service account operating across internal networks.
- Step 2: execution tracing: Audit tool usage, API invocations, and database queries initiated by autonomous runtimes.
- Step 3: identity delegation: Implement scoped OAuth2 Token Exchange (RFC 8693) to ensure agents operate under strict downscoped permissions tied directly to the delegating human user.
For a limited time, you can create a complimentary Ory account and turn on observe mode to learn how best to build enforcement.
“Scaling authentication to 1.2 billion weekly active users proves that identity is no longer just a security checkbox; it is a core distributed systems challenge.”
Scaling authentication to 1.2 billion weekly active users proves that identity is no longer just a security checkbox; it is a core distributed systems challenge.
As software shifts from human-driven UI interactions to high-velocity AI agent execution, engineering teams must evaluate whether their identity stack can handle exponential API volume. Decoupled, stateless-first identity engines offer the low latency, data sovereignty, and predictability modern platforms need to scale into the agentic era.

articles.title: Cloudflare Opens Quicksilver to Customers as Workers KV Instant, Inside a 1 MB Envelope
articles.text:
Cloudflare recently made Quicksilver available to customers for the first time, as a new mode for Workers KV called KV Instant. Reads resolve in 1.62 ms at the 99th percentile, compared with 287 ms for classic KV. What determines whether a team can use it isn't the latency, but the envelope around it.
Quicksilver is Cloudflare’s own configuration store, introduced in 2020. Nearly every request to Cloudflare looks up at least one key in it, Rob Sutter writes, and it has never been a customer-facing product. Brendan Irvine-Broque, who works on Cloudflare’s developer platform, announced the change on X:
we have this crazy key-value store at Cloudflare called Quicksilver
instantly updates keys across our whole network. microsecond reads from every location. stupid fast
our customers have asked us for years to make it available
we finally did – in a way we think is quite simple - as a new mode for Workers KV
The published figures, measured to over 300 edge locations:
| Mode | p99 reads (all) | median write replication | p99 write replication | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Instant | 1.62 ms | 107 ms | 256 ms | 
| Classic | 287 ms | under 1 s | 4.38 s | 
Cloudflare notes it has no sub-second fidelity for replication lag in classic mode, so the classic median and p95 figures are upper bounds rather than measurements. p95 reads in Instant mode are reported in microseconds.
The API is the Workers KV one, with three differences. Mode is set at namespace creation with a "mode": "instant" attribute, and cannot be changed afterward. Metadata is unsupported, so getWithMetadata always returns null. And list returns every matching key with no pagination.
Then the limits. A namespace holds at most 10,000 key-value pairs and one megabyte in total, with keys up to 300 bytes. Writes are capped at one per namespace per second, which Cloudflare contrasts with classic KV’s one write per key per second, on the grounds that a single system of record "makes it easier for you to reason about update order in your application." That difference is the one most likely to catch a team migrating: a pattern classic KV permits across many keys concurrently becomes a single serialised queue.
Pricing points the same direction, and Cloudflare says so plainly: "storage and Class A operations are significantly more expensive than Workers KV."
|  | Reads (Class B) | Writes, deletes, lists (Class A) | Storage | 
|---|---|---|---|
| KV Instant | $0.20 per million | $0.10 per operation | $100 per MB, per month | 
| Classic KV | $0.50 per million | $5.00 per million | $0.50 per GB, per month | 
Reads cost 60% less. A write costs ten cents, against five dollars per million in classic mode. Storage runs $100 per megabyte per month, and since a namespace tops out at one megabyte, that is also the ceiling. Multi-key reads bill per key, so requesting three keys in one get costs the same three Class B operations as three separate calls.
Irvine-Broque set out the reasoning in the same thread:
just like how we use Quicksilver ourselves, it’s for small data that is read often and updated infrequently
pricing reflects this - reads actually cost 60% less than even Workers KV
Writes cost what they cost, he added, because writing a key replicates it to hundreds of locations. This is a store priced so that you read from it constantly and write to it rarely.
Benjie Malinao, also on X, read the fit the same way:
This is the config store agents actually need. Sub-2ms p99 reads and global writes landing in about a quarter second at p99, on the same KV API. Feature flags and agent settings without waiting on a TTL. I’d move hot-path config over first.
Feature flags, routing tables and agent settings fit that shape. Session state, user records and anything with a write path do not.
The comparison practitioners reached for was Vercel. Developer Shawn Mclean asked Irvine-Broque directly:
I’m looking into using Vercel Global Config for a middleware read. They claim 15ms. If I move my workloads to CF, are you saying I can read from middleware for a platform tenant domain mapping in 2ms?
The answer did not quite confirm it:
even p50 of Workers KV (non-instant) from 2 years ago was ~5ms. KV Instant is even faster than that (see numbers in the post)
Cloudflare’s own worked example is a launch flag read on every request and flipped at a keynote, which is precisely the workload: one key, one write, read everywhere immediately.
Classic Workers KV, which launched during Birthday Week in 2018, remains the recommendation for large or frequently updated data. The two modes now sit under one API with opposite economics.
KV Instant is in private beta with a sign-up form, and Cloudflare says it plans to open it up more widely. No general availability date is given.

articles.title: Anthropic says it will be burning lots of natural gas to feed the AI boom
articles.text:
Anthropic says it will be burning lots of natural gas to feed the AI boom
Anthropic reveals spending threats associated with fossil fuels as it prepares to go public
- Anthropic is becoming increasingly reliant on fossil fuels as the queue to join the power grid grows
- Competing with other hyperscalers and conflict in the Middle East is increasing fuel costs
- Trump is trying to increase fossil fuel energy production while simultaneously killing renewable energy projects
In order to meet the massive power demands of AI data centers, Anthropic is becoming increasingly reliant on natural gas to fuel its buildout.
The United States power grid is lagging behind on the demands of an enormous number of requests for grid connections from data centers, prompting many developers to equip their sites with natural gas burning turbine generators.
While this does counter having to build the necessary grid infrastructure and anger from consumers over rising electricity prices, it has left Anthropic vulnerable to fluctuations in fossil fuel prices made worse by conflict in the Middle East.
Data centers turn to fossil fuels
“Competition for access to electrical supply and data center locations with adequate power availability is intense,” Anthropic said in documents filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission as the company prepares to go public.
Anthropic also acknowledged in the same filing that increasing global temperatures - caused by climate change - would contribute towards increased operating costs, leaving the company in something of an impasse. To remain competitive, the company needs to continue expanding data center capacity, and the only way to do that is to rely on fossil fuels.
But the same tactic that Anthropic is using to cut down wait times for grid connections is also being used by other hyperscalers and AI companies. Anthropic has predicted that “This competition could drive up the price of natural gas.”
The Trump administration has attempted to make it easier than ever for new fossil fuel projects to be approved, scrubbing the climate-improving red tape in favor of quick input to the energy grid. Old fossil fuel sites, shuttered and set for demolition by the Biden administration, have also been brought back online in an attempt to quell the growing backlog of new grid connections.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
But in order to appease some of the dissatisfaction of Americans dissatisfied with the enormous buildout of data centers and the associated downstream costs, Trump has urged developers to shoulder the costs of new grid infrastructure and contributory price increases - which Anthropic said “could adversely affect our cost structure and limit our ability to scale our compute infrastructure, develop and deploy our models, and service our customers.”
Anger against data centers is snowballing
From the harms to local environments and the wider climate, to noise pollution and lowered property values - data centers have become a great unifier across the political spectrum as Democrats and Republicans oppose the unprecedented buildout of AI data centers across the US.
Two-thirds of Americans said they oppose the construction of new facilities, and it has become a key issue in the lead up to the most important election of 2026: the November midterms. Candidates aligned with Trump’s AI first rhetoric have been buoyed by political action committees, but face a difficult time at the polls.
One of the biggest issues facing everyday Americans is the cost of living. Rising energy prices caused in tandem by the US war on Iran and the increased demand from AI data centers is at the front of voters' minds, and prices are unlikely to come down any time soon.

articles.title: Why better data could be the key to AI-driven food R&D
articles.text:
Why better data could be the key to AI-driven food R&D
As food companies navigate increasingly complex product development and safety requirements, connected data and generative AI could help scientists make better-informed decisions, reduce manual work and identify potential risks earlier.
Picture a product developer creating a plant-based protein drink for three different markets. The product concept is clear; the information needed to build it is not. Supplier specifications are locked inside PDFs. Trial results sit in spreadsheets. Regulatory requirements arrive by email. Even a single ingredient can carry a different name in each document: “haldi” in one file, “turmeric” in another and “Curcuma longa” in a regulatory note. None of these files is wrong. The problem is that the information is scattered.
As a result, the developer spends more time searching, matching, and verifying data than working on the product itself. This has become common across food, beverage, and wellness R&D. Creating a product is no longer only about getting the taste and texture right. It is also about managing and connecting an ever-growing volume of data.
Why the data load keeps growing
Food product development is becoming more complex, and food safety sits at the centre of that complexity. The World Health Organization’s 2026 estimates, which cover 42 foodborne hazards, found that unsafe food caused an estimated 866 million illnesses and 1.5 million deaths worldwide in 2021. Chemical hazards accounted for 73% of these deaths, with inorganic arsenic and lead alone responsible for 42% and 31% of chemical-related deaths, respectively. The economic toll is just as stark: WHO puts the productivity lost to foodborne disease at $310 billion in 2021.
The challenge multiplies when companies develop products for several markets at once. Each market brings its own allergen rules, contaminant limits, permitted claims and labelling norms, and the ingredients themselves vary. In wellness products, for instance, the composition of a botanical can shift with its source, harvest season and processing. With every new ingredient, supplier and market, the volume of information that must be checked and connected keeps growing.
Giving data a common language
The answer is not another database. It is a shared vocabulary with the relationships built in, which is exactly what an ontology provides. FoodOn, an open food ontology described in npj Science of Food in 2018, was created to tackle a familiar problem: food data siloed across disparate languages and data dictionaries. Still actively maintained, it now contains tens of thousands of classes covering food products, their plant and animal sources, and the processes used to make them.
Inside a company, the principle is simple. Turmeric is turmeric, whatever name appears in a spreadsheet, supplier document or regulatory file. An ontology can link that one ingredient to its specification, supplier lot, test results, claims and market requirements. Instead of merely matching keywords across thousands of documents, AI can recognise that different names refer to the same ingredient and connect it to the details that matter. A question such as “Which approved ingredients could breach the lead limit in Market B?” then shifts from a slow, manual exercise to a rapid, data-driven check.
Where GenAI fits
Generative AI can read supplier documents, scan scientific literature, suggest alternative ingredients and help draft R&D reports. But when information is fragmented, AI can miss important connections or produce answers that are hard to verify. In some cases, it may generate details that sound plausible but are simply not true.
An ontology can help address this by grounding GenAI in structured, connected facts. Rather than guessing from loose text, the model can draw on linked information about an ingredient, its supplier, its test history, the rules it must satisfy and the claims made for it, and show where each answer came from. This makes AI outputs easier to check and, ultimately, easier to trust. The ontology provides the map; GenAI makes that map usable.
Safety built in, not bolted on
In most organisations, even when quality checks run throughout development, some risks only become visible late, once a finished batch reaches the lab. Connected data can bring those risks into view at the design stage. If a developer selects a rice-based protein, the system can flag a potential inorganic arsenic risk well before a pilot batch is made, since rice absorbs arsenic from soil and water more readily than most other cereals. If a recipe changes, implications for allergens and cross-contact can surface immediately. This matters because many foodborne illnesses are preventable, and catching risks upstream reduces rework, delays and costly product recalls.
The scientist stays in the loop
AI can produce a formulation that is confident and wrong. It cannot taste bitterness, feel grittiness or predict how a blend will behave after months in a humid warehouse.
Consider one high-protein beverage project. The AI recommended a pea protein isolate with added calcium and a stabiliser system, a combination that met every target for protein, nutrition and ingredient constraints on paper. In the lab, however, the proteins aggregated after heat processing, leading to visible settling and a chalky mouthfeel. The team had to rework the mineral load and the stabiliser system before the formulation could move forward.
The working rule is simple: AI proposes; scientists decide. Every suggestion should trace back to a source, be tested at the bench and be signed off by a qualified person. This matters most in safety and regulatory decisions, where accountability cannot be delegated to software.
What comes next
The future of food R&D is not about robot chefs. It is about shorter development cycles, because no one has to waste time hunting for information. It is about keeping institutional knowledge within the organisation, even after a scientist moves on. And it is about building safety and compliance into a product from day one, rather than adding them at the end.
The messy, unglamorous work of cleaning, naming and connecting data will decide who gets real value from AI. The advantage may not go to the company with the most powerful model, but to the one whose data both people and machines can understand.
(Vicky Dodani is the Co-founder of Agrizy)

articles.title: "My grandfather fell and remained on the floor for an entire day" - Magic Vision raises €600k for monitoring tech | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Magic Vision, an Italian DeepTech startup developing AI and computer vision technologies to monitor and support older people and vulnerable individuals, has closed a €600k funding round.
Investors include SixS, the Italian company behind Gecos, a management software platform for the nonprofit sector, alongside a group of Italian business angels with expertise in law, compliance and business development.
“Population ageing is putting pressure on care systems, which must meet growing needs with increasingly limited resources and staff. Technology can make a practical contribution by enabling continuous monitoring and timely intervention when needed,” says Lorenzo Mauri, co-founder and CEO of Magic Vision.
Magic Vision’s funding comes alongside several European investments in technology-enabled care during 2026.
Germany’s Patronus raised €11 million for its elderly emergency-response technology, while Spain’s Tucuvi secured €17 million for AI-powered nursing follow-up and Portugal’s Hope Care closed a €6 million round for remote patient monitoring.
Together with Magic Vision, these account for approximately €34.6 million in funding. In Italy, Rome-based VoiceMed reported reaching €1 million in cumulative funding for its device-free respiratory monitoring technology.
“Wearable devices, emergency buttons and other available systems had significant limitations. We therefore decided to use our expertise in artificial intelligence to develop technology capable of recognising risks without requiring a person to wear a device or call for help,” adds Federico Lanzani, co-founder and CTO of Magic Vision.
Magic Vision is an Italian startup founded in 2023 by six co-founders with expertise in AI and computer vision. Based in Meda, in the province of Monza and Brianza, it develops Silver Eye, an environmental monitoring system for older people and vulnerable individuals, designed to support their independence and assist families and care professionals.
Silver Eye uses proprietary AI and computer vision algorithms to analyse people’s activity and rest patterns , identify behavioural anomalies and detect critical events such as falls. Operating through environmental sensors without wearable devices, the system enable individual behavioural monitoring even in dynamic, shared settings, including senior living facilities, cohousing and private homes.
The technology is designed to protect privacy: data is processed locally using edge AI, without storing or transmitting images. Rather than functioning as a video surveillance system, it analyses the information needed to identify potential risks, alerting caregivers only when necessary.
The aim is to support prevention and help older people maintain their independence, providing technology for care models ranging from shared housing and home care to traditional residential and nursing care facilities.
During its growth journey, the startup has benefited from incubation at PoliHub and support from ComoNExT’s NExT Accelerator and Paradigma Exponential Hub , which helped connect the founders with investors. It has also received a €30k award from the Milan Monza Brianza Lodi Chamber of Commerce through the Switch2Product programme.
The funding has enabled Magic Vision to complete development and bring Silver Eye to market.
Already deployed in pilot and commercial projects with Italian care providers, Silver Eye has more than 200 sensors installed, with a target of monitoring over 100 people by the end of 2026.
“The idea for Silver Eye came from a personal experience: when my grandfather fell and remained on the floor for an entire day, I started looking for a solution that could prevent something similar from happening again,” says Federico.
The company is also preparing a €1.5 million funding round to accelerate commercial growth, build a network of partners and distributors across Italy, and begin its European expansion, with the aim of securing its first international customer within 24 months.

articles.title: Apple Creator Studio ahora tiene agentes de IA: así cambia la forma de editar en Mac, iPad y iPhone
articles.text:
Apple anunció una actualización de Apple Creator Studio con nuevas funciones de inteligencia artificial y herramientas para editar vídeo, imágenes, música y documentos. La colección incorporará contenido de MotionVFX en Final Cut Pro, Relleno generativo en Pixelmator Pro y asistentes inteligentes en Logic Pro, Keynote, Pages y Numbers. Las novedades llegarán a la App Store en noviembre de 2026 y estarán incluidas para quienes ya estén suscritos.
Aunque el titular de la actualización apunta a los agentes de IA, las funciones varían según la aplicación. Algunas ayudan a realizar tareas mediante instrucciones en lenguaje natural; otras conectan herramientas de terceros con las aplicaciones para leer y modificar contenido. Apple las presenta como una forma de facilitar flujos de trabajo y ayudar a los usuarios a aprender a utilizar sus programas.
Final Cut Pro integra contenido de MotionVFX
Final Cut Pro para Mac ofrecerá acceso integrado a miles de elementos de MotionVFX, entre ellos plantillas, gráficos, títulos y transiciones, además de recursos para rotoscopia, seguimiento y gradación de color. Los suscriptores también podrán abrir desde la aplicación un centro de contenido seleccionado por Apple con vídeos, fotografías y fondos de archivo.
La actualización conectará Final Cut Pro con Pixelmator Pro. Los editores podrán abrir una imagen de la línea de tiempo en esa aplicación, modificarla y guardar los cambios directamente en el proyecto. Apple también señala que será posible generar imágenes a partir de descripciones de texto y aplicar ediciones rápidas.
Entre las mejoras del flujo de trabajo figuran nuevas opciones para suavizar fotogramas clave, la posibilidad de separar clips de la historia principal y colocarlos en otras partes de la línea de tiempo, y la incorporación de 23 idiomas de transcripción. Según la compañía, esto facilitará la creación de subtítulos y la búsqueda de momentos dentro del material grabado.
Motion también sumará complementos de MotionVFX y herramientas para generar y editar imágenes mediante texto. Compressor, por su parte, podrá codificar vídeos grabados en modo Cine con el iPhone 18 Pro y el iPhone Duo.
Pixelmator Pro permitirá editar imágenes con instrucciones
La principal novedad de Pixelmator Pro es Relleno generativo. La herramienta permite seleccionar una zona de la imagen y describir qué cambio se quiere realizar. También se puede delimitar el área con las opciones de selección libre, rápida o magnética de la aplicación.
Apple afirma que la función adapta la iluminación, la perspectiva y la textura para integrar el elemento añadido en la imagen. Los resultados podrán ampliarse con superresolución y combinarse con las capas del proyecto, ya sea como parte de una capa existente o como una nueva con máscara inteligente.
Asistentes de IA en Logic Pro y las aplicaciones de productividad
Logic Pro para Mac incorporará un asistente inteligente en versión beta, basado en modelos de Apple y OpenAI. Podrá orientar a los usuarios en tareas de producción, ayudar a comenzar una canción o configurar una pista vocal mediante una instrucción. La beta estará disponible en inglés de Estados Unidos y requerirá macOS 27 Golden Gate o posterior en un Mac compatible con Apple Intelligence.
Keynote, Pages y Numbers también tendrán asistentes beta para suscriptores. En Keynote, ayudarán a diseñar y perfeccionar diapositivas; en Pages, a redactar y reorganizar textos; y en Numbers, a organizar y visualizar datos, recomendar gráficos y crear tablas a partir de instrucciones. Estas funciones también exigirán un dispositivo compatible con Apple Intelligence y un sistema operativo de la versión 27 o posterior.
Las tres aplicaciones añadirán compatibilidad con Model Context Protocol (MCP), que permitirá a herramientas y agentes externos leer contenido, realizar ediciones y ejecutar acciones automatizadas. Keynote admitirá además el formato abierto .keyx, diseñado para que sistemas externos puedan acceder a sus archivos.
Disponibilidad y precios
Las actualizaciones llegarán en noviembre y serán gratuitas para los suscriptores actuales. En Estados Unidos, la suscripción costará 12,99 dólares al mes o 129 dólares al año, con un mes de prueba. Estudiantes universitarios y docentes podrán acceder por 2,99 dólares mensuales o 29,99 anuales. Hasta seis personas podrán compartir la suscripción mediante En familia.
Apple mantendrá también las versiones de compra única de varias aplicaciones en la Mac App Store. Las funciones beta de IA, en cambio, tendrán requisitos de sistema y compatibilidad específicos, por lo que no estarán disponibles en todos los dispositivos.

articles.title: The data center boom has an upside: innovation for the US grid | TechCrunch
articles.text:
The AI boom has led to a gargantuan surge in energy demand across the country. Critics say this upswell in connections is enacting a stress test on America’s aging grid infrastructure. Worries abound that, in the short term, the energy crunch could lead to surging electrical bills and, in the long term, may eventually lead to outages or other technical problems.
At TechCrunch Disrupt earlier this month, industry insiders tempered much of this criticism with optimism about how the flood of new energy connections could actually be opening the door for grid modernization. Apoorv Bhargava, founder and CEO of WeaveGrid, Tim Heidel, CEO of Veir, and Kristin Eberhard, VP of policy at Rewiring America, said that though the grid faces new challenges, there are also plenty of new opportunities as well.
“It’s a very different electric grid, right?” said Bhargava. “We’re dealing with a ton of new variables, including renewable energy. We’re dealing with a ton of new load in the form of electric vehicles and data centers and heat pumps, and the ability to manage and orchestrate is fundamentally what utilities are now grappling with.”
While all of those new connections are driving an ever larger amount of stress to the grid, Bhargava’s company hopes to provide the kind of load orchestration and management that helps utilities maximize the potential of the current system. WeaveGrid’s software can help organizations efficiently deploy energy while also optimizing connections to reduce utility payers’ bills, the founder said.
Heidel, on the other hand, runs a company that is working to build out and expand the physical infrastructure of the grid, while also making it run much more efficiently. Veir sells superconductive power lines that promise to transfer energy at a much more efficient rate than traditional ones. Veir’s cables can carry power five times farther than traditional cables while also requiring 20 times less space, the company has said. Earlier this month the startup raised $110 million in a Series C funding round.
“The scale of the investment in AI infrastructure is driving a tremendous amount of innovation,” said Heidel. “There’s a ton of new technologies that are coming off the shelves and starting to get to scale that, pulled together, can actually really make sure that data centers are the best community neighbors and citizens they can possibly be.”
He added: “I think that we really need to look at ways that we can really adopt all of that as fast as possible to ease this next stage of growth.”
Eberhard, whose organization advocates for household electrification, also said that while the surge in data center energy demand has spurred a new urgency to the modernization cause, it has also created an environment where industries are ready to try new things.
“I feel like this era of AI and load growth is a very improv era,” Eberhard said. “There’s a lot of yes-and-ing going on. So yes, we need more transmission lines. Yes, we need more centralized power plants, and we also need to make sure that we’re taking advantage of all this other stuff that we had previously been leaving on the table when we didn’t have this urgency of the AI demand.”

articles.title: Google begins certifying Registered App Stores for Android, but not in the US
articles.text:
Running an app ecosystem has gotten a lot more complex for Google after its loss in the Epic Games antitrust case. While US users can access app stores in Google Play by court order, international users will use Google’s voluntary Registered App Stores program. Google has announced that stores wishing to be part of that program are now free to apply, and support will roll out to some Android devices later this year.
App stores accepted into the program will enjoy preferential treatment on the Android platform. Users of approved stores will be able to install apps with a single click, similar to the experience in the Play Store. These stores will also be allowed to update apps silently in the background like Google’s store does.
“In March, we announced the Registered App Stores program to give third-party app stores a more streamlined way to reach users while maintaining the safety and security of the Android ecosystem,” said a Google spokesperson. “Eligible app stores outside the US can now apply to register their stores ahead of the new simplified installation experience rolling out to users later this year.”
The Android Registered App Stores program was initially Google’s backup plan. After losing its appeal of Judge James Donato’s verdict, Google was faced with a number of remedies, like allowing third-party billing and sharing app catalogs with rival stores. The most dramatic shift was the court’s requirement that Google distribute third-party stores within Google Play.
Google and Epic, having patched things up following the trial, attempted to settle the case in a way that gave Google more control. Registered App Stores were intended as a replacement for hosting the stores in Google Play, provided they could adhere to a baseline level of trust and safety. Google intended to use this program in the US and internationally, but the companies withdrew the settlement when the court signaled it would not be approved.

articles.title: 'VisionQuest' recupera por sorpresa a uno de los primeros villanos de Marvel: no le veíamos desde 'Iron Man'
articles.text:
ATENCIÓN: El artículo contiene SPOILERS de VisionQuest 1x06.
El estreno de los nuevos episodios de VisionQuest esta semana ha devuelto a los fans de Marvel a un personaje totalmente inesperado. La serie protagonizada por Paul Bettany sigue el camino de la nueva Visión Blanca. Atrapado en su propio conflicto interno, el personaje no es capaz de conectar emocionalmente con los recuerdos de su versión anterior. Pero no por ello dejará de intentar sentirse, de verdad, humano.
En ese camino se cruza con Tommy Shepherd, que asegura ser el hijo de Wanda y Visión. Sin embargo, el villano Paladín, cuyo nombre real es Paul Denning, le secuestra con el fin de atraer a Visión a una trampa y poder capturarle para entregárselo a su misterioso Cliente. Pero lo cierto es que esta peligrosa figura, cuya identidad sigue siendo desconocida, ha puesto punto y final al contrato que les unía.
Bajo este contexto, todos los personajes se reúnen en Madripoor. Allí, Visión y el Paladín se enfrentan en una vertiginosa escena de acción, con Tommy como recompensa. Pero, de pronto, ambos se ven sorprendidos por una banda que comienza a tirotearles. Y el líder de todos ellos no es otro que Raza Hamidmi al-Wazar. Los fans más veteranos de Marvel recordarán perfectamente a este personaje porque era el líder de la banda terrorista de los 10 Anillos que secuestraron a Tony Stark en Iron Man.
En aquella película, Raza Hamidmi al-Wazar parecía morir traicionado por Obadiah Stane, que mandaba a sus hombres para asesinarlo. Sin embargo, jamás vimos su cadáver. Y ahora, casi veinte años después, el actor Faran Tahir ha regresado como Raza en la serie de VisionQuest. Una confirmación de que este villano se ha mantenido vivo y activo en las sombras.
¿Es Raza Hamidmi al-Wazar el Cliente de VisionQuest?
Con esta impactante revelación del retorno de Raza Hamidmi al-Wazar a Marvel, muchos podrían pensar que el villano es el verdadero Cliente, el gran antagonista en las sombras de VisionQuest. Pero pronto salimos de dudas. Resulta que no, Raza no es esta misteriosa figura, sino otro de sus mercenarios.
El Cliente ha contratado a Raza y sus hombres para poner fin al desastre generado por el Paladín y, de paso, secuestrar definitivamente a Visión. De hecho, como vemos en VisionQuest 1x06, está a punto de conseguirlo. Al final, los protagonistas se salvan porque E.D.I.T.H. consigue tomar control de los drones de los terroristas. El propio Paladín es quien le da el golpe definitivo a Raza para dejarle fuera de combate.
Date de alta en Disney+ ahora y ahorra gracias a la suscripción anual, con la que podrás disfrutar de todo su catálogo de series y películas. Acceso a los últimos estrenos, al catálogo de Star y ESPN* y a los mejores documentales de National Geographic.
*ESPN solo está disponible en Latinoamérica. Ahorro respecto a 12 meses de suscripción mensual.
Tras este breve pero intenso regreso de Raza Hamidmi al-Wazar a Marvel, se desconoce si volveremos a ver al personaje en el futuro. No ha muerto, por lo que no hay nada descartado. Pero lo cierto es que todo apunta a que su retorno no era más que un guiño a los fans de la saga y una nueva manera de conectar la nueva serie al resto de la franquicia. Los dos últimos episodios de VisionQuest se estrenarán en Disney+ el 3 y el 10 de noviembre (el 4 y el 11 de noviembre en España), respectivamente.

articles.title: Google built AI agents a world to practice in. The physics still aren’t quite right.
articles.text:
Google built AI agents a world to practice in. The physics still aren’t quite right.
Google DeepMind introduced Genie 4 on Tuesday, a world model that renders interactive environments in real time with simulated physics, human motion, and native audio. The photorealistic demos are seriously impressive, but arguably the real draw for anyone building AI agents is that Genie 4 gives them somewhere to run multi-step tasks before it counts.
Tejas Kulkarni, a research director at Google DeepMind, describes the approach at a press briefing as a move toward “these hybrid world models,” with Gemini writing the code and text and Genie turning it into a running scene. It gives developers a way to generate test environments on demand, although how closely those simulations reflect real-world conditions remains an open question about reliability.
It gives developers a way to generate test environments on demand.
How Gemini steers Genie 4
Genie 4 uses several Gemini models to keep its simulations running. Gemini Omni helps shape the environment, while Gemini 3.8 Flash follows what’s happening, plans the next steps and adjusts when something changes.
Instead of producing a finished video, Genie 4 lets users interact with the world as it’s generated. They can move through it with a keyboard, change the camera angle or use text prompts to alter the environment without restarting the simulation.
Instead of producing a finished video, Genie 4 lets users interact with the world as it’s generated.
Rehearsing robots in simulation
Google’s clearest example puts Apptronik’s Apollo humanoid through a game of checkers, with Gemini 4 Argon planning each move and Genie 4 rendering the results as captions steer the scene.
The company is also exploring how the technology could support its Gemini Robotics research, which gives developers the ability to test agents in changing environments without having to rebuild each simulation from scratch.
Where the physics breaks down
The catch is that Genie 4 can’t always keep those environments consistent. Objects can shift position or behave unpredictably during longer sessions, and Google acknowledges that the physics isn’t always accurate.
That complicates agent evaluations, particularly when tasks involve remembering locations or returning to earlier states. A failed run could reflect a problem with the agent or the simulation itself, and Google hasn’t demonstrated that Genie 4 can replace traditional physics engines in high-stakes testing.
Game developers are using Genie 4 to explore prototypes and test game mechanics before writing engine code, while enterprise partners are looking at ways to generate their own testing scenarios.
The company hasn’t published benchmarks showing how Genie 4 performs across repeated agent tests.
The company hasn’t published benchmarks showing how Genie 4 performs across repeated agent tests. This includes whether the same prompt produces consistent results, leaving leaves developers with little to go on when deciding whether to use it in automated testing.
Who gets Genie 4 access
For now, only trusted testers have access. Google plans to expand availability to Google AI Ultra subscribers through Project Genie and select partners through the Gemini API and Google AI Studio. There’s no word yet on pricing, a wider release or performance guarantees.

articles.title: Introducing Build-A-Chip-Bench: From Workload Specification to GDS
articles.text:
Home >
                                                                    Systems & Design >
                                                                Introducing Build-A-Chip-Bench: From Workload Specification to GDS                                                    
Systems & Design
                        WHITEPAPERS
		
Evaluate AI agents from workload specification through GDS layout, using open-source tools and an open-source PDK to assess their ability to complete the chip-design workflow.
								October 28th, 2026 - 
								By: ChipAgents
								
							
Existing chip design benchmarks test isolated steps, such as writing RTL from a specification, and are increasingly saturated. ChipAgents is developing Build-A-Chip-Bench with contributions from Nvidia to the benchmark suite and scoring rubric. The benchmark evaluates AI agents from workload specification through GDS layout, using open-source tools and an open-source PDK to assess their ability to complete the chip-design workflow. Each design must pass a hard gate, covering functional correctness against a hidden verification IP as well as routability, hold timing, and DRC, and designs that pass are scored on PPA against the task’s constraints. The best agent passes the hard gate on 65% of tasks and reaches an overall score of 16.6%. Frontier agents struggle to revisit earlier decisions, protect working behavior while optimizing, and plan around slow tool runs.

articles.title: Quantum Computing’s Energy Bill Is Coming, and It’s Unpriced - EE Times
articles.text:
UN researchers project that by 2030, data centers will use twice the power and water they used in 2025, largely because of AI. Energy has become a key constraint to consider in scaling up compute. The same goes for scaling up quantum computing, yet progress is still often only measured in raw qubit count and fidelities. Those are key, of course, but by themselves they fail to tell you what amount of useful compute power your system brings. In the end, we’re pushing our technology to get it to a useful scale, which in the most basic sense means that value per solution must outweigh cost per solution.
Quantum computers hold real promise in utility applications, be it in faster drug discovery, accelerating materials research, or enabling more efficient machine learning once they run at a useful scale. Getting there means taking the cost of running these machines as seriously as the physics behind them to make them economical. A better understanding of how much useful compute power systems generate for each unit of energy or dollar you put into it is key for that.
At utility scale, compute per watt is what counts
There are two parts of that equation. The denominator is power: Cooling and control electronics in a quantum computer draw power continuously. That power draw will be significant, as large-scale quantum computers will consume tens of megawatts. However, because quantum compute can scale exponentially with the size of the processor, the numerator of the equation is much more important. What matters most is the amount of compute power the system generates for every watt it consumes. This is driven by the QPU architecture of the system.
Classical computing encountered similar issues. For years, processors were judged by clock speed. But as data centers scaled, power became the bottleneck, and performance per watt became the metric that mattered. Since 2007, the Green500 has ranked the world’s supercomputers by computations per watt, next to the TOP500’s ranking by raw speed.
Following the emergence of AI and the hyperscale compute buildout, compute demand is still outrunning supply. The industry has spent the years since catching up, adding power and cooling retrospectively rather than designing for it from the start. Operators are now resorting to on-site gas generators to power new data centers, which is a step back. With quantum, we need to build an energy-efficient architecture before we hit that same inflection point.
From qubit count to compute per watt and per dollar
This is why the industry needs a better yardstick. Compute-per-watt should be the core metric: the amount of useful computation you get for each watt the system consumes. It pushes buyers and builders to weigh output against the energy that produced it, rather than counting the qubits and assuming the rest follows.
The metric counts the power drawn by cooling, control electronics, and classical computing on one side, and the useful quantum computation delivered on the other. If buyers and builders adopt compute-per-watt as a common measure, the whole industry will optimize for the useful processing power it can get from each unit of energy. The same logic applies to cost: Compute-per-dollar weighs that output against what the system costs to build and run.
The fix is in how the chip is built
Getting more compute per watt comes down largely to how a chip is built. On the power side, the way you design your chip and system architecture determines how much power is needed for cryogenics, control hardware, and classical compute.
On the compute side, the differences between architectures are much larger. There are two main scaling approaches for quantum computers: scaling up and scaling out. Scaling out means taking today’s QPUs and networking them together to scale your quantum computer. Scaling up means overcoming today’s scaling bottlenecks and scaling the QPU itself. Both scale qubit count, but scaling qubit count is not the same as scaling compute power.
A recent study quantifies this, showing that quantum computers built around large QPUs generate up to exponentially more compute power than a networked quantum computer. The difference is explained by the network links, which are significantly slower and more lossy than connections within a single QPU.
This networking penalty is often overlooked when the industry talks about scaling quantum computers, but it can make the difference between running a workload for one hour on 100,000 qubits and running the same workload for 10 years on 100 billion qubits. Networking will be important, but later. We first need to scale up, then scale out.
The decisions get made now
The architecture and manufacturing processes for these systems are being decided today, and those decisions set the course for the next decade. Quantum is at an earlier stage than AI, so the industry still has a choice AI didn’t: We either start measuring progress in a way that accounts for the economics and power usage today or face the consequences of neglecting these key considerations.
