articles.title: KI-Simulation in Echtzeit: So funktioniert Googles neues Weltmodell Genie 4
articles.text:
KI-Simulation in Echtzeit: So funktioniert Googles neues Weltmodell Genie 4
Google Deepmind hat sein neues Weltmodell Genie 4 als Research-Preview veröffentlicht. Laut einem Beitrag des Unternehmens soll es die bisher fotorealistischsten und interaktivsten Welten generieren können. Nutzer:innen haben die Möglichkeit, während der Simulation Eingaben zu machen, um die Szene in Echtzeit zu verändern. Google beschreibt das Modell als „von Haus aus multimodal“: Es kann neben Videos auch passende Musik, Umgebungsgeräusche und Dialoge erstellen.
Google will der Konkurrenz voraus sein
Ein Weltmodell ist ein KI-System, das weiß, wie eine Umgebung funktioniert. Dafür lernt es, welche Objekte, Zusammenhänge und möglichen Zukünfte es gibt. So kann es die Folgen bestimmter Handlungen vorab simulieren, anstatt nur auf Basis von Beobachtungen das nächste Wort oder Bild zu erzeugen. Weltmodelle spielen besonders dort eine Rolle, wo Technologie autonom handeln muss, also beispielsweise bei selbstfahrenden Autos, Robotik oder der Simulation von Wetterereignissen. Sie ermöglichen es, Risiken virtuell durchzuspielen, bevor sie auf die echte Welt übertragen werden.
Laut Techcrunch ist die Branche für Weltmodelle derzeit dabei, sich zu konsolidieren. Bisher gab es einige gut finanzierte Startups, die sich auf diesen Bereich konzentrierten. Diese werden zunehmend aufgekauft oder von großen Konzernen überholt. Die Veröffentlichung von Genie 4 könnte demnach Googles Versuch sein, in diesem hart umkämpften Feld die Nase vorn zu behalten. Laut Angaben des Unternehmens kann das neue Modell eine konsistente Szene bis zu zwei Minuten lang aufrechterhalten. Das ist doppelt so lange wie das Vorgängermodell. Zudem bietet Genie 4 eine verbesserte Physik sowie menschenähnlichere Charaktere.
Alles ist möglich: So funktioniert Genie 4
Gemini, Googles KI-Modell, ist jetzt enger in Genie 4 integriert und fungiert als eine Art KI‑Regisseur. Es plant Schritte und überprüft Einzelbilder, während Genie die visuellen Elemente erstellt. „Gemini Omni verankert die Simulationen in einem realistischen Erscheinungsbild und Verhalten, während andere Gemini-Modelle die komplexen Schlussfolgerungen liefern, die erforderlich sind, um die Kohärenz und Kontinuität einer Simulation aufrechtzuerhalten”, heißt es im Beitrag von Google Deepmind. „Auf dieser Grundlage können Sie ein Ereignis in Gang setzen und Genie 4 simuliert, was als Nächstes geschieht: Wie die Welt reagiert, wie sie klingt und wie sich die Menschen darin bewegen, reagieren und sprechen.“
In einem Video zeigt das Labor, wie sich Videos in Echtzeit anpassen lassen. Nutzer:innen verändern die Simulation per natürlicher Sprache. So können sie beispielsweise das Wetter ändern oder ein neues Objekt hinzufügen. Zwischen den Eingaben überwacht und steuert Gemini die Szene, damit sich die Welt nahtlos weiterentwickelt. Laut dem Unternehmen setzt Genie 4 dabei neue Maßstäbe für den Realismus in der interaktiven Echtzeit-Simulation. Dank eines fortgeschrittenen physikalischen Verständnisses könne es realistische Szenarien wie Aerodynamik und Kollisionen simulieren. Google Deepmind erklärt zudem, dass das Verstehen und Simulieren der Welt ein entscheidender Aspekt bei der Entwicklung einer AGI sei.
Nur für ausgewählte Tester:innen verfügbar
Bei der Entwicklung von Genie 4 hat Google eigenen Angaben zufolge mit Tester:innen aus den Bereichen Journalismus, Bildung, Gaming und Ingenieurwesen zusammengearbeitet. Ziel war es, zu verstehen, wie interaktive Weltmodelle reale Arbeitsabläufe unterstützen können. Als kommerzielle Anwendungsfälle nennt das Unternehmen interaktives Lernen und Robotik. Genie 4 ist vorerst allerdings nur für „vertrauenswürdige Tester:innen“ verfügbar. In den kommenden Wochen sollen Abonnent:innen von Google AI Ultra, Early-Access-Partner der Gemini-API und von Google AI Studio sowie Nutzer:innen von Project Genie folgen. Interessierte können sich schon jetzt für eine Warteliste eintragen.

articles.title: ANYbotics begins delivery of legged inspection robot built for explosive atmospheres - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
ANYbotics begins delivery of legged inspection robot built for explosive atmospheres
ANYbotics AG, a leading provider of four-legged inspection robots for heavy industry, today announced it’s shipping the world’s first legged robot designed to operate in dangerous environments where a spark or fire could trigger an explosion.
The new robot, named ANYmal X, is a dog-like robot that can patrol and inspect equipment where specialist technicians otherwise move between heavy equipment wearing dampened gear and avoid situations that might trigger an explosion.
The platform is now shipping to several oil, gas and chemical industry leaders, including multinational energy company Equinor ASA and Swiss-Dutch specialty chemical company DSM-Firmenich AG.
“Four years of pioneering engineering with more than ten patents went into ANYmal X,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Péter Fankhauser. “Many experts thought a legged robot could never be made safe for explosive atmospheres. Oil, gas and chemical plants are among the most hazardous and most costly places to operate.”
Energy and chemical industry leaders BP p.l.c., Equinor, Shell plc, Petroliam Nasional Berhad, Petróleo Brasileiro S.A., BASF SE and SLB N.V. began testing the ANYmal robots in 2023 across hundreds of onshore and offshore facilities through ANYbotics early access program. They used the data and knowledge from their participation to refine the platform into the industrial-grade robot being shipped today.
Making a legged robot safe around flammable gases is not simply a matter of giving it a tougher shell. It means controlling potential ignition sources throughout the machine so its electrical components and hot surfaces cannot set off the surrounding atmosphere.
Legged robots are made up of complex components, which must be isolated from the atmosphere. As a result, they are banned from oil, gas and chemical refineries and other hazardous atmospheres where explosions can happen. In these environments, preventable downtime can translate into massive profit losses.
Autonomous inspection robots target a growing industrial market, with research firms estimating global oil-and-gas inspection robotics revenue at roughly $800 million to $1 billion annually, according to Fortune Business Insights. The broader opportunity includes chemical plants and spending on conventional inspection services, although published estimates do not consistently isolate that combined market.
Undetected equipment failures can cost companies roughly $1.4 trillion each year in downtime, according to ANYbotics. In the oil and gas sector alone, Siemens AG reported a single hour can translate to almost $500,000 and the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health reported that historically extraction workers in the United States face dangerous conditions, creating fatality rates seven times the national average.
Robots to go where no human should
“We asked one question over and over: Which credible event in the life of a walking robot could create an ignition source, and how do we make sure it never does?” said Chief Technology Officer Andrea Corda.
Companies make fixed equipment compliant by housing it in heavy, explosion-proof enclosures, with limited exposure to the outside environment. Legged robots are a completely different endeavor, with exposed cameras and sensors required for navigation and ports needed for docking. Every component must be certified explosion-proof so it won’t ignite a spark, or, if it does, it will prevent heat sources or combustion from spreading to outside environments — all while maintaining payload capacity, agility and operating speed.
The company said it engineered ANYmal X from the ground up to comply with oil, gas and chemical industry safety standards. ANYbotics performed comprehensive ignition risk assessments and implemented safeguards for every potential ignition source.
“Today, more than 50 power, metals and materials customers use this system to run over 120,000 autonomous inspections every month,” said Chief Revenue Officer Thierry Obédé.

articles.title: Après Ledger, deux autres géants des portefeuilles crypto victimes d'un incident de sécurité
articles.text:
2026 est une année noire pour les fabricants de portefeuilles crypto (hardware wallets). Ces boîtiers de petite taille servent à stocker hors ligne des bitcoins, et d’autres cryptomonnaies, afin de les protéger contre d’éventuelles tentatives de piratage. Malheureusement, ce sont désormais les concepteurs de portefeuilles qui se retrouvent dans le colimateur des cybercriminels.
Récemment, la licorne française Ledger a subi une attaque dite « de la chaîne d’approvisionnement ». Des composants espions ont été dissimulés dans certains appareils avant même qu’ils n’arrivent chez les clients. Ces composants étaient programmés pour s’emparer des clés privées des utilisateurs. Plus de 200 millions de dollars de pertes ont été enregistrés par les victimes. Les portefeuilles vendus par certains revendeurs, dont Mediamarkt en Europe, ont été retirés des rayons. Ledger parle d’une « attaque localisée sur un canal de distribution », et non d’une cyberattaque d’envergure à l’encontre de son infrastructure.
  À lire aussi : Ceci n’est pas un smartphone – le géant des cryptos Ledger dévoile Atom, un « coffre-fort » sous Android
Phishing, faille et piratage
Dans le sillage de Ledger, deux autres entreprises spécialisées dans les hardware wallets ont été victimes d’un incident de sécurité récemment. Le fabricant américain Foundation a alerté ses clients d’une vague de phishing qui paraissent tout d’abord anodine. La société révèle que des e-mails d’hameçonnage se sont mis à circuler afin de piéger les investisseurs. Le message, excessivement alarmiste, prétendait que « vos fonds sont en danger », car « un module d’affichage de l’un de nos fournisseurs a été modifié avant de nous parvenir ». Comme on s’y attendait, les pirates cherchent à surfer sur l’inquiétude laissée derrière l’affaire Ledger, en évoquant une attaque de la chaîne d’approvisionnement.
  ANNOUNCEMENT: SPAM EMAILS HAVE BEEN SENT THAT APPEAR TO HAVE COME FROM OFFICIAL FOUNDATION DOMAINS. We have traced this back to one or more compromised API keys on Cloudflare, and have already revoked all API keys. The malicious domain in the spam email has been taken down. Funds stored on Passport are safe and Passport hardware is not compromised. We are working nonstop to discover exactly what happened and will put out a report ASAP.
— FOUNDATION (@FoundationHQ) October 26, 2026
Les mails provenaient bel et bien des domaines officiels de l’entreprise, ce qui tend à endormir la méfiance des cibles. L’entreprise a retracé l’origine des mails à une ou plusieurs clés d’API Cloudflare compromises. Zach Herbert, cofondateur et PDG de la marque, a ensuite précisé qu’une partie de l’infrastructure de Foundation a été piratée.
L’attaquant s’est appuyé sur une faille d’une application qui donnait accès à la boîte mail du support client de la marque. Une fois dans la messagerie, ils ont pu envoyer de faux e-mails en se faisant passer pour Foundation. Foundation assure avoir colmaté la brèche et que ses portefeuilles physiques restent sécurisés. Les fonds des clients ne sont pas en danger. Néanmoins, l’incident suscite l’inquiétude des utilisateurs, car des données personnelles ont été exfiltrées.
Près de 19 000 appareils à détruire
Keystone, un autre fabricant de wallets, s’est également retrouvé dans le colimateur des truands quelques jours plus tôt. Le fabricant a détecté un accès non autorisé à son site le 20 octobre. Un intrus a pu récupérer les données de livraison des clients (noms, coordonnées, adresses, détails de commande) sans déclencher la moindre alerte de sécurité. Au total, 25 964 fiches clients ont été volées.
  We owe you an apology. On October 20, we detected unauthorized access to our official website. After verifying API activity with Shopify, we confirmed on October 23 that a third party obtained customer shipping information. You trusted us with those details, and we’re sorry we didn’t keep them safe. Exposed: names, contact details, shipping addresses, and order details (items and prices). Not exposed: payment card or bank details, recovery phrases, private keys, or wallet passwords. We’ve blocked access, fixed the vulnerability, opened an investigation, and are emailing affected customers. Scammers may pose as Keystone by phone, text, email, or mail, offering refunds, replacement devices, or “fixes” for your order or address. None of it is from us. NEVER share your recovery phrase or private keys, and NEVER enter your recovery phrase into a device you didn’t order. We will never ask for them. Don’t click links in unexpected messages. Type https://t.co/7km8AZM288 yourself. A detailed report is coming soon. Until then, trust only our official channels. If anything feels off, email [email protected]. We’d rather hear from you than have you take a chance. Again, we’re truly sorry to everyone affected.
— Keystone Hardware Wallet (@KeystoneWallet) October 24, 2026
Pire, l’attaquant a mis la main sur la clé d’authentification unique inscrite du groupe. Elle permet à Keystone de vérifier qu’un appareil est authentique. Gravée en usine, elle est impossible à effacer. Avec la clé en mains, des pirates vont théoriquement pouvoir fabriquer des appareils piégés qui ressemblent à des appareils authentiques. Dos au mur, l’entreprise va détruire les 18 835 appareils de son stock qui reposent sur la clé compromise. En miroir de Foundation, Keystone insiste sur le fait que les clés privées et les phrases de récupération des clients n’ont pas été touchées. Les appareils et les fonds sont en sécurité.
Des incidents qui se ressemblent
Dans les trois incidents, c’est une entité qui gravite autour des fabricants de wallets qui est à l’origine de la cyberattaque. Dans le cas de Ledger, il s’agit d’un maillon de sa chaîne d’approvisionnement. Chez Foundation, il s’agit d’une application tierce. Du côté de Keystone, c’est son site de vente qui a été compromis. Dans tous les cas, les portefeuilles entre les mains des clients sont restés intouchés.

articles.title: Intel's APX offers 'better performance' in Windows 11 according to new Insider setting — Microsoft begins early enablement for Advanced Performance Extensions on Nova Lake CPUs
articles.text:
Intel's APX offers 'better performance' in Windows 11 according to new Insider setting — Microsoft begins early enablement for Advanced Performance Extensions on Nova Lake CPUs
Advanced Performance Extensions, or APX, will bring improved performance to some apps, but there are no chips that support it just yet.
A new "Advanced Performance Extensions (APX)" option has been spotted in a version of Windows 11 made available to Windows Insiders on October 23, with the feature set to enable a boost in application performance on compatible chips. At the moment, those chips don't exist. But when they do, this feature is the one that you'll want to flick on if you're using one of them. The new toggle was reported by Neowin after it was first spotted by a poster on the X social network. The feature debuted in build 29295 as an Experimental build, so it's unlikely that it will make its way to the version of publicly available Windows 11 anytime soon.
Intel announced APX back in 2023, confirming that it features 16 additional general-purpose registers and three-operand instruction formats with a new data destination register for many integer instructions. Doubling the number of general-purpose registers from 16 to 32 will allow code compiled with APX to run with 10% fewer loads and 20% fewer stores than Intel 64's baseline, says Intel. APX has been available in the GCC compiler since version 14, with subsequent versions up to GCC 17, which is targeting a 2027 code freeze, adding additional support. LLVM and MSVC have preliminary support, as well. Although enablement has been going steady for the past two years, developers will still need to recompile their applications with the proper flags for APX-capable CPUs to leverage those instructions.
Not that there's any real need to rush just yet. The fact that no APX-capable chips are on sale yet means that enabling the feature in Windows 11 build 29295 does nothing currently. But it's clear that Microsoft is getting its ducks in a row ahead of time. Intel's Nova Lake Core Ultra 400-series chips are expected to be the first to feature APX support, but they won't break cover until early 2027. Even then, it's likely that the 28-core version will debut first, with the 52-core model made to wait until later in the year. These are consumer chips, of course, with Intel's Xeon 7 'Diamond Rapids' bringing APX support and up to 256 cores to the data center, also in 2027.
The good news is that you might not have to buy a new chip to enjoy improved Windows 11 performance. Five years after Windows 11's debut, Microsoft has already said that it's working to make its operating system play more nicely with machines with just 8GB of RAM. But what Microsoft gives with one hand, it soon takes away: an expansion of the Windows 11 Memory Integrity feature will reduce gaming performance on some systems.

articles.title: Avant l'arrivée de GTA 6, ce SSD Lexar de 1 To compatible PS5 baisse son prix pour faire de la place
articles.text:
Depuis plusieurs mois, le prix des SSD grimpe. La pénurie de composants, aggravée par la demande des centres de données pour l’IA, se répercute sur le stockage grand public. Ça tombe mal pour les joueuses et les joueurs PS5. GTA 6 sort le 19 novembre, et Rockstar ouvre le préchargement le 12. L’éditeur n’a pas encore communiqué officiellement sur le poids de GTA 6, mais le jeu pèserait 210 Go sur PlayStation 5. C’est beaucoup.
Pour ajouter de l’espace sans tout désinstaller, PC Componentes vend le Lexar NQ790 de 1 To à 167,99 €. Le disque est vendu et expédié par l’enseigne, avec livraison et retour gratuits. La livraison est annoncée pour début novembre, donc avant l’ouverture du préchargement de GTA 6.
Le SSD se trouve également au prix de 174,99 € sur Amazon.
C’est quoi, le SSD Lexar NQ790 ?
Le NQ790 de Lexar est un SSD au format M.2 2280. C’est une petite barrette de 22 x 80 mm, qui pèse 6 g et s’enfiche directement sur la carte mère d’un PC ou dans l’emplacement d’extension de la PS5. Il passe par l’interface PCIe 4.0 avec le protocole NVMe. Lexar annonce jusqu’à 7 000 Mo/s en lecture et 6 000 Mo/s en écriture, et dépasse les 5 500 Mo/s recommandés par Sony pour un SSD M.2 destiné à la PS5. Il répond donc au critère de débit, même si les performances réelles dépendent aussi des conditions d’utilisation.
Côté endurance, le Lexar NQ790 est annoncé à 600 TBW, soit 600 To de données pouvant être écrites au total. Pour vous donner un ordre d’idée, cela représente environ 2 800 installations d’un jeu de 210 Go comme GTA 6. Il faut toutefois prendre en compte que le SSD est livré sans dissipateur thermique, alors que Sony en exige un sur la PS5. Il faudra donc prévoir quelques euros de plus pour un dissipateur adapté. Le modèle de Glotrends, vendu 5,99 € sur Amazon, convient très bien.
À ce prix, le Lexar NQ790 est-il une bonne affaire ?
Il y a quelques années, 167,99 € pour 1 To aurait paru cher. Dans le marché actuel, c’est un prix correct pour un SSD PCIe 4.0. Rien ne dit que les prix vont redescendre d’ici la fin d’année. En commandant maintenant, le disque devrait arriver avant le 12 novembre. Vous aurez le temps de l’installer et de le formater. GTA 6 peut ensuite se précharger sans que vous ayez à sacrifier certains jeux de votre bibliothèque. Vous pourrez arriver à Vice City sans faire le ménage dans vos jeux installés la veille de la sortie.

articles.title: OPINION: Scaling is the real test of Europe’s AI boom | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Europe’s AI funding boom is not benefiting every part of the market equally. Recorded Series A–C investment rose by approximately 66% in the first nine months of 2026, yet funding in rounds worth €22.2 million to less than €88.9 million declined by around 8%.
This middle segment is particularly important for AI startups moving beyond their first customers. Expanding internationally, hiring teams and securing larger enterprise contracts can require substantial capital, even for companies operating on a much smaller scale than Europe’s leading AI developers.
The contrasting funding trends raise questions about how Europe’s next generation of AI companies will finance their expansion. While overall investment continues to grow, the more important test may be whether startups can progress from early funding rounds to sustainable businesses without becoming overly dependent on their next investment.
The findings are based on an analysis of Crunchbase funding-round data for the first nine months of 2025 and 2026, using consistent dates and funding stages and correcting identified data issues. The original dollar-based categories were retained, with euro thresholds rounded for readability. Figures follow Crunchbase’s classifications and currency conversions and may differ from public announcements.
How Europe’s AI funding splits across the market
The adjusted Crunchbase sample recorded approximately €15.04 billion in announced Series A–C funding in the first nine months of 2026, up from €9.06 billion a year earlier. The number of recorded funding events increased from 203 to 232. Of these, 196 events in 2025 and 218 in 2026 were included in the round-size breakdown. These figures cover companies tagged as Artificial Intelligence by Crunchbase and do not represent all European AI funding stages.
The growth was concentrated in larger transactions. Rounds worth €88.9 million or more increased from 18 to 33, accounting for approximately 74% of disclosed funding in 2026, up from 59% the previous year. Although the ten biggest investments represented about half of the total, funding outside these transactions also grew.
Smaller rounds became more frequent, increasing from 108 to 124 for investments below €22.2 million. The middle of the market, however, moved in the opposite direction. The €22.2–88.9 million segment saw its share of disclosed funding fall from approximately 29% to 16%. Across all rounds below €88.9 million, recorded funding barely increased, growing by just 2.7% to €3.86 billion.
This uneven growth suggests that Europe’s AI investment boom has not been felt equally across different funding sizes. While more smaller rounds were recorded and large investments attracted substantial capital, the segment between them contracted.
Some of the largest announcements also require caution. NEURA Robotics announced a Series C of up to €1.24 billion, while Multiverse Computing described a round targeting up to €500 million. Excluding both amounts reduced the sample’s overall funding growth from approximately 66% to 47%.
The increase therefore remained substantial even without these transactions, but the headline amounts should not be interpreted as confirmation that all the funding had already been received.
From €98 million to €3 billion: The different costs of scaling AI
Taktile, a Berlin-founded company developing decision technology for financial institutions, raised approximately €51 million in a Series B in February 2025. By June 2026, it had secured another approximately €98 million in Series C funding. The company operates in enterprise software, where expansion means winning more customers and making its technology work inside complex banking systems.
Mistral raised €3 billion in a Series D in September 2026. Developing frontier AI models requires enormous computing resources and research investment. The financing needs of these two companies differ considerably, yet their announcements contribute to the broader picture of an AI funding boom. These examples provide context separately from the statistical sample: Taktile is absent from the European-headquartered export, and Mistral’s Series D falls outside the stages analysed.
Funding activity also increased across all three stages. Series A events rose from 133 to 148, Series B from 51 to 58, and Series C from 19 to 26. Median round sizes grew at every stage, with the most pronounced increase at Series C, where the median rose from €49.3 million to €93.3 million.
These figures do not indicate a broad decline in Series B or C activity. However, they cannot show how easily individual companies secured funding or what conditions investors attached to their investments.
Taktile shows that companies can successfully move through successive funding stages. For other founders, planning that transition means making expensive decisions before they know when the next round will arrive or what terms investors will offer.
The cost of depending on your next funding round
A company may raise capital to enter new markets, hire sales teams and expand its customer base. These plans often assume that another funding round will follow once the business reaches its next growth targets. But expansion can become expensive long before the company reaches those targets.
For an enterprise AI business, new contracts may require extensive customisation and ongoing engineering support. Revenue grows, yet the company spends more than expected to deliver it. Hiring commitments and operating costs continue even when progress falls behind the original plan.
This leaves founders in a difficult position. If they need fresh capital to maintain operations, they have less control over the timing of fundraising and the terms investors offer. A more measured expansion strategy may look less impressive in the short term, but it gives management greater freedom to choose when and how to raise its next round.
The next test for Europe’s AI boom
The next test for Europe’s AI funding market will come in 2027 and 2028, when some of the startups raising smaller amounts today will need substantially more capital to expand. Whether they can secure investments of €27 million, €44 million or more on favourable terms will help determine their ability to grow.
The current data does not show how many companies sought funding unsuccessfully, how long fundraising took or how much capital they needed. It therefore cannot establish a shortage of growth capital across Europe.
The next stage will also put more pressure on business fundamentals. Enterprise AI companies that can retain customers and expand without a corresponding rise in operating costs should have an advantage when seeking further investment. Others may face difficult choices about how quickly they can grow and how much capital they can afford to raise.
It will be worth following the companies that secured smaller rounds in 2025 and 2026. Their progression to larger investments, the time between funding rounds and the terms they receive will help establish whether Europe has a genuine growth-capital constraint.
Europe may continue setting AI investment records. The more consequential development over the next few years will be how many of today’s funded startups manage to reach the next stage and build sustainable businesses. That is where the depth of Europe’s AI funding market will become much clearer.

articles.title: Nio devait arrêter ses stations d'échange de batteries en Europe, il en ouvre une nouvelle
articles.text:
Sur l’A7, entre Francfort et Hanovre, les conducteurs de Nio ne trouvaient aucune station pour changer de batterie. Le constructeur chinois vient d’ouvrir une station près de Kassel, alors qu’il avait assuré à ses clients européens qu’il ne construirait plus aucune station.
C'est un sacré ascenseur émotionnel pour les propriétaires européens de Nio, après avoir appris au printemps que la marque ne construirait plus « ni stations ni bornes en Europe », nous explique Numerama. Chez Nio, le client achète sa voiture sans batterie et loue celle-ci au mois. En Europe, Nio achète seul ces batteries et les garde dans ses comptes, faute de partenaire financier, et chaque station de troisième génération est conçue pour stocker jusqu’à 21 batteries pleines. Plus Nio ouvre de stations, plus il doit donc acheter de batteries. En ouvrant la station de Kassel, il continue de les payer seul, et les conducteurs de sa citadine Firefly ne pourront pas l’utiliser.
Faute de partenaire, Nio paie seul ses batteries européennes
William Li, fondateur et P.-D.G de Nio, avait posé le problème devant des clients norvégiens. « En Europe, nous n’avons ni partenaire ni société de ce type, ce qui veut dire que tous les actifs de batteries fournis via le BaaS seront détenus par nous, dans notre bilan », expliquait-il. Ce partenaire, Nio l’a trouvé en Chine, mais pas en Europe.
Le constructeur a malgré tout ouvert une station sur l’A7, là où ses clients manquaient le plus de solutions. Les conducteurs qui quittaient la station de Reiskirchen, au nord de Francfort, devaient jusqu’ici rouler 290 kilomètres avant la suivante, près de Hanovre. Les propriétaires qui partent du sud de l’Europe vers la Scandinavie sont les premiers concernés. « Ce site comble un vide important sur les axes de circulation nord-sud de l’Europe », a fait valoir l’entreprise.
Geely pourrait apporter à Nio le partenaire qui lui manque. Le groupe chinois s’est engagé à prendre 30 % de NIO Power, qui gère l’échange et la recharge des voitures de Nio, en apportant sa filiale Yiyi Power et 640 millions de yuans. Des responsables de Geely ont ensuite interrogé William Li sur l’Europe. « Tout à l’heure, des collègues de Geely me demandaient aussi si nous devions, l’an prochain, lancer notre plan de réseau d’échange de batteries en Europe et l’annoncer ensemble », a raconté le patron de Nio dans un entretien vidéo diffusé en Chine. Il n’a dit ni quels pays seraient couverts, ni si Geely financerait ce réseau.
Aucune station pour la Firefly, la citadine conçue pour l’Europe
L’obstacle de la Firefly est technique. Nio a dessiné cette petite citadine en priorité pour l’Europe, avec une batterie de 42,1 kWh incompatible avec les stations de troisième génération installées sur le continent, dont celle de Kassel. En Chine, le constructeur a réglé le problème avec des stations de cinquième génération ouvertes aux trois marques du groupe. Devant les propriétaires réunis aux Pays-Bas, la direction européenne avait en revanche exclu ces nouvelles stations du continent, d’après le participant.
Les premières Firefly livrées en Europe ont donc été vendues avec leur batterie, sans abonnement, faute de stations adaptées, et leurs conducteurs rechargent sur une borne. Un conducteur français a encore moins de choix. Nio a installé ses stations en Allemagne, aux Pays-Bas, en Suède, en Belgique et en Norvège, mais aucune en France. Si vous partez de France au volant d’une Nio, vous devrez passer la frontière belge ou allemande avant de pouvoir changer de batterie.
Le BaaS est un modèle où la voiture est vendue sans batterie : l’utilisateur loue la batterie via un abonnement et peut l’échanger en station. Ce système implique que quelqu’un finance et possède le stock de batteries nécessaires aux échanges. En Europe, faute de partenaire financier, Nio doit acheter et détenir lui-même ces batteries comme des actifs dans son bilan, ce qui immobilise beaucoup de capital. Plus le réseau de stations s’étend, plus le besoin en batteries « en réserve » augmente mécaniquement.
Une station d’échange automatise le retrait de la batterie vide et l’installation d’une batterie chargée, puis recharge la batterie retirée en interne. Pour garantir un échange rapide, la station doit disposer d’un stock de batteries pleines, dimensionné selon la fréquentation. Une station de troisième génération peut stocker jusqu’à 21 batteries, ce qui représente un inventaire coûteux à financer et à maintenir. Ce stock est aussi un point critique opérationnel : s’il est insuffisant ou mal adapté aux modèles compatibles, l’échange perd son intérêt face à la recharge sur borne.
L’échange de batterie exige une standardisation stricte : dimensions du pack, points de fixation, connectique haute tension, interfaces de communication et procédures de sécurité doivent correspondre exactement à ce que la station sait manipuler. La Firefly utilise une batterie (42,1 kWh) conçue avec des caractéristiques physiques et/ou d’interface différentes de celles gérées par les stations de troisième génération déployées en Europe. Résultat : même si la station est sur le trajet, elle ne peut pas effectuer l’échange pour ce modèle. En attendant un réseau compatible, les propriétaires de Firefly se reposent sur la recharge classique sur borne, avec batterie achetée plutôt que louée.

articles.title: Nvidia Vera Rubin : baisse des spécifications et de la bande passante GPU — Frandroid
articles.text:
Les caractéristiques de la nouvelle plateforme Vera Rubin ne sont plus tout à fait celles que Nvidia avait annoncées en janvier dernier au CES 2026, puis reprises à la GTC 2026, près d’un an après la première présentation de ces nouveaux GPU à la GTC 2025. La firme les installe progressivement chez les hyperscalers et les laboratoires d’IA de ses gros clients depuis cet été.
Comme l’a relevé cette semaine VideoCardz, la firme a discrètement abaissé, sur la page officielle du Vera Rubin NVL72, la bande passante mémoire des modules HBM4 intégrés aux GPU Rubin, mais aussi le débit des liaisons NVLink de 6e génération. Ces deux changements touchent les GPU Rubin pris isolément, mais aussi les racks Vera Rubin NVL72 et la plateforme HGX Rubin NVL8, note le site spécialisé.
Jusqu’à 26 % de bande passante HBM4 en moins pour certaines configurations
Dans le détail, Nvidia a par exemple réduit de 12,7 % la bande passante des 288 Go de mémoire HBM4, par GPU, prévue sur les racks Vera Rubin NVL72, passant des 22 To/s initialement promis à « seulement » 19,2 To/s. La bande passante NVLink 6 baisse elle aussi, de 3,6 To/s à 3 To/s par GPU, soit 16,7 % de moins.
Le coup de rabot concerne aussi les racks Vera Rubin NVL72 au grand complet, combinant 72 GPU Rubin à 36 CPU Vera. Nvidia avait promis pour ces racks une bande passante HBM4 totale de 1 580 To/s et une bande passante NVLink de 260 To/s. Désormais, la firme parle à la place de 1 400 To/s et 216 To/s, respectivement.
Comme le souligne VideoCardz, la plateforme HGX Rubin NVL8, équipée de huit GPU, est encore plus durement touchée. Sa capacité HBM4 est passée de 2,3 To à 2 To, tandis que sa bande passante mémoire a été ramenée de 176 To/s à 130 To/s (-26 %). La bande passante de son commutateur NVLink recule aussi, de 28,8 To/s à 24 To/s. Nvidia a aussi revu à la baisse les performances d’entraînement annoncées pour cette plateforme, qui passent de 280 à 270 PFLOPS en NVFP4 et de 140 à 130 PFLOPS en FP8.
D’après les versions archivées de la page officielle, consultées par Wccftech, Nvidia a effectué ces changements entre le 1er et le 11 septembre dernier. Ce coup de rabot a donc plus d’un mois, et compte tenu de la ruée vers les solutions Nvidia, il y a peu de chances qu’il freine les ventes de Vera Rubin.

articles.title: Government working to utilise procurement process for promoting startups: DPIIT Secretary
articles.text:
Government working to utilise procurement process for promoting startups: DPIIT Secretary
Elaborating on the move to enhance participation of startups in government procurement, DPIIT Additional Secretary Ateesh Kumar Singh said that there are already certain facilities available in the form of relaxations to the GFR (General Financial Rules).
The government is working to leverage the procurement process to promote startups, a top official of the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade said on Tuesday.
Speaking at the curtain-raiser event for National Startup Awards 6.0, Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) Secretary Amardeep Singh Bhatia said that there is a need for more private initiatives to engage with startups and bring them into their supply chain network.
"We are also working with other agencies to see how government procurement can also be better used for promoting startups by providing them with at least early access to demand," he said.
Elaborating on the move to enhance participation of startups in government procurement, DPIIT Additional Secretary Ateesh Kumar Singh said that there are already certain facilities available in the form of relaxations to the GFR (General Financial Rules).
"Also, here are certain circulars which have been put out by various agencies to make the pathway into the government procurement process easier. The partaking of those benefits still remains a challenge. It is there where we are trying to make sure that the offerings are available to them," he said.
Singh said that a lot of problems also occur due to information asymmetry.
"One part of the problem is to tell people what is available. The second part of the problem is partaking in those things. We are also trying to address challenges in our existing system. We are working with various ministries, including the Department of Finance, Public Enterprises and MSME. This is ongoing work and we will come up with a new framework," he said.
He said that the number of startups in the country has grown to over 2.5 lakh, with more than half of them located in tier 3 and smaller towns.
Under the 6th Edition of the National Startup Awards (NSA 6.0), winning startups across the 20 sectoral categories and the two startup-focused special categories will be eligible for a cash prize of Rs 25 lakh per category, subject to the applicable award guidelines.
The student innovator and aspiring entrepreneur award will carry a total prize pool of Rs 25 lakh across four sub-categories.
In addition to monetary recognition, the National Startup Awards seek to facilitate mentorship, investor engagement, market access, industry partnerships and enhanced visibility within India’s startup ecosystem.
The 20 categories will also include three special categories comprising women-led startups, startups from the north-eastern region and student innovators or aspiring entrepreneurs.

articles.title: Japan's GMO urges customers to shut down PCs amid ransomware threat
articles.text:
The GMO Group has urged customers to disconnect their systems from the internet and shut down computers after a threat actor who breached the company’s Onamae Desktop Cloud threatened to launch a ransomware attack today.
The company later confirmed that data belonging to both the company and its customers had been published online.
The alert concerns a cyberattack on Onamae Desktop Cloud, a popular VPS provider in Japan operated by GMO Internet, a member of GMO Internet Group and one of Japan's largest domain registrars.
Last week, the company announced it detected an intrusion on October 20 that could have installed malware on up to 26,739 customers' servers.
To minimize the risk, the company shut down the servers and reduced service availability before launching an investigation.
The internet company assured customers that their payment information had not been exposed but warned that MetaTrader 4 and MetaTrader 5 (MT4/MT5) credentials and trading-account details may have been exposed or compromised. It urged customers to reset their passwords and terminate active sessions.
Cyberattack escalation
Subsequent updates from the company confirmed that data had been stolen and that the attacker was demanding a ransom of ¥8 billion ($50 million), which GMO said it would not pay. Instead, the company announced it would compensate each customer ¥5,000 ($30) for the inconvenience caused.
On October 26, GMO warned that threat actors planned to leak customer information online and trigger a ransomware payload planted on customer servers earlier in the attack.
The next day, the company asked customers to disconnect their PCs from the internet, shut them down, and unplug all cables before noon, while it worked with Trend Micro to recover from the cyberattack.
“Once you have a backup, disconnect the network, power it down, and unplug the cord that connects to your PC,” advised GMO to customers.
The company said it was scanning customer systems to determine whether malware was still present, and offered equivalent PC replacements to those who suffered damages from a ransomware attack.
In a report published earlier today, GMO confirmed that the threat actor had published company and customer data, prompting efforts to verify the authenticity of the leaked information.
For customers whose information was exposed, GMO said it will consider additional financial compensation.
It appears that the attacker never acted on their threat, as no ransomware was activated on customer machines.
The company warned people and the media not to disseminate the exposed information, announcing it will take legal action against those who do, while reaffirming its refusal to pay the attackers.

It’s Day 1 at Moonshot 2026! ☀️
Let’s talk at Moonshot!
You’ve been reading our stories. Now, we’d love to hear yours.
If you’re attending Moonshot today, we’re inviting TC Daily readers to sit down with members of the TechCabal newsroom for a conversation.
Bring us an African tech story you’re trying to understand, a question you’ve been meaning to ask, or even a take of ours you disagree with. We’d love to talk about it.
We’re setting aside a few 15-minute slots at the TechCabal booth on October 28 and 29. Pick a time that works for you, tell us what you’d like to discuss, and we’ll see you there.
Read smart insights about Francophone Africa’s tech ecosystem—weekly.
Banking
FirstRand goes bank shopping in Kenya, again
FirstRand has spent about 14 years window-shopping Kenya’s banking sector. The South African banking group may finally be ready to buy.
What happened? FirstRand, the parent company of First National Bank (FNB) and Rand Merchant Bank (RMB), has stepped up its search for a Kenyan lender. Mary Vilakazi, the bank’s chief executive officer, said the group would rather buy a smaller bank at the right price and grow it than pay a premium for one of Kenya’s biggest lenders.
No target has been named. FirstRand is also looking beyond banking at businesses such as insurance and investment banking as it tries to build a broader East African operation.
Explain like I’m new here: FirstRand is not new to Kenya. In 2012, it opened a representative office in Nairobi, mainly through RMB, to arrange infrastructure and project-finance deals. But a representative office cannot take deposits or run a full retail bank.
Even then, FirstRand said it wanted to buy a mid-sized Kenyan lender. It never did. High valuations made acquisitions difficult, so the group spent years operating on the market’s edges instead.
Between the lines: Kenyan banks made KES 241.65 billion ($1.9 billion) in combined profits last year, up 16.3%. At the same time, smaller lenders are under pressure to build enough capital to meet a KES 10 billion ($77 million) minimum by 2032, which could create more willing sellers.
FirstRand therefore does not need to win a bidding war for a trophy bank. Buying a smaller lender would give it a banking licence, deposits, and customers, then let it add FNB’s retail products and RMB’s corporate business over time.
Zoom out: South Africa’s banks are crowding into Kenya. Nedbank has completed its 66% acquisition of NCBA, while Standard Bank already operates Stanbic and is looking for more scale.
FirstRand has watched Kenya for more than a decade. The interesting part now is whether rising consolidation finally produces a bank at a price it is willing to pay.

Companies
Safaricom fires 118 employees over fraud
Safaricom fired 118 employees for fraud in the year to March, roughly one every three days. It is the fourth year in a row that the number has risen at Kenya’s largest telecom company and M-PESA’s operator.
What happened? Dismissals jumped from 113 in the previous year. Safaricom also issued three disciplinary warnings and referred 14 cases to law enforcement. The misconduct included theft, falsifying company records, and unauthorised access to customer call records.
Safaricom separately recovered KES 953 million ($7.4 million) in inflated commissions paid to agents after its monitoring systems flagged irregular payments. The company has not linked those recoveries directly to the 118 employees who were fired.
Explain like I’m new here: Fraud is particularly sensitive at Safaricom because the company sits on much more than phone records. M-Pesa processed KES 41.68 trillion ($323 billion) across 46.4 billion transactions in the year to March. Employees, dealers and agents can therefore access customer identities, SIM registrations and a payments network used by tens of millions of people.
Safaricom has dealt with insider fraud for years, including unauthorised system access, fraudulent SIM swaps and misuse of M-PESA processes. It has steadily added automated monitoring and machine-learning tools to catch suspicious activity.
Between the lines: More dismissals do not automatically mean fraud is getting worse. Safaricom has expanded the operations its fraud reporting covered in recent years, while better analytics can uncover misconduct that previously went unnoticed.
A more useful measure is whether actual losses and successful attacks fall. Safaricom says its new SIM-swap system, which runs 18 automated checks before a line can be replaced, has already cut fraudulent swaps by 65%.
What to watch: Safaricom is increasingly taking sensitive decisions away from individual employees and agents and putting them into automated systems. If those controls work, future fraud reports should eventually show more than people getting caught. They should show fewer successful fraud attempts in the first place.

Fintech
Moniepoint is restructuring its engineering and product teams
On October 19, Moniepoint, a Nigerian fintech unicorn, informed employees of an internal restructuring affecting roles across backend, frontend, mobile, quality assurance, and product management. The company says some positions will become redundant as it moves to smaller teams that own products from start to finish. Moniepoint has offered affected employees five months’ salary to leave voluntarily, while saying it will first look for suitable roles elsewhere in the business. The company has not disclosed how many employees will be affected.
Explain like I’m new here: Moniepoint became a unicorn in 2024 after raising $110 million, bought a 78% stake in Kenya’s Sumac Microfinance Bank in March, and says its subsidiaries now process more than $400 billion in annual digital payments. In October, one employee said the company hired more than 120 people, while Moniepoint has previously said it was struggling to fill hundreds of senior technical roles. However, in August, Moniepoint phased out MonieWorld, its UK-Nigeria remittance product, less than 18 months after launch.
Why the restructuring? The fintech says the restructuring is part of a regular strategic review as the business moves into its next growth stage. It is moving to a platform-group model, where smaller teams own specific product areas, and it is also creating platform architect roles to oversee the shared technology underneath those teams. The restructuring and growth reflect a company still expanding, but becoming more selective about where it puts people and money.
The bigger picture: Moniepoint is also joining a tech-industry shift towards smaller teams. Block, the parent company of Square and Cash App, cut about 40% of its workforce earlier this year, citing AI and a leaner organisational structure. Jumia and Zap Africa have also tied workforce changes to efficiency and AI. Moniepoint says AI is not the reason for this restructuring, although the company has discussed internally how AI could streamline product-management work.

Funding
South Africa’s CrissCross gets Circle backing for stablecoin expansion
Stablecoins are having their moment in African payments, and Circle, the company behind USDC, is backing the infrastructure that wants to make them actually useful.
What happened? CrissCross, a South African cross-border payments company, has received an undisclosed investment from Circle Ventures, Circle’s corporate venture arm. The investment was made through CrissCross’s parent company, Stitch Group. The money will help CrissCross expand its payment connections and liquidity across Africa, while building out stablecoin settlement for enterprise customers.
Explain like I’m new here: Stablecoins such as USDC are digital tokens designed to maintain a stable value against a currency, usually the US dollar. That makes them useful for moving dollar value between markets. African fintechs are beginning to build around this idea.
Flutterwave announced a Circle Ventures investment in July and added USDC settlement to its payments platform. Onafriq has also been working with Circle on regulated stablecoin settlement across its network of more than 40 African markets. CrissCross partnered with Velocity in October to connect institutional stablecoin liquidity to local collections and FX across more than 30 African markets.
Why Circle is interested: Every new payment platform that builds USDC into its infrastructure potentially creates another route for the stablecoin to move through the financial system. Sub-Saharan Africa also received more than $205 billion in on-chain crypto value between July 2024 and June 2025.
CrissCross says it operates across more than 30 markets and supports more than 20 currencies. The investment should help it deepen those local connections and give enterprises more ways to move between stablecoins and local currencies.

articles.title: Meta gets $3 billion from Nvidia, team up to make Muse AI faster and cheaper to run
articles.text:
What just happened? One day after Meta announced plans to raise $95 billion to fuel its AI spending, Nvidia has confirmed it will invest $3 billion in Meta's equity offering. Team Green calls the move a strengthening of the companies' AI partnership, one that will deepen their collaboration on the Muse AI models.
When Meta announced its stock offering yesterday, it was reported that Nvidia, AMD, and Broadcom had indicated interest in buying up to $5 billion worth of the company's shares collectively. The world's largest company by market cap has now confirmed its contribution.
The original fundraising plans comprised roughly $35 billion in initial offerings and a separate $60 billion share-sale program, expected after Meta's new nonvoting Class C shares begin trading in early 2027. That later program remains subject to final terms. Reuters reports that Meta increased the overall fundraising figure to $97.5 billion on Tuesday.
Nvidia says the expanded partnership will focus on improving training and inference performance across Muse and its family of models, while reducing the cost of running them. The companies claim Muse has delivered strong benchmark results and surging downloads since launch, though there are no included figures.
There is, unsurprisingly, more Nvidia hardware involved. Meta plans to expand its deployment of Vera Rubin systems and Vera CPUs, alongside Spectrum-X Ethernet networking and BlueField-4 technology. The aim is to squeeze more performance from each watt and improve the movement of data across its infrastructure.
The pair are also considering further work on Nvidia's OpenShell framework for deploying agents safely and Sentry for monitoring their behavior.
Muse sits at the center of Mark Zuckerberg's push for personal superintelligence. Meta describes it as an agent that can take action across everyday services, from sending emails to booking travel, with users deciding how much access to grant it.
Meta expects capital expenditure of $135 billion to $145 billion this year, nearly all of which is fueling its AI infrastructure buildout. The tech giant's latest quarterly results showed revenue rising 26% to $64.6 billion.
For Nvidia, investing in a customer that plans to deploy more of its hardware adds to more questions about circular financing across the AI industry, which comes down to chip suppliers backing the companies that buy their products.

articles.title: Uber Moves beyond CPU Cores with Performance-Aware Scheduling for Stateful Workloads
articles.text:
Uber has introduced Normalized Compute Units (NCUs) to make CPU allocation more consistent across its highly heterogeneous server fleet. The approach, implemented in Uber's Odin stateful orchestration platform, accounts for differences in processor performance rather than treating every CPU core as equivalent.
Odin manages around 5 million CPU cores across on-premises data centres and public clouds, including multiple generations of x86 hardware and ARM processors. Uber found that single-threaded performance can vary by almost a factor of two between the fastest and slowest cores. Consequently, the same workload can require significantly different numbers of physical CPU cores depending on where it runs.
The problem creates two competing risks. Allocating resources according to the slowest hardware can waste capacity on faster machines, while allocating according to average usage can leave workloads under-provisioned when they move to slower servers. For stateful workloads, where moving traffic to another machine is often not possible, the latter can become a reliability problem.
Uber's solution is to separate the amount of compute performance a workload requires from the physical cores used to provide it.
Odin assigns each server type a performance factor, using an older server generation as a baseline of 100. Newer hardware can have considerably higher values; Uber reports factors approaching 190 for some servers. These factors are initially determined during hardware qualification and then refined using production workload data.
CPU usage is converted into normalized units using these factors. Odin can then determine that a workload requires a particular amount of compute capacity and translate that requirement into a different number of physical cores depending on the server hosting it.
A workload on faster hardware may therefore receive fewer cores, while the same workload on slower hardware receives more. The objective is not to make the number of cores identical, but to make the computational capacity more comparable.
Uber also found that performance factors differ between technologies. Its measurements for Kafka, for example, showed substantially different performance between ARM, older on-premises hardware, and newer x86 systems. The company therefore updates factors using production measurements rather than relying exclusively on synthetic benchmarks.
For stateless services, differences between servers can often be addressed through load balancing. Traffic can be directed towards less-loaded or faster machines.
Stateful systems do not have the same flexibility. A request may need to reach the server containing a particular shard or piece of data. Moving the request elsewhere does not solve the underlying resource problem.
In the post, Uber describes workloads where a leader consumes more than ten times the CPU of its followers. If that leader moves from a fast server to a slower one, its CPU consumption can increase substantially, potentially causing resource pressure even though the workload itself has not changed.
Uber has rolled the approach out across approximately 1.4 million CPU cores of automatically scaled Odin workloads. For Kafka, CPU utilisation initially varied by around eight percentage points between server types, with the hottest hardware running at approximately 50% higher utilisation than the coldest.
After introducing performance-aware allocation, the difference fell to around three percentage points, with the hottest hardware only about 10% higher than the slowest. Uber also reduced total Kafka CPU allocation by approximately 8%, with much of the reduction occurring on faster hardware where the savings are potentially more valuable.
The approach differs from the CPU abstraction used by Kubernetes, where CPU requests are expressed as cores or millicores. Kubernetes deliberately treats a CPU unit as an absolute quantity of CPU time, regardless of the size of the underlying machine. That abstraction works well for portable workload definitions, but it does not inherently express the relative performance of different processor generations.
Uber's NCU model addresses a somewhat different problem: making the resource itself performance-aware. Rather than primarily deciding how many workloads should fit on a machine or how much CPU a workload should receive, it asks how much computational capacity a CPU allocation actually represents.

articles.title: Microsoft lanza un parche de emergencia por una falla crítica en Brotli que afecta a .NET
articles.text:
Microsoft publicó un parche de seguridad de emergencia para corregir una vulnerabilidad crítica en Brotli que afecta a .NET 8, .NET 9, .NET 10 y .NET 11 Release Candidate 3. La compañía emitió la actualización fuera de su calendario habitual, un domingo, después de confirmar que el fallo puede permitir la lectura o corrupción de memoria dentro de un proceso.
La corrección importa para desarrolladores, empresas y administradores de sistemas que utilizan aplicaciones .NET en Windows, Mac y Linux. La vulnerabilidad, identificada como CVE-2026-111497, está vinculada al procesamiento de datos comprimidos con Brotli, un algoritmo creado por Google y utilizado para reducir el tamaño de archivos que circulan por internet.
El fallo puede provocar filtraciones, bloqueos y ejecución de código
Rahul Bhandari, gerente sénior de programas de Microsoft .NET, confirmó que la vulnerabilidad fue descubierta el 22 de octubre y que corresponde a un desbordamiento de búfer. Este tipo de error ocurre cuando un programa intenta almacenar más información de la que puede manejar un área de memoria determinada.
Según la advertencia difundida por Microsoft, un atacante no autenticado podría leer o corromper la memoria de un proceso afectado. Las consecuencias potenciales incluyen divulgación de información, denegación de servicio y escalada de privilegios.
La falla también podría permitir la ejecución de código arbitrario mediante un flujo comprimido con Brotli manipulado. Esto significa que un actor malicioso podría intentar aprovechar datos especialmente preparados para alterar el comportamiento de una aplicación vulnerable.
El Centro de Respuesta de Seguridad de Microsoft clasificó el problema como crítico. Aunque la vulnerabilidad ya fue divulgada públicamente, la empresa indicó que no tiene pruebas de explotación activa. Sin embargo, su análisis de riesgo considera que la explotación es “más probable”.
Brotli permite comprimir datos sin perder información
Brotli es un algoritmo de compresión sin pérdida desarrollado por Google en 2015. Su función consiste en reducir el tamaño de datos como texto, código o imágenes sin modificar su contenido original. De esta manera, los archivos pueden trasladarse con mayor rapidez por internet.
El sistema utiliza un diccionario interno de palabras, frases y elementos de código. En lugar de repetir una secuencia completa de caracteres, puede reemplazarla por una referencia más corta que permite reconstruirla al descomprimir el archivo.
También identifica repeticiones dentro del contenido comprimido. Si una frase o bloque de información vuelve a aparecer, Brotli puede sustituirlo por una referencia en vez de enviarlo de nuevo completo. Esta lógica permite ahorrar espacio y mejorar la transferencia de datos.
Brotli puede ser cerca de un 20% más eficiente que sistemas de compresión anteriores, como Gzip. Esa ventaja explica su presencia en aplicaciones, servicios web y herramientas que necesitan procesar grandes volúmenes de información.
Las aplicaciones ASP.NET Core y HttpClient pueden estar expuestas
Microsoft advirtió que las aplicaciones pueden verse afectadas si procesan datos comprimidos con Brotli en varios escenarios. Entre ellos se encuentra la descompresión de solicitudes en ASP.NET Core, la descompresión automática de respuestas mediante HttpClient y el uso de las interfaces de Brotli incluidas en System.IO.Compression.
El riesgo aparece cuando una aplicación recibe y descomprime contenido manipulado. Por ello, la recomendación de la compañía es instalar las actualizaciones disponibles lo antes posible en todos los entornos afectados.
La medida alcanza a proyectos en desarrollo, servidores de producción y equipos que ejecuten versiones vulnerables de .NET. En organizaciones con múltiples aplicaciones, la revisión debe incluir tanto los sistemas expuestos a internet como los servicios internos que procesen archivos o respuestas comprimidas.
Microsoft también corrigió un fallo en Authenticator para Android
La actualización de .NET coincide con otra corrección de seguridad reciente de Microsoft. La empresa publicó un parche para una vulnerabilidad en Microsoft Authenticator para Android que podía permitir que una aplicación maliciosa instalada en el mismo teléfono obtuviera tokens de acceso de una cuenta laboral.
El fallo, identificado como CVE-2026-80097, afectaba versiones anteriores a la 6.2606.4246. Para aprovecharlo, una aplicación dañina debía estar instalada previamente en el dispositivo, por ejemplo, tras una descarga desde una fuente no confiable.
En el caso de Brotli, la prioridad es actualizar los entornos .NET afectados. En el de Authenticator, los usuarios deben comprobar la versión instalada desde Google Play Store y evitar aplicaciones descargadas fuera de tiendas oficiales.

articles.title: Ex-CEO do GitHub lança Entire, plataforma rival feita para IA e humanos • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Ex-CEO do GitHub lança Entire, plataforma rival feita para IA e humanos
Thomas Dohmke, ex-CEO do GitHub, lançou a plataforma Entire para competir com a sua antiga empresa.
Já mencionamos Thomas Dohmke aqui no Tecnoblog. A razão é simples: ele foi CEO do GitHub entre 2021 e 2025. O executivo está de volta, mas agora na condição de fundador da Entire, uma empresa de hospedagem e colaboração Git que surge para competir justamente com o GitHub.
A Entire foi apresentada em julho, mas o seu lançamento oficial se deu nesta semana. No anúncio de lançamento, o serviço foi descrito da seguinte forma:
A Entire está lançando a primeira plataforma Git criada para que agentes e humanos trabalhem juntos, uma alternativa ao GitHub que oferece a velocidade necessária para que as equipes integrem alterações tão rapidamente quanto os agentes de programação as criam.
Repare que a descrição acima menciona “agentes”. Trata-se de uma forma de dizer que a Entire foi projetada não só para o trabalho de desenvolvedores humanos, como também para tarefas executadas por agentes de inteligência artificial. Na prática, isso significa que a plataforma foi preparada para suportar as altas cargas de trabalho que esses agentes podem demandar.
Mas as diferenças com relação ao GitHub não acabam aí. No lugar de pull requests, que são recursos comuns no GitHub que permitem ao usuário informar a outros desenvolvedores sobre alterações no repositório de determinado projeto, a Entire usa Trails.
Trails são uma forma de registrar e comunicar mudanças em código de modo que outros desenvolvedores possam não só entender o que mudou, mas também como e por quê. Não por acaso, a Entire compara a interface dos Trails à visão que um piloto tem do painel de um avião (não no sentido de complexidade, mas de acompanhamento da operação).
Dohmke e sua turma enfatizam que o desempenho é outro diferencial da plataforma: “a Entire é construída em um novo servidor de controle de versão compatível com Git, com pushes até 89 vezes mais rápidos do que o GitHub e seis vezes mais rápidos do que o Cursor Origin”, descreve o comunicado oficial.
Sim. Pelo menos nesta fase de lançamento, a Entire não cobra nada pelo uso da plataforma para repositórios de código e Trails. Porém, o usuário precisa comprar créditos para o uso de agentes de IA. A boa notícia é que cada conta criada no serviço recebe um crédito de US$ 100 como “boas-vindas”.
O site oficial é entire.com.

articles.title: Guidewire buys Hyperexponential for $1.7B in cash | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Insurance tech company Guidewire announced Tuesday the acquisition of the agentic underwriting insurance company Hyperexponential for $1.7 billion in cash.
The deal, expected to close sometime next year, is to help bring AI agents to work alongside humans to underwrite, analyze, and price decisions. The deal is worth around $2 billion in total, with $400 million in additional capital reserved if certain revenue targets are hit.
Backed by Andreessen Horowitz and Battery Ventures, Hyperexponential was founded in 2017 and has raised nearly $90 million to date, according to PitchBook. So this marks a significant return for investors. The U.K.-based AI startup says nearly 600 insurers across 40 different countries use its software.

articles.title: Vibe genes? Natural(ish) language comes to protein, genome design software
articles.text:
Protein design tools may be getting increasingly sophisticated, but you still need a sophisticated understanding of protein structure for them to work. This can include knowing enzyme mechanisms down to the positions of specific amino acids, as well as the water molecules that also occupy the area where catalysis takes place. Once you specify these, the tools can build the rest of a protein around this target.
A large collaboration of researchers based in China, however, decided to bring protein design to the masses, making a tool that can take natural language prompts and use them to produce proteins with the function you specify. If your measure for success is a working protein, then the success rate may not be great. But they still manage to get the job done. And, in a separate announcement, Hugging Face shared that it’s now hosting a tool that does similar things on the DNA level.
The equivalent of vibe coding may have come to protein design—at least if you have access to a lab where you can sort the good designs from the dozens of failed ones.
Focusing on function
Some of the best protein design tools we have available right now work through a two-step process. First, you specify a set of constraints, such as the need to bind another molecule or to have a specific arrangement of amino acids. One AI tool then generates a protein shape that meets those constraints. Once that’s done, a separate tool populates that shape with a specific sequence of amino acids that can ensure the protein folds into the appropriate configuration to match the shape.
Obviously, doing that often requires a fair bit of technical knowledge. If you’re designing a catalyst, for example, then you not only need to know what amino acids are critical to get a chemical reaction to happen, but you have to know where they should be located within a 3D space. That, not surprisingly, requires a fairly sophisticated understanding of protein chemistry and the ability to express that understanding in whatever form that the protein design tools require.
The thing is, if two experts were talking to each other, they wouldn’t need to get that specific. If one said “serine protease,” for example, the other would know a lot of what was implied by that in terms of the specifics of the reaction mechanism. We need to get specific when communicating with an AI tool because, while our current generation of tools are great at working through the 3D arrangements of amino acids, they’re kind of stupid about the functions that those 3D arrangements enable.
In the work of the team behind the new tool, called Pinal, this doesn’t necessarily have to be the case. We have databases full of millions of protein sequences tagged with notes about the functions those proteins perform. With the proper training, the researchers reasoned, it should be possible to just use the same terminology in those tags to get a system that outputs a sequence that performs exactly like what you’re looking for.
Proteins plus language
Pinal, on some levels, works quite like the standard tools, following a two-step process of building a backbone for the protein and then filling in the details of the amino acids that populate that backbone through a separate process. But there are very significant differences—beginning with what you need to do to start the process.
Rather than specifying some details of a few amino acids in the design product, you simply tell the system what you want. “The first stage is handled by T2struct, a text-to-structure module that translates a natural language prompt into a structural blueprint,” as the system’s developers describe it. T2struct doesn’t output a 3D shape, either; it simply produces a linear array of tokens that correspond to the spatial relationship between each amino acid and its nearest neighbors and assign a probability to each.
That gets handed off to a system called SAProt-T, which uses a combination of the original text and the output to T2struct to construct the sequence of amino acids in the final protein design. Here, the probabilities generated earlier matter, since SAProt-T performs a global re-evaluation. According to the authors, this avoids the risk of “overlooking a slightly less probable structure that can accommodate a far superior functional sequence.”
How do you develop a system that can do all of this? The researchers decided the best way was to use massive amounts of data. For each set of tags that describe a protein’s function, they fed the tags into an LLM and had it provide a plain-language description and used both the tags and the description as part of the training. They used protein sequences from three different databases, paired with structural information predicted by AlphaFold; just one of these databases contained 800 million keyword–protein pairs.
It’s noteworthy that AlphaFold is not 100 percent accurate in its predictions, so if you’re trying to generate something related to a relatively obscure protein, this could be a problem. But many common proteins have structural data available, which presumably would ensure AlphaFold made informed predictions.
In any case, apparently enough of the structural data was right for the training to work.
Functional proteins
To test Pinal, the researchers asked it to design four very different proteins: a fluorescent one, two enzymes, and one that takes part in a large multi-protein complex. While the details vary a bit from case to case, there was a similar process for each; we’ll use the fluorescent protein as an example.
The classic example of a fluorescent protein, which won its discoverer a Nobel, is GFP, the green fluorescent protein. Pinal was asked to produce 50,000 proteins that could fluoresce like GFP. This massive list was then filtered down by a number of criteria. For starters, the researchers rejected anything with a sequence that looked like a known fluorescent protein. But they selected for a couple of key features found in GFP: the ability to form a barrel-like structure, and the presence of a key amino acid that can be chemically modified to enable fluorescence.
In short, they wanted it to be a bit like GFP in general, but not very similar in terms of the specific amino acid sequence. That filtering left them with a high-priority list of just 29 candidate proteins, all of which were made in E. coli. A grand total of one of them fluoresced.
All the other examples were done similarly: start with a massive list, narrow it down computationally, then test a few dozen designs, of which only a few would work.
It would be tempting to dismiss this as a horrifically low success rate. But remember that a lot of the suggestions that were most likely to work would look a lot like known GFP proteins, and so be weeded out. The researchers also didn’t even bother to test whether things that didn’t form a structure similar to GFP might work, so they may have rejected a huge range of alternative fluorescent proteins based on that.
Not just proteins
Last week also saw the introduction of something very similar but focused on DNA sequences. A collaboration of the AI company Hugging Face, the Zhongguancun Academy, and the University of Naples “Federico II” introduced what they’re calling Carbon X, an open-weight model that can run on local hardware. It is based on a human-language model called Qwen3-14B but was retrained using DNA, followed by reinforcement learning and supervised fine-tuning.
The re-training (technically termed mid-training) required a careful balancing act: “A low learning rate preserves English but leaves DNA at chance, and a high one learns DNA but forgets English.” But the result is a single model that can speak both DNA and English and translate between them. So, like large genome models, you can prompt it with a DNA sequence, and it will attempt to predict sequences that might come after it in a typical genome. But you can also prompt it with a mix of DNA and natural language, asking it things like “what would the consequence of changing this G to an A be?”
While the team has not released a publication describing the behavior of the system, their internal performance suggests it’s quite good, being competitive with large, specialized commercial models like GPT-6.1 Sol. That said, it also includes a few cautions. The system is not especially good at noting specific positions, especially on longer sequences. It can also be prone to hallucinations if the prompt isn’t specific enough. So, the usual cautions when using an AI tool definitely apply.
Hugging Face points out two major reasons why Carbon X might be a better option than commercial models, even for tasks where the commercial models tend to perform a bit better, both of them related to the fact that Carbon X can be run locally. The first is simply cost; the company’s demonstration video was done using a MacBook, so it can be run repeatedly on relatively affordable hardware. The second is that there are many situations where, for proprietary or privacy reasons, people will not want to share the inquiries they’re making with a commercial entity.
Keeping it plain
It’s easy to think this is dumbing biology down so anyone with the slightest bit of knowledge can start making custom proteins and viruses. That’s not entirely accurate. They can easily get the sequences out of the tool. But they will then likely need to use a lot of specialized tools to screen through these in order to find sequences that are more likely to be functional. And then there’s the issue of testing them, which requires a well-equipped biology lab and trained specialists.
Biologists have clearly not been taken out of the equation.
In many cases, this may solve ongoing issues faced by experimental biologists. In the post-genome era, there have been lots of questions that are best answered via computers. But a lot of tools made to get these answers were made by bioinformaticians who did not go out of their way to make their tools approachable. Many biologists can understand a relatively English-ish phrase like “find me all the enhancers that control the expression of this gene.” But far fewer will know which combination of tools are needed to answer that question, much less how to configure them.
Giving those biologists a tool that can answer these questions without the need to consult multiple software manuals has potential to accelerate research. But it may take a few years before it becomes clear that biologists find this capability useful.
John is Ars Technica's science editor. He has a Bachelor of Arts in Biochemistry from Columbia University, and a Ph.D. in Molecular and Cell Biology from the University of California, Berkeley. When physically separated from his keyboard, he tends to seek out a bicycle, or a scenic location for communing with his hiking boots.

articles.title: EIZO Expands Touch Panel Monitor Lineup with Active Stylus
articles.text:
Tuesday, October 27th 2026
EIZO Expands Touch Panel Monitor Lineup with Active Stylus
EIZO Corporation (TSE: 6737) today announced the release of three new DuraVision touch panel monitors optimized for stylus-based input: the DuraVision FDF2182WT-AS (21.5-inch), FDF1983WT-AS (18.5-inch), and FDF1683WT-AS (15.6-inch). As derivative models of EIZO's established touch panel monitor lineup, the new products retain the core specifications and reliability of their respective base models while adding a dedicated active stylus for smooth digital writing.
As organizations continue transitioning from paper-based processes to digital workflows, many tasks across offices, healthcare facilities, manufacturing sites, and public service systems still depend on handwritten input. To support these workflows, the new monitors combine projected capacitive (PCAP) touch technology with a dedicated active stylus engineered for accurate, responsive pen input. Users can comfortably write, annotate, sign, and draw directly on the screen, bringing the precision and familiarity of pen-and-paper interaction to digital environments.The bundled active stylus provides highly responsive input for a natural writing experience and supports 4,096 levels of pressure detection, allowing line thickness to vary according to writing pressure. A hover function displays the cursor position before the stylus touches the screen, enabling users to place the pen accurately and write with greater precision.
The monitors incorporate palm rejection technology that ignores unintended touch contact while writing. This allows users to rest their hand naturally on the screen surface, providing a more comfortable and intuitive writing experience.
In addition to stylus input, the monitors support up to 10 simultaneous touchpoints, enabling smooth finger-based operation and intuitive multitouch gestures such as pinch-to-zoom, rotation, dragging, and flicking. This flexibility allows users to seamlessly switch between touch and pen input depending on the task at hand.
The FDF2182WT-AS is equipped with EIZO's LaidBack stand, which allows the screen to be reclined for a comfortable writing angle. The adjustable design makes it easy to position the monitor for annotation, document review, and other interactive tasks.
By expanding its touch panel monitor lineup with dedicated active stylus models, EIZO offers customers greater flexibility in creating paperless workflows that combine the efficiency of digital systems and the precision and familiarity of handwritten input. The monitors are built for 24-hour operation and are backed by a 3-year manufacturer's warranty, ensuring long-term reliability in professional environments.
Availability
The FDF2182WT-AS, FDF1983WT-AS, and FDF1683WT-AS are now shipping. The date of availability varies by country or region.
