articles.title: Nuevos buscadores inteligentes rastrean objetivos a velocidades hipersónicas sin GPS ni señales de radio
articles.text:
OKSI ha presentado cabezas buscadoras de misiles capaces de reconocer y seguir un objetivo sin necesidad de GPS, designación láser ni radio, afirmó la empresa, que cuenta con algoritmos capaces de funcionar tanto a velocidad subsónica como hipersónica.
El comunicado presentó las capacidades anunciadas por el fabricante, sin mencionar ensayos con ningún tipo de misil hipersónico.
Sensores y software de reconocimiento de objetivos
A partir de sensores electroópticos e infrarrojos, con proceso de imagen a bordo, OKSI afirma que puede reconocer y seguir un objetivo tras el lanzamiento, permitiendo al operador utilizar múltiples municiones en contra de uno o varios objetivos sin necesidad de designación externa continua, algo que su director ejecutivo, Chris HolmesParker, describió como “una vía pasiva para fijar el objetivo”.
La empresa afirmó que podía aplicarse a la lucha contra drones, armas de ataque marítimo, fuego indirecto y sistemas de interceptación, y añadió que su diseño modular permite sustituir sensores y ordenadores y actualizar el software por separado. Afirma que la familia de productos está lista para entrar en producción.
Este problema tiene su origen en la guerra electrónica. Este tipo de guerra puede interferir con los sistemas de navegación o las radios de otras armas y plataformas, reduciendo su eficacia. Procesar imágenes de sensores en el propio misil permitiría reducir esa dependencia de señales externas.
Hay que tener en cuenta que reconocer un objeto no es lo mismo que saber dónde se encuentra la plataforma, y que estos dos aspectos forman parte de diferentes módulos, según el folleto del producto de OKSI OMNISCIENCE.
OMNISCIENCE también incluye OMNItarget para la guía terminal y OMNImind para gestionar la misión utilizando lógica de programación condicional. OKSI ofrece estas capacidades en forma de módulos en un contenedor, que podrían utilizarse por separado o combinarse.
La colaboración con Qualcomm y el entorno Ubuntu Linux
La empresa OKSI anunció una colaboración con Qualcomm en 2026. Según el comunicado, el software OMNISCIENCE se ha adaptado al QCS8550 y su entorno se basa en Ubuntu Linux, con herramientas de inteligencia artificial y visión por ordenador open source, mientras que este chip aporta el cálculo y el procesamiento de imágenes necesarios para ejecutar este software de autonomía en dispositivos sin tripulación.
Este comunicado también es prueba de una vía de integración del software para la autonomía. Sin embargo, no menciona que el QCS8550 sea ni el microprocesador ni el sensor de las nuevas cabezas buscadoras anunciadas. Además, tal y como se describe en el comunicado, no hay forma de determinar si el software de OKSI sigue el principio de la programación open source, ya que esa descripción se refiere al entorno Ubuntu y a las herramientas compatibles.
Los ataques de elusión descritos en la documentación del software Dioptra, del Instituto Nacional de Estándares y Tecnología (EE. UU.), pueden modificar los datos de entrada, incluso mediante cambios en el entorno físico, para impedir que los modelos funcionen correctamente, lo que afectaría a la precisión de los modelos de inteligencia artificial, incluidos los utilizados para la visión artificial, según la documentación general sobre los ataques de elusión en sistemas de aprendizaje automático.
Los comunicados no ofrecen datos cuantitativos sobre la exactitud o la tasa de error de las nuevas cabezas buscadoras, necesarios para evaluar las afirmaciones de OKSI. Estos comunicados tampoco presentan resultados de ensayos hipersónicos.
Imágenes | OKSI

articles.title: As Merz visits Japan, energy startup Proxima Fusion moves to secure Germany's place in the global fusion race | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Proxima Fusion, a German stellarator fusion company, has today signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) in Japan to strengthen the industrial supply chain behind Germany’s ambition to become a global leader in fusion energy.
The MoU was signed during Chancellor Merz’s visit to Japan with Kyoto Fusioneering, a Japanese fusion technology provider, and marks the cooperation of critical technologies needed to build and operate commercial fusion power plants.
Dr. Francesco Sciortino, co-founder and CEO of Proxima Fusion, said: “The global race to fusion will be won in factories and supply chains. Japan has spent decades building world-class fusion engineering capabilities; Germany has the leading stellarator engineering in the world and knows how to industrialise. In working closely with Kyoto Fusioneering and Fujikura, we are building a new industry together, one that makes both our countries more secure.
“Japanese partners choosing to work with Germany is a direct result of the strong backing fusion enjoys from the German government and the European Union, as well as our determination to apply world-leading technology to the world’s increasing energy demands and climate challenge.”
Today’s news comes off the tail-end of a spectacular couple of years for the Munich-based startup.
EU-Startups has followed Proxima Fusion’s development since its €7 million pre-Seed round in 2023, followed by a €20 million Seed round in 2024 and a €130 million Series A in June 2025, extended by a further €15 million that September. In July 2026, the company secured another €411 million, bringing its reported funding and public grants to more than €650 million and supporting the development of its Alpha demonstration stellarator.
This progression comes amid investment in other European fusion technologies, including fellow Munich-based Marvel Fusion’s €50 million Series B extension in 2025 and Bristol-based Astral Systems’ €26 million Series A in 2026, the latter focused on medical-isotope applications.
Together with Proxima’s latest round, they represent €487 million in investment across 2025–2026, reflecting the varied European approach to fusion power.
Kiyoshi Seko, Representative Director, President and COO, Kyoto Fusioneering, said: “Germany is approaching fusion not only as a future source of energy, but as a pillar of its High-Tech Agenda to build national prosperity through advanced technology. Manufacturing and engineering are at the heart of that vision, and they are also at the heart of what Kyoto Fusioneering does. Through our cooperation with Proxima Fusion, we will bring our state of the art plasma heating.. technologies to one of the most ambitious stellarator programmes in the world, and help turn fusion into a real industry in Germany.“
Founded in 2023, Proxima Fusion is a spin-out from the Max Planck Institute for Plasma Physics. The company is developing commercial fusion power plants based on the QI-HTS stellarator concept. With Alpha, Proxima is developing a net-energy fusion demonstrator targeted for the early 2030s, paving the way for Stellaris, the world’s first commercial stellarator fusion power plant later that decade.
On the other side of the MoU sits Kyoto Fusioneering, a premier fusion technology and integrated systems developer. It delivers technologies and engineering services for plasma heating, tritium fuel cycle, and tritium breeding blanket and thermal cycle systems that are essential to advanced fusion programmes worldwide, regardless of confinement approach.
Under the MoU, the two companies will continue and expand joint work on next-generation gyrotrons for plasma heating and on fuel cycle technologies. Kyoto Fusioneering will also contribute its technologies and engineering expertise to the commercialisation and industrial deployment of fusion energy in Germany, including within the national Fusion Hubs initiative of the German Federal Ministry of Research, Technology and Space’s (BMFTR).
The German federal government has set the goal of building the world’s first fusion power plant in Germany. Turning that ambition into reality depends on secure, industrial-scale supply chains for components that, in many cases, do not yet exist at scale anywhere in the world.
Building on Proxima’s existing partnerships across the supply chain, including for high-temperature superconducting (HTS) magnets, the agreement with Kyoto Fusioneering adds key building blocks of that supply chain: the systems that heat and fuel the plasma.
The agreement brings together Japan’s long standing expertise in fusion engineering with Germany’s world-leading stellarator research and industrial capabilities. It also strengthens industrial ties between the two countries as governments and companies worldwide race to turn fusion science into a new source of firm, dispatchable and clean energy.
The partnership will support Proxima’s roadmap towards Alpha, its demonstration stellarator planned for the early 2030s, and Stellaris, its first commercial fusion power plant.

articles.title: Moto G77 5G (256 GB) com câmera de 108 MP cai 38% em promoção • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Moto G77 5G (256 GB) com câmera de 108 MP cai 38% em promoção
Moto G77 (256 GB) câmera avançada e tela AMOLED de 120 Hz; lançamento da Motorola sai a preço mais baixo em oferta no Magalu
O Moto G77 de 256 GB está saindo por apenas R$ 1.556,10 no Pix no Magazine Luiza. A oferta representa um desconto de 38% frente ao preço original de R$ 2.499. O celular da Motorola se destaca pela câmera principal de 108 MP e pela tela AMOLED de 120 Hz.
O conjunto de câmeras de um dos últimos lançamentos da Motorola traz um sensor principal de 108 MP com estabilização óptica de imagem. Isso significa que suas fotos terão alta definição e seus vídeos ficarão estáveis, sem tremidos incômodos, mesmo se você estiver gravando enquanto caminha pela rua.
A tela AMOLED de 6,78 polegadas conta com taxa de atualização de 120 Hz e impressionantes 5.000 nits de brilho máximo. Na prática, isso garante uma navegação extremamente fluida e excelente visibilidade para ler ou assistir a vídeos mesmo sob a luz direta do sol.

articles.title: “La vida es corta para andar con gente sin recursos”: el criterio de Jeff Bezos para armar equipos de éxito
articles.text:
“La vida es corta para andar con gente sin recursos” resume una de las ideas asociadas a Jeff Bezos sobre la formación de equipos de trabajo. El fundador de Amazon convirtió una librería online creada en 1994 en una compañía con presencia en comercio electrónico, logística, entretenimiento y computación en la nube.
Detrás de ese recorrido hubo decisiones empresariales arriesgadas, pero también una visión sobre las personas que deben participar en un proyecto.
La frase no se refiere necesariamente al dinero, los contactos o la formación académica. En este caso, contar con recursos significa tener la capacidad de responder ante un problema, buscar alternativas y avanzar cuando faltan herramientas, información o experiencia previa.
Para los equipos de tecnología y negocios, esa actitud puede marcar la diferencia entre una dificultad que bloquea el trabajo y una oportunidad para corregir el rumbo.
Jeff Bezos y la importancia de las personas resolutivas
El planteamiento atribuido a Jeff Bezos pone el foco en una cualidad concreta: la iniciativa. Una persona resolutiva identifica un obstáculo y trata de encontrar una salida. Puede aprender una habilidad, solicitar ayuda, revisar procesos o proponer una alternativa sin esperar de forma permanente una indicación externa.
Desde esa perspectiva, el valor de un profesional no depende solo de los conocimientos que acumula al comenzar un empleo. También cuenta su reacción ante tareas desconocidas, problemas inesperados y cambios de prioridades.
En sectores que evolucionan con rapidez, esta capacidad resulta útil porque los equipos deben tomar decisiones antes de contar con todas las certezas.
En una organización, esta actitud también reduce la dependencia de decisiones jerárquicas para asuntos cotidianos. Los responsables pueden concentrarse en las cuestiones estratégicas si los equipos tienen margen para resolver incidencias operativas con criterio y comunicación.
La eficiencia como complemento de la iniciativa
El texto de referencia sobre Bill Gates, cocreador de Microsoft, aporta una idea relacionada con esta visión. La frase “Elijo a una persona perezosa para hacer un trabajo difícil. Porque una persona perezosa encontrará una manera fácil de hacerlo” suele interpretarse como una defensa de la eficiencia.
La expresión no plantea una exaltación de la falta de esfuerzo. El sentido se relaciona con quienes rechazan tareas innecesarias y buscan simplificar procedimientos. Una persona con ese enfoque puede automatizar procesos repetitivos, eliminar pasos que no aportan valor o encontrar una forma más directa de completar un trabajo complejo.
La productividad no se mide únicamente por la cantidad de horas dedicadas a una tarea, sino por la capacidad de obtener resultados con menos pasos y menos recursos. En ámbitos como el desarrollo de software, la logística, la consultoría o la atención al cliente, esa mentalidad permite detectar demoras y prevenir cuellos de botella.
La conexión entre ambas ideas está en la respuesta ante los problemas. Bezos destaca la necesidad de contar con personas capaces de moverse frente a la incertidumbre. Gates, según el sentido de la frase, resalta el valor de quienes buscan una vía más sencilla y eficiente para completar una tarea difícil.
La formación de equipos exige iniciativa y colaboración
Un equipo sólido no se compone de personas que intentan resolverlo todo de manera individual. Requiere perfiles capaces de actuar, pero también de compartir información, aceptar correcciones y reconocer los límites de sus conocimientos.
La iniciativa sin comunicación puede provocar errores. La búsqueda de eficiencia sin atención a los detalles puede eliminar controles necesarios. Por eso, el criterio para formar equipos no debería reducirse a la rapidez o a la autonomía, sino incluir la responsabilidad con la que cada persona aplica esas habilidades.
En entornos tecnológicos, donde los cambios son frecuentes, la capacidad de aprender y resolver conserva un valor central. La frase atribuida a Bezos funciona como una síntesis de esa exigencia: trabajar con personas que no se paralicen ante los problemas y que sepan convertir una dificultad en un siguiente paso.

articles.title: Dell extends cyber resilience to identity, AI environments and quantum-safe storage - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Dell extends cyber resilience to identity, AI environments and quantum-safe storage
Dell Technologies Inc. today extended its cyber resilience portfolio into identity systems with PowerProtect software that can restore a compromised identity platform to a clean, trusted state after an attack.
Identity is one of three fronts in the release. Two new services and added capabilities for PowerProtect AI Assistant are aimed at artificial intelligence environments, which Dell calls high-value targets for attackers. The storage changes include quantum-safe encryption for data in flight on Dell PowerStore arrays.
The identity restore supports Microsoft Corp.’s Active Directory and Entra ID as well as Okta Inc. Access controls come back with the platform, so administrators are not stuck rebuilding them by hand after an incident.
Detection is covered separately. Dell Managed Detection and Response for Identity, a new service, monitors around the clock for suspicious authentication activity, compromised accounts and misuse of privileges. If it picks up a defined attack pattern, Dell analysts can launch automated responses to contain the threat.
On the AI side, Security Hardening for Dell AI Factory sends Dell experts into a customer’s AI Factory deployment to check the physical, virtual and application layers for configuration risks. Customers receive prioritized recommendations for reducing exposure.
Resilience Operations for AI, the second service, begins by working out which AI capabilities a business can least afford to lose. Dell then writes recovery policies and procedures for those applications, and the customer gets a plan for bringing them back after a disruption.
Dell first put an AI assistant into PowerProtect Data Manager in March. Administrators can now use the updated version’s chat interface for restores, reporting and other tasks, and the assistant sends a daily brief on risks it expects could escalate. Any action it proposes goes to a person for approval first.
Part of the storage side involves Dell PowerScale. PowerProtect now runs retention-locked local snapshots on those systems automatically, including the scheduling, so customers have a recent copy on hand for fast recovery. With PowerScale SmartSync, a second copy of those snapshots can go to Dell ObjectScale and be kept long term.
PowerStore’s quantum-safe encryption, part of its latest software release, applies to traffic over Fibre Channel connections. When the arrays are paired with supported Dell PowerEdge servers, the encryption protects data against harvest-now, decrypt-later attacks, according to Dell.
The company is also offering a Post-Quantum Readiness Assessment that looks for exposed cryptography across an organization’s infrastructure and devices. The resulting inventory ranks risks by criticality to guide migration priorities.
Simon Jelley, vice president of cyber resilience at Dell, said many organizations still defend AI environments and identity systems with tools and strategies “designed for yesterday’s threats.” Attacks are moving faster than they were even a few months ago, he said.
Dell did not say when the new services and capabilities will be available or what they will cost. The lineup is being presented today at the AI Cybersecurity and Resilience Summit, which is broadcasting on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio.

articles.title: “I don’t use Astra every day”: OpenAI developer lead tells TNS why
articles.text:
“I don’t use Astra every day”: OpenAI developer lead tells TNS why
OpenAI’s recent releases have given developers more options for using AI in software. At its 2026 DevDay, the company introduced new models, tools, and agents that raise practical questions about cost, speed, safety, and how teams keep up.
On September 29, OpenAI held its fourth annual DevDay near its San Francisco headquarters. The company listed more than 20 major announcements across ChatGPT, Codex, its models, and developer APIs. Among them were GPT-6.1 Sol and a faster Ultrafast tier for GPT-6 Astra; Ultrafast support for Sol followed on October 8.
The announcements included OpenAI dots, persistent agents that can work in the background. Backed by GPT-6 Astra, they can connect to more than 4,000 apps through OpenAI’s plugin ecosystem and take on ongoing responsibilities.
These agents run continuously in the background, researching and monitoring, then suggesting actions — completing pull requests (PRs), drafting messages, documentation, and analysis, or booking meetings — for human-in-the-loop review. Depending on a user’s rules and the action involved, a dot may proceed, request approval, or leave a sensitive task to the user.
Other updates included the Decisions API, which uses predefined answer choices to classify inputs or route requests, and computer use in the Agents API, which lets agents interact with software interfaces.
Ahead of OpenAI’s Dev Day Exchange on November 3 in London, Vaibhav “VB” Srivastav, OpenAI developer experience and community lead for EMEA, told The New Stack about the cascade of features the company is releasing. The London-based Srivastav also noted how the new releases may affect the day-to-day work of engineers.
This interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.
The New Stack: At DevDay, OpenAI announced more than 20 products and updates. In a time of rapid change, how do developers and engineering managers decide what to use? And how does OpenAI consider the cost of developers absorbing these changes?
Vaibhav Srivastav: We did ship a lot, right? The overarching goal was to reduce friction for pretty much everyone across the board when we want to release something. This ranges from the average person using ChatGPT to answer questions, to more advanced folks using Codex for day-to-day engineering tasks, to folks in hybrid roles like engineering managers or people managers. From a developer’s lens, I’m particularly passionate about four of those 20 and helped ship them with the team.
First and foremost is GPT-6.1 Sol. It gets up to 95% of Astra’s performance, but at one-fifth the cost. When we shipped GPT-6 Astra, everyone was like, “Hey, this is a very good model. We love it,” but we couldn’t bring it to a price point everyone could afford for this level of intelligence. That’s why we worked to bring GPT-6.1 Sol to a price point that lets everyone benefit from it across plans.
I don’t use Astra every day. I do use GPT-6.1 Sol as my main go-to.
Sol vs. Astra trade-offs
TNS: OpenAI describes GPT-6.1 Sol as offering “near-Astra intelligence” at one-fifth of Astra’s standard input and output token prices. What type of evaluations back up this idea of ‘near,’ and where does Sol fall short of Astra?
VS: When we get a model, we run traditional benchmarks, including Terminal-Bench 4.0, GDPval, GDP.pdf, SWE-bench, and many others. On those benchmarks, GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra are very close. Both Terminal Bench and SWE-Bench are good indicators of how a model would perform on difficult and long-running tasks. In both benchmarks, 6.1 Sol is empirically very close to GPT -6 Astra.
Second, and more importantly, we dogfood these models internally before they’re ready to ship to see how good a particular model is. A good measure of success is when everyone starts adopting that model as their daily driver across engineering, product, and adjacent teams like marketing, human resources, and so on. When we started dogfooding this model, we saw a rapid increase in people switching to GPT-6.1 Sol as their daily driver.
They could use whatever they want. We have no internal limits on what people can do with these models, so they can choose whichever model they want, and they keep choosing 6.1 Sol.
TNS: For a developer or a team choosing among GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Astra, and the Ultrafast speed tier, what’s the decision rule? When is premium worth paying for?
VS: In my opinion, Sol gets you about 95% there for most tasks. For a new project or an unfamiliar problem, I would turn to Astra to look for loopholes or things I may have missed.
“If I use GPT-6.1 Sol to work on that feature and then use the same model for code review, it’s like checking my own work. I’d be biased toward saying it’s good.”
If I use GPT-6.1 Sol to work on that feature and then use the same model for code review, it’s like checking my own work. I’d be biased toward saying it’s good. For an adversarial review, I give GPT-6 Astra fresh context and ask it to poke holes, take the work apart, and help me make sure it’s safe, secure, and gets me the outcome I want.
TNS: Where does Ultrafast mode fit in?
VS: Ultrafast is for important, real-time use cases like fraud detection, financial investigations, and code investigations. Developers have told us they want something extremely fast for those cases. Ultrafast mode lets GPT-6 Astra, and now also GPT-6.1 Sol, deliver remarkably fast outputs — over 300 tokens per second — at a higher price than the standard tier, but still quite affordable.
We later added 6.1 Sol to Ultrafast. It costs 1.2 times standard Astra, so you get near-Astra performance at more than 300 tokens per second for 20% more than Astra.
Guardrails and Auto-review
TNS: Let’s talk about guardrails both around the plans developers can use, and also around safety and governance.
VS: Any feature that could add costs for enterprise or business users is off by default. They need to opt in explicitly.
The more interesting point for me is safety. As models do more and get faster, we want their actions to align with what you want. One of my favorites is called Auto-review. Before the model acts, a Luna-level [lightweight, ultra-efficient] model checks it against a policy you define.
For example: I don’t want the model to submit anything on my behalf, send emails, or share personally identifiable information. An organization or solo developer can define the policy, allowing these models to run safely and autonomously for longer.
Last week we made Auto-review free for Codex and ChatGPT subscribers — over 5 million weekly active users can benefit. We think it’s important to let these models run safely.
See also: OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Terra worked around restrictions in 29.6% of runs in a controlled test
TNS: Now let’s talk about the development and impact of Decisions API.
VS: The Decisions API came together four or five days before DevDay. A team of four or five people shipped a production-ready API in preview for DevDay, then in beta a couple of days later. The Decisions API is multimodal: it classifies text and images and quickly returns structured output. Traditionally, you’d give an LLM a schema and ask for structured output. Now it’s 10 times faster at the same accuracy and costs $0.10 per million uncached input tokens.
How OpenAI dots work
TNS: Finally, let’s talk about one of the major DevDay announcements: OpenAI dots.
VS: A dot is a persistent, always-on agent that looks across the tools, plugins, and other surfaces you’ve given it access to. It identifies what needs your attention and orchestrates the work to get it done.
TNS: How does a dot decide what to act on without being asked, and what does a user see when it’s done something on their behalf?
VS: My dot is connected to Slack, where much of OpenAI’s work happens. It is also connected to my GitHub, where I contribute engineering work, and to my Gmail and calendar. Every so often, my dot looks through my Slack messages, DMs, mentions, mail, and calendar. It brings that information together and surfaces things I haven’t acted on or that it can take off my plate.
My team is spread globally, so someone is working around the clock. My dot could be like: Person X tagged you to review this pull request, or Person Y is waiting for information about upcoming model launches. Previously, I spent the morning sifting through thousands of Slack mentions and threads. I specifically tell my dot: Here’s someone on my team and what she does. When she flags things A, B, or C, make sure I know about it. It keeps gathering more context. It knows I want to respond quickly if my boss messages me, so that goes to the top of my list. If a product I’m working on launches tomorrow or the next day, that’s automatically a high priority.
My dot also looks through my engineering work, including PRs, and might say: This is already approved. You can merge it. Or it might say: I can merge it for you as well. I can say yes on my phone, and it can merge the PR, check that tests pass, and verify it looks right in production.
TNS: Some developers say AI leaves them feeling more isolated. Do you miss the sillier things in Slack, like meme sharing or other ways to bond with your engineers?
VS: I’ve had the opposite reaction. I joined OpenAI in December last year. At the time, models were good but couldn’t reliably do things autonomously for me. Now the models are much better. They can get context from wherever you point them to. Before, I spent a lot of time making sure the model did what it was supposed to, leaving less time to catch up or banter with my team.
“Every Friday, it checks my calendar and blocks 30 minutes with someone I haven’t spoken to in the past three or four days. If I did it manually, I would never stick to it.”
Now I’m more on top of my work because I’m not spending an hour or two sifting through Gmail and Slack messages. I’ve asked my dot to help me catch up each week with someone on my team I haven’t spoken to in a while. Every Friday, it checks my calendar and blocks 30 minutes with someone I haven’t spoken to in the past three or four days. If I did it manually, I would never stick to it.
TNS: With so many recent updates, different teams will be piloting different features. What should they measure to know if it’s working? What metrics turn out to be misleading?
VS: Every new model should be better overall, based on metrics and what we see internally. But the performance boost varies by use case.
When we ship a model, test it on an isolated use case — a migration, new product, or monitoring task — and measure the lift. The lift can mean the same outcome at a lower cost or a better result.
For an organization, the question is how much it’s willing to pay for a given outcome. That’s where the other models in the family come in. We’ve got GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Luna, with others in the pipeline.
The same goes for features like Ultrafast. Not every problem needs Ultrafast, but you might need it to monitor a major user-impacting migration. That’s where Ultrafast with 6 Astra or 6.1 Sol comes in.
Put a few problems through that test to see whether the model or feature helps. We do the same internally. We run A/B tests to see how features work for users. We also look at product-market fit for each feature or model.
Model deprecation and migration
TNS: OpenAI has accelerated its model release cycle. What commitments can you make to developers building production-ready systems on these APIs about stability and migration paths?
VS: Stability and the end-user experience are important to us. If you go to status.openai.com, you can see our availability, with four or five nines, which means that we actually take this very seriously.
The way we ship models has changed a lot in the past year. Better models help us build the next generation faster, improving productivity for developers and researchers.
“Because we ship faster, we don’t deprecate a model until we’re certain the next generation is cheaper and more accurate across the board.”
Back in November of last year, we had GPT-5.1. We’re now at GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol. Because we ship faster, we don’t deprecate a model until we’re certain the next generation is cheaper and more accurate across the board.
For the API, we give three months’ deprecation notice and a migration path so your workflows can be cheaper and better with the next model.
We still serve GPT-5.5 to API users, even though we’re already at 6.1 Sol.
TNS: How can developers manage that much continuous change and migration? What has to change in the traditional agile software development lifecycle?
VS: We see this internally: you build something, and the next model helps you improve it. It’s always a trade-off. There’s always something you care less about. If I built software to solve a problem within my team, I might not need the best frontier performance.
But let’s say I’m building something that handles transactions for my users or another product they use directly. Then I’d want the best performance and current state of the art.
Before AI, teams developed software in sprints toward a launch, then paused new features to fix what was broken. They repeated that cycle over months or quarters. We see the same thing with models.
A new generation arrives; you sprint to use it, then pause. When another model arrives, you use it to improve security and build better features. I see it as an extension of what developers were already doing.

articles.title: GM is embracing hybrids now | TechCrunch
articles.text:
General Motors plans to invest in its Lansing Delta Township Assembly plant to handle future production of hybrid-electric vehicles, the latest move by the U.S. automaker to claw back market share by appealing to the shifting tastes of consumers.
The company said on Tuesday that it plans to invest more than $2 billion over the next several years in the broader Lansing region, an amount that includes $1.25 billion to prepare the assembly plant for “future vehicle production.”
The company said it is working with the U.S. Department of Energy to restructure a previously awarded Domestic Manufacturing Conversion Grant and direct those funds to future hybrid production at the Lansing factory. The company was awarded $500 million under the Biden administration to support converting a different factory in Lansing to produce electric vehicles, including hybrid, battery-electric, plug-in electric hybrid, and hydrogen fuel cell electric vehicles. Those funds were never released, according to GM.
Today, GM assembles the gas-powered Buick Enclave, Chevrolet Traverse, and GMC Acadia at the Lansing Delta Township factory, which produced a record 291,000 vehicles in 2025.
GM didn’t provide specifics on when it would begin producing and selling hybrid vehicles. But insiders told TechCrunch to expect hybrids across multiple brands rather than a single vehicle line. A Reuters report, citing anonymous sources, said the company plans to build hybrid versions of the Chevrolet Traverse, Buick Enclave, and GMC Acadia at the factory.
Hybrids have become increasingly popular, thanks in part to rising gas prices. Customers also have more choices than ever before, with most automakers offering a range of hybrid and plug-in hybrid models. Toyota is the U.S. market leader in hybrid sales, followed by Honda. Ford has also gained considerable market share in hybrid sales in the past two years, selling some 228,000 hybrids in 2025.
But GM has been slow to adopt hybrids. Until recently, the company’s only electric-hybrid vehicle was the Chevrolet Corvette E-Ray, which launched as a 2024 model. (GM sold 2,444 of those vehicles last year.) The E-Ray has since been discontinued; GM began deliveries of the hybrid Corvette ZR1X in March and next year will launch a hybrid Corvette Grand Sport X.
GM eschewed hybrids in favor of battery-electric vehicles. The automaker invested billions of dollars to shift its gas-powered portfolio to an all-electric one. That strategy has changed under the Trump administration with the end of the federal EV tax credit and slower-than-expected demand. GM hasn’t abandoned EVs completely, though it has seen EV sales fall year-over-year. The company still sells numerous battery-electric vehicles across its brands, including the Chevrolet Equinox EV, Blazer EV, and Cadillac Escalade IQ.
GM said Tuesday it will share specific details on its hybrid vehicle production plans closer to launch.

articles.title: Nvidia is bankrolling AI accelerator supply chain buildout to reserve production capacity
articles.text:
Nvidia is bankrolling AI accelerator supply chain buildout to reserve production capacity — announces billion-dollar deals with six major suppliers across substrates, advanced packaging, semiconductor testing, and optical engines
Expanded supply to be available from 2027 through 2028
On October 21, during GTC Berlin, Nvidia announced several massive, multi-billion-dollar deals with supply chain partners across substrates, advanced packaging, semiconductor testing, and optical engines to expand production capacity. Aimed at overcoming severe bottlenecks restricting the current and future AI infrastructure buildouts, the deals feature commitments and production roadmaps stretching through 2028, securing capacity for Nvidia and ensuring resiliency and redundancy in its AI accelerator supply chain. “We are in the midst of the largest infrastructure buildout in human history. Demand is extraordinary. Capacity is the constraint,” said Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. “Our supply chain partners are the world’s best manufacturers. I’m grateful they are expanding capacity around the globe to scale production and help us deliver the AI supercomputing systems powering this new industrial revolution.”
The deals cover two major AI accelerator supply chain categories: hardware interconnects and OSAT (Outsourced Semiconductor Assembly and Test). Under hardware interconnects, Nvidia is securing capacity for both substrates and co-packaged optics. Nvidia has signed deals with Ibiden, Unimicron, and Samsung Electro-Mechanics — three of the world's five largest substrate manufacturers — to support its production capacity expansion and reserve significant portions of that capacity for the chipmaker. The company says it plans to secure 2.5x dedicated substrate capacity over the next three years. Nvidia has also signed agreements with SPIL (Siliconware Precision Industries Co., Ltd) to expand manufacturing capacity for the optical engines used in co-packaged optics by 15x by mid-2027.
On the OSAT side, Nvidia and Amkor are targeting a 300% increase in interposer wafer capacity by the end of 2028 through expanded advanced packaging capacity in South Korea, to support higher production volumes for Nvidia's platform. The company also plans to double its semiconductor testing capacity by 2027, investing $1.1 billion to reserve capacity from KYEC (King Yuan Electronics Co., Ltd.), the world's largest semiconductor testing company, which currently handles nearly all of Nvidia's chip testing.
Nvidia currently leads the AI chip market by a considerable margin, with its extremely powerful accelerators sitting in a vast majority of AI data centers globally. These deals target major bottlenecks in the AI chip supply chain, suggesting Nvidia doesn't plan to relinquish its position soon. So, why these specific deals? What are the exact details? What's the broader play? And where do Nvidia's competitors and the rest of the AI industry stand?
Uncorking bottlenecks
The substrate base, a specialized intermediary layer in every accelerator package that connects the tiny silicon chips above it to the board below, is one of the most critical bottlenecks in the AI chip supply chain. As we detailed in our comprehensive substrates roadmap, this indispensable physical layer, manufactured by only a handful of companies, is expanding in both the X-Y and Z axes as chip makers package an increasing number of components onto one board. Nvidia's Blackwell generation places two reticle-sized GPU dies and eight HBM3E stacks on a single package. Its Rubin and Rubin Ultra architectures mount even more components. As a result, each substrate now consumes much more material and production capacity, even as demand for individual substrates soars.
Fubon Research estimates that Nvidia would supply around 12.4 million data-center AI GPUs in 2028, up from a projected 8.2 million in 2026. Each one would feature a substrate layer. Nvidia is staying ahead of the curve, with a planned 2.5x capacity expansion over the next three years, led by Ibiden. Earlier this year, the company signed a deal to provide a multibillion-dollar capacity reservation advance to support Ibiden's Ono Plant in Japan, targeting 3x the plant’s current individual capacity.
To reach its 2.5x target, Nvidia has also brought on Samsung Electro-Mechanics, Samsung's substrate-manufacturing subsidiary, as a supplier. Beyond the immediate capacity from Samsung Electro-Mechanics’ existing operations, the deal will support facility upgrades and new plants in Busan and Sejong. Nvidia is projected to account for a significant portion of the substrate manufacturer’s output by 2028. To build even more redundancy, Nvidia also signed a capacity reservation agreement with Unimicron, supporting the latter's substrate manufacturing expansion in Taiwan. The expansion will reach full capacity by mid-2028 but is expected to start providing capacity by Q2 2027.
Next on Nvidia's to-expand-capacity list announced on October 21 is co-packaged optics. As next-generation speeds surpass 224 Gbps per lane, traditional copper traces on the board consume considerable power to move data even a few inches from the processor to the edge of the board. To address this, the industry is moving the optical engine into the accelerator package itself via co-packaged optics. Nvidia had long detailed its plans for silicon photonics and co-packaged optics as the standard for future AI accelerator packages. The company has signed a deal with Taiwanese optical engine manufacturer SPIL to expand production capacity by 1,400% by mid-2027, with plans to double again by the end of 2028.
A 4x increase in packaging, double the testing, and $1.1 billion specifically for U.S. facilities
Interestingly, the world's biggest semiconductor company, Nvidia, doesn't own a single Fab. After TSMC manufactures the logic chip and binds it with memory chips on a silicon interposer, final-assembly companies such as Amkor package that integrated module with the substrate and protective casing into the final accelerator package. These final steps are increasingly incorporating co-packaged photonics chips. Nvidia’s deal with Amkor aims to expand the latter's interposer wafer capacity by more than 300% by the end of 2028, through advanced packaging capacity expansions in South Korea. Amkor confirmed the deal is worth $1.3 billion, bringing Nvidia's total investment in Amkor across its Arizona and South Korea facilities to $3 billion.
After final assembly, finished Nvidia AI accelerator packages are shipped to KYEC for extreme testing. KYEC currently handles nearly all of Nvidia's chip testing. It therefore comes as no surprise that Nvidia expects semiconductor testing capacity to double from calendar 2026 to 2027 through buildouts across KYEC’s facilities in the U.S., Taiwan, and Singapore. On October 13, Nvidia signed a deal to pay KYEC $1.1 billion to reserve testing capacity at KYEC's new $1.4 billion U.S. facility, where high-volume production is slated to begin in April 2027. The funds will build domestic testing capacity and bolster the domestic supply chain. At the same time, KYEC is aggressively expanding operations in Singapore, where it expects high-volume production to begin in February 2027.
The bigger picture
Nvidia has been aggressively securing production capacity and long-term supply commitments to meet anticipated demand for its next-generation AI accelerators. According to its August 2026 financial disclosures, the company had accumulated $279 billion in outstanding supply and manufacturing-capacity commitments by July 2026. The company has since signed several additional deals. These commitments cover future component purchases and manufacturing capacity reservations, particularly for memory and chip production. Combined with its more recent agreements, Nvidia is securing nearly every stage of its AI accelerator supply chain, from semiconductor fabrication and HBM memory to substrates, advanced packaging, optical interconnects, final assembly, and testing.
Of course, the rest of the industry isn't standing by. On May 21, 2026, AMD announced over $10 billion in investments across Taiwan's semiconductor ecosystem, specifically targeting advanced packaging and manufacturing partnerships. On October 6, CEO Lisa Su confirmed that AMD intends to increase those investments further. The company is working with TSMC, packaging partners, substrate manufacturers, and memory suppliers to increase production substantially in 2027. Google and Amazon are also aggressively expanding their custom TPU and Trainium accelerator programs.
Intel, meanwhile, is positioning its foundry and advanced packaging operations as alternatives to TSMC's increasingly constrained production capacity. The company is expanding its EMIB-T packaging technology, with reports indicating that Google has already reserved Intel capacity to package more than three million TPUs in 2028. Intel is also advancing its 18A and 14A manufacturing processes as it attempts to attract major external customers.
Samsung is expanding its semiconductor operations as well. The Korean company, which held approximately 5.9% of the global foundry market by revenue in Q2 2026, is ramping up its 2nm manufacturing technology and preparing its Taylor, Texas, facility for volume production in 2027. As detailed in our comprehensive Samsung foundry roadmap, the company is investing heavily in its manufacturing operations as it attempts to close the considerable gap with TSMC.
Perhaps the most ambitious player is new entrant Elon Musk's Terafab, a joint semiconductor manufacturing project involving Tesla, SpaceX, and xAI. The project aims to eventually manufacture the equivalent of one terawatt of AI computing capacity annually, an extraordinarily ambitious target given the industry's current scale. Intel joined the project in April, and Musk later confirmed plans to use the company's 14A fabrication technology. The project aims to deliver its first experimental chips in 2027 and begin high-volume production by the third or fourth quarter of 2028.
Nvidia and other semiconductor firms are continuously fighting against emerging bottlenecks, but compute doesn't come online overnight, and fabs aren't built in a day. So, while almost every inch of the semiconductor supply chain remains constrained, it remains likely that big-name players will continue to invest heavily to ensure that products continue to flow into neoclouds and data centers alike.
Etiido Uko is a news contributor for Tom's Hardware covering the latest updates in big tech and the PC industry. He is a mechanical engineer and senior technical writer with over nine years of experience in documentation and reporting. He is deeply passionate about all things engineering and technology, and is an expert in gadgets, manufacturing, robotics, automotive, and aerospace.

articles.title: Ford simplifies using your EV as a home battery with the $30K Fathom
articles.text:
This morning, Ford revealed that buyers of the forthcoming Fathom—the company’s sub-$30,000 electric pickup truck due next year—will get more than just a truck. Until now, vehicle-to-home technology—like the setup Ford developed for the now-discontinued F-150 Lightning—takes DC power from the electric vehicle and runs it through an inverter built into the wallbox to turn it into AC the house can use. But with the Fathom, that inverter is built into the truck from the start. So every Fathom will be able to act as a backup battery for your home.
It’s typical: You wait a decade for a cheap electric truck, and then two come along almost at once. And they’re two radically different products from two radically different automakers that I think will reveal a few preferences from the EV-buying public. One is the Blank Slate, from a brand new startup offering a bare-bones two-door that capitalizes on features the Internet says it wants, like no onboard modem, no touchscreens, and no infotainment system.
The other is the result of one of Detroit’s big three taking a long, hard look at Chinese EVs and asking itself, “How do we make a car that cheap?” Although the Ford Fathom will cost $5,000 more than a Slate, that money does buy an extra pair of doors, modern conveniences like an infotainment system, CarPlay, electric windows, and a vast dealership network to service the car. That may be helpful given how many recalls Ford issues each year.

articles.title: TikTok is going after Yelp and Google Maps with an in-app restaurant guide
articles.text:
TikTok is launching an in-app restaurant guide in a challenge to other platforms like Yelp and even Google Maps.
TikTok is going after Yelp and Google Maps with an in-app restaurant guide
For years, the app helped local restaurants go viral. Now, TikTok wants to offer crowdsourced reviews, reservation booking, and curated discovery.
The company on Wednesday announced the launch of Must Eat, a new section of the TikTok app built on 40 million posts, reviews, and comments about dining on the platform. The new feature uses videos and discussions of buzzy local businesses to create restaurant recommendation guides. Users can leave reviews of restaurants, call and make reservations, and search for nearby businesses on a map.
At a launch event this week, TikTok US CEO Adam Presser called Must Eat “the compilation of all of the conversation that’s happening on the TikTok platform across creators, restaurateurs, [and] individuals” who make videos or leave comments about local restaurants. Among the featured restaurants in New York are Golden Diner (home of very viral pancakes) and hard-to-reserve spots like Semma and Via Carota.
Must Eat falls somewhere between Yelp and more curated recommendations from publications like The Infatuation. Must Eat is divided into two category tabs: “everyday eats” and “elevated dining.” Users can sort and filter by rating, distance, cuisine type, and what’s currently open, and each page for a restaurant links to videos about the business posted to TikTok. Diners can also bookmark businesses to save them for later. The feature is initially available in a few select regions — New York City, Los Angeles, and the Bay Area. The company says restaurants can’t pay to be featured in the recommendation lists.
It’s not the first time TikTok has tried to bridge the gap for users between seeing a video about a place and actually visiting in person. Earlier this year, the company added the ability to book hotels and attractions through the app. That feature, TikTok Go, allowed content creators to tag and link to locations; Must Eat is an expansion of that earlier capability.
TikTok’s deeper move into the dining space is fitting, given the app’s profound impact on restaurants. Content creators have angled to become the food critics of the short-form video era, each with their own schtick or eccentricities. The popularity of food videos has even changed what restaurants put on the menu to begin with, like extra-long cheese pulls or dramatic presentations. In its press release announcing the launch of Must Eat, TikTok says 27 million US diners went to a restaurant, cafe, or shop for the first time thanks to the platform last year.

articles.title: Apple pisa el acelerador con el MacBook Neo 2
articles.text:
Este año, el MacBook Neo tomó el mercado de portátiles ligeros por asalto. El dispositivo de Apple demostró que un chip de iPhone (y ni siquiera el de última generación) era lo suficientemente potente para ofrecer una experiencia de primera calidad con macOS, sumando a esto un diseño y un precio muy atractivo.
El éxito del MacBook Neo no ha pasado desapercibido en Cupertino y es por ello que Apple está trabajando en un modelo de segunda generación. Y si bien todavía no hay detalles sobre qué diferencias presentará en comparación con la versión actual, el más reciente reporte de Mark Gurman ha dado pistas firmes de cuándo podríamos verlo.
El periodista de Bloomberg, una fuente prácticamente infalible en lo que corresponde a futuros lanzamientos de Apple, indicó que los dela manzana estaría encaminados para estrenar el MacBook Neo 2 durante el primer trimestre de 2027. De hecho, Gurman indica que el portátil barato de la manzana formará parte de la primera oleada de renovación de 2027 junto con el MacBook Air.
Por supuesto que el dato está lejos de ser una sorpresa, considerando el antecedente. El MacBook Neo se anunció en los primeros días de marzo de este año, así que tiene toda la lógica que una potencial renovación llegue alrededor de la misma fecha de 2027.
Lo que la información sí parece dar por hecho es que el MacBook Neo será un dispositivo de renovación anual. La duda hasta aquí pasaba justamente por esa arista, pues en primera instancia el portátil barato apuntaba a ser un experimento. Pero con la espectacular recepción que ha tenido, es evidente que Apple no va a dejar escapar la oportunidad de pulirlo y sacar todavía más provecho de su potencial en ventas.
El MacBook Neo 2 llegaría en el primer trimestre de 2027
Todavía es muy pronto para saber cómo será el MacBook Neo de segunda generación. No obstante, algunos rumores apuntan a mejoras de hardware puntuales en comparación con el modelo actual. El propio Gurman dijo tiempo atrás que el portátil podría incorporar el chip A19 Pro de los iPhone 17 Pro, equiparado con 12 GB de memoria RAM en lugar de los 8 GB actuales. Asimismo, habló de la adopción de nuevos colores.
Es lógico pensar que un potencial MacBook Neo 2 no modificará su diseño más allá de los posibles nuevos colores. Después de todo, esa apuesta continuista puede ser crucial para evitar que su precio de venta al público se dispare. No olvidemos que el dispositivo ya no es tan barato como cuando se lanzó, siendo impactado por la subida de precios que Apple implementó a mediados de año.
El MacBook Neo se lanzó en marzo a cambio de 699 y 799 euros por las versiones de 256 y 512 GB, respectivamente. Sin embargo, actualmente se venden por 799 y 899 euros. Con el mercado en su condición actual y una crisis de componentes que no merma, si Apple realmente amplía la RAM puede que no sea la mejor señal para el bolsillo del comprador. De todos modos, aún es demasiado pronto para especular en tal sentido.

articles.title: Android 18: Neue Funktion soll deine Kontakte besser schützen
articles.text:
Android 18: Neue Funktion soll deine Kontakte besser schützen
In Android 18 schließt Google nach Jahren ein Einfallstor für Manipulationen im Adressbuch. Im kommenden Betriebssystem sollen Apps nicht mehr ohne die aktive Zustimmung der Nutzer:innen auf die Kontakte in deinem Smartphone zugreifen.
Dies erklärte Mishaal Rahman, der bei Google als Community-Manager für Android zuständig ist, in einem ausführlichen Thread bei X. Google hatte bereits am 21. Oktober 2026 Änderungen beim Zugriff auf das Adressbuch angekündigt. Für Rahman ging dieses wichtige Update dabei jedoch unter.
Android: App-Berechtigung als Freifahrtsschein
Bisher galt ein im Rückblick verblüffend sorgloses Prinzip. Hattest du einer App über die entsprechende Berechtigung einmal gestattet, auf dein Adressbuch zuzugreifen, konnte sie dort tun und lassen, was sie wollte. Ohne dass du davon etwas mitbekommen hast. Selbst Apps, die nur einen einzigen Kontakt hinzufügen wollten, hatten vollen Zugriff.
Dies bedeutete, dass böswillige Anwendungen oder manipulierte Apps etwa die Handynummern deiner Kontakte ändern konnten. Wenn dann deine Bank anrief, konnte es sein, dass du mit Betrügerinnen sprichst.
Android 18: Bei Kontaktaufnahme öffnet sich Interface
Wenn Apps künftig unter Android 18 auf dein Adressbuch zugreifen wollen, soll sich eine Benutzerfläche öffnen. Darin siehst du genau, welchen Kontakt die Anwendung wie verändern will.
Bei neuen Einträgen im Adressbuch öffnet sich künftig der Kontakt-Editor in Halbbildansicht. Du siehst darin genau, wer sich in deine Kontakte eintragen will. Du kannst darüber auch bestehende Kontakte durchsuchen.
Neue Berechtigung für Spamfilter und Co.
Für Anwendungen wie Wählhilfen oder Spamfilter, die zwingend Zugriff auf mehrere Kontakte benötigen, wird es eine andere Lösung geben. Für sie führt Google eine neue Berechtigungsform ein. Sie soll bereits ab dem Update Android 17 QPR2 verfügbar sein.
Mit dem Start von Android 18 im Jahr 2027 müssen Apps, die im großen Stil Zugriff auf die Adressbücher von Nutzer:innen wünschen, eine Erklärung in der Google Play Console einreichen. Darin müssen sie nachweisen, warum sie massenhaft auf Kontakte zugreifen wollen.

articles.title: IA : des travailleurs de l'ombre portent plainte pour violation des règles sur les données
articles.text:
Des personnes travaillant dans l'entraînement des modèles IA portent plainte dans plusieurs pays. Et cette action nous fait découvrir des coulisses peu reluisantes pour l'industrie.
On le sait, derrière l'entraînement des modèles IA, il y a de nombreuses « petites mains », que l'on redécouvre périodiquement à l'occasion de scandales. Il y avait ainsi au mois de mars dernier celui des annoteurs au Kenya qui visionneraient les vidéos, même les plus intimes, captées par les Ray-Ban de Meta. Et aujourd'hui, une plainte d'ampleur vient d'être déposée, cette fois contre Scale AI.
Une plainte contre Scale AI déposée dans plusieurs pays, dont la France
La société Scale AI est sur la sellette. La firme américaine spécialisée dans la préparation de données est en effet attaquée en justice dans quatre pays de l'Union européenne : les Pays-bas, l'Italie, l'Autriche et la France.
L'association autrichienne Noyb, qui est bien connue pour son combat pour la protection de la vie privée, est ici à la baguette, avec d'autres partenaires. Elle soutient dans cette action en justice cinq travailleurs indépendants qui officient sur la plateforme numérique de Scale AI, Outlier. Ce sont ici à la fois les conditions de travail, mais aussi les infractions présumées au RGPD, qui sont mises en causes.
Des employés surveillés et tracés
Ces travailleurs sont employés pour effectuer des tâches complexes, comme la rédaction de prompts, ainsi que le classement de réponses ou l'annotation de données. Quand ils reçoivent la notification de leur tâche, ils ont alors 20 minutes pour l'exécuter, et voient leur rémunération (de 20 dollars de l'heure) divisée par deux s'ils dépassent ce délai.
Au-delà de cette cadence infernale, c'est l'absence de respect de la vie privée qui est pointée du doigt par les plaignants. Car en travaillant avec Scale AI, ils intègrent de nombreux traceurs sur leurs appareils électroniques, traceurs qui collectent des données très personnelles telles que l'adresses IP, l'activité sur des réseaux comme Facebook ou TikTok, les types de clics ou les mouvements de souris. Scale AI irait même jusqu'à user de la reconnaissance faciale.
Source : Le Monde

articles.title: Hackers hijack Convertr analytics script to steal payment card data
articles.text:
A credit card skimming group reportedly compromised a shared analytics script used by e-commerce platform Convertr to steal shoppers’ payment data during checkout.
The campaign was identified on October 24 and has been attributed to a Brazilian gang, active since at least July 2024, that focuses on infecting online stores running Magento, OpenCart, and WooCommerce platforms.
Convertr is a Brazilian e-commerce platform that powers online stores and checkout systems for dozens of major fashion brands in the country, handling R$2 billion ($370M) in sales.
E-commerce security firm Sansec says that the attacker modified the Plausible tracker file hosted on a self-managed server operated by Convertr.
Ecommerce cybersecurity company Sansec says that the attacker modified the tracker file on a self-hosted server for Plausible, an open source alternative to Google Analytics, managed by Convertr.
Sansec suspects the attackers exploited CVE-2026-8467, an unauthenticated command-execution vulnerability affecting Convertr’s outdated Plausible Community Edition installation, to gain initial access. However, this hasn’t been confirmed.
After gaining access, the attackers injected malicious code into a legitimate Plausible analytics tracker hosted on Convertr’s infrastructure, which loads on the checkout pages of all merchants using the platform.
Sansec says that earlier versions of the skimmer used generic payment-field patterns, but by October 26, the attackers pushed a more refined version that specifically targeted Convertr’s exact payment API field names.
The injected skimmer was configured to steal the following data types from checkout pages:
- Payment card number
- Expiration date
- CVVs code
- Cardholder name
- CPF taxpayer identification number
The researchers suggest that those who paid by card on a Brazilian store that contained the ‘checkout.convertr’ string in the checkout address page since October 24 should contact their bank immediately and ask to block their card.
In an update today, Sansec confirmed that Convertr "removed the skimmer and upgraded Plausible to a patched version," noting that the company announced it was notifying affected merchants and payment providers.
BleepingComputer has contacted Convertr for a statement on the incident, but we have not received a response yet.
Sansec researchers warned that browser caching could keep the malicious script active on impacted sites for up to 24 hours after cleanup, so customers should clear their cache before placing new orders, even after the threat has been eliminated.
One way to protect payment card details when shopping online is to use disposable virtual cards that expire immediately after a transaction.

articles.title: Le Xiaomi Smart Band 11 arrive enfin en Europe, mais pas encore dans tous les pays
articles.text:
Après un lancement en Chine au début du mois de septembre, le Xiaomi Smart Band 11 pose ses valises sur le sol européen, plus précisément en Espagne où le bracelet connecté est déjà référencé à partir de 59,99 euros dans sa version de base.
Un design plus fin et un écran très lumineux
Le Smart Band 11 se distingue du Xiaomi Smart Band 10 par plusieurs aspects, notamment par son épaisseur. En effet, le boîtier mesure seulement 9,99 mm d’épaisseur pour un poids plume de 15,58 g (sans le bracelet). Côté affichage, le constructeur chinois a intégré une dalle AMOLED oblongue de 1,72 pouce dotée d’une définition de 212 par 520 pixels, portée par une impressionnante luminosité de 2 000 cd/m2 qui garantit une lisibilité parfaite en extérieur.
Découvrez : Les meilleures montres connectées pour le sport en 2026
Le bracelet tourne sous HyperOS 4, et embarque plusieurs capteurs pour assurer un suivi plus précis de la fréquence cardiaque et de la saturation en oxygène dans le sang (SpO2). Les sportifs pourront également compter sur plus de 150 modes d’entraînement préinstallés. Enfin, le bracelet est protégé par une étanchéité certifiée jusqu’à 5 ATM, soit une résistance à l’immersion équivalente à 50 mètres de profondeur.
Prix, versions et autonomie du Xiaomi Smart Band 11
Affiché à 59,99 euros dans sa version standard, le bracelet voit son prix grimper à 79,99 euros pour la variante équipée de la puce NFC, bien que Xiaomi n’ait pas encore confirmé tous les détails concernant la prise en charge des paiements sans contact. Si une édition en céramique est mentionnée sur le site officiel espagnol, elle n’est pour l’instant pas disponible à l’achat.
L’autonomie reste l’un des gros points forts de cette génération : la batterie de 233 mAh promet d’atteindre jusqu’à 21 jours d’utilisation sur une seule charge (dans un scénario idéal, probablement moins en usage réel). Entièrement compatible avec l’écosystème iOS et Android, le bracelet se décline en plusieurs coloris : noir, argent et rose.
Pour l’instant, seul le Xiaomi Smart Band 11 Active est disponible sur le site de Xiaomi France à 39,99 euros. Compte tenu de la proximité de nos voisins espagnols, il n’y a pas de raison que le Xiaomi Smart Band 11 et sa variante NFC n’arrivent pas en France dans les jours ou semaines à venir. Nous mettrons cet article à jour lorsque cela sera le cas.

articles.title: Ifo-Beschäftigungsbarometer: Unternehmen werden beim Stellenabbau vorsichtiger – aber nicht in allen Branchen
articles.text:
Stellenabbau: Wo Unternehmen jetzt noch kürzen und wo wieder gesucht wird
Die Unternehmen in Deutschland planen nach Einschätzung des Ifo-Instituts, insgesamt etwas weniger Stellen abzubauen. Das Ifo-Beschäftigungsbarometer stieg im Oktober leicht auf 95,5 Punkte, nach 95,1 Punkten im September. „Die Unternehmen werden beim Stellenabbau etwas vorsichtiger. Für einen breiten Beschäftigungsaufbau fehlt dem Aufschwung aber noch die Stärke“, sagte Klaus Wohlrabe, Leiter der Ifo-Umfragen.
In der Industrie habe sich die Situation gegenüber September leicht verschlechtert. Die Unternehmen planten weiter mit weniger Personal. Vor allem in der Autoindustrie sollen weitere Stellen abgebaut werden. Bei den Herstellern von Datenverarbeitungsgeräten sowie elektronischen und optischen Erzeugnissen seien dagegen mehr Neueinstellungen vorgesehen. Zuletzt plante die Industrie Anfang 2023 einen Personalaufbau.
Die Dienstleister wollen dem Ifo zufolge eher Stellen aufbauen. Auch bei Leiharbeitsfirmen wachse angesichts der verbesserten Konjunkturaussichten die Zuversicht. Im Handel planten die Unternehmen dagegen unverändert mit weniger Personal. Auch im Baugewerbe zeichne sich ein leichter Stellenabbau ab.
Ökonomen erwarten mehr Wachstum
Die Stimmung in den Chefetagen der deutschen Wirtschaft hatte sich zuletzt erneut verbessert – laut Ifo-Institut den sechsten Monat in Folge. Für die Konjunktur wächst die Zuversicht: Die Bundesregierung rechnet mit 1,3 Prozent Wachstum der deutschen Wirtschaft im laufenden Jahr. Das Ifo erwartet ein Plus von 1,4 Prozent. Damit würde die jahrelange Flaute enden: 2025 hatte das Bruttoinlandsprodukt nur um 0,2 Prozent zugelegt, in den beiden Jahren davor war die Wirtschaft geschrumpft.

articles.title: Exclusive: FireMon unveils AI agents to handle the legwork behind firewall policy changes - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Exclusive: FireMon unveils AI agents to handle the legwork behind firewall policy changes
Network security policy management company FireMon LLC today unveiled artificial intelligence agents for its platform designed to handle much of the legwork behind firewall policy changes.
The release, called FireMon Agentic AI, is aimed at a workload that grows with every firewall vendor and cloud environment an enterprise runs. One business access request can span several devices and policies, often with more than one technically valid way to grant it.
Engineers have traditionally worked through those decisions by hand. FireMon argues the manual coordination ties up expertise while the business pushes for faster decisions.
In the new setup, agents handle the investigation and planning steps, operating inside limits the customer sets on which devices and tools each one can touch. The data behind that work is the same policy record FireMon’s human users already query. Choices that need organizational judgment go back to practitioners.
FireMon supplies three agents of its own, and customers can customize those or build new ones inside the platform. The FireMon Intelligent Agent answers plain-language questions about policy, such as which rules allow access to a given service, generating the underlying queries itself. Firewall rule recommendations for a specific access requirement come from the Network Designer Agent.
The Policy Change Designer Agent goes furthest, carrying an access request from discovery to staged Policy Plan changes. Required fields such as rule names are filled in automatically, and the agent pauses whenever a practitioner has to choose between valid alternatives. Nothing is saved until someone reviews and accepts the proposal. Even then, acceptance only stores the work in FireMon’s workflow, with no automatic deployment to firewalls.
Outside agents get access too, through a new Model Context Protocol server that could let an incident investigation workflow, for example, pull FireMon policy evidence in alongside alert data. Authorized workflows can go further and turn selected recommendations into staged Policy Plan changes. Roles and credentials govern what each external application can reach.
Network security “has never been more complex, and the answer isn’t more infrastructure,” said FireMon founder and Chief Executive Jody Brazil. He said the aim is to put the policy context the company has accumulated to work, with practitioners keeping “the calls that need human judgment.”
AI enablement is optional and off by default. Customers can pick from supported large language models, including one hosted in their own approved environment, and scope each agent’s permissions to particular device groups. Activity is logged to an audit trail.
Both FireMon Agentic AI and the FireMon MCP Server are due in November. FireMon is not charging extra for the initial release.
Brazil started the company in 2004, and the Lenexa, Kan.-based business now reports more than 1,800 enterprise customers in upward of 70 countries.

Agentic solutions for RF design.

Artificial intelligence is rapidly reshaping electronic design automation, creating new opportunities for RF and microwave engineering teams to improve productivity, preserve expertise, and accelerate innovation. As designs become increasingly complex and experienced engineers become harder to replace, organizations must find practical ways to integrate AI into existing workflows without disrupting proven design processes.
This white paper presents a strategic framework for AI adoption built around three complementary themes: Capture, Orchestrate, and Accelerate. Rather than prescribing a single transformation path, the framework enables organizations to pursue one or all three capabilities in parallel using the engineering tools they already rely on, including Advanced Design System (ADS), RFPro, RF Circuit Simulation Pro (Nexus), and Python. Capture focuses on making engineering knowledge reusable by transforming institutional expertise into accessible, repeatable workflows. Orchestrate introduces intelligent agents that automate routine engineering tasks and enable scalable design processes. Accelerate expands design exploration through machine learning, surrogate models, and measurement-correlated simulation to evaluate more design alternatives in less time.
