articles.title: The hidden failure paths that affect Kubernetes control plane availability
articles.text:
The hidden failure paths that affect Kubernetes control plane availability
Kubernetes control planes are designed to contain individual failures, but their availability still depends on how components in the critical path behave under pressure. At fleet scale, a component does not have to crash to contribute to an outage. A valid mechanism can amplify a local defect through shared metadata, synchronized startup work, or an overly aggressive health check.
For example, an informer gives a controller a local view of cluster state, letting its workers make progress without repeatedly querying the API server. This is efficient when controllers start independently. When many controllers restart simultaneously across a fleet, rebuilding those views can place significant pressure on the control plane. The informer mechanism itself becomes the amplifier.
“At fleet scale, a component does not have to crash to contribute to an outage. A valid mechanism can amplify a local defect through shared metadata, synchronized startup work, or an overly aggressive health check.”
This article examines three cases. In the first, an extension API server published an invalid schema after a dependency upgrade and blocked clients that had never used its API. In the second, DaemonSet agents restarted across a large fleet, turning routine startup work into a request storm the API server couldn’t absorb. In the third, a deep liveness check on a component in the API request path treated a dependency outage as a process failure and drove repeated restarts while the dependency remained unavailable.
These cases matter for teams running extension APIs, controllers that watch large object collections, and components in the API request path that rely on deep dependency checks.
1. Extension API Servers: How a Dependency Upgrade Broke Unrelated Clients
In one of the cluster, Helm deployments started failing for charts that contained only standard Kubernetes resources. The charts had no relationship to the extension API that caused the failure. Users who had never heard of the extension saw validation errors before their requests reached the API server. The failure path ran through metadata, through a schema document that combined definitions from APIs registered in the cluster.
Understanding why requires knowing how Kubernetes exposes API metadata to clients.
Kubernetes can be extended through aggregated API servers, which add new APIs without modifying the core API server. To users, an aggregated API looks native: it has a group, version, kind, and resource paths, and kubectl accesses it through the cluster’s normal API endpoint. An extension API server generates an OpenAPI schema describing its objects and fields. Clients retrieve this schema to understand and validate resources before sending requests.
OpenAPI v2 and v3
Kubernetes exposes this schema contract in two forms, and the difference determines the blast radius of a broken extension. OpenAPI v2 is a single combined document available at /openapi/v2, containing definitions from the core API server and aggregated extension APIs. OpenAPI v3 separates schemas by API group and version. That separation narrows the impact because clients using a core API don’t need to retrieve every extension’s document.
“The v2 format creates a shared failure domain: an invalid definition from one extension can prevent clients from parsing the document used to validate unrelated resources.”
The v2 format creates a shared failure domain: an invalid definition from one extension can prevent clients from parsing the document used to validate unrelated resources.
Explicit OpenAPI model names
Kubernetes PR #131755 made OpenAPI model names explicit. Before this change, Kubernetes could derive a model name from a Go package path. That made it easy to start with a valid schema, but it also tied published model names to implementation details. Moving code or reorganizing packages could change a name that OpenAPI clients saw. The newer approach lets API authors declare a stable model package, and code generation uses that declared value when building schema definitions and references.
Before the change, a schema could expose a definition derived from the raw Go package path:
{
   "com.example.platform.pkg.apis.metrics.v1.MetricReportSpec": {
     "type": "object"
   }
 }
After the change, once the package declares an OpenAPI model namespace, the same definition uses an explicit, stable name:
{
   "com.example.platform.metrics.v1.MetricReportSpec": {
     "type": "object"
   }
 }
A missing declaration
One extension API server upgraded the Kubernetes API machinery dependency without including the +k8s:openapi-model-package annotation required by the updated model name generation. Its generated code continued to supply raw Go package paths when building schema definitions. Earlier API machinery transformed those paths into OpenAPI-safe names; the newer behavior expects the extension to provide a declared model package. Without that declaration, the extension began publishing raw package paths as OpenAPI model identifiers. Because those paths contain /, they made the resulting schema invalid.
The extension server started successfully and continued serving its API. Process health checks do not validate the OpenAPI document a process publishes. The problem appeared in clients that read OpenAPI v2. Because v2 combines API schemas into one document, an invalid definition from one extension can cause a client to report an error before it sends the requested API call, even when the requested resource belongs to a different API.
Helm’s behavior made this especially visible. Depending on the Helm version, command, and validation settings, Helm retrieves the OpenAPI v2 document before applying a chart. A chart using only ordinary Kubernetes resources can fail because an unrelated aggregated API publishes an invalid schema. Clients using v3 for core resources follow a narrower path: they retrieve the relevant core API document rather than the extension schema that contains the problem.
Test the schema you publish
The most revealing test validates the artifact that clients actually receive. After an upgrade, start the extension and fetch both schema formats:
kubectl get --raw /openapi/v2 > openapi-v2.json
 kubectl get --raw /openapi/v3/apis/<group>/<version> > openapi-v3.json
Parse and validate those documents before enabling the extension in production. Also test with clients that validate requests against the OpenAPI v2 schema. These tests follow the user path and reveal problems that endpoint health checks cannot detect.
2. When a rolling restart becomes a request storm
The cost of rebuilding a local view
A DaemonSet runs one copy of a Pod on every node in a cluster. It suits monitoring, network policy, logging, and security agents that need an up-to-date view of cluster Pods. For example, a network agent may need to map an IP address to its owning Pod for policy or telemetry.
The standard way to maintain that view is through an informer: a client mechanism that lists the required objects and then watches for changes to keep a local cache current.
On a cluster with a few thousand nodes, a cluster-wide Pod informer means a few thousand potential initial list operations. When agents start at different times, the load spreads across the API server’s capacity without incident.
When recovery synchronizes the work
The cost changes when recovery synchronizes the work. In one incident, a DaemonSet ran across thousands of nodes, and its agents repeatedly crashed across much of the fleet. An operator initiated a rolling restart to recover them. The DaemonSet’s maxUnavailable setting seemed protective because it limits how many Pods an update may make unavailable at once.
Those Pods were already unavailable. Their replacements did not necessarily face the same pacing constraints. Many agents started nearly simultaneously.
Each new agent creates its informer. Each informer begins by listing the same collection of Pods. A recovery operation intended to reduce the failure footprint can therefore create a large, synchronized population of requests against the API server.
The cost of a list request
Informers commonly make their initial request with the resourceVersion parameter set to 0. By using 0, the client allows the API server to answer from its watch cache in memory rather than performing a direct read from etcd, the API server’s backend datastore. This is normally the fast path. It avoids repeated storage reads and uses a view of the state the API server has already assembled for watches.
For years, that path had an unintuitive limitation. The watch cache could not provide pagination in the same way that lists served from etcd could. A client could include limit=500 and reasonably believe it had bounded the response to 500 objects. In affected request paths, when the list was served from the watch cache with resourceVersion=0, the API server could ignore the limit and return every matching object.
On a large cluster, a response containing all Pods may include tens of thousands of objects and occupy hundreds of megabytes while the API server decodes, filters, serializes, and sends it. When thousands of replacement agents request the same full collection together, the server can exhaust available memory and CPU constructing many copies of the same answer. Ordinary control plane traffic then waits.
Reducing the startup load
The Kubernetes community has improved this part of the stack. API Priority and Fairness list-cost estimation was corrected in Kubernetes 1.31. WatchList can also replace the traditional list-then-watch startup path in clients that support it. These improvements reduce the per-request cost, but they do not change the broader design calculation: a cluster-wide informer in a DaemonSet still multiplies its startup cost by the number of nodes, and a retry policy can still synchronize that cost during a failure.
The question for an agent owner is: what is the smallest Kubernetes resource collection this informer can watch and still fulfill its function?
An agent that only needs Pods in one namespace should not list all Pods cluster-wide. An agent that needs Pod metadata should consider a metadata-only informer rather than transferring full Pod specifications. An agent interested in service backends may be able to use EndpointSlices instead of listing every Pod because EndpointSlices describe service endpoints directly and are typically much smaller than the full Pod inventory.
An agent that truly needs Pod-to-IP ownership, labels, or other Pod metadata may still need to watch Pods, but it should restrict that watch to the relevant namespaces, nodes, or labels whenever its semantics allow. The goal is not to eliminate Pod informers. It is to avoid reconstructing more cluster state than the agent can use, especially when recovery causes many instances to start together.
3. When a liveness check restarts what it cannot fix
A liveness probe that checks downstream dependencies will restart a process whenever those dependencies are unavailable. If the process sits in the API request path, each restart can interrupt API traffic. When the dependency outage persists, the probe drives a cycle of restart, initialize, fail dependency check, and restart again. Each iteration adds latency without repairing the dependency.
“The probe may faithfully execute its contract. The contract may still be wrong.”
The probe may faithfully execute its contract. The contract may still be wrong.
Static stability depends on cached key material
Kubernetes control planes may depend on an external Key Management Service, or KMS, to encrypt Secrets. The KMS provider uses that service for key operations, while the API server can retain cached encryption material in memory. That cached state is part of the system’s availability design. A transient loss of KMS connectivity may delay operations that require fresh key material without immediately making the API server unable to serve useful requests.
A Liveness probe that tested the wrong thing
In one incident, an encryption provider that integrated Kubernetes with an external KMS had a liveness probe monitored by the kubelet. The probe performed a fresh encryption operation, followed by a decryption operation, against the external KMS every few seconds. When a network impairment made the KMS endpoint unreachable, the probe failed, and the kubelet restarted the provider. The restarted provider couldn’t establish a new KMS session, so it kept restarting while the dependency remained unavailable.
The probe accurately reported that the KMS endpoint was unreachable. It could not determine whether the provider process could no longer serve its local interface, or whether the API server had exhausted the cached encryption material that let it keep working. Neither conclusion followed from a failed call to the external KMS.
The cascade through API server health
The risk was broader because the API server’s composite /healthz check included the KMS provider’s status. A failed provider could therefore replace an API server with usable cached encryption state. The new API server had no warm encryption cache, needed to establish a new KMS session, and faced the same unreachable dependency. Repeated replacements could turn a transient KMS impairment into a loss of control plane serving capacity.
Preserve capability during an impairment
This is the difference between testing dependencies and testing capabilities. KMS reachability was a useful monitoring signal, but it was not sufficient evidence that either the provider process or the API server had lost all useful capability. The liveness probe should determine whether the provider is stuck or unable to serve its local interface. A separate dependency check can alert operators that KMS is unavailable without automatically triggering a restart.
The same reasoning applies to any component in the control plane path. A cached credential, an established connection, or an in-memory view of state may be the only thing allowing useful work to continue while an upstream service recovers. This behavior is already built into components such as kube-proxy and CoreDNS: kube-proxy continues using its last-known Service and Endpoint state, while CoreDNS continues answering from the Kubernetes data it already has, even when the API server is temporarily unavailable.
“Each case shares a structural property: a mechanism can operate correctly within its own contract yet still violate the availability contract of the system it belongs to. Component-level correctness is necessary but insufficient.”
Restarting every process that cannot reach every dependency discards cached state, increases the amount of state that must be rebuilt, and creates synchronized demand on an already impaired dependency.
Each case shares a structural property: a mechanism can operate correctly within its own contract yet still violate the availability contract of the system it belongs to. Component-level correctness is necessary but insufficient for system availability.
The general design principle is to evaluate every mechanism on the critical path for its behavior when its assumptions are violated. Schema aggregation assumes extensions publish valid schemas. Rolling restart pacing assumes Pods are available to become unavailable. Liveness probes assume restart moves a process closer to health. When those assumptions break, the mechanism can amplify the failure it was designed to contain.
For platform teams operating shared control plane components at scale, these are practical review criteria for upgrades, recovery exercises, and health-check design:
- Validate the schema artifacts that clients receive, not only the extension process.
- Limit informer scope and startup work to the smallest resource collection the component requires.
- Separate dependency monitoring from liveness decisions when a component can retain useful capability during an impairment.
- Test recovery behavior when many replicas restart simultaneously.
These practices help keep a local failure local, preserve useful capability during dependency outages, and prevent ordinary recovery work from becoming a control plane incident.
For additional resilience guidance, see the Amazon EKS Best Practices Guide.

articles.title: Akamai expands its AI Cloud platform with dedicated inference and agent execution environments - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Akamai expands its AI Cloud platform with dedicated inference and agent execution environments
Akamai Technologies Inc. is expanding its AI Cloud infrastructure platform with a pair of new foundational components called Akamai Inference and Akamai Agent Sandbox.
They provide its enterprise customers with a highly customizable managed environment from which they can serve and execute artificial intelligence workloads and agents on any infrastructure, from its cloud data centers to the network edge.
The company says it’s addressing the growing enterprise demand for more flexible yet reliable serving infrastructure and a way to integrate AI with proprietary and third-party data sources with strict governance protocols. As autonomous AI agents take on more software coding responsibilities, organizations also need harder boundaries to secure those systems.
The Akamai AI Cloud aims to provide all of that, and more, offering customers everything they need to get their AI workloads and agents up and running: compute, cloud storage, networking and security. It also offers a vast choice of graphics processing units and other AI accelerators available from more than 4,350 edge locations. The Akamai Cloud platform sits at the heart of the company’s AI strategy, which envisions AI inference running closer to end users and the data it needs in order to minimize latency.
Given its ambitious goals, the launch of Akamai Inference is a big deal. Akamai said it’s a managed service offering that provides customers with access to dozens of open-weight and custom AI models through OpenAI-compatible application programming interfaces. The main advantage of Akamai Inference is that it allows teams to deploy new AI applications and agents at the edge without rewriting any code.
At launch, enterprises will be able to choose from 12 open-weight models ranging from 8 billion to 2.8 trillion parameters, including Nvidia Corp.’s Nemotron 3 Ultra, OpenAI Group PBC’s gpt-oss-120b and Google LLC’s Gemma 4. There’s also a selection of specialized “embedding” models for retrieval-augmented generation pipelines. These are meant to connect the open-weight models with Akamai’s managed database services to ensure their responses are grounded in enterprise data.
The Akamai Agent Sandbox, meanwhile, is all about secure execution. It’s an isolated execution space for running AI agents that work autonomously on behalf of human users. Within the sandbox, AI agents run on Akamai Functions, with their code contained in isolated WebAssembly environments managed by the open-source Spin framework. With these sandboxes, enterprises will be able to enforce granular control over everything from the agent’s compute and memory to their system APIs and outbound network access, ensuring they never overstep their boundaries.
Adam Karon, chief operating officer and general manager of Akamai Cloud, said the company believes inference is going to become the main focus for the vast majority of enterprises in future. “Our customers have already proved that thesis,” he said. “They want to build, run and protect AI on the same platform. Akamai Inference and Akamai Sandbox add the inference and execution layers that turn our AI infrastructure into a full AI stack, and our security portfolio protects every layer of it.”
The company is also keen to give customers more choice over the hardware they use to power their AI workloads, which is why it also revealed it’s expanding its fleet of GPU platforms within Akamai AI Cloud. It now offers access to Nvidia Blackwell Ultra clusters, in particular RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs. Each eight-GPU Blackwell Ultra node provides up to 2.3 terabytes of total HBM3e memory, enabling support for long-context reasoning, Akamai said.
Akamai is also planning to expand its fleet further with Nvidia’s next-generation Vera Rubin GPU platform, which will be made available in the new year, it said.

articles.title: Ghost Rider : le prochain film Marvel fait un choix qui n’a pas été fait depuis 15 ans
articles.text:
L’information a été publiée ce mardi 27 octobre 2026 par The Hollywood Reporter, qui cite des sources proches du projet. Le tournage de Ghost Rider commencera à New York en 2027. Kevin Feige, président de Marvel Studios, a construit l’univers Marvel sur les caméras numériques et les fonds verts. La surprise, c’est que la nouvelle adaptation de Ghost Rider, annoncée en juillet à la Comic-Con de San Diego, sort de ce cadre. Pour le motard maudit, Marvel mise sur une image plus brute que d’habitude.
La fin du « tout-numérique » pour Marvel avec Ghost Rider en tête
Il faut remonter aux débuts de l’univers Marvel au cinéma, avec Thor de Kenneth Branagh et Captain America : First Avenger en 2011, pour retrouver un film Marvel Studios tourné sur pellicule 35 mm. Depuis, le studio tourne en numérique, le plus souvent avec des caméras Arri Alexa, et s’appuie massivement sur les fonds verts et les effets visuels.
Cette méthode laisse beaucoup de souplesse au studio, mais l’image des films Marvel est régulièrement critiquée pour son aspect plat et grisâtre. Avec la pellicule, Shawn Levy mise sur le grain et le rendu plus chaud du film argentique.
Linus Sandgren, un défenseur de la pellicule à la caméra
Linus Sandgren est l’un des défenseurs les plus déclarés de la pellicule à Hollywood. Il a signé l’image de La La Land et de First Man pour Damien Chazelle. Sur Dune 3, il a convaincu Denis Villeneuve, qui avait tourné les deux premiers volets en numérique, de passer à la pellicule, y compris en IMAX 65 mm.
Ryan Gosling devrait incarner Johnny Blaze, un cascadeur à moto qui a vendu son âme au diable, même si Marvel n’a pas officiellement précisé quelle version du personnage il jouera. Pour ce personnage, la pellicule peut donner une image plus sombre et plus granuleuse. Le crâne enflammé du héros passera toujours par les effets visuels, mais il sera intégré à des images au grain argentique, ce qui peut le rendre plus inquiétant.
La pellicule impose plus de rigueur sur le plateau. Contrairement au numérique, elle oblige à fixer la lumière et la mise en scène dès la prise de vue. Les images sont ensuite numérisées pour les effets visuels, indispensables pour un héros au crâne en feu.

articles.title: Halloween : Intego ONE Advanced passe à 65,99€ pour 2 ans sur Mac (-40 %)
articles.text:
Pour Halloween, Intego retire 40 % à la formule de sa suite Mac qui ajoute le nettoyage du disque à l’antivirus et au pare-feu. Intego ONE Advanced revient à 65,99 € pour deux ans, sous son plus bas des 30 derniers jours, mais notre test a relevé un moteur anti-malware gourmand en mémoire.
Intego ONE a remplacé au printemps 2026 l’ancienne gamme X9 de l’éditeur, avec une application unique pour protéger et entretenir un Mac. La suite se décline en trois formules : Essential réunit l’antivirus et le pare-feu, Advanced y ajoute SmartClean, Complete y ajoute encore un VPN.
L’offre Intego ONE Advanced à 65,99 € pour deux ans couvre un Mac, avec 40 % de réduction. Elle vise ceux qui veulent une protection pensée pour macOS et un disque désencombré, sans payer pour un VPN dont ils n’ont pas l’usage.
Intego ONE Advanced pour 1 Mac pendant 2 ans passe à 65,99 € au lieu de 109,99 € sur le site d’Intego, soit 2,75 € par mois.
Pourquoi choisir Intego ONE Advanced ?
- Une détection confirmée par un laboratoire : En mars 2026, AV-Test a attribué à Intego ONE la note maximale de 6/6 en protection, performance et utilisation, avec 100 % de détection sur 405 malwares macOS récents. Les fichiers suspects sont placés en quarantaine.
- Un pare-feu qui montre qui se connecte : Le pare-feu affiche les connexions de vos applications, souvent en arrière-plan, et vous laisse les autoriser ou les bloquer une par une.
- SmartClean pour récupérer de l’espace : C’est l’apport de la formule Advanced : SmartClean repère les fichiers inutiles, les caches et les journaux, montre comment le stockage est occupé et désinstalle une application sans laisser de fichiers résiduels.
Protéger un Mac et faire de la place, dans la même application
Au quotidien, l’antivirus surveille les téléchargements, les pièces jointes et les fichiers partagés, avec des analyses rapides, complètes ou personnalisées que l’on peut planifier. Il détecte aussi les malwares Windows, utile quand des fichiers passent d’une machine à l’autre. SmartClean suit l’usage du processeur, de la mémoire et du disque, et vous laisse choisir ce qui part à la corbeille. Sur un Mac dont le SSD sature, c’est lui qui justifie Advanced plutôt qu’Essential.
Dans notre test d’Intego ONE, nous avions apprécié une interface claire et visuelle, mais relevé deux réserves qui comptent à l’usage. Au premier lancement, le pare-feu multiplie les alertes et demande de valider chaque application installée. Surtout, l’ensemble des processus occupait environ 1,3 Go de mémoire au repos, dont 1,03 Go pour le seul moteur anti-malware. Sur un Mac doté de 8 Go, le minimum exigé par l’éditeur, cette empreinte pèsera davantage que sur une machine de 16 Go.
Advanced, la formule du milieu face aux suites concurrentes
Advanced ne contient ni VPN, réservé à la formule Complete, ni contrôle parental, ni filtre anti-phishing dédié. Bitdefender Total Security, deuxième de notre comparatif des meilleurs antivirus pour Mac, intègre justement une protection web et anti-phishing et propose un essai de 30 jours, quand Intego mise sur une garantie satisfait ou remboursé de 30 jours. Norton 360 vise plutôt les familles. Intego ONE garde la première place de ce classement, pour sa suite pensée pour macOS.
✅ Les points forts
- Note maximale chez AV-Test en mars 2026, avec 100 % de détection
- Pare-feu avec règles par application
- SmartClean pour nettoyer le disque et désinstaller proprement
- Prix sous le plus bas des 30 derniers jours
- Garantie satisfait ou remboursé de 30 jours
❌ Les limites
- Environ 1,3 Go de mémoire occupée au repos selon notre test
- Alertes du pare-feu nombreuses au premier lancement
- Ni VPN, ni contrôle parental, ni anti-phishing dédié
- Renouvellement automatique à 109,99 € tous les 2 ans
L’offre Halloween ramène Intego ONE Advanced à 2,75 € par mois pendant deux ans, sous son plus bas des 30 derniers jours.
Passer sous le plus bas des 30 derniers jours donne à cette remise Halloween un intérêt réel. La formule réunit une protection validée par AV-Test, un pare-feu complet et un outil de nettoyage utile sur un Mac à l’étroit. Elle convient aux propriétaires de Mac qui veulent une suite unique, pensée pour macOS, et qui ont déjà un VPN ou n’en voient pas l’utilité.
Elle convaincra moins sur un Mac limité à 8 Go de mémoire. Si le phishing vous inquiète davantage que les malwares, une suite comme Bitdefender, dotée d’un filtre web, colle mieux à votre besoin. Pensez aussi au renouvellement automatique à 109,99 € dans deux ans : noter l’échéance dès l’achat vous laisse le temps de comparer avant de rempiler.

articles.title: Poland’s Autofixer raises €3 million in venture debt to scale its online car parts platform | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Autofixer, a Polish online car parts platform, has raised €3 million in venture debt financing to expand further across Europe, develop its platform and grow its team.
The financing came from Orbit Capital, a growth-stage venture debt and growth equity firm, whose portfolio includes Preply, Booksy, MEWS, Rohlik, among others. The venture debt financing allows Autofixer to access capital without diluting existing shareholders.
“The company’s rapid growth and strong business metrics demonstrate both clear product-market fit and the effectiveness of its business model. At this stage, venture debt is a natural way to support further growth, providing additional capital to scale the business without diluting existing shareholders,” said Wiktor Namysł, General Partner at Orbit Capital.
Autofixer was founded in 2021 by the team behind Renee and born2be, two e-commerce brands that were later consolidated under AZA Group. The group generated approximately €114 million in annual revenue at its peak, and the founders are bringing that expertise to the automotive parts market. The earlier growth was backed by Montis Capital, which invested in the company in both 2023 and 2025.
The premise is simple: buying car parts online is harder than it looks. The 360 million vehicles in Europe require a wide range of components, and even within a single model, parts can differ significantly across production years and trim levels. Another problem being that parts that look alike are not always interchangeable, while the information needed to identify the right component remains scattered across manufacturers and distributors.
Autofixer, as the name clearly implies, fixes this problem by combining vehicle data with parts catalogues, supplier listings, and records of previous part-to-vehicle matches. Autofixer’s platform relies on automation and AI to organise product descriptions and part numbers, helping drivers find components that are compatible with their specific cars.
“For a driver, buying the wrong part means more than returning a product. It means starting the search again and delaying the repair. We want to help drivers make an informed choice before placing an order. We bring together information about their car and the available parts so they can choose the right product without having to search through and compare multiple catalogues themselves,” said Szymon Jezierski, CEO of Autofixer.
The platform is not only designed for vehicle owners but also distributors, who can expand into new European markets without having to build a full e-commerce operation in each country. Autofixer integrates distributor listings and handles customer acquisition, marketing, and customer service.
In the first ten months of 2026, Autofixer processed more than 840k orders and expects to cross one million by the end of the year. The company has generated approximately €41 million in revenue so far this year, with full-year revenue expected to reach around €52 million. Since July, the company has recorded positive monthly EBITDA.
The €3 million will support Autofixer’s continued expansion in Europe, with Czechia as the next market and sales expected to begin within a month. The company also plans to use the fund to improve its platform technology and grow the team.
“The financing from Orbit Capital gives us the resources for our next stage of growth. We will invest in improving the platform, expanding our team and entering more European markets. As sales grow, we want to make the shopping experience more convenient for drivers too,” Jezierski added.
Autofixer plans to build AI-powered tools that guide drivers through the parts-selection process, as well as a companion app designed to support day-to-day car ownership.

articles.title: Healthy snack brand Troovy raises Rs 100 Cr in Series B round led by Fireside Ventures
articles.text:
Healthy snack brand Troovy raises Rs 100 Cr in Series B round led by Fireside Ventures
Gurugram-based Troovy will use the funding for R&D, expanding its manufacturing capacity, and scaling distribution across quick commerce and offline channels.
Troovy, a food and snacks brand, has raised Rs 100 crore in a Series B round of funding led by Fireside Ventures, with participation from Sharrp Ventures and other investors.
The Gurugram-based brand will use the funding for R&D, expanding its manufacturing capacity, and scaling distribution across quick commerce and offline channels, as it looks to launch a wide range of products.
Troovy was founded in 2023 by Mansi Baranwal and Aditya Mukherjee with the goal of providing nutritious food. Its portfolio spans categories such as snacks, sauces and spreads, and millet pasta. It says its vacuum-cooked potato chips have 10-12% oil and high protein, compared with 35-40% oil in mainstream chips. It also promises clean-label ketchups and seasonings without synthetic additives or preservatives.
Troovy's co-founder & CBO Aditya Mukherjee said, "This backing (investment) is a vote of confidence in a model most food companies don't use: building with the people who'll actually eat what you make. When you build with users, you have to push innovation, because users don't settle. It's not enough to replace the oil and sugar; you have to reduce them dramatically.”
Troovy says it has engaged with over 100 mothers and their children through community-led discussions, recipe brainstorming, and product tastings. These conversations have helped shape the brand’s approach to creating snacks with good ingredients, without harmful preservatives or additives, while maintaining the taste that children expect, the company said.
Ankita Balotia, Principal, Fireside Ventures, said, "Troovy grew 5x in the eight months following our last investment, and that is what made us double down. The team has executed incredibly well on growth, and the backend supply chain.”
Troovy had raised $5 million in a Series A round of funding in January this year.

articles.title: Un tournant historique pour l'IA : Anthropic s'apprête à entrer en Bourse avec une croissance monstrueuse
articles.text:
Anthropic, l’entreprise derrière Claude, s’apprête à entrer à la Bourse de Wall Street pour vendre une partie de ses actions. Et avec le succès de l’intelligence artificielle générative, il se pourrait bien que ce soit un succès. Succès a priori paradoxal puisque la société perd des dizaines de milliards de dollars à chaque semestre. À l’approche de cette entrée en Bourse, Anthropic a partagé son dossier d’introduction qui permet d’en apprendre plus sur sa santé financière.
Une croissance hors norme, mais avec de lourdes pertes
Au premier trimestre de cette année, Anthropic a enregistré un chiffre d’affaires de 16,286 milliards de dollars, contre 1,1 milliard un an plus tôt. Ce qui représente une croissance annuelle d’environ… 1 300%. Et sur l’ensemble de l’année 2025, ses revenus avaient atteint près de 4,6 milliards de dollars, après avoir été multipliés par 12.
Si cette croissance est impressionnante, elle ne se fait pas à n’importe quel prix. La perte nette du premier semestre 2026 est évaluée à 80,75 milliards de dollars, contre 13 milliards un an plus tôt. L’essentiel, soit environ 72 milliards de dollars, provient de charges comptables liées à la variation de la valeur d’obligations convertibles en actions, qui avaient été émises lors de précédentes levées de fonds. Autrement dit, lorsque la valorisation d’Anthropic augmente, la valeur de ces obligations augmente aussi. Ce mécanisme gonfle la perte nette, sans que cela ne corresponde réellement à de l’argent sorti des caisses de l’entreprise.
Mais la trajectoire semble s’améliorer : Anthropic a indiqué à ses investisseurs potentiels que son chiffre d’affaires du troisième trimestre avait progressé de 45% par rapport au trimestre précédent. La croissance ralentit, mais la croissance est toujours là. Restent des coûts très difficiles à réduire, liés à la puissance de calcul. Sur les six premiers mois de l’année, Anthropic a dépensé près de 9 milliards de dollars, soit presque quatre fois plus que l’année dernière sur la même période. Par ailleurs, le dossier d’introduction en Bourse évoque aussi une dépense potentielle pouvant atteindre 750 milliards de dollars dans les années à venir. Elle doit permettre de sécuriser davantage de capacité de calcul, le nerf de cette guerre de l’IA menée contre OpenAI, Google et autres.
L’entrée en Bourse d’Anthropic s’annonce historique
Anthropic, en publiant ce dossier, continue de préparer son entrée en Bourse ; elle a déposé son formulaire S-1 auprès de la SEC (organisme américain chargé de réguler et surveiller les marchés financiers) ce 26 octobre. Elle vise une cotation au Nasdaq sous le symbole ANT, avec une introduction attendue à la mi-novembre, juste avant Thanksgiving. Pour le moment, on ignore quel sera le nombre d’actions proposées ou même la fourchette de prix : Anthropic doit les préciser dans un amendement publié prochainement.
Comme le raconte Reuters, analystes et investisseurs évoquent une valorisation comprise entre 1 500 milliards et 2 000 milliards de dollars. Si ces chiffres sont atteints, Anthropic entrerait dans le top 10 des entreprises les plus valorisées au monde et pourrait se retrouver devant Meta dans le classement.
Cette introduction sert aussi de test pour la valorisation des entreprises d’IA : si Anthropic parvient à lever massivement tout en affichant des pertes considérables, Wall Street validera l’idée que la croissance des revenus et son avancée technologique peuvent justifier une valorisation aussi exceptionnelle. Cependant, si la valorisation est revue à la baisse, cela enverrait un autre signal pour le secteur, notamment pour OpenAI, dont les besoins de financement sont comparables.

articles.title: Ante la amenaza de la gripe A, España va a optar por vacunar a humanos antes que por seguir sacrificando aves
articles.text:
La amenaza de la gripe aviar ha dejado de ser un problema que afecta únicamente a los veterinarios, puesto que también ha aparecido en la agenda de la salud pública europea. Y España está muy interesada en ello, puesto que los últimos datos del Centro Europeo para la Prevención y el Control de Enfermedades (ECDC) apuntan a que nuestro país es una de las tres regiones europeas, junto a Noruega y Croacia, para iniciar una campaña de vacunación en humanos contra el virus de la gripe A.
Lo que sabemos. El informe del ECDC publicado a principios de este mismo mes expone el mapa actual de la vacunación zoonótica en Europa, y tras encuestar a 30 países de la UE, el panorama es desigual, ya que ocho países ya tienen recomendaciones nacionales, ocho las están desarrollando y once carecen de planes. Y aquí España entra en el grupo de los que lanzarán su campaña a corto plazo, pero con matices.
Y es que, mientras que en el resto de países europeos las recomendaciones de vacunación se aplican a todas las personas de los grupos de riesgo como ganaderos, trabajadores de mataderos o veterinarios, España ha restringido el cerco. Aquí nuestro país limita la profilaxis exclusivamente a aquellos profesionales expuestos que, además, tengan alguna enfermedad de base que pueda incrementar su riesgo de padecer una gripe más fuerte.
Algo respaldado. Esta postura conservadora se alinea en parte con la del propio ECDC, que actualmente considera que la evidencia científica no es suficiente para respaldar una vacunación amplia en toda la Unión Europea, relegándola a una "medida complementaria opcional" para los trabajadores expuestos.
La vacuna. El arma elegida para esta campaña profiláctica es la Zoonotic Influenza Vaccine Seqirus, que cuenta con la aprobación de la Agencia Europea de Medicamentos (EMA) desde octubre de 2023. En este caso se busca inmunizar contra la cepa más predominante en la circulación global.
No obstante, el problema que se recoge en su ficha técnica es que hay una limitación importante al no existir un marcador inmunitario de protección establecido para la gripe A por subtipos H5, y se desconoce cuánto tiempo dura la protección tras la pauta primaria.
Los resultados. Parecen prometedores, puesto que en personas no vacunadas previamente la protección alcanzó niveles muy altos. Además, se generaron anticuerpos capaces de neutralizar cepas del virus detectadas en granjas peleteras finlandesas y en el ganado bovino de Estados Unidos.
El reto. Tener la vacuna es solo la mitad del camino, puesto que todavía hay que convencer a la población objetivo para que se vacune. En este caso, los datos de los que se dispone nos llegan desde Finlandia y aquí solo el 8,6% e la población acudió a recibir la primera dosis, y apenas un 7,5% completó la pauta completa.
En España, la maquinaria burocrática y de salud laboral ya está en marcha. Como referencia, tenemos el informe del Centro de Coordinación de Alertas y Emergencias Sanitarias correspondiente a la temporada 2025-2026, donde se apunta a que en España no se ha diagnosticado ningún caso humano de gripe aviar autóctono. Sin embargo, la circulación en animales es intensa, con 188 focos detectados y la inmensa mayoría en aves silvestres.

articles.title: Microsoft releases Windows OOB updates to distrust eMudhra certificates
articles.text:
Microsoft has released out-of-band (OOB) Windows updates to remove trust in certificates tied to compromised eMudhra certificate authority keys, protecting systems that do not receive automatic certificate trust updates.
The KB5134133 update for Windows 11 versions 24H2, 25H2, and 26H2 and the KB5134125 update for Windows 10 versions 21H2 and 22H2 were released on October 26.
The updates are for systems without Internet access, devices that cannot access Microsoft's certificate-update service, and those where automatic Certificate Trust List (CTL) updates have been disabled.
The updates were released after the discovery of eight eMudhra intermediate certificate authority private keys that were so weak they could be recovered almost instantly.
All eight keys were generated in April 2025 and had values smaller than 256, allowing anyone to recover them by testing just 256 possible numbers.
The compromised keys could have allowed attackers to forge certificates for legitimate websites and intercept encrypted communications.
After the disclosure, eMudhra revoked the eight compromised intermediate certificates, and Mozilla, Google, Apple, and other software vendors also began revoking them.
In response, Microsoft previously updated the Windows Disallowed Certificate Trust List to block the eight affected intermediate certificate authorities, including six used for TLS and two for code signing.
The company also released a CRLSet update for Microsoft Edge and WebView2 to block affected TLS certificates, which enabled the block without requiring a browser update.
Microsoft is now taking further steps by removing seven certificates associated with the affected certificate hierarchies from its Windows trust list.
"On October 26, Microsoft released an out-of-band Windows update that removes seven certificates associated with the affected hierarchies: six eMudhra G3 roots and an AAA Certificate Services cross-sign, from the Windows trust list," Microsoft explained.
The new update goes further by also removing trust in the eMudhra root certificates used to verify other certificates issued by the CA.
Microsoft says the same seven certificates will also be removed from the Edge trust list on October 27.
"Removing a root from a trust list is not the same as revoking the known impacted intermediate certificate authorities," explains Microsoft.
"This is a separate trust decision, broader than blocking the identified compromised intermediate keys. Organizations with a specific compatibility need may choose to trust a certificate locally, subject to their own security assessment and policies."
The company advises admins to install the update on disconnected Windows systems and identify any certificates that depend on the removed roots, as they may need to be replaced.
Microsoft is also investigating the remaining eMudhra roots and may make additional trust changes as needed.

articles.title: CrissCross raises undisclosed investment from Circle Ventures
articles.text:
CrissCross, the South Africa-headquartered cross-border payments infrastructure company, has secured an undisclosed investment from Circle Ventures, the corporate venture arm of Circle Internet Group, the company that issues USD Coin (USDC), a digital stablecoin.
The investment, made through Stitch Group, CrissCross’s parent company, will help the company expand its local payment connections and liquidity, build more stablecoin settlement capabilities for enterprise customers, and grow the team supporting clients across the continent.
Stablecoins are increasingly being used to move money across borders, making them a growing part of Africa’s payments infrastructure. Circle’s investment marks its second notable bet on the sector in 2026. In July, it invested in Nigerian fintech Flutterwave as the company expanded USDC settlement across its payments platform, allowing businesses to collect payments locally and settle in USDC. s.
“Africa’s cross-border payments market is massive, complex, and underserved,” James Cope, general manager at CrissCross, said in a statement. “Circle Ventures’ investment validates what we’ve been building: infrastructure that can handle that complexity at scale.”
Lex Campbell and Byron Coetsee founded CrissCross to make cross-border payments more efficient for enterprise businesses operating in African markets. The company was acquired early by Stitch and now sits within Stitch Group, the South Africa-based payments group. CrissCross provides businesses with a single application programming interface (API) to collect money, make payouts, manage funds and exchange currencies across African markets.
For collections, CrissCross lets customers pay merchants using familiar local methods such as bank transfers, mobile money and cards. For payouts, businesses can send individual or bulk payments directly to local bank accounts and mobile wallets. Its treasury tools let companies manage funds across multiple currencies, while its foreign exchange infrastructure lets them convert between local currencies, US dollars, and euros.
CrissCross connects blockchain-based settlement to local fiat payment networks. A business can move value between markets using stablecoins, while the recipient can receive local currency in a bank account. The company says it chooses between stablecoin and fiat rails based on a client’s requirements. It makes money from the payments and currency conversions it processes for clients, and says its pricing varies depending on the markets, payment methods, and services each customer uses.
“Stablecoins help funds move between markets quickly and transparently, and the money is delivered in local currency to the recipient’s bank account or mobile wallet,” the company said in a statement shared with TechCabal. “We use stablecoin or fiat rails depending on what each client needs for speed, cost and compliance.”
CrissCross is trying to close the gap between global stablecoin liquidity and local payment infrastructure. In October, CrissCross partnered with Velocity, a stablecoin payments and treasury platform, to connect institutional on-chain liquidity with local collections, payouts and FX. The partnership aimed to connect global stablecoin liquidity to local bank accounts and payment rails.
Sub-Saharan Africa received more than $205 billion in on-chain crypto value between July 2024 and June 2025, up 52% from the previous year. As crypto activity grows, so does demand for infrastructure that connects digital assets to local payment systems and enables cross-border payments.
“We’re excited to support CrissCross as they bring stablecoin-powered payments infrastructure to scale across African markets — some of the most complex and underserved corridors in the world,” said Brian Schultz, vice president of corporate development and ventures at Circle.
CrissCross says it currently operates across more than 30 markets spanning West, Central, East, Southern and North Africa, including both CFA franc zones, and supports more than 20 currencies. Its customers include multinational enterprises, financial institutions and platforms that need to move money across complex African payment corridors. The company wants to become the infrastructure that lets global businesses treat Africa as one connected market rather than a collection of separate payment systems.
“We want global businesses to find it as easy to collect and pay out across African markets as anywhere else they operate,” it said. “A company operating in Nigeria, Senegal or Kenya should be able to do it through the same infrastructure, with predictable settlement and full visibility over its funds. More enterprises are building their growth plans around African markets, and we want CrissCross to be the payments infrastructure they use to do it.”
Stablecoins are becoming the layer underneath payments for African payments companies. In June, Flutterwave announced an investment from Ripple as part of its Series E and said it would integrate RLUSD, Ripple Payments, and the XRP Ledger into its payment infrastructure. It has also partnered with Polygon and Tempo to build out stablecoin settlement infrastructure.
Onafriq, which operates across more than 40 African countries, has taken a similar route. In February, it partnered with Conduit to use stablecoins such as USDC to fund accounts and rebalance treasury holdings, and announced another partnership in July with digital-asset infrastructure provider Privy to develop regulated stablecoin-powered payment services for financial institutions.
Yellow Card has shifted its focus towards businesses, providing stablecoin payment infrastructure, fiat settlement rails, custody, and local stablecoin issuance. Once associated with crypto trading, dollar-backed stablecoins are now being positioned as a way for businesses to settle transactions and move money across borders.
True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. We’ve filtered the noise out of Moonshot 2026, optimising the conference strictly for high-calibre connections between startup founders, global financial operators, enterprise leaders and individuals rewiring Africa’s technical frameworks. articles.title: Sony ELF-MN1 : environ 300 euros pour cet écran 3D sans lunettes qui met vos personnages en relief sur votre bureau — Frandroid
articles.text:
Sony a officialisé ce mercredi 28 octobre, au Japon, l’ELF-MN1, un écran de 6 pouces qui affiche en relief et sans lunettes des personnages et des objets en 3D. Il se branche en USB-C à un smartphone ou à un PC.
Il rejoint la gamme matérielle XYN (prononcé zin), l’écosystème de Sony consacré aux contenus spatiaux. XYN regroupe les logiciels et les appareils que Sony propose pour faciliter la création de contenus 3D. L’ELF-MN1 sert à afficher des avatars, des personnages et des objets numérisés avec la solution de capture XYN, avec un relief qui donne l’impression qu’ils sont posés dans la pièce.
Un changement de cible
Alors que les écrans de réalité spatiale de Sony étaient jusqu’ici des outils professionnels, ils s’ouvrent désormais à un plus large public. L’ELF-SR1 de 15,6 pouces a été lancé en 2020 à environ 500 000 yens hors taxes au Japon (environ 2 850 euros au cours actuel) et à près de 5 000 dollars aux États-Unis (environ 4 500 euros).
L’ELF-SR2 de 27 pouces a suivi en 2023 à 550 000 yens TTC (environ 3 100 euros). Tous deux visaient les designers, les créateurs 3D et les showrooms. Le nouveau venu, beaucoup plus petit et dix fois moins cher, s’adresse donc à un usage personnel.
Une dalle LCD de 403 ppi et un suivi des yeux infrarouge
L’ELF-MN1 s’appuie sur une dalle LCD verticale de 6 pouces, recouverte de microlentilles optiques, affiche une définition de 1080 x 2160 pixels au format 2:1. Elle atteint une densité de 403 ppi, la plus élevée des écrans de réalité spatiale de Sony selon la marque, avec une luminosité de 470 cd/m² et un contraste de 1350:1. Sony met en avant ce niveau de détail pour rendre visibles les expressions des visages ou les ornements des costumes des personnages.
Le relief repose sur un capteur de suivi du regard de troisième génération (l’ELF-SR2 utilisait la deuxième), placé en haut de l’écran. Il repère en temps réel la position des yeux et envoie une image distincte à chacun. Quand on bouge la tête, l’angle de vue sur le personnage change en conséquence. Sony y a ajouté un capteur infrarouge, qui permet de garder le suivi des yeux dans une pièce sombre ou peu éclairée, par exemple en soirée à côté d’un moniteur.
Un procédé qui a ses limites
Le relief n’est visible que par une seule personne, à une distance de 30 à 80 cm et dans un angle de 25° autour de l’axe de l’écran. Sony recommande d’incliner l’écran à 25°. L’appareil mesure 77 x 154 x 94,5 mm et pèse 300 g (350 g avec son support). Il consomme 14 W en fonctionnement et embarque des haut-parleurs stéréo de 1 W ainsi qu’un micro.
Connexion, compatibilité et contenus
Le branchement passe par un câble USB-C compatible DisplayPort Alternate Mode. La boîte contient un câble USB-C d’un mètre, un support et un cadre. L’adaptateur secteur et le câble de charge sont vendus séparément. Avec un chargeur USB Power Delivery de 45 W, l’écran peut alimenter le smartphone pendant l’utilisation. Toutefois, Sony ne garantit pas la recharge : selon le téléphone et l’application, la batterie peut continuer à baisser.
L’écran fonctionne avec un PC sous Windows ou un smartphone Android ou iOS. Il ne transforme pas en 3D les jeux ou l’interface du téléphone : il faut une application compatible. Parmi les premières, on trouve HoloModels, le service de figurines numériques de Gugenka, surtout centré sur des personnages officiels d’anime. Trois autres applications sont déjà compatibles : Deskrium, Animates et Fenestra: my focus, her future. Les développeurs disposent de SDK pour Windows et pour smartphone, compatibles Unity et OpenXR. Ils sont déjà téléchargeables sur le site développeurs de Sony, qui propose aussi des tutoriels pour Unity.
Côté PC, le site développeurs demande au minimum Windows 11, un Core i5-9600 ou un Ryzen 5 3600, une GeForce RTX 2060 ou une Radeon RX Vega 64, et 8 Go de mémoire. La configuration recommandée monte à un Core i7-9700, une RTX 2070 Super ou une Radeon RX 5700, et 16 Go. Le PC doit aussi disposer d’un port USB-C capable de sortir un signal 4K à 60 Hz, ou d’une sortie DisplayPort 4K à 60 Hz associée à un port USB 2.0 avec un câble adaptateur.
Côté smartphones, Sony a validé les Xperia 1 V à 1 VIII et le Xperia 5 V, les Galaxy S23 à S26 (modèles standard et Ultra), les Pixel 10 et 11 (standard et Pro), et les iPhone 15 à 18 (standard et Pro).
Prix et disponibilité
L’écran Sony ELF-MN1 sortira le 11 décembre au Japon, le seul pays annoncé à l’heure de l’écriture de ces lignes. Sony n’a rien dit sur une commercialisation en France ou en Europe, ni sur un prix en euros. La marque estime le tarif de marché à environ 54 000 yens TTC, soit un peu plus de 300 euros au cours actuel. Les précommandes sont déjà ouvertes sur le Sony Store, qui le vend 53 900 yens.
Avant la sortie, l’écran sera présenté à partir du 20 novembre dans les Sony Store de Ginza (Tokyo) et de Nagoya. Il sera possible d’y essayer des contenus de créateurs et des figurines HoloModels.

articles.title: AWS Shows Use of AI Agents to Triage Linux Kernel CVEs
articles.text:
Engineers from Amazon Web Services (AWS) have described how the team that maintains the Linux kernel for EC2 infrastructure handles kernel CVEs. The process combines an automated filter, an AI agent and human review. The team also argues that it needs to move to newer long-term-support (LTS) kernels, as older branches collect fixes that are never backported.
Dylan Johnson and Justinien Bouron gave the talk at the Linux Plumbers Conference in Prague earlier this month. At the start of the recording, Johnson explains that the team maintains the kernel used within EC2 infrastructure. This is separate from Amazon Linux and from the kernels that customers run in their virtual machines.
After the kernel project became a CVE Numbering Authority in February 2024, the team saw about two kernel CVEs a week before 2024 and about 16 a day afterwards, with 848 published on 15 August 2026. The kernel CVE documentation states that the project cannot know how a given system uses the kernel, so users must decide which CVEs apply to them.
The first stage of AWS's process does not use AI. Bouron explained that kernel CVE records are published in JSON and list the affected versions and source files. A script discards a CVE if the kernel version is outside the affected range, or if none of the listed files are built into the image. In AWS's environment this removes about 70% of CVEs, although Bouron said the figure depends heavily on kernel configuration.
The remaining CVEs go to an AI agent. It receives AWS's kernel source tree, the configuration for each platform, a description of the environment and threat model, and a severity rubric. The agent produces a table that records the affected subsystem, the vulnerability type and the attack vector. Bouron said the team ignores CVSS scores, because they are not specific to its environment.
"We're really using it as a very fancy classifier."
Dylan Johnson
Two engineers usually review the table. According to the slides, the agent needs about 3.4 seconds per CVE, compared with minutes for a person. Bouron said review is now the slowest step in the process, and that the team does not intend to remove it.
"We don't want to hinge our entire security posture on the output of an LLM agent."
Justinien Bouron
When asked about accuracy, Bouron estimated that between 5% and 10% of the agent's decisions were problematic. This was an informal estimate, and the talk did not describe a formal evaluation.
The team also disabled kernel features it did not need, to reduce the number of applicable CVEs. Bouron called this approach "deceptively difficult". The slides list more than 32,000 configuration options, and removing the wrong one can cause bugs or performance regressions that appear months later.
The team's data also shows that older LTS branches receive fixes later and carry more unfixed CVEs. For CVEs affecting all six branches studied, the median time from a mainline fix to an LTS release was 31.8 days for Linux 5.10 and 18.1 days for 6.18. On 16 September, 1,709 known CVEs were unfixed in 5.10, compared with 229 in 6.18. These are counts for each branch, and they do not show how many affect AWS's own kernel.
Backporting fixes in-house brings its own risks. Bouron pointed out that CVE records often name only the final fixing commit. A team that misses the prerequisite commits may still be vulnerable after applying the listed fix.
AWS has shortened its own upgrades. Johnson said the move from 4.19 to 5.10 took about two years, measured from the start of porting work to full production deployment. The next upgrade took about a year, and the move to 6.18 took about six months. During the 5.10-to-6.12 upgrade, 43% of tracked issues were fixed in userspace, where workloads depended on older kernel behaviour. Johnson said the team will now run stable kernels in testing through the year, and move the fleet when each new LTS release appears.
Microsoft's Azure Linux team described a similar pipeline at the same conference. Its triage verdicts come from a rule table, and AI only suggests inputs to it. The team uses agents for backporting, and reported that a build-and-test feedback loop raised its success rate from about 50% to 80%. Google DeepMind's CodeMender, which InfoQ covered in October 2025, focuses on writing fixes. Its announcement stated that human researchers review every patch before it is submitted upstream.
Berend de Boer, CTO of Process Focus, commented on LinkedIn about the work involved in running cloud infrastructure. He listed host patching and Linux CVEs among the work that organisations take on when they build their own cloud. "Focus on what makes your business valuable to your customers," he wrote.
AWS has not released the tools. Asked about open-sourcing them, Johnson said the team would like to explore sharing the filtering tool. He also acknowledged that AWS's internal users make it easier to disable features than it would be for a general-purpose distribution.

articles.title: TLS Flaws Found in GoAhead Web Server Used in Hundreds of Millions of Devices
articles.text:
Cybersecurity firm FoxIO has disclosed three vulnerabilities in GoAhead’s handling of TLS. They could keep revoked client certificates working, let eavesdroppers decrypt some traffic, or help attackers get around a cap on certificate chain length.
GoAhead, a lightweight web server made by EmbedThis, runs the management interfaces of networking equipment, printers and industrial systems. According to FoxIO, it is present on hundreds of millions of devices across the IoT, OT, firewall and military sectors.
FoxIO’s Sébastien Féry, who documented the flaws this week, said each one affects only a subset of deployments. Which GoAhead devices are at risk depends on the TLS library the manufacturer built into the firmware and how it configured certificate checks.
The critical flaw, CVE-2026-115881 (CVSS score of 9.1), impacts GoAhead 3.4.5 through 6.1.0 when built with OpenSSL or a compatible library and configured for mutual TLS (mTLS) with a certificate revocation list (CRL). The server reads the list but never tells OpenSSL to consult it.
On these builds, a certificate an administrator has revoked, such as one tied to a stolen or compromised device, is still accepted, even with issuer verification switched on. Nothing at startup warns that revocation checks are inactive.
The eavesdropping risk comes from the second bug (CVSS score of 5.9, no CVE), found in GoAhead 4.0.2 through 6.1.0 builds that use Mbed TLS. A coding error weakens the encryption of some TLS 1.2 connections enough that recorded sessions can be decrypted offline, but only if the client accepts the flawed parameters.
The chain-length bypass, CVE-2026-115884 (CVSS score of 7.4), affects GoAhead up to version 6.1.0 built with LibreSSL 3.2.x or 3.3.2 through 3.3.6. It only works against servers that require client certificates but accept them from any issuer, so the length cap is the only safeguard attackers get past.
“None of these defects prevents the affected handshake from completing,” Féry wrote.
GoAhead 6.1.1, released on Aug 2, resolves the OpenSSL and Mbed TLS issues, and advisories for all three flaws were published on Oct 12. Mbed TLS builds can also be protected by turning off finite-field DHE cipher suites or moving to the OpenSSL backend.
For the LibreSSL issue, FoxIO recommends enabling issuer verification with a trusted CA bundle, or switching to OpenSSL or LibreSSL 4.x.
The firm has also released proof-of-concept code and fingerprints that defenders can use to spot internet-facing GoAhead servers and determine which TLS library they rely on.
In a post on X, FoxIO founder and CTO John Althouse named Palo Alto Networks, Comcast, D-Link, HP, Canon, Honeywell, GE, Oracle, Siemens, Rockwell, Digi, Lockheed Martin and Boeing among the companies whose devices rely on GoAhead. FoxIO has not specified whether any of their products use a vulnerable configuration.
Althouse cautioned that the availability of an upstream fix “doesn’t mean there’s a patch available for the devices yet — that’s up to the manufacturer.”

articles.title: Detienen a una mujer en Cangas por una estafa bancaria de más de 47.000 euros
articles.text:
La Guardia Civil ha detenido a una mujer de 29 años en Cangas do Morrazo (Pontevedra) por su presunta participación en múltiples sucesos de hurto y una estafa continuada, con un perjuicio económico superior a los 47.280 euros, según las investigaciones. La mujer habría sustraído carteras y teléfonos móviles al descuido, utilizando los datos y las tarjetas de las víctimas para acceder a sus aplicaciones de banca electrónica.
La sospechosa habría realizado transferencias y compras, enviado dinero mediante Bizum, retirado efectivo de diferentes cajeros automáticos con HalCash y solicitado préstamos personales no autorizados. Los investigadores no especifican cuánto dinero perdió cada una de las víctimas ni la cantidad que corresponde a cada tipo de operación.
La investigación surgió a raíz de tres denuncias presentadas en enero de 2026. Los hurtos eran similares y se produjeron los martes y viernes, días de mercado en Cangas. Las investigaciones revelaron que la misma persona retiraba efectivo en todos los cajeros automáticos.
La detención y el paso por el juzgado
Fue el 17 de octubre cuando la sospechosa intentó robar un bolso en una cafetería y huyó junto a otros dos hombres en un vehículo, que fue interceptado por una patrulla de la Guardia Civil. Al identificarlos, los agentes se dieron cuenta de que la mujer ya estaba siendo investigada por actividades delictivas similares.
Tras su detención, la mujer fue puesta a disposición del Tribunal de Instancia de Cangas junto con las diligencias, y quedó en libertad mientras continúa investigada por los hechos. No hay información sobre cómo accedió a las contraseñas ni qué comprobaciones de autenticación se saltó.
Las funciones antirrobo de Android y iPhone
Los propietarios de teléfonos Android pueden proteger sus dispositivos frente al robo y al acceso no autorizado a sus datos utilizando funciones de protección antirrobo. Estas opciones se pueden encontrar en Ajustes, Google, Todos los servicios y Protección antirrobo, y constan de varias funciones de seguridad.
El bloqueo por detección de robo utiliza los sensores de movimiento y las conexiones del dispositivo y puede bloquear la pantalla si alguien arrebata el móvil y huye. Sin embargo, la disponibilidad de estas funciones puede variar en función del modelo del teléfono; un ajuste atenuado indica que no es compatible con esa función.
La guía de protección antirrobo de Android describe el funcionamiento de las herramientas. El bloqueo remoto exige, entre otros requisitos, que el número de teléfono esté verificado, la tarjeta SIM esté activa y que la función “Localizador” esté activa en el móvil, tal y como se indica en las instrucciones de Google. Si el dispositivo no tiene conexión a internet cuando se solicita el bloqueo remoto, el teléfono se bloqueará automáticamente una vez que se restablezca dicha conexión.
Los iPhones ofrecen funciones de protección antirrobo similares; sin embargo, algunas acciones exigen Face ID o Touch ID, sin que el código pueda usarse como alternativa. Dichas funciones requieren autenticación biométrica para acceder a contraseñas guardadas cuando se cumplen las condiciones de esta protección. Además, si se intenta cambiar las opciones de seguridad, como la contraseña de la Cuenta de Apple, tendrá que esperar una hora y utilizar Face ID/Touch ID una segunda vez para confirmar su identidad.
La protección antirrobo adicional del iPhone se aplica por defecto fuera de lugares conocidos, como casa o el trabajo. La opción “Siempre” permite exigir estas medidas también en esas ubicaciones. Las funciones de protección antirrobo deben activarse antes de que se produzca un robo.
Si ya se han realizado pagos fraudulentos, el Instituto Nacional de Ciberseguridad (INCIBE) aconseja contactar con el banco para intentar anularlos y, en su caso, bloquear la tarjeta y denunciar el problema. El bloqueo del teléfono y la reclamación de las operaciones son actuaciones distintas.

articles.title: Une plateforme en ligne permet désormais aux propriétaires de ficher les locataires qui ne paient pas leur loyer et de vérifier leurs impayés avant de leur louer un logement
articles.text:
Une plateforme en ligne permet désormais aux propriétaires de ficher les locataires qui ne paient pas leur loyer et de vérifier leurs impayés avant de leur louer un logement
Les propriétaires ont désormais accès à une plateforme pour savoir si un candidat à la location cumule au moins 3 mois de loyers impayés. Il s’agit de Sigilio, un fichier privé accessible aux professionnels de l’immobilier qui gèrent des locations en France. Pour un locataire qui est déjà en difficulté, être inscrit dans ce fichier consultable peut peser lourd sur un dossier.
Sigilio se présente comme le "répertoire communautaire national des incidents locatifs". Pour l’utilisation, c’est simple. Il faut que le professionnel renseigne le nom, le prénom, la date et la ville de naissance du candidat. Ensuite, sur son écran apparaît la réponse entre "INSCRIT" ou "NON-INSCRIT”, sans précision de la somme due. L’adresse, le numéro de téléphone ou quelconque donnée bancaire n’apparaissent pas dans le résultat.
Un fichier pour consulter et inscrire les locataires
À noter qu’un propriétaire qui gère seul son bien n’a pas accès à Sigilio. C’est uniquement lorsque le propriétaire confie son logement à une agence adhérente que la vérification peut avoir lieu via un professionnel. Sigilio est donc un outil de contrôle pour les professionnels au moment d’étudier un dossier de location.
Un locataire peut être inscrit dans Sigilio quand sa dette atteint au moins 3 mois de loyers impayés, charges comprises. Avant le fichage, il y a une mise en demeure puis ensuite la plateforme informe le locataire par courriel. Si la dette repasse sous le seuil des 3 mois, le professionnel a 5 jours ouvrés pour supprimer l’inscription. Si elle ne repasse jamais en dessous, Sigilio efface automatiquement les données 5 ans après la dernière inscription, sans historique.
Sigilio admet qu’un professionnel peut refuser un dossier si un candidat apparaît comme "INSCRIT". Sauf que voilà, cela n’explique pas pourquoi il y a une dette. Certains locataires font face à une perte d’emploi, une maladie incapacitante ou une séparation qui provoque plusieurs mois d’impayés. La Confédération nationale du logement dénonce un risque d’exclusion en plus pour les ménages fragiles.
Le sujet est d’autant plus sensible que les impayés progressent. À la fin du mois de septembre 2026, le baromètre Rivage a étudié 6 577 baux gérés par des agences clientes de sa plateforme. Sur ces baux, 3,4 % présentaient au moins un mois d’impayé. Pour les dossiers concernés, la dette médiane atteignait 1 998 €, soit 2,9 mensualités charges comprises. Un niveau très proche de celui retenu par Sigilio.
3 € facturés pour chaque recherche effectuée
En 2020, un projet comparable à Sigilio a provoqué la polémique. À l’époque, la Fédération nationale de l’immobilier souhaitait créer un fichier mutualisé des incidents de paiement. La CNIL est alors intervenue pour rappeler qu’une base de données pareille pouvait exclure une personne d’un contrat de location et exigeait de fortes garanties. Finalement, le projet fut abandonné.
Mais ensuite, le RGPD est entré en application en 2018 et un fichier comme Sigilio ne passe plus par une autorisation préalable de la CNIL. Mais la plateforme a toutefois transmis une analyse d’impact sur la protection des données à l’autorité. Arthel Digital s’occupe du traitement des données et de la conformité du fichier.
Le mois dernier, le ministre du Logement a relancé l’idée d’un suivi national des dettes locatives, même si aucun texte de loi n’est programmé à court terme. Sigilio est donc une initiative privée distincte de ce souhait du ministre du Logement. Sigilio n’est pas payant pour le moment, la consultation est gratuite depuis la phase de lancement. Ensuite, chaque recherche coûtera 3 € HT aux professionnels adhérents.
