articles.title: Scientists overcome a hidden obstacle to more powerful quantum computers
articles.text:
Scientists overcome a hidden obstacle to more powerful quantum computers
- Date:
- October 25, 2026
- Source:
- RIKEN
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered a way to operate multiple silicon qubits simultaneously with remarkable accuracy, overcoming a major challenge in scaling up quantum computers. Their new technique maintained accuracy of approximately 99.9% even when all five qubits were running at once, opening the door to larger and more powerful quantum processors.
- Share:
Silicon spin qubits could play a major role in the future of quantum computing because they can be produced using the same semiconductor manufacturing methods that make today's computer chips. However, researchers have faced a significant challenge. When multiple silicon qubits are controlled at the same time, their operations tend to become less accurate. Building practical, large quantum computers will require scientists to control many qubits simultaneously while keeping errors to a minimum.
Researchers at the RIKEN Center for Emergent Matter Science and their collaborators have now made important progress toward solving this problem. In a study published in Nature Physics, the team demonstrated highly accurate control of several silicon spin qubits operating simultaneously. Their experiments used an array of five qubits connected to a shared microwave control line. By identifying a major cause of errors during simultaneous operation, the scientists developed a technique to reduce those errors and maintain precision.
Leon Camenzind, a RIKEN research scientist and co-first author who supervised the experiments, explains the significance of the results: "This shows that high-fidelity control can be maintained even when several qubits are operated at the same time and represents an important step toward scaling up silicon-based quantum processors."
Scientists Identify a Hidden Source of Quantum Computing Errors
Unlike conventional computers, which store information as bits representing either 0 or 1, quantum computers use quantum bits, or qubits, that can exist in combinations of both states. Silicon spin qubits store this information using the spin of individual electrons confined within silicon. Performing reliable quantum calculations requires extremely precise control over these electron spins.
Microwave signals provide that control, but operating multiple qubits simultaneously can create unwanted effects that interfere with their accuracy. The researchers traced much of this problem to a phenomenon called the AC Stark shift.
This effect occurs when microwave control signals alter a qubit's effective energy levels, producing changes in the phase of its quantum state. Those phase shifts can disrupt the intended operation of individual qubits, particularly when several are being controlled at once.
To counteract the problem, the team created a calibration method that compensates for these unwanted shifts. Rather than separately calibrating every possible combination of qubits, the technique relies on calibrations performed between pairs of qubits. This makes the approach more practical for systems containing larger numbers of quantum bits.
"Rather than requiring an entirely separate calibration procedure for every possible combination of qubits, our method uses calibrations between pairs of qubits to compensate for the unwanted phase shifts," explains Yi-Hsien Wu, the first author who carried out the experiments as part of his PhD research.
Quantum Qubits Achieve Accuracy Above 99.99%
The researchers combined their calibration technique with an improved device design and carefully adjusted microwave control pulses. Their results showed that exceptionally high accuracy could be maintained even when multiple qubits were operating simultaneously.
When the five qubits were tested individually, each achieved single-qubit gate fidelity well above 99.99%, with the highest approaching 99.999%. Fidelity describes how closely a quantum operation matches its intended result.
The team then tested how well the system performed when several qubits were active together. With as many as three qubits operating simultaneously, fidelity remained above 99.99%. Even when all five qubits were controlled at once, accuracy stayed at approximately 99.9%, approaching the levels needed for practical fault-tolerant quantum computing.
Although the calibration method greatly reduced errors, it did not eliminate them entirely. The researchers found that the remaining loss of accuracy was linked to drive-induced decoherence, an effect caused by the greater microwave power required to operate multiple qubits simultaneously.
Unlike the unwanted phase shifts corrected by the new technique, decoherence involves the loss of the delicate quantum coherence needed for reliable operations.
According to Camenzind, "This is a limitation, but further improvements to device design could help mitigate this source of error."
A New Path Toward Larger Quantum Processors
The findings show that controlling several silicon spin qubits at the same time does not necessarily require a major sacrifice in accuracy. By correcting a key source of errors, the researchers have demonstrated a promising approach for operating more qubits through shared microwave control lines.
This is especially important for the development of large quantum processors. Giving every qubit its own independent control system would make increasingly complex devices difficult to manage. Shared control lines could offer a more practical way to expand these systems while maintaining the precision needed for quantum calculations.
"By addressing a key source of control errors through pairwise calibration," says Camenzind. "Our study supports the use of shared control lines as a practical approach to scaling up quantum processors. Combined with silicon's compatibility with established semiconductor manufacturing, we believe that this advance could help pave the way toward larger quantum processors capable of performing increasingly complex computations."
The broader objective is to develop quantum computers that can reliably perform calculations despite the errors and disturbances that affect quantum systems. Such machines, known as fault-tolerant quantum computers, will require precise, dependable control over large numbers of qubits.
"Our long-term goal is to build a fault-tolerant quantum computer based on silicon spin qubits, and reliable parallel control is an essential step toward that goal," adds Seigo Tarucha, project manager of a silicon quantum computing project under JST's Moonshot Goal 6.
Story Source:
Materials provided by RIKEN. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Yi-Hsien Wu, Leon C. Camenzind, Patrick Bütler, Ik Kyeong Jin, Akito Noiri, Kenta Takeda, Takashi Nakajima, Takashi Kobayashi, Giordano Scappucci, Hsi-Sheng Goan, Seigo Tarucha. Simultaneous high-fidelity single-qubit gates in a spin qubit array. Nature Physics, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41567-026-03466-2

articles.title: Who's really in charge at Anthropic after the IPO? | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Anthropic was founded in 2021 to ensure humanity can control AI and benefit from it in the long-term. As the frontier lab approaches its initial public offering, however, there’s one class of humanity that is being shut out of control: anyone who buys its stock on public markets.
Complex structures that allow founders like Elon Musk or Mark Zuckerberg to control their public companies without owning most of them are nothing new in Silicon Valley. But Anthropic’s obsession with AI safety has resulted in a truly baroque style of corporate governance that will leave common shareholders with little say over most major decisions at the AI company, including who sits on its board.
First, Anthropic is a public benefit company — a for-profit corporation legally allowed to weigh a public mission alongside profit — with the goal of promoting AI safety. That status protects the board’s ability to make decisions about AI safety that aren’t driven entirely by shareholder value without being sued by angry investors.
Right now, the board is chaired by Anthropic president Daniela Amodei and includes CEO Dario Amodei (her brother), Netflix cofounder Reed Hastings, former Microsoft and GM CFO Christopher Liddell, Novartis CEO Vas Narasimhan, and Spark Capital partner Yasmin Razavi. There is one vacancy on the board.
Second, Anthropic has allocated significant control of its board to a Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT), an independent panel meant to keep the company focused on mission to benefit humanity. The trust owns a class of stock that gives it the ability to elect and remove a majority of the company’s board, known as Class T directors. The LTBT is chaired by Neil Shah, a global health expert who was managing director at GiveWell, a nonprofit that ranks charities, and includes former Federal Reserve chair Ben Bernanke, national security expert Richard Fontaine, and Harvard physicist Christopher Stubbs. There is one vacancy on the LTBT right now. The existing members will themselves choose who fills it.
Third, Anthropic’s seven founders also jointly own a special class of stock that gives a majority of them 50.1% of shareholder voting power, allowing them to elect three members of the board of directors. If, for whatever reason, there’s no majority among the founders, only then are their shares voted in proportion with holders of common stock.
Finally, the board can put a check on the LTBT. When the LTBT nominates a “Specified” one of its four directors, or removes that director without cause (that is, without alleging misconduct), the board’s nominating committee can decline to approve the move and throw the decision to the company’s employees for a vote.
Here’s what all that looks like:
The dynamics of such a complex structure are hard to predict. We’ve already seen one notable instance where a similar structure was essentially overthrown: OpenAI’s so-called blip, when OpenAI’s board briefly fired CEO Sam Altman over concerns that he was not being candid with them. Thanks to the loyalty of the company’s employees to Altman, the board backed down, reinstated him, and a new governance structure was put in place. Anthropic’s structure seems to formalize that kind of employee power.
At Anthropic, cracks in the founders’ unified front could lead to common shareholders having more say than expected, while employees can overrule the LTBT on board seats if they back the board over the assembled luminaries.
The founders’ control won’t last forever: Ten years after the IPO, the founders can choose to end their control of the company, or their control will end automatically when fewer than three of them remain. At that point, the LTBT will continue until 85% of common shareholders vote to end it, or it decides to step down with approval from the board.
If and when neither special class of shareholder exists any more — hopefully not because of an AI-driven catastrophe — common shareholders finally get control.

articles.title: Siete días metiéndose en agua a 14 °C: lo que de verdad dice (y lo que no) el último estudio del “cold plunge”
articles.text:
La inmersión en agua fría era algo que parecía reservado para deportistas que necesitaban tener una buena recuperación física tras un esfuerzo considerable, como ocurre, por ejemplo, en futbolistas. Pero esto es algo que ha pasado a convertirse en un ritual para cualquier persona con el objetivo de mantener los tejidos sanos y sobre todo jóvenes. Aunque la pregunta que de verdad nos debemos hacer es: ¿sirve para algo estar bajo agua fría durante mucho tiempo?
Un estudio publicado en la revista Advanced Biology hace unos años quiso responder a esta pregunta, reclutando a 10 chicos jóvenes de unos 23 años y físicamente activos. Con esta muestra, comenzaron a sumergirlos en agua fría para analizar qué ocurría en sus células mononucleares que viajan por todo su organismo. El problema es que no hubo ningún tipo de grupo control para poder hacer una comparativa real.
Aquí lo que se buscaba era observar la batalla que había entre dos procesos celulares que son fundamentales, como son la apoptosis, es decir, la muerte celular programada, y la autofagia, que es el sistema de reciclaje y limpieza de nuestro cuerpo.
Los resultados mostraron que la aclimatación es real, pero no inmediata, ya que en los primeros cuatro días el cuerpo sufre por estar bajo una temperatura mínima. Y sufría porque se detectaron signos de una autofagia que no estaba funcionando correctamente y también se vio un aumento de la caspasa-3 escindida, que es un marcador que nos habla de que las células están muriendo por estrés.
Sin embargo, el día 7 todo cambió, puesto que las células aprendieron a defenderse. De esta manera, el sistema de limpieza fue más eficiente y la destrucción celular volvió a sus niveles basales. En cuanto a la inflamación si que hubo un poco de decepción, puesto que los marcadores clásicos como la interleucina-6 no variaron mucho entre estar fuera de un baño de agua fría o dentro. Es por ello que la conclusión a la que llegaron fue que la exposición repetida al frío solo mejoraba la tolerancia celular a bajas temperaturas.
La fuente de la juventud todavía parece estar dentro de los libros más fantasiosos porque aún no la hemos encontrado. Este estudio no llegó tan lejos, y solo podemos sustentarnos en las declaraciones de una de las autoras que extrapoló los resultados a una supuesta prevención del envejecimiento celular, aunque en ningún momento se midió alguna de las variables que nos hablaran de esto.
Lo que sí sabemos. Pero si nos salimos de la necesidad de ser prácticamente eternos, sí que encontramos beneficios para poder darse un baño de hielo. Uno de los más evidentes nos lo da una revisión publicada este mismo año que confirma que sumergirse en hielo ayuda con la recuperación rápida, reduciendo las agujetas. El problema es que, si se usa este sistema de manera constante después de entrenar, se está perjudicando a las ganancias de fuerza y también al crecimiento muscular.
Si pensamos en los beneficios psicológicos, la verdad es que a día de hoy no hay evidencia que nos permita afirmar que el agua fría mejore el estado de ánimo o reduzca el estrés, puesto que muchos de los estudios que hay tienen un sesgo muy elevado.
El verdadero peligro. Más allá de que los beneficios antienvejecimiento no estén contrastados, meterse en agua helada no es un juego inofensivo. Aquí hay que tener en cuenta que, en el momento de tocar el agua helada, el cuerpo responde con una hiperventilación y una taquicardia que busca compensar la disminución de la temperatura corporal. Un efecto que es conocido como 'cold shock response'.
Y esto es un problema, puesto que hablamos de un riesgo cardiovascular importante que puede llevar a la muerte en el caso de darse estos baños en aguas abiertas o sin supervisión.

articles.title: Apple se rinde ante la IA y lanza una gran actualización para sus aplicaciones más usadas
articles.text:
Apple ha lanzado una actualización que integra la IA en Pages, Numbers, Keynote y otras aplicaciones. Siguiendo la estrategia de Microsoft, los de Cupertino añadieron un asistente inteligente en sus aplicaciones creativas y de productividad. Apple usará sus modelos y los de OpenAI para ofrecer funciones de edición de imágenes o vídeos, generación de documentos y más.
De acuerdo con el comunicado de prensa, Apple se ha subido por completo al tren de la IA al ofrecer herramientas generativas dentro de sus aplicaciones. En la Creative Suite, Pixelmator Pro añadió el Generative Fill, una función de relleno inteligente que permite modificar o completar áreas de una imagen mediante un prompt. Al igual que vemos en Photoshop, los usuarios solo tienen que seleccionar la parte a editar y escribir lo que necesitan usando lenguaje natural.
El relleno generativo utiliza valores como la iluminación, perspectiva y textura del entorno que lo rodea para calcular la edición. Los elementos generados por la IA pueden fusionarse en las capas existentes o insertarse como nuevas capas usando un enmascarado inteligente. Sumado a esto, Pixelmator Pro también debuta una función llamada Super Resolution que agranda las imágenes sin perder detalle o nitidez.
Otra app que recibe funciones de IA es Logic Pro, la cual integra un asistente inteligente que usa modelos de OpenAI y Apple para iniciar una nueva canción, configurar una pista vocal a partir de un prompt o perfeccionar un proyecto activo. La actualización también añade una herramienta de análisis de audio para clasificar y etiquetar los sonidos añadidos a la colección, de modo que sean más fáciles de buscar y arrastrar al proyecto.
Pages, Numbers y Keynote dan el salto a la IA
La parte más interesante de esta actualización son las aplicaciones como Pages, Numbers y Keynote. Tras años de mantenerse al margen, Apple dobló las manos y dejó que la inteligencia artificial ocupe un lugar central en su suite de productividad de un modo similar a lo que hace Copilot en Microsoft Office. Las tres aplicaciones permitirán acceder a un asistente inteligente impulsado por la IA de OpenAI y los modelos internos de Apple.
Según la compañía, la IA puede comprender el contexto de los documentos para ayudar a redactar textos, generar contenido o automatizar determinadas tareas. En Keynote es capaz de diseñar y animar diapositivas, mientras que en Numbers puede calcular, visualizar y organizar datos o construir tablas personalizadas. Apple también ha añadido soporte para MCP, un estándar que permite conectar agentes y herramientas de IA externas para ejecutar acciones y acceder a la información en sus aplicaciones.
Por último, Apple ha actualizado Final Cut Pro integrando las herramientas de MotionVFX de forma nativa. Los usuarios tendrán acceso a plantillas, gráficos, transiciones y otras herramientas usadas por profesionales. La nueva versión habilita el acceso al Content Hub dentro de la aplicación, desde el cual se ofrecerá una selección de vídeos, fotos y fondos de stock seleccionados por Apple. Las imágenes de la línea de tiempo podrán abrirse en Pixelmator Pro para hacer ediciones sin necesidad de reimportar, e incluso se podrá usar la IA para generarlas.
La actualización estará disponible en noviembre de 2026 para los suscriptores de Creator Studio sin coste adicional. No está de más mencionar que las funciones de IA requieren un dispositivo compatible con Apple Intelligence que ejecute iOS 27, iPadOS 27 o macOS 27 o posterior.

articles.title: Almost all of Amazon’s new Echo gear is available now
articles.text:
Amazon used to blast out dozens of products onstage at annual hardware events. If this October is any indication, the company has wisely changed its strategy to put more focus on each new product with its own launch. The latest round of launches focuses on Echo products, including speakers, smart displays, as well as a smart photo frame.
Almost all of Amazon’s new Echo gear is available now

A 10-inch anti-glare touchscreen that comes in a few design options. It’s a frame that features Alexa, and doubles as a smart speaker. It works with Amazon Photos, which offers unlimited storage for Prime members.

articles.title: Micron Plans 400-Layer 3D NAND with Wafer-to-Wafer Bonding in 2027
articles.text:
Tuesday, October 27th 2026
Micron Plans 400-Layer 3D NAND with Wafer-to-Wafer Bonding in 2027
Micron is actively working on bringing its next-generation G11 NAND Flash technology to production, as the company has announced that G11 will be its first 3D NAND Flash. With the current G9 technology shipping across Micron's product portfolio, the company has created NAND Flash storage modules using over 200 layers of scaling. However, as the current technology reaches its limitations, the next phase involves exploring vertical stacking. With G11, Micron aims to use wafer-on-wafer 3D NAND stacking to double the capacity of NAND modules. Micron is now officially following in the footsteps of Chinese NAND giant YMTC, which has been making 3D stacked NAND for some time using Xtacking technology.
This is achieved by splitting each wafer into separate components. One is designed as a memory cell wafer, while the other contains peripheral logic circuits. These are combined using hybrid bonding technology in wafer-to-wafer stacking. Hybrid bonding creates a permanent bond between two silicon chips using embedded metal bumps that fuse together to form a single chip. Multiple dies or entire silicon wafers can be connected by stacking the back ends of two chips together. In this way, Micron plans to ship 400-layer NAND in the second half of 2027, which is less than a year away, and we are about to see more commercialization of 3D silicon.For capacity and speed, Micron advertises that G11 will double the density per square millimeter. From 21 Gb/mm² for G9, the G11 generation is targeting 42 Gb/mm². Other improvements include a much faster I/O speed, increasing from 3,600 MT/s in G9 to 5,400 MT/s with G11, while efficiency is expected to be significantly improved with 25% lower energy transfer per bit. Real-world performance will depend on the number of these 3D NAND chips in the SSD, as well as the controller, firmware, and interface that the SSD uses to communicate with the host system. Therefore, we don't yet know what kind of speeds consumers can expect, but rest assured, we will be benchmarking them in the future.

articles.title: How Much Can Semiconductor Models Hide?
articles.text:
Advanced packaging requires models to cross company boundaries without exposing proprietary processes, but hiding too much can make the prediction break down.
Key Takeaways:
The goal seems simple — share the model without sharing the process. A materials supplier shouldn’t have to reveal a proprietary formulation just so a customer can predict how it will behave in a package, and a foundry shouldn’t have to hand over its recipe to provide a useful model of a chiplet. But advanced packaging is making that separation much harder to maintain.
For years, engineers moved much of what they needed between companies through datasheets, design rules, and qualification specs, while the manufacturing knowledge stayed with the supplier. That arrangement held as long as the pieces behaved independently, but what one company keeps inside its process now shapes how another company’s part of the package performs once everything is assembled. The process may still belong to the supplier, but its consequences no longer end at the factory gate.
“There’s been some initial work on this challenge, but how do you insert a membrane between the companies so they can share a certain amount of data, but not all,” said Greg Prewitt, director of product management for Exensio Test Operations at PDF Solutions. “Do you obfuscate it? Do you normalize it? How much do you share so both teams can solve a problem without seeing any of the IP that’s proprietary to one company or another?”
The difficulty is deciding what that membrane should let through. Hide too little and the supplier gives away process knowledge it spent years developing. Hide too much and the model may lose the behavior, variation, or limits that the engineer on the other side needs to make a useful prediction. That leaves a harder question — how much can disappear inside it before it starts hiding something the prediction actually needs?
Materials show the problem in its simplest form. Engineers may need to know how a material changes with temperature, whether a substrate will warp enough to affect assembly, or how process variation propagates into electrical performance without needing the proprietary details that produced those behaviors. A customer doesn’t need a material company’s formulation to model how one of its materials will behave, but a few static numbers on a datasheet may not be enough either.
“Although proprietary formulations cannot be shared, material characterization across the range of conditions relevant to the intended application can provide a more comprehensive representation of material behavior, allowing models to better reflect real-world conditions and improve prediction accuracy,” said Hanlin Chen, senior research associate and team lead at Brewer Science. “A digital twin that uses single fixed values for material inputs will always underrepresent real-world risk.”
The data handoff challenge
The need for more detailed models is growing because an advanced package brings together pieces whose engineering histories accumulated in different places. They may pass through several companies before the finished package reaches the system, but by then no single company necessarily has the whole history.
“Advanced packaging is enabled by a highly collaborative supply chain,” said Joon Ahn, vice president of global factory IT and automation at Amkor. “Dies, substrates, materials, and design information are contributed by multiple partners. Each participant owns unique expertise and data associated with their portion of the value chain.”
That distributed ownership becomes a problem once the design flow needs manufacturing information before everything has been built. The process can remain inside one company, but enough of its behavior has to become usable somewhere else.
What reaches the next engineer is usually enough to describe the part as designed, but not necessarily enough to explain how it will behave after assembly. Nominal dimensions and basic electrical or material properties are relatively easy to pass along. Production variation and the history behind those numbers are much less likely to make the trip.
“I don’t think we need complete data transparency to create a connected digital thread,” said CP Hung, vice president of corporate R&D at ASE. “What we really need is a trusted way to share enough information for the next engineering decision to be made.”
That doesn’t mean every upstream detail belongs in the model. Some can disappear without changing the prediction, while others matter only when something elsewhere in the package exposes their effect. For example, a chiplet’s thermal response may be enough for one analysis, but process variation can change that response in a way the downstream model can’t see.
The question therefore isn’t simply how much information can be shared. It’s which information still matters after the process itself has been hidden. A model that preserves the right behavior can protect the recipe underneath it. Hide the wrong thing, however, and the uncertainty disappears from the model even though it never disappeared from the package.
How much physics can a model hide?
Reduced-order and surrogate models solve a similar computational problem in different ways. A reduced-order model simplifies a higher-fidelity physical representation, while a surrogate approximates behavior across a sampled design or process space. Both make analysis practical when running the underlying model every time would take too long, but they don’t become more trustworthy because they run faster.
“The surrogate model can be trusted if the simulated data used to create the surrogate model is accurate,” said Eric Guichard, senior vice president and general manager of AI Manufacturing at Silvaco. “For the simulation data to be accurate and predictive, the physical models used to generate them must be calibrated. The calibration can only be done against experimental data. Those experimental data are usually available and not proprietary. Physical model calibration is only one part of the equation. The second part is the knowledge of the detailed process recipes.”
The problem splits into two very different kinds of information. Experimental measurements can provide the evidence needed to calibrate a model without revealing much about the process itself, but building a predictive representation may still require details the company would never hand directly to a customer.
What makes that workable is an asymmetry between building the model and using it. The organization creating the model may need to know enough about the process to establish why it behaves the way it does. The engineer consuming the model may only need access to that behavior. A substrate model, for example, might expose thickness, material response, and the effects of process variation without revealing how the supplier achieves those characteristics in manufacturing.
“If only some key knobs are exposed to the user of the surrogate model, we can reasonably believe that the proprietary process details are preserved,” Guichard said.
The recipe doesn’t disappear. It moves behind the model boundary. But that only relocates the disclosure problem rather than solving it, because the model builder still needs what the supplier is trying to protect.
“Availability of detailed process recipes is actually the challenge,” Guichard added.
Encryption protects proprietary data
Encryption creates a way to separate useful behavior from proprietary implementation. Synopsys’ HFSS (High Frequency Structure Simulator) supports encrypted electromagnetic models that a component supplier can share for use in a customer’s simulation without exposing the underlying geometry and material information.
“These encrypted models solve a significant but non-technical hurdle — how to share simulation models of an electronic part with your customers without revealing your trade secrets,” said Lang Lin, product management director at Synopsys.
Encryption handles the disclosure problem neatly. The engineer receiving the model can use it without gaining access to what’s sealed inside. What encryption can’t tell that engineer is whether the model is still valid for the problem being asked.
“That has always been one of the key concerns about simulation, in general,” Lin said. “How well does it actually match reality?”
A model can be secure and still be wrong for the conditions in which it’s being used. If it was built around one package or process window, the result may remain numerically precise long after the design has moved beyond those conditions. Encryption can make that harder to catch because the user can’t look inside and see where the original assumptions stop holding. The IP can stay perfectly protected while the engineering decision doesn’t.
Model sharing therefore needs something outside the encrypted model itself. The recipient may not need to know how the model works internally, but they still need to know the conditions under which it can be trusted.
When the model stops working
Materials make that problem easier to see. A datasheet can be perfectly accurate and still describe only one moment in a material’s life. Once that material is cured, assembled, and put into service, the properties used to build the model may start to move.
“A datasheet gives you a snapshot, CTE, modulus, adhesion, viscosity, measured under one set of conditions at one point in time,” said Brewer’s Chen. “Mechanical and thermal properties shift with degree of curing. Crosslink density may continue to evolve after processing, and adhesion strength is highly dependent on the specific bonding interface. CTE also varies, particularly in the temperature region near the polymer’s Tg (glass transition temperature). Treating any of these as a single static number causes a lot of simulation-to-silicon gaps.”
The supplier doesn’t have to reveal the formulation to account for that behavior. What has to survive the handoff is enough information to show how the material changes under the conditions the package is likely to see. A nominal value may be enough at one point in the design space but misleading somewhere else.
Surrogate models make the same validity problem particularly visible. They can be highly accurate inside the region represented by their training data and still return a plausible-looking answer after the user has wandered outside it. The model hasn’t necessarily failed at that point. It’s being asked a question its underlying data was never meant to answer.
“The fundamental principle is that surrogate models are reliable when interpolating within the region represented by their training data and less reliable when extrapolating beyond it,” Guichard said.
The difficulty is that nothing in the output necessarily flags the crossing. A number returned from outside the training region can look exactly like a number returned from inside it.
A useful black box therefore needs a visible envelope around it. The recipe can remain hidden, but the conditions that establish where the model applies can’t. The engineer using it needs to know when the question has moved outside the territory the model actually knows. The model builder has to make that territory visible, and the user still has to respect it.
The interfaces add complexity
The problem gets harder at the interfaces because the IP line often falls in the same place where two independently built models have to begin describing the same physical behavior.
A material, substrate, or die model may be perfectly valid for the conditions its supplier intended. The trouble starts when those models are joined and the assumptions underneath them don’t line up. One may treat a temperature, geometry, or other condition as fixed while another allows it to move.
“The challenge is that the data often comes in different formats, at different levels of detail, and with different assumptions behind it,” said ASE’s Hung. “A material property, for example, only really means something if we know how it changes with temperature, moisture, time, and process history. A component model may also work perfectly well on its own but not tell us enough about what happens once it’s integrated into the package.”
Those assumptions become harder to separate once the package is assembled. Heat generated in the die moves through the structures around it, while the resulting temperature changes material behavior and mechanical stress elsewhere in the assembly. The models may have been created separately, but the package doesn’t operate that way.
“The real challenge isn’t simply moving data from one company to another,” Hung said. “It’s making sure the physical meaning of that data doesn’t get lost along the way.”
Thermal analysis shows how quickly the information problem follows. Substrate and interposer data may exist upstream, but the downstream design flow needs it in a form that can be combined with the rest of the package.
“When you’re talking about thermal, it’s not just the dies,” said Amlendu Shekhar Choubey, senior director of product management at Synopsys. “This is an integrated problem. You need the whole stack.”
But having all the pieces still doesn’t guarantee they fit. One supplier may characterize behavior under one set of conditions while the model on the other side of the interface assumes another. Even the same nominal parameter can mean something different if it was measured at another temperature, derived from a different process state, or intended for a different range of operation.
The harder problem isn’t getting more data across the interface. The handoff has to preserve enough of the assumptions behind the data for the next model to know how to use it, or every model can be right on its own while the package they describe together is wrong.
What models need to carry
The model itself is becoming a kind of engineering contract between companies. One side doesn’t promise to expose how a process works. It promises to describe enough of what that process does for another engineer to use the result within an agreed set of conditions. The formulation, recipe, or implementation can stay hidden as long as the model exposes the behavior the next engineer actually needs. The receiving engineer still needs to know what kind of promise is being made.
“Uncertainty and model validity need to move with the model,” said Kenneth Larsen, senior director of 3D-IC product management at Synopsys. “It is not enough to exchange geometry, material properties, or simulation results. Each model also needs to carry the context that determines whether it can be trusted — where the data came from, how it was measured or calibrated, what assumptions were used, what range it is valid over, and what decisions it is intended to support.”
That context matters most when the model is abstracted or encrypted. A model useful for architecture exploration may not be trustworthy for final closure, and a surrogate built inside one process window doesn’t automatically stay predictive after the package changes. The output alone gives the engineer no indication that the original promise no longer applies.
The practical answer isn’t to demand that everything become visible. It’s to make the model’s useful behavior and its limits visible enough that the company receiving it can decide whether it applies.
Supplier boundaries won’t disappear, and neither will the competitive value of the processes behind them. In many cases those proprietary details are exactly why a customer selected the supplier in the first place. What’s changing is how much engineering information can stop at the boundary with them. A traditional black box could hide both the process and most of its behavior because the customer mainly needed a specification. A model shared into a tightly coupled package has to conceal the recipe while leaving enough of its consequences visible for someone else to make a defensible decision.
Conclusion
For years, the black box was a workable bargain. A supplier could protect how something was made, the customer could design around a specification, and enough margin usually existed between the two to absorb what neither side could see. Advanced packaging is narrowing that margin because the behavior of one piece increasingly depends on what happened to another before the two ever met.
That doesn’t make proprietary process knowledge less valuable. If anything, the process may become more valuable as packages demand materials, assembly methods, and manufacturing windows tuned to a particular architecture. But the model now has to carry something the old specification often didn’t — enough evidence about what that hidden process does, where that behavior changes, and when the representation should no longer be trusted.
The companies that solve this best probably won’t be the ones that share the most. They’ll be the ones that can turn proprietary process knowledge into models other engineers can use without being able to reconstruct what’s underneath. The recipe can stay private, but the consequences cannot.

articles.title: Cross-border payments startup Taja surpasses 50,000 users across 7 African markets - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Pan-African fintech startup Taja has surpassed 50,000 users and is now processing millions of dollars in transaction volume each month, two years after launching its cross-border payments platform.
Launched in 2024, Taja has built a platform that allows individuals and businesses to send, receive, convert and spend money globally. It offers multi-currency wallets and accounts, international collections, cross-border payouts, real-time currency conversion, virtual cards and digital-asset settlement capabilities.
The startup is live in Nigeria, Ghana, Kenya, Senegal, South Africa, Benin and Ivory Coast, connecting users to major global currencies and payment networks in the United Kingdom and United States.
“We built Taja because moving money across borders shouldn’t feel like navigating a labyrinth,” said David Orovwiroro, the startup’s CEO.
“Surpassing 50,000 users and processing millions of dollars in monthly transaction volume demonstrates the growing demand for accessible, borderless financial infrastructure. We remain committed to ensuring that African creators, freelancers and business owners have the financial tools they need to participate and compete in the global economy.”
The startup said it plans to continue expanding across Africa and into international markets, with a focus on strengthening its payment infrastructure.

articles.title: Apple releases iMac with M6 to make the all-in-one home computer more powerful than ever - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Apple has upgraded the iMac desktop computer with the new M6 chip to help users with everyday productivity and advanced AI performance.
The new iMac is aimed at everyday consumers and families who want a powerful home computer with remarkable capabilities to meet all your computing needs, as well as access to Apple Intelligence and Siri AI.
The iMac design has not changed – it has a 24-inch 4.5K Retina display and is still a remarkably thin and includes a keyboard and your choice of a mouse or trackpad.
It is also available in seven vibrant colours so it can transform your home or workspace.
The new M6 chip adds noticeable performance and power improvements to allow users to complete tasks like video and photo editing and play the latest games.
The display has 500 nits of brightness and the ability to display more than a billion colours.
The new iMac also has a 12MP Centre Stage camera to keep you framed and centred on video calls.
On the audio side it has two pairs of force-cancelling woofers with two tweeters that offer room-filling bold, bass-rich sound and Spatial Audio with support for Dolby Atmos you can enjoy an immersive entertainment experience.
The new iMac includes Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 along with 2.5Gb Ethernet that delivers up to 2.5 times faster wired connectivity than the previous model.
Its internal SSD (solid-state drive) has read and write performances that are two times faster than the M4 iMac.
The new iMac with M6 is available with up to four Thunderbolt 4 ports to enable fast data transfers and to connect a range of accessories, including external storage and up to two 6K external displays.
PRICING AND AVAILABILITY
The new iMac with M6 is available to preorder from October 29 and will go on sale on Friday, November 6.
Pricing for the iMac with M6 featuring a 10-core CPU and 10-core GPU starts at $2,399.

articles.title: Un juge croit reconnaître un texte rédigé avec Claude dans un recours, une étudiante condamnée
articles.text:
Le tribunal administratif de Rennes a condamné une étudiante à 750 euros d’amende, coupable d'un recours abusif. Sa requête contre un refus d’admission en master portait, selon le juge, les marques d’une intelligence artificielle de type Claude, d'Anthropic.
Le 22 octobre 2026, le tribunal administratif de Rennes a infligé une amende de 750 euros pour recours abusif à une étudiante ayant été refusée en master de psychologie à l’université Rennes 2, vient d'apprendre Clubic. Saisi plus de quatre mois après ce refus, le juge des référés a rejeté sa demande d’inscription provisoire. Il a aussi relevé, dans la requête, différents marqueurs typographiques qu’il attribue à l’intelligence artificielle générative.
Ni urgence ni doute sérieux pour le tribunal administratif
L'affaire a démarré avec un refus d'admission en première année de master de psychologie, opposé par l'université Rennes 2 à Delphine*, une étudiante qui ne voulait pas en rester là. La décision était datée du 3 juin 2026, mais le juge des référés n'a été saisi qu'il y a quelques jours, le 18 octobre. L'étudiante a notamment demandé la suspension de la décision et une inscription provisoire sous huit jours.
Elle a expliqué ce délai entre la décision et le recours par un été chargé, avec la phase complémentaire de la procédure nationale, la gestion des désistements, une saisine du recteur le 20 juillet, puis une demande d'aide juridictionnelle le 17 août. Sur le fond, elle conteste le refus sur quatre points. Le chef d'établissement se serait cru tenu de suivre l'avis de la commission. L'acte fixant les capacités d'accueil et les critères de sélection serait introuvable sur le site de l'université. Les membres de la commission n'auraient pas été régulièrement désignés. Et enfin, la signature électronique du refus serait irrégulière, car l'homologation du téléservice Mon Master ne couvrirait plus ses conditions d'utilisation.
Forte de ces arguments et pour obtenir gain de cause, la jeune femme est passée par un référé-suspension, une procédure d'urgence qui permet de geler une décision en attendant que le tribunal la juge sur le fond. Encore faut-il réunir deux conditions : une véritable urgence et un doute sérieux sur la légalité du refus. Le juge n'en a retenu aucune et a rejeté la demande sans même organiser d'audience. Concernant l'urgence, il a estimé que les démarches faires durant l'été n'empêchaient pas d'agir plus tôt, que les cours ont sans doute commencé depuis plusieurs semaines et qu'une nouvelle candidature reste possible pour 2027-2028. Côté légalité, aucun argument ne le convainc, et l'absence de documents sur le site de l'université, par exemple, ne prouve pas qu'ils n'existent pas. Le dossier de la candidate ne plaide pas non plus pour elle. Quatorze autres masters de psychologie l'avaient refusée sans même l'inscrire en liste d'attente, et six autres l'avaient classée, à une exception près, entre la 152e et la 357e place.
Un recours jugé abusif et marqué par l'usage de l'intelligence artificielle générative
Le juge aurait pu s'arrêter là, mais il a pourtant choisi d'utiliser l'article R. 741-12 du code de justice administrative, qui permet de sanctionner une requête abusive jusqu'à 10 000 euros. Selon lui, la demande de Delphine ne remplissait aucune des conditions du référé. Elle visait de plus une formation dont la candidate n'avait manifestement pas le niveau. Le texte comporte en outre des erreurs révélatrices. Une « Madame B. » apparaît plusieurs fois dans les arguments, une « Mme C. » surgit dans la partie sur les frais, et une autre requête à l'objet analogue a été enregistrée. Le juge s'est posé des questions sur des recours considérés comme stéréotypés, produits en masse, et pas même entièrement mis à jour. Vous nous voyez venir ?
L'intelligence artificielle a alors fait son entrée dans la discussion. Le magistrat a fait état d'un mélange d'apostrophes courbes et droites, de nombreux tirets cadratins, des puces en ronds noirs et une argumentation très ordonnée, pédagogique, mais bien trop répétitive, ce qui peut être caractéristique d'un recours à l'IA. Le juge cite même Claude.ai, le chatbot d'Anthropic, comme potentiel outil d'« intelligence artificielle générale » utilisé. Ces indices restent discutables, car un simple copier-coller depuis un traitement de texte peut laisser les mêmes traces. La sanction est tombée malgré tout, et elle est de 750 euros, à la charge de l'étudiante elle-même.
*nous avons modifié son prénom

articles.title: Lessons in Chemistry: 5 Takeaways from Bonnie Garmus’ Novel
articles.text:
Lessons in Chemistry: 5 Takeaways from Bonnie Garmus’ Novel
Discover five powerful lessons from Lessons in Chemistry by Bonnie Garmus about equality, ambition, independent thinking, and self-worth.
Lessons in Chemistry by Bonnie Garmus is a thought-provoking novel about ambition, gender inequality, motherhood, and the courage to challenge social expectations.
Set in the 1960s, the story follows Elizabeth Zott, a brilliant chemist whose professional ambitions are constantly challenged by a society that believes women belong in the kitchen rather than the laboratory.
When Elizabeth unexpectedly becomes the host of a cooking television show, she uses the opportunity to teach more than recipes. Through science, she encourages women to think independently, question established beliefs, and recognise their own abilities.
The novel offers several meaningful lessons about self-worth, equality, and the importance of refusing to let society define who we can become.
5 Powerful ideas in Lessons in Chemistry by Bonnie Garmus
1. Never let society define your potential
One of the most important lessons in Lessons in Chemistry is that your potential should never be determined by society's expectations.
Elizabeth Zott is an exceptionally talented scientist, but she faces discrimination because she is a woman working in a male-dominated field. Instead of being judged solely on her knowledge and abilities, she repeatedly encounters people who underestimate her because of her gender.
Her experiences highlight how social stereotypes can prevent talented individuals from reaching their full potential. Elizabeth refuses to accept these limitations as the truth about herself. She continues pursuing her interests and challenges the assumptions that attempt to hold her back.
The lesson is simple: your abilities are not limited by what others believe you can achieve. Whether in your career, education, or personal life, you deserve the opportunity to explore your potential without being restricted by outdated expectations.
2. Question everything instead of accepting it blindly
Elizabeth approaches life with the curiosity of a scientist. She believes in examining evidence, asking questions, and understanding why things happen rather than accepting conventional wisdom without thinking.
This mindset becomes particularly important when she begins hosting her cooking show, Supper at Six. Although the programme is designed around cooking, Elizabeth introduces scientific explanations and encourages her audience to understand the processes behind everyday tasks.
Her approach transforms an ordinary television show into an opportunity for women to learn, think critically, and develop confidence in their own intelligence.
The novel reminds readers that questioning established ideas is not necessarily an act of rebellion. Sometimes, it is the first step towards progress.
In everyday life, this means examining the beliefs we inherit, questioning unfair traditions, and making decisions based on reason rather than fear of judgement. Independent thinking allows us to recognise when something needs to change.
3. Women deserve equal opportunities and respect
Gender inequality is a central theme throughout Lessons in Chemistry. Elizabeth encounters professional discrimination, unequal treatment, and assumptions about what women should do with their lives.
Her experiences reflect a broader social problem: women's achievements have often been overlooked simply because they do not fit traditional expectations.
Through Elizabeth's journey, Bonnie Garmus illustrates how exhausting it can be to prove one's competence in an environment where others are unwilling to offer equal opportunities. Elizabeth must work harder to have her knowledge recognised, even when her qualifications speak for themselves.
However, the novel also demonstrates the importance of women supporting one another and recognising their shared potential.
The lesson extends beyond the workplace. Equality means respecting women's choices, valuing their contributions, and allowing them to pursue careers and ambitions without being forced into predefined roles.
A person's capabilities should determine their opportunities, not their gender.
4. Intelligence and confidence can change the way people think
Elizabeth's transformation into a television personality demonstrates that knowledge can be a powerful tool for challenging social attitudes.
Rather than abandoning her scientific background to fit the expectations of a cooking show, she brings science into the kitchen. She explains cooking through chemistry and treats her viewers as intelligent individuals capable of understanding complex ideas.
Her approach challenges the assumption that domestic responsibilities and intellectual pursuits must exist separately. It also gives women a platform to engage with science in a way that traditional institutions have often denied them.
Elizabeth's confidence is not about proving that she is better than everyone else. It comes from knowing the value of her knowledge and refusing to make herself smaller to satisfy other people's expectations.
This lesson encourages readers to embrace their expertise, communicate their ideas clearly, and trust their ability to make a difference.
Sometimes, changing people's perspectives begins with one person who is willing to challenge the familiar and present a different way of thinking.
5. Family and personal identity can exist beyond traditional roles
Another meaningful lesson from Lessons in Chemistry is that people should be allowed to define family and identity on their own terms.
Elizabeth's life challenges conventional ideas about motherhood, relationships, and women's responsibilities. Her experiences show that being a mother does not mean abandoning one's ambitions, just as pursuing a career does not make someone less capable of caring for a family.
The novel explores how people navigate grief, parenthood, relationships, and the expectations placed upon them. It presents a more nuanced understanding of what it means to build a fulfilling life.
Elizabeth refuses to accept that she must choose between being intellectually ambitious and being a devoted parent. Instead, she creates a life that reflects her circumstances, values, and priorities.
For readers, the lesson is that there is no single formula for a meaningful life. People have different ambitions, responsibilities, and definitions of happiness.
Rather than measuring ourselves against conventional milestones, we can focus on building lives that align with our own values and allow us to grow.
Final thoughts
Lessons in Chemistry by Bonnie Garmus is more than a novel about a scientist navigating a world that underestimates her. It is a story about challenging inequality, embracing curiosity, and refusing to let other people's assumptions determine your future.
Through Elizabeth Zott's experiences, readers are reminded that intelligence deserves recognition, women deserve equal opportunities, and personal ambition should not be sacrificed to satisfy society's expectations.
The five lessons from the book encourage us to question outdated beliefs, trust our abilities, and create lives that reflect who we truly are. Whether you are navigating your career, questioning social norms, or discovering your own identity, Elizabeth's journey offers a powerful reminder that you do not have to fit into someone else's definition of success.
Ultimately, Lessons in Chemistry encourages readers to approach life with curiosity, courage, and the confidence to challenge what they have been told is possible.

articles.title: Microsoft propose un plan de départ volontaire à 60 000 salariés pour faire des économies
articles.text:
Les investissements massifs dans l’IA et l’explosion des dépenses de Microsoft dans les infrastructures et les centres de données pour répondre à la demande galopante en calcul sur le Cloud pour alimenter des modèles d’intelligence artificielle ne seront pas sans conséquence sur les effectifs de la firme de Redmond.
Celle-ci vient en effet d’annoncer la mise en place d’un programme de départ volontaire de grande ampleur. Il concerne quelque 60 000 salariés éligibles, ce qui représente près de 27 % de la masse salariale globale de l’entreprise qui comptabilisait encore 223 000 employés en juin dernier.
L’annonce de ce plan de départs volontaires, qui a été faite en interne par Amy Coleman, la directrice des ressources humaines du groupe, a été partagée publiquement dans un billet de blog publié sur le site de Microsoft.
Des départs volontaires négociés poussés par les investissements dans l’IA
Ce programme de départ volontaire mis en place par Microsoft, qui n’a pas fixé d’objectif chiffré de nombre de départs, est temporaire et doit permettre aux employés éligibles et qui le souhaitent de partir avec un soutien financier, mais aussi un accompagnement pour une reconversion.
L’offre, qui s’adresse aux salariés situés au Canada, aux États-Unis, au Royaume-Uni et en Inde, court a priori jusqu’au début du mois de décembre, avec des départs effectifs fixés au 31 décembre prochain.
Ce plan de départs volontaires intervient six mois après la mise en place d’un plan de départ en retraite volontaire en avril dernier, après le licenciement de plus de 4800 employés au début de l’été 2026, et après une longue série d’autres licenciements entamés par la firme de Redmond depuis plusieurs années. Si Microsoft n’a rien confirmé à ce sujet, cet énième plan de départs volontaires pourrait être les prémices de futures nouvelles vagues de licenciements.
Il faut dire que le contexte financier actuel est plutôt compliqué pour l’entreprise. Microsoft accélère ses investissements dans les datacenters pour répondre à l’explosion de la demande en IA. Une expansion indispensable, mais qui requiert un calcul financier stratégique, alors que le flux de trésorerie disponible de la firme de Redmond, bien que positif, a subi une baisse de 23 % sur la dernière année.

articles.title: Warp discloses breach exposing AI agent logs, user telemetry data
articles.text:
Agent decision logs and telemetry data belonging to Warp agentic development environment users were exposed in an attack on a third-party vendor in the project’s infrastructure.
The company’s founder and CEO, Zach Lloyd, estimates that "roughly 1% of Warp users may have been impacted," but external experts are helping with the ongoing investigation.
Warp is a popular developer tool that started as a modern terminal and evolved into an agentic development environment (ADE) that allows developers to direct AI agents to write and test code and deploy software.
The environment provides a terminal, a code editor, task orchestration, and agent review tools in a single workspace. The project's website says the platform has at least 800,000 users.
“On Friday, we became aware of what we believe to be an active and narrow-banded exploitation of a vendor in Warp's infrastructure,” Lloyd stated.
“We detected the operation within hours and were able to remediate and mitigate the impact,” the CEO added.
Although agent traces and telemetry were identified as potentially affected data, the company did not clarify whether the exposed information included source code, prompts, credentials, or other sensitive details.
Analysis of the incident suggests that the attack was powered by "an agent swarm" that relied on "a very sophisticated penetration and escalation technique."
Lloyd said that Warp has contacted the third-party vendor about the vulnerability, but no details have been shared. The platform has notified users identified to be impacted.
The cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike has also been engaged to assist with the investigation, while the platform has also informed law enforcement authorities.
The incident at Warp follows an incident at AI coding platform OpenCode, which notified users last week that a security breach exposed stored API keys used with external providers.
The incident affected a small percentage of OpenCode users, about 1.4%, and led to unauthorized charges of up to $1,700 for some.
Warp users are advised to remain vigilant, monitor account activity, and treat unsolicited communications with increased caution.

articles.title: 👨🏿🚀TechCabal Daily – Fined National Bank - TechCabal
articles.text:
It’s Moonshot week! ☀️ ️️️
We’re officially renaming Q4 the “IPO quarter.” Any company that went public before October may have to do the whole thing again, properly this time.
But on a serious note, Anthropic, the AI company behind Claude, filed to list on Nasdaq under the ticker “ANT” on Monday, joining an already busy quarter for public market debuts.
Closer to home, Quickmart, Kenya’s second-largest supermarket chain, has expanded the cornerstone allocation in its KES 15 billion ($116 million) IPO to 48% after three more institutional investors joined the offer.
Read smart insights about Francophone Africa’s tech ecosystem—weekly.
Startups
Klump shuts down after five years of trying to make BNPL work
Klump wanted to make taking a loan feel as quick as buying a pair of shoes online. Five years later, the Nigerian buy-now-pay-later (BNPL) startup is shutting down after discovering that fast credit still needs one expensive ingredient: money to lend.
What happened? Klump, founded in 2021 by Celestine Omin and Olufunbi Falayi, has closed after raising about $1.2 million across two rounds. The startup let shoppers split purchases into instalments at checkout and eventually powered financing for hundreds of merchants, including Jumia, Konga, SLOT, and iStore. Seedcamp, the UK-based investor, led its $780,000 pre-seed round in 2022.
Explain like I’m new here: Klump initially funded loans from its own books. Owning the loan book meant it could decide who qualified and return a credit decision in minutes, exactly what an online checkout needed.
But lending at scale requires far more capital than building software, Omin wrote on October 25. Klump tried to raise debt to fund more loans but could not secure enough.
So it changed the model. Instead of lending, Klump became the pipe connecting shoppers and merchants to banks and other lenders. By July, shoppers on e-commerce platform Jumia could choose financing from multiple lenders directly at checkout.
Between the lines: The pivot solved one problem and created another. Klump no longer needed to finance every purchase, but its growth now depended on banks. Integrations took six to 18 months, sometimes years. Lenders decided which sectors they would finance, how much they would lend, and how much risk they would tolerate.
Klump’s problem captures BNPL’s difficult economics. Finance the loans yourself, and you need a deep pool of debt. Let banks fund them and your product moves at bank speed.
Zoom out: Klump explored acquisition options before shutting down, including talks with Kenya’s Lipa Later, which itself entered administration in 2025. Its founders now say BNPL may work better as a feature inside a larger financial services company than as a standalone business.
Klump proved people wanted instalments at checkout. It could not build enough control over the capital behind them.
Upgrade your business today
Pay with OPay is live on Fincra. Customers approve payments straight from their OPay wallet, and you get confirmation back on your site. Available now for NGN collections! Upgrade your business today with Fincra pay with OPay.
Banking
FNB, South Africa’s second-largest bank, fined $60,000 for exposing private customer data
Because of their business, banks usually hold valuable and sensitive customer information—names, ID numbers, addresses, salaries, account details, and loan applications. Keeping that data safe is a great responsibility. When banks fail to do so, it sends ripples throughout the ecosystem.
First National Bank (FNB), South Africa’s second-largest lender, unfortunately became susceptible to that risk. On October 23, the Information Regulator fined the bank R1 million ($60,000) for that failure.
What happened? South Africa’s privacy regulator said FNB violated the country’s data protection law, the Protection of Personal Information Act (POPIA). An error in FNB’s banking system wrongly classified some account holders as employees, giving 696 unauthorised people access to personal information belonging to 88 home-loan applicants.
Explain like I’m new here: South Africa’s POPIA governs how organisations handle personal data. The regulator found that FNB breached several provisions, including unlawfully processing an account number. It also said FNB was alerted twice, in March and May 2022, but only acknowledged the second complaint in September.
There’s more: The regulator also flagged how FNB collected and kept personal data. It said the bank wrongly used newspaper reports to build databases on people linked to money laundering and politically exposed persons, because newspaper articles do not count as public records under POPIA.
FNB’s retention policy was also criticised for keeping some records—including cancelled tax certificates, asset ownership records, and securities registers—indefinitely without a stated legal basis.
What now? FNB has 30 days to pay the R1 million ($60,000) fine, agree to pay in instalments, or take the matter to court. If it does none of these, the regulator can recover the fine as a civil judgment.
More value with Mycoverai
You already have a great product. With MyCover.ai, create tailored insurance for your customers across fintech, e-commerce, logistics and more, built around your product, and their needs. Get started here.
Ecommerce
Pick n Pay closes 19 more stores as losses narrow
Pick n Pay is shrinking in size to get healthy again. The South African supermarket chain has closed another 19 stores over the past year, while its half-year headline loss narrowed nearly 32% to R299 million ($18 million).
What happened? Pick n Pay’s turnover was almost flat at R36.4 billion ($2.2 billion) in the six months to August, but gross profit rose 3.9%, and its trading loss narrowed 16.9% to R516 million ($31 million). Online sales were a bright spot, growing 35.4%.
The company now has 520 supermarkets and is targeting a return to profit in its 2029 financial year.
Explain like I’m new here: Pick n Pay is one of South Africa’s oldest and best-known supermarket brands. Raymond Ackerman bought four stores in Cape Town in 1967 and built them into a national retailer. But more than a decade of losing market share to rivals such as Shoprite—the country’s largest supermarket chain by revenue and store count—eventually left its core supermarket business in trouble.
The rescue began in 2024. Pick n Pay raised R4 billion ($240 million) through a rights issue, then sold 34.4% of its faster-growing Boxer discount chain for R8.5 billion ($510.5 million). The money reduced debt and bought the company time to repair the Pick n Pay business.
Between the lines: The turnaround is entering a different phase. Closing bad stores, cutting costs, and staff management can improve the numbers. Now Pick n Pay needs shoppers back.
It is also turning to sports to drive that strategy after backing Springboks, South Africa’s world-champion national rugby team. Its six-year Springboks sponsorship is part of that push. Rugby collectables are bringing customers into stores, while Pick n Pay has exclusive rights to sell cheaper Springbok merchandise. Sean Summers, the company’s chief executive officer, said merchandise sales have been “absolutely phenomenal.”
The first phase of the turnaround was about survival. The next is about relevance.
What to watch: Same-store sales. Pick n Pay’s company-owned South African supermarkets recorded 2.4% same-store sales growth in the first half of 2026. Closing another weak store improves the cost base; getting more people through the remaining stores is what eventually gets Pick n Pay back to profit.

True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. We’ve filtered the noise out of Moonshot 2026, optimising the conference strictly for high-calibre connections between startup founders, global financial operators, enterprise leaders and individuals rewiring Africa’s technical frameworks. Join us on October 28 & 29, 2026. Get your ticket.
Pay-TV
DStv is cutting Kenya prices to win back viewers
DStv, the pay-TV platform owned by MultiChoice, has been reshuffling its prices and packages. First in South Africa, now in Kenya. What caught our attention is that MultiChoice has unbundled sports into a standalone package in both markets. Meanwhile, Nigeria is still waiting for the same treatment.
What happened? Canal+-owned MultiChoice is replacing six DStv packages with four in Kenya. From November 5, prices will range from KES 750 ($6) for Starter to KES 7,300 ($56) for Ultimate, down from KES 11,700 ($90) for Premium. That is a 38% cut at the top end.
The Sports package will cost KES 3,000 ($23) and include Premier League and UEFA Champions League matches, plus UFC and WWE.
Explain like I’m new here: DStv is trying to stop a subscriber decline that has been building for years. MultiChoice ended 2025 with 14.4 million subscribers, down from 14.9 million in the previous year. Canal+ has responded with a €100 million ($112 million) growth plan built around simpler packages, lower entry costs and stronger distribution, while shutting down loss-making Showmax to cut costs. MultiChoice expects a €140 million ($157 million) loss in 2026, hit by weaker revenue and rising costs
Will cheaper DStv bring people back? DStv has already tried cheaper packages and promotions in markets such as South Africa, but price alone cannot fix the subscriber problem. Its competition is no longer limited to pay-TV rivals such as StarTimes and Zuku.
Viewers can instead spend their time and money on Netflix, YouTube, TikTok, and other streaming services. Interestingly, Netflix, one of Africa’s widely-streamed platforms, is facing its own problems, as watch hours decline globally.
Is it an attention span problem, electricity outages, cost, or are users just deprioritising entertainment services in the pecking order?
MultiChoice is approaching the problem from all angles that it can control. GOtv gives price-sensitive customers another option within the same group. Canal+ is betting that cheaper entry points and easier access to sports will give DStv a reason to stay in the monthly budget.

articles.title: "Se acabó, la IA ganó": Google Gemini 4 Argon destruye una conjetura de fusión nuclear de 59 años en solo unas pocas horas
articles.text:
Gemini 4 Argon de Google ha ayudado a descubrir nuevas soluciones matemáticas relacionadas con la fusión nuclear. Los primeros candidatos se encontraron en cuestión de horas, según los investigadores. Esto supone una mejora con respecto al trabajo anterior, que refutó una conjetura formulada en 1967. Las aplicaciones prácticas se refieren a las pruebas del software que simula campos magnéticos para la investigación en fusión.
La conjetura lleva el nombre del físico Harold Grad. Aborda las ecuaciones que rigen el equilibrio del plasma y el campo magnético que lo rodea. El objetivo es identificar equilibrios estacionarios tridimensionales compatibles con un conjunto dado de condiciones de presión y simetría.
Cómo se encontraron las nuevas soluciones
La investigación que se publicó en arXiv es el resultado del esfuerzo conjunto de Opal Issan, Jonathan Citrin, Matt Landreman y Brendan Tracey. Los autores generalizaron las dos familias de soluciones anteriores mediante un parámetro en cada una, que rompe la simetría de stellarator. Los stellarators son dispositivos de fusión que utilizan campos magnéticos tridimensionales para contener el plasma.
Con el fin de encontrar generalizaciones de las familias de soluciones conocidas, los autores entregaron la investigación de Landreman y sus preguntas abiertas a un pequeño equipo de agentes de Gemini 4 en Google Antigravity. Los avances mencionados por los investigadores se lograron en cuestión de horas.
El Argon de Google también contribuyó a la escritura de partes del manuscrito, así como a la codificación de comprobaciones simbólicas y numéricas. Los autores humanos supervisaron el proceso de investigación y realizaron varias rondas de revisión adversarial, así como la reescritura del manuscrito.
Los investigadores volvieron a derivar y comprobar simbólicamente cada desarrollo y asumieron la responsabilidad del resultado final. El tiempo mencionado se refiere al periodo en el que unos agentes de IA encontraron los primeros candidatos prometedores.
A la vista del ejemplo mencionado anteriormente, cabe afirmar que se repartió el mérito. Gómez-Serrano, Liehr y Taylor habían expuesto otros contraejemplos a Grad el 21 de septiembre de 2026. Sus soluciones no presentan las simetrías de reflexión planar, axial o helicoidal que postula la conjetura. El resumen de su investigación incluye un sello de aprobado en Lean 4, un asistente de prueba matemática.
A continuación, Landreman presentó sus soluciones analíticas el 22 de septiembre de 2026. Según contó, las soluciones analíticas que él pudo encontrar con la ayuda del GPT-6 Astra Pro fueron comprobadas manualmente por él. La versión revisada se publicó el 28 de septiembre. Cuando se les presentó el problema a los agentes de Gemini, ya disponían tanto de las soluciones de Landreman como de preguntas concretas que requerían respuestas.
El sello de aprobado en Lean 4 figura en la investigación de Gómez-Serrano y sus colaboradores. El artículo de Gemini también menciona otra comprobación. Los investigadores también realizaron cálculos que se verificaron simbólicamente. El manuscrito mencionado anteriormente no declara un sello de aprobado en Lean para los hallazgos. La mención del código de comprobación simbólica y numérica tampoco permite dar por sentado dicho sello.
El acceso a Argon y la publicación científica
En la hemeroteca de septiembre de 2024 hay más ejemplos de formas en que la inteligencia artificial ha facilitado la investigación en fusión nuclear. Los científicos han utilizado la nueva tecnología en la investigación de patrones de turbulencia y en la detección de defectos en soldaduras.
Google mencionó la investigación cuando anunció el 13 de octubre de 2026 el lanzamiento del Argon para su uso comercial. Argon está ahora disponible a través de la API y para suscriptores de Google AI Pro y Ultra en la aplicación Gemini y en el Modo IA del buscador, y de Google AI Ultra en Antigravity.
Se han abierto también las solicitudes para que 10.000 científicos reciban gratuitamente seis meses de acceso al nivel de mayor uso de Antigravity, sujetos a los requisitos de acceso, la capacidad y la selección del programa.

articles.title: “Ces nouveaux entretiens ont des conséquences importantes” : Proton va trier ses employés selon leur usage de l'IA
articles.text:
“Ces nouveaux entretiens ont des conséquences importantes” : Proton va trier ses employés selon leur usage de l'IA
Selon un email interne de la direction de Proton à ses employés, ces derniers vont devoir passer de "nouveaux entretiens" pour savoir comment ils utilisent l'IA. Les conséquences s'annoncent sérieuses.
Alors que les licenciements à cause de l'IA se multiplient dans la tech et le jeu vidéo, à petite ou à grande échelle comme c'est d'ailleurs le cas aujourd'hui chez Microsoft (Jamais Microsoft n’avait fait ça : pour financer l’IA, plus de 25 % de ses salariés sont incités à partir d’ici la fin de l’année), voici venir un autre type de décision en provenance de chez Proton.
La société suisse, souvent citée parmi les meilleures solutions pour se passer de Google et renforcer sa vie privée avec des outils comme Proton Mail, Proton Pass, Proton VPN ou Proton Calendar, aime aussi l'IA. En témoigne son chatbot maison Lumo, mais aussi l'email interne adressé à ses employés que 404 Media a pu se procurer.
Proton veut se réorganiser (et licencier) en fonction de l'IA
Dans les grandes lignes, cet email annonce qu'une partie des employés de Proton va devoir repasser un entretien d'embauche ("re-interviewing") pour savoir comment ils utilisent l'IA dans leur travail. L'email l'indique sans s'en cacher : "Ces nouveaux entretiens ont des conséquences importantes".
Plus exactement, le courrier précise : "Les évaluateurs consigneront leurs évaluations, qui serviront de base à l'analyse globale de notre organisation et de nos ressources humaines." Jusqu'ici, pourquoi pas. Dans une période où l'IA change en profondeur de nombreux métiers, vouloir faire un point à ce sujet se défend.
	
Nous avons besoin de personnes capables de mettre à profit les capacités de l'IA pour créer de meilleurs produits, améliorer l'efficacité opérationnelle et mettre en place de nouvelles méthodes de travail — et qui abordent ce changement avec curiosité, discernement et un sentiment d'urgence.
Mais la suite est moins réjouissante : "Cette analyse pourra déboucher sur des changements au niveau des fonctions, des responsabilités et de la poursuite de l'emploi. Les résultats individuels seront communiqués directement dès que les décisions auront été finalisées." Ainsi, le risque de perdre son emploi si une personne n'utilise pas correctement ou suffisamment l'IA semble bien réel.
Dans une autre phrase qui semble enfoncer une porte ouverte, Proton ajoute : "Nous sommes conscients que ce processus est source d'incertitude. Nous ferons clairement savoir ce qui a été décidé et ce qui reste en suspens." Il est précisé que les interviewers, des spécialistes de l'IA, proviendront d'en dehors de l'entreprise.
Une nouvelle décision contestable
Pour les utilisateurs enfin, qui se tournent souvent vers Proton pour profiter d'un produit européen sécurisé et éloigné de Google et du tout IA, il s'agit d'une nouvelle mauvaise nouvelle sur la politique et la stratégie de la firme. Il y a quelques mois, la firme et son PDG Andy Yen étaient déjà au cœur d'une polémique après avoir financé un clip publicitaire dans la vidéo d’un influenceur français d’extrême-droite. La défense à l'époque était alors que "Proton soutient la liberté d’opinion, mais Proton lui-même doit rester neutre."
