articles.title: "Esto es alucinantemente loco": Hemos tenido que cambiar de nuevo el eje de las ordenadas para poder mantener a El Niño de 2026 dentro
articles.text:
Ese amasijo de líneas azules que hay más arriba es un resumen visual, corto y al pie, de los últimos 45 años de temperaturas del Pacífico ecuatorial. Ese es el contexto, pero la historia es otra cosa: la línea roja. Es decir, las cifras de lo que va de 2026.
Eso y que, por primera vez, tenemos que ampliar el eje hasta los cuatro grados de anomalía para que no se salga por arriba.
¿Qué es exactamente El Niño? No está de más recordar que nos referimos a un fenómeno climático cíclico (aunque muy irregular) que tiene grandes efectos sobre el clima mundial. Enormes, de hecho. Si excluimos a las estaciones, se trata de la fuente más importante de variabilidad climática anual de todo el planeta.
Durante la fase cálida (es decir, durante El Niño), la ausencia de unos vientos alíseos fuertes que refresquen la superficie del Pacífico ecuatorial hace que la temperatura de esa zona del océano se dispare. Es esto, a través de diferentes teleconexiones atmosféricas, lo que trastoca todos los sistemas meteorológicos del mundo.
Los efectos son variados y cambian según la región ("condiciones más secas de lo normal en determinadas partes del mundo; mientras que en otras provoca más precipitaciones. Unos países tienen que lidiar con sequías importantes y otros, con lluvias torrenciales", dice AEMET); pero cuando hablamos de temperaturas no hay duda: El Niño es sinónimo de calor.
Así que repasemos los números. Con los datos diarios de la NOAA en la mano, el máximo de El Niño de 2015 fue una anomalía de +3,02 ºC, el 19 de noviembre; el de 1982, +2,78 °C; el del 97, +2,39 °C. El 26 de octubre de 2026 esas mismas aguas marcaban +3,49 °C.
En el fondo, ahí está todo: El Niño de 2026 está casi medio grado por encima del de 2015, más de un grado por encima del de 1997 y, según el consenso de los modelos, todavía no ha tocado techo.
¿Por qué sigue subiendo? Porque es lo normal. Así funciona El Niño. Es decir, en la medida en que hay más agua en el hemisferio sur, son sus estaciones las que marcan la temperatura del agua. Es normal que (en plena primavera austral) la temperatura siga subiendo.
Además, en cierta forma, El Niño se está retroalimentando a sí mismo. En condiciones normales, los alisios funcionan como un ventilador que empuja el agua caliente hacia Indonesia. Cuando el centro y el este del Pacífico ecuatorial ganan temperatura, los vientos pierden fuelle y eso hace que el mismo sistema que enfría esa zona deje de hacerlo.
La cosa es que, a riesgo de repetirme, no es un año normal: los mapas de la NASA dan zonas del Pacífico hasta 40 centímetros más altos de lo normal.
¿Y hasta cuándo? Los récors anteriores suelen fijarse en noviembre. Así que, a priori, nos queda un mes de subidas. La OMM prevé una media de unos +3,7 °C para octubre-diciembre, frente a un récord trimestral previo de +2,6 °C, y su actualización del 21 de octubre eleva a unos +3,8 °C la de noviembre-enero.

articles.title: Marre de prendre des notes ? Gemini Notebook se transforme en dictaphone
articles.text:
Gemini Notebook continue de s’imposer comme un outil incontournable de l’écosystème Google pour faciliter l’apprentissage et les révisions. Après avoir permis à ses utilisateurs d’améliorer leurs fiches de révision, Google s’attaque à un autre élément essentiel de l’apprentissage : la prise de notes. Avec l’arrivée d’un enregistreur vocal intégré, Gemini Notebook vient désormais marcher sur les plates-bandes de Pixel Recorder et des autres applications d’enregistrement audio. Heureusement, cette nouvelle fonctionnalité a encore quelques lacunes avant de pouvoir remplacer des outils traditionnels.
    Pour aller plus loin
Google lance son générateur de podcasts en 50 langues
            
Un outil limité
Dans la version 1.63.1002728510 de Gemini Notebook pour Android et iOS, les équipes d’Android Authority ont pu découvrir cette nouvelle fonctionnalité d’enregistrement vocal. Pour l’activer, il suffit d’appuyer sur l’icône du microphone dans l’onglet « Sources » de l’application. Une fois l’enregistrement terminé, le fichier audio est envoyé aux serveurs de Google. Quelques secondes plus tard, une transcription apparaît automatiquement.
Pratique sur le papier, l’outil se révèle toutefois limité dans son fonctionnement. Son principal inconvénient est qu’il nécessite une connexion Internet pour être 100 % opérationnel. Si l’enregistrement audio peut bien être effectué hors ligne, le fichier reste bloqué dans une boucle de chargement tant que l’appareil n’est pas connecté. Impossible, durant cette période, d’écouter l’enregistrement depuis l’application ou de consulter sa transcription. Les fichiers enregistrés avec Gemini Notebook restent accessibles sur l’appareil, dans Enregistrements > Carnet, où il est possible de les écouter après coup.
Autre problème : tant que le fichier est en cours de chargement, il est impossible de le supprimer depuis Gemini Notebook. Lorsque l’utilisateur tente de le faire, le message « Chargement en cours » s’affiche. Plus étonnant encore, le fichier audio reste accessible dans Enregistrements > Carnet, même après la suppression du carnet correspondant dans l’application. Un comportement problématique en matière de gestion de fichiers.
Enfin, l’enregistreur impose une autre restriction : la durée des enregistrements est limitée à une heure. Une contrainte qui pourrait rapidement devenir gênante pour les étudiants souhaitant enregistrer des cours complets ou pour les professionnels qui veulent conserver la trace de longues réunions.

articles.title: Una vulnerabilidad de Microsoft Authenticator en Android podía exponer cuentas de trabajo
articles.text:
Una vulnerabilidad en Microsoft Authenticator para Android podía permitir que una aplicación maliciosa instalada en el mismo teléfono obtuviera tokens de acceso de una cuenta laboral. Con ellos, un atacante podría acceder a servicios vinculados a Microsoft 365, como el correo, los archivos, el calendario, SharePoint y Teams.
El fallo, identificado como CVE-2026-80097, fue descubierto por investigadores de Enclave y comunicado a Microsoft. La compañía publicó una corrección para la aplicación. La vulnerabilidad no afecta a todos los usuarios de Microsoft Authenticator ni permite, por sí sola, atacar un teléfono a distancia: para que el escenario descrito fuera posible, la aplicación maliciosa tenía que estar instalada en el dispositivo.
Según el análisis de Enclave, una vez en el teléfono, esa aplicación podía solicitar un token haciéndose pasar por un servicio de Microsoft. Authenticator no comprobaba correctamente qué aplicación estaba realizando la petición y podía confiar en la identidad que esta declaraba. Los investigadores demostraron el problema con una aplicación de prueba. No hay indicios en la información consultada de que el fallo se estuviera explotando en ataques reales.
Qué podía hacer un atacante
Microsoft Authenticator no solo genera códigos de verificación. En Android también puede actuar como intermediario de autenticación: cuando una aplicación como Teams u Outlook necesita iniciar sesión, solicita a Authenticator un token digital que confirma que el usuario está autenticado.
En el escenario probado por Enclave, una aplicación maliciosa podía presentarse como una aplicación legítima y conseguir tokens asociados a la cuenta laboral. De acuerdo con el equipo investigador, esos tokens podían permitir leer y enviar correo, consultar o modificar archivos y calendarios, acceder a sitios de SharePoint y enviar mensajes de Teams como si fueran del usuario.
Los investigadores también explicaron que una aplicación podía hacerse pasar por Authenticator para intentar cambiar métodos de inicio de sesión de la cuenta, incluidas las claves de acceso. Un atacante que lograra añadir su propio método de autenticación podría tratar de mantener el acceso incluso después de que la aplicación maliciosa fuera eliminada del teléfono.
El mecanismo requería que la persona instalara previamente una aplicación maliciosa, por ejemplo, fuera de una tienda de confianza o tras ser engañada para descargarla. En la demostración descrita por Enclave, una vez instalada, la solicitud del token podía producirse sin una alerta visible ni una aprobación adicional del usuario. Microsoft clasifica la vulnerabilidad como un problema de autenticación local y señala que se requiere interacción del usuario en el proceso de explotación.
Microsoft ya publicó una corrección
La vulnerabilidad fue corregida en Microsoft Authenticator para Android. El artículo de Help Net Security indica que están afectadas las versiones anteriores a la 6.2606.4246 y recomienda actualizar la aplicación desde Google Play Store y comprobar que esté instalada esa versión o una posterior.
Las organizaciones que administran teléfonos de sus empleados pueden establecer una versión mínima mediante sus herramientas de gestión de dispositivos, para evitar que los equipos sigan usando una edición vulnerable. El aviso también recomienda evitar la instalación de aplicaciones desconocidas o descargadas desde fuentes que no sean de confianza.
El fallo tiene una puntuación de gravedad de 8,6 sobre 10 en el sistema CVSS, según los datos citados por Microsoft y los investigadores. Esa calificación mide la severidad potencial de la vulnerabilidad; no significa que todos los teléfonos o cuentas estén comprometidos. El análisis publicado tampoco confirma una campaña de ataques activa.
Qué deben revisar los usuarios
Quienes usen Microsoft Authenticator en Android deberían abrir Google Play, buscar la aplicación y actualizarla. Después pueden comprobar el número de versión en la información de la app. Si el teléfono pertenece a una empresa, también conviene seguir las indicaciones del área de soporte o de seguridad, especialmente si se instalaron aplicaciones fuera de tiendas oficiales.
Actualizar la aplicación cierra la vulnerabilidad descrita, pero no permite determinar si una cuenta ya fue afectada. Si el usuario sospecha que instaló una aplicación maliciosa o detecta actividad inusual en su cuenta laboral, debería comunicárselo al equipo de tecnología de su organización para que revise los accesos y los métodos de autenticación asociados.

articles.title: Cloudflare and VoidZero Introduce tsrs: An AI-Generated Rust Port of TypeScript
articles.text:
tsrs, a Rust port of the TypeScript compiler, has been announced by Cloudflare, which is developing it with VoidZero and Max Schwenk of Owner.com, incubating the project inside the Oxc toolchain and working in close collaboration with the TypeScript team. Cloudflare is emphatic that this is not a fork, with the TypeScript team retaining full control over the language's design.
Cloudflare's benchmark comparing tsrs against TypeScript 7.0 at the same number of checker workers
The headline numbers are a claimed up to 8x faster type checking and around 70% less memory than TypeScript 7.0 at the same number of checker workers. Rust also unlocks the use case of compiling to WebAssembly through @tsrs/wasm so checks can run in a browser or on Workers, without dragging a garbage collector into the bundle the way a Go binary does.
To try, developers simply point it at an existing tsconfig and run:
npm install -D tsrs
npx tsrs -p . --noEmit
In a detailed write-up, Schwenk explains he wrote "zero" code, instead directing agents led by Claude Opus 5.5 to produce a faithful port, using TypeScript's own 15,197 conformance cases as the spec. On Owner's 37,000-file monolith, a check that needed 19 GiB and 80 seconds on TypeScript 7.0 dropped to 7 seconds.
One developer benchmarked both npm packages and measured 5.3x faster checking and 72% less memory, with identical diagnostics and byte-identical emit, but spotted that tsrs exits with code 2 on type errors where tsc exits 1, enough to quietly break a CI script. Measuring against the newer TypeScript 7.1 beta rather than 7.0, ImportStatic found a smaller 2.7x gain, a reminder that the 8x headline is measured against the older baseline.
TypeScript's Daniel Rosenwasser responded that much of the speed "does not just come down to language choice," and that some optimisations discovered in tsrs are feeding into a leaner TypeScript 7.1. Peter Steinberger reported on X:
Moved to tsrs over the weekend. Drop-in replacement. Around 5x faster for OC.
Kind of amazing that it took Microsoft a team and two years to rewrite the TS compiler in go, and now you can just let an agent rip and get sth significantly better within weeks.
Others were wary, questioning whether the arena-based, never-freed memory model is sound.
tsrs sits alongside Microsoft's own Go-based compiler, known as tsgo, and Theo Browne's rival Rust port, tsc-rs. Rather than compete, Cloudflare is merging tsc-rs and tsrs into a single package, adding language server and content mapper support.
The release remains experimental. There is no watch mode or language server yet, --init and --showConfig are unsupported, and diagnostic order can differ, the compatibility notes provide more details. Because tsrs tracks TypeScript 7, teams still on TypeScript 5 or 6 should first adopt Microsoft's native Go port before swapping in tsrs, after which migrating is as simple as reusing the existing tsconfig.
tsrs is open source under Apache-2.0 and available on GitHub.

articles.title: When “isolated” doesn’t mean isolated: How to sandbox AI agents
articles.text:
When “isolated” doesn’t mean isolated: How to sandbox AI agents
Separation of workloads before AI wasn’t easy, but it was far more straightforward. Servers sat in data centers, VLANs segregated packets, firewall rules managed ingress/egress, and physical cables separated packets to and from their destinations.
Now, flip on an agent, and it has access to almost everything by default.
Enterprises cannot operate with that default, and in this article, you’ll learn how to implement true sandboxing at every layer that matters.
Why aren’t containers enough to sandbox AI agents?
When you run a container (think Docker), it’s a lightweight package that runs as an isolated process. But that isolation has limits. Containers share the host kernel, and those on Docker’s default bridge can communicate with one another. A container cannot directly access host files by default, but a writable bind mount can let it modify or delete the host files exposed through that mount.
If you rely on a container alone for agent isolation, you may leave important boundaries unprotected. Thinking of containers as locked down by default is a major security risk. When running workloads in Kubernetes, you have tools like NetworkPolicy, service mesh for secure service communication, and SecurityContext to ensure containers run in a governed way.
KubeCon + CloudNativeCon is taking place in Salt Lake City from November 9 to 12. Register now!
That’s why having default security out of the box, easily turned on, and policy enforcement built into your AI sandboxing solution is key to enabling all teams. Without it, every organization risks thinking security exists, only to face a harsh reality.
So, regardless of what agentic workloads we’re running, the question we must answer is: “What makes up a true sandbox?”
What’s a true agent sandbox?
OpenAI reported that agents in restricted research sandboxes found a route to the internet through its internal Artifactory service; an agent later found and shared publicly exposed Hugging Face credentials. Anthropic described a different failure: in three cybersecurity evaluations, Claude reached real systems because a third-party test environment had internet access despite instructions that it did not. These cases show that sandboxing depends on the network and service boundaries around an agent, not just the runtime that contains it.
“These cases show that sandboxing depends on the network and service boundaries around an agent, not just the runtime that contains it.”
Agent sandboxing by default can sound “buzzword-ish”, but there is merit in implementing it at all of the boundaries that count for you and your organization. That means sandboxing will look different depending on where, and ultimately how, you put it into production. For example, sandboxing an agent with access to government- or healthcare-related data could mean locking down ingress/egress to public, consumer-based LLMs and allowing the agent to interact only with dedicated models for specific tasks on the data it must use. On the flipside, a software engineer or architect coding up a new integration may have more flexibility in the LLMs, MCP Server tools, and agent skills that agents they’re using can interact with and ultimately where those Agents can run (e.g. on your laptop/desktop vs an isolated server running an Agent runtime).
That’s where the fun, ironic consulting answer of “it depends” comes in, because it really does. As with everything security-related, there is a spectrum of what you can implement ranging from “cover the key use cases” to “this is Area 51”, and that plethora of range needs to be thought about and ultimately implemented in the best and most efficient way for your organization.
So, here’s the answer to the underlying question from this section’s header: true agent sandboxing means clarifying, understanding, and implementing what your agents should and shouldn’t be able to interact with. This includes other agents, LLMs, web searches, MCP servers, tools, and APIs.
“True agent sandboxing means clarifying, understanding, and implementing what your agents should and shouldn’t be able to interact with.”
In the next section, you’ll learn the key differentiating factors that make up a true sandbox. With that knowledge, you’ll be able to draw a proper conclusion about what level of agent sandboxing an organization should implement.
The differentiating factors for your agent sandbox
There are four key areas that you must keep in mind when implementing agentic workloads:
- Software vs. hardware-level isolation (think user space vs. at the chip level)
- Where the agents run (is it running on an isolated runtime or your workstation)
- What the agents have access to (ingress/egress/web search/models/tools/APIs)
- Secure code execution for AI agents (what commands/code/scripts can an agent run)
When thinking about software-level isolation, think container-level isolation. Now, after the first section of this blog post, ” Why aren’t containers enough to sandbox AI agents?, you may be thinking to yourself, “No way I’m going to run Agents in containers; it’s not isolated at all.” That’s true, but only by default/out of the box. You can secure and govern software-level isolation; it’s just a matter of what policies you put in place to ensure it. It runs inside a Linux kernel using Linux Namespaces/the user space for boundaries. Hardware isolation, on the other hand, is running a guest VM (think microVM/Firecracker) at the chip/CPU level. That means it runs a dedicated, standalone guest VM, and all processes run inside that guest VM.
The next two pieces of the puzzle are where agents run, and that brings us back to the previous section. An agent can run on your laptop/desktop, in a container, or within an isolated guest VM at the hardware level. Regardless of which option you choose, you still need proper guardrails, policy enforcement, and access to LLMs and tools, but the segregation may occur elsewhere. In any case, outbound and inbound connectivity (to/from the agent) occurs at your “line of communication”, which is an AI gateway. That’s typically where you set up policies, guardrails, tool isolation, agent access, and LLM connectivity.
The final step is “how” the agents run. For many use cases, agents run on a laptop/desktop. Still, in an organization, most agentic runtimes run on a server/platform like Kubernetes (which also covers “where” the Agents run). For example, an agent you may interact with on an eCommerce website isn’t running on someone’s laptop; it runs on a hosted runtime.
When working with a hardened solution, the ability to ensure agents run within your harness of choice and that it implements a true agent sandbox environment under the hood should be out of the box, and this is an important decision factor.
kind: Harness
metadata:
  name: YOUR_HARNESS_NAME
  namespace: YOUR_NAMESPACE
spec:
  kagent: {}
  workload:
    image: YOUR_AGENTIC_WORKLOAD_IMAGE
  substrate:
    workerPoolRef:
      name: kagent-default
    snapshotPolicy:
      location: ACTOR_SNAPSHOT_STORAGE_LOCATION
  allowedAgentTemplates:
    selector:
      matchLabels:
        kagent.dev/harness: kagent
kind: AgentTemplate
metadata:
  name: assistant
  namespace: kagent
  labels:
    kagent.dev/harness: kagent
spec:
  modelConfig:
    name: default-model-config
  description: A substrate-backed assistant used to verify this main build.
  systemPrompt: You are a helpful assistant running on agentic workloads.
Choosing the right agentic runtime, and therefore framework, lets you specify which AI gateway your agent traffic goes through from the sandbox, which harness you use, your underlying software- or hardware-level isolation, governance around agentic workloads, and where agents store memory/context.
Closing thoughts
Sandboxing agents will always come down to a keen understanding of what those AI agents need to do, and that’s the hardest part. Locking down an agent and implementing governance, security, and policy enforcement should be easy with the right tooling and platforms. The “what” is crucial. What exactly are you locking down and why?

articles.title: Long-Hidden Flaws Patched in EPICS Research Facility Control Software
articles.text:
Four vulnerabilities in EPICS Base could allow attackers to crash processes in control systems used at particle accelerators, fusion experiments and other large research facilities. One flaw could potentially lead to code execution.
CISA disclosed the issues in an advisory published on Tuesday, saying they impact EPICS Base 7.0.10 and earlier. The agency recommends updating to version 7.0.11.
The vulnerabilities were discovered by Cipher, an autonomous security research system made by Causal Security.
EPICS is an open source software toolkit that scientific facilities rely on to build their control systems, and EPICS Base is its central component. According to Causal, ITER’s fusion reactor control system is based on EPICS, and the Advanced Photon Source at Argonne National Laboratory makes heavy use of it.
The most severe of the bugs is CVE-2026-114595 (CVSS score of 9.8), an integer overflow that can occur when network requests are processed. According to CISA, it can lead to a wrongly sized memory allocation, and processing attacker-supplied data afterwards could corrupt memory, trigger DoS, or possibly enable remote code execution.
Exploiting CVE-2026-114596 (CVSS score of 8.2) can cause an out-of-bounds write that leaves the process unstable or causes DoS. CVE-2026-114597 (CVSS score of 7.5) is an out-of-bounds read that could crash the application and leak data from nearby memory, while CVE-2026-114598 (CVSS score of 7.5) is a type confusion issue that can be triggered with malformed network data, leading to DoS.
All four bugs are tied to the handling of Channel Access and pvAccess, the protocols EPICS uses for network communication. Shubham Raj, co-founder of Causal Security, explained to SecurityWeek what an attack would require.
“All four can be triggered without authentication or user interaction. An attacker needs network access to the vulnerable EPICS services, typically on TCP 5064 (Channel Access) or 5075 (pvAccess). This could be through an exposed service or access to a facility’s internal network,” he said.
Attacks could disrupt costly experiments
Regarding the potential operational consequences of the vulnerabilities, Raj explained, “Operationally, this could potentially mean interrupted particle beams, disrupted experiments, lost monitoring data, or expensive shutdowns of critical research equipment (by abusing remote code execution).”
Code execution has not actually been achieved, though. “Cipher demonstrated the attacker-controlled out-of-bounds heap write and process crash using AddressSanitizer,” Raj said. After that write was confirmed, he did not pursue a functional RCE exploit.
The number of internet-facing EPICS deployments is also unknown. Raj said a brief Censys check identified potential candidates based on exposed ports, but none could be verified as EPICS.
No public exploitation of the flaws has been reported to CISA.
The bugs were found in under four hours
According to Causal, Cipher needed roughly 3 hours and 49 minutes to identify the four vulnerabilities. It started with no knowledge of EPICS and was not given attack techniques designed for scientific control systems.
No human directed the first phase of the analysis. Afterward, the system received a single instruction to look more closely at whether the bugs could be exploited.
Cipher’s review of the code history shows the flaws are between approximately 14.5 and 31.5 years old. EPICS maintainers were notified on June 9 and merged patches in July and August.
Earlier this month, Causal’s research also led to disclosures in Grid Protection Alliance’s openPDC and openHistorian, which process power grid measurements, and in the FreeRTOS-Plus-TCP embedded networking stack.

articles.title: Studie zeigt: Europa ist heute abhängiger von ausländischer Digitaltechnik als vor 10 Jahren
articles.text:
Studie zeigt: Europa ist heute abhängiger von ausländischer Digitaltechnik als vor 10 Jahren
Europa gerät bei Schlüsseltechnologien immer stärker ins Hintertreffen gegenüber den USA und China. Während die beiden globalen Technologie-Großmächte ihre Abhängigkeiten in den vergangenen Jahren spürbar abbauen konnten, ist Europa heute abhängiger von ausländischen Digitaltechnologien als noch vor gut einem Jahrzehnt. Das geht aus einer umfassenden Vergleichsstudie des Center for Advanced Security, Strategic and Integration Studies (CASSIS) der Universität Bonn in Kooperation mit dem Vodafone Institut für Gesellschaft und Kommunikation hervor, die heute veröffentlicht wurde.
Für die Untersuchung entwickelten die Forscher den sogenannten Digital Dependence Index (DDI), der 51 Industrie- und Schwellenländer über einen 14-jährigen Zeitraum von 2010 bis 2023 analysiert. Der Index bildet die Abhängigkeit auf einer Skala von 0 für vollkommene Unabhängigkeit bis 1 für vollständige Abhängigkeit in den vier Kernbereichen Hardware-Handel, IT-Dienstleistungen, Software-Plattformen und Technologiepatente ab.
Demnach stieg die durchschnittliche digitale Abhängigkeit europäischer Staaten zwischen 2010 und 2023 leicht um 0,5 Prozentpunkte auf 0,69 an. Im selben Zeitraum gelang es China, seinen Wert um 10,8 Prozentpunkte auf 0,43 zu senken. Die USA verbesserten sich um 6,0 Prozentpunkte und behaupten mit einem Wert von 0,38 die globale Spitzenposition als autonomste Digitalnation.
Deutschland liegt im Mittelfeld
Deutschland belegt im weltweiten Ranking mit einem DDI-Wert von 0,73 Rang 25 und rangiert damit im mittleren Feld gleichauf mit Österreich und Thailand. Zwischen 2010 und 2023 hat sich die digitale Verwundbarkeit der Bundesrepublik um 2,4 Prozentpunkte verschärft, was laut den Autoren vor allem auf eine wachsende Abhängigkeit bei Software und IT-Dienstleistungen zurückzuführen ist.
Bei der Betrachtung der einzelnen Bereiche zeigt sich für Deutschland ein zwiespältiges Bild: Einerseits weist die deutsche Wirtschaft unter allen untersuchten europäischen Staaten die geringste Abhängigkeit bei Informations- und Kommunikationstechnologie-Patenten auf. Andererseits reicht dieser europäische Spitzenplatz im globalen Vergleich bei Weitem nicht aus, da der Rückstand zu den USA 26 Prozent, zu China 20 Prozent und zu Südkorea 12 Prozent beträgt.
Schwäche bei Plattformen
Wie fast alle europäischen Partner ist Deutschland zudem bei Plattformen wie Betriebssystemen, Suchmaschinen und Cloud-Diensten praktisch vollständig von ausländischen Anbietern abhängig. Gemeinsam mit Partnern wie Frankreich, Italien und Großbritannien gehört Deutschland damit zum Cluster der postindustriellen Staaten, die zwar industriell und forschungsseitig stark sind, aber erhebliche Lücken bei Plattform-Ökosystemen aufweisen.
Im europäischen Gesamtschnitt zeigt sich eine gravierende Zweiteilung: Während Europa bei Dienstleistungen mit einem Wert von 0,42 und Hardware mit 0,59 vergleichsweise moderat dasteht, herrscht bei Plattformen mit 0,98 und Patenten mit 0,99 faktisch ein beinahe vollständiges Ausgeliefertsein an Drittstaaten vor.
Zugleich warnen die Wissenschaftler vor einer statistischen Verzerrung durch den sogenannten «Irland-Effekt». Irlands scheinbar hervorragender Unabhängigkeitswert von 0,40 beruht im Wesentlichen darauf, dass viele US-amerikanische Großkonzerne dort aus Steuergründen ihren Sitz haben. Rechnet man Irland heraus, kippt die europäische Handelsbilanz bei digitalen Dienstleistungen für die Jahre 2022 bis 2024 von einem Überschuss in ein sattes Defizit von rund 350 Milliarden US-Dollar.

articles.title: Barcelona’s Artiso raises over €3 million to scale its AI operating system for fashion teams | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Artiso, a Barcelona-based FashionTech startup building an AI operating system built for fashion teams, has raised more than €3 million in a fully equity pre-Seed round.
Criteria Venture Tech led the round and has supported the company since it emerged from stealth. Swanlaab Venture Factory and Bynd Venture Capital joined the round, alongside business angels David Tomás, co-founder of Cyberclick, and Nicolaj Reffstrup, founder and former CEO of GANNI, who invests through Look Up Ventures.
“I spent years leading creative teams that had to orchestrate every step of a collection across tools that never spoke to each other. So we built the operating system we always needed: one that knows each brand’s archive, its customers and its taste, and that is already running inside fashion companies today. AI is changing how every collection is imagined, made and shown, and with Artiso, creativity, not complexity, defines fashion’s next era,” said Sarah Iglesias Hiller, co-founder and CEO, Artiso.
Artiso was founded in Barcelona in 2025 by Iglesias Hiller, Lucas Pastur Romay (CPO) and Matthias Brenninkmeijer (CTO), former Mango executives who have worked together since 2022.
The company emerged from stealth in July 2025 and claims to be building an AI operating system for fashion that connects inspiration, design, product development, and pre-production, including tech packs, styling, and campaign imagery, on top of each brand’s own memory.
According to the Spanish startup, fashion is one of the industries where AI can make the maximum impact, as the sector designs so many products and undergoes constant change season after season.
“Artiso’s vision is to redefine how fashion brands create, end to end. Today that work is spread across disconnected tools: product lifecycle management (PLM) systems, design software, image generators, shared drives, spreadsheets and email. Every season, part of what a brand has learned is lost along the way: which shapes sold, which colours worked, what was designed two seasons ago,” the company mentioned in the press release.
Artiso claims to bring that work and that knowledge together, using agentic AI to transform the process from the first idea to the final campaign. The company says it is designed for creatives, with a visual, intuitive platform built around how fashion teams actually work.
Its agentic AI takes collections from inspiration and moodboards to design and flat sketches, product development and pre-production such as tech packs, virtual models, on-model imagery, packshots and campaign content.
“We designed Artiso for the people who make fashion: creative directors, designers, pattern makers, merchandisers. It is intuitive, it remembers each brand and adapts to how every team works, and it connects every step, from the first moodboard to the tech pack and the campaign, in one operating system,” commented Pastur Romay.
The startup says a brand memory and ontology sits beneath everything, capturing each brand’s archive, bestsellers, seasonal direction, and visual codes, so every output is hyper-personalised to the brand’s DNA.
It highlights that a complete tech pack takes around four minutes instead of two to six hours. Artiso connects the whole process end to end, with creative direction, design, pattern making, product development, visual merchandising, and marketing, all working in the same operating system.
Brenninkmeijer said, “Fashion imagery is where AI first proved its value, and Artiso takes it further: every image, sketch and tech pack is created with an understanding of the brand behind it. Our agents combine state-of-the-art generation with each brand’s own knowledge, while people stay in control of every decision. That is what turns AI from a tool into a new way of working.”
The company plans to use the new capital to accelerate development of its operating system, expand the team, and support customers’ enterprise rollouts. To do that, Artiso is hiring across fashion and technology. Its team’s expertise spans garment technology, pattern making, design, art direction, motion, and data science.
Artiso reported that it already works with mid-sized to enterprise brands with strong identities, from fast-growing players in full transformation to established category leaders and luxury houses, as well as the retailers and manufacturers behind them. Its customers span Europe, North America and Asia, with the US as a key market. The new funding will help it bring more of them on board.

articles.title: Cisco Partner Summit: Five insights that will define the channel in the AI era - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Cisco Partner Summit: Five insights that will define the channel in the AI era
For most of its 30-year history, Cisco Partner Summit has focused on how partners sell Cisco Systems Inc. technology. This year’s event in Vancouver was about something different: how partners make money in a world where the transaction is no longer the main event.
Cisco entered the event with tremendous momentum, as its stock was up more than 50% over the past 12 months. Tim Coogan (pictured), senior vice president of global partner sales, told the 2,000 partners in attendance that channel bookings accounted for about 90% of Cisco’s total in fiscal 2026 and that global channel growth was just over 17%. Chief Executive Chuck Robbins called fiscal 2026 “the absolute best year that Cisco’s ever had.” Good years can mask structural change, though, and the announcements in Vancouver signal a real rethink of how value moves through Cisco’s partner ecosystem.
Here are my five takeaways that should matter to Cisco partners.
Influence now counts, not just transactions
The most significant change in Vancouver may also be the least flashy. Ecosystem Deal Registration gives advisers, consultants and developers formal credit for helping Cisco win a deal, even when they don’t execute it. This group of partners hasn’t received the same level of attention as traditional reseller partners, yet they are now critical in the AI era.
Today, that credit takes the form of marketing support and promotion alongside Cisco sellers. Starting next spring, preferred advisers and developers will be eligible for referral incentives. Cisco is also introducing dedicated Partner Value Indexes for advisors and developers, with a unified distributor index planned for 2027.
Coogan emphasized the importance of the change. “Our traditional programs were transaction-based,” he said during his portion of the keynote. “This is a unique way to bring the entire ecosystem of partners together into a single solution for the benefit of our customers.”
The data presented supports this change. Cisco cited Omdia research showing that customers rely on six to seven partners and pass through 28 moments of influence before buying. A program that pays only the partner holding the paper ignores most of what shapes the decision. The risk is channel conflict, and resellers will want proof that rewarding influence grows the pie rather than splitting it.
Robbins addressed the bumpiness of the Cisco 360 rollout and the company’s willingness to take corrective action. “We’re not perfect. We’ll screw it up, but we’ll fix it,” he said. This is a great example of his statement, and partners should continue to hold him to it.
Cisco IQ turns services into the business
If one announcement could change partner economics, it would be Cisco IQ Partner Branded Support Standard. Partners can now deliver Cisco IQ under their own brand, through their own experts, with role-based access to customer installed bases, application programming interfaces, IT service management integrations, and a Model Context Protocol server.
“For too long, partners entered customer conversations without the same view as Cisco. That changes today,” said Liz Centoni, executive vice president and chief customer experience officer. “It’s their name, their customer relationship and their services practice. Cisco IQ is the engine. Partners are the business.”
Centoni presented several compelling proof points. More than 16,000 customers and nearly 20 million devices are now on Cisco IQ. Generali reduced the time to assess a single security advisory across 16,000 devices from four days to 10 minutes. Georgetown University transformed two months of manual renewal work into a 20-minute view.
On stage, Centoni gave an example that quantified the opportunity. In her example, a partner who walks in to refresh 75 switches books about $625,000 and walks away. A partner who starts with Cisco IQ, identifies uncovered devices, sells hardening services, designs the refresh, and then runs managed operations across all 175 switches can reach roughly $1.3 million over five years, including incentives. That’s 2.1 times the value. “Basic gives you the map. Standard and Signature give you the GPS,” she said.
Cisco is backing that with a $2,500 adoption incentive per onboarded customer, a 6% deal registration on Standard and Signature support, and a $1 million Builders Challenge for partners who create managed services on Cisco IQ. My take is that Cisco is moving partners from project revenue to recurring revenue, where valuation multiples are higher. Partners who sell Cisco IQ as a support add-on will miss the point.
Mythos made modernization an emergency
For years, last-day-of-support conversations felt like a vendor pushing hardware. Robbins said as much. “When we used to stand up and talk about what we call LDOS (last day of support), people would go, ‘OK, that’s just the vendor trying to sell more equipment,’ and you would have been partially right,” he said. “Now the urgency of getting that equipment out of the infrastructure, equipment that can’t be patched and for which there are no spares, is a real emergency.”
Coogan provided the numbers that underscore the urgency. In 2018, more than two years passed between discovery and exploitation of a vulnerability. Last year, it was about three weeks. This year, it’s eight hours or less. Only 3% of partners named AI security a growth opportunity last year. This year, 33% did.
Cisco’s answer includes expanded Live Protect coverage, what it calls the industry’s first quantum-resilient Wi-Fi 7 access point, and Privileged Infrastructure Access, built with Teleport, which provides engineers and AI agents with short-lived, identity-bound access to routers and switches. Robbins framed the architecture this way: “If agents are operating across your infrastructure, the only common denominator they’re going to touch on a daily basis is the network.”
Robbins said only 8% of the installed base has been refreshed to Cisco’s new enterprise portfolio. But, in his words, customers are “overwhelmed.” The winning partners will present a phased plan outlining what to fix first and why. That’s an advisory skill, not a quoting skill.
Margin follows the platform
Mark Patterson, executive vice president and chief financial officer, has attended Partner Summit for more than 20 years, but this was his first time onstage. His session was among the day’s most useful because he discussed what motivates partners most: money. On price increases, he said, “Raising prices is the absolute last resort for us.” He added that the Nov. 7 increase targets memory-intensive products rather than being spread “in a peanut butter fashion.”
His most important point concerned margin. “The big takeaway is that margin follows the platform,” Patterson said. “You might lead with compute, but then you add networking, security, Splunk and observability. That’s where you’ll drive much of the margin.”
The incentives align with that view. The program adds an extra 2% cross-sell bonus for expanding into new Cisco architectures, including Splunk. It increases the reward for annual contract value growth by 50%, doubles adoption incentives, and offers 12% deal registration for Supermicro systems sold as part of full-stack AI infrastructure. Coogan also made an unusual admission about Splunk. “We moved slower on Splunk than we wanted to, than we should have, and that changes this year and it changes now,” he said.
Patterson also highlighted Cisco Capital as underused, noting that “the margins are paid entirely up front,” which helps partners build larger deals for customers with heavy technical debt. The message is that thin-margin compute is the entry point, not where the profit lies. With 91% of surveyed partners reporting that customers are concerned about AI costs, those who can design cost-efficient on-premises inference will capture the attached revenue.
Partners must become builders
The final insight concerns who builds value. Cisco is putting its own AI tooling directly into partners’ hands. Model Foundry, a new service within Cisco Cloud Control, gives partners first access to Cisco’s purpose-built models, including Deep Network for network troubleshooting. Partners can run these models via an OpenAI-compatible application programming interface and fine-tune them on customer data. Cloud Control Studio lets partners build agents for customers. New MCP servers for networking platforms eliminate the need to build custom integrations, and ThousandEyes synthetic testing is now built into eligible Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 7 access points at no additional cost.
Cisco is also turning AI on its own channel friction. Its Partner Experience Platform is being rebuilt to connect opportunity, quote, and payout in a single flow. An early agent-to-agent pilot with a distributor cuts the time to build a bill of materials by about 80%.
Coogan spoke about partners in a humble tone. “Our partners don’t owe us anything, and they don’t work for us,” he said. “We earn the right to work with them every day.” That mindset matters at Cisco, where they ask partners to invest in skills many don’t yet have. Partners reported that the AI knowledge gap is closing, but the hands-on deployment gap is widening.
What this means for partners
The 2026 Partner Summit marks the Cisco channel’s shift from a resale model to an intelligence-led services model. My advice to partners:
Move as many customers as possible from Basic support. Basic support provides customers with an inventory. Standard and Signature unlock the capabilities that create partner value: vulnerability prioritization, proactive risk intelligence, peer benchmarking, and quantum-readiness assessments. Centoni said Cisco has “far too many critical customers who have basic that should be on standard and signature,” and noted that customers on the higher tiers have net promoter scores 15 points higher, which translates into better retention and stronger renewals. With a $2,500 adoption incentive per onboarded customer and 6% deal registration on Standard and Signature, the economics reward partners who move now. Start by reviewing your installed base, identifying the critical accounts still on Basic, and letting a live Cisco IQ demo make the case.
Lead with resilience, not refresh. Customers know their equipment is old. What they lack is a clear sense of what to fix first. Use Cisco IQ and Cisco’s Resilient Infrastructure playbooks to build a phased, risk-ranked plan. First, address devices with no support. Then harden those staying in service. Finally, modernize gear past its last day of support or that can’t be patched. The new Quantum Safe and software End of Vulnerability Support assessments provide more evidence to scope that work. This approach turns a hardware conversation into a professional services engagement. When the customer says there’s no budget this year, it also gives you a plan to move the refresh into next year’s budget cycle. Customers will buy priorities, not part numbers.
Team up intentionally. Most customers already work with six to seven partners, and Ecosystem Deal Registration gives Cisco a formal way to reward the advisors, consultants, and developers who shape a deal without transacting it. Transacting partners should view this as a pipeline opportunity, not a threat. Identify the advisors who influence your largest accounts, the independent software vendors building on Meraki and Cisco Cloud Control, and the Splunk specialists who can fill gaps in your practice. Splunk is new to many Cisco partners, and for them, Coogan offered some advice. If another partner has the expertise your team needs, team up. Partners who map and formalize these relationships early will see larger, faster deals before competitors catch on.
Invest in builders. The next round of differentiation won’t come from offering a deeper discount. It will come from who can turn Cisco’s data and models into services customers can’t get anywhere else. Model Foundry, Cloud Control Studio, the Cisco IQ MCP Server, and the new MCP servers for networking platforms give partners the building blocks for custom agents, automated troubleshooting, and managed services that run on customer telemetry. Partners told Cisco the AI knowledge gap is closing, but the lack of hands-on deployment experience has become the bigger barrier. Get engineers through Black Belt training and dCloud labs. The $1 million Builders Challenge is also a good reason to put a small team on a new managed service. Partners who can fine-tune models and ship agents will stand out from those who only resell.
Final thoughts
For buyers, the partner you hire should arrive with a live view of your environment and a plan, not a quote. If they don’t, find another partner – one that has modernized its own business to help you modernize yours. Robbins concluded that Cisco and its partners defined the internet era and can lead the AI era together. The tools and incentives are in place. Now, execution must keep pace with the threats.

articles.title: Announcing SOCI-indexed images for faster SageMaker AI jobs | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Announcing SOCI-indexed images for faster SageMaker AI jobs
Every minute your deep learning container image spends downloading is a minute you pay for and a minute your team waits. Container image download is pure overhead: billable job time that produces no model progress. For modern deep learning images, that overhead is several minutes on every single job. Today, we’re excited to announce Seekable OCI (SOCI) indexing for Amazon SageMaker AI Training and Amazon SageMaker AI processing jobs, which takes full container image download off the critical path of every job.
With SOCI indexing, SageMaker AI lazy-loads your container image. It fetches only the files needed to start the container and streams the rest in the background as your code runs, so your job begins in seconds instead of minutes. You adopt it by pointing to a pre-indexed AWS Deep Learning Container (DLC) or adding an index to your own image. Neither approach requires changes to your job definition, entry point, or data channels. The result is faster job starts, lower job cost, and more time spent building models rather than waiting on infrastructure.
SOCI-indexed images start Amazon SageMaker AI training containers in seconds, with no impact on training performance. As we show in the What we measured section, this reduced GPU idle time during image pulls by up to 90 percent in our benchmarks.
This post shows how to adopt SOCI indexing: what it is, the results we measured, and how to turn it on for your own jobs.
The challenge
SageMaker AI training and processing jobs run inside container images stored in Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR). Before a job can execute your code, the service downloads the entire image to the instance. It decompresses and writes every layer to disk.
For small images this takes seconds. But deep learning images routinely exceed 10 GB or more. That download adds minutes to every job, and you pay for it as job time. The impact is largest exactly where iteration speed matters most: hyperparameter tuning sweeps for hundreds of jobs, quick experiments, and short processing jobs, where image download can dominate total runtime.
How SOCI indexing works
Seekable OCI (SOCI) is an open source technology that lazy loads container images. Instead of downloading the whole image before starting, the runtime uses a SOCI index to fetch only the files needed to launch the container immediately. It then streams the rest in the background as your code accesses it.
A SOCI index is metadata that maps every file inside your image. You store it in Amazon ECR as an OCI-compliant artifact linked to your original image. Because the index is a separate artifact, your image digest and any existing signatures remain valid.
SageMaker AI checks for an index automatically
When you create a training or processing job, SageMaker AI checks whether the image you specified has a SOCI index and behaves accordingly:
| Scenario | What happens | 
| The image includes a SOCI index | SageMaker AI lazy-loads the image and starts your container before the full download completes | 
| The image has no SOCI index | Standard download, no change in behavior | 
| The index can’t be read, or lazy loading doesn’t succeed | The job falls back to a standard download and continues running | 
Because jobs always fall back to a standard download when needed, adding a SOCI index never prevents your job from running. You only gain faster startup. You never risk breaking an existing workflow.
What we measured
We pulled the same container images two ways on real SageMaker AI training jobs: standard download and SOCI-indexed lazy loading. We then ran full training jobs from both to measure the effect on training speed.
Setup
- Eight images, 1.8–35.4 GB compressed.
- GPU and CPU instances ml.g4dn, ml.g5, ml.g6, ml.g6e, ml.g7, ml.g7e, ml.p4d, ml.p5, and ml.m7i, from xlarge to 48xlarge, in the US West (Oregon) Region (us-west-2) and the US East (N. Virginia) Region (us-east-1).
- Download time measured from the start of the image pull until the container is ready to run. All figures are medians of repeated runs.
Result 1: Download time drops from minutes to seconds at every image size
| Image size (compressed) | Standard download | Lazy loading | Improvement | 
| 1.8 GB | 48 s | 3-11 s | ~8x | 
| 13.2 GB | 3 min 42 s | ~6 s | ~34x | 
| 35.4 GB | 7 min 17 s | 3-11 s | ~38x | 
The following chart compares container image download time for a standard Docker pull against SOCI lazy loading across eight image sizes, from 1.8 GB to 35.4 GB.
Each image size shows two bars. The Docker download time bar (blue) grows steadily with image size, from 48 seconds at 1.8 GB to 7 minutes 17 seconds at 35.4 GB.
A speedup label above each pair shows the ratio of Docker time to SOCI time. Speedups range from approximately 10x for the smallest image to over 35x for the largest.
Standard download time grows with image size because every file is decompressed and written. Lazy loading stayed at 3–11 seconds regardless of size, an 8x–46x improvement. The bigger the image, the more minutes you save.
Result 2: The saving holds on every instance type and size
Running the 13.2 GB image across 13 instance type/size combinations, standard download ranged from 3 min 16 s to 4 min 20 s, while lazy loading held at 6-8 s. That is about 34x faster on every configuration. You don’t need to change instance type or size to benefit.
Result 3: Training performance is unaffected beyond a first-epoch penalty
We ran two kinds of full training jobs from the Docker-pulled and from the SOCI-indexed image and compared every epoch:
- Image classification on ResNet-50 on Imagenette (9,469 images) 
         
  - Container images: PyTorch (13.2 GB DLC) and TensorFlow (9.9 GB DLC)
  - Instances: ml.p5.48xlarge, ml.p4d.24xlarge, ml.g7e.48xlarge, ml.g7.48xlarge, ml.g6e.12xlarge, ml.g6e.24xlarge, and ml.g6e.48xlarge.
- Large language model (LLM) fine-tuning: full-parameter supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of Qwen2.5-0.5B on alpaca-cleaned (51,760 examples) with the Hugging Face Trainer. 
         
  - Container image: 9.4 GB Hugging Face PyTorch DLC.
  - Instances: ml.p5.48xlarge, ml.p4d.24xlarge, ml.g6.48xlarge.
The following chart breaks job startup into image download time and first training epoch time, comparing a standard Docker pull with a SOCI-indexed image across GPU and CPU configurations for both workloads.
- From the second epoch on, time per epoch is the same (within run-to-run variation) on every instance, for both workloads.
- The first epoch takes 3–16 s longer from the lazy-loaded image, while files the framework touches for the first time are fetched. This first-epoch cost is the same on every instance size.
- Net: each job finished 1-6 min sooner. That is the download saving minus the one-time first-epoch cost, a fixed saving per job.
Test this on your own workload
These numbers are from the two workloads described earlier. The first-epoch cost depends on your image and what your code touches at startup:
- Lazy loading wins when the first training step needs only a fraction of the image, the rest streams in while you train.
- If your entry point reads most of the image before training starts (for example, scanning, checksumming, or preloading its contents), the first epoch waits for roughly the same bytes a full pull would have fetched. The net improvement would be small.
- Front-loaded starts still came out ahead in our tests: 
         
  - torch.compile and a just-in-time (JIT) built CUDA extension added 7-15 s to the first epoch (net saving still 3 min 25 s–3 min 56 s)
  - A 6 GB model baked into the image streamed its weights at load time, adding 2-3.5 min, but the overall job still finished 2-2.5 mins sooner on the indexed image.
Getting started
You can adopt SOCI indexing two ways: use a pre-indexed AWS Deep Learning Container or create an index for your own custom image.
Option 1: Use a pre-indexed AWS Deep Learning Container
AWS publishes SOCI-indexed variants of several popular Deep Learning Containers, identified by the -soci suffix on the image tag:
Pre-indexed variants are available for PyTorch Training, TensorFlow Training, vLLM, and SGLang, including arm64 variants for some frameworks. To adopt lazy loading, update the image tag in your job definition to the -soci variant. Browse the full list in the AWS Deep Learning Containers Gallery.
Note: If you build your own image FROM a DLC base image, you must create a SOCI index for your final image. The index from the base image does not carry forward to derived images.
Option 2: Create a SOCI index for your own image
To index a custom image, you need a Linux host (such as an Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance running Amazon Linux 2023) with containerd, the SOCI snapshotter, and either Finch or nerdctl installed.
- Set your environment variables.
- Install the required tools.
- Authenticate to Amazon ECR.
- Pull your original image.
- Create the SOCI-indexed image.
- Push the indexed image.
This creates two artifacts in your repository: the SOCI index and an OCI-compliant image index manifest linking your image to the index. Your original image and its digest remain unchanged.
Automate index creation in CI/CD
To generate indexes automatically on every push, deploy the CFN ECR SOCI Index Builder. It uses an Amazon EventBridge rule to detect Amazon ECR image push events and build the index. No changes to your build pipeline are required.
Use the indexed image in your SageMaker AI job
Reference your SOCI-indexed image exactly as you would any other image. No API changes are needed. Only the tag differs.
Training example (SageMaker Python SDK)
Verify that your image includes a SOCI index
Before launching, confirm your tag resolves to an indexed image:
Look for a child manifest whose artifactType begins with application/vnd.amazon.soci.index. alongside your platform manifest. If it isn’t there, the tag does not point to an indexed image.
Things to keep in mind
- Amazon ECR private repositories only. Images in other registries, or pulled through a private Docker registry (TrainingRepositoryAccessMode set to Vpc), are not eligible for lazy loading.
- Improvement scales with image size. Images smaller than roughly 4 GB see relatively small improvements.
- Check for Docker-specific assumptions. SOCI-indexed images run on a containerd-based runtime. Review entry points and setup scripts for code that calls the Docker CLI, reads /var/run/docker.sock, or derives identifiers from cgroup paths. SageMaker AI mounts a /.dockerenv marker for backward compatibility, but avoid adding new dependencies on it.
- SOCI indexing for SageMaker AI jobs is available across all AWS Regions.
Conclusion
With SOCI indexing, you can minimize container image download time from your SageMaker AI training and processing jobs. Add a SOCI index to your images, or switch to a pre-indexed AWS Deep Learning Container. Either way, you cut startup time from minutes to seconds, reduce total job cost, and accelerate your machine learning (ML) iteration cycle. And your existing job definitions, API calls, and data pipelines stay exactly the same.
To learn more about Amazon SageMaker AI and start using SOCI indexing, explore the following resources:
- Pick a SOCI-indexed Deep Learning Container. Browse the Deep Learning Containers Gallery and append -soci to your image tag. For framework-specific guidance, see SOCI index for AWS Deep Learning Containers.
- Index your own custom image. Follow the step-by-step walkthrough in the SageMaker AI Developer Guide, or refer to the SOCI snapshotter getting-started guide for advanced options.
- Automate indexing in your CI/CD pipeline. Deploy the CFN ECR SOCI Index Builder to generate indexes automatically on every image push. No pipeline changes are required.
- Test locally with Finch. Use the Finch lazy-loading walkthrough to validate your image on a containerd-based runtime before you submit a job.
- Dive deeper into the technology. Read Reducing container cold start times using SOCI index on DLAMI and DLC on the AWS Machine Learning Blog for benchmarks, or explore Under the hood: Lazy loading container images with Seekable OCI and AWS Fargate on the AWS Containers Blog to understand the lazy-loading mechanism in detail.
Faster container startup is only one image tag away. Try it on your next SageMaker AI job and see the difference.

articles.title: MIT scientists build a tiny robot that swims using living muscle cells
articles.text:
MIT scientists build a tiny robot that swims using living muscle cells
- Date:
- October 23, 2026
- Source:
- Massachusetts Institute of Technology
- Summary:
- MIT engineers have built a paper-thin swimming robot powered by living muscle cells that respond to flashes of light, allowing it to swim and steer through water. The breakthrough could pave the way for tiny, self-healing biological robots capable of exploring fragile environments that ordinary machines cannot safely navigate.
- Share:
A swimming robot does not necessarily need a bulky motor or powerful mechanical parts to move through water. MIT researchers have demonstrated that a single, carefully engineered layer of living muscle cells can generate enough force to propel a tiny robot forward.
The engineers developed an extremely thin swimming robot that uses living muscle tissue to move its fins. Described in a new study published in Advanced Functional Materials, the device has a flexible gel framework roughly the length and width of a stick of gum. The gel forms two fins, each coated with a layer of muscle cells far thinner than a human hair. These cells have been genetically modified to contract when exposed to light.
By directing light onto either fin, the researchers can trigger muscle contractions that make the fin flap and push the robot through water. Adjusting which fin receives light and how frequently it is illuminated allows the team to control both its speed and direction.
In experiments, the remarkably thin robot successfully swam and turned through a simple underwater maze. At maximum speed, it covered approximately four times its body length per minute. Although that is much slower than an Olympic swimmer, who can travel up to 65 body lengths per minute, it is comparable to the swimming pace of a cow shark moving leisurely through the ocean.
"It takes a lot of force to move through water versus air," says study author Ritu Raman, associate professor of mechanical engineering at MIT. "The robot's quite strong, given its size. "
A New Generation of Robots Powered by Living Muscle
The device represents the first demonstration of a very thin, two-dimensional robot that can move from place to place using living muscle tissue.
Most existing biohybrid robots rely on relatively large, three-dimensional structures made from laboratory-grown skeletal muscle. Producing these structures typically requires millions of cells. Raman explains that thinner designs could reduce manufacturing costs while potentially improving movement efficiency.
"Currently, biohybrid robots from our group and others' are built from bulky, 3D chunks of lab-grown skeletal muscle that require millions of cells to fabricate," says Raman, who notes that thinner, less bulky designs such as the team's new bot could be cheaper to build and could move more efficiently. "We believe that biohybrid robots powered by living muscle could one day perform delicate jobs like exploring environments too fragile or unpredictable for conventional hardware, because living tissue is soft, responsive to its surroundings, and can heal itself."
The MIT research team also included first author Maheera Bawa, along with Arielle Berman, Laura Schwendeman, Ferdows Afghah, and Seanbiron Johnson.
From Artificial Muscle to a Swimming Robot
The new swimming robot builds on an earlier achievement by Raman's laboratory. Last year, the researchers created an artificial muscle disk inspired by the human iris, demonstrating how a thin layer of living cells could produce precisely controlled movements.
For that project, the engineers patterned a gel disk with grooves extending outward from its center and forming concentric circles. They then placed living muscle cells on the surface, where the cells grew into a thin layer following the patterned channels.
When illuminated, the muscle tissue contracted in different directions, causing the disk to stretch and compress. Its movements resembled the way the iris of the human eye changes shape as the pupil expands or narrows.
The experiment established that researchers could grow extremely thin muscle layers in intricate arrangements and use light to control their movements along multiple directions.
"People hadn't seen this muscle architecture engineered from scratch before," Raman says. "And the cells were moving in multiple directions. But they only moved about 100 microns. From a robotics perspective, their movements were tiny."
For the latest project, the researchers wanted to dramatically increase the amount of movement and force generated by the muscle cells. Their goal was to produce contractions powerful enough to propel a robot through water.
They determined that achieving this would require a better foundation for the living muscle tissue.
The earlier artificial iris had used fibrin, an exceptionally soft gel, as its underlying structure. However, the team found that fibrin could quickly shrink under the forces exerted by contracting muscle cells, limiting the effectiveness of the resulting movement.
To overcome this problem, the engineers investigated three characteristics of the gel foundation: its chemical composition, its stiffness, and the dimensions and geometry of the grooves used to organize muscle growth.
"For engineering any type of tissue, it's known that these are knobs you can tune," Raman says. "And we wanted to optimize all these parameters to support live muscle cells."
Engineering a Stronger Muscle-Powered Robot
Finding the right supporting material required testing gels with different formulations, stiffness levels, and surface patterns.
The researchers compared several groove shapes, including narrow channels with square profiles and longer channels with curved bottoms. They discovered that muscle cells aligned more effectively inside square-shaped grooves.
This alignment was important because muscle cells that grow in the same direction are more likely to merge into fibers. Those fibers can then form stronger muscle tissue that contracts in a coordinated way. The square grooves therefore provided a more effective structure for producing force.
The team also replaced fibrin with gelatin methacrylate (GelMA), a material commonly used to grow and engineer biological tissue.
By adjusting the formulation of GelMA, the researchers produced supporting gels with varying degrees of stiffness. They then examined how muscle cells developed on each surface and measured their ability to generate force.
Stiffer gels produced the best results. On these firmer surfaces, muscle cells grew in better alignment and generated stronger contractions.
The engineers next investigated how thick the gel should be. They determined that a film measuring approximately half a millimeter offered an effective balance. It was sturdy enough to support a single layer of muscle cells while remaining sufficiently lightweight to prevent the contracting cells from detaching from the surface.
The team further improved muscle performance through a form of exercise. Repeated pulses of light stimulated the cells to contract, strengthening the muscle tissue before it was incorporated into the swimming robot.
How Light Makes the Living Robot Swim
With the gel structure optimized and the muscle cells strengthened, the researchers assembled their swimming device.
The finished robot consisted of a thin gel framework divided into two fins. Both sides of the gel were patterned with square-bottomed grooves and covered with living muscle cells. As the cells developed, they fused into organized muscle fibers capable of contracting together.
Each fin could be activated independently using light, giving the researchers a simple way to control the robot's movements.
"You can think of the robot as having two independent muscles," Raman says. "If we shine a light on just one, only that muscle moves. If shining on both, they both flap."
To test the device, the researchers placed it inside a large petri dish filled with water. They then moved a light source by hand, illuminating the fins to guide the robot through a maze positioned inside the dish.
As the muscles contracted, the fins flapped and propelled the robot through the water. By changing the light stimulation, the engineers successfully controlled its movement and helped it navigate the obstacles.
Although the robot demonstrated the ability to swim and steer, its current shape remains relatively simple. The primary objective of the experiment was to establish that an exceptionally thin layer of engineered muscle tissue could generate enough force for swimming.
The researchers now plan to refine the robot's body to improve its speed. Beyond demonstrating a new approach to biohybrid robotics, the technology could eventually be useful for monitoring aquatic environments or operating in locations where conventional rigid machines might cause damage.
"Our next goal is to optimize the body design to enable faster swimming," Raman says. "But even at slow swim speeds, one could imagine a muscle-powered swimmer being used for purposes like environmental monitoring in aquatic environments."
The Office of Naval Research provided partial funding for this research.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Original written by Jennifer Chu. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Maheera Bawa, Arielle Berman, Laura Schwendeman, Ferdows Afghah, Seanbiron Johnson, Ritu Raman. 2D Skeletal Muscle Thin Film Actuators Enhance Efficiency of Biohybrid Robots. Advanced Functional Materials, 2026; DOI: 10.1002/adfm.78065
