articles.title: African startups invited to apply for Yamaha’s TRANSPOSE Innovation Challenge 2026 - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
African startups are invited to apply for the second edition of Yamaha’s TRANSPOSE Innovation Challenge, a Yamaha-backed programme that will see winning founders receive funding and support to build the future of sound and entertainment.
The Japanese music and audio giant is looking for startups that can help it reimagine how people experience music, live events and entertainment, with selected companies offered project funding, technical resources and mentorship to test, validate and scale their products.
The inaugural edition of the challenge last year attracted 314 applications from startups across 63 countries.
This year’s edition is structured around four challenge tracks. The Venue track seeks solutions that elevate live events, sports and concerts through immersive technology, visuals and crowd interaction, while the Senior track focuses on harnessing music and entertainment to support active ageing, cognitive health and intergenerational connection.
The Game track is looking for startups combining gaming mechanics, audio and intellectual property (IP) to add playfulness to everyday life, while the Timeless track targets solutions that turn temporary live entertainment experiences into lasting digital or physical assets.
Successful startups will have the opportunity to co-create with Yamaha using its proprietary technologies, domain expertise and assets, and will also gain access to exclusive fundraising discussions with the company’s corporate venture capital (CVC) team.
The Grand Prix Award winner will receive up to JPY5 million (US$32,000) in proof-of-concept (PoC) funding, as well as the chance to collaborate with Yamaha and its partners. The Yamaha Award comes with up to JPY2 million (US$13,000) in PoC funding and a collaboration with Yamaha, while the YMI Fund Award offers direct fundraising discussions with members of the Yamaha Music Innovations Fund.
Applications are open here until October 31.

articles.title: Google Cloud’s Gemini voice AI wants to do more than just talk
articles.text:
Google Cloud’s Gemini voice AI wants to do more than just talk
What if AI could do more than answer the phone? At TechSparks 2026, Google Cloud’s Naren Kachroo showed Gemini voice AI handling bookings, sales negotiations and multilingual conversations.
Imagine asking an AI assistant to find a customer, negotiate a price and help close a sale, all without typing a single prompt. Voice AI is moving beyond answering questions to taking on tasks, and Google Cloud wants businesses to put it to work.
At TechSparks 2026, Naren Kachroo, Head of AI Go-to-Market at Google Cloud, demonstrated how Gemini’s voice AI capabilities could help businesses handle customer conversations, restaurant bookings and sales negotiations.
From talking to taking action
Until now, much of the AI experience has revolved around asking questions and getting answers. Kachroo said the next step is AI that can access information, use tools and take action on a user’s behalf.
“We don't want to focus on voice AI just being an experience to talk to AI,” he said. “We want voice AI to be powered through agentic experiences where the task is actually accomplished with AI.”
To show what that means, Naren Kachroo played a demonstration of an AI assistant booking a restaurant table for eight. The assistant answered questions about bringing a birthday cake, identified a dish from an image, discussed vegetarian options and switched between English and Spanish during the conversation.
In other words, it did more than take a booking. It handled the questions that came with it, too.
Kachroo also introduced Gemini Live voice capabilities, alongside models for text-to-speech, speech-to-text and translation. He showcased Live Avatar, which combines voice interaction with a visual AI presence.
Meet the AI sales assistant
The standout demonstration involved a fictional safety equipment business with 500 helmets sitting in its inventory. Its owner, Rajesh, wanted to sell them quickly and instructed an AI voice agent to find a suitable lead, contact the customer and negotiate a price above Rs 400 per helmet.
The assistant checked the business’s leads, identified a construction company that needed 500 helmets and initiated a call in Hindi. When the prospective buyer pushed for a lower price, the AI negotiated while sticking to the owner’s pricing instruction.
It was a glimpse of how AI could help small businesses manage sales without handling every step themselves. The agent could draw on internal business information, speak to a customer and respond to objections, rather than simply recommend what the owner should do next.
Kachroo said the demonstration showed how the agent maintained context as it moved from internal information to a customer conversation.
Why India needs voice AI
Voice could be particularly useful in India, where people speak many languages and have different levels of comfort with typing or navigating digital interfaces.
“I believe that India and Indian consumer is continuing to go as voice first,” Naren said.
He highlighted Google’s work on Indian languages, accents and cultural nuances, and pointed to Equal AI, an Indian company building voice assistants that can handle calls on users’ behalf.
For Kachroo, the goal is to make voice AI useful in everyday business processes, not just impressive in a demo. That means building systems that understand context, handle interruptions and follow instructions while completing tasks.
The real test, then, is not whether AI can hold a conversation. It is whether it can get the job done. And for businesses exploring voice AI, that could be the difference between another chatbot and a genuinely useful assistant.

articles.title: Jackie Chan creó una escuela de especialistas de artes marciales. Hoy es el motivo de que 'Phantom Blade: Zero' parezca una película
articles.text:
Cuando vimos por primera vez 'Phantom Blade: Zero' en el PlayStation Showcase de mayo de 2023, muchos pensaron que aquellos combates tan rápidos y espectaculares parecían secuencias de una película de acción. No era casualidad. El proyecto del estudio chino S-GAME lleva años desarrollándose con una idea muy concreta: trasladar al videojuego la precisión, las acrobacias y la contundencia del cine de artes marciales y qué mejor referencia que el propio Jackie Chan. El resultado ha convencido a la crítica y está a punto de llegar al mercado: se estrena el 29 de octubre para PC y PlayStation 5.
El sello de Jackie Chan. Como detallaron nuestros compañeros de 3DJuegos tras viajar a China, detrás de los combates del juego no hay simples trucos de animación, también está el estudio de captura de movimiento Flying Goat en Shanghái, que cuenta con acróbatas experimentados y la certificación del mismísimo Jackie Chan.
En 1976, Jackie Chan creó su propio equipo de especialistas, el Jackie Chan Stunt Team, con el que desarrolló algunas de las coreografías más reconocibles de su carrera. El actor convirtió las acrobacias y los combates en una de sus señas de identidad, una tradición que ha perdurado y está presente en el nuevo juego de S-GAME.
Cables y sensores al milímetro. El rodaje en el plató combina la destreza física de los acróbatas con la tecnología necesaria para capturar tanto los movimientos corporales como las armas de combate. Para reproducir las acrobacias aéreas más espectaculares cuentan con un sistema de cables, poleas y contrapesos instalados en el techo. La tecnología captura todos los movimientos y permite trasladar esa interpretación física a los personajes digitales, logrando un efecto mucho más natural que con sólo animación tradicional.
China juega en primera división. Aunque S-GAME enseñó el proyecto en 2023, en realidad llevaba desde 2018 en marcha. Uno de los motivos de que se haya demorado tanto es precisamente la ambición de los combates con especialistas reales. A eso se suma el diseño de escenarios, enemigos y jefes, con un nivel de producción propio de un triple A.
'Black Myth: Wukong' ya demostró el potencial internacional de una superproducción desarrollada en China y ahora S-GAME busca hacerse un hueco con una propuesta propia, apoyada en una gran ambición técnica y en las artes marciales chinas como seña de identidad.
Las críticas están por las nubes. Cuentan en Vidaextra que las primeras reseñas de 'Phantom Blade: Zero' están siendo excelentes. El juego ya ha cosechado un 88 de 100 en Metacritic y apunta a convertirse en un éxito de ventas. Estará disponible para PC y PlayStation el próximo 29 de octubre.

articles.title: Fix evaluation bias to unlock better models on Amazon Bedrock | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Fix evaluation bias to unlock better models on Amazon Bedrock
This post was co-authored with Khaled Thabit, Meriem Boughrara, and Mohamed Desouky from Property Finder.
The engineering team at Property Finder, a digital real estate application, discovered that 96.8 percent of their evaluation labels had been inherited directly from a single model’s predictions rather than verified by human experts. Their ground truth was systematically skewed toward the incumbent model, making every alternative appear to underperform. The labels also had errors, but the bias was what blocked objective model comparison. They uncovered this when migrating their vision AI workload to a more cost-effective option on Amazon Bedrock.
Property Finder processes tens of thousands of property images every day across the Middle East and North Africa (MENA). Their system evaluates 11 quality attributes per image. These cover watermark detection, room classification, furnishing status, photo quality, and construction indicators. That’s thousands of new property listings with an average of 15 images each. All need quality assessment before going live.
Property Finder needed a more cost-effective option. But measured against those labels, any alternative was at a disadvantage.
The hardest part was not finding a better model. It was discovering that their evaluation methodology itself was the blocker.
In this post, we share how Property Finder identified evaluation bias, built unbiased ground truth, and applied evolutionary prompt optimization to select the right model on Amazon Bedrock, achieving higher accuracy at 86 percent lower cost. We walk through the methodology and iteration examples, with lessons you can apply to your own workloads.
The following figure illustrates the prompt optimization loop that Property Finder and the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center team used to iteratively improve classification accuracy on Amazon Bedrock.
The diagram shows the iterative prompt optimization cycle. A property image is processed by Amazon Bedrock, which outputs the predicted attributes in JSON format. During optimization, these predictions are scored with Micro F1 against the 256-image expert-annotated development set. Error analysis then inspects failed images and identifies visual patterns, which inform the next prompt version. The loop ran from v0 to v27. AI assistants helped refine the prompts, and later versions used automated optimization.
Your evaluation might be lying
Many teams encounter this scenario. You want to compare vision models, so you build an evaluation dataset. The most common way to get labels is to run your current model and treat its outputs as ground truth. The model has been running in production and nobody complained, so the labels must be good enough.
But this creates a circular evaluation where any alternative gets judged by how closely it matches the incumbent’s behavior, not by actual correctness.
Property Finder’s evaluation dataset had exactly this problem. Of their labeled samples, 96.8 percent came directly from the predictions of the existing vision language model (VLM) rather than independent human verification. Any alternative model was structurally disadvantaged before a single image was even processed.
Hidden errors confirmed the severity. Watermark text extraction had character-level mistakes marked as correct, including hallucinated brand names and missing characters. Photo classification forced single labels onto images containing multiple room types.
In the remaining 3.2 percent of human-labeled samples, annotators had introduced categories outside the original specification, like Office appearing where no such label existed in the prompt. A model comparison loses validity when the answer key was written by the model you are trying to replace.
Building ground truth you can trust
To break the cycle, you need human experts with real domain knowledge doing fresh annotations independently. No reference to previous model outputs. No access to what the incumbent predicted.
Dataset scope
Property Finder’s team hand-annotated 356 UAE images and a separate set of Egypt images. The team selected these from unlabeled production listings across representative industry segments. This post reports results on the UAE images. The Egypt images served as a cross-regional check on 230 images and are not reported here. The first 256 UAE images to be annotated formed the development set for tuning. The evaluation set for the final model comparison uses all 356, adding 100 images annotated after the development runs. A set of 356 images is roughly sufficient to detect moderate differences between models. Rare classes within individual attributes have fewer examples, so smaller differences on those attributes might not be detectable.
Expert annotation
A strategy and analytics expert annotated all images. They brought specialized knowledge of real estate listing quality standards. The AWS Generative AI Innovation Center team conducted systematic quality reviews through dedicated clarification sessions. Those reviews settled ambiguous cases and kept the labeling consistent across the dataset.
Multi-label transition
Real estate images frequently show multiple rooms through doorways or display overlapping quality characteristics. The switch from single-label to multi-label classification alleviated a major source of artificial ambiguity.
A hallway photo showing a bedroom through a doorway is genuinely both. After you allow multiple labels, you measure what the model gets right rather than penalizing it for reasonable secondary predictions.
A hybrid approach could complement this methodology: models from different families surface candidate labels and disagreements, and human experts adjudicate every case, so no model output is used directly as a label. This would reduce the annotation burden for future dataset expansion.
Metrics selection
Micro F1 served as the primary metric because it weights each prediction equally, which matches the business goal of overall label correctness. Macro F1 was reported alongside it because Micro F1 is dominated by frequent classes and can hide weak performance on rare attributes. Per-label precision and recall helped identify specific failure modes. Per-sample intersection over union (IoU) measured how closely each image’s predicted labels overlapped the expert’s labels. The nine single-label attributes, such as rotation or watermark detection, have one right answer per image. The AWS team also scored them with exact-match accuracy, the share of images where the answer matches the expert label.
Prompt optimization as reinforcement learning
With unbiased evaluation in place, you can start improving. You cannot improve what you cannot measure correctly.
The optimization follows a loop analogous to reinforcement learning. Think of each prompt version as an agent, the Micro F1 score as the reward signal, and error analysis as the gradient for improvement. The idea resembles GEPA (Genetic-Pareto reflective prompt evolution), where you mutate prompt components, evaluate fitness, select survivors, and iterate. In this engagement, the AWS team refined most versions from error analysis, with AI assistants reviewing failed images and proposing changes.
MIPROv2, an automated prompt optimization framework from the DSPy library, complemented this manual process for the photo classification task in v27.
Where it started
The first prompt (v0) used generic classification instructions, simplified here for illustration:
        “Classify this image into one of the following categories: Living Room, Kitchen, Bedroom, Bathroom…”
Proprietary model A, Property Finder’s production baseline, scored a Micro F1 of 0.55 on the 256-image development set. It used v22, a prompt tuned for its model family. Scores before v21 used the earlier single-label setup and aren’t directly comparable.
Iteration by iteration
The AWS team tested early versions on several candidate models and added structured output formatting and attribute-specific definitions.
The most instructive fix came from image-level error analysis. In the early single-label versions, the model consistently classified rooms visible through doorways as the secondary room type. The AWS Generative AI Innovation Center team added explicit instructions to classify based on the room occupying the majority of the frame. The later switch to multi-label output kept the main room as a label and allowed rooms visible through doorways as additional labels.
Regional customization produced the next gain. In some regions, listing photos carry decorative Arabic text overlays that are not watermarks. Rules for that text removed a whole category of false positives.
The v21 prompt switched photo classification and room category to multi-label output and became the shared starting prompt for every model. With it, Llama 4 Maverick 17B Instruct from Meta scored a Micro F1 of 0.75 on the development set. From there, the AWS team tuned each model’s prompt separately. For this model, v24 targeted room size overestimation, multi-label handling, and output format. Then v25, an automatically optimized version, moved the critical tasks first. In v27, MIPROv2 restructured the photo classification task, and the model’s Micro F1 on that task reached 0.76.
Where it ended
The final prompt, v27_PF, is v27 plus rules that Property Finder added for renders, images with borders or frames, and corridors. Like v27, it keeps the Arabic text rules and output format instructions. A normalization step after each model call handles remaining format differences.
With v27_PF, Llama 4 Maverick 17B Instruct scored a Micro F1 of 0.80 on the 356-image evaluation set, where proprietary model A scored 0.56 with v22. The evaluation set includes the 256 development images, and both models’ prompts were tuned on those images. These scores are therefore optimistic.
The switch from proprietary model A to Llama 4 Maverick 17B Instruct, each on its own tuned prompt, lifted Micro F1 from 0.55 to 0.81 on the development set. That is a 47 percent relative gain. Prompt tuning alone, on Llama 4 Maverick 17B Instruct, raised it from 0.75 with the shared v21 prompt to 0.81 with v27.
Lessons from failed approaches
Not everything succeeded. The 2-bucket approach put the watermark attributes and the other attributes in two separate API calls. It brought no meaningful accuracy gain. Boxed-image detection also dropped sharply. Without the watermark attributes in the same prompt, the models mistook watermark overlays for image borders.
Generic prompts also failed regardless of which model you ran them on. Real estate imagery has too much domain specificity for a one-size-fits-all instruction.
Results: Cost, accuracy, and speed
The AWS Generative AI Innovation Center team evaluated multiple models on Amazon Bedrock with the unbiased evaluation framework. All models started from the shared v21 prompt and were then tuned for their model family on the development set. Proprietary model A got one tuning round, v22. Llama 4 Maverick 17B Instruct got several, v24 to v27, plus Property Finder’s edge-case rules, so it had more tuning effort behind it. The final comparison against proprietary model A used the 356-image evaluation set. Property Finder selected Llama 4 Maverick 17B Instruct for their production workload based on accuracy across all 11 attributes and cost efficiency. For model availability by Region, refer to Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock.
The following table shows the exact-match accuracy that Llama 4 Maverick 17B Instruct (v27_PF) reached on each single-label attribute, scored on the 356-image evaluation set. It scored 90 percent or higher on six of the nine, and matched or exceeded proprietary model A on all 11 attributes. On photo classification, which can have several labels per image, the two scored the same.
| Attribute | Exact-match accuracy | 
| Rotation detection | 100% | 
| People detection | 97% | 
| Boxed-image detection | 97% | 
| Watermark detection | 94% | 
| Render detection | 93% | 
| Furnished status | 91% | 
| Room under construction | 81% | 
| Room size | 65% | 
| Watermark text extraction | 55% | 
Cost per 1,000 images
Property Finder scores tens of thousands of images a day, so per-image cost matters. Llama 4 Maverick 17B Instruct is a cost-effective open-weight model, and the pipeline gets all attributes for an image in a single call.
| Result | Value | 
| Estimated cost per 1,000 images | $2.35 | 
| Cost reduction compared with Property Finder’s previous setup | 86% | 
These figures are estimates as of December 2025 in the US East (Ohio) Region. The Llama 4 Maverick 17B Instruct figure assumes 9,000 input tokens and 200 output tokens per image, from the original two-call cost analysis. A single call with the production prompt carries about 7,500–8,000 input tokens, so this is an upper estimate. The 86 percent compares it with the cost analysis estimate for Property Finder’s previous setup, which used the v21 prompt. The accuracy comparison used v22, which was tuned from v21, so its cost might differ. For current pricing, refer to Amazon Bedrock pricing.
Inference speed
Property Finder runs this optimized pipeline in production, processing tens of thousands of images daily with Llama 4 Maverick 17B Instruct on Amazon Bedrock. In their own monitoring, Property Finder observed a 40–60 percent reduction in inference latency compared with their previous setup.
Apply this to your workloads
Start by auditing your evaluation labels. If they came from model predictions rather than human experts, you have the same bias problem Property Finder found.
Build domain-expert ground truth for a few hundred representative samples, and keep a separate test split that you never use for tuning. Adopt multi-label metrics where your classification task involves overlapping attributes. Then iterate on prompts using image error analysis, treating each iteration as a generation in an evolutionary optimization loop.
When you deploy a pipeline like this, add responsible AI controls. For example, you can use Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to enforce content policies and filter inappropriate model outputs. The attribute predictions in this pipeline don’t come with a calibrated confidence score, so use a practical signal to choose images for human review. Model disagreement is one such signal. When two models give different answers for an attribute, the image is often ambiguous. A second model on every image adds cost, so you can start with a sample. Check how often the signal catches real errors on your development set before you rely on it.
Conclusion
In this post, we walked through how Property Finder identified evaluation bias, built unbiased ground truth, and applied evolutionary prompt optimization to achieve better accuracy at lower cost through model selection on Amazon Bedrock.
Three elements needed to come together for this result: unbiased evaluation to measure honestly, the flexibility to evaluate and switch between model families without re-platforming, and carefully evolved prompts tailored to the domain. Amazon Bedrock provided the foundation. It gave Property Finder access to multiple model families through a single API, inherited AWS governance and security controls, and the ability to adopt new models as they become available without changing their infrastructure.
To get started with model evaluation and selection on Amazon Bedrock, visit the Amazon Bedrock documentation. If you process vision workloads at scale and want help building an unbiased evaluation framework, reach out to the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center.
Share your experiences with model evaluation and prompt optimization in the comments.
Acknowledgments
Additional contributors from AWS include Yousuf Albannai, Amine Sehili, Thomas Ounnas, Aris Tsakpinis, Rafik Soliman, Nikhil Ulhas Pandit, and Sneh Sharma.

articles.title: He probado el vivo X500 Pro Max y lo tengo claro: hay vida (y muy buena) más allá del iPhone
articles.text:
Se presentó hace un mes en China, pero ahora llega al mercado europeo para demostrar que hay vida más allá del iPhone, del Samsung de gama alta de turno y de los cientos de móviles Xiaomi. El nuevo vivo X500 Pro Max es uno de los móviles más prometedores del año. Llega con un apartado fotográfico muy interesante, un conjunto de especificaciones que no decepciona. Pero también, con la misma pregunta de siempre: ¿realmente merece la pena frente a toda su competencia?
Porque admitámoslo: a estas alturas ya no es suficiente que un móvil tenga una buena pantalla, un procesador potente o una batería capaz de aguantar todo el día. Los móviles de gama alta han alcanzado un nivel tan alto elevado que las diferencias entre un modelo y otro son casi imperceptibles. Por eso, lo importante ahora está no solo en los detalles, sino en esos extras que hacen especial a un móvil: accesorios que suman y aportan mas experiencia, un software que va más allá de animaciones bonitas y fluidez, etc. Aquí es, precisamente, donde este vivo X500 Pro Max quiere hacerse un hueco.
Llevo un mes probando este móvil a fondo. Incluso viajé a Shanghái hace un mes para asistir a su presentación oficia, donde pude probar en profundidad aspectos como su cámara, su batería, su pantalla o su rendimiento. Un mes es tiempo más que suficiente para ir más allá de unas primeras impresiones y comprobar si lo que ofrece este dispositivo realmente merece la pena o no.
Ahora, toca responder a la pregunta: ¿es este vivo X500 Pro Max una alternativa real a los grandes referentes de la gama alta? ¿O estamos entre otro móvil que promete mucho, pero que termina en nada?
Sin sorpresas ni decepciones
El vivo X500 Pro Max es uno de esos móviles que no decepcionan; ni por su diseño, ni por su construcción. Es un móvil elegante, muy resistente y con detalles muy bien pensados para mejorar su ergonomía, como ese doble acabado con una parte mucho más gomosa, que evita que el móvil se te resbale de las manos y por ejemplo no se te caiga al agua (aunque también cuenta con certificación IP69).
El vivo X500 Pro Max también es muy bonito. Destaca por su gran cámara circular, por sus marcos en un acabado mate o su gran pantalla, que en este caso es de 6,85 pulgadas. Es un panel AMOLED con una resolución de 1400 x 3168 píxeles, un brillo de 2.000 nits (con picos de hasta 4.000 nits) y una tasa de refresco de 144 Hz. Es una pantalla muy brillante, con una nitidez excelente y con una interpretación de los colores muy buena: el panel OLED los satura ligeramente, pero sin pasarse, y presenta unos muy buenos ángulos de visión.
El rendimiento del vivo X500 Pro Max tampoco desentona con su diseño o su pantalla. En este caso, nos encontramos un procesador Dimensity 9600 Pro, un SoC de gama alta que está acompañado con 12 o 16 GB de memoria RAM. Dicho procesador ofrece un rendimiento excelente para el día a día y una potencia más que suficiente para ejecutar tareas de IA, tanto de edición como de productividad.
Respecto a la autonomía, este vivo X500 Pro Max tiene una de 6.750 mAh. Se trata de una batería de sicilio-carbono que ofrece una autonomía más que decente para el día a día, aunque un poco justa en condiciones de uso más intensivo. Cuenta, además, con carga rápida de 90W y una carga rápida inalámbrica de 40W.
Así son las cámaras del vivo X500 Pro Max
Hablemos del que, sin duda, es el apartado más importante de este Vivo X500 Pro Max: sus cámaras. Este modelo cuenta con un sensor principal de 50 megapíxeles y una apertura f/1.6, así como una cámara ultra gran angular de la misma resolución (aunque con una apertura f/2.0). Le acompaña, además, un teleobjetivo periscopio de 200 megapíxeles, que permite tomar fotografías con un zoom de 3.5X. Todas estas cámaras se han desarrollado con Zeiss, como fruto de una colaboración entre ambas compañías consolidada ya durante varios años.
La cámara es: impresionante. Hacia tiempo que no disfrutaba tanto haciendo fotos con un móvil. Ofrece un detalle excelente en la mayoría de situaciones, incluso en condiciones de baja luminosidad.
Tiene una interpretación de los colores muy buena, cuida mucho las sombras y consigue una exposición más que correcta en todos los escenarios. Lo fuerte es que estos resultados se consiguen incluso con el modo automático. Además (y algo que me encanta) es que puedes escoger entre diferentes filtros desarrollados por Zeiss, que le dan un toque artístico a las imágenes y consigue, incluso, imitar a las cámaras tradicionales.
Eso sí, no es oro todo lo que reluce. La cámara del vivo X500 Pro Max tiene un pequeño inconveniente relacionado con el procesado a la hora de hacer fotos a personas. En muchas ocasiones la cámara tiende a "deformar" los rostros de las personas. Es algo que se nota solo al hacer zoom, y que es claramente un "error" del procesado con IA que realiza la cámara.
El vivo X500 Pro Max también es compatible con el kit fotográfico que incluyen los otros modelos. Aunque, ojo, necesitas comprar uno específico para este modelo, pues el kit incluye una funda y un anillo adaptado a este tamaño. Dicho kit incluye también dos objetivos: Uno de 200 mm y otro de 400 mm. Es un añadido muy bienvenido si quieres tomar fotografías con más zoom o centrarte aún más en los detalles. Eso sí, colocar el objetivo es un proceso bastante engorroso. Por no hablar de que tienes que quitarlo si quieres utilizar el resto de cámaras.
¿Merece la pena el nuevo móvil de vivo?
He de reconocer que este vivo X500 Pro Max es uno de los mejores móviles del mercado. Es bonito, tiene una muy buena pantalla, su rendimiento es excelente, también su batería, su apartado fotográfico es increíble y sus extras hacen que sea un móvil mucho mas versátil y atractivo que cualquier otro modelo de gama alta.
Ahora bien, hablemos del precio. El vivo X500 Pro Max sale a la venta por 1.599 euros (1.499 euros con la promoción de lanzamiento) o 2.199 euros si quieres el kit fotográfico con los dos objetivos. Sin el kit, el terminal prácticamente iguala el precio de los mejores móviles del mercado. Además, el smartphone tiene argumentos suficientes para competir de tu a tu frente a los mejores móviles del mercado. La cuestión es si esos argumentos son suficientes para justificar un desembolso tan elevado.
Si buscas un móvil que destaque especialmente por sus cámaras y que ofrezca una experiencia sobresaliente a la hora de tomar fotografías, este es tu móvil. El vivo X500 Pro tiene una de las cámaras más versátiles que he probado nunca, y uno de los puntos más positivos es que, a diferencia de otros modelos con características similares, no necesitas ser un experto en fotografía. El modo automático, reitero, consigue unos resultados excelentes, y con un poco de aprendizaje puedes conseguir auténticas maravillas con el modo pro.
El Kit fotográfico, por su parte, es una propuesta muy particular y que puede resultar muy atractiva para aquellos que buscan experimentar más con la fotografía móvil. No obstante, no es para mi. Salvo que esté disponible a través de alguna oferta o promoción, no veo necesario gastarse 700 euros en este añadido. Sobre todo teniendo en cuenta que la cámara ya hace fotografías muy buenas.
En definitiva, el vivo X500 Pro Max es un móvil sobresaliente que tiene argumentos de sobra para plantar cara a los grandes del mercado. No es barato, precisamente, pero si el presupuesto no es un problema, estamos ante uno de esos teléfonos que conviene tener en cuenta antes de decidir qué móvil comprar. No obstante, también es importante tener en cuenta que el Vivo X500 Pro Max es muy parecido al Vivo X300 Ultra (el modelo anterior), por lo que si estás pensando en comprar este modelo y no te importa tener lo último de lo último, tal vez te interese optar por la generación anterior a cambio de un precio más reducido; apenas vas a notar diferencia.

articles.title: The Download: Anthropic’s IPO, smarter power grids, and exercise pills
articles.text:
The Download: Anthropic’s IPO, smarter power grids, and exercise pills
Plus: Anthropic's listing could determine the future of the AI investment boom.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
Will the real Anthropic please stand up?
After weeks of frenzied speculation, Anthropic has filed its IPO prospectus. The 335-page document (100 pages or so are focused on risks) lays out the company’s unique view of the technology it is building and how it believes it will change the world.
But Anthropic has been honing its storytelling skills for years. Its public messaging is a master class in narrative capture, presenting it as different things to different people: an AI safety organization, a profit-driven megacorp, and a group hell-bent on creating superhuman technology.
These roles come with huge tensions. Will the IPO reveal the company behind the mask, or lean deeper into the myth-making? Take a new glimpse inside Anthropic.
—Will Douglas Heaven
This story is from The Algorithm, our weekly AI newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Monday.
How solid-state transformers could help power the AI boom
Transformers are a crucial but nearly invisible part of the US grid, helping efficiently move power across long distances. But they’re complicated and in short supply, and their basic design hasn’t changed much in about a century.
As electricity demand rises from EVs, data centers, and more, researchers and companies are looking to modernize these grid staples. Solid-state versions could help ease supply concerns and cut power losses.
The technology is still in development, but it could become a crucial part of our future grid.
Find out how solid-state transformers could help meet rising electricity demand.
—Casey Crownhart
Are we there yet? Exercise in a pill
We all know exercise is good for us. It builds muscle, strengthens bones, lowers blood pressure, and boosts mood. By deciphering how movement benefits the body, researchers hope to develop medicines that can offer some of the same perks, without the workout.
The idea isn’t to replace exercise but to bring its upsides to people who struggle with frailty, disability, or chronic illness.
Discover how close researchers are to developing an exercise pill.
—Cassandra Willyard
This story is part of “Are we there yet?” from the new Impossible issue of MIT Technology Review. The series takes stock of six technologies that have long promised to change the world—and scores them on a progress meter. Over the next six days, we’ll explore each one in The Download.
The must-reads
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.
1 Anthropic has filed for its blockbuster IPO
The listing could determine the future of the AI investment boom. (CNBC)
+ The filing warns of catastrophic AI risks and huge compute costs. (BBC)
+ And exposes safety failures and a month-long training pause. (Reuters $)
+ The prospectus reveals soaring revenues but also staggering losses. (NYT $)
+ Anthropic’s founders will retain voting control after the IPO. (Verge) 
2 Solar is quietly overtaking nuclear as a global power source
Cheap panels and batteries are accelerating the shift. (BBC)
+ The balcony solar boom is coming to the US. (MIT Technology Review)
3 OpenAI has announced three new science discoveries
They span mathematics, computer science, and physics. (Verge)
+ It’s enlisted expert "shepherds" to publish its breakthroughs. (Gizmodo)
4 Microsoft is offering buyouts to a quarter of staff amid rising AI costs
Around 60,000 employees are eligible for the buyout program. (Bloomberg $)
+ Microsoft plans $190 billion in AI spending this year. (NYT $)
5 The plastics industry knew microplastics could enter the body decades ago
Company documents reveal concerns dating back to 1974. (LA Times $)
+ No part of the globe is free of human fingerprints. (MIT Technology Review) 
6 A demonstration of lighting Earth from space has sparked alarm
Startup Reflect Orbital used space mirrors for the California test. (Guardian)
+ The tech could jeopardize the night sky. (MIT Technology Review)
7 The US has designated helium a critical material
The move is due to its importance to semiconductor production. (AP)
8 Hundreds of Boston Dynamics staff have protested its ICE deal
They’ve called for a halt to sales of the robot dogs. (Ars Technica)
9 Treatments for age-related infertility are being developed at last
Two startups aim to reduce chromosome errors in eggs. (Economist $)
+ Here’s how tech transformed babymaking. (MIT Technology Review)
10 Grok says its AI-generated Odyssey is “not historically accurate”
The bot itself admitted Elon Musk’s filmmaking plan has failed. (Wired $)
Quote of the day
“It’s as if they’re making a promise and crossing their fingers behind their backs.”
—Kate Brennan, who leads policy at the AI Now Institute, tells the New York Times that the voluntary safety pledges AI executives recently made are toothless and unenforceable.
One more thing
The problem with thinking you’re part Neanderthal
There’s a theory that many of us have an “inner Neanderthal.” The idea is that Homo sapiens and its cousin species once bred, leaving some people today with a trace of Neanderthal DNA.
This DNA is arguably the 21st century’s most celebrated discovery in human evolution. But in 2024, a pair of French geneticists called into question the theory's very foundations.
They proposed that what scientists interpret as interbreeding could instead be explained by population structure—the way genes concentrate in smaller, isolated groups.
Find out what it all means for human evolution.
—Ben Crair
We can still have nice things
A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line.)
+ See how fast the planets spin with this dizzying animation that puts faces on each one.
+ A flask of mercury, a little neon, and some shaking produce this mesmerizing homemade light.
+ What can the USA’s earliest restaurants teach us about the country? This digital collection explores the answers.
+ Rick and Morty asked the crucial question: could a lightsaber really drill its way to Earth’s core? Science now has an answer.

Plus: 22 nations have called for a new global body to oversee AI.

articles.title: Some iPhone Duo screens are already failing, Apple says only a "small number" are affected
articles.text:
The iPhone Duo launched last week, offering anyone willing to spend $2,000 a chance to experience Apple’s first foldable phone. For some early buyers, the morning after isn’t going great. Despite the company’s big talk about its “precision-engineered” hinge, some devices appear to have a hardware flaw that destroys the device’s impressive internal display within hours (or minutes) of use.
The Internet is currently overflowing with images of busted iPhone Duos, all sporting almost identical damage. The OLED is marred by several bright lines originating just below the midpoint of the display. These bands of damaged pixels extend all the way to the bottom and right edges. Some units also show lines of dead pixels following the crease from the top to the area where the bright lines begin.
Anyone who has seen a damaged OLED panel will be familiar with this type of defect. When the layers of the display are damaged, the pixels no longer receive the correct voltage to illuminate them. Instead, they get the full driving voltage and are permanently on at maximum brightness. Some pixels can get no voltage, leaving them totally black. The only fix is to replace the OLED, but swapping the iPhone Duo’s screen reportedly costs half as much as the device itself.
It sounds like most affected devices are failing within about a day of use. But a few unlucky buyers note they only opened and closed the phone a few times, and in some cases, they hadn’t even finished the initial setup process. Some customers have reported success taking their defective phones to Apple stores for replacement, but spares may be in short supply right now.
A look inside
In the absence of any official explanation, iFixit may be the next best thing. The site has already torn an iPhone Duo apart and taken a close look at the affected area. After years of seeing other foldables fail, there are a few suspects to check. Since foldables need to pass data and power across the hinge, there’s always a cable tucked in there that could press on the screen. The iPhone Duo has a wide cable with “accordion-like pleats,” according to iFixit, but this doesn’t quite match the accounts of the damage.

articles.title: Amazon’s new Echo line is here: the 6 biggest updates
articles.text:
Amazon has just taken the wraps off a bunch of new devices as part of a string of fall announcements. Today’s news focuses largely on new Echo speakers, with a few new smart home gadgets sprinkled in.
Amazon’s new Echo line is here: the 6 biggest updates
There are plenty of updates to Amazon’s existing Echo devices, and a few new ones, too.
Here’s a roundup of all of the updates Amazon revealed on Wednesday.
Amazon’s new Echo Show 16 has a 16-inch display in an anodized aluminum frame that the company says is nearly 40 percent thinner than its predecessor. There’s a new Nanomatte display option to reduce glare, along with an audio architecture with micro woofers and two tweeters for clearer audio.
The Echo Show 16 features a wide-angle 13-megapixel camera, which Amazon says offers the “widest field of view” on an Echo Show device so far. It has 20 percent more computing power and an upgraded Omnisense fusion platform, allowing Alexa to turn up the heat when the room is too cold or turn on a light when you enter the room.
The Echo Show 16 is available for preorder today and costs $499.99, with the Nanomatte option priced at $569.99.
Amazon is launching a new digital photo frame with a semi-matte, 10-inch touchscreen. The device syncs with Amazon Photos, allowing Alexa Plus to automatically pull up pictures based on who’s in it, when it was taken, and sentiment. You can also choose people you want to feature in your frame, as well as ask the device to show you specific pictures.
The Alexa Photo Frame costs $199.99 with a black frame or $229 for the birch and walnut frames.
Amazon is rolling out an upgraded Echo Dot with a built-in smart home hub that can control devices around your home without a separate hub. Like the Echo Show 16, the Echo Dot also has the company’s Omnisense fusion platform to detect room temperature and presence. It has Amazon’s custom AZ3 chip as well, along with four microphones, a new full-range driver for 50 percent more bass than the previous generation, and a built-in Eero Wi-Fi extender. You can buy the Echo Dot today in black, white, green, and pink for $99.99.
Amazon built a camera into the Echo Studio. With this update, you can tap into a livestream of the room while you’re away from home, or ask Alexa questions about something in front of the camera. As an example, Amazon says you can hold up a board game to ask about the rules, or show it a box of cereal to order a different flavor. The Echo Studio with Home Camera will soon connect with compatible Fire TVs, too, giving you the ability to hold video calls on a larger screen.
The Echo Studio with Home Camera is available in black for $249.99, while its optional stand costs $39.99.
Amazon has revealed the Echo Time, a smart alarm clock with a circular, 3.2-inch touchscreen that you can customize with different clockfaces and layouts.
The Echo Time offers an optional smart alarm feature that can wake you up when you’re in a lighter sleep — 10 to 60 minutes before your alarm — rather than at the exact time you want to wake up. It uses Amazon’s Omnisense technology to determine when to wake you up based on temperature and presence. The display also adjusts throughout the day, gradually brightening in the morning before dimming at night.
The Echo Time is available today for $199.99 in black, white, and pink, while a Kids Echo Time starts at $209.99. There’s also an adjustable stand available for $39.99.
A new Alexa Home Map feature creates an interactive 3D map of the inside and outside of your home. It displays your Echo devices, Ring and Blink cameras, Fire TV, lights, locks, thermostats, and other smart home devices, which you can control directly through the map.
Amazon says you can create a map by entering your home address, scanning each room with a compatible iPhone, and then placing each smart home device. You can access your map in the Ring app, too, where you can view live animations of people and cars outside your home.
Alexa Home Map is rolling out in preview later this year on iOS in the Alexa Home Map, Alexa, and Ring apps. It’s also coming to larger Echo Show devices, the Ember Artline Fire TV, and new Alexa Tablets.

articles.title: Q&A: Koho’s Daniel Eberhard on unicorns, leadership, and striving to stay humble | BetaKit
articles.text:
Daniel Eberhard has hit some milestones not many founders have. Last summer, the CEO and founder of Toronto FinTech company Koho saw the company’s valuation reach unicorn status following a $130-million Series E round, joining an increasingly exclusive club of non-AI startups to do so in the post-2023 era.
En route to securing a banking license that, if obtained, will vault Koho into the Canadian challenger bank category, Eberhard sat down with BetaKit Editor-in-Chief Douglas Soltys for a conversation about what he’s learned about leadership on the road from startup to billion-dollar valuation, why he’s not game for prediction markets, and the very peculiar list he keeps in his office. An excerpt from that conversation is below.
The following interview has been edited for clarity and length.
You raised a Series E round earlier this year that got Koho over a $1-billion valuation. What does that mean for the company after a decade?
Internally, I still don’t really think of Koho as a unicorn, even though we are. The cool part is it’s a validation of the team, the work that we’ve done to get here, and the capital in itself is very useful.
There are on the order of 150 unicorns minted each year in the world. Roughly 70 percent of those are AI companies right now. So it’s 40 companies each year that do what we’ve done.
The other part is that only eight percent of companies that make billion-dollar valuations go on to build $10-billion businesses. Fifty percent of them never raise another round, never get acquired. So, 50 percent of them are zombie unicorns. If you just do that math, you’re like: OK, we have a one-in-10 shot.
On the other side, what keeps you humble is that we didn’t do this to be a unicorn. In that respect—who cares? It’s incidental to what we’re trying to do as a business.
Has the perspective around valuation changed in the post-2023 AI era? Do you see Koho and FinTech in a different space relative to what’s going on in AI?
I don’t really care. We are not out to chase valuations; we’re here to build a wonderful business. There’s a nature of cyclicality to what we do, and I don’t spend a lot of time losing sleep over it.
It’s been a 10-year journey for Koho, and you’re coming up to this major milestone of obtaining a banking license. I’m wondering what’s still driving you to get to the end of the beginning?
The team is really good, and I’m having a lot of fun. If the job today was like it was during the first five to eight years, I don’t think I’d have the gas in the tank. I’m at a different phase in life now. I have two young kids, and I’m trying to figure out how I can do this job for the next 25 to 30 years. At the same time, even if I did stop, what would I do? I like this business. I think we’re positioned better than anyone in the country to go solve our version of the problem. We’ve worked our butts off for a decade plus to position ourselves this way, and I do think it takes 25 to 30 years to build a truly generational company.
RELATED: Koho secures $190 million CAD in equity and debt to bolster banking licence efforts
What changed from those first seven or eight years to the point where you’re now having fun?
It’s a confluence of factors. Certainly part of it is existential risk that is not present in Koho the way it used to be. Before, if we ran out of money, we died. We’re in a better position now, and it makes it much easier. The distribution of outcomes is very different.
The other thing is that the team is really good. As you get to this stage, the folks you have around the table are very competent and much better than me in many ways.
There was a Maclean’s interview you did recently; it was revealed that on the wall of your office, you have several motivating, inspirational things. But there’s also a list of names of people that have burned you, or didn’t believe in you. What’s going on there?
I’m happy to talk about it. There are two things on my wall. One of them is a poem called If by Rudyard Kipling and another called Defeat by Kahlil Gibran. But yes, I have a list of people. I used to lean on it a lot more. I kind of consider it dirty fuel and I think there’s a certain utility to that which is like anger or spite. There’s a part of you that’s like “Fuck you, I’m going to prove you wrong.” I think that’s important and useful. There’s obviously much healthier ways to get your energy, though, and building from a place of wholeness and completeness, and that’s what I’m trying to do now.
In the Maclean’s article, there was a reference to what happened in 2021, kind of at the very end of the zero interest rate period (ZIRP) and the end of Tiger Global coming in and throwing checks at a bunch of Canadian companies. What happened at that moment?
In 2021 it was really interesting because it was ZIRP and I was listening to certain members of my board a lot, and I kind of thought of them as the adults in the room; these folks were telling me to grow, grow, grow, double headcount every year, that kind of stuff. Then ZIRP went away, and I was way too deferential to these folks, and they were like, “Why is your burn so high?” It was a total 180-degree flip, and it got really contentious, and I just remember thinking I could follow these people’s advice perfectly, and even then, if it doesn’t work, the bag’s with me. So, I may as well fail or succeed on my terms. That was a really clarifying moment for me as a CEO. It almost killed the company.
So, there is this kind of thing of people that I do want to prove wrong. I don’t look at it that much anymore.
Are you still in contact with those people?
Yeah. We have a great relationship. They’re still on my board. We still have to have productive working relationships. We have a really good board with a lot of healthy conversation and mutual respect.
RELATED: Koho wants to be the new bank on Bay Street
At NACO Summit this year, you talked about the idea of launching a telco. Talk to me about the strategy there.
We don’t have anything to announce right now, but the question we always ask ourselves is: can we give people more agency in their life if we give them better financial tools? If part of that better financial tool is a telco, or access to phone plans at $20 a month, then we’re fairly agnostic about what types of things we’re delivering, assuming it’s useful for the user and we can deliver it in a cohesive way.
There’s been some new competition in Canada, and it mostly seems to be coming from international FinTechs. We’re starting to see some US-Canadian partnerships. Is the real competition going to be international incumbents or disruptors?
I welcome competition, one, for the reason that it makes us better as a company, and two, that it makes the products and services better in Canada. I don’t want Koho to win because we’ve had an insulated market where we didn’t go up against the best companies in the world. That’s not interesting to me. And we like our position because it’s taken us five years to get a banking license, and we may bank some of these entities as they come into Canada. We have a lot of call options in terms of how we think about it.
We’ve seen that the 2015 cohort of young, shiny FinTechs has grown up to capture a meaningful share of the market, yet I haven’t seen too much change from the larger financial institutions. How do you see the market changing?
I think the banks have proven they largely, with few exceptions, have a very, very hard time changing. That said, we are all still incredibly small relative to the banks. So when we talk about this at Koho, with 2.5 million accounts, we think, cool, let’s go directly impact two-and-a-half million people. The way you indirectly impact the entire landscape of the country is when you start showing up on a bank’s earnings reports. That’s how they go: oh yeah, maybe we should stop paying savings rates of 0.01 percent.

articles.title: Charge bidirectionnelle : le tacle de Ford à l’écosystème coûteux de Tesla
articles.text:
La charge bidirectionnelle est-elle en passe de devenir le nouveau champ de bataille de la voiture électrique aux États-Unis ? « Rendre la meilleure technologie accessible à la majorité, pas seulement à quelques-uns », a publié Jim Farley, le grand patron de Ford, sur LinkedIn ce mardi 27 octobre 2026. Le message sonne comme une attaque directe contre Tesla.
Cette technologie (V2H, pour Vehicle-to-Home) permet à une voiture électrique de se transformer en groupe électrogène géant pour alimenter une maison lors d’une coupure de courant. Avec la multiplication des catastrophes climatiques, la fonction intéresse de plus en plus, d’autant qu’elle peut aussi alléger la facture d’électricité. Or, la solution proposée par Tesla s’accompagne d’une installation particulièrement coûteuse. Ford veut, de son côté, rendre cette fonction plus abordable avec son futur pick-up vendu moins de 30 000 dollars (environ 27 000 euros).
Ford Fathom : 10 kW dans la maison, sans onduleur hors de prix
L’arme de Ford pour cette nouvelle guerre contre Tesla s’appelle le Fathom. Ford a même fixé ce mardi 27 octobre son prix de départ à 28 350 dollars. Les précommandes ouvriront début 2027, pour des livraisons plus tard dans l’année. Tesla promet depuis des années une voiture électrique sous ce seuil, sans jamais l’avoir proposée aux acheteurs américains.
Dans son communiqué, Ford promet que le Fathom sera capable de délivrer plus de 10 kW de puissance directement au réseau domestique. L’originalité technique ne réside pas dans la puissance en elle-même, mais dans la méthode : l’équipe d’ingénierie a réussi à intégrer l’onduleur directement dans le véhicule.
Concrètement, cela signifie que le courant continu (DC) de la batterie est transformé en courant alternatif (AC) par le pick-up lui-même avant d’être réinjecté dans le réseau domestique. Il supprime ainsi l’obligation pour le client d’acheter et de faire installer un onduleur mural séparé facturé plusieurs milliers de dollars. Une simple borne de recharge domestique compatible sera nécessaire, à un tarif que le patron de Ford promet particulièrement bas.
Dans l’idée, le véhicule peut servir de générateur de secours en cas de panne complète du réseau, mais il peut aussi permettre d’éviter les heures les plus coûteuses en électricité pour réduire les factures d’énergie. Le principe parlera aux abonnés français de l’offre Tempo d’EDF, même si le Fathom n’est annoncé que pour le marché nord-américain.
Pour éviter que la recharge bidirectionnelle ne tourne au casse-tête administratif, Ford a aussi monté, dès juillet 2026, un groupe de travail avec cinq fournisseurs d’électricité nord-américains (PG&E, American Electric Power, BC Hydro, Consumers Energy et Exelon). Objectif : définir des règles communes de raccordement au réseau avant l’arrivée du Fathom.
Le pied de nez à l’écosystème Tesla
Chez Tesla, la vision de l’énergie domestique passe par un écosystème propriétaire. Si vous voulez secourir votre maison avec votre Model Y ou Model 3, Tesla vous pousse logiquement vers ses propres solutions de conversion et de stockage stationnaire. La facture d’installation peut alors rapidement doubler le prix d’entrée dans le monde du V2H. C’est un peu différent avec le Cybertruck, dont l’installation minimale est plus légère (mais pas le prix du véhicule). Tesla ne garantit d’ailleurs la fonction que sur les Model 3 et Model Y commandées depuis le 1er octobre 2026, alors que la marque l’avait annoncée dès mars 2023.
Ford prolonge ce qu’il avait lancé avec le F-150 Lightning (souvent utilisé comme source d’énergie sur les chantiers), un pick-up électrique dont il a depuis arrêté la production, mais cette fois sur un modèle bien moins cher. Pour Ford, la voiture doit servir de batterie à la maison en cas de tempête, sans obliger à acheter en plus une batterie domestique à plus de 10 000 dollars (environ 8 600 euros), comme chez Tesla.
En taclant frontalement l’approche élitiste et verrouillée de Tesla, Ford joue habilement la carte du constructeur populaire. Sur les réseaux sociaux, les acheteurs du Ford F-150 Lightning restent pour le moment sur la réserve concernant cette annonce : ils ont vécu la même exaltation, avant d’être déçus par la marque sur ce point. Espérons pour Ford que les promesses seront à la hauteur des attentes des acheteurs cette fois.

articles.title: La demande d'iPhone Duo s'effondre : les scalpers pourraient bien perdre leur pari, et leur argent
articles.text:
Les scalpers qui comptaient fermement sur les pénuries d'iPhone Duo pour se faire une marge confortable se prennent un retour de bâton. Ces derniers voient ainsi leurs espoirs d'argent facile réduits à peau de chagrin, au gré des problèmes matériels de ce dernier.
En sumérien, ça se prononce "cheh". Les revendeurs qui avaient précommandé en grand nombre l'iPhone Duo, le premier smartphone pliable d'Apple, se retrouvent aujourd'hui contraints de brader leurs stocks. En cause : une série de problèmes matériels qui ont terni le lancement de l'appareil et dissuadé de nombreux acheteurs potentiels.
Des prix de revente revus à la baisse en Chine
Selon des informations en provenance de Chine, plusieurs revendeurs (scalpers) ont dû réduire significativement leurs tarifs. Le modèle 1 To de l'iPhone Duo a ainsi vu son prix chuter de plus de 400 dollars depuis vendredi 23 octobre, date de lancement officiel de l'appareil.
Cette baisse de prix a toutefois eu un effet : certains consommateurs, jusqu'alors hésitants, ont profité de la chute des tarifs pour finaliser leur achat, entraînant un léger regain d'intérêt pour le produit.
Des précommandes tendues, des mois d'attente
Le 16 octobre, jour d'ouverture des précommandes pour l'iPhone Duo, la demande avait été particulièrement forte. De nombreux revendeurs avaient alors acheté d'importantes quantités de l'appareil dans l'optique de les revendre ensuite à des prix bien plus élevés, jouant sur les pénuries.
Mais voilà, tout ne s'est pas passé comme prévu. Quatre jours après son lancement, l'iPhone Duo a fait l'objet de multiples signalements concernant des écrans fissurés et des charnières défaillantes.
Apple reconnaît un problème sur certains appareils
Interrogée par Mark Gurman, correspondant en chef d'Apple pour Bloomberg, la firme de Cupertino a confirmé être au courant de problèmes affectant l'écran interne "d'un nombre limité d'unités de l'iPhone Duo". Apple recommande aux clients concernés de contacter le service AppleCare afin d'obtenir gratuitement le remplacement de leur appareil.
L'entreprise a précisé que la majorité des unités commercialisées ne présentaient pas ce défaut. Ce souci, s'il doit se produire, arrive assez rapidement après l'acquisition du smartphone selon la marque à la pomme. C'est toutefois un peu facile à dire au bout de seulement quelques jours de commercialisation. Le nombre exact d'appareils concernés par ce problème matériel n'a pas été communiqué par Apple.
Lors de ses premiers smartphones pliables en 2019 et 2020, Samsung avait été victime de problèmes similaires. Si ces défauts pouvaient être tolérés à une époque primitive pour les smartphones pliables, leur réapparition sur un appareil de 2026 pose question.
Source : PhoneArena

articles.title: Workshaala targets Rs 1,000 Cr revenue as it scales enterprise workspace business
articles.text:
Workshaala targets Rs 1,000 Cr revenue as it scales enterprise workspace business
Operating 75,000 seats across 25 centres in 10 cities, Workshaala is betting on pan-India expansion, technology-led operations, and growing demand from GCCs to drive its next phase of growth.
India's offices are being reinvented, and Workshaala wants to be the company that runs them. The enterprise workspace provider has set out a Rs 1,000 crore revenue vision for its next phase of growth, built on a footprint that already spans 3.5 million sq ft of serviceable area: 75,000 seats across 25 centres in 10 Indian cities.
The announcement follows a landmark moment for the company. Workshaala recently delivered what it describes as the world's largest service-platform workplace transaction, a deal that is now live within its existing footprint.
For the company's leadership, that transaction is less a finish line than a proof point. It shows the model works at the very top end of enterprise demand, and that it is ready to be replicated across the country.
From proof point to growth platform
Workshaala is clear that the Rs 1,000 crore target is not a fundraising story or a projection built on potential. It is a revenue roadmap anchored in a model the company has already tested at the largest scale in its category.
The timing reflects a market at an inflection point. India's technology and services economy is expected to add millions of white-collar seats over the next decade. Grade-A workspace demand is outpacing supply in every major city. And enterprises are taking a hard look at the economics of traditional real estate, seeking flexibility, cost predictability and operational efficiency without the weight of long-term leases.
That is precisely the gap Workshaala was built to fill. With execution already proven, the company sees scaling not as an option, but as the logical next step.
Four pillars to Rs 1,000 crore
Rather than a single bet on one city or one client segment, Workshaala's growth plan rests on four pillars, each already in motion.
1. Pan-India expansion. The company is growing across Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune, Chennai and Mumbai, with emerging Tier II hubs such as Indore, Coimbatore and Chandigarh close behind. Enterprises increasingly want a single partner that can deliver consistent workspace standards in every city they operate in. Workshaala's playbook is designed to travel.
2. A technology layer beneath the real estate. Workshaala runs a platform that manages occupancy, utilization, service delivery and facility operations in real time. This lets it operate 75,000 seats across 25 centres with the discipline of a technology business rather than the margins of a facilities operator, and allows revenue to scale faster than headcount.
3. Enterprise-grade service delivery. Large corporates do not switch workspace partners lightly. They need assurance on uptime, compliance, safety, and consistency at scale. Workshaala's landmark transaction gives prospective clients a live reference they can visit before they sign, rather than a promise in a pitch deck.
4. Strategic ecosystem partnerships. Instead of competing with developers, landlords and corporate real estate teams, Workshaala works alongside them. It positions itself as the operating layer that makes large commercial assets enterprise-ready, a model that compounds as more partners plug into the platform.
Taken together, the pillars describe a company that is not chasing growth for its own sake, but extending a model it has already validated at scale.
Built for the GCC wave
No discussion of enterprise workspace demand in India is complete without Global Capability Centers, and this is where Workshaala sees its sharpest fit.
GCCs come with distinct expectations. Parent companies mandate strict security and compliance standards. Headcount plans can double within a year. And the space has to feel world-class from day one.
Workshaala's answer is to pair real estate execution with its live occupancy and service-delivery platform. Instead of waiting months for a customized build-out, a GCC can move into managed, technology-enabled space that is enterprise-ready from the outset. It can then grow from 200 seats to 2,000 without renegotiating its entire real estate strategy.
Standardized service levels across 25 centres in 10 cities mean every GCC location runs on the same playbook, with the uptime guarantees, compliance rigor, and reporting discipline a global headquarters expects.
As India cements its role as the world's hub for innovation and operations, GCCs are emerging as one of the fastest-growing segments of Workshaala's enterprise pipeline.
The road ahead
The next decade will decide how enterprise India works, and where. Companies want space that scales with them, runs reliably in every city and frees capital from long leases.
Workshaala is betting that the winners in this market will be operators who combine physical execution with a technology backbone, and that a model proven at the largest scale can be repeated city by city.
The Rs 1,000 crore milestone is the company's way of measuring that bet. With 75,000 seats already live, a reference transaction enterprises can walk into, and a growing GCC pipeline, Workshaala is entering its growth decade from a position of proof rather than promise.

articles.title: Ugandan startup XenFi helps hotspot operators sell, manage Wi-Fi access - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Ugandan startup XenFi is helping internet service providers (ISPs) and Wi-Fi hotspot operators sell internet access, manage customers and collect payments via mobile money from a single platform.
Founded in 2025, XenFi has built a hotspot billing and management platform that also lets operators monitor transactions and manage multiple MikroTik routers from a centralised dashboard.
“Many hotspot operators need to manage customer access, sell vouchers, collect payments, monitor revenue and administer multiple routers. Handling these processes through disconnected tools or manual systems can make it difficult to track transactions, maintain operational efficiency and scale,” said Charles Wasswa, XenFi’s CEO.
“XenFi brings these functions together through a centralised platform that supports mobile money payments and simplifies the management of hotspot businesses.”
The startup is self-funded by its founders, which Wasswa said forced discipline from the start.
“Starting without relying on external investors required us to be disciplined in how we allocated resources, developed our technology and acquired customers,” he said.
That approach has paid off. XenFi is already profitable and employs more than 100 people.
“Rather than treating profitability as the end goal, we are using it to strengthen our technology, expand our operations and reach more customers,” Wasswa said.
The platform serves approximately 6,000 active users in Uganda and has customers in close to 15 African countries, including Ghana, Kenya, Nigeria, Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi and Gabon. XenFi has also set up a physical presence in Kenya.
“Uptake has been encouraging,” said Wasswa. “Beyond Uganda, we are seeing adoption across other African markets, with businesses welcoming our system as a solution for managing their hotspot operations and payments.”
XenFi makes money through platform charges and billing and transaction fees, which vary by service and market.
“As our customers grow and process more activity through our platform, we have opportunities to grow our revenue alongside them,” Wasswa said.
The startup competes with international hotspot billing platforms, regional providers, locally developed billing tools and operators still relying on manual systems. Wasswa said XenFi stands out through its focus on African market needs, payment integration and ease of use.
Expansion has brought its own challenges.
“Payment systems, customer expectations, connectivity infrastructure and regulatory requirements differ from country to country, making international expansion a continuous learning process,” Wasswa said.
“Customers need reliable systems that support their businesses consistently, so we place considerable importance on product reliability, customer support and continuous improvement.”
XenFi now plans to deepen its presence in existing markets, strengthen local partnerships and move into more African countries.
“We are proud of how far we have come, but we see this as the beginning of a much larger journey,” said Wasswa.

articles.title: iPhone Duo : Apple tient l'une des promesses phares de la keynote
articles.text:
Selon le toujours très bien informé Mark Gurman, Apple aurait considéré la création d’un stylet entièrement dédié à l’iPhone Duo. Cependant, intégrer un tel accessoire sur la fine charnière du téléphone pliant aurait constitué un véritable casse-tête pour l’entreprise. Nous le savons maintenant, Apple a dû faire des compromis lors de la création de l’iPhone Duo, et l’abandon d’un stylet conçu sur mesure en fait partie. Mais lors de sa keynote de rentrée, Apple avait fait une promesse : son téléphone pliant allait être compatible avec l’Apple Pencil. Cette promesse est aujourd’hui tenue grâce à la mise à jour d’iOS 27.2.
L’iPhone Duo est désormais compatible avec l’Apple Pencil
Grâce à la mise à jour iOS 27.2, l’iPhone Duo est compatible avec l’Apple Pencil. Point important à retenir : cette compatibilité concerne seulement l’Apple Pencil USB-C. Le modèle doté d’un connecteur Lightning n’est quant à lui pas supporté par l’iPhone pliant. Pour pouvoir bénéficier de la mise à jour iOS 27.2, il suffit de se rendre successivement dans Réglages, Général et Mise à jour logicielle. Une fois la mise à jour disponible, vous pourrez donc donc utiliser l’Apple Pencil USB-C sur l’iPhone Duo.
Notons au passage qu’iOS 27.2, à destination de l’iPhone Duo, améliore les appels vidéo avec Edge Light (un anneau lumineux virtuel est affiché sur le pourtour de l’écran pour illuminer votre visage) et intègre SynthID pour identifier les images générées par IA. Pour les téléphones non pliants, la mise à jour colmate plus de 160 failles de sécurité dénichées sur l’iPhone et renforce Siri IA (toujours indisponible en Europe), qui peut désormais parler français, portugais et espagnol. La mise à jour apporte également des corrections de bugs et des profils personnalisés dans Apple TV.
Comment apparier l’Apple Pencil à l’iPhone Duo ?
Pour jumeler l’Apple Pencil USB-C à votre iPhone Duo, faites coulisser l’extrémité du stylet pour accéder à son connecteur USB-C. Branchez-y le câble de recharge USB-C fourni avec le téléphone, puis reliez l’autre extrémité à l’iPhone Duo. Une fenêtre vous invitant à jumeler l’Apple Pencil devrait alors s’afficher à l’écran.
Une fois le jumelage effectué, vous pouvez débrancher le câble. Le stylet restera associé à votre iPhone Duo jusqu’à ce que vous redémarriez le téléphone, désactiviez le Bluetooth ou jumeliez l’Apple Pencil avec un autre appareil, précise Apple. Si vous choisissez de ne pas le jumeler, il se rechargera simplement tant qu’il restera branché.

articles.title: Tailscale warns of SSH flaws allowing root privilege escalation
articles.text:
The Tailscale security team is working to patch almost a dozen security vulnerabilities that could be exploited to steal credentials, crash servers, gain root privileges, and more.
Tailscale develops a software-defined mesh virtual private network (VPN) built on WireGuard that lets users connect computers, servers, and cloud instances from anywhere to the same encrypted mesh network ("tailnet") via direct peer-to-peer (P2P) connections.
Cyberdione Labs discovered 11 flaws (collectively known as Tailworm) that still lack patches during a security audit of Tailscale 1.104.2 and the self-hosted headscale v0.29.5 control server.
"All findings were verified by reproduction in a lab environment on unmodified, released software (tailscale v1.104.2, headscale v0.29.5)," said Erica Windisch, founder of Cyberdione Labs, who reported the flaws to Tailscale and publicly released the details.
"It is the opinion of the researchers that rapid awareness of these flaws will expediate remediation across impacted devices. These vulnerabilities were not introduced by the researchers, but were discovered, and discovered with low effort."
The table below classifies the security issues by the component they affect. The most critical issue is in Tailscale's SSH server and could let authorized attackers gain code execution with root privileges through Unix-socket forwarding on a targeted tailnet.
| Component / feature | Mechanism (what breaks) | Attacker requirement | Principal outcome | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Tailscale SSH (tailscaled's embedded SSH server, running as root) | Unix-socket forwarding ( ssh -R/-L) performs path checks and file operations as root; races and missing privilege drop let an ordinary session replace, dial, or delete privileged resources | One approved device + one SSH policy rule (forwarding granted automatically on headscale; per-rule on SaaS) | Root execution on target servers; capture of enrollment keys; arbitrary root-file deletion | 
| Tailscale app connectors (conn25, experimental) | Connector translates traffic to attacker-chosen destinations with no validation; network ACLs are never consulted for the true destination | A device granted the connector capability | Reach cloud metadata (credential theft), internal LANs, and — in Kubernetes — every cluster service | 
| headscale control server (self-hosted deployments) | Unauthenticated resource exhaustion (memory growth, cache eviction) | Internet reachability; no account | Control-server crash loop; blocking of new-device onboarding org-wide | 
| Tailscale DERP client (relay connection in every agent) | Unbounded read of a malicious relay's response | Ability to position/point a client at a hostile relay | Client-agent memory exhaustion | 
| tailscale serve (local service exposure) | TCP-forward to a unix socket lacks a guard present on the HTTP path; plus a race in per-mount authorization | Operator configures the forward (or a peer races the mount check) | Remote administrative-API access to the node; minority of requests bypass app authz | 
On Monday, the Tailscale team said it received Cyberdione Labs' report and was working on patches to address these security issues by the end of today.
The developers also confirmed that the reported flaws are "serious" as they could let threat actors with permissions on targeted systems take actions with escalated privileges.
"Most of the Tailscale SSH issues we've identified concern privilege escalation. In some circumstances, someone already authorized to connect over Tailscale SSH may be able to perform actions beyond the permissions of their configured local user, including potentially gaining elevated privileges," Tailscale said.
"These are serious security issues, and we're treating them accordingly. Exploitation depends on the permissions granted to the connecting user or device, the system's configuration, and other conditions. We're continuing to verify the full scope of the findings and which configurations may be affected."
However, despite the severity of the issues, Tailscale said it doesn't recommend that users disable the Tailscale SSH feature.
"If you want to jump to the most important part, based on our current assessment, we're not recommending that everyone disable Tailscale SSH," said Mike Shaver, VP of Engineering at Tailscale.
Instead, the Tailscale team shared measures that should mitigate some of these flaws:
- Review SSH access policies. Limit access to the users and devices that need it.
- Disable SSH forwarding if you don't need it. Set TS_SSH_DISABLE_FORWARDING=1 in the tailscaled service environment and restart the service. This disables SSH forwarding without disabling Tailscale SSH entirely, and mitigates several of the more serious findings.
- Review access to sensitive systems. Consider temporarily tightening your Tailscale SSH access policies while we investigate, so that only the specific users and devices that need access can connect.
The Tailscale devs aim to push a new version that fixes these issues by the end of Tuesday, October 27, and urged users to prepare to update and "apply the patched Tailscale client release when it becomes available."
Once attackers have valid credentials, only 37% of their actions are blocked
Overall prevention scores can hide what happens after initial access. Once attackers are using valid credentials, prevention drops sharply.
