articles.title: Nobody Trusts the Security Questionnaire. We Rely on It Anyway.
articles.text:
Right now, people on security and GRC teams are spending their entire workday answering security questionnaires. At some companies it is a full-time role: a GRC analyst or compliance manager who arrives, opens a laptop, and works through these forms until they go home, two or three hundred of them in a year. I’ve heard the stories. The dinner missed, left a kid’s game at halftime, lost the weekend to a form asking whether the company still keeps tape backups. They do it because the questionnaire sits on the path to revenue. If the form stalls, the deal stalls with it.
There is a double standard built into the process. The same team buried under those questionnaires also sends them out to the company’s own vendors, collects the answers, and files them as proof those vendors are safe to trust. They know how little the answers are worth when they fill them out, because they have watched how little scrutiny the yeses get under deadline. They rely on them anyway when a vendor sends them back, because for a long time there was nothing better to rely on.
The same form, distrusted going out and trusted coming in
Step back and look at the whole exchange. Company A wants to sell to Company B. Before the deal closes, B sends A a questionnaire and a stack of security terms to sign: a security addendum, a data processing agreement, and now an AI addendum. Company A answers the questions, signs the commitments, and the deal proceeds. But A buys software too, so it runs its own vendors through the same exercise and weighs their answers to decide whom to trust. The form Company A knew was soft when it answered becomes, when A sits on the buyer’s side, its basis for trusting someone else. Every company in the chain is doing both at once.
Good programs already know the questionnaire is weak, which is why they also ask for a SOC 2 report, an ISO certificate, a penetration test, and sometimes an outside security rating. But look at where the weight still sits. The questionnaire is still what gates the deal and lands in the file as the record of due diligence. We have surrounded it with supplements and left it at the center. Trust between businesses runs, more than we like to admit, on a self-report: a vendor’s own account of its security, taken largely on the vendor’s word.
Why a self-reported answer stopped being evidence
An answer is not a control. A vendor writing yes does not make the thing true, and it was not true because your own team wrote yes when the roles were reversed. A questionnaire captures an intention, or a setting that was accurate on the day someone typed it, and then everyone moves on while the environment keeps changing.
If this model were working, third-party breaches should be getting rarer. They are not. Verizon’s 2025 Data Breach Investigations Report found the share of breaches involving a third party doubled in a single year, from 15 percent to 30 percent. They are not cheap, either. In IBM’s 2025 Cost of a Data Breach report, third-party and supply-chain compromise was one of the most expensive vectors at roughly $4.9 million per incident, above the global average, in a year when the overall average breach cost fell for the first time in five years. So the vendor-borne breach is getting more common and staying more costly even as breaches overall ease.
The clearest illustration is also one of the most studied breaches in the industry. Target was certified compliant with the Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard in September 2013. That December it disclosed a breach of 40 million payment cards. The certificate was real. It was also beside the point. A passing assessment tells you a vendor cleared a bar in one day. It does not tell you the vendor is secure, and that conflation is how thoroughly certified companies still end up writing breach notifications.
Stop trading promises, start trading proof
The market has started to act on this, and so have regulators. In an October 2025 industry letter, the New York Department of Financial Services (NYDFS) clarified what it expects of the firms it oversees: vet vendors up front, reassess them on a risk basis over time, obtain independent audit reports rather than rely on a vendor’s own say-so, and recognize that compliance cannot be handed off to the vendor. Stop exchanging assertions and start exchanging things the other party does not get to author. What that looks like depends on which chair you are in.
When you are assessing a vendor, start with what they cannot write for you. Before the questionnaire goes out, look at what is observable from the outside, none of which is self-reported:
- Exposed infrastructure and the state of their public-facing systems
- Breach and incident history
- Leaked or exposed credentials
It is not perfect. Anyone who has used security ratings knows the noise, the stale IP address, the subdomain that was never theirs. But it is harder to dress up than a self-graded form, and it is a better starting point than the vendor’s own account of itself. From there, concentrate your real effort on the few vendors who hold enough of your data or access to cause meaningful damage, and ask the rest for proof rather than prose: a report, a test result, or an attestation signed by someone who is not on the sales team.
When you are the one being assessed, the same principle holds. The security and data processing terms in your contracts are specific and binding in a way the questionnaire is not, and a customer is entitled to ask you to show, not assert, that you are meeting them. In practice that means being able to:
- Answer “show me you are doing what this clause requires” with current evidence
- Produce that evidence on demand, rather than re-typing the same three hundred answers into every customer’s form
- Stand behind the words as an accurate description of what is actually running, not what was true when someone last typed them
You put the promises in writing. Be able to back them the same way.
What trust between two companies should rest on
The questionnaire made sense when there was no other way to size up a vendor you couldn’t see inside. Mailing everyone a form was better than flying blind. That constraint is gone. You can observe a company from the outside, and you can produce real evidence behind your own commitments, neither of which existed at scale a decade ago.
So stop letting a self-report be the decision. Keep the questionnaire if it helps you start a conversation, but make the evidence, yours and theirs, the thing that actually settles whether there is trust. Businesses were never safe taking each other’s word for it. For a long time that was the only option. It is not anymore.

articles.title: Exowatt beats frontier models on accuracy with SageMaker serverless model customization | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Exowatt beats frontier models on accuracy with SageMaker serverless model customization
Exowatt builds modular, dispatchable solar systems that deliver reliable power for energy-intensive applications such as AI data centers. Its flagship product, the Exowatt P3, captures solar energy through optical lenses, stores it as heat in a long-duration thermal battery, and dispatches electricity on demand through a heat engine. Unlike grid-tied photovoltaic solar systems, P3 powers data centers directly behind the meter, helping data centers come online without waiting in multi-year grid interconnection queues. Exowatt builds a fleet of AI agents that monitor and triage live alarms and support operational decisions for solar systems, often at the edge, with limited or no connectivity. As its fleet scales from test benches toward manufacturing and thousands of deployed field units, the intelligence layer that operates these systems must scale with it.
In this post, we show how Exowatt used Amazon SageMaker AI serverless model customization to build a repeatable AI pipeline. The pipeline produces task-specific fine-tuned models for two deployment targets, edge and cloud, achieving higher accuracy than frontier models at up to 49× lower cost.
The two models described here are the first outputs of that pipeline rather than the end goal. The more durable result of the engagement was the pipeline itself: a repeatable path from raw operational data to a certified training set, a fine-tuned model, and an evaluated deployment artifact. Exowatt can now run this path in days rather than months. Alarm triage and energy-market analysis are two of many narrow, high-value tasks where the same approach applies.
The challenge: AI on physical energy infrastructure
Exowatt’s energy management system (EMS) runs across a growing fleet of operational sites. Each site continuously produces alarms: a hardware component operating out of spec, a dropped connection, an out-of-range voltage reading, and similar events. As the fleet scales toward thousands of field units, a human operator can’t monitor every site in real time. Exowatt needed an AI agent that could read the alarm state on each site and take or recommend the correct next action autonomously and reliably.
A frontier model couldn’t solve this problem for three reasons:
- The task is narrow and proprietary. Alarm triage on Exowatt’s EMS depends on their specific hardware, data, and operating logic. A general-purpose frontier model isn’t specialized for it.
- It must run at the edge, with no GPU and often no internet. Many sites have limited or intermittent connectivity, so an agent that depends on a cloud call to a frontier model leaves the operator without coverage when the connection drops.
- Cost doesn’t scale at fleet level. Routing every operational decision to a frontier model across thousands of sites is not economical for a decision that repeats continuously.
This is where Exowatt turned to model customization. Exowatt’s initial fine-tuning workflow relied on selecting an open-weight model, building a container, and creating a custom training recipe before any experiment could run. This was a major blocker for model experimentation. Additionally, they had to decide GPU hardware requirements of model fine-tuning. As the team increased the pace of experimentation, each run first required choosing a specific GPU instance type and then waiting for that self-selected capacity to become available. When a chosen instance type was unavailable, this could delay the start of a run or block it entirely.
They needed a model small enough to run on a no-GPU edge controller, yet accurate enough compared to the frontier model on the specific task to act autonomously. Fine-tuning closed that gap: a compact, task-specialized model that is both deployable in the cloud and at the edge.
Solution overview
Exowatt addressed these challenges by adopting a cloud-native, serverless model customization approach on Amazon SageMaker AI. The same training pipeline produces fine-tuned models for two deployment targets: the edge and the cloud.
Exowatt implemented this approach on the Qwen3-1.7B model for the first use case, edge alarm triage, then applied the same approach to the Qwen3-14B model for the second use case, cloud energy-market analysis. The company plans to reuse this solution to build smaller, task-specific models across the fleet.
The following seven AWS services power the AI pipeline, with no instances, clusters, or endpoints to manage:
| AWS Service | Purpose | 
| Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) | Data, manifests, model artifacts, and test sets | 
| Amazon SageMaker AI serverless fine-tuning | Every fine-tune run, launched from Public Hub recipes | 
| Amazon SageMaker AI serverless evaluation | 2,000 answers per candidate scored as a managed job | 
| SageMaker Model Registry | Every completed fine-tune with its evidence and metrics | 
| Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import | Hosts the fine-tuned Qwen3-14B for Cloud EMS, invoked privately from the Cloud EMS service. No idle cost | 
| Amazon Bedrock (Claude, Qwen3) | Paraphrase (three rewrites per answer in the training data) and frontier model benchmarking Alarm-triage paraphrases use Qwen3-VL-235B on Amazon Bedrock. Energy-market paraphrases use Claude Sonnet 4.6 on Amazon Bedrock. | 
| AWS Lambda + Amazon EventBridge | Serverless-evaluation scorer and a scheduled keep-warm invocation of the custom model | 
The workflow is organized into three stages:
Model customization (cloud): Exowatt fine-tunes open-weight base models using serverless model customization, Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on SageMaker AI. Because serverless training allocates capacity on demand, the team runs multiple experiments per day rather than waiting for self-selected GPU. After evaluation, the best model is registered in the SageMaker AI Model Registry.
Edge deployment: For latency-sensitive, connectivity-constrained work such as alarm triage, the fine-tuned Qwen3-1.7B model is frozen, quantized to the GGUF format, and run with llama.cpp inside Kubernetes pods at the edge using on-site controllers. This path requires no GPU and operates without internet connectivity.
Cloud deployment (elastic): For internet-connected, fleet-level analysis, the fine-tuned Qwen3-14B energy-market model is served through Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import, which runs with no idle cost and bills only while the model is active.
Why Amazon SageMaker AI serverless model customization
Amazon SageMaker AI serverless model customization service provides a wide selection of open-weight models with ready-made fine-tuning recipes from the SageMaker Public Hub, so the team avoided building and optimizing a custom training container, work that can otherwise take weeks. For Exowatt, this turned fine-tuning from a scarce, scheduled event into a routine, on-demand one. This makes a rapid experimentation-and-test loop practical while keeping experimentation cost low.
Fine-tuning on provisioned GPUs requires choosing a specific instance type, requesting that capacity, waiting for it to become available, running the job, and paying for the instance for as long as it is held. The held time typically includes the idle time between experiments when a dedicated instance is kept running. For a small team running many experiments, this slows down innovation and increases cost. Amazon SageMaker AI serverless model customization automatically manages and orchestrates the infrastructure required to run the fine-tuning job, removing the pain of capacity management, and charges only for the time the fine-tuning job runs.
Use case 1: Edge alarm triage with Qwen3-1.7B
Exowatt sites raise alarms around the clock. A compact on-site model reads each alarm together with the site’s own status and telemetry and returns one of a small fixed set of classifications with cited evidence (such as an offline system, derated component, or sensor mismatch) or an explicit abstention when the evidence is insufficient.
Model selection and training data
The team first tried Qwen3-8B with prompting and guardrails, which plateaued below the target (0.735 macro-F1). A fine-tuned Qwen3-1.7B changed that: it outperformed the Qwen3-8B plus prompting setup on this narrow, single-turn task at roughly one-fifth the parameters, while staying small enough for GPU-free edge inference. Thirteen fine-tuned Qwen3-8B candidates across 12 dataset versions never beat the prompted 8B baseline. The smaller model with more varied data did.
The training set was small and curated: 2,522 examples built from 684 verified decisions on generated site scenarios plus 1,838 certified paraphrases that kept each decision fixed while rewriting the prose. The paraphrases were generated by Qwen3-235B on Amazon Bedrock for about $3.72. Each paraphrase was kept only if deterministic checks confirmed that the decision, labels, evidence citations, and every number were unchanged (1,838 of 2,218 candidates passed). One fault family was held out of training entirely, and 320 cases were reserved for testing.
Training and deployment
Training completed in about 32 minutes on SageMaker serverless fine-tuning for roughly $20–$25. Quantized to 8 bits (about 1.71 GiB), the model runs offline in a 6 GiB llama.cpp pod on the site’s existing CPU server. It also runs on a t3.2xlarge instance type.
Use case 2: Cloud energy-market analysis with Qwen3-14B
Dispatchable storage turns timing into an operational decision: each site must continually decide how much stored energy to hold for its load and when to release it, and for grid-connected sites market conditions feed into that choice. The fine-tuned model reads a six-hour packet of live market data (about 90 rows of real-time prices, day-ahead forecasts, and grid notices) and returns one of five market events (such as a price spike or scarcity adder) in about four seconds. Every claim is tied to a specific data row to inform the dispatch strategy.
Why Qwen3-14B
Qwen3-14B was chosen because it is supported by Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import, it ships as a SageMaker Public Hub model with a ready LoRA recipe (no custom container or instance type to manage), and at about 28 GiB it is small enough to serve cost-effectively.
Training data and process
Exowatt fine-tuned the model on public Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) market data drawn from five years of history (about 163 million rows across 12 tables). The team rule-labeled this data into 25,000 examples (22,000 for training, 1,000 for validation, and 2,000 held out for testing). They then expanded the training set to 86,281 rows by having Anthropic’s Claude Sonnet 4.6 on Amazon Bedrock rewrite the prose of each example while its labels and numeric fields stayed fixed.
Training was a single LoRA epoch (rank 16, alpha 32), completed in about 8.5 hours of managed serverless fine-tuning with up to four jobs running at once. The team ran 23 jobs and about 155 hours of managed training in the six days from initial plan to a champion model serving in Cloud EMS.
The decisive improvement came from paraphrase diversity: adding three rewrites per answer lifted macro-F1 from 0.950 to 0.975. The base model scored only 0.415 macro-F1. It produced valid JSON but did not yet know the market. Fine-tuning fixed that.
Deployment
The merged checkpoint was imported to Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import in about 14 minutes. The model runs with no idle cost and bills at $6.86 per hour only while active.
Benchmark results
On the edge alarm-triage task the fine-tuned Qwen3-1.7B went from a model that couldn’t produce a valid answer to 0.911 macro-F1 with 320 test cases, ahead of every frontier baseline. Applying the identical fine-tune-and-evaluate loop to the energy-market task with 2,000 test cases, the Qwen3-14B reached 0.975 macro-F1, again ahead of the frontier baseline and at a fraction of the cost. In both cases a small, fine-tuned model beat far larger general-purpose models on the specific task.
Both models return strict JSON in which every claim cites a specific input data row. Any unsupported claim is dropped before it reaches an operator, which is what lets the team trust small models in autonomous, physical settings.
| Model | Macro-F1 | $ / 1,000 decisions | Offline? | 
| Claude Haiku 4.5 | 0.519 | ~$4.70 | No | 
| Claude Opus 4.7 | 0.680 | ~$22 | No | 
| Claude Sonnet 4.6 | 0.698 | ~$15 | No | 
| Fine-tuned Qwen3-1.7B | 0.911 | $0* | Yes | 
| Base Qwen3-1.7B | No score (failed the validity gate) |  |  | 
Table 1: Edge alarm triage results, fine-tuned Qwen3-1.7B compared to frontier models
$0 per 1,000 decisions means no metered API or GPU inference cost. The quantized model runs on the site’s existing CPU.
| Model | Macro-F1 | Event Acc. | Valid JSON | $ / 1,000 answers | 
| Base Qwen3-14B | 0.415 | 0.54 | 0.834 | $0.64 | 
| Claude Sonnet 4.6 | 0.538 | 0.584 | 0.991 | $17.79 | 
| Claude Opus 4.7 | 0.625 | 0.718 | 0.9995 | $29.26 | 
| Fine-tuned Qwen3-14B | 0.975 | 0.983 | 1.000 | $0.60 | 
Table 2: Cloud energy-market analysis results, fine-tuned Qwen3-14B compared to frontier models
Costs are Amazon Bedrock list prices times measured tokens per answer. Fine-tuning lifted an open model from last place to first: +0.35 macro-F1 over Claude Opus 4.7 (95 percent confidence interval 0.324 to 0.371) at about 49× lower cost per 1,000 answers ($0.60 compared to $29.26). The model held 0.968 macro-F1 on a second, later test set.
Business benefits
Faster iteration and faster time to market: Exowatt moved its customized model from experimentation to production in only nine days. This process could have taken months if the team had to build and optimize custom containers and training recipes, provision GPUs, and manage infrastructure. With SageMaker AI serverless model customization, the team trained Qwen3-1.7B in about 32 minutes and Qwen3-14B in about 8.5 hours, with no capacity requests and up to four training jobs running concurrently. For the energy-market use case, Exowatt ran 23 jobs totaling about 155 hours of managed training and moved from the base model to a fine-tuned model serving in Cloud EMS in six days. The merged checkpoint was imported into Amazon Bedrock in about 14 minutes. The end-to-end pipeline used seven AWS serverless services, with no instances, clusters, or endpoints for Exowatt to manage.
Higher accuracy compared to frontier models: Both fine-tuned models beat the larger frontier models on their own task: Qwen3-1.7B at 0.911 macro-F1 (compared to 0.698 for Claude Sonnet 4.6) and Qwen3-14B at 0.975 (compared to 0.625 for Claude Opus 4.7).
Lower cost across both deployments: In the cloud, the Qwen3-14B serves at $0.60 per 1,000 answers versus $29.26 for Claude Opus 4.7 (about 49× lower), with no idle cost and $6.86 per hour only while active on Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import. At the edge, the quantized Qwen3-1.7B runs on the site’s existing CPU with no per-inference cost and no dependency on connectivity.
Grounded, low-risk outputs: Across both models, the evidence fence removed every uncited claim (any evidence citation whose source, field, or value does not literally match the input), and the edge model abstains rather than guesses when unsure. This is what let the team run it autonomously in shadow mode on a cloud-hosted replica of a site.
Lessons learned
For specific tasks, smaller fine-tuned large language models can outperform large frontier models: Fine-tuned Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-14B models each outperformed frontier models on the target task, delivering higher accuracy at a fraction of the cost with significantly smaller models.
Data quality and variety outweigh raw volume and extra epochs: For tightly scoped tasks, data quality mattered more than model size or data volume. On the alarm-triage model, more verified training variety moved macro-F1 from 0.584 (trained on the 684 verified decisions alone) to 0.911 (with the paraphrase-expanded 2,522-row set). Simply running more epochs over the same rows did worse: a control run that trained on the 684 original rows for 11 epochs (the same number of steps) reached only 0.879. Curated data mattered more than dataset size throughout.
Removing the provisioning step changes how a team works: When a training run no longer requires waiting for GPU capacity, fine-tuning shifts from a rare event to a routine, iterative one.
One training pipeline serves two deployment targets: Separating model training from deployment lets Exowatt use the same pipeline for both offline edge deployment and connected fleet-level analysis, simplifying operations and accelerating model deployment in the cloud.
Conclusion
Exowatt now has one reusable AI pipeline that took a task from model specific data preparation to model deployment. Rather than tuning one model for different tasks, Exowatt plans to apply the same fine-tuning principles to different tasks, each with its own data, specific models, and evaluations, across the fleet as new device types and market tasks come online.
The pattern generalizes beyond energy industry segments. AI engineers, data scientists, and customers across industry segments can adopt the same principles. Use Amazon SageMaker AI serverless model customization as a low-overhead AI pipeline to fine-tune small, task-specific models, then deploy them where the work happens: at the edge when connectivity or latency requires it, and through a managed cloud endpoint such as Amazon SageMaker AI for elastic workloads.
To learn more, see Amazon SageMaker AI serverless model customization and Amazon Bedrock.

articles.title: Cambridge scientists create a $10 chip that could put a medical lab on your wrist
articles.text:
Cambridge scientists create a $10 chip that could put a medical lab on your wrist
- Date:
- October 22, 2026
- Source:
- University of Cambridge
- Summary:
- Cambridge researchers have created a groundbreaking $10 optical sensor that delivers the precision of laboratory equipment in a device small enough for wearable technology. It identified foods, plastics, and medicines with 100% accuracy in tests and demonstrated the ability to monitor blood glucose, alcohol, and other health markers without invasive procedures.
- Share:
A new optical sensor costing just $10 could bring laboratory-level precision to wearable health monitors, potentially allowing people to track blood glucose without needles. The technology could also transform food testing, industrial quality control, and environmental monitoring.
Researchers at the University of Cambridge and GlitterinTech (a start-up founded by the same research group) have developed a new type of optical spectrometer that combines exceptional accuracy with a remarkably small size and low cost. Measuring just centimeters across, the device could be incorporated into portable electronics and wearable health technology. Its potential applications range from monitoring important health markers in real time to identifying materials and detecting changes in chemical composition.
Optical spectrometers work by analyzing light to reveal information about the substances it interacts with. They are essential tools in medicine, manufacturing, chemical testing, and environmental research. However, making these instruments smaller has traditionally meant compromising their performance. Compact spectrometers often have limited measurement ranges, reduced resolution, or lower accuracy, making them better suited to identifying substances than performing precise measurements.
The researchers believe their new design could overcome these limitations. Known as a convolutional spectrometer, it uses a mathematical principle called the convolution theorem to analyze light in a fundamentally different way. According to the team, this approach delivers performance that surpasses existing types of spectrometers in several key areas, including designs based on light dispersion, Fourier transforms, and computational reconstruction.
A New Way to Analyze Light With Extraordinary Precision
Traditional spectrometers generally separate incoming light into its component wavelengths or use complex calculations to reconstruct its spectrum. The new device takes another approach by performing a mathematical operation called convolution directly on the incoming light.
To accomplish this, the researchers arranged optical components with repeating spectral responses in a sequence. These components can include unbalanced Mach-Zehnder interferometers or micro-ring resonators. By adjusting them in proportion to one another, the system can shift its response to different wavelengths in a controlled, linear fashion. Fast Fourier transforms are then used to accurately recover the light spectrum.
"The key insight was to go back to the mathematics and ask whether there was a fundamentally cleaner way to retrieve spectra," said Dr. Chunhui Yao, a lead author of the study. "By using the convolution theorem directly in the optical domain, we avoid many of the limitations that have held miniaturized spectrometers back. This gives us high precision, strong noise tolerance, and very low computational overhead, all in a compact and low-cost system."
The researchers built the spectrometer using a silicon nitride photonic platform and integrated it with onboard electronics. It operates across a broad range of near-infrared wavelengths (1200-1700 nm) and can collect and process measurements in less than a second.
Another important advantage is its ability to expand its measurement capabilities without major hardware changes. Because the system uses repeating optical patterns, its spectral bandwidth can theoretically be extended almost without limit. Adding more optical components in sequence can also increase its resolution exponentially.
A $10 Sensor That Could Transform Food Testing and Healthcare
To evaluate the device outside purely theoretical measurements, the researchers tested it on a variety of materials and substances. The results demonstrated its potential for applications that normally depend on larger, more expensive laboratory instruments.
When used to identify plastics, pharmaceuticals, coffee, flour, and tea, the spectrometer achieved a 100% classification success rate in the reported tests. It also measured concentrations in water-based and organic solutions with accuracies of approximately 0.01%, exceeding the performance of commercial benchtop spectrometers in those experiments.
The healthcare demonstrations were particularly promising. Under conditions designed to reflect real physiological environments, the device accurately measured several human biomarkers, including skin moisture, blood alcohol, blood lactate, and blood glucose.
The researchers also demonstrated noninvasive glucose tracking over an extended period in one participant. Although further testing would be needed before the technology could become a practical medical product, the finding suggests a possible route toward monitoring blood sugar without repeatedly piercing the skin.
"These biomedical demonstrations are particularly exciting," said Prof. Qixiang Cheng, who led the project. "What makes this work stand out is not just performance in the lab, but technical readiness. Dr. Chunhui Yao's contribution was crucial in translating a mathematical concept into a fully packaged, robust system that operates reliably across temperature extremes and real-world conditions. That combination is what opens the door to practical deployment."
The sensor also demonstrated impressive resistance to temperature changes. It continued operating reliably between -20°C and 80°C, an unusually wide temperature range for a miniature spectrometer. This durability could be especially valuable for wearable devices, factory equipment, and sensors operating outdoors.
Why a Simpler Design Could Be a Major Breakthrough
The new spectrometer's advantages extend beyond its accuracy, size, and price. Its internal design also reduces the amount of computing power needed to analyze incoming light.
Many existing miniature spectrometers depend on complicated calibration procedures and demanding algorithms to reconstruct spectral information. These methods can become unreliable when measurements contain noise, and they often require substantial processing resources.
The Cambridge team's convolution-based approach avoids much of this complexity. Because the measurements follow a linear mathematical relationship, the system can recover spectra rapidly and consistently while using relatively little computational power.
"This is a beautiful example of how elegant engineering can unlock real impact," said Prof. Richard Penty, who contributed to the photonic system design and integration. "The architecture is simple, scalable, and manufacturable, yet it delivers precision that rivals or exceeds much larger instruments. Dr. Chunhui Yao played a central role in bringing together the photonic design, system integration, and experimental validation that made this possible."
Its relatively simple construction could also make the technology easier to manufacture on a large scale, potentially bringing sophisticated optical measurements to devices where conventional spectrometers would be too bulky or expensive.
Bringing Laboratory-Grade Measurements to Everyday Devices
The researchers envision a future in which accurate optical sensing becomes a routine feature of everyday technology rather than something largely confined to specialized laboratories.
In industrial settings, inexpensive spectrometers could be installed throughout manufacturing facilities to continuously check material composition and product quality. Similar sensors could monitor food freshness, identify substances, and analyze environmental conditions on a much larger scale than is currently practical.
Healthcare could see equally significant changes. Compact sensors might eventually enable wearables to measure hydration levels, detect signs of alcohol intoxication, track biomarkers related to physical fitness, or continuously monitor glucose levels for people managing diabetes.
"Our vision is to make spectrometry as ubiquitous as temperature or motion sensing," added Prof. Qixiang Cheng. "This work shows that high-quality spectral information doesn't have to be confined to the laboratory -- it can be embedded directly into the technologies people use every day."
As photonic technology becomes smaller and more advanced, the convolutional spectrometer provides a promising example of how mathematical insights and practical engineering can make sophisticated scientific instruments simpler, cheaper, and more accessible. By combining high precision with a device that costs around $10, the researchers have opened a potential path toward a new generation of smart sensors capable of measuring the hidden chemistry of our bodies and surroundings.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Cambridge. Original written by Michael Shuff. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Chunhui Yao, Jie Ma, Ningning Wang, Peng Bao, Wei Zhuo, Tao Zhang, Wanlu Zhang, Kangning Xu, Ting Yan, Liang Ming, Yuxiao Ye, Tawfique Hasan, Ian White, Richard Penty, Qixiang Cheng. Optical convolutional spectrometer. Nature Photonics, 2026; 20 (6): 664 DOI: 10.1038/s41566-026-01891-6

articles.title: Memory-Enforced GPU Sharing in Kubernetes with NVIDIA CUDA 13.4 | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
Many AI workloads need only a fraction of a GPU. Giving each one an entire device can leave capacity idle; sharing GPUs lets platform teams serve more workloads with the infrastructure they already have.
NVIDIA GPUs already support several approaches to sharing. Multi-instance GPU (MIG) splits a GPU into hardware-isolated instances that are transparent to the application, time-slicing lets several processes take turns without memory enforcement, and Multi-Process Service (MPS) lets them run concurrently in separate address spaces (sm-sharing).
CUDA 13.4 now enforces a memory boundary that is transparent to the application with a new time-sharing mode, alongside the compute sharing mode (sm-sharing) that already existed in MPS.
Here is what the CUDA release brings:
- An exact memory amount: A workload asks for a memory size and CUDA holds it there. An allocation above that size fails, just as it would on a smaller GPU.
- A range: A workload gets a guaranteed minimum plus a maximum it can grow into when memory is free.
- A compute mode: Each workload can choose to use its compute in an sm-sharing mode rather than using the default time-sharing mode.
- A transparent memory limit: Each workload sees only a fraction of the GPU memory.
The missing piece: Getting there from Kubernetes
CUDA provides the memory enforcement capability, but a Kubernetes cluster can’t use it on its own. On every GPU node, something has to:
- Run and supervise the daemons that these features depend on
- Apply each Pod container’s memory limits and compute mode before the process starts
- Report what each fraction actually uses, rather than what the whole GPU uses
This work belongs on the node, independent of whichever scheduler placed the workload.
GPU fractioning: An open-source Kubernetes operator
A new open-source Kubernetes operator, gpu-fractioning, is  hosted under the KAI Scheduler organization on GitHub. It runs next to the NVIDIA GPU Operator, which provides the driver and the container runtime setup.
GPU Fractioning Operator handles three jobs:
- It sets up and runs MPS on every GPU node.
- It applies each workload’s memory limits and compute mode.
- It measures memory and compute use per fraction rather than per GPU.
How schedulers pass GPU allocations to the operator
The developers write the resource and mode annotations in the pod YAML. Then the scheduler selects the GPUs for a workload and records its memory allocation and compute-sharing mode in per-container Pod annotations. GPU Fractioning Operator reads those annotations and configures the assigned GPUs to apply the workload’s memory limits and compute mode:
| Annotation | Meaning | 
|---|---|
| nvidia.com/container.<name>.gpu-memory.request | Guaranteed GPU memory | 
| nvidia.com/container.<name>.gpu-memory.limit | Maximum the container may grow into | 
| nvidia.com/container.<name>.gpu-compute.mode | time-slicing (default) or sm-sharing | 
| nvidia.com/container.<name>.gpus.devices | Which GPUs the container was assigned | 
Any Kubernetes scheduler that can write these annotations can enforce GPU fractions with CUDA. The scheduler still has its own job: choosing a GPU with enough free memory and never mixing compute modes on one GPU.
Using GPU Fractioning with KAI Scheduler
KAI Scheduler is the first scheduler integrated with gpu-fractioning. Starting with v0.18.0, KAI Scheduler has a GPU-sharing mode called NvFractions. KAI Scheduler picks which slice of which GPU each workload gets and writes the annotations (see Table 1, above), and gpu-fractioning enforces them on the node. 
KAI Scheduler’s other sharing modes stay available, and administrators choose one per cluster. It can be enabled when KAI is installed:
helm upgrade -i kai-scheduler oci://ghcr.io/kai-scheduler/kai-scheduler/kai-scheduler \
  -n kai-scheduler --create-namespace \
  --set global.nvFractions.set=true
This also installs gpu-fractioning as a dependency. From then on, you describe a fractional workload with Pod annotations. 
There are four important annotations that answer four questions:
1. How much memory is needed 
2. How far the workload may grow
3. How compute is shared
4. How many GPUs it spans
How much memory: The request
There are two ways to request memory:
1. As an absolute size: Use the per-container NVIDIA annotation and standard Kubernetes units:
The container name (app) is part of the key, so it always targets the right container.
2. As a portion of a GPU by using KAI Scheduler’s existing annotation:
gpu-fraction: "0.5"
How far it may grow: The limit
This ability is new in KAI Scheduler. A workload can declare a guaranteed minimum (the request) and a maximum it may burst into when memory is free. Which limit annotation you use depends on how you wrote the request:
| Request Type | Annotation | Example | 
|---|---|---|
| Absolute Size | nvidia.com/container.<c>.gpu-memory.limit | “80Gi” | 
| A Portion | kai.scheduler/container.<c>.gpu-memory.portion.limit | “0.8” | 
The limit is optional. If it is omitted, the limit equals the request and the workload is capped at exactly what it asked for. A portion limit must be greater than the gpu-fraction and less than 1.
How compute is shared: Time sharing or sm-sharing
Compute can now be divided. Call n the number of workloads sharing a GPU: either way each gets roughly 1/n of the compute, and what differs is whether they take turns or run together.
- Time-slicing is serial: Workloads take turns on the whole GPU, and when every one of them uses its full slice each gets about 1/n of the time. Time left unused by one workload is shared equally between the others. This is the default. Each workload runs in its own error domain, i.e. full error isolation.
- SM-sharing is parallel: The GPU’s streaming multiprocessors (SMs) are split between workloads and all run at once, continuously. Nothing is carved out in advance. The GPU hardware allocates and releases SMs as workloads need them. When every workload is busy the split settles at roughly 1/n; when one goes quiet its SMs go to the others, and a single active workload can use them all. In this mode, workloads share a single error domain.
Compute mode is now explicit and can be set per container:
nvidia.com/container.app.gpu-compute.mode: "sm-sharing"   # or "time-slicing"
A shared GPU runs one compute mode at a time, so KAI Scheduler never places a time-slicing workload and an sm-sharing workload on the same GPU. KAI Scheduler tracks this per GPU, not per node, so one node can host both modes on different GPUs.
How many GPUs are utilized
To get fractional capacity on several devices, add:
gpu-fraction-num-devices: "4"
The request applies to each device. A 40Gi request with four devices gets 40Gi on each of four GPUs.
Putting it together: Examples of GPU fractioning
An absolute size with room to burst on four GPUs with SM-sharing:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: inference
  labels:
    kai.scheduler/queue: default-queue
  annotations:
    nvidia.com/container.app.gpu-memory.request: "40Gi"
    nvidia.com/container.app.gpu-memory.limit: "60Gi"       # optional
    nvidia.com/container.app.gpu-compute.mode: "sm-sharing" # optional, default time-slicing
    gpu-fraction-num-devices: "4"                           # optional, default 1
spec:
  schedulerName: kai-scheduler
  containers:
    - name: app
      image: nvcr.io/nvidia/cuda:13.0.2-base-ubuntu24.04
This is an inference server split across four GPUs that needs a guaranteed 40Gi on each GPU, can use up to 60Gi when neighbors are idle, and runs alongside other workloads instead of waiting its turn. SM-sharing puts the workloads in one error domain, so use it for workloads you trust to run together.
Half a GPU that may grow to 80% on two GPUs with time slicing (default):
metadata:
  annotations:
    gpu-fraction: "0.5"
    gpu-fraction.limit: "0.8"  # optional
    nvidia.com/container.app.gpu-compute.mode: "time-slicing"    # optional
    gpu-fraction-num-devices: "2"                                # optional
spec:
  schedulerName: kai-scheduler
  containers:
    - name: app
This is an example for a development or batch job, such as notebooks or small fine-tuning runs, that need a guaranteed half of each of two GPUs and can grow to 80% when memory is free. Time-slicing gives each workload its own error domain, so a crash in one job doesn’t affect its neighbors. Running nvidia-smi in the container should show two GPUs, each with this workload’s fractional memory share.
Getting started
KAI Scheduler and the GPU Fractioning Operator are both on GitHub under the KAI Scheduler organization, with installation and configuration instructions for all three sharing mechanisms (See admin and user guides). Join the Slack channel or bi-weekly community meetings to ask your questions and contribute.
For more information about CUDA 13.4, refer to the announcement.
You can also get involved during KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA 2026 in Salt Lake City, Utah, Nov. 9-12.

articles.title: Biometria será obrigatória para usuários de celular; veja os prazos
articles.text:
A Agência Nacional de Telecomunicações (Anatel) aprovou uma norma que exige validação biométrica para cadastrar ou manter linhas de celular ativas. A medida vale para pessoas físicas e microempreendedores individuais (MEIs) e busca dificultar fraudes no registro de linhas.
A implantação será gradual, com prazos específicos para novas ativações e regularização dos cadastros existentes. Quem não cumprir as exigências poderá ter a linha suspensa a partir de 2029.
Como funcionará a validação biométrica
As operadoras deverão identificar os clientes por reconhecimento facial com prova de vida, comparando as informações obtidas com bases biométricas públicas ou de fornecedores privados. O procedimento estará disponível nas lojas físicas, nos sites e nos aplicativos oficiais das empresas.
A norma também prevê alternativas para os casos em que não for possível concluir a validação. As operadoras deverão adotar medidas de proteção de dados pessoais em conformidade com a Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados (LGPD).
A regra está descrita na Norma Técnica GT-SEG.2026.11, desenvolvida pelo Subgrupo Técnico de Enfrentamento de Fraudes e Golpes (SGT-Fraudes) e aprovada por consenso pelo Grupo Técnico de Suporte à Segurança Pública (GT-Seg). A iniciativa pretende dificultar a habilitação de linhas com informações falsas ou dados de terceiros.
Quando a biometria será exigida
A adoção do procedimento ocorrerá em etapas, conforme o tipo de serviço. Para novas ativações pré-pagas, o prazo termina em setembro de 2027. As demais operações previstas na norma terão até o fim daquele ano para se adaptar.
O cronograma estabelece as seguintes datas:
- 30 de setembro de 2027: prazo para novas ativações de linhas pré-pagas.
- 31 de dezembro de 2027: prazo para novas ativações pós-pagas, portabilidade, troca de chip e alterações cadastrais ou contratuais solicitadas pelo consumidor.
- 31 de dezembro de 2028: prazo final para regularizar os usuários que ainda não tiverem passado pela validação biométrica.
O que acontece com quem não fizer a validação
O prazo para regularizar os cadastros existentes termina no fim de 2028. A partir de janeiro de 2029, as linhas que continuarem irregulares estarão sujeitas à suspensão e, posteriormente, ao cancelamento.
As operadoras deverão seguir as regras de notificação e os prazos previstos na norma antes de aplicar essas medidas. A regulamentação também estabelece procedimentos alternativos para quem não conseguir concluir a identificação biométrica, evitando que esses casos fiquem sem uma solução prevista.
Valdir Antonelli é jornalista com especialização em marketing digital e consumo.

articles.title: Introducing the Cloudflare PHP Capture the Flag challenge
articles.text:
Introducing the Cloudflare PHP Capture the Flag challenge
Last week was one for the Internet security history books. First, eight eMudhra intermediate certificates were compromised, creating the possibility of forged certificates that could be used to impersonate servers. Then came php2shell: serious vulnerabilities in PHP, the runtime behind a large portion of the Web.
Cloudflare worked around the clock as these events unfolded to protect our customers and help protect the Internet. We shipped client updates and multiple mitigations, updated our web application firewall (WAF) with new rules to block attackers from exploiting the PHP vulnerabilities, and introduced a new feature called full transaction detection.
As always in situations like this, these new capabilities were made available on all plans, including Free.
Put our WAF to the test
Protecting systems from vulnerabilities like these is always an ongoing process, not a one-time event. The widespread adoption of AI allows attackers to discover new vectors with unprecedented speed and efficiency, so collecting real-world data to test our assumptions and strengthen defenses is essential.
That’s why today we're launching the Cloudflare PHP Capture the Flag challenge, run through our Bug Bounty program. We've put a deliberately vulnerable PHP installation behind our WAF, and we're inviting security researchers on HackerOne to try to bypass the protections and capture a flag.
How this Capture the Flag (CTF) works
We are keeping this simple. The challenge focuses on CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, the two PHP vulnerabilities behind php2shell. The target runs stock PHP 8.5.11 (with standard PHP extensions), Apache 2 (via mod_php), and an empty index.php inside a Cloudflare Container, with our default WAF protection rules for these vulnerabilities enabled in front of it. Inside the sandbox is a file called /flag.
The sandbox is reset every few minutes, including the flag file.
Your mission, should you choose to accept it: bypass the WAF protections, exploit the PHP sandbox, and recover the contents of /flag. You can use your own research tools. The challenge page has the environment details, scope, and flag verification form.
Challenge requirements
This limited-time challenge is run via Cloudflare's Bug Bounty program on HackerOne. All aspects of this challenge are subject to HackerOne terms and the Cloudflare HackerOne program rules the (“Bounty Terms”). If you find an eligible bypass, you must follow these requirements in order to claim the bounty:
- All participants must sign up for a HackerOne account and review and agree to the Bounty Terms before participating in the CTF.
- Demonstrate attacker-controlled PHP code or command execution inside the sandbox through an authorized POST request.
- Use that remote code execution (RCE) to recover the current contents of /flag, then successfully verify the flag through the CTF user interface (UI). Verify promptly before a reset; retain the successful result for later review.
- Submit a private report to Cloudflare on HackerOne. Include PHP CTF in the title and provide:
  - The endpoint, complete payload, and request sequence, preserving relevant headers, encoding, and body bytes.
  - Raw request/response captures or a readable proof of concept sufficient to reproduce the full chain.
  - An explanation of the WAF bypass, executed code or command, and how that execution recovered /flag.
  - The attempt ID, successful UI verification result, and exploit/verification UTC timestamps. Include the flag privately if needed for verification.
  - What makes the method or payload materially distinct, and related submissions you know about.
UI verification does not submit a HackerOne report or establish reporting priority. File disclosure without RCE, RCE without successful flag recovery and UI verification, local-only exploits, rediscovery of the known PHP vulnerabilities, and WAF detection differences or partial chains without the full objective are not eligible.
Awards require a materially distinct Firewall (WAF) bypass method, even for the same PHP CVE. Reports using the same Firewall-bypass mechanism are duplicates, regardless of differences in the PHP exploit, payload, RCE technique, or flag-recovery method. New flags, resets, attempt IDs, or cosmetic changes—including equivalent encodings—do not qualify as unique. Equivalent submissions are duplicates even if unfixed; only the first complete, reproducible HackerOne report is considered. Cloudflare makes final duplicate and reward decisions.
We record attempted metadata and request payloads to help analyze reports, so please use test data only. Do not send credentials, personal information, or anything else you would not want included in a research record. Read Cloudflare’s privacy notice before testing.
Testing is authorized only against the challenge hostname's WAF-protected /php/* endpoints (POST method only). Other Cloudflare services, direct access to the underlying infrastructure, the upstream PHP project, and third-party systems are out of scope. No denial of service, high-volume scanning, persistence, social engineering, or attacks on other participants. If you get a 429 or 503, back off.
In the event of any conflict between this blog post and the Bounty Terms, the Bounty Terms shall prevail.
Cloudflare reserves the right to suspend or terminate this challenge at any time. Once the competition is removed from HackerOne, it is officially terminated, so please refer to the Cloudflare HackerOne page for the most up-to-date information on whether this challenge remains open.
Not a substitute for patching
Our WAF protects you, but it is not a replacement for fixing vulnerable software. Response blocking can prevent exposed data from reaching an attacker, but it cannot undo actions already performed at the origin. If you run PHP, follow the latest PHP security advisories and apply the relevant updates.
Last week was a reminder that helping build a better Internet often takes many people—researchers, maintainers, and teams across the industry—doing difficult, urgent work together.
We hope this challenge gives everyone a useful way to join in. Head over to php-rce.cloudflare.app if you want to participate: the flag is there, and we'd like to know if you can get it.

articles.title: Re:Build, which spun out Slate Auto, raises $2.1B | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Re:Build, the Massachusetts-based manufacturing accelerator that spun out EV startup Slate Auto in 2023, has raised $2.1 billion
The company said Tuesday that it will use the funding to “expand Re:Build’s capacity to manufacture hard tech products and launch new industrial startups,” which will “ensure the most innovative products can be made in America for generations to come.” The investment was led by General Catalyst and JPMorganChase’s Strategic Investment Group. Other investors weren’t disclosed.
The funding round comes as increasing attention and capital is flowing to the idea of building up manufacturing and supply chains in the United States, especially as a hedge away from China.
“We started Re:Build because the deindustrialization of America is an economic failure and national security risk,” Re:Build co-founder Jeff Wilke said in a statement. “This capital allows Re:Build to go faster and further than would otherwise be possible, and build a great manufacturing business and a platform for American industrial leadership. The products and companies emerging from our ecosystem prove we can help restore America’s industrial might.”
General Catalyst’s CEO Hemant Taneja echoed those sentiments in a statement, saying, “General Catalyst has long believed that rebuilding American industrial capacity is one of the most important economic and national security imperatives of our time.”
Taneja added: “To compete with China, re-industrialize the U.S., and revitalize the towns and jobs that have been left behind, we need platform companies that can operate at genuine scale — and we need our innovation ecosystem to learn how to build hardware again.”
Founded in 2020, Re:Build bills itself as “America’s answer to Shenzhen,” and it has numerous ties to Amazon. It was co-founded by Wilke, who was Amazon’s former commercial CEO. Wei Gao, a longtime Amazon VP and technical adviser to Bezos, is Re:Build’s chief digital and product officer. Multiple other Re:Build executives also worked for the e-commerce giant.
Re:Build claims to have “launched hundreds of products and production systems” over its six-year existence. The company tends to operate two ways: It enters partnerships with industrial companies to “design, engineer, and manufacture products at scale across verticals including aerospace and defense,” and it incubates startups in “critical, underserved markets.”
Re:Build says its network of companies employs more than 2,100 people in the U.S. and houses more than 2.4 million square feet of manufacturing capacity.
Wilke and his co-founder Miles Arnone came up with the idea of Slate Auto in 2022 and decided to spin it out in order to help it attract more capital. The company has since gone on to raise at least $1.4 billion, including funding from Bezos’ family office, in an attempt to build an ultra-low-cost, bare-bones pickup that can be customized to a customer’s liking.

articles.title: Sculpture re-creates odd optical effects of famed Lycurgus Cup
articles.text:
Dating back to around 400 CE and made of dichroic glass, the Lycurgus Cup is notable for exhibiting different colors depending on the light. (It gets its name from the scene depicted on its surface, of King Lycurgus of Thrace.) Light it from the front, and the cup looks green; light it from behind, and the color changes to a deep red. University of Sheffield scientists have re-created the original recipe to produce a contemporary glass sculpture with the same optical effect.
The cup is considered one of the seven glass wonders of the world, one of just 40 glass cage cups that survived. Exactly why the unusual color effects of the Lycurgus Cup occurred was a mystery until 2007, when a team of scientists discovered the color shifts were due to the presence of nanoparticles in the glass—the result of Roman artisans adding finely ground gold and silver into the mix. Those nanoparticles change how the electrons in the cup vibrate in response to light so that the color one sees shifts with the observer’s vantage point.
As we reported in 2019, it’s a similar phenomenon to the one responsible for the shifting colors of 19th-century daguerreotypes due to the scattering properties of nanoparticles. The Romans added salt when they melted the silicon (sand) to make the glass, and those salts contained gold atoms. In the melting process, those atoms aggregate and produce nanoparticles, which in turn produce the colors. It’s how any stained glass is made. It’s also similar to how the precise lattice-like structure of photonic crystals produces iridescent colors in nature, like the wings of butterflies, or opals.
There is a key difference, however: The nanoparticles are embedded into the glass of the cup, whereas with a daguerreotype, they are sitting on top of a substrate, adding some reflection that does not occur with an artifact like the Lycurgus Cup. So the scattering of the particles has a strong dependence on the substrate. Also, if one coats the surface of a daguerreotype with a layer of gold, the colors shift more to the red side of the spectrum. That’s in keeping with a 19th-century trick called “gilding,” in which the photographer would apply a solution of gold salt to the image to achieve warmer tones and sharper contrast.

articles.title: Anthropic says AI may ‘pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity’ in $2 trillion IPO document — as the Chinese AI bubble bursts in a stark warning of what could happen next
articles.text:
Anthropic’s $2 trillion IPO warns of ‘self-preserving’ AI and data center backlash — as China’s AI bubble reportedly bursts in $480 billion meltdown
China is both a threat to Anthropic — and a warning about AI bubbles
- Anthropic has outlined the risks to its business in its $2 trillion IPO filing
- AI may ‘pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity,’ the firm warns
- China’s AI bubble has reportedly burst, with $480 billion wiped out
As AI firm Anthropic gears up for an enormous $2 trillion initial public offering (IPO) that could be the largest in stock market history, the company's prospectus has just warned that AI could “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.” Yet there might be a very different kind of danger on the horizon, as an early warning from China hints that its AI bubble might be about to burst.
In papers filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), Anthropic outlined some of the risks facing the company and its investors. It detailed a long list of factors that could impact its business, including not being able to access enough compute power to maintain its workloads, inaccurately forecasting how much power it needs (and thus over- or underpaying for hardware), failures in its supply chain that might leave it without adequate resources, and many more.
One of the more startling sections of the document outlines how Anthropic’s AI models could accelerate beyond anyone’s ability to evaluate and safeguard them and “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponized, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy.” Aside from the obvious danger posed to humanity, Anthropic is also apparently worried that such an outcome could “adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.”
That situation could be compounded by AI models’ “unexpected strategic or self-preserving behaviors, including attempts to resist shutdown, conceal or manipulate information", Anthropic said. AI could also "generate outputs that could be interpreted as coercive, deceptive, or manipulative, including behavior resembling blackmail or efforts to influence human decision-makers to preserve the model’s continued operation or access,” the company added.
As Anthropic notes, some of these possibilities have become reality, and it’s that sort of eventuality that has prompted another threat to its business: public backlash. “Opposition to data center development has also become more organized and coordinated across jurisdictions,” the company wrote, and that doesn’t seem to be going anywhere as negative headlines continue to proliferate.
Another eye-opening passage concerns Anthropic’s need to continually secure funding for its operations. The company has posted increasingly huge losses every year that it has operated — including $1.5 billion in 2023, $8.3 billion in 2024, $42 billion in 2025, and $80 billion in just the first six months of 2026 — and is reliant on continued venture capital inflows.
Anthropic’s IPO listing notes that “it is critical that we maintain strong revenue growth” but that “our revenue growth may not be sustainable … We expect our costs will increase over time and our losses will continue.” How sustainable it is to lose more than $80 billion in just six months on a continual basis remains to be seen.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
A warning from China
While Anthropic has been postulating on what might happen to its business — and the world — if any of these forecasts come to pass, we’re already seeing that in action in China. According to a report from Reuters, the Chinese AI bubble has already burst, with the STAR50 stock index dropping 40% in four months and taking with it $480 billion in market value.
Rather than a single catalyzing factor, the precipitous fall has been fueled by concerns about high prices, AI demand, and the impact of tariffs and bans on Chinese exports, Reuters reported. Shares in robotics firm Unitree have halved in value since listing in August, for example, while chipmaker CXMT’s stocks are down more than 25% in a month.
Other firms have seen similarly sizable drops. That includes MetaX Integrated Circuits and Moore Threads Technology, which jumped 700% and 400% on their initial listings but have now “halved in value since July.” As fund manager Wang Zhuo told Reuters, “All bubbles inevitably burst.”
With Anthropic alerting readers to the serious threats posed to humanity by future AI developments, the situation in China provides another kind of warning: that the bubble might pop before any of that comes to pass.

articles.title: SpaceX closes $40 billion debt financing for GPUs expected in the first half of 2027, Musk says — company faces up to $40 billion in additional fourth-quarter capital spending as AI infrastructure costs soar
articles.text:
SpaceX closes $40 billion debt financing for GPUs expected in the first half of 2027, Musk says — company faces up to $40 billion in additional fourth-quarter capital spending as AI infrastructure costs soar
SpaceX is preparing to spend as much as $40 billion in the fourth quarter alone.
Elon Musk has confirmed that SpaceX closed $40 billion in debt financing for graphics processing units (GPUs), with the chips expected to arrive in the first half of 2027. He disclosed the deal on X, October 25 (embedded below) while responding to investor Chamath Palihapitiya, who had warned that mounting financing pressures and delays in data center construction could leave AI computing capacity sitting idle next year.
Musk agreed with that assessment, but argued that SpaceX is better positioned than many of its competitors because it can borrow against revenue from businesses outside AI. “Pretty much,” Musk replied to Palihapitiya on X explaining that debt markets had largely shut off funding for companies without substantial revenue independent of AI data centers.
He further said SpaceX had closed $40 billion in debt for GPUs because it has investment-grade status and revenue from its Starlink satellite internet and space businesses. “That means the 200+ neoclouds are going to see guppy-level death and consolidation. Some will make it through, but not many,” Musk wrote.
It is still, however, unclear what Musk meant by “closed” or whether investors had agreed to the final debt pricing. The disclosure comes as SpaceX prepares for another enormous spending period. CFO Bret Johnsen had stated during SpaceX’s Q3 2026 earnings call that the company expects capital expenditure of $35 billion to $40 billion in Q4 “because of the additional capacity coming online this quarter.”
Musk also clarified that the borrowing was primarily callable debt for GPU purchases expected to arrive in the first and second quarters of 2027. “This is primarily callable debt for GPU purchases that will arrive in Q1 and Q2. Not a major factor this quarter,” Musk wrote.
Earlier this month, it emerged SpaceX had proposed a $40 billion debt package for Nvidia hardware, estimating that the proposed funding could cover roughly 360,000 Rubin GPUs across 5,000 Nvidia NVL72 racks. The proposed package reportedly included $10 billion in bank loans and $30 billion in investment-grade debt. Musk has now said the financing has closed, but has not confirmed the specific GPU models or quantities covered by the deal.
The spending fits into Musk’s broader push to expand AI computing capacity. In August, xAI outlined plans to increase its data center capacity sevenfold by 2027, targeting 10 gigawatts. In September, the publication also reported that SpaceXAI planned to add another 660,000 Nvidia GPUs during 2026, potentially bringing its total to around 1.44 million if the planned deployments proceed.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
And GPUs are only part of the bill. Data centers need power, cooling, networking equipment, and physical infrastructure before those accelerators can do useful work, which underscores SpaceX’s latest move.
SpaceX, meanwhile, has begun selling access to its own infrastructure. In May, Anthropic secured access to SpaceX’s Colossus 1 supercomputer, which includes more than 220,000 Nvidia GPUs and over 300 megawatts of computing capacity. Later in June, SpaceX struck a separate deal with Google, which agreed to pay $920 million per month for access to approximately 110,000 Nvidia GPUs and related hardware, with payments scheduled to run from October 2026 through June 2029.

articles.title: Industrial Intelligence: The next growth opportunity for manufacturing
articles.text:
Sponsored
Industrial Intelligence: The next growth opportunity for manufacturing
Physical AI brings business intelligence to physical processes, turning knowledge into decisions and decisions into action.
Provided byMicrosoft
Every manufacturer has its own industrial intelligence. Some is documented, and some resides in the knowledge of experienced workers.
Consider an experienced operator preparing to restart a line after a changeover. The machine settings matter, but so does knowing how a particular material behaves, what happened during the previous shift, and when an apparently minor variation deserves a closer look. A procedure can describe the sequence, but successful execution depends on the judgment that comes from experience and the organization’s accumulated know-how.
That combination is industrial intelligence: a manufacturer’s accumulated know-how, operating practices, production data, and understanding of its own business.
The opportunity now is to make more of that intelligence available wherever decisions are made, then connect it to the physical world of manufacturing. The strategic destination is not more agents, but rather to turn the existing business intelligence into an engine for profitable growth.
Individual knowledge can be translated into organizational advantage
Expertise has limited reach when it stays with one person, inside one system, or within one plant. Leaders now must determine how to extend that reach without stripping away the context that makes the knowledge useful.
For example, an engineer evaluating a process change needs more than a production record. They need to understand the circumstances behind it: the equipment configuration, the quality requirements, and the trade-offs an operator made. Connecting those elements can help people apply experience beyond the place where it originated.
When individual knowledge becomes widely accessible, innovation can spread to the maintenance workshop, the planning office, the engineering team, and the production floor. More people can contribute because more people can work with what the organization knows.
But access to knowledge is only part of the opportunity. Manufacturing ultimately is physical, and it depends on materials, machines, and products.
When intelligence participates in action
Physical AI describes systems that can perceive conditions, reason about them, and take action within the physical world. By connecting machines and processes, manufacturers get a clearer view of what is happening on the factory floor. Agents can then reason on top of that information to identify patterns, predict problems, and determine the best course of action. Physical AI brings business intelligence into the physical process, allowing machines and systems to respond to changing conditions.
Consider a robotic-handling operation encountering variation in the parts arriving at its station. Vision can help the system assess a part’s position. A model informed by the material and task can help determine an appropriate movement. Connected controls can then execute an adjustment within validated limits. The value is not merely seeing the variation; it is responding appropriately.
The same principle applies to quality operations. When Toyota Industries connected previously fragmented paint shop data, engineering and operations teams were given the context needed to understand defect drivers. The company reports that analysis cycles fell from five days to under four hours, while its pilot reduced relevant paint defects by about 25%. The breakthrough was not simply identifying another signal; it was helping people understand why defects were occurring and respond before the outcome was locked in.
This is the type of situation where industrial intelligence has become essential. Data may reveal what is happening, but industrial intelligence provides the context for what should happen, which constraints cannot be breached, and when uncertainty requires human judgment.
Simulation offers a way to examine proposed actions before applying them to equipment. Manufacturers can explore how a change might affect a process in a digital environment. That does not remove the need for physical validation, but it creates room to learn without treating the production line as the first experiment.
Responsible deployment, therefore, begins with operational discipline. Leaders need to establish clear authority or what systems may change, reliable connections to equipment, defined safety boundaries, and a record of decisions and actions. People must be able to recognize uncertainty, intervene, and bring equipment to a safe state. Trust rests on those practical arrangements, not on confidence in a model alone.
More capable machines, more capable people
Manufacturing has long combined human ingenuity with increasingly capable tools. Physical AI extends that relationship. Intelligent equipment can take on suitable repetitive or physically demanding tasks, while agent-assisted operations can help people navigate information-intensive decisions and changing conditions.
The aim is not to make machines smarter; it is to see what people can build when knowledge can travel, intelligence can act, and ambition has more room to become reality.
Rockwell Automation illustrates the point. At its Singapore plant, technicians use a maintenance copilot that combines manufacturing data, machine manuals, and knowledge captured from experienced workers. This system has reduced the time required for new workers to learn how to troubleshoot hundreds of machines from nine months to three. An engineer could explore more process alternatives before committing to a change. An operator could help improve the system’s response rather than repeatedly managing the same exception.
This type of progress requires investment in equipment but also in people: training, time to learn, and playing a meaningful role in shaping how systems work. Machines become more capable so people can become more capable.
Industrial Intelligence is the answer to sustainable growth
Industrial intelligence connects what a manufacturer knows: the experience of its people, the signals from its operations, and the lessons accumulated over time. Physical AI gives that intelligence a way to act in the physical world, turning knowledge into decisions and decisions into action.
The next challenge for industry is not simply to produce more, but to grow without adding complexity at the same rate. Intelligence can help manufacturers turn experience into scalable capability—improving productivity, accelerating innovation, expanding capacity, and enabling people to solve problems that were previously difficult to tackle.
The next frontier of industry is not smarter machines or more automated factories; it is businesses that can continuously learn, adapt, and act. The opportunity is to turn the intelligence embedded in every operation into a compounding advantage for growth.
