articles.title: Mira el asombroso nuevo tráiler de 'Dune 3', el épico final de la saga
articles.text:
Por fin, el tráiler final de Dune 3 acaba de ver la luz. El esperado desenlace de la épica saga de ciencia ficción de Denis Villeneuve llegará a los cines cinco años después de su primera entrega. Será un filme que adapte la historia del segundo libro de la franquicia, El Mesías de Dune. Y por lo que podemos ver en el avance, va a volver a ser una película grandiosa y brutal.
El tráiler de Dune 3 nos lleva de vuelta a Arrakis. Pero, esta vez, su historia se ambienta 17 años después de los eventos ocurridos Dune 1 y 2. Ahora, Paul Atreides deberá lidiar con las consecuencias de su lucha por la libertad de los Fremen tras ascender como Emperador Muad’Dib al derrotar a los Harkonnen y al anterior Emperador Shaddam IV Corrino.
Paul se ha convertido, por tanto, en un emperador despiadado y ambicioso que lidera a sus ejércitos en campañas de conquista. De esta forma, Dune 3 indagará ese círculo de violencia del que el protagonista parece incapaz de escapar. La guerra se antoja inevitable en su camino, marcado por oscuras traiciones y luchas de poder.
Mira el tráiler final de Dune 3
Obsesionado por visiones del colapso Imperialista y la reaparición de su antiguo amor perdido, en el tráiler de Dune 3 Paul es absorbido por una conspiración radical, con Chani en el centro del misterio. Ante el fragor de la rebelión y la aproximación de los enemigos, Paul debe enfrentarse al verdadero precio del poder y el destino de aquellos a los que más quiere.
El reparto de Dune 3 lo conforman Timothée Chalamet como Paul Atreides, Zendaya como Chani, Javier Bardem como Stilgar, Rebecca Ferguson como Lady Jessica y Florence Pugh como la emperatriz Irulan. También está Jason Momoa, que regresa como un clon de Hayt tras la primera película. Y los nuevos fichajes, Robert Pattinson como Scytale, Anya Taylor-Joy como Alia Atreides e Isaach De Bankolé como Farok.
La película será la última de la saga. O, al menos, la última que dirigirá Denis Villeneuve, que ya ha asegurado que el resto de libros no le interesan tanto. En definitiva, Dune 3, que se estrena en cines el 18 de diciembre, será un épico cierre a una de las mayores trilogías del cine de ciencia ficción de este siglo.

articles.title: Voters in Texas agree: They hate data centers
articles.text:
Ask Texas NAACP president Gary Bledsoe what it’s been like to see data center developers descend upon Austin and its surrounding suburbs and he can rattle off project after project facing opposition from locals.
Voters in Texas agree: They hate data centers
Some are even mad enough to vote for Democrats.
Voters in Texas agree: They hate data centers
Some are even mad enough to vote for Democrats.
There’s the fight in Taylor over plans to build a data center at a site that’s supposed to be a park. Temple, around 40 miles away, is another sore spot, Bledsoe says. The mayor and City Council members there face recall attempts over data center developments. And some 30 miles outside of Austin, San Marcos became the first city in all of Texas to ban data centers.
Nowhere in the world are data centers growing more explosively than in Texas. With the midterm elections looming, the data center fight “is the issue in Texas,” says Bledsoe. The state’s NAACP recently joined dozens of other groups across the political spectrum to form a coalition to stop — or at least stall — data center construction. Their grievances are just as diverse as their membership: concerns about how much water the industry consumes in a state as dry as Texas, qualms about tax subsidies, and objections to new gas plants and wind farms built to meet rising electricity demand. Together, Bledsoe estimates the coalition — named We the People Texas — represents as many as 1 million voters across the state.
If there’s one thing a broad range of voters can agree on this election season, it’s that they hate data centers and are unhappy with the status quo. A majority of Texans — 57 percent — oppose the construction of data centers, an August poll found. That included 43 percent of Republicans, 75 percent of Democrats, and 54 percent of independents.
“We have almost nothing in common in so many other ways. And yet you get us in the room with this issue, and it’s like a wall”
After initially proclaiming his state the “epicenter of AI development,” Texas Gov. Greg Abbott is now fighting for reelection against underdog Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who is seen as having a rare shot at taking a reliably red state. The state’s high-profile Senate race is no less of a nail-biter, with Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton running neck and neck against Democrat James Talarico. In each race, candidates have to win over voters who think data centers are coming for their water, land, and livelihoods. Republican and Democratic hopefuls alike are trying to distance themselves from an industry that’s taken deep root in the state — and so far, voters aren’t buying it.
“You’re talking about Democrats, libertarians, independents, Republicans, all in one fight … we have almost nothing in common in so many other ways. And yet you get us in the room with this issue, and it’s like a wall … fighting one big enemy,” says Jet Parker, who cofounded a group called Save Rural Texas that is now part of the We the People Texas coalition.
Save Rural Texas came together this year after a local county commissioners’ meeting about plans to build a new data center in the Texoma area that borders Oklahoma. Residents, including Parker, successfully delayed that project. That victory led Parker, a corporate coach and speaker, to write up a handbook for other communities trying to block data center projects, and she now spends much of her time traveling around the state to train grassroots groups.
She’s got a warning for Republicans: If they keep backing data centers, they’ll lose Texas. “You just pissed off a lot of people in rural Texas who are supposed to carry you across the [finish] line,” Parker says.
Abbott is in particularly hot water. “You brung it, so you dance with it. That’s Texas talk, you know,” Parker says. “That’s what Abbott’s done, but we’re the ones having to dance with it … we didn’t want to be in the dance at all.”
For years, however, Texas has taken among the most welcoming stances toward data centers in the country. The state passed a sales and use tax exemption for data centers in 2013 under former Gov. Rick Perry. In 2015, Abbott expanded the exemption to include hyperscale data centers, which can span millions of square feet and house tens of thousands of GPUs. As a result, qualifying data center developers don’t have to pay state taxes on equipment and electricity for up to 20 years. That essentially rolled out the red carpet for companies that need abundant electricity to power energy-hungry data centers.
Since then data centers have had a massive growth spurt in order to support new generative AI models — and that’s costing the state. The tax exemption was initially expected to cost taxpayers $14.6 million in 2014 and 2015. But in 2025, state officials estimated that the tax break would lead to $3.2 billion in lost sales tax revenue over two years.
“You brung it, so you dance with it.”
The state’s energy woes go further than that. Electricity bills have grown by 35.4 percent on average over the past five years as demand rises and utilities build expensive new infrastructure to meet that demand. Bledsoe is concerned about air pollution for communities around new gas plants. Data center electricity demand could erase decades of air quality gains in Texas, one recent study found. Parker, meanwhile, can’t stand solar and wind farms built near farmland. Neither wants to see new transmission lines snaking through their communities.
Data centers can also put pressure on already stressed water supplies, especially in a drought-prone state like Texas. While they can reuse water used on-site to cool servers, the larger part of data centers’ water footprint comes from electricity use. Data center proposals have driven a surge of gas and nuclear power projects, both of which need a lot of water for their own cooling systems.
Data center electricity demand could increase nearly tenfold by 2030, the state’s largest grid operator estimates. Meanwhile, data centers in Texas consumed about 25 billion gallons of water last year, around 0.4 percent of total water use, according to the Houston Advanced Research Center (HARC). By 2030, that figure could grow to up to 2.7 percent of the state’s total annual water use, HARC estimates. And water consumption can be much higher when zooming into certain communities. Another study by the University of Texas at Austin estimated that data center water use statewide could rise to as high as 9 percent by 2040.
Virginia has historically been the state with the most data centers, but it’s running out of space. Virginia still beats Texas 287 to 170 when it comes to the number of planned data center projects as of April, according to Pew Research. But as data centers get bigger, they’re moving out of cities and into rural areas — particularly in Texas. Data center capacity is typically measured by how much power it draws, and in this measure, Texas already takes the crown with 26GW of existing and under-construction capacity compared to 13GW in Virginia.
Facing backlash to data centers, Abbott has changed his tune. In June, he directed the state Public Utility Commission to require that data center operators cover the costs of new infrastructure built to serve them. Since then, he has also announced statewide moratoriums on permits for data center projects pending audits on their electricity and water use. He’s also said that he would support a repeal of the sales tax exemption for data centers and greater oversight of data centers’ water and electricity use.
Even so, he’s reportedly taken millions in campaign contributions from data center interests, and We the People Texas coalition members are not convinced he’s turned the page. “Is he doing enough? Absolutely not,” Parker says.
The NAACP sent a letter to Abbott’s office last month criticizing his moratoriums for not going far enough because the state is only auditing projects that connect to the power grid. However, more so than any other state, Texas has data centers building their own power supply on-site, without needing to connect to the grid. Bledsoe’s concerned that these private energy projects will be subject to less regulatory scrutiny, while also harming air quality in nearby neighborhoods. Projects that already have permits are still being built. And an October investigation by advocacy group Public Citizen and FracTracker found public records indicating that state agencies are still processing permits for data centers, although Abbott’s office denies that they have issued any approvals since he directed them to pause permitting. To Bledsoe and other coalition members, he says, the temporary moratorium looks like “an attempt to run out the clock before the election.”
Data center hyperscalers including AWS, Microsoft, Google, Meta, and others have formed their own trade group called the Data Center Coalition (DCC). For what it’s worth, DCC isn’t endorsing any candidates. But in an interview with The Verge, Jess Heck, the group’s director of Texas government affairs, says, “It’s very clear that our members share the same goals as Gov. Abbott and the legislature. We want to be true partners, good neighbors in every Texas community where we operate.” Heck didn’t confirm whether any of its members are providing any campaign support for Abbott.
“An attempt to run out the clock before the election”
Eduardo Leal, press secretary for Abbott’s campaign, said in an email to The Verge that “Under [Abbott’s] standards, data centers must pay for their own electric infrastructure, add power instead of only adding demand, reuse their own water, reduce the cost of electricity for Texans, not disrupt residential neighborhoods, and eliminate reliance on outdated taxpayer-funded incentives.”
Abbott signed a state Senate bill into law last year that directs the Public Utility Commission of Texas to reassess how it allocates transmission costs in order to keep rates from rising disproportionately for residential customers. And this June, he proposed more measures to force companies to cover the costs of infrastructure upgrades needed to serve their data centers.
Abbott’s biggest competitor, state Rep. Gina Hinojosa, has eked out a narrow lead recently in some polls after strengthening her language against data centers — calling for a moratorium on development until the state legislature passes more protections. “I think her campaign has made a ton of inroads into moderate Republican communities because of her stance on data centers,” says Anthony Elmo, public education funding defender for Good Jobs First, which recently cofounded another coalition pushing for data center reforms in Texas alongside other advocacy groups.
Hinojosa has skyrocketed from a relatively obscure local official to a serious contender for the governor’s seat, largely on a populist message that caters to residents’ frustration with Big Tech companies grabbing land for data centers. Even so, she might not be convincing enough for conservative rural voters.
Candidates from both sides of the aisle were pretty soft on data centers up until the party conventions earlier this year, says Miriam Cobb, who cofounded the Texas Coalition Against Data Centers earlier this year (which is also part of We the People Texas). Texans can see the political posturing from Hinojosa, too, she says. One of Hinojosa’s major donors has been the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers, which recently formed an “American Infrastructure Alliance” with OpenAI and data center developers.
“[Voters] know she wasn’t against it from a place of understanding or sincerity, it’s something she knows she has to say now,” Cobb tells The Verge, adding that she’ll be writing in an independent candidate come Election Day. Even with many conservatives — some of them now claiming to be single-issue voters on data centers — skeptical of both parties’ candidates, Cobb still expects Republicans to lose seats.
Paxton, the Republican candidate for Senate, is attempting to atone for his previous support of data centers. He voted for the sales tax exemptions as a state senator in 2013, although he now says he’d support a repeal. In September, he announced an investigation into hundreds of data centers’ water use. Paxton also launched an investigation into the case in Taylor over whether it’s legal for land deeded for parkland to be developed into a data center. And he’s aligned himself with Abbott’s proposals to impose stronger light and noise restrictions on data centers, limit construction in rural areas, and push developers to cover the costs of new energy infrastructure. But he also reportedly received hundreds of thousands of dollars in campaign funding this year from data center interests.
“Trump keeps saying, you know, ‘Let them in, let them in, let them in’”
Talarico, meanwhile, has a similar plan to stop data centers “from jacking up our utility bills.” But he also claims to want to “empower local communities to decide whether they want a data center in their town,” a jab at Republicans including Paxton who have either stayed mum on whether counties should be allowed to make permitting decisions on data centers rather than the state or have actively curtailed their ability to do so. Abbott signed the so-called “Death Star” bill into law in 2023 barring counties and municipalities from crafting regulations that contradict state law. Some Republicans have cited the Death Star law in legal challenges to local moratoriums on data centers.
While the Senate race between Talarico and Paxton is in the national spotlight over the prospect of a Democrat flipping the seat, it’s probably less important for Texans concerned most about data centers, advocates tell The Verge. The race is too politically polarized to flip voters on the single issue, Cobb says, and neither candidate has given a very convincing position on how to rein in data centers anyway. Neither campaign responded to press inquiries from The Verge.
Working at the federal level, the best thing the senator-elect could do would be to push back against President Donald Trump’s data center agenda and ensure Texas can moderate data center development without interference, she says.
“We want assurances that you’re gonna let us deal with it instead of what’s been happening, where Trump keeps saying, you know, ‘Let them in, let them in, let them in,’” Cobb tells The Verge.
Cobb still sees construction traffic clogging two-lane rural roads leading to data center projects that have avoided Abbott’s partial moratorium. Residents are worried about the traffic jams blocking emergency vehicles, especially when fire weather kicks up. In some areas, Texans have seen property values drop, she adds. Farmers are giving up land that their families have tended to for generations. In other neighborhoods, an influx of new workers arriving for the data center “gold rush” is exacerbating housing shortages and making rent more unaffordable for locals. In either case, data center opposition coalition members say they’re worried about a loss of culture.
“It’s not for nothing,” Cobb says. “They have real community … and now they’re losing it.”

articles.title: Women-led companies dominate top ranks of 2026 Deloitte Fast 50 | BetaKit
articles.text:
For the first time, half of Canada’s 10 fastest-growing companies are led by women, according to the 2026 Deloitte Technology Fast 50.
The annual list recognizes Canada’s fastest-growing technology companies across three categories based on their revenue growth percentage over the past three or four years, depending on the category.
The top of the flagship list featured more women-led companies than usual this year, including Toronto-based rewards platform Chexy, which placed second with a four-year revenue growth rate of 23,183 percent. Other women-led companies at the top of the list include legaltech company BorderPass, led by co-CEO Sally Daub, in third place; cleantech software WeavAir, led by CEO Natalia Mykhaylova, in fourth; AI automation platform SimplyAsk.ai, led by CEO Shuli Gortler, in fifth; and online therapy provider Total Life, led by CEO Neelam Brar, in sixth place.
Women-led companies featured more prominently than usual on this year’s list, taking spots two through six.
In a statement, Chexy CEO Liza Akhvledziani-Carew said the company has proved its rent-to-rewards model, and that the growth rate indicates it’s “onto something much bigger.” Earlier this year, the company raised a $14-million Series A round led by Khosla Ventures, one of Silicon Valley’s most reputable venture firms, to help its users earn credit card rewards on more everyday expenses.
The list’s top spot went to Toronto-based Finni Health, which sported a four-year revenue growth rate of 46,754 percent. The Y Combinator alum, founded by Canadian Bucky Khan, provides a platform for autism care providers in the United States to start, run, and grow their practices.
The average revenue growth rate of this year’s Fast 50 was 3,079 percent, a jump from last year’s average growth of 2,623 percent. Other companies on the 2026 Fast 50 include, in descending order, Toronto-based legaltech Spellbook, Québec City-based pipeline inspector Flyscan, Montréal-based digital lender Nesto, and Vancouver-based private stock marketplace Clarity (formerly known as Hiive).
In addition to the Fast 50, Deloitte also recognized 15 Canadian companies on its Enterprise—Industry Leaders ranking and another 17 on its Companies to Watch list, which showcases companies with the potential to be future Fast 50 program winners.
Richmond, BC-based last-mile delivery company UniUni topped this year’s industry leaders list, sporting a 2,143-percent four-year revenue increase. While its reported revenue increase vastly exceeded others below it on the list, UniUni has faced trouble recently. The company’s attempt to go public through a special purpose acquisition company (SPAC) fell through after the SPAC terminated the deal, citing UniUni’s deteriorating business and financial performance.
RELATED: Neo Financial completes first-ever hat trick of Deloitte Technology Fast 50 rankings
Other companies on the Enterprise—Industry Leaders list include Toronto-based FinTech firm Koho, which placed second with a 580-percent four-year revenue increase, Calgary-based PurposeMed (which is set to be acquired by Grindr) in seventh, and Ottawa-based surveillance tech firm Solink in tenth.
Ottawa-based Turbopuffer, which provides a fast data search engine, decisively took the top spot on the Companies to Watch list with a 65,443-percent growth rate, confirming founder Simon Hørup Eskildsen’s fears that he runs Canada’s fastest-growing company. In a distant second was another Ottawa-based company, defence tech firm Tactiql, with a 4,395-percent growth rate.
Companies on the flagship Fast 50 list are automatically eligible for the broader North American Technology Fast 500, which will be released on November 18. Deloitte says 80 Canadian companies made that list this year, down from 114 last year.
Feature image courtesy Chexy.

articles.title: Alibaba obtient gain de cause contre une décision du Pentagone : une petite victoire dans une longue affaire
articles.text:
Entre la Chine et les États-Unis, c'est une guerre commerciale sans fil qui s'opère depuis des années. Le Pentagone, armée américaine, avait indiqué que les entreprises du secteur de la défense avaient interdiction de travailler avec l'IA chinoise, mais un juge opère un retournement de situation.
Un juge fédéral américain a temporairement bloqué une règle du Pentagone qui menaçait de priver certaines entreprises de leurs contrats de défense si elles employaient des lobbyistes également au service d'Alibaba. Le tribunal californien a accordé lundi la demande d'injonction formulée par Alibaba, dans l'attente de l'issue de son recours juridique plus large contre le ministère américain de la Défense.
Un litige qui date de plusieurs mois
L'affaire remonte à juin dernier, lorsque le Pentagone a inscrit Alibaba sur une liste d'entreprises qu'il considère comme apportant un soutien à l'armée chinoise. Cette décision est le fruit de décisions globales de durcissement des restrictions américaines visant les technologies chinoises. Le département du Trésor a par ailleurs mis en place des limitations concernant les investissements américains dans l'intelligence artificielle et les biotechnologies chinoises.
L'inscription sur cette liste du Pentagone ne déclenche pas de sanctions formelles. Cependant, elle limite les partenariats du ministère de la Défense américain avec les entreprises qui exploiteraient des solutions du géant chinois. À partir de 2027, ces restrictions devraient également s'appliquer aux achats de leurs produits effectués via des fournisseurs tiers.
Une loi distincte sur les lobbyistes
Une loi américaine séparée interdit aux prestataires du Pentagone d'employer des lobbyistes qui représentent également des entreprises figurant sur cette liste. Ainsi, les cabinets partageant des lobbyistes avec Alibaba feraient face au risque de perdre leurs contrats avec le ministère de la Défense.
Après l'inscription d'Alibaba sur la liste en juin, l'entreprise aurait mis fin aux missions de plusieurs dizaines de ses lobbyistes à Washington.
Une décision judiciaire renverse une partie des sanctions
La décision rendue lundi empêche temporairement le gouvernement d'appliquer la restriction relative aux lobbyistes à l'encontre d'Alibaba. Elle ne retire en revanche pas l'entreprise de la liste du Pentagone, cette question faisant l'objet d'un volet distinct de la procédure judiciaire engagée par l'entreprise.
Alibaba avait saisi la justice américaine en juin, estimant que son inscription sur cette liste n'avait « aucun fondement factuel ou juridique ». L'entreprise affirme servir des consommateurs, des entreprises de livraison et des clients professionnels, et dément bien évidemment tout lien avec l'armée chinoise.
Pour l'heure, ni Alibaba ni le département de la Défense n'ont commenté cette décision.
Un contentieux qui dépasse Alibaba
La contestation envers la liste du Pentagone dépasse la seule cause d'Alibaba. Le laboratoire pharmaceutique chinois WuXi AppTec avait obtenu en août une décision de justice lui permettant de ne pas y figurer.
En septembre, deux filiales du constructeur automobile BYD ont également engagé une action en justice contre la restriction sur les lobbyistes, estimant qu'elle porte atteinte à leur liberté d'expression. Le fabricant de drones DJI conteste par ailleurs son inscription sur cette liste, après qu'une cour d'appel a ordonné au gouvernement de revoir sa décision.
Source : TheNextWeb

articles.title: The Huntress Tragic Quadrant: Ranking Threats Hitting Businesses Hardest
articles.text:
Cyber headlines often focus on the flashy attacks, but the ones that actually cause OH $#!T moments are the tactics that abuse the tools and workflows you already trust. If you run a small or mid-sized organization, whether you handle IT yourself or outsource it, it’s a constant race to keep up with attackers and their evolving tactics.
The bottom line is that you need to know which attacks are landing in environments like yours, and how to prioritize your defenses against them.
The Tragic Quadrant at a Glance
That’s why Huntress created the Tragic Quadrant, a ranked list of the cyber tactics putting businesses at risk, built to show you where to focus regardless of what’s trending week to week.
Fix These Threats First: The OH $#!T Corner
Each of these tactics hides inside something your team uses every day, like a remote access tool or a Microsoft 365 login.
RMM Abuse Is Steady and Holding
Remote monitoring and management (RMM) tools are a staple for IT teams, which is exactly why attackers abuse them. One rogue RMM install gives an attacker persistent access that looks like ordinary admin work.
In Q1 2026, 45% of endpoint-related incidents Huntress investigated involved RMM abuse. Attackers are also using AI to build convincing fake document shares and service agreement lures that trick users into installing unwanted RMMs.
Mailbox Manipulation Is an Entry Point to BEC
So far in 2026, 24.6% of Identity Threat Detection and Response (ITDR) signals point to mailbox manipulation and persistence. With mailbox access, an attacker can change inbox rules and send vendor replies to folders nobody is watching, like RSS Feeds or Archive.
From there, they can tweak invoice details and redirect payments to their own accounts, all without any malware for detection tools to flag.
Account Takeover That Sidesteps MFA
Adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) attacks made up 18.9% of all identity-based threats Huntress tracked in 2025. The attacker sits between the victim and the real Microsoft 365 login page, steals the session token in transit, and forwards everything along so nothing looks off to the user.
As long as that session is valid, the attacker can access the account without a password or a fresh MFA prompt.
If you were hit with ransomware, what would you do?
Your files are encrypted, your operations are down, an attacker has named their price, and they're waiting for you to respond. Do you pay? Do you negotiate? Do you even engage at all?
Choose your next move in a simulated ransomware incident, built from tactics Huntress has seen used against real businesses. You'll see how ransomware operators behave when they think they're in control, and what steps you can take for catching an attack before it becomes a negotiation.
Try the Simulator →
Your Next Stop: The Other Three Corners
Once you’ve covered the top-right tactics, the others still deserve a plan. Each one is evolving fast, potentially moving toward the OH $#!T corner at any time.
Device Code Phishing Turns Low-Key Deadly
Device code phishing is less common, but it rides on Microsoft’s real device code login flow, so “check the URL” advice doesn’t help. A convincing prompt nudges someone to enter a short code on a genuine Microsoft page, and the attacker walks away with an access token that can outlive a password reset.
In one 16-day window, a phishing-as-a-service (PhaaS) kit called EvilTokens hit 344 organizations across five countries. Defenders should be suspicious of unusual device code prompts and odd token activity.
ClickFix Is a Daily Intrusion Pest
ClickFix leans on the copy-paste muscle memory people use to get past everyday friction. A fake CAPTCHA or “verification failed” prompt tricks someone into pasting a malicious command into their terminal. The paste itself triggers the malicious code, so no exploit chain is involved, and it can lead to infostealer malware or ransomware.
ClickFix accounts for about 2.2% of Managed Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) detection signals so far in 2026, but nearly 99% of those detections are high severity.
AI Platform Abuse Is Overhyped, for Now
This one sits in the overhyped corner because it’s still an emerging pattern. Attackers hide malicious content behind real AI tools and workflows people trust.
A fake “desktop client” or “productivity helper” might live inside a shared conversation or a hosted artifact on a trusted AI domain like Claude or ChatGPT, which makes it tricky to tell what’s malicious.
In one case, FakeAgent used a malicious Claude Artifact on the real claude.ai domain to send people looking for Claude Desktop to SectopRAT, reaching 29 organizations in two days.
Make the Tragic Quadrant Your Starting Point
The Tragic Quadrant helps you pick what to fix first when everything feels urgent.
Start in the top right corner and ask a few simple questions: Which remote tools are approved, and how do we catch mailbox rule changes and odd session behavior before they turn into something worse?

articles.title: iPhone 18e : sur cette fonctionnalité très attendue, Apple ne ferait aucun effort
articles.text:
Partagées par le leaker souvent bien informé Digital Chat Station sur le réseau social chinois Weibo, de nouvelles informations viennent détailler ce à quoi pourrait ressembler la fiche technique de l’iPhone 18e. Attendu pour le premier trimestre 2027, comme l’iPhone 17e avant lui, le smartphone Apple le plus abordable fait déjà beaucoup parler pour ses choix conservateurs qui auraient de quoi faire grincer des dents.
Un écran et un appareil photo très (trop ?) familiers pour l’iPhone 18e
L’iPhone 18e s’appuierait ainsi sur une dalle OLED LTPS de 6,12 pouces qui resterait bloquée à un taux de rafraîchissement de 60 Hz, comme le nouvel iPad mini. Un choix plus que discutable à l’heure où les smartphones Android d’entrée de gamme ou de milieu de gamme profitent de 90 Hz ou 120 Hz depuis des années.
Côté photo, n’attendez pas non plus de miracle. On s’attend en effet au retour de l’unique capteur de 48 Mpx, ce qui viendrait doucher les espoirs de ceux qui rêvent d’un ultra grand-angle ou d’un téléobjectif que l’on trouve couramment chez la concurrence dans cette tranche de prix.
Toujours plus de puissance, mais pas que
S’il y a bien un domaine dans lequel Apple n’est pas avare, c’est bien celui des performances. La marque à la pomme préparerait en effet quelques évolutions notables pour son iPhone 18e, à commencer par une puce Apple A20 gravée en 2 nm, épaulée par 9 Go de RAM, toujours selon les rumeurs. On parle également d’une caméra selfie qui passerait à 24 mégapixels, contre 12 mégapixels sur l’iPhone 17e.
Découvrez : Les meilleurs smartphones à moins de 800 euros en 2026
Apple a toujours été très conservateur (pour ne pas dire radin) sur les évolutions matérielles de ses smartphones d’entrée de gamme au fil des années. Ajoutez à cela une crise des composants qui oblige même certains concurrents comme Samsung à prendre des décisions radicales, et vous avez un cocktail peu reluisant pour ceux qui espéraient des évolutions notables pour l’iPhone 18e, que l’on attend au premier trimestre 2027.

articles.title: Disruptive raises $10B fund to make big bets on at least 10 companies | TechCrunch
articles.text:
The Dallas-based investment firm Disruptive, whose past bets include Palantir, Airbnb, and Spotify, announced a $10 billion fund to back at least 10 late-stage companies, with checks of up to $1 billion, it said Tuesday.
It’s one of the biggest fundraises of the year so far, aiming to back (what else?!) the capital-intensive fields of AI and defense. The Wall Street Journal first reported earlier this month that the firm was seeking to raise the fund and by then had already secured at least $7.5 billion in capital commitments.
The firm was founded in 2012 by Alex Davis, grandson of billionaire oil magnate Marvin Davis.
This is technically the firm’s first blind-pool fund, meaning investors commit money without knowing which companies it will back. Until now, the firm raised money through deal-by-deal special purpose vehicles. Disruptive has nonetheless made headlines in recent years for pouring money into companies like chip startup Groq and the AI voice-generation startup ElevenLabs. Bloomberg reported that the firm told LPs it has returned more than $6 billion on the roughly $1.9 billion it has put into startups.
According to the Dallas Business Journal, the new vehicle is the largest venture fund raised in Texas history.

articles.title: Loon clears key regulatory hurdle to offer Canadian dollar-backed stablecoin | BetaKit
articles.text:
Calgary-based FinTech startup Loon has secured the green light from domestic securities regulators to issue its Canadian dollar-backed CADC stablecoin in Canada.
Loon announced on Tuesday that its newly established CADC Reserve Trust has received receipt for its final prospectus from the Ontario Securities Commission (OSC), giving it exemptive relief to offer the blockchain-based token. Paytrie, the Calgary company that originally created CADC—and from which Loon spun out of last year—has also been granted exemptive relief to distribute CADC.
Though Loon still has more work to do to ensure compliance, including migrating legacy CADC over to this new contract, this marks the completion of one of the key and final regulatory steps required for Loon to issue CADC, and for Paytrie to deliver it, Paytrie co-founder and Loon co-founder and CEO Kevin Zhang told BetaKit in an interview. He claimed that the two firms have carved out a new framework around stablecoin distribution in the process.
“If you’re a new stablecoin company in Canada and you wanted to issue a Canadian dollar stablecoin, you should be doing it exactly the same way we just did it.”
Kevin Zhang, Loon
“If you’re a new stablecoin company in Canada and you wanted to issue a Canadian dollar stablecoin, you should be doing it exactly the same way we just did it, because this will allow Canadians full access the same way that you expect a stablecoin to work, like USDC,” he said.
The value of stablecoins is pegged to another reserve asset beyond crypto. In the case of fiat-backed stablecoins, that asset is typically a currency like the US dollar. Stablecoins are usually, though not always, less volatile than other digital currencies. For each CADC token purchased, $1 CAD will be deposited into a reserve trust account with ATB Financial.
Loon is one of several Canadian firms that have been working to deliver a regulated, CAD-backed stablecoin to alleviate friction for domestic users and reduce the value exported by using US dollar-backed alternatives. Toronto-based Stablecorp secured similar approval to Loon last year for its QCAD offering, while Calgary’s Tetra Trust is pursuing a slightly different path for its own CADD stablecoin.
This appears to make Paytrie the second non-cryptocurrency trading platform to secure the relief necessary to offer stablecoins in Canada, after US-based ZeroHash, as an “authorized participant.”
RELATED: Government of Canada unveils proposed stablecoin regulations
These milestones come days after the Government of Canada released its proposed stablecoin regulations, which Zhang described as “a positive step forward” with no big surprises, noting that it follows many of the same principles as the United States GENIUS Act.
Led by Zhang and other former Paytrie staff, Loon launched last year with $3 million CAD to focus exclusively on CADC, which the startup acquired from Paytrie in 2025. Paytrie built CADC as an experiment as it set up its core stablecoin on- and off-ramp business, and since its launch in 2021, the stablecoin has facilitated over $1 billion CAD in transactions.
Zhang and his team began working with regulators while they were still at Paytrie, beginning with the Alberta Securities Commission before they were redirected to the OSC. He claimed that Tuesday’s announcement required “18 to 24 months of intense back-and-forth,” and “significant” legal investment on both companies’ behalf.
The biggest issue Loon faced, Zhang said, was how long it has taken Canada’s Stablecoin Act to become law, adding that delay “created a huge gap in the market.” Were it in effect earlier, Loon’s path would have looked a lot different: the company would have simply sought approval directly from the Bank of Canada, the CEO said.
RELATED: Paytrie spinout Loon raises $3 million to oversee Canadian dollar-backed stablecoin
With stablecoins increasingly used for payments, accessing them through a crypto exchange for this application “can be quite limiting,” Zhang argued. He claimed Paytrie’s capacity to deliver CADC will enable a wider array of cross-border and decentralized finance use-cases.
Zhang said the feds’ draft stablecoin regulation rules contained “nothing too out of the box, which could be a good thing or bad thing.” It also appears to signal that the federal government intends to soften its ban on stablecoin yield.
One thing it does not do, however, is create a regulatory advantage for CAD-backed stablecoins compared to their US-dollar counterparts; rather, it establishes a level playing field, he said. Zhang was hoping that policymakers would push the legislation “a little bit further” to help CAD-backed stablecoins compete domestically and abroad.
BetaKit’s Prairies reporting is funded in part by YEGAF, a not-for-profit dedicated to amplifying business stories in Alberta.
Feature image courtesy Loon.

articles.title: Amazon’s first digital picture frame lets you add voice notes to photos
articles.text:
Amazon’s screen-equipped smart speakers have long been able to display your family’s photos, but its new Alexa Photo Frame is purpose-built for that task. It’s designed to compete with other digital picture frames from companies like Aura, and Amazon’s incorporates a smart speaker with access to Alexa Plus’ capabilities through voice commands. However, unlike the Echo Show and Amazon’s other smart home hubs, the Alexa Photo Frame only ever displays your photos, and you’ll never be served an ad.
Amazon’s first digital picture frame lets you add voice notes to photos
The Alexa Photo Frame can use the smart assistant to choose your best photos based on lighting, smiles, and the season.
The Alexa Photo Frame is available starting today; it’s $199.99 for a black frame or $229 if you want to upgrade to a frame made from birch or walnut wood. It pulls images from Amazon Photos, which offers unlimited storage for Prime members, but otherwise the frame doesn’t require a subscription. The Amazon Photos app can back up photos from your Android or Apple devices and pull images from iCloud Photo, but importing from Google Photos isn’t supported yet.
The frame has a 10-inch touchscreen display with a “semi-matte, anti-glare finish” to simulate the look of physical prints. A light sensor adjusts the display’s brightness throughout the day, and it sits on a detachable stand.
You can select specific people or albums through Amazon Photos, or let Alexa Plus curate what’s displayed. Alexa selects the best images based on lighting, when people are smiling, and the current season, so you may get more Halloween costumes this time of year, while intelligently skipping images like receipts or screenshots. Alexa can also display similar photos with unique connections as side-by-side pairs, such as pics of a child 10 years apart with a similar pose. If there’s something specific you want to see, like last summer’s beach trip, you can just ask Alexa to dig those up.
You can use the Amazon Photos app to add voice notes to images that will play through the frame. An option to record them on the frame itself is coming later. If you plan to buy the Alexa Photo Frame as a gift and purchase it through Amazon, you can preload photos or albums with voice notes that play once the recipient sets it up.

How solid-state transformers could help power the AI boom
articles.text:
How solid-state transformers could help power the AI boom
New technology could help cut power losses and reinvent a staple of the grid.
Transformers are a crucial but nearly invisible part of our grid. The devices help efficiently move power across long distances, but they’re complicated and in short supply. And given that their basic design hasn’t changed much for about a century, they could use an upgrade.
As the world races to meet rising electricity demand from EVs, data centers, and more, researchers and companies are looking to modernize transformers. New, solid-state versions could help relieve some of the supply concerns and make sure the grid can handle the growing pressure.
Conventional transformers generally rely on huge amounts of specialized steel alloys and miles of copper wire to do their work of transferring electricity between circuits. Solid-state models, in comparison, combine magnetic components with high-power semiconductors, making them more compact and allowing for more control over the flow of electricity.
These devices are still in development, and can’t replace all traditional transformers today, especially the largest ones that work at the high voltages necessary for long-distance transmission. But a new generation of transformer technology could be a crucial part of our future grid.
The grid’s backbone
Moving electricity through the grid isn’t perfectly efficient: As electricity flows through power lines, some gets lost as heat. How much varies—the higher the voltage, the lower the current, and the less electricity gets lost. So a key function for the grid is stepping voltage up and down.
Consider, for example, your local solar plant. For that electricity to efficiently travel to your home hundreds of miles away, it needs to reach a higher voltage than what’s generated by the solar plant. Enter transformers.
In its path from the power plant to your outlets, electricity might go through one transformer at the solar farm and another at a substation nearby, stepping up the voltage twice to reach a high enough level to travel on high-voltage transmission lines. Solar panels also produce direct current (DC) electricity, which needs to be converted to alternating current (AC) via an inverter before it flows into a transformer. Closer to its destination, the voltage will be stepped down again, probably at least twice: once at another substation and again at a smaller transformer in your neighborhood.
If you’re in the US, electricity from a solar plant might be converted to AC by an inverter at around 480 volts, get stepped up to 115,000 volts for the transmission lines, and finally get stepped back down to 120 volts and 240 volts for your home.
Conventional transformers do this work using what essentially amount to loops of wire. The core of a transformer is typically made of a special type of steel called grain-oriented electrical steel. Coils of copper wire sit on either end of that core.
The number of loops in each coil determines the voltage on either end of the transformer: If there are more loops on the secondary coil than the primary, the voltage steps up, and if there are fewer, it steps down. When incoming electricity passes through loops on the upstream end of the transformer, that forms a magnetic field in the core. That field induces a voltage in the loops on the other side of the device, which is what allows the energy to continue flowing at a new voltage. This process is called magnetic induction.
Transformers form the backbone of electricity transmission and distribution, says Srdjan Lukic, a professor of electrical and computer engineering at North Carolina State University. In addition to doing the job of stepping up and down voltage, transformers also often provide what’s called galvanic isolation, meaning there’s no direct electrical path flowing through them. That can help limit disturbances from moving through the grid, improving safety.
The problem is that today’s transformers are big and bulky, and they’re also difficult and expensive to replace, Lukic says.
A solid option
Solid-state transformers essentially add so-called power electronics—semiconductors that convert and control electricity to the typical blueprint of today’s transformers.
While a conventional transformer operates at the frequency of the part of the grid it’s connected to, a solid-state transformer actually controls the frequency of the current. Typically, a solid-state transformer first converts incoming AC power from the grid to DC power, and then to a higher-frequency AC power using switches made of a semiconductor like silicon carbide.
From there, a magnetic component changes the voltage. Because the advanced semiconductors allow transformers to exert so much control over the frequency and stability of the current, the magnetic core can be much smaller than in a conventional transformer. Some come in at roughly one-tenth the size but have the same capacity, Lukic says.
Finally, additional power electronics convert the electricity from high-frequency AC to its required form—generally back to DC power and finally to lower-frequency AC.
Today, stepping voltage up and down is many transformers’ only job. But solid-state transformers can do much more. They absorb the jobs of devices like rectifiers and inverters (which convert AC to DC power and vice versa), shrinking the total footprint of the electrical equipment and potentially cutting the amount of power lost in the system.
In August, the New York Power Authority and the Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI) tested a one-megawatt solid-state transformer under realistic utility conditions at EPRI’s test site. The device was built in Lukic’s lab, and it was the first such test for a transformer of that capacity, he says.
The prototype was roughly 98% efficient—meaning it lost only 2% of the energy fed in. An equivalent conventional transformer and rectifier, by comparison, would be about 96% efficient together, Lukic says. A difference of 2% might seem small, but it is significant, since it means the solid-state transformer could cut power losses from conventional equipment in half, Lukic says.
One major goal of the project was to help utilities gain more confidence in these new components, Lukic says. That’s crucial, since these devices could be used on the power grid in the future. In the near term, solid-state transformers could be used within data centers to provide electricity for server racks.
The prototype is still a relatively low-voltage system, operating at about 15,000 volts. Industrial facilities like larger data centers often require higher-voltage connections, and transmission lines typically operate at hundreds of thousands of volts. Adapting solid-state transformers to these higher voltages will require further engineering development. But the test was a successful demonstration that solid-state transformers can work under real conditions, Lukic says.
Companies developing solid-state transformers are largely focused on data centers right now, Lukic says. There’s an influx of money to support developing the new technology, and the voltage requirements aren’t as high as they will be for larger transformers that will be needed for long-distance transmission.
In February, Heron Power raised $140 million to commercialize its solid-state transformer, which the company calls the Heron Link. The technology could be used in data centers, solar power arrays, and grid batteries, says Drew Baglino, the founder and CEO. The company is starting to test its technology at larger scales now, Baglino says. Ten megawatt-hours’ worth of batteries at Heron’s headquarters in Scotts Valley, California, will soon undergo testing with Heron transformers. The company is also planning a pilot with a nearby solar farm, Baglino says.
One challenge for solid-state transformers is that their power electronics have more failure modes than conventional transformers. In a traditional device, a failure means that the entire device will typically be taken offline, resulting in power interruptions. But Heron designs with that in mind, Baglino says: The company uses a modular design, with many small devices that work together. If one fails, the rest of the system keeps working until the affected bit can be replaced, which doesn’t require shutting the whole thing down.
Heron Power is currently building a $100 million factory in California to make advanced transformers. The facility should begin production in 2027 and reach its full production rate of 40 gigawatts’ worth of transformers per year in 2029.
The future of the grid
In recent years, companies that make grid equipment have put $1.7 billion into the US supply chain for power transformers, which are used in high-voltage transmission, says Benjamin Boucher, a supply chain analyst at Wood Mackenzie. There’s been an additional $1.3 billion invested for distribution transformers, the smaller devices that help transform power for homes and businesses, he adds.
But even this investment isn’t keeping pace with the rapid growth of the grid. Wait times for large conventional transformers—the kind needed to connect new power plants, long-distance transmission, and high-demand sites like data centers—are stretching as long as five years.
“Transformers have become one of the biggest bottlenecks for utilities, generation developers, and even data centers,” Boucher says. The big challenge is that it’s difficult to get new transformer manufacturing up and running, because it’s a quite technical process that requires a lot of specialized labor. So even facilities announced years ago are still years from opening, Boucher says.
Solid-state transformers could help ease some of that pressure. But high-voltage devices needed for power plant connections and transmission lines are the holy grail for solid-state transformers, Lukic says. Existing solid-state technology can’t be used for those applications yet, so the industry will need to develop new materials and designs to support high voltages and handle electricity safely in a compact device.
“We’re facing a big risk related to grid infrastructure,” Boucher says. “Without the transformers, you don’t really have an electrical grid.”

articles.title: La moda de los dispositivos sin pantalla y por qué cada vez hay más
articles.text:
La moda de los dispositivos sin pantalla y por qué cada vez hay más
La IA y el cansancio digital impulsan dispositivos que funcionan sin pantalla, sin iconos y, en algunos casos, sin necesidad de sacar el móvil del bolsillo
Durante años, la industria tecnológica parecía obsesionada con una idea: poner una pantalla en cualquier objeto imaginable; y cuanto más grande, mejor. Teléfonos, relojes, electrodomésticos, coches, altavoces e, incluso, frigoríficos se llenaron de superficies repletas de iconos y notificaciones. Sin embargo, en los últimos tiempos ha comenzado a emerger una tendencia aparentemente opuesta: la de los dispositivos que reducen o eliminan por completo la pantalla.
No se trata de un regreso al pasado, sino de una nueva forma de relacionarse con la tecnología. La inteligencia artificial generativa, los asistentes de voz y los sistemas capaces de interpretar lenguaje natural han abierto la puerta a productos que prometen ofrecer información o ejecutar tareas sin necesidad de que el usuario mire constantemente una pantalla.
Tecnología invisible
Los expertos llevan años alertando sobre la fatiga asociada al exceso de notificaciones y al tiempo de exposición a dispositivos digitales, como demuestran estudios como el llevado a cabo por investigadores de la Universidad Cornell en 2020. Frente a ello, muchas empresas han comenzado a explorar lo que algunos diseñadores denominan “tecnología ambiental” o “tecnología invisible”: dispositivos que permanecen en segundo plano y solo aparecen cuando son necesarios.
Y la llegada de la IA generativa ha dado, además, un nuevo impulso a este movimiento. Si un sistema es capaz de comprender preguntas complejas y responder de forma conversacional, la necesidad de navegar por menús o aplicaciones disminuye. Uno de los ejemplos más conocidos fue el Humane AI Pin, presentado en el Mobile World Congress (MWC) en el año 2024, un pequeño dispositivo que se llevaba prendido en la ropa y que aspiraba a sustituir parcialmente al teléfono móvil.
Su propuesta consistía en interactuar mediante voz, gestos y una proyección luminosa sobre la mano del usuario en lugar de utilizar una pantalla convencional. Sin embargo, el producto no logró convencer al mercado y fue retirado menos de un año después de su lanzamiento tras la adquisición de gran parte de la empresa por HP. Su fracaso, no obstante, no ha frenado la búsqueda de alternativas.
Los altavoces inteligentes son el caso más evidente de que es posible usar un dispositivo sin pantalla y no echarla de menos. El Amazon Echo Dot, el Apple HomePod Mini o el Google Nest Mini funcionan principalmente mediante voz y han normalizado la idea de que una interfaz puede ser invisible. De hecho, millones de usuarios se han acostumbrado a pedir música, consultar el tiempo o controlar dispositivos domésticos simplemente hablando.
De forma similar funcionan los auriculares inteligentes provistos de asistentes integrados o las gafas inteligentes. En estos productos, el usuario recibe información directamente por audio sin necesidad de tener que sacar el teléfono del bolsillo. En las últimas semanas, además, hemos visto que firmas como Fitbit han renovado su catálogo con una pulsera de actividad —Fitbit Air— con un diseño que pasa totalmente desapercibido (y sin pantalla, por supuesto) a la vez que registra todo tipo de métricas. También destaca la ēllu band, una pulsera especialmente indicada para niños y adolescentes que integra localización en tiempo real, avisos y funciones de seguridad; o Amazfit Helio Strap, un entrenador deportivo diseñado para conseguir objetivos de entrenamiento y mejorar en la recuperación.
En el ámbito doméstico, sensores, termostatos, cerraduras inteligentes o asistentes para el hogar conectado funcionan cada vez más de forma automática, sin requerir una pantalla propia. La tecnología se integra en el entorno y desaparece de la vista.
Las ventajas (y las que no lo son tanto)
La principal promesa de estos dispositivos es reducir la dependencia visual. En teoría, permiten acceder a información o realizar acciones sin interrumpir una conversación, una caminata o cualquier otra actividad cotidiana. También pueden simplificar el uso de la tecnología. Hablar suele ser más rápido que navegar por varias aplicaciones cuando se trata de tareas sencillas como consultar una cita, encender una luz o reproducir una canción. Además, algunos diseñadores consideran que estos equipos ayudan a combatir la llamada “economía de la atención”, un modelo en el que las aplicaciones compiten constantemente por captar la mirada del usuario.
Pero eliminar la pantalla también implica renuncias. Las interfaces visuales siguen siendo extremadamente eficientes para mostrar grandes cantidades de información, comparar opciones o realizar tareas complejas. Y la privacidad es otro desafío importante. Al basarse en micrófonos y procesamiento de voz, estos dispositivos generan preguntas sobre la recopilación y tratamiento de datos personales. Tanto es así que diversos estudios académicos han analizado riesgos potenciales relacionados con el tráfico de datos, la elaboración de perfiles de usuario y la seguridad de las interacciones por voz.
¿Un futuro sin pantallas?
Probablemente no. La mayoría de los expertos coinciden en que las pantallas seguirán siendo imprescindibles para multitud de tareas y, por lo tanto, lo que parece más plausible es un escenario híbrido. Así, en lugar de desaparecer, podrían convertirse en un recurso secundario. La interacción cotidiana se realizaría mediante voz, inteligencia artificial o automatizaciones, mientras que la información compleja seguiría mostrándose visualmente cuando fuera necesario.

articles.title: L’iPad mini pourrait avoir un écran 120 Hz : Apple l’a-t-il bridé à 60 Hz ?
articles.text:
L’iPad mini 8 change d’écran, mais pas de fréquence. Avec sa nouvelle tablette annoncée le 26 octobre 2026, Apple adopte une dalle OLED de 8,5 pouces, aux noirs plus profonds et au contraste plus élevé. Pour profiter de la fluidité du 120 Hz, en revanche, il faudra encore regarder du côté des iPad Pro : le mini reste à 60 Hz, sans ProMotion.
Une affirmation relayée le 27 octobre par IT Home, dont l’article reste consultable chez Sina, alimente les critiques. Selon le blogueur chinois @有没有搞措, la dalle serait capable de fonctionner à 120 Hz, mais limitée par logiciel. Apple aurait donc installé un écran plus performant que ce qu’elle permet à ses clients d’utiliser.
Cette accusation, également reprise dans plusieurs messages sur X, reste à vérifier. Elle pose néanmoins une question : pourquoi Apple conserverait-il le 60 Hz si le matériel permettait d’aller plus loin ?
Le 120 Hz a aussi un coût pour la batterie
Une première explication serait l’autonomie. C’est notamment l’hypothèse du blogueur Kang, rapportée dans le même article chinois. Rafraîchir un écran 120 fois par seconde rend les animations et le défilement plus fluides, mais demande aussi davantage d’énergie qu’à 60 Hz, à conditions comparables.
Pour limiter cette consommation, les écrans à rafraîchissement adaptatif réduisent leur fréquence lorsque le contenu bouge peu. Pendant que l’on fait défiler un article, une fréquence élevée est utile. Une fois la page arrêtée pour lire, elle l’est beaucoup moins. C’est le principe de ProMotion, la technologie de rafraîchissement adaptatif des iPad Pro.
Encore faut-il que l’écran sache ralentir efficacement. Dans son analyse de la polémique, Max Weinbach, de Creative Strategies, avance que l’iPad mini utiliserait probablement une dalle OLED LTPS plutôt que LTPO. Il évoque un choix moins coûteux, mais aussi des contraintes de consommation et de calibration.
Ces acronymes désignent les technologies des transistors qui commandent les pixels. Le LTPO associe notamment des transistors à oxyde qui réduisent les fuites électriques, comme l’explique Samsung Display. Cela permet de conserver une image stable plus longtemps entre deux rafraîchissements, et donc de descendre à de basses fréquences pour économiser de l’énergie.
Avec le LTPS, ce fonctionnement est plus délicat : les fuites de courant peuvent entraîner du scintillement ou des variations de luminosité lorsque la fréquence devient trop basse. Son utilisation pourrait donc rendre le 120 Hz moins intéressant pour l’autonomie qu’avec une dalle LTPO.
Le LTPS n’empêche pas le 120 Hz
Cela ne signifie pas qu’un écran LTPS est condamné à rester à 60 Hz. Il peut fonctionner à 120 Hz et proposer plusieurs modes de rafraîchissement. En revanche, passer de l’un à l’autre demande des réglages pour conserver des couleurs et une luminosité homogènes. Chaque mode nécessite sa calibration, puis des contrôles pour éviter des changements visibles à l’écran.
Le choix pourrait ainsi se jouer dès la conception : une solution LTPS moins coûteuse, utilisée à 60 Hz, ou un écran plus sophistiqué permettant de profiter du 120 Hz tout en limitant sa consommation. Si Apple a retenu la première option, l’absence de fluidité supplémentaire serait la conséquence d’un arbitrage économique et technique. Pas la preuve que le 120 Hz était impossible.
Il reste aussi à vérifier ce que recouvre l’affirmation sur la dalle. Sa capacité à supporter 120 Hz ne garantit pas que le contrôleur et les circuits qui la pilotent soient prévus pour cette fréquence. Pour savoir si une mise à jour suffirait, il faudrait connaître les caractéristiques de l’ensemble de l’écran.
Garder un avantage pour les iPad Pro
L’explication pourrait également être commerciale. Dans la gamme actuelle, Apple réserve ProMotion aux iPad Pro. Maintenir le mini à 60 Hz conserve une différence immédiatement perceptible entre ses tablettes, même après l’arrivée de l’OLED sur le petit modèle.
Cela ne prouve pas qu’Apple a volontairement désactivé une fonction disponible. Mais les contraintes techniques n’excluent pas une volonté de distinguer les gammes : le fabricant choisit aussi combien investir dans chaque écran et quelles fonctions proposer à chaque prix.
Préserver l’autonomie, réduire les coûts et garder un avantage pour les modèles Pro sont des explications qui peuvent se cumuler. Aucune n’est confirmée pour cet iPad mini. L’absence de 120 Hz reste donc critiquable, sans qu’il soit encore possible d’affirmer qu’Apple cache un mode prêt à être activé.

articles.title: Apple étend Siri AI à 5 nouvelles langues, mais les utilisateurs européens restent exclus
articles.text:
Siri AI débarque en français, mais toujours pas en France sur iPhone, iPad et Apple Watch. Cependant, les restrictions d'usage se feront nombreuses avec le plan d'utilisation gratuit.
Apple a annoncé l'ajout du français, du japonais, du coréen, du portugais et de l'espagnol à Siri AI avec la mise à jour vers la version 27.2. Cette nouvelle version, si intéressante soit-elle, n'est toutefois pas encore disponible en France ni dans certains pays d'Europe.
Siri boosté à l'intelligence artificielle
Cette version repensée de l'assistant vocal mise sur l'intégration d'Apple Intelligence pour apporter plus de contexte à l'utilisateur. L'objectif est de permettre à Siri de retrouver des informations dans les messages, les mails, les photos et d'autres contenus, lorsque l'utilisateur en a besoin.
Parmi les fonctionnalités proposées figurent la rédaction de mails depuis une simple instruction, ainsi que des outils d'édition et de partage de photos. Siri AI intègre également une fonction de reconnaissance de l'écran, lui permettant de répondre à des questions ou d'exécuter des actions en lien avec le contenu affiché. L'assistant dispose en plus d'une base de connaissances générales et peut fournir des informations actualisées sur de nombreux sujets.
Toujours pas disponible dans l'UE
Apple précise, dans les mentions légales accompagnant l'annonce, que Siri AI demeure en version bêta pour l'ensemble des systèmes d'exploitation intégrant la mise à jour 27.2. Son utilisation nécessite par ailleurs un matériel compatible avec Apple Intelligence.
La fonctionnalité reste indisponible dans l'Union européenne sur iOS, iPadOS et watchOS. La marque à la pomme indique travailler à trouver une solution permettant son déploiement chez nous. Siri AI n'est pas non plus accessible aux utilisateurs de moins de 13 ans.
- Intégration transparente dans l'écosystème Apple
- Respect de la confidentialité des données
- Outils d'écriture puissants
Pour profiter de Siri AI, il faudra impérativement un appareil sous iOS 27.2, iPadOS 27.2, macOS 27.2, visionOS 27.2 ou watchOS 27.2 compatible avec Apple Intelligence.
Un déploiement progressif et quelques limites
Cette mise à jour s'ajoute à la prise en charge existante de l'anglais. Apple prévoit de poursuivre cette extension linguistique d'ici la fin de l'année avec l'intégration du chinois traditionnel, du norvégien, du turc et du vietnamien.
L'entreprise californienne rappelle également que certaines fonctionnalités d'Apple Intelligence reposent sur des modèles hébergés sur ses serveurs et sont, à ce titre, soumises à des limites d'utilisation quotidiennes. Cela concerne notamment Siri AI, les outils d'édition de photos basés sur l'intelligence artificielle, Image Playground, ainsi que les modèles AFM 3 Cloud utilisés dans l'application Raccourcis. Apple devrait par ailleurs proposer des abonnements payants à l'avenir, pour élargir l'accès à ces fonctionnalités actuellement plafonnées.
Source : NeoWin

articles.title: No bank account required: how blockchain works at the last mile - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
African technologists and entrepreneurs are applying blockchain in innovative ways, creating a new financial infrastructure for the continent with wide-ranging benefits, including for the humanitarian sector.
Through its Blockchain Ventures investment programme – supported by Ethereum Foundation and GSR Foundation – UNICEF Office of Innovation provides funding and technical assistance to emerging market startups building innovative blockchain-based solutions.
Kenya-based Kotani Pay’s co-founder Samuel Kariuki, spoke with us about what the early work with UNICEF taught the team and how the company grew from a feature phone ready SMS wallet into a business serving multiple markets.
What did you see in those early days that told you there was a problem Kotani Pay could solve?
We started as a bunch of educators teaching people in Nairobi about blockchain, around 2018. We soon hit a problem: Africans pay through mobile money, and mobile money couldn’t connect to the blockchain. In one basic-income pilot in Nairobi’s informal settlements, people received digital money they couldn’t spend. A local agent swapped it for cash, and he quickly became a target.
We thought someone should be able to move from the blockchain to Kenya shillings, and from Kenya shillings back to the blockchain, using the readily available payment channel, which is mobile money. We experimented, and it was a eureka moment for us. We felt we had a product we could build a team around.
What did your first product allow someone receiving money to do?
Through our work with UNICEF Office of Innovation, we did projects in Ghana and Kenya, mainly with people living in refugee camps. If you look at Africa as a whole, the people who struggle financially – whether refugees or others – have feature phones and have trouble connecting to the internet. By designing infrastructure where someone can use any device to connect to the blockchain, what we provided was an SMS wallet: a user could simply dial a code to see what funds they had received and convert it into, local currency through mobile money making it possible to spend digital funds.
What did working with those early users teach you about building the product?
It was a phenomenal experience, to customize a product that resonates. Building a product that meant blockchain payments worked on basic phones and seeing the excitement of someone actually spending that money in the local economy, was very good for us, because it made a case that this is a product that can be replicated at scale.
UNICEF supported Kotani Pay to develop its model. What did the experience give you beyond funding?
The early projects also made a case for us to raise money, because we could tell investors: look, this is what we have been able to achieve, this is what we have been able to learn, these are some of the gaps we are identifying, and we think we can do more.
Beyond that, we had amazing support in terms of product design, market penetration and understanding the fundamentals of the business, and all of this was given for free.
Kotani Pay began with an SMS wallet and now provides payment infrastructure to businesses. What led to that change?
We decided to focus specifically on Application Programming Interfaces (API), tools that allow different software systems to connect and exchange information. With the projects in Kenya and Ghana, we had built a platform that could be used to transfer funds into two different markets, and that’s a very big value proposition. People in the Web3 ecosystem were asking whether they could have a pathway to move crypto into local currency in different countries.
How does Kotani Pay’s payment infrastructure work?
Money moves through something we call the ‘stablecoin sandwich’. The first leg of a transaction is fiat [traditional currency], the second leg is stablecoin, and the last leg is fiat again. Our API is multi-chain infrastructure: on one end it connects to local payment channels – whether that’s banking or mobile money – and on the other end it connects to the blockchain protocols.
Why is blockchain finding such practical uses in Kenya?
Most emerging markets tend to be victims of how financial services are structured. For me to make a trade with someone in Uganda, I have to exit from Kenya shillings into the dollar, then exit from the dollar into Ugandan shillings!
Say I sell phones on a street in Nairobi. I go to a local bank and tell them I want to make a payment to China to import goods. The process of settlement is so long, and most of this business is first-come-first-served, so if it takes one week for my funds to reflect on the other side, the product may have been sold to someone else. These frustrations are forcing people to look for alternatives, and one of the strongest alternatives has always been crypto, specifically stablecoins.
Kotani Pay now focuses on businesses. Is the social purpose of your early work still part of the company?
Social good is still something so close to our hearts. We still believe in it. We open-sourced our solution, and being in the UNICEF portfolio, we are known as people who have infrastructure that people can experiment with.

articles.title: Healthtech startup Cent raises $15M in Series A
articles.text:
Healthtech startup Cent raises $15M in Series A
Cent said it will use the funding for R&D and to build out its AI, engineering, and clinical teams.
Healthtech startup Cent has raised $15 million in a Series A funding round through a combination of debt and equity, led by Blume Ventures and existing investor South Park Commons.
The round also saw participation from individual investors, including Arun Sarin, former CEO of Vodafone; Srinivas Narayanan, former CTO (B2B) of OpenAI; and Sharath Narayana, Krishna Sridhar, and Aprameya Radhakrishna.
Cent said it will use the funding for R&D and to build out its AI, engineering, and clinical teams.
Cent was founded by Shashank ND, Arpit Garg, and Anshul Khandelwal in 2025 and is positioned as a preventive health intelligence company. Shashank ND is the founder of Practo, while Anshul Khandelwal was the former CMO of Ola Electric, and Arpit Garg was the former product head at Lenskart.
Cent is building a vertically integrated preventive health platform that combines purpose-built hardware, AI-driven radiology and diagnostics, and bioinformatics. The startup says the platform can help detect diseases well before symptoms appear.
Cent has also acquired Medsee, an AI-powered radiology reporting workflow platform founded by Chitra Singh and designed for qualified medical professionals. The platform drafts structured reports and highlights findings for radiologist review, enabling Cent to deliver faster, more consistent reporting as scan volumes grow.
"India's healthcare system is still built to treat illness, not to find it early. We believe the next shift is preventive care that is precise and accessible at scale. This investment lets us go deeper into AI, medical imaging and clinical research, and build preventive health infrastructure in India that can serve the world," said Anshul Khandelwal, Co-Founder, Cent.
According to Cent, it has completed 10,000 preventive whole-body scans across Bengaluru, Mumbai and Delhi since inception. It is targeting 10 million scans by 2035.
“We are believers in the Cent's vision to extend this from India to the world over time, and it is in line with our conviction around health tech for a decade now," said Karthik Reddy, Co-founder and Managing Partner, Blume Ventures.

articles.title: Un ChatGPT moins cher et plus puissant : le nouveau modèle GPT-6.1 Terra d'OpenAI a trouvé sa recette
articles.text:
Le modèle Terra d’OpenAI était resté jusque là sur la génération GPT-5.6 (arrivé en juillet dernier). Désormais, il passe à GPT-6.1 et devient plus puissant, mais surtout deux fois moins cher. Ce modèle est vu par OpenAI comme capable de travailler sur plein de tâches différentes, et il est déjà disponible.
GPT-6.1 Terra est là : qu’est-ce qui change vraiment ?
Sur la page dédiée à ce modèle, OpenAI explique que GPT-6.1 Terra est un modèle dit intermédiaire (pas le moins cher, mais pas le plus puissant) conçu pour analyser ce qui s’affiche sur votre écran, puis agir. Cliquer, saisir du texte, remplir un formulaire, passer à un autre logiciel… il peut à peu près tout faire. Il succède donc à GPT-5.6 Terra, dont la sortie avait été suspendue par l’administration Trump au nom de la sécurité nationale. Seuls quelques partenaires sélectionnés avaient pu le tester. Un système nécessaire puisqu’il y a encore quelques jours, deux agents IA d’OpenAI ont effectué des actions surprenantes. Quelques jours plus tard, le modèle était enfin sorti.
GPT-6.1 Terra est taillé pour le travail professionnel, avec des usages variés : rédiger un mail, interpréter un plan technique, extraire les données d’une facture pour les saisir dans un logiciel comptable, assister un montage vidéo, etc. OpenAI le présente donc comme un modèle associant raisonnement visuel détaillé et utilisation précise d’un ordinateur.
Sur le benchmark Agent’s Last Exam, cette version est 15% plus performante que la version précédente (sur un exercice de transformation de plans architecturaux en modèles 3D et en analyse d’un film d’animation). GPT-6.1 Terra est d’ores et déjà disponible dans ChatGPT Work et Codex. Mais pour le moment, il est réservé aux abonnés à ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Enterprise et Edu.
Un modèle d’IA deux fois moins cher que sa version précédente
Aujourd’hui, la gamme de modèles d’OpenAI compte quatre niveaux, du moins cher au plus puissant : Luna, Terra, Sol et Astra. Terra est donc dans une position intermédiaire, entre le plus accessible qu’est Luna et des modèles plus coûteux comme Sol et Astra. GPT-6.1 Terra est annoncé à 1 dollar par million de tokens en entrée et 5 dollars par million de tokens en sortie. Pour rappel, sur GPT-5.6 Terra, c’était deux fois plus cher.
Au regard de la grille tarifaire d’OpenAI, ce modèle est dix fois plus cher que le modèle le moins cher, à savoir GPT-6 Luna. Mais il est dix fois moins cher que le modèle le plus puissant, GPT-6 Astra, tout en ayant des performances qui s’en rapprochent. OpenAI semble donc en faire un modèle avec le meilleur rapport performances-prix possible.

articles.title: Apple backports CoreGraphics zero-day patches to older iPhones
articles.text:
Apple has backported security patches released last month to older iPhones and iPads, addressing a zero-day bug exploited in "extremely sophisticated" targeted attacks on iOS devices.
Apple patched the same vulnerability in September for devices running iOS 26.7.1 and iPadOS 26.7.1, macOS Tahoe 26.7.1, and macOS Sequoia 15.8.1.
Meta Product Security discovered this out-of-bounds write weakness (tracked as CVE-2026-86950) in CoreGraphics, a framework used for two-dimensional vector graphics, text drawing, and image rendering across iOS, macOS, iPadOS, watchOS, and tvOS.
Successful exploitation of out-of-bounds write security issues can let attackers crash programs, corrupt data, or gain remote code execution by writing data outside the allocated memory buffer.
"Apple is aware of a report that this issue may have been exploited in an extremely sophisticated attack against specific targeted individuals on versions of iOS before iOS 27," Apple warned on Monday.
"Processing a maliciously crafted file may lead to arbitrary code execution. An out-of-bounds write issue was addressed with improved bounds checking."
With this week's security patches, Apple has now also addressed this vulnerability on iPhone XS, iPhone XS Max, iPhone XR, iPad 7th generation, iPad Air 4th generation and later, iPad 9th generation and later, and iPad mini 6th generation and later.
While Apple said CVE-2026-86950 is exploited only in highly targeted attacks, it is strongly advised to install these backported patches to block potential attacks.
With this vulnerability, Apple has fixed two zero-days exploited in attacks this year. The other (CVE-2026-20700), an arbitrary code execution vulnerability in dyld (the Dynamic Link Editor used by Apple operating systems) also exploited in "extremely sophisticated" targeted attacks, was patched in February.
Earlier this year, Apple also fixed a high-severity Beats Studio Buds flaw (CVE-2025-20701) that lets attackers in Bluetooth range spy on users' conversations, and patched older iPhones and iPads against four vulnerabilities targeted in cyberespionage and crypto-theft attacks using the Coruna exploit kit.
Once attackers have valid credentials, only 37% of their actions are blocked
Overall prevention scores can hide what happens after initial access. Once attackers are using valid credentials, prevention drops sharply.
