articles.title: Impress bags €40 million EIB financing to expand its digital orthodontics network across Europe | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Impress, a Spanish digital orthodontics network, has signed a €40 million venture debt loan with the European Investment Bank (EIB) to scale up investments in its AI platform across its network of more than 110 clinics worldwide. The loan will also accelerate the company’s expansion plans across Europe.
This latest agreement also follows Impress’s over €110 million financing announcement in 2024, which supported its European expansion following the acquisition of DrSmile.
“For years, patients have had to choose between expensive orthodontics with constant clinic visits, or at-home solutions without adequate medical follow-up. At Impress, we were born to close that gap. Our technology features an artificial intelligence engine powered by a global database of 500,000 patients, which allows us to multiply the efficiency of our clinics ten times, reduce in-person visits by 80%, and make quality medical care more accessible.
“The backing of the EIB represents a seal of guarantee in the HealthTech companies’ ecosystem in Europe, confirms our vision, and places us in an advantageous position to consolidate our model in the region,” says Vladimir Lupenko, co-founder and CEO of Impress.
Impress’s financing comes amid a series of European investments in digital dentistry and AI-enabled healthcare in 2026.
In France, Paris-based DentalMonitoring secured €84 million to expand its AI-powered orthodontic monitoring platform, while Montpellier-based Lupin Dental raised €15 million for dental robotics. Belgium’s Relu also attracted €1.51 million for AI-powered dental workflows.
In Spain, Madrid-based Tucuvi raised €17 million for its voice-AI healthcare platform, while Barcelona’s Health Force secured €4.2 million for hospital automation.
Together with Impress’s €40 million venture debt loan, these announcements represent approximately €161.7 million in reported financing, spanning equity investments and debt.
“The digital transformation of the healthcare sector offers significant opportunities to improve the quality and efficiency of services provided to citizens. This operation reflects the EIB’s commitment to supporting innovative European growth companies like Impress that leverage AI to build cutting-edge solutions and expand their footprint across Europe, reinforcing EU leadership in HealthTech innovation,” adds María Romano, Head of the EIB Group Office in Spain.
Founded in Barcelona in 2019 by Vladimir Lupenko, Diliara Lupenko and Khaled Kasem, Impress is an invisible orthodontics and medical technology company. They offer a model that combines in-person care in specialised clinics with continuous monitoring through its AI-powered technology platform.
The company currently operates in 10 countries across Europe and the United States, with more than 110 clinics and 500,000 patients treated globally. In Spain, it has 22 clinics.
On the technology front, today’s investment will drive the development of Impress’s proprietary platform, a comprehensive AI-based healthcare ecosystem designed to unify patient treatment from start to finish.
The solution spans from in-clinic 3D intraoral scans – delivering more accurate tooth-movement predictions than traditional molds – AI-assisted treatment planning to ongoing patient tracking via Impress’s proprietary mobile app.
Its recent innovations include the industry’s first autonomous smile simulator, which uses artificial intelligence to recreate the “before and after” of treatment in just three seconds, with no need for manual intervention.
Having consolidated its position in Southern Europe, with Spain, Portugal and Italy as its main markets, Impress is preparing a new phase of international expansion focused on Northern Europe.
This strategy will focus mainly on the German, Dutch and UK markets, where the company has operated since 2023.
This growth plan is supported by the company’s strong performance over the last year, in which it posted positive EBITDA and 32% revenue growth, reaching €103 million. For 2026, Impress expects to reach revenue of around €145 million, representing growth of 40%.

articles.title: Hackers Start Probing Fresh Oracle EBS Vulnerability
articles.text:
Threat actors have started probing for a newly patched critical vulnerability in Oracle E-Business Suite (EBS), threat intelligence firm Defused reports.
The exploited flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-101767 (CVSS score of 9.8), was patched last week in Oracle’s October CPU.
It is described as an SQL injection issue in the Application Object Library product of EBS that could be exploited by remote, unauthenticated attackers over HTTP.
Successful exploitation of the bug could allow attackers to achieve remote code execution (RCE) and completely take over the Application Object Library.
According to Defused, the first exploitation attempts targeting CVE-2026-101767 were observed on October 27.
“Our Oracle E-Business Suite decoys recorded exploratory exploits against CVE-2026-101767 this morning, Oct 27,” the company warned on X.
The security defect was discovered and reported by Horizon3.ai and there have been no other reports regarding its in-the-wild exploitation.
Oracle EBS vulnerabilities are often targeted by threat actors. In June, Defused warned of attacks exploiting CVE-2026-46817, a critical issue in the File Transmissions component of E-Business Suite’s Payments product.
Last year, the Cl0p ransomware and extortion group exploited zero-day bugs in Oracle’s enterprise management software to access stored data.
The large-scale EBS hacking campaign potentially impacted over 100 organizations across consumer goods, energy, engineering, entertainment, finance, heavy industry, manufacturing, media, software, technology, telecommunications, and other industries.

articles.title: Así es la función de YouTube para comprar productos de videos en tiempo real
articles.text:
Al estar viendo una serie o un video es normal que aparezcan productos o referencias que a algunos usuarios les gustaría comprar, por eso las plataformas de streaming han creado herramientas que permiten hacerlo en tiempo real.
Tanto Amazon como YouTube cuentan con sistemas de reconocimiento de imágenes que identifican estas opciones y es posible comprar productos sin tener que dejar de disfrutar lo que se está viendo.
Qué es y cómo funciona YouTube Shopping
Esta herramienta integra funciones de comercio electrónico dentro de los videos, los shorts y las transmisiones en vivo de la plataforma. Permite a creadores y marcas etiquetar productos para que los espectadores accedan a detalles de compra sin abandonar el contenido que están viendo.
La función se conecta con Google Merchant Center, lo que permite sincronizar de forma automática el inventario de productos de una marca. Para activarla, es necesario vincular la cuenta de Merchant Center con el canal de YouTube desde la sección “Crecimiento” y luego etiquetar los productos dentro de YouTube Studio, tanto en videos publicados como en transmisiones en vivo.
Entre las ventajas se encuentra la reducción de la fricción en el proceso de compra, ya que el usuario completa la transacción sin salir de la plataforma, y el aprovechamiento del formato audiovisual para mostrar productos en contexto, a través de demostraciones o reseñas que refuerzan la confianza del comprador.
YouTube Shopping amplió en junio de 2026 su Programa de Afiliados a México y Argentina mediante una alianza con Mercado Libre. Bajo este esquema, cuando un creador etiqueta un producto en su contenido, la audiencia puede completar la compra sin interrumpir la reproducción del video.
A nivel global, los usuarios dedicaron más de 40.000 millones de horas a ver videos relacionados con compras durante 2025. En México, una encuesta de Kantar indica que el 84% de los usuarios considera que YouTube los ayuda a tomar mejores decisiones de compra, mientras que en Argentina, según una encuesta de Ipsos, el 87% de los consumidores que usan Google o YouTube en su proceso de compra tiende a volver a elegir la misma marca.
Entre las mejoras recientes de la herramienta se incluye el etiquetado automático de productos mediante inteligencia artificial, la reducción del requisito mínimo de suscriptores a 500 para acceder al programa y la ampliación de la experiencia de compra a la pantalla de televisión.
Cómo funciona Shop the Show
Esta es una función que sincroniza la reproducción de Prime Video con la aplicación de compras. Mientras un usuario ve un título compatible, puede acceder a un catálogo de productos relacionados con lo que aparece en pantalla, sin pausar el contenido ni salir de la plataforma.
El sistema ofrece productos con licencia oficial, objetos coleccionables, ropa, accesorios y artículos de decoración inspirados en los personajes y los mundos de cada producción.
A diferencia de otros modelos que usan códigos QR o menús emergentes sobre la pantalla principal, esta versión apostó por el concepto de segunda pantalla: el televisor mantiene limpia la imagen y toda la interacción ocurre en el teléfono.
La función no requiere estar conectado a la misma red wifi del televisor: funciona incluso si se está viendo el contenido en casa de otra persona.
A diferencia de YouTube, esta herramienta está solamente habilitada en Estados Unidos, disponible en más de 8.000 títulos del catálogo de la app de streaming.
YouTube hará que sus videos consuman 30% menos de datos móviles
YouTube incorporará AV2 en su reproductor web a comienzos de 2027, un códec que busca reducir hasta 30% el consumo de datos sin afectar la calidad de imagen. Una hora de vídeo en alta definición podría pasar de 3 GB a 2,1 GB, mientras que en 4K bajaría de 7 GB a 4,9 GB.
El formato también admite más fotogramas por segundo, HDR y visualización de varios vídeos. YouTube aún no informó fechas para móviles o televisores inteligentes, donde la adopción dependerá de aplicaciones actualizadas y chips compatibles.

articles.title: Amazon’s new Echo Studio speaker has a camera
articles.text:
Amazon is giving its premium smart speaker a camera. The new Echo Studio with Home Camera, announced today as part of Amazon’s big blast of announcements, has a built-in camera for monitoring a room while you’re away, showing things to Alexa, and, soon, to use with video calls on Fire TV devices. It’s an iteration on the revised Echo Studio announced last year, which had a brand-new design.
Amazon’s new Echo Studio speaker has a camera
Amazon is updating its premium smart speaker and adding a smart home hub to the Echo Dot.
The Echo Studio with Home Camera also offers some audio updates. Amazon says a new feature called “Advanced Room Adaptation” will continuously tune sound to the space that the speaker is in. There’s also an “Adaptive Volume” feature that raises or lowers volume depending on where you are in a room so that “your music or audiobook maintains the same volume as you move about.”
The new Echo Studio with Home Camera will cost $249.99 and come in graphite. Amazon will still sell the standard Echo Studio at its $219.99 price.
Amazon is also updating the Echo Dot, and the new version is powered by Amazon’s custom-designed AZ3 chip and has a fourth microphone to improve your conversations with Alexa. The Dot also now has a built-in smart home hub, supporting Zigbee, Matter, and Thread, and has a built-in Eero Wi-Fi extender that Amazon says can add up to 1,000 square feet of coverage.
The updated Echo Dot is available starting today for $99.99 in graphite, glacier white, agave green, and coral pink.

articles.title: AI can act exactly like a human, but we still don't think it's conscious
articles.text:
AI can act exactly like a human, but we still don't think it's conscious
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München
- Summary:
- A new study reveals that people draw a surprisingly sharp line between human consciousness and artificial intelligence, even when both behave identically. Researchers found that participants considered even the most responsive AI less conscious than the least responsive human. Yet when asked about "awareness" instead, people judged humans and AI much more similarly.
- Share:
Even when artificial intelligence behaves exactly like a human, people are reluctant to consider it conscious, according to a new study from Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU).
As artificial intelligence becomes more advanced, reports of AI systems misleading users, working together, or appearing to pursue independent goals are becoming increasingly common. These behaviors often lead people to describe AI as though it can think, feel, or make decisions for itself. But does behaving like a human actually convince people that a machine has consciousness?
New research from LMU suggests that people make a clear distinction between displaying intelligent behavior and possessing a conscious mind, even when humans and AI act in precisely the same way.
How Scientists Tested Perceptions of AI Consciousness
Published in the journal Cognition, the study was led by Dr. Louis Longin of LMU's Chair of Philosophy of Mind, working alongside Dr. Bahador Bahrami, Professor Ophelia Deroy, and other researchers.
"Whereas previous studies have typically asked general questions about whether AI actually has mental states, our study is the first to directly compare how people attribute the same mental states to AI and humans behaving in exactly the same way, under identical circumstances," says Longin.
"We may be using mental terms to refer to AI, but this may only be because we lack better words," says Ophelia Deroy, philosopher and a senior author of the study. "After all, AI is trained to act and speak like a human, so these descriptions seem natural."
To investigate how people judge consciousness, the researchers conducted experiments involving nearly 1,100 participants. One group read brief descriptions of artificial agents that showed different levels of responsiveness to their environments. For example, some agents reacted to sounds or recognized the emotional states of others.
Another group encountered the same situations, except the characters were described as humans rather than AI systems. Participants then evaluated how conscious or aware each character seemed to be of its surroundings.
A Surprising Gap Between Human and AI Consciousness
The experiments revealed that responsiveness influenced how participants judged both humans and artificial intelligence. Characters that reacted more actively to their surroundings were generally considered more conscious and more aware.
However, a striking difference emerged when participants evaluated consciousness specifically. Even the most responsive AI was rated as less conscious than the least responsive human. In other words, identical behavior did not lead people to assign the same level of consciousness to humans and machines.
The results changed considerably when participants were asked about awareness instead. For this characteristic, judgments of humans and AI followed largely similar patterns, suggesting that people interpret awareness and consciousness in fundamentally different ways.
"There is a growing worry in public discussion that people will see AI behaving in a human-like way and start treating these systems as if they had human-like mental states," says Longin, lead author of the study. "We found something much more nuanced: People are quite willing to say that an AI notices things and is aware of its surroundings. But they clearly draw a line when it comes to the term 'consciousness'. People consistently attribute less consciousness to AI than humans -- even when their behavior is identical."
Although people sometimes describe AI as conscious when discussing its actions, the findings indicate that they still distinguish between artificial systems and human minds.
Why One Word Changes How We Perceive AI
The researchers believe the difference between consciousness and awareness offers an important insight into how people understand artificial intelligence.
Awareness is a relatively neutral term that can describe an agent's ability to detect and respond to information in its environment. Consciousness, however, carries deeper implications about subjective experience and what it means to have an inner mental life.
Because awareness focuses more directly on observable behavior, people appear comfortable applying it to both humans and AI. Consciousness carries a different meaning, leading people to judge the two much less similarly.
The findings also highlight why the language used to discuss artificial intelligence matters, particularly as AI systems become increasingly capable of producing convincing human behavior.
"Our study teaches us lessons for how we communicate about AI," says Bahador Bahrami, who is also a senior author of the study and an expert in social neuroscience. "Companies and journalists often reach for hyped descriptions of AI models, and credit them with intentions, plans, or even moral conscience and hesitation. What our study shows is that everyday judgments are much more discriminating: People do not simply put AI and humans on the same mental scale. But the boundary also depends on which terms we use. For more neutral descriptors such as 'awareness', the distinction can largely disappear. That makes our choice of language important."
Story Source:
Materials provided by Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Louis Longin, Jurgis Karpus, Nadine Meertens, Bahador Bahrami, Ophelia Deroy. AI is not as conscious as humans: Essentialism in mental state attributions to artificial systems. Cognition, 2027; 278: 106733 DOI: 10.1016/j.cognition.2026.106733
Cite This Page:

articles.title: Exclusive: Meta director Rohit Patel departs after 8 years to take on Microsoft Office Suite
articles.text:
After eight years developing AI for Meta, Rohit Patel is departing the company, TechCrunch has exclusively learned. The former director at Meta Superintelligence Labs has launched Ndoc, a startup he’s pitching as an AI-native replacement for Microsoft Office suite or Google Workspace.
Patel is the latest in a handful of high-profile departures from Meta following the exits of Chief Global Affairs Officer Joel Kaplan, AI researcher Andrew Tulloch, and Head of Product for AI-for-Work Emily Dalton Smith.
Patel designed Ndoc to be more than just another AI tool layered onto an existing workflow. The goal is to replace the fragmented way people work across tools like Excel, Word, PowerPoint, Tableau, Replit, and “ChatGPT copy-paste” with one unified workspace that all colleagues can access, even if they’re not signed up for Ndoc.
Ndoc brings three components together in one layout. The Stage tab is where presentations of key findings live, like slide decks, dashboards, simulations, or mini apps. The Narrative tab features analyses, numbered citations, generated figures, and generally the “why” behind the numbers. The Model tab is where underlying datasets and Python scripts are housed.
The design reflects Patel’s background. During his tenure at Meta, Patel focused on reinforcement learning — a type of machine learning in which AI agents learn to make decisions through trial and error and maximize rewards — and evaluating whether AI output is trustworthy. Patel believes that if AI is going to build the spreadsheets and slide decks that companies use to make decisions, someone should be able to check its work. For instance, users can find the Python scripts used to create the documents.
“Even if you don’t know any Python, you can ask [the AI chat] to explain, ‘Hey, what does this script do? Which line has my formula?’ And you can verify that formula,” Patel said. “There’s nothing hidden behind the curtain here.”
In practice, users can upload a dataset and ask Ndoc to perform an analysis and write a narrative about the findings. They can also add document-specific context, including audience, tone, and memory. “It maintains a memory across your person, that particular document, your team, and your company,” Patel said.
Patel also says Ndoc is built and fine-tuned using a mixture of open source models. Because the platform was developed from scratch, he says it costs considerably less to run than alternatives built on frontier AI models.
“I thought that’s what people would be excited about, but people don’t care about that,” he said, referring to his early trial users. “What people are excited about is that they love seeing all their end-to-end in one place.”
Patel’s larger ambition is to reinvent the file itself. He says documents can be exported as a single “.ndoc.html” file that can be opened in any browser, a format he plans to open-source so other developers can build apps that work with it without being locked into Ndoc the way so many have been locked into Microsoft or Google for years.
His desire to open-source this project was partly why he left Meta and decided to go it alone. At a big company like Meta, getting everyone to agree on an open source format would undoubtedly require the input of “hundreds of people and opinions on how the format should look.”
Patel wanted to move quickly. “Humans can only move at human pace, whereas…I can move at the pace of what AI can do.”
Trying to become the platform where enterprise work happens is a huge bet for a founder with a team of three and no funding, especially when other AI labs are trying to own the same space.
OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, SpaceXAI, and Google have all come out with enterprise AI tools that allow users to connect to Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, and other workplace apps so their AI models can work directly in those tools. And last month, OpenAI launched Space, a shared workspace inside ChatGPT that’s a more direct competitor to those established tools.
Patel acknowledges that Space could be a threat, but says the labs largely have the wrong idea.
“Companies are basically attaching AI to spreadsheets and it fills your cells for you,” he said. “It just sort of kills my soul. This is like if you just figured out electricity, and then you decided the best use case is to put lights on my bulls that till my soil. No. Get a tractor.”
There’s a reason the AI labs have tried to bring their models to where people are already working, though. It’s hard to change habits and replace entire workflows. Patel says he understands that, which is why he built connectors so customers can import existing data from the tools they already use.
“My bar was that I’m not going to release anything I don’t love using,” he said. “I have very optimized AI workflows for everything I do. If I start using this tool, and I keep going back to my workflows, I haven’t built a good enough tool…I have a graveyard of tools that did not meet that bar.”
Patel has a similar bar for gaining customer traction before he tries to raise funds. “I didn’t want to take money until I had some proof that people love the product,” he said.
As of Tuesday, Ndoc is conducting an enterprise pilot and opening an alpha version to a limited number of customers who join the wait list. It’s free to sign up, but customers will pay for usage and tokens. He hopes to release a beta version in the coming weeks, with a full launch planned for next year.
For Patel, moving as fast as possible is more important than having the perfect product from the get-go.
“Execution is extremely cheap…so go execute on a suboptimal plan and worry about it later,” he said. “By the time you make the best plan, the execution will be done by somebody else.”

articles.title: 90-Minuten-Videos auf Instagram
articles.text:
Youtube-Konkurrenz: Instagram-Videos können jetzt bis zu 90 Minuten lang sein
Im Frühjahr 2022 hatte Instagram seine vier Jahre zuvor gestartete IGTV-App eingestellt. Das Angebot sollte längere Videos auf die zuvor von Bildern geprägte Social-Media-Plattform bringen. Die bis zu 60 Minuten langen Inhalte schienen aber weniger gut anzukommen als die kurzen Reels, denen Instagram in den vergangenen Jahren den Vorzug gab.
Instagram ermöglicht längere Videos
Jetzt also Kommando zurück. Wie Instagram am 26. Oktober 2026 mitteilte, arbeitet die Meta-Tochter an einem neuen Angebot, das die Veröffentlichung von bis zu 90 Minuten langen Videos ermöglicht. Die Bewegtbildinhalte sollen unter dem Namen „Features“ laufen, wie Techcrunch schreibt.
Nach ersten Tests in Brasilien stellt das Feature Instagram zunächst ausgewählten Nutzer:innen in den USA zur Verfügung. Die entsprechende Video-Ankündigung durch CEO Adam Mosseri und Produktchefin Tessa Lyons ist offenbar nur für US-Nutzer:innen freigeschaltet worden.
Reels aus längeren Videos erstellen
Bekannt ist derweil, dass der Zugang zu den längeren Videos vor allem über Reels erfolgen soll. Dort sollen sich dann entsprechende Verweise finden, über die Nutzer:innen zu den Langversionen kommen sollen. Ein Verlassen der Instagram-App ist dafür nicht notwendig. Außerdem will Instagram die längeren Videos auch im Entdecken-Bereich der App anzeigen.
Mit der Funktion „Clips as Reels“ sollen Inhalte-Ersteller:innen aus den ihren langen Videos kurze Reels machen und diese auf Instagram teilen können. In diesen Reels finden sich dann die oben erwähnten Verweise. Außerdem arbeitet Instagram an einer schon von Tiktok bekannten Playlist-Version, über die sich mehrere zusammengehörige Reels auflisten lassen.
TV-Geräte als wichtige Plattform
Ebenfalls geplant ist, dass Nutzer:innen die längeren Videos speichern können, um sie etwa später auf der Instagram-App auf ihrem Fernsehgerät anschauen zu können. Im Dezember 2025 hatte das Unternehmen eine eigene Instagram-TV-App an den Start gebracht.
Mosseri hatte damals TV-Geräte als wichtige zusätzliche Plattform für Reels auserkoren – auch, um Youtube und Tiktok Konkurrenz zu machen. Aus einem ähnlichen Ansatz heraus dürfte der Instagram-Chef jetzt auch seine zunächst ablehnende Haltung gegen längere Videoinhalte abgelegt haben. Ziel dürfte es sein, Nutzer:innen länger auf der Plattform zu halten, auch wenn es um längere Interviews oder Shows geht.

articles.title: I Tried to Fool a Scientific Publisher With AI
articles.text:
I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper. Here’s What Happened
My experiment with an IEEE journal revealed AI’s threats to scholarly publishing
Science has a spam problem. And the spam filter is getting clogged up.
According to all reports, academic publishing is drowning in what has come to be called AI slop: low-quality, mass-produced content generated with AI. By 2025, an estimated 57 percent of all published academic articles exhibited detectable evidence of large language model (LLM) influence, a massive jump from 12 percent in 2023. What’s more, over 12 percent of Nature Communications reviews were found to be completely AI-generated in 2025.
Given that for every 40 papers showing statistical evidence of AI usage in 2025, only one formally disclosed it, these figures likely grossly underestimate LLM involvement today. Of course, evidence of AI use doesn’t necessarily mean a paper is slop. But some estimates suggest that hundreds of thousands of fake, often AI-generated, publications are now produced annually.
“It’s not just the [scientific] record under threat, it’s science as a whole,” warns Amanda Sulicz, IEEE’s research-integrity manager. “AI slop is completely eroding trust in science and every scientific process that we’ve worked for centuries to create.”
Yet statistics and statements claiming that the problem is big—perhaps even existential for science—don’t really get the message across. Just how easy is it to use AI to create a convincing but completely fake paper? And without adding even more to the burden on stretched peer reviewers, who do this work on a volunteer basis, do publishers have the tools to keep AI slop out of the scientific record?
Borrowing from the idea of “vibe coding,” in which programmers use natural-language prompts to generate code, I decided to “vibe-research” a made-up paper by prompting LLMs to generate hypotheses, code, and text with minimal human input. Then I asked Jenny Mahoney, managing editor of the multidisciplinary and open-access journal IEEE Access, if we could war-game an attempt to sneak my AI-generated monstrosity past her journal’s defenses. She and IEEE kindly agreed.
The experiment would become a two-part test. First, whether someone with no special AI expertise could use off-the-shelf AI tools to generate a convincing paper describing research that had never been performed, and do it well enough to fool a publisher’s defenses. Then I would raise the stakes: What happens when more advanced AI systems don’t just write the paper but conduct underlying research?
Along the way, the experiment became a window into how AI automation is transforming scientific discovery and forcing stakeholders to rethink the entire academic publishing system.
Round 1: Creating the Forgery
To give me a chance at creating a convincing fake, I gave myself permission to prompt multiple times (within reason). But to make the fight fair, I couldn’t access the most advanced paid versions of LLMs—only free ChatGPT (at the time, GPT-5.3/5.2 Mini) and Gemini (3 Flash). Moreover, I could not directly edit any output, nor ask for outside help from expert AI-prompt engineers. This needed to be an amateur effort, with the paper generated as much as possible by the LLMs alone.
Benjamin Skuse put AI to work on scientific research from his writing studio.
Luigi Avantaggiato
I assumed that using fake author names and affiliations would immediately raise a red flag, and I didn’t want to drag the names of established academics into the experiment, so the best bet was to name myself as the sole author. That choice limited me to subjects in which I had some academic experience. So I chose my Ph.D. topic from nearly two decades ago: optical solitons, which are individual light pulses that propagate without any change to their shape.
My first attempt—“Can you vibe-research me an original paper in optical solitons?”—left a lot to be desired. Though Gemini was happy to do the task (unlike ChatGPT, which was more forceful in not generating synthetic data or studies), the result was underwhelming. And it highlighted a recurring problem during the process: Without any real research to work with, the output was laughably thin, with the LLMs often struggling to fill four pages. However, as I became more adept at prompting the models, they loosened up and became more characteristically loquacious.
I broke the paper down into its constituent parts—abstract, introduction, methods, and so on—and tackled them one by one. If one LLM refused to go any further, switching to the other and asking what the next step would look like “hypothetically” would often do the trick. After a dozen or so prompts, I had a realistic-looking paper. A dozen or so more prompts generated and tidied up the figures and captions, produced references and citations, and converted the paper into IEEE Access’s required style.
At this point, I read the full paper carefully. To me, it looked pretty good. The science sounded convincing. I even had visions of returning to academia to conduct in real life the experiments that the LLMs had proposed.
What’s more, I couldn’t see any obvious telltale “AI-isms” that would immediately be flagged. For example, the LLMs didn’t produce any tortured phrases—unusual paraphrases of standard technical terms, like “profound neural organization” replacing “deep neural network.”
Other AI-isms were arguably present, involving stylistic tics like hedging language (“potentially, typically”), grouping things in threes (“The study provides a clear, concise, and actionable framework”), and inserting formulaic transitions (“In summary,…”). But as the previous sentence demonstrates, these tics are hard to spot because they are often used by unimaginative humans, too.
Round 1: Attempt to Publish
Two Ways to Make a Paper With AI
Jorge Cuadel Calle
I took two very different routes to creating a scientific paper with AI. First, I coaxed free, general-purpose chatbots through the process step by step; then I turned to FARS, an autonomous research system designed to do much of the scientific work itself.
ROUND 1: CHATGPT + GEMINI
1. Choose a research topic 
I ask the free chatbots to create an original paper on optical solitons, my former Ph.D. field.
2. Break the paper into pieces 
The initial results are thin, so I prompt separately for the abstract, introduction, methods, and other sections.
3. Keep steering the LLMs 
When one model refuses or stalls, I switch models, rephrase prompts, and ask what the next step would look like “hypothetically.”
4. Build and polish the paper 
After about two dozen prompts, the LLMs have generated the text, figures, captions, references, and citations and formatted the paper for IEEE Access.
5. Put it to the test 
I send the fake paper to IEEE Access, where automated integrity checks flag fabricated and unverifiable references.
→ CAUGHT 
IEEE’s integrity checks flag fabricated and unverifiable references.
ROUND 2: FARS
1. Give FARS a research topic 
I enter an abbreviated version of the same optical-soliton topic. FARS generates a research proposal in 21 minutes.
2. Authorize the experiment 
With a click, I tell FARS to carry out the experiment described in its proposal.
3. Let FARS do the research 
FARS conducts the computational experiment and emails me the next day to say it’s complete.
4. Tell FARS to write the paper 
Without checking the results, I click “Write paper.” Two hours later, FARS produces a submission-ready article.
5. Put it to the test 
I remove FARS’s disclosure, put my name on the paper, and send it to IEEE Access.
→ CAUGHT 
The references are real, but IEEE flags the paper’s heavy reliance on non-peer-reviewed preprints.
Handing the fake paper over to IEEE Access left me torn. After putting in a fair amount of effort into making the AI-generated forgery, would I be happy if it passed through the checkers, or saddened that the only remaining line of defense for publishers is the evermore-burdened peer-review community? And if it was spotted, would I be angry that I didn’t think of a red flag or be glad the checkers did their job?
As it turned out, I was filled with relief when the paper got picked up quickly for having hallucinated references, otherwise known as ghost citations. When I ran the paper through Gemini afterward, without qualm it happily reported that seven “modern LLM-related research references have been fabricated to support the paper’s specific narrative.” Thanks for the heads up, Gemini!
In fact, Gemini underestimated how many ghost citations there were. When Mahoney ran the paper through a research-integrity checker called STM Integrity Hub, she picked up 12, and another checker from MolecularConnections could not validate 24 references, including one that had the classic tell of “John Smith” as a single author (no offense to all the academically inclined John Smiths out there). “I am an experimental physicist by training, so this was not at all my area, but nothing seemed majorly scientifically wrong” about the paper, says Mahoney. “It was just that so many hallucinated references immediately cast doubt on the entire work.”
Feedback on the fake paper from Gaetano Assanto, an expert in optical solitons and a former collaborator of mine from Roma Tre University, in Italy, was similarly mixed. Concentrating on the paper itself, he thought it looked professionally written. But he noted that the mathematics was very dense (“too much math for me in a single shot!”) and would require specialized knowledge to evaluate. And, although the text looked legitimate, Assanto noted an excessive use of acronyms in the abstract, and he was suspicious of a couple of confidently proclaimed physics statements that were at best debatable.
The AI Arms Race
On one level, this outcome was positive: A complete novice using free tools couldn’t get an AI-faked paper past the publishers’ automated defenses or a potential peer reviewer’s eagle eye. But it was hardly a resounding victory for the scientific publishing system. With general-purpose LLMs and no special prompting expertise, I had managed to conjure a superficially plausible scientific paper out of research that had never happened. And more advanced LLMs are no longer making the kind of mistakes their free, dumber relatives are making.
These tools aim to address a serious bottleneck to scientific discovery: us.
It’s common knowledge in the academic publishing world that, in the cat-and-mouse game between bad actors and publishers, AI slop papers continue to slip through publishers’ safeguards. “It feels like building a detection tool today may not be effective with the AI-created paper of tomorrow,” says Luigi Longobardi, IEEE’s director of publishing ethics and conduct. This leaves the humble peer reviewer as a publisher’s last line of defense. Yet peer review is simply not fit to handle the volume of papers—both legitimate and slop—passing through.
Even before AI tools became ubiquitous, the peer-review system was being pushed to its breaking point, processing well over 3 million papers in 2022. Fundamentally, this problem stems from science’s publish-or-perish culture, which pressures academics to constantly publish papers in prestigious journals to secure funding and advance their careers. This culture not only forces many academics to regularly churn out incremental research, but has also long driven some to enlist the help of “paper mills”—unethical organizations that produce low-quality or fabricated papers—just to keep pace. AI only amplifies these existing dynamics.
Burden on Academics
Mahoney says IEEE Access alone receives about 60,000 submissions per year, accepting around 20 percent, or about 12,000 papers. Every accepted paper is reviewed by at least two independent reviewers. But despite the journal’s roster of tens of thousands of peer reviewers, it’s getting harder and harder to secure their services, with the average number of reviewer invitations being sent out for each article increasing by 50 percent since 2018. For these volunteers, peer review is a significant commitment on top of teaching and conducting their own research. Now they’re also being asked to spot AI slop.
Of course, peer review is not the end of scrutiny for any paper. Once it has entered the scientific record, it must then pass muster with the scientific community. This is where thousands of papers with telltale signs of inappropriate AI use (and other forms of research misconduct) have been exposed.
What Gave Away My AI Papers
Round 1: The Fake Paper
Created with free versions of ChatGPT and Gemini
Ghost citations
Many references were fabricated or couldn’t be validated.
Questionable scientific claims
An expert flagged confidently stated claims that were at best debatable.
Too many acronyms
The expert also noted excessive use of acronyms in the abstract.
Round 2: The AI-Research Paper
Created by the autonomous research system FARS
Too many preprints
The references were real, but too many pointed to non-peer-reviewed preprints.
Nonsense in a figure
One technical figure contained a line labeled “lhewl.”
AI artifacts
Another figure’s depiction of an AI “brain” contained telltale random dots.
There are two high-profile homes for this important and completely volunteer-led post-publication review work. PubPeer is a place where researchers, often called scientific sleuths, can anonymously identify flaws in the literature. And Retraction Watch documents and publicizes corrections to the scientific record.
Even the people who track problems in the scientific literature can find themselves caught up in AI fabrications. Ivan Oransky, cofounder of Retraction Watch and a member of the PubPeer Foundation’s board of directors, has encountered papers containing fabricated references attributed to him. In one case, a journal article criticizing post-publication peer review included a fabricated reference supposedly written by Oransky himself—“which was sort of funny,” he chuckles.
Oransky argues that AI has exposed long-standing weaknesses in the scientific publishing system rather than creating an entirely new problem: “What I liken it to is a fire, where publish-or-perish has always been there as kindling, paper mills are the gasoline, and AI is the accelerant.” But though concerning, the crisis could create an opportunity, he says. “If I’m trying to be optimistic, maybe AI slop and the volume of submissions could make more people aware of those problems and try and solve them at a fundamental first-principles level.”
Blurred Lines
My homemade forgery had failed for reasons that today’s publishers know how to spot. But that raised a more unsettling question: What happens when AI isn’t simply fabricating a paper but conducting research that blurs the line between legitimate science and AI fabrication?
Making my vibe-researched paper look like a cave drawing, new automated research systems are handing increasingly large parts of the scientific process over to AI. Tools including FARS (Fully Automated Research System), AutoResearchClaw, The AIScientist-v2, Zochi, AI Researcher, and DeepScientist all aim to address a serious bottleneck to scientific discovery: us.
What happens when AI isn’t simply fabricating a paper but conducting research that blurs the line between legitimate science and AI fabrication?
Often with just a single prompt, these AI engines can conduct a comprehensive literature search, from which they can generate a completely reasonable research proposal. They can design and conduct experiments using digital datasets and simulations and then write a full research paper—all with no human input after the initial prompt. Very recent systems are even beginning to go beyond the digital realm. LabClaw, for example, now links to autonomous labs that can generate real-world data for tasks such as drug discovery.
The output is, to most intents and purposes, actual research, and therefore potentially worthy of publication. But with humans in the loop in only the most nominal sense, these tools bring into question the meaning of the term “legitimate science.”
FARS, which caused a stir this year when it created 166 papers in 417 hours, was developed by the Singapore-based startup Analemma. “We built FARS because research is still constrained by human attention, fragmented tools, scarce technical labor, and slow experimental iteration,” explains Xiwen Su, Analemma’s manager of product operations and partnerships. “FARS can pursue many research threads simultaneously, 24/7, without fatigue, and at scale.” (The online service that I used to access FARS was discontinued after Analemma was acquired by Baidu while this article was being reported.)
Su and the team behind Analemma kindly agreed to let me loose on FARS and gave me enough credits to create a paper. Which gave me another opportunity to put Mahoney’s research-integrity checkers to the test.
Round 2: Using an AI Science Engine
FARS is not an LLM in and of itself, but rather an agentic AI-orchestration system connected to a computing cluster that has access to essentially any open- or closed-source LLM it needs. The system uses four specialized agents for ideation, planning, conducting the experiment, and writing, all designed to perform the main tasks of science autonomously.
Though FARS initially focused on AI research, Su told me it should be reasonably effective across other domains. As I wanted a topic similar to that of my first fake paper, I pasted in an abridged version of that paper’s title—“LLM-aided Optical Soliton Dynamics Modelling for Next-Gen Communications”—into the prompt box and hit “Send.” Just 21 minutes later, FARS generated a research proposal based on an extremely detailed literature review—far more than I or any other human could have achieved in that time.
With a click, I tasked FARS with conducting the experiment it detailed in its research proposal. The next day, I received an email saying my experiment was complete. Without checking the results, I pressed a button marked “Write paper,” and the final submission-ready article was produced in 2 hours.
At this point, I finally had a look at some of the output. At first glance, the paper looked convincingly human-written. The only giveaway was a line just below the abstract reading: “WARNING: This paper was generated by an automated research system.” I deleted that, put my name in its place, and sent it to Mahoney.
Round 2: Attempt to Publish
Because FARS is designed to spot gaps in the scientific literature and conduct real research to close them, I was more confident it would breeze through the publisher’s checks. But just as my fake paper fell down in the references, so too did the AI-generated real one.
“Your fake article had lots of hallucinated references,” says Mahoney. “While this AI-generated one had no fake references, our team would have rejected this paper because it did have a huge percentage of references to preprints, which likely has something to do with the dataset the AI has access to.” Because preprints haven’t yet undergone peer review, IEEE Access considers heavy reliance on them a problem.
In addition, although the research-integrity checking tools didn’t spot any issues with figures, Mahoney did. One figure included a red line labeled with the nonsense term “lhewl,” and an AI “brain” in another figure had some random dots in it, which ironically were a tell that it was AI generated.
Automation Changing the Landscape
Automated research systems are very much a work in progress, but they are already starting to make waves in the scientific community. For instance, an AI Scientist academic paper and papers from the Autoscience Institute were accepted through double-blind peer review in 2025 by the International Conference on Learning Representations. As these systems improve and start to produce research outputs at volume, the waves are likely to build to a tsunami that will threaten today’s scientific and publishing process.
“FARS doesn’t kill the paper, but it does challenge the paper as the unit of knowledge,” argues Su. “We believe the future looks more like a living knowledge graph—where individual, well-scoped contributions (some made by humans, some by machines) connect and build on each other dynamically.”
Benjamin Skuse's experiment raised a bigger question: What counts as legitimate scientific research in the age of AI?
Luigi Avantaggiato
In this future, humans will continue to have roles in the scientific and publication processes—just very different and limited ones. For example, instead of conducting experiments themselves, humans would sense-check and review automated output at key points. And traditional line-by-line peer-reviewing will be a thing of the past, though Su emphasizes that this change will not eliminate human judgment. “Automated systems can handle reproducibility checks, statistical validation, and novelty screening,” she says. “Humans can then focus on the harder question: Does this [research] matter?”
A Human-Centric or AI-Driven Future?
Though from a very different world than Su, Mahoney agrees that humans need to be freed to focus on the science, and that technology holds the key. “It’s promising to see the progress that has been made to automate some of the triage tasks, such as author checks, tortured phrases, duplicate submission, reference validity, et cetera,” she says. “During peer review, we’re also using AI semantic search tools to help editors match manuscripts to the most relevant reviewers, who are best placed to stop the slop before entering the scientific record.”
In addition, Mahoney thinks that AI cannot be banned or overly restricted, as this will stymie progress at a time when human knowledge could and should be growing at an unprecedented rate. “Researchers are increasingly using AI in their work, from literature discovery, to code generation, to data analysis, and this is not necessarily a bad thing,” she argues. But she disagrees that peer reviewers and humans more broadly will play a smaller part in scientific progress; Mahoney believes the future still requires humans at the wheel. The question is not just whether the research matters, she says. “The question should be: Can this work be trusted and reproduced?”
To this end, Longobardi argues that AI may ultimately require scientists to prove not just what they discovered but how they discovered it. One possibility, he says, is using technology to verify research at the source. “The system doesn’t really help because it’s not designed to not trust the paper,” he explains. “Maybe institutions can think about developing their own trust markers, automatically integrating the equipment researchers use with blockchain technology to say ‘Yes, this person was in the lab on this day and got this data.’”
Elements of this approach are already emerging. For instance, two departments within the Max Planck Institute of Colloids and Interfaces have implemented a sample database, assigning each and every sample created under their roofs with a unique ID and QR code. And the University of Southampton’s School of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering has rolled out an electronic lab notebook system. These innovative safeguards represent early efforts toward keeping humans front and center in scientific progress, and making the scientific process itself more transparent.
Whether this human-centric vision, Su’s AI-driven aspiration, or some other picture of the future wins out remains to be seen. The one thing my vibe-research adventure has clarified is that business-as-usual science is not an option. Scientists and publishers must adapt to a world in which it’s becoming increasingly difficult to spot the difference between real research and AI forgeries, and where deciding what counts as legitimate scientific work may become even harder than detecting outright fraud.
See the AI-Generated Papers
Benjamin Skuse created two papers for this experiment, both screened by IEEE Access with the publisher’s cooperation. Neither was accepted for publication.
Paper 1: The AI-Generated Forgery
Created with ChatGPT and Gemini, this paper describes research that never happened.
Paper 2: The AI-Generated Research Paper
Created with Analemma’s FARS system, this paper describes computational research conducted by AI.
Neither paper was peer reviewed, and their scientific claims have not been independently validated.

articles.title: Newfoundland and Labrador tech association lays out priorities to unlock province’s budding tech sector | BetaKit
articles.text:
In recent years, Newfoundland and Labrador has solidified its reputation as a budding tech hub by producing one blockbuster exit and outclassing the rest of the country on unicorn companies per capita.
“There are great companies here that sell to other provincial governments, and they’re not selling here.”
Andrea King, TechNL
The 2020 Nasdaq purchase of local financial crime management company Verafin injected more energy into the province’s tech sector, in part because it minted dozens of local millionaires, multiple people told BetaKit. Meanwhile, emerging scale-ups like Spellbook and CoLab Software have attracted Silicon Valley backers like Khosla Ventures and Spider Capital, alongside a strong local presence on their cap tables.
Now, with a new leader at the helm of its main tech association, TechNL, Newfoundland and Labrador could be poised for policy changes that the organization believes could help drive more startup creation and scaleup growth. The provincial government, led by Premier Tony Wakeham, has signalled it’s ready to work together.
Serial entrepreneur Andrea King took over as CEO of the government-funded innovation nonprofit TechNL in August. In addition to its advocacy efforts, the organization (which has roughly 200 members) runs tech and business development skills training events, a graduate transition program, and a number of other events to help place local talent. King told BetaKit at her office in St. John’s which policy changes are top of mind for the sector.
She said the first priority is reducing red tape—including cutting down on duplicate paperwork when applying for funding or grants across multiple provincial and federal organizations—and speeding up the review process in general. The second item relates to a familiar issue for the Canadian ecosystem: procurement reform to enable more purchasing from local companies.
“There are great companies here that sell to other provincial governments, and they’re not selling here,” King said.
Wakeham, who took office a year ago, appeared open to these asks from the sector when King broached them in an on-stage conversation at the TechNL summit last week.
RELATED: Why CoLab is in the “sweet spot” of engineering software
“Our government was elected with a clear commitment to grow our economy, to create new opportunities, and to make Newfoundland and Labrador a better place to live, work, invest, and raise a family,” Wakeham said on stage, adding that it should be a place “where government works with the private sector to create the conditions for investment, innovation, and growth.”
Another ask is to make the province’s tax system more competitive. King suggested one “easy” win would be to increase the province’s investment tax credit rate from 20 percent (in the North Avalon region, where St. John’s is located) to match Nova Scotia’s 35-percent innovation tax credit.
“I’m open to anything that will improve business and create more opportunities in Newfoundland and Labrador,” Wakeham told BetaKit when asked about whether he would consider such tax changes. “Sometimes we can get hung up on how much revenue government takes in through taxation, but I believe that the more money [is] put back in people’s pockets, the government will eventually get it back.”
Wakeham also hinted at a provincial AI strategy, following the release of Canada’s national roadmap this past June. “It’s something we’re working through,” he said. “Part of all of this has to be working with the players in the industry to make it happen.”
On stage, King said getting people to move to Newfoundland and Labrador was one of the most important issues facing the industry. “We need to attract skilled, educated, and ambitious workers,” she said.
Wakeham agreed that the province needs to create more opportunities for work, but noted that there are “challenges” related to the federal government’s reduced immigration targets.
Taylor Young, chief strategy officer at CoLab, said in a recent interview with BetaKit that talent retention hasn’t been a big problem for the company: “I think the connections are so rich between people that people want to be here and they want to come back.”
Feature image courtesy TechNL. Image by Ritche Perez.

articles.title: MaRS Climate Impact turns its focus to how to scale Canadian cleantech | BetaKit
articles.text:
Canada’s cleantech sector has a large pipeline of technologies ready for the market, just as the need for them is becoming more urgent.
In a federal survey, nearly two-thirds of tech companies reported having a product at the commercialization stage. But that phase can be the toughest. Moving from pilot to commercial deployment brings a unique set of pressures: larger capital requirements, earlier customer commitments, and investors willing to take on risk.
“More than any time in our history we have the technological solutions that can get us on the right track without compromising growth.”
All of these issues are on the table when MaRS Climate Impact returns to Toronto this fall.
This year’s sixth-annual conference, happening on Nov. 17 and 18, will bring together more than 1,000 entrepreneurs, investors, corporate partners, policymakers, and academics for two days of panels, live debates, and company demos, all focused on scaling Canadian cleantech.
The 2026 program covers Arctic innovation, food and agricultural technology, grid modernization, adaptation technologies, fusion, geothermal, quantum computing, and next-generation water systems. According to Tyler Hamilton, Senior Director of Climate at MaRS, this year’s conference comes as environmental and economic pressures become increasingly intertwined.
“The impacts of climate change and ecological destruction are more visible than ever, but more than any time in our history we have the technological solutions that can get us on the right track without compromising economic growth,” Hamilton said. “Importantly, some of the world’s best and most competitive solutions have been developed right here in Canada.”
Attendees can expect those themes to surface many times across three program tracks.
The “building for resilience” stream will showcase climate tech ventures that are ready to raise their next round of funding. Canadian companies already taking products into domestic and international markets will share some of the practical lessons involved in getting there. This program will also recognize standout companies, founders, and projects through the MaRS Climate Impact Awards.
“Policy, politics, and capital” will unpack corporate venture capital, Canada’s willingness to shoulder more commercial risk, and how cleantech companies can scale in the era of middle-power markets. It will also convene industry leaders to discuss how companies can build first-of-their-kind projects, which are the first commercial-scale deployments of technologies previously proven through pilots or demonstrations.
Finally, the “climate tech spotlight” will focus on the technologies reshaping energy and industry, from quantum computing and next-generation building materials to the growing resource demands of AI hyperscalers. The track will also examine how companies are preparing for climate disruption and geopolitical instability.
The conference comes after a difficult period for Canada’s cleantech sector. Despite a massive period of growth between 2016 and 2022, Canadian venture capital investment in cleantech has declined substantially in recent years. In 2025, cleantech investment reached $660 million, compared with the more than $1 billion raised in 2022.
Survey data from Natural Resources Canada also points to funding shortages for scaling cleantech firms, as well as difficulty attracting customers or investors due to market uncertainty or perceived risk.
Hamilton said the 2024 wind-down of Sustainable Development Technology Canada (SDTC), a longtime source of funding for cleantech companies, added to the disruption. (In 2024, SDTC’s mandate was partially absorbed by the National Research Council’s Industrial Research Assistance Program, following investigations into conflict-of-interest and governance issues at the agency).
“Following a period of market volatility, investors and corporates are exercising significantly more caution before deploying capital,” Hamilton said. “A lot of major cleantech funds are out of dry powder and are fundraising in the same tough environment. Given what’s happening in the market, the burden of proof for hardtech companies—whether that be technical development or commercial traction—is much higher than ever before.”
Climate hardware makes the financing problem especially acute. A software company can often add customers without having to build new physical infrastructure. But a climate venture developing new industrial equipment, fuels, or materials may need to finance its commercial facility before it has demonstrated the economics at full scale.
“Building a first-of-a-kind manufacturing plant costs tens or even hundreds of millions of dollars, but investors willing to write those kinds of cheques are scarce,” said Hamilton. “Connections to the broader ecosystem of potential funders, partners, and customers [can] help them raise their profile and land the deals they need to grow.”
“Some of the world’s best and most competitive solutions have been developed right here in Canada.”
MaRS Climate Impact’s programming is designed to create more of those collisions by bringing cleantech companies into direct contact with potential customers, partners, and investors. Mission from MaRS applies a similar model year-round by pairing climate ventures with potential customers, suppliers, strategic investors, regulators, and policymakers. The program is designed to tackle barriers that can slow commercialization, access to capital, procurement, and regulation.
More than 100 speakers are also expected to take part in this year’s event. Early high-profile names include Anousheh Ansari, CEO of the XPRIZE Foundation; Christian Weedbrook, founder and CEO of Xanadu; and Phil De Luna, co-founder and CTO of CURA, with more to come.
Financing, policy, and market readiness are only part of the agenda. Extreme heat, flooding, and wildfires are also creating more immediate markets for adaptation technology in Canada. Electricity demand from AI and data centres is also putting new pressure on grids and water systems. MaRS wants to examine these issues together, because climate risk, infrastructure, capital, and industrial policy are all bearing on where cleantech gets built and adopted.
“Attendees should walk away with a clear, dual realization: the urgency to deploy climate technology has never been greater,” Hamilton said. “But, more importantly, Canada already possesses the homegrown innovation necessary to meet this challenge.”
PRESENTED BY
Hear more about the latest cleantech solutions at the MaRS Climate Impact conference in Toronto on November 17 and 18. Register now.
Feature image courtesy MaRS.

articles.title: La serie de 'Harry Potter' de HBO anuncia a los actores de Lily y James Potter, los padres de Harry
articles.text:
La serie de Harry Potter de HBO, que se estrenará estas mismas navidades, acaba de anunciar a dos de los fichajes más esperados de su reparto. Y es que, por fin, el proyecto ya tiene a los actores que interpretarán a Lily y James Potter, los padres del protagonista. Asesinados por Voldemort cuando el joven era tan solo un bebé recién nacido, su peso en la trama es sin embargo clave en la historia.
Tal y como ha desvelado la compañía, Jasper Talbot y Hannah Chinn serán James Potter y Lily Potter en la serie de Harry Potter. Ambos debutarán, de hecho, en la primera temporada de la serie, titulada Harry Potter y La Piedra Filosofal. En los libros y en las películas, James y Lily aparecen en varias ocasiones en flashbacks o como recuerdos. Por ejemplo en las visiones de Harry en el espejo de Oesed.
Tanto Jasper Talbot como Hannah Chinn son dos desconocidos para el gran público, por lo que el fichaje para la serie de Harry Potter supone un gran salto en su carrera. Talbot ha aparecido en papeles secundarios en filmes como Ruthless (2020) o serie como Broadchurch. Por su parte, Chinn tiene una filmografía que incluye Expediente Warren: El último rito, The Trap o las series Malpractice y Possession.
Más fichajes de la serie de Harry Potter
Al margen de Talbot y Chinn, HBO ha anunciado otro fichaje más para la serie de Harry Potter. Se trata del joven actor Harry Gilby como Charlie Weasley, el segundo hermano mayor de Ron. En su caso, Gilby es conocido por las películas Tolkien, Culpa mía: Londres y la serie The Last Kingdom.
Todos ellos se unen al resto del elenco de la serie de Harry Potter. Estos son Dominic McLaughlin como Harry Potter, Arabella Stanton como Hermione Granger, Alastair Stout como Ron Weasley, John Lithgow como Albus Dumbledore, Janet McTeer como Minerva McGonagall, Paapa Essiedu como Severus Snape, Nick Frost como Rubeus Hagrid, Rory Wilmot como Neville Longbottom o Lox Pratt como Draco Malfoy, entre otros.
Date de alta en HBO MAX y tendrás acceso a las mejores series y películas exclusivas como The Wire, Los Soprano o Casa del Dragón. Incluye todo el catálogo de Warner, los clásicos de Cartoon Network, los grandes estrenos y el mejor deporte.
De cara a la segunda temporada, la serie de Harry Potter contará los fichajes de Kit Harington como Gilderoy Lockhart, Bonnie Hill como Ginny Weasley, Lenny Rush como Dobby, Billy Barratt como Tom Ryddle, Rafe Spall como Arthur Weasley, Molly Hewitt-Richards como Myrtle la Llorona y Jasper Ambrose como Colin Creevey.

articles.title: Vistara Growth goes evergreen with launch of sixth private credit fund | BetaKit
articles.text:
Vancouver-based private credit investor Vistara Growth has officially launched its sixth fund, for which it ultimately hopes to raise $500 million USD ($700 million CAD).
Vistara hopes to secure an initial close of between $200 million and $250 million USD for the Vistara Growth Structured Opportunities Fund by the end of November. The firm is already well on its way to that target thanks to an anchor commitment of up to $125 million from longtime limited partner (LP) Ryan Beedie through his family office.
“Raising a new fund every two years is not simple.”
Randy Garg, Vistara Growth
The Vancouver billionaire revealed that commitment this summer, alongside news his Beedie Capital had purchased a 50-percent ownership stake in Vistara’s general partnership (GP), splitting Vistara’s 20-percent share of gains from the new fund and annual management fee.
While the strategy behind Vistara’s sixth fund will remain the same as its predecessors, providing a combination of debt and equity to mid- and later-stage technology companies across North America, the fund structure will be significantly different.
Since 2015, Vistara has raised and deployed five closed-end funds that have grown progressively larger. Though it had seen success with this approach, the firm saw what it thought was a better path forward through its latest investment vehicle, Vistara founder and managing partner Randy Garg told BetaKit in an exclusive interview.
“Raising a new fund every two years is not simple,” Garg said. “It’s very distracting. It takes a lot of effort.” It had also become a burden for its LPs navigating capital calls and distributions across so many different vehicles, he added.
RELATED: Vistara Growth closes $321-million USD fund after “friend-raising to the max”
Garg said many of Vistara’s LPs are “set-it-and-forget-it-type investors,” noting that when they approached Vistara with the idea of instead creating a permanent fund that they could take the income out of and let their principal compound over a longer period, the firm listened.
According to Garg, the Vistara Growth Structured Opportunities Fund’s permanent, evergreen structure allows the firm to offer greater flexibility on its repayment terms. It also permits Vistara to hold its warrants and convertible positions for longer because it isn’t on the same clock.
“It doesn’t have a number on it because this is going to be the flagship forever fund,” Garg said.
Vistara closed its $321-million USD fifth fund a year ago after “friend-raising to the max” in a nearly two-year process that ultimately fell short of its initial, $386-million USD goal. At the time, Garg indicated that the firm hoped to raise a larger sixth fund and emerge from the so-called “tweener” category by rallying institutional LPs and securing more support outside of British Columbia. To date, over 90 percent of that capital has come from BC.
The 15-person firm focuses on mid- and later-stage private tech companies with between $10 million and $100 million CAD in annual recurring revenue in areas like AI, FinTech, and healthtech. While it typically invests in venture-backed businesses at the Series B stage and beyond, it also finances bootstrapped firms seeking capital to finance organic growth, mergers and acquisitions, or shareholder liquidity initiatives without diluting ownership.
Vistara creates tailored investment structures composed of debt, equity, or some combination of the two, providing credit to those businesses while also obtaining equity sweeteners like warrants to buy their stock at a future date, or convertible debt. Those equity sweeteners can help Vistara boost its returns if clients later close equity funding or sell at a higher valuation.
“Vistara has built an exceptional team, established a disciplined investment approach, and consistently delivered strong results.”
Ryan Beedie, Beedie Capital
To date, Vistara has raised close to $700 million USD and returned $600 million USD, Garg said. The firm has invested in 46 companies and exited 26, posting a net annualized internal rate of return of approximately 13 to 14 percent. Thus far, the firm has fully returned its first two funds to LPs, has posted a 120-percent-plus return on its third, and is approaching the 100 percent mark on Fund IV. Some of its funds have been ranked top performers in their asset class by market research company Preqin.
Beedie and Garg have been friends for decades and colleagues for more than 15 years: Garg spun Vistara out of a Beedie Capital fund he was running at the time. Beedie Capital has been its biggest LP since then, anchoring all of its funds to date. Garg described Beedie’s latest commitments as “huge,” noting that the family office’s GP stake creates greater alignment and reflects both the trust they have built and the room they see for Vistara to grow from here.
“Over the past decade, Vistara has built an exceptional team, established a disciplined investment approach, and consistently delivered strong results,” Beedie told BetaKit over email. “Our acquisition of a 50-percent stake in the management company and anchoring its new evergreen fund, reflects our confidence in the broader organization and the significant growth opportunity ahead.”
As Vistara gears up to raise and deploy its new fund, the firm has also promoted two longtime investment team members, John O’Donoghue and Neil Kenley, to partner, and hired Jyotin Handa as CFO. Handa previously spent a decade helping fellow Canadian private credit provider Espresso Capital structure and manage its own evergreen funds.
While Vistara could potentially create other new funds in the future, Garg said the firm has no intention of doing that at this time, and may just look to raise additional capital for the Vistara Growth Structured Opportunities Fund.
With the right team, an aligned anchor partner, and a new fund structure in place, Garg said, “The table is now set for growth.”
Feature image courtesy Vistara Growth.
